meta.title: Psychometric Course · Quantitative & Verbal Reasoning
meta.sourceNote: The completed algebra, word-problem and geometry content is preserved. Verbal reasoning adds Active Reading and new English questions based on the supplied teaching approaches. Each verbal topic has seven additional independent-practice questions; the short analogy and completion units are retained within their topic practice sets.
meta.adaptationNote: English scripts use clear spoken language, adapted scenarios and explicit NEXT cues. Verbal adaptations preserve reasoning mechanics rather than Hebrew wording; English-specific scope and vocabulary are taught directly. Original source blocks remain available for comparison.
changes: Reversed foundations reordered from introduction through summary practice.
Questions precede their matching solution videos.
Self-practice has written solutions and no explanation videos.
The nine-question fraction bank gains one source-aligned comparison question.
Twenty independent expressions questions were added to fill the requested practice set.
The first ten exponent questions form the core drill; five additional bank questions remain accessible.
Duplicate equation and expression variants remain in additional practice, without duplicate recordings.
The duplicate equation subtitle attachment is represented once.
All example choices, solutions, and videos reference one canonical question record.
Added the nine word-problem topics in subtitle order.
Replaced repeated generic explanation introductions with the question’s own reasoning.
Added seven questions to each existing independent-practice set and a root extension.
Added fast calculation with seven practice questions.
Added slide-specific pen annotations with undo, clear, colour and width controls.
Printable questions and worked solutions use the same records as the online course.
Geometry follows the new Hebrew subtitles, with recreated vector figures shared by the course and paper books.
Question vocabulary follows the supplied English psychometric examination papers.
Verbal reasoning starts with Active Reading: quick paraphrases, inner emphasis, precise markings, opinion ownership and paragraph roles.
Analogies prioritize defining the dependent word through its partner; formal logic combines the condition/result slide deck with the subtitle methods.
The optional translated JSON bank is treated as an unverified draft. New English questions use the supplied exam register and retain the intended reasoning mechanics.
Eleven verbal topics add 97 question-before-video walkthroughs, 547 independent questions, 24 original passages and seven extra practice questions per topic.
meta.verbalAdaptation: English questions are newly written around the source reasoning mechanics. Bilingual examination papers guide register and terminology. The optional machine-translated JSON bank is not treated as an authoritative answer key. Difficulty labels are instructional judgements, not calibrated exam-equivalence claims.

topics.title: Algebraic Fundamentals
topics.description: Integer arithmetic from the ground up: addition and subtraction with negatives, multiplication and division techniques, order of operations, and the core vocabulary of algebra — natural numbers, opposites, reciprocals and primes.
topics.subject: Algebra

topics.title: Fractions — Fundamentals
topics.description: Everything a fraction can do: expanding and reducing, mixed numbers and improper fractions, the four operations on fractions, and decimal fractions — the computational toolkit every later fraction question builds on.
topics.subject: Algebra

topics.title: Fractions
topics.description: Exam-level fraction work: complex fractions, symbolic fractions with letters, comparing and ordering close fractions, and reasoning about which expression is largest or smallest under given constraints.
topics.subject: Algebra

topics.title: Expressions — Fundamentals
topics.description: Combining like terms, multiplying monomials, expanding brackets, the three multiplication formulas ((A+B)², (A−B)², A²−B²) , and factoring perfect squares and differences of squares.
topics.subject: Algebra

topics.title: Expressions
topics.description: Working with algebraic expressions at exam level: continued fractions, sign-flip quotients like (a−b)/(b−a) , common factors, factoring quadratics, rational-expression simplification, and the number-substitution technique for eliminating wrong answers.
topics.subject: Algebra

topics.title: Equations — Fundamentals
topics.description: Solving linear equations and systems of two equations: isolating the variable, clearing fractions, substitution and elimination, rational equations with domain restrictions, and the special cases of identities and contradictions.
topics.subject: Algebra

topics.title: Equations
topics.description: Exam-level equation techniques: when dividing by an unknown is (and isn't) legal, counting solutions, deriving "must be true" relationships, computing composite expressions without solving for each variable, chained ratios, coefficient matching, and equation decomposition.
topics.subject: Algebra

topics.title: Exponent Laws — Fundamentals
topics.description: The core exponent facts — a¹ = a , a⁰ = 1 , negative exponents, and the product, quotient, and power laws — drilled through fifteen fundamentals questions, plus the power tables worth knowing by heart.
topics.subject: Algebra

topics.title: Roots — Fundamentals
topics.description: Square roots, cube roots, and higher roots from the ground up — combining and splitting roots, rationalizing, estimating irrational values, and the reference table of roots every test-taker should memorize.
topics.subject: Algebra

topics.title: Laws of Exponents & Roots — Fundamentals
topics.description: The combined exponents-and-roots toolkit: converting to shared prime bases, simplifying sums and quotients of roots, solving exponential and root equations, and a forty-question review across theory, practice, and a summary drill.
topics.subject: Algebra

topics.title: Laws of Exponents & Roots — Advanced
topics.description: Higher-difficulty exponent and root problems: multi-variable simplification, conjugate and factoring tricks with roots, exponential equations with parameters, and estimation-based comparisons — the level at which these questions actually appear on the exam.
topics.subject: Algebra

topics.title: Inequalities
topics.description: Solving linear and compound inequalities, flipping the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative, squeezing whole-number solutions, and reasoning about products, squares and rational expressions under inequality constraints.
topics.subject: Algebra

topics.title: Absolute Value
topics.description: Absolute value as distance from zero: solving |x| equations and inequalities by case-splitting, sign analysis with products and quotients, and classic identities such as equal squares meaning equal absolute values.
topics.subject: Algebra

topics.title: Prime Numbers
topics.description: Primes, divisors and prime factorization: recognizing primes, counting divisors, building greatest common divisors and least common multiples from prime powers, and parity arguments with sums and differences of primes.
topics.subject: Algebra

topics.title: Division & Remainder
topics.description: Divisibility rules and remainder arithmetic: quick tests for 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 and 11, expressing numbers as "quotient times divisor plus remainder", combining two remainder conditions, and divisibility of algebraic expressions.
topics.subject: Algebra

topics.title: Integers
topics.description: Sign rules for products and quotients, consecutive integers and their algebraic form, even/odd (parity) arguments, and divisibility facts built from products of consecutive integers.
topics.subject: Algebra

topics.title: The Number Line
topics.description: Ordering and comparing expressions built from numbers in different ranges — greater than 1, between 0 and 1, between −1 and 0, below −1 — and how powers, roots and reciprocals grow or shrink values in each range.
topics.subject: Algebra

topics.title: Exercises with Letters
topics.description: Digit puzzles where letters stand for digits: expanding two- and three-digit "letter numbers" by place value, using digit constraints and units-digit behavior to pin down the unique solution.
topics.subject: Algebra

topics.title: Defining a New Operation
topics.description: Questions that invent a custom operation symbol, define it by a formula, and ask you to substitute, nest, reverse-engineer or reason about it — including piecewise and recursive definitions.
topics.subject: Algebra

topics.title: Algebraic Understanding
topics.description: Reasoning about what is forced, possible or impossible from algebraic givens — counting arguments, pigeonhole logic, structural constraints on integers, and validating formulas against required behavior.

explanation: 1 is odd (true), 1 is a natural number (true), and 1 divides every integer (true). But 1 is not prime — a prime must have exactly two distinct divisors, 1 and itself, while 1 has only one divisor. So statement (2) is the false one.

q-422.stem: Alan claims: "Every number divisible by both 4 and 6 without remainder is also divisible by 24." Beth claims: "Every number divisible by both 4 and 6 without remainder is also divisible by 12." Which of the following statements is correct?
q-422.stemHtml: Alan claims: "Every number divisible by both 4 and 6 without remainder is also divisible by 24." Beth claims: "Every number divisible by both 4 and 6 without remainder is also divisible by 12." Which of the following statements is correct?
explanation: A number divisible by both 4 and 6 is divisible by LCM(4, 6) = 12 — that's exactly Beth's claim, always true. Alan's claim fails on a counterexample: 12 itself is divisible by 4 and by 6, but 12 is not divisible by 24. (24 is only the PRODUCT of 4 and 6 divided by nothing — the product overshoots because 4 and 6 share the factor 2.)

q-426.stem: A number leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 3. Which of the following expressions could represent the number (x is an integer)?
q-426.stemHtml: A number leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 3. Which of the following expressions could represent the number (x is an integer)?
explanation: Reduce each expression modulo 3. (1) 3x + 5 = 3(x + 1) + 2 — remainder 2, never 1. (2) 6x + 8 = 3(2x + 2) + 2 — remainder 2, never 1. (3) (3x + 4)² = 9x² + 24x + 16 = 3(3x² + 8x + 5) + 1 — remainder 1, always ✓. (4) (3x + 6)² = 9(x + 2)² — remainder 0, never 1.

q-438.stem: Tom has x marbles, which he divides equally among his 4 children. The eldest child then divides his share equally among 3 friends (no remainder), and the second child divides his share equally among 5 friends (no remainder). What is the minimum value of x?
q-438.stemHtml: Tom has x marbles, which he divides equally among his 4 children. The eldest child then divides his share equally among 3 friends (no remainder), and the second child divides his share equally among 5 friends (no remainder). What is the minimum value of x?
explanation: Each child receives x:4 . This share must be divisible by 3 (eldest) and by 5 (second), so x:4 must be divisible by LCM(3, 5) = 15 — meaning x is divisible by 4·15 = 60 . The minimum is x = 60 : each child gets 15, and 15 splits evenly among 3 and among 5.

q-444.stem: A is an even positive integer. Given: n = {A}^{3} + 12\,{A}^{2} + 32\,A. Then n is necessarily divisible by:
q-444.stemHtml: A is an even positive integer. Given: . Then n is necessarily divisible by:
explanation: Factor: n = A(A² + 12A + 32) = A(A + 4)(A + 8) . Write A = 2m : n = 2m(2m + 4)(2m + 8) = 8·m(m + 2)(m + 4) . The numbers m, m + 2 , m + 4 cover all three residues mod 3, so one of them is divisible by 3. Hence n is divisible by 8·3 = 24 , always. The other choices fail on counterexamples: A = 2 (m = 1) gives n = 8·1·3·5 = 120 , and neither 18 nor 32 divides 120; A = 14 (m = 7) gives n = 8·7·9·11 = 5,544 , and 60 does not divide 5,544. Only 24 divides every case.

q-445.stem: Lior has 80 lockers numbered 1 to 80, all closed. In round 1 he opens every locker. In round 2 he switches the state of every 2\,nd locker (2, 4, 6, …). In round 3 he switches every 3\,rd locker, and so on, up to round 80 (switching locker 80 only). Which of the following lockers is open at the end?
q-445.stemHtml: Lior has 80 lockers numbered 1 to 80, all closed. In round 1 he opens every locker. In round 2 he switches the state of every locker (2, 4, 6, …). In round 3 he switches every locker, and so on, up to round 80 (switching locker 80 only). Which of the following lockers is open at the end?
explanation: Locker k is switched once in every round d where d divides k — so it's toggled exactly as many times as k has divisors. Starting closed, it ends open only after an ODD number of toggles, and only perfect squares have an odd number of divisors (divisors pair up d with k:d except when d = √k ). Among the choices only 49 = 7² is a perfect square (its divisors 1, 7, 49 give three toggles: open–close–open). 50, 55 and 78 have evenly many divisors and end closed.

q-452.stem: A taxi company's phone number consists of 5 identical digits (for example, 33333). The company's fax number equals the phone number plus 1. What will be the remainder if the sum of the fax number's digits is divided by 5?
q-452.stemHtml: A taxi company's phone number consists of 5 identical digits (for example, 33333). The company's fax number equals the phone number plus 1. What will be the remainder if the sum of the fax number's digits is divided by 5?
explanation: Let the repeated digit be d. Adding 1 changes only the last digit (from d to d + 1 , no carry for d ≤ 8 ), so the fax digits are d, d, d, d, d + 1 . Their sum is 5d + 1 — a multiple of 5 plus 1 — so the remainder mod 5 is always 1. Example: phone 33333 → fax 33334, digit sum 16 = 5·3 + 1 ✓.

q-460.stem: Let x and y be positive integers. Given: ( x+y ) is odd. Which of the following statements guarantees that the expression x^y + y^x + 7 + 6x will necessarily be odd?
q-460.stemHtml: Let x and y be positive integers. Given: ( x+y ) is odd. Which of the following statements guarantees that the expression x^y + y^x + 7 + 6x will necessarily be odd?
choicesHtml: y is and x is
x is and y is
the expression can never be
explanation: Since x + y is odd, exactly one of x, y is even and the other is odd. Case 1 — x even, y odd: x^y = even^odd = even ; y^x = odd^even = odd ; 7 is odd; 6x is even. Even + odd + odd + even = even . Case 2 — x odd, y even: x^y = odd^even = odd ; y^x = even^odd = even ; 7 odd; 6x even. Odd + even + odd + even = even . Both possible cases give an even result, so the expression can never be odd — no extra condition can rescue it. (Choice (1) is impossible anyway: x = y would make x + y even.)

q-462.stemHtml: x and y are integers. Given: . Which of the following expressions will necessarily be even?
explanation: x − y = 4 (an even difference) means x and y share the same parity — both even or both odd. Factor: x² − y² = (x−y)(x+y) = 4(x+y) , which is a multiple of 4 and so always even, regardless of the shared parity. The others depend on the case: if x, y are both odd (say x=5 , y=1 ), then 2x−y = 9 is odd, x²+y²+5x = 25+1+25 = 51 is odd, and 5x²+2y = 125+2 = 127 is odd — so none of them is necessarily even.

Either way x is odd, while a's own parity is completely unconstrained.

q-471.stem: Given: m, p, q, r are integers, and 2\,m + 1 = {\left(p + 1\right)}^{2} \cdot  {q}^{5} \cdot  {\left(r - 1\right)}^{2}. Which of the numbers m, p, q, r are necessarily odd?
q-471.stemHtml: Given: m, p, q, r are integers, and . Which of the numbers m, p, q, r are necessarily odd?

q-474.stemHtml: In class A, every child has 4 pencils, and in class D every child has 5 pencils. The number of children in class D is odd. The total number of pencils of all the children in classes A and D together is necessarily a number that is —
explanation: Total = 4·(children in A) + 5 ·(children in D). The first term, 4 times anything, is always even. The second term is 5 (odd) times an odd number of children — odd × odd = odd . q-512.stemHtml: A, B, C and D are letters representing digits from 0 to 9. Given: (with AB and CB being two-digit numbers and DDB being a three-digit number, each letter being the digit in that position).
explanation: Expand by place value: AB + CB = (10A+B) + (10C+B) = 10(A+C) + 2B , and DDB = 110D + B . Equating: 10(A+C) + 2B = 110D + B , so 10(A+C) + B = 110D . The left side ends in digit B while 110D ends in 0, forcing B = 0 . Then A + C = 11D ; since A + C ≤ 18 , we get D = 1 and A + C = 11 . So A + C + D = 11 + 1 = 12 . Example: A=5 , C=6 : 50 + 60 = 110 = DDB with D=1 , B=0 ✓.

q-520.stem: Given: x is a two-digit number. x equals its units digit cubed, plus the sum of its digits. What is the tens digit of x?
q-520.stemHtml: Given: x is a two-digit number. x equals its units digit cubed, plus the sum of its digits. What is the tens digit of x?
explanation: Let T be the tens digit and U the units digit, so x = 10T + U . The condition says 10T + U = U³ + (T + U) . Subtracting T + U from both sides: 9T = U³ . So U³ must be a multiple of 9 with T a digit: U = 3 gives U³ = 27 and T = 3 ✓ ( U = 6 gives 216, T = 24 — impossible; U = 9 gives 729 — impossible; U = 0 gives T = 0 , not a two-digit number). So x = 33 : check 3³ + (3+3) = 27 + 6 = 33 ✓. The tens digit is 3.

q-583.stem: Nadia chose 13 positive integers, all different from each other. Within the group of numbers she chose, there necessarily exist two numbers whose difference is divisible by —
q-583.stemHtml: Nadia chose 13 positive integers, all different from each other. Within the group of numbers she chose, there necessarily exist two numbers whose difference is divisible by —
explanation: Pigeonhole principle: there are only 12 possible remainders upon division by 12 (0 through 11). With 13 numbers, at least two must share the same remainder mod 12, and their difference is then divisible by 12. This is not guaranteed for 13, 14 or 15: thirteen numbers can occupy thirteen distinct remainders in those larger moduli (e.g. the numbers 1..13 have all-different remainders mod 14), leaving no pair with a difference divisible by them.

wp21-p01.stem: A maker has 120 wooden pieces: circles, squares, and triangles. There are equally many circles and squares, and more circles than triangles. Which could be the number of triangles?
wp21-p01.stemRich: A maker has 120 wooden pieces: circles, squares, and triangles. There are equally many circles and squares, and more circles than triangles. Which could be the number of triangles?
wp21-p01.stemHtml: A maker has 120 wooden pieces: circles, squares, and triangles. There are equally many circles and squares, and more circles than triangles. Which could be the number of triangles?
explanation: If there are 34 triangles, 86 pieces remain. Splitting those equally gives 43 circles and 43 squares, and 43 is greater than 34. With 21 triangles the remaining 99 cannot split equally. With 44 or 50 triangles, each other group would be smaller than the triangle group.
wp21-p01.answerHtml: If there are 34 triangles, 86 pieces remain. Splitting those equally gives 43 circles and 43 squares, and 43 is greater than 34. With 21 triangles the remaining 99 cannot split equally. With 44 or 50 triangles, each other group would be smaller than the triangle group.

methods.title: Check the choices
steps: If there are 34 triangles, 86 pieces remain. Splitting those equally gives 43 circles and 43 squares, and 43 is greater than 34. With 21 triangles the remaining 99 cannot split equally. With 44 or 50 triangles, each other group would be smaller than the triangle group.

methods.title: Use an equation and a bound
steps: Write the circle and square counts as c and the triangle count as t. Then 2c+t=120. Since c>t, we have 120>3t, so t<40. The total is even, so t must also be even. Only 34 among the choices is both even and below 40.

wp21-p02.stemRich: Nora owns 8–14 sketchbooks and fewer than 6 brush cases. Sam owns fewer than 7 sketchbooks and 3–9 brush cases. Counts can be zero unless a lower bound is stated. What are the exact ranges for their combined sketchbooks and combined brush cases?
wp21-p02.stemHtml: Nora owns 8–14 sketchbooks and fewer than 6 brush cases. Sam owns fewer than 7 sketchbooks and 3–9 brush cases. Counts can be zero unless a lower bound is stated. What are the exact ranges for their combined sketchbooks and combined brush cases?
explanation: For sketchbooks, the smallest total is 8+0=8 and the largest is 14+6=20. Fewer than 7 means at most 6. For cases, the smallest total is 0+3=3 and the largest is 5+9=14. Each endpoint can actually occur.
wp21-p02.answerHtml: For sketchbooks, the smallest total is 8+0=8 and the largest is 14+6=20. Fewer than 7 means at most 6. For cases, the smallest total is 0+3=3 and the largest is 5+9=14. Each endpoint can actually occur.

methods.title: Add the smallest and largest counts
steps: For sketchbooks, the smallest total is 8+0=8 and the largest is 14+6=20. Fewer than 7 means at most 6. For cases, the smallest total is 0+3=3 and the largest is 5+9=14. Each endpoint can actually occur.

methods.title: Write integer intervals
steps: Nora’s ranges are 8≤N≤14 and 0≤B≤5. Sam’s are 0≤S≤6 and 3≤C≤9. Adding the lower bounds and upper bounds gives the exact intervals. Because the individual ranges contain every integer between their endpoints, there are no missing totals inside the combined intervals.

wp21-p03.stem: A player pays for a game item with exactly four vouchers, each worth 2, 7, or 12 credits. No change is given. Which price is impossible?
wp21-p03.stemRich: A player pays for a game item with exactly four vouchers, each worth 2, 7, or 12 credits. No change is given. Which price is impossible?
wp21-p03.stemHtml: A player pays for a game item with exactly four vouchers, each worth 2, 7, or 12 credits. No change is given. Which price is impossible?
explanation: Four 2-credit vouchers total 8. Replacing a 2 with a 7 adds 5; replacing it with a 12 adds 10. Every possible total so differs from 8 by a multiple of 5. The difference 31−8=23 is not a multiple of 5, so 31 is impossible.
wp21-p03.answerHtml: Four 2-credit vouchers total 8. Replacing a 2 with a 7 adds 5; replacing it with a 12 adds 10. Every possible total so differs from 8 by a multiple of 5. The difference 31−8=23 is not a multiple of 5, so 31 is impossible.

methods.title: Start with four smallest vouchers
steps: Four 2-credit vouchers total 8. Replacing a 2 with a 7 adds 5; replacing it with a 12 adds 10. Every possible total so differs from 8 by a multiple of 5. The difference 31−8=23 is not a multiple of 5, so 31 is impossible.

methods.title: Build the other prices
steps: 18=12+2+2+2; 28=12+12+2+2; 38=12+12+12+2. Each uses exactly four vouchers. These three prices are possible, leaving 31 as the impossible option.

wp21-p04.answerHtml: The three museum passes cost 180. For the minimum, buy five film passes: 180+150=330. For the maximum, buy five workshop passes: 180+600=780. Both purchases meet the condition of exactly three museum passes.

steps: The three museum passes cost 180. For the minimum, buy five film passes: 180+150=330. For the maximum, buy five workshop passes: 180+600=780. Both purchases meet the condition of exactly three museum passes.

wp21-p05.stem: A card shop sells half its stock each day. At closing, it adds three new cards for every card sold that day. It starts Monday with 24 cards. How many cards does it have at the end of Wednesday?
wp21-p05.stemRich: A card shop sells half its stock each day. At closing, it adds three new cards for every card sold that day. It starts Monday with 24 cards. How many cards does it have at the end of Wednesday?
wp21-p05.stemHtml: A card shop sells half its stock each day. At closing, it adds three new cards for every card sold that day. It starts Monday with 24 cards. How many cards does it have at the end of Wednesday?
explanation: On Monday it sells 12, keeps 12, and adds 36, ending with 48. Tuesday ends with 24+72=96. Wednesday ends with 48+144=192. Each closing count is the next morning’s starting count.
wp21-p05.answerHtml: On Monday it sells 12, keeps 12, and adds 36, ending with 48. Tuesday ends with 24+72=96. Wednesday ends with 48+144=192. Each closing count is the next morning’s starting count.

methods.title: Follow the three days
steps: On Monday it sells 12, keeps 12, and adds 36, ending with 48. Tuesday ends with 24+72=96. Wednesday ends with 48+144=192. Each closing count is the next morning’s starting count.

methods.title: Find the daily multiplier
steps: Starting with N cards, the shop keeps N divided by 2 and adds 3N divided by 2. Together that is 2N, so the stock doubles each day. Three days give 24×2³=192.

wp21-p06.stem: The sequence is 1,\ \frac13,\ \frac19,\ \frac1{27},\ldots. Which statement is not true?
wp21-p06.stemRich: The sequence is $1,\ \frac13,\ \frac19,\ \frac1{27},\ldots$. Which statement is not true?
wp21-p06.stemHtml: The sequence is . Which statement is not true?
choices: Every term is three times the following term
Each term after the first is smaller than the previous term
The gap between neighboring terms gets smaller
choicesRich: Every term is three times the following term
Each term after the first is smaller than the previous term
The gap between neighboring terms gets smaller
choicesHtml: Every term is three times the following term
Each term after the first is smaller than the previous term
The gap between neighboring terms gets smaller
explanation: Each term is obtained by dividing the preceding positive term by 3. Dividing a positive number by 3 keeps it positive, so no term becomes negative. The values get closer to zero without crossing it. The gaps also divide by 3 each time.
wp21-p06.answerHtml: Each term is obtained by dividing the preceding positive term by 3. Dividing a positive number by 3 keeps it positive, so no term becomes negative. The values get closer to zero without crossing it. The gaps also divide by 3 each time.

methods.title: Look at the repeated operation
steps: Each term is obtained by dividing the preceding positive term by 3. Dividing a positive number by 3 keeps it positive, so no term becomes negative. The values get closer to zero without crossing it. The gaps also divide by 3 each time.

methods.title: Use the nth term
steps: The nth term is 3 raised to the power 1−n. A positive base raised to any integer power is positive. The gap between term n and term n+1 is twice 3 raised to the power −n, which stays positive and gets smaller.

wp21-p07.stem: Twenty-eight badges are divided among n teams. Each team receives a different positive integer number of badges. Which value of n is impossible?
wp21-p07.stemRich: Twenty-eight badges are divided among n teams. Each team receives a different positive integer number of badges. Which value of n is impossible?
wp21-p07.stemHtml: Twenty-eight badges are divided among n teams. Each team receives a different positive integer number of badges. Which value of n is impossible?
explanation: Eight teams would need at least 1+2+3+4+5+6+7+8=36 badges. There are only 28, so eight teams are impossible. Seven teams can receive 1 through 7, totalling 28. Three or four teams can also receive distinct positive counts.
wp21-p07.answerHtml: Eight teams would need at least 1+2+3+4+5+6+7+8=36 badges. There are only 28, so eight teams are impossible. Seven teams can receive 1 through 7, totalling 28. Three or four teams can also receive distinct positive counts.

methods.title: Give each team as little as possible
steps: Eight teams would need at least 1+2+3+4+5+6+7+8=36 badges. There are only 28, so eight teams are impossible. Seven teams can receive 1 through 7, totalling 28. Three or four teams can also receive distinct positive counts.

methods.title: Check the possible choices constructively
steps: For three teams use 1,2,25. For four teams use 1,2,3,22. For seven teams use 1,2,3,4,5,6,7. All these allocations are legal. The remaining choice, eight, fails because even its smallest allocation already exceeds 28.

wp21-p08.stemHtml: Seats at an event are numbered 1 through 270. Every sixth seat has a red label, and every ninth seat has a blue label. How many seats have both labels?
explanation: A seat has both labels when its number is divisible by both 6 and 9. Their least common multiple is 18, so the labelled seats are 18,36,…,270. There are 270 divided by 18, or 15.
wp21-p08.answerHtml: A seat has both labels when its number is divisible by both 6 and 9. Their least common multiple is 18, so the labelled seats are 18,36,…,270. There are 270 divided by 18, or 15.

steps: A seat has both labels when its number is divisible by both 6 and 9. Their least common multiple is 18, so the labelled seats are 18,36,…,270. There are 270 divided by 18, or 15.

methods.title: Look at the blue-labelled seats
steps: There are 30 multiples of 9. Every second one is also a multiple of 6: 18,36,54, and so on. Half of the 30 blue-labelled seats so have both labels.

wp21-p09.stemHtml: Six musicians and eight actors are invited to a school event. Exactly nine attend. Each musician brings two posters; each actor brings four. What is the exact range of the total number of posters?
explanation: At most six attendees can be musicians, so at least three must be actors. That gives 6×2+3×4=24 posters. At most eight can be actors, leaving one musician and giving 8×4+2=34. Both endpoints are possible.
wp21-p09.answerHtml: At most six attendees can be musicians, so at least three must be actors. That gives 6×2+3×4=24 posters. At most eight can be actors, leaving one musician and giving 8×4+2=34. Both endpoints are possible.

steps: At most six attendees can be musicians, so at least three must be actors. That gives 6×2+3×4=24 posters. At most eight can be actors, leaving one musician and giving 8×4+2=34. Both endpoints are possible.

methods.title: Start with two posters per attendee
steps: Nine people would bring 18 posters if each brought two. Every actor adds two more. The number of actors ranges from 3 to 8, so the total is 18+2a, ranging from 24 to 34.

wp21-p10.stemHtml: A quiz has 48 questions. A correct answer earns 3 points, a wrong answer loses 2 points, and a blank earns zero. Layla answers exactly 42 questions. Which could be her score?
explanation: Forty-two correct answers would earn 126 points. Changing one answer from correct to wrong reduces the score by 5: three points are lost and a two-point penalty is added. Possible scores are 126,121,116,111,… . Of the choices, only 116 appears.

steps: Forty-two correct answers would earn 126 points. Changing one answer from correct to wrong reduces the score by 5: three points are lost and a two-point penalty is added. Possible scores are 126,121,116,111,… . Of the choices, only 116 appears.

methods.title: Use the number of correct answers

wp21-p11.stem: A two-sided card is drawn and replaced seven times. One side awards 5 points and the other 2 points. The total score is divisible by 8. What is the total?

wp21-p11.stemHtml: A two-sided card is drawn and replaced seven times. One side awards 5 points and the other 2 points. The total score is divisible by 8. What is the total?
explanation: Seven 2-point results give 14. Every 5-point result adds 3, so the possible totals are 14,17,20,23,26,29,32,35. Only 32 is divisible by 8.
wp21-p11.answerHtml: Seven 2-point results give 14. Every 5-point result adds 3, so the possible totals are 14,17,20,23,26,29,32,35. Only 32 is divisible by 8.

methods.title: Check the answer choices with an equation
steps: If h draws give 5 points, the total is 5h+2(7−h)=14+3h. A total of 32 gives h=6 and one 2-point draw, so it is legal. Totals 16 and 24 give fractional h, while 40 exceeds the maximum possible total of 35.

wp21-p12.stem: There are 18 robots in room A. At least half move to room B. At least four of the robots remaining in A are blue. What is the smallest and largest possible number of blue robots that move to B?
wp21-p12.stemRich: There are 18 robots in room A. At least half move to room B. At least four of the robots remaining in A are blue. What is the smallest and largest possible number of blue robots that move to B?
wp21-p12.stemHtml: There are 18 robots in room A. At least half move to room B. At least four of the robots remaining in A are blue. What is the smallest and largest possible number of blue robots that move to B?
explanation: For zero blue robots to move, let nine non-blue robots move and leave nine blue robots, so every condition holds. For the maximum, leave exactly four blue robots in A and move the other fourteen blue robots. There are not enough robots to move more than fourteen while leaving four blue robots behind.
wp21-p12.answerHtml: For zero blue robots to move, let nine non-blue robots move and leave nine blue robots, so every condition holds. For the maximum, leave exactly four blue robots in A and move the other fourteen blue robots. There are not enough robots to move more than fourteen while leaving four blue robots behind.

methods.title: Construct the two extremes
steps: For zero blue robots to move, let nine non-blue robots move and leave nine blue robots, so every condition holds. For the maximum, leave exactly four blue robots in A and move the other fourteen blue robots. There are not enough robots to move more than fourteen while leaving four blue robots behind.

methods.title: Separate the condition about movers from their colour
steps: At least half moving means at least nine robots move, but it says nothing about the colour of those movers. The lower bound on blue movers is so zero. At least four blue robots must stay, so blue movers cannot exceed 18−4=14. Both bounds are achievable.

explanation: Three 8-kg packages and two 2-kg packages total 28 kg. Their cost is 3×10+2×3=36. To prove this is best, begin with five 2-kg packages, costing 15. Eighteen more kilograms are needed. An upgrade from 2 to 8 kg adds 6 kg for 7 credits, the cheapest available upgrade per kilogram, and three such upgrades fit exactly.
wp21-p13.answerHtml: Three 8-kg packages and two 2-kg packages total 28 kg. Their cost is 3×10+2×3=36. To prove this is best, begin with five 2-kg packages, costing 15. Eighteen more kilograms are needed. An upgrade from 2 to 8 kg adds 6 kg for 7 credits, the cheapest available upgrade per kilogram, and three such upgrades fit exactly.

methods.title: Use cheap weight in the larger packages
steps: Three 8-kg packages and two 2-kg packages total 28 kg. Their cost is 3×10+2×3=36. To prove this is best, begin with five 2-kg packages, costing 15. Eighteen more kilograms are needed. An upgrade from 2 to 8 kg adds 6 kg for 7 credits, the cheapest available upgrade per kilogram, and three such upgrades fit exactly.

methods.title: Check all possible numbers of 8-kg packages
steps: With three 8-kg packages, the remaining two must be 2 kg each: cost 36. With two 8-kg packages, the cheapest remaining weights are 6,4,2: cost 37. With one 8-kg package, the cheapest remaining weights are 6,6,6,2: cost 37. With none, the only five weights summing to 28 are four 6s and one 4: cost 38. Four 8-kg packages are already too heavy.

wp21-p14.stem: Four players play a game. Each round lasts five minutes and has exactly one winner. The game stops as soon as one player wins four rounds. What is the longest the game can last?
wp21-p14.stemRich: Four players play a game. Each round lasts five minutes and has exactly one winner. The game stops as soon as one player wins four rounds. What is the longest the game can last?
wp21-p14.stemHtml: Four players play a game. Each round lasts five minutes and has exactly one winner. The game stops as soon as one player wins four rounds. What is the longest the game can last?
explanation: Each player can have three wins without ending the game. Four players can so play 12 rounds before anyone must have a fourth win. The next round ends the game. Thirteen rounds of five minutes take 65 minutes.
wp21-p14.answerHtml: Each player can have three wins without ending the game. Four players can so play 12 rounds before anyone must have a fourth win. The next round ends the game. Thirteen rounds of five minutes take 65 minutes.

methods.title: Delay the first fourth win
steps: Each player can have three wins without ending the game. Four players can so play 12 rounds before anyone must have a fourth win. The next round ends the game. Thirteen rounds of five minutes take 65 minutes.

methods.title: Use a capacity argument
steps: Imagine four boxes, one for each player, each able to hold three wins without triggering the stop. Together they hold 12 wins. The thirteenth win must go into a box that already has three. Giving every player three wins first shows that this maximum can actually be reached.

wp21-p15.stem: A bag contains 3–9 yellow counters and 5–8 black counters, and no others. What is the greatest possible fraction of the counters that are yellow?
wp21-p15.stemRich: A bag contains 3–9 yellow counters and 5–8 black counters, and no others. What is the greatest possible fraction of the counters that are yellow?
wp21-p15.stemHtml: A bag contains 3–9 yellow counters and 5–8 black counters, and no others. What is the greatest possible fraction of the counters that are yellow?
explanation: Use nine yellow counters and five black counters. The yellow share is then 9 out of 14. Adding yellow counters increases their share; adding black counters decreases it. Therefore no other allowed pair gives a larger share.
wp21-p15.answerHtml: Use nine yellow counters and five black counters. The yellow share is then 9 out of 14. Adding yellow counters increases their share; adding black counters decreases it. Therefore no other allowed pair gives a larger share.

methods.title: Maximise yellow and minimise black

methods.title: Compare yellow to black first
steps: The yellow-to-black ratio is at most 9:5. Converting that ratio into a fraction of the whole gives nine yellow parts out of fourteen total parts. Do not use the black count alone as the denominator: the question asks for the share of all counters.

wp21-p16.stem: A 148-meter fence is painted in 3-meter stripes, with 2-meter unpainted gaps between stripes. Stripes must be complete. What is the greatest possible number of painted stripes?
wp21-p16.stemRich: A 148-meter fence is painted in 3-meter stripes, with 2-meter unpainted gaps between stripes. Stripes must be complete. What is the greatest possible number of painted stripes?
wp21-p16.stemHtml: A 148-meter fence is painted in 3-meter stripes, with 2-meter unpainted gaps between stripes. Stripes must be complete. What is the greatest possible number of painted stripes?
explanation: With n stripes there are n−1 gaps, because no gap is needed after the last stripe. The length is 3n+2(n−1)=5n−2. For n=30 it is 148 metres exactly. A thirty-first stripe would require 153 metres.
wp21-p16.answerHtml: With n stripes there are n−1 gaps, because no gap is needed after the last stripe. The length is 3n+2(n−1)=5n−2. For n=30 it is 148 metres exactly. A thirty-first stripe would require 153 metres.

methods.title: Count stripes and gaps separately
steps: With n stripes there are n−1 gaps, because no gap is needed after the last stripe. The length is 3n+2(n−1)=5n−2. For n=30 it is 148 metres exactly. A thirty-first stripe would require 153 metres.

methods.title: Add one imaginary final gap
steps: Add a 2-metre gap after the fence’s last stripe. The imagined length is 150 metres and now consists of equal 5-metre blocks, each containing one stripe and one gap. There are 30 blocks, so 30 real stripes. The added gap is a counting aid, not part of the actual fence.

methods.title: Build the other three options
steps: Eleven and a half metres is 10 plus half of 3. Eighteen is one full ribbon. Twenty-eight is 18+10. All use each ribbon at most once. Seven fails after listing the short-piece possibilities, so it is the only impossible choice.

wp21-p19.stem: A team has 27 volunteers, each working as either an editor or a translator. One third work remotely. There are more editors than remote volunteers, but fewer editors than translators. What is the exact range of the number of translators?
wp21-p19.stemRich: A team has 27 volunteers, each working as either an editor or a translator. One third work remotely. There are more editors than remote volunteers, but fewer editors than translators. What is the exact range of the number of translators?
wp21-p19.stemHtml: A team has 27 volunteers, each working as either an editor or a translator. One third work remotely. There are more editors than remote volunteers, but fewer editors than translators. What is the exact range of the number of translators?
explanation: There are 9 remote volunteers, so there must be at least 10 editors. Editors are fewer than translators and the total is 27, so there can be at most 13 editors. Subtracting from 27 gives between 14 and 17 translators. These bounds are reached with 13 and 10 editors respectively.
wp21-p19.answerHtml: There are 9 remote volunteers, so there must be at least 10 editors. Editors are fewer than translators and the total is 27, so there can be at most 13 editors. Subtracting from 27 gives between 14 and 17 translators. These bounds are reached with 13 and 10 editors respectively.

methods.title: Bound the editors first
steps: There are 9 remote volunteers, so there must be at least 10 editors. Editors are fewer than translators and the total is 27, so there can be at most 13 editors. Subtracting from 27 gives between 14 and 17 translators. These bounds are reached with 13 and 10 editors respectively.

methods.title: Use inequalities for the requested count
steps: Let t be the translator count, so editors number 27−t. More than 9 editors gives t<18. Fewer editors than translators gives 27−t<t, so t>13.5. Since t is an integer, 14≤t≤17.

wp21-p20.stem: A volunteer working alone sorts 8 parcels per hour. For this task, each additional volunteer increases every volunteer’s rate by 3 parcels per hour. Seven volunteers work together for one hour. How many parcels do they sort?

wp21-p20.stemHtml: A volunteer working alone sorts 8 parcels per hour. For this task, each additional volunteer increases every volunteer’s rate by 3 parcels per hour. Seven volunteers work together for one hour. How many parcels do they sort?
explanation: The first volunteer is joined by six others, not seven. Each volunteer’s rate becomes 8+6×3=26 parcels per hour. Seven volunteers so sort 7×26=182 parcels in one hour.
wp21-p20.answerHtml: The first volunteer is joined by six others, not seven. Each volunteer’s rate becomes 8+6×3=26 parcels per hour. Seven volunteers so sort 7×26=182 parcels in one hour.

methods.title: Count the six increases per volunteer
steps: The first volunteer is joined by six others, not seven. Each volunteer’s rate becomes 8+6×3=26 parcels per hour. Seven volunteers so sort 7×26=182 parcels in one hour.

methods.title: Separate the base output and the teamwork gain
steps: Without the rate increase, seven volunteers would sort 7×8=56 parcels. Each of the seven gains 18 parcels per hour from the six extra teammates, adding 7×18=126 parcels. The total is 56+126=182. Do not add the gain only once for the whole team.

wp21-p24.stemHtml: In a row of 52 lockers, every block of four neighboring lockers contains exactly one red locker. Locker 2 is red. Which locker is necessarily also red?
explanation: A red locker repeats every four positions: 2,6,10,14,… . Moving from one block of four to the next removes one locker and adds one, so the new locker must match the removed locker’s colour. Position 46 fits the pattern.
wp21-p24.answerHtml: A red locker repeats every four positions: 2,6,10,14,… . Moving from one block of four to the next removes one locker and adds one, so the new locker must match the removed locker’s colour. Position 46 fits the pattern.

methods.title: Extend the repeating pattern
steps: A red locker repeats every four positions: 2,6,10,14,… . Moving from one block of four to the next removes one locker and adds one, so the new locker must match the removed locker’s colour. Position 46 fits the pattern.

methods.title: Check the remainders
steps: Red positions are 2+4k. Since 46−2=44 is divisible by 4, 46 is red. The other choices do not leave remainder 2 when divided by 4.

wp21-p25.stem: There are 16 boxes containing a total of 58 pencils. Every box has at least three pencils. What is the smallest possible number of boxes containing exactly three pencils?
wp21-p25.stemRich: There are 16 boxes containing a total of 58 pencils. Every box has at least three pencils. What is the smallest possible number of boxes containing exactly three pencils?
wp21-p25.stemHtml: There are 16 boxes containing a total of 58 pencils. Every box has at least three pencils. What is the smallest possible number of boxes containing exactly three pencils?
explanation: Giving every box three pencils uses 48, leaving ten extra pencils. To make as many boxes as possible have more than three, put one extra in each of ten boxes. The remaining six stay at exactly three.
wp21-p25.answerHtml: Giving every box three pencils uses 48, leaving ten extra pencils. To make as many boxes as possible have more than three, put one extra in each of ten boxes. The remaining six stay at exactly three.

methods.title: Spend the extra pencils
steps: Giving every box three pencils uses 48, leaving ten extra pencils. To make as many boxes as possible have more than three, put one extra in each of ten boxes. The remaining six stay at exactly three.

methods.title: Prove the lower bound
steps: If k boxes have exactly three, the other 16−k have at least four. Thus the total is at least 3k+4(16−k)=64−k. Since only 58 pencils are available, k≥6. Six boxes with three and ten with four reach 58.

wp21-g004.stem: A game begins with 2 large crystals. Breaking a large crystal replaces it with 4 small crystals. Breaking a small crystal removes it. After exactly 3 breaks, which crystal count is possible?
wp21-g004.stemRich: A game begins with 2 large crystals. Breaking a large crystal replaces it with 4 small crystals. Breaking a small crystal removes it. After exactly 3 breaks, which crystal count is possible?
wp21-g004.stemHtml: A game begins with 2 large crystals. Breaking a large crystal replaces it with 4 small crystals. Breaking a small crystal removes it. After exactly 3 breaks, which crystal count is possible?
explanation: The first break has to hit a large crystal, because there are no small ones yet. One large crystal disappears and four small ones appear. We now have one large and four small: five crystals in total.

For the second break, choose the remaining large crystal. It becomes four more small crystals. Now all eight crystals are small. The third break removes one of them, leaving seven. That gives a complete legal sequence, so seven is possible.

We can also explore the other branch. If the second break removes a small crystal, we have one large and three small. Breaking the large next gives seven; breaking another small gives one large and two small, or three total. So the only possible totals are three and seven.
wp21-g004.answerHtml:
The first break has to hit a large crystal, because there are no small ones yet. One large crystal disappears and four small ones appear. We now have one large and four small: five crystals in total.

For the second break, choose the remaining large crystal. It becomes four more small crystals. Now all eight crystals are small. The third break removes one of them, leaving seven. That gives a complete legal sequence, so seven is possible.

We can also explore the other branch. If the second break removes a small crystal, we have one large and three small. Breaking the large next gives seven; breaking another small gives one large and two small, or three total. So the only possible totals are three and seven.

methods.title: Draw the possible branches
steps: The first break has to hit a large crystal, because there are no small ones yet. One large crystal disappears and four small ones appear. We now have one large and four small: five crystals in total.

For the second break, choose the remaining large crystal. It becomes four more small crystals. Now all eight crystals are small. The third break removes one of them, leaving seven. That gives a complete legal sequence, so seven is possible.

We can also explore the other branch. If the second break removes a small crystal, we have one large and three small. Breaking the large next gives seven; breaking another small gives one large and two small, or three total. So the only possible totals are three and seven.

methods.title: Track the change in the total
steps: Every large break adds three to the count overall: remove one and add four. Every small break subtracts one. If b of the three breaks hit large crystals, the final count is 2+3b−(3−b)=4b−1.

At least one large crystal must be broken, and at most two can be broken. Therefore b is one or two, giving totals three or seven. Both values can be achieved by the branches we drew. This second method turns the game into a short calculation without losing the rule about what can be hit.

wp21-g005.stem: A queue contains at least one delivery van of length 5 m and at least one scooter of length 2 m. There is a 1 m gap between consecutive vehicles and no gap counted at either end. Which total queue length is impossible?
wp21-g005.stemRich: A queue contains at least one delivery van of length 5 m and at least one scooter of length 2 m. There is a 1 m gap between consecutive vehicles and no gap counted at either end. Which total queue length is impossible?
wp21-g005.stemHtml: A queue contains at least one delivery van of length 5 m and at least one scooter of length 2 m. There is a 1 m gap between consecutive vehicles and no gap counted at either end. Which total queue length is impossible?
explanation: Start with the required van and scooter. Their lengths plus the single gap total 5+1+2=8 metres, so eight is possible. Each extra scooter adds its own two metres and one new gap: three metres. Adding one or two scooters gives eleven and fourteen.

Ten lies between the minimum eight and the next possible total eleven. An added van would contribute six metres, which is even larger. We cannot add only a gap or part of a vehicle, so ten is impossible.
wp21-g005.answerHtml:
Start with the required van and scooter. Their lengths plus the single gap total 5+1+2=8 metres, so eight is possible. Each extra scooter adds its own two metres and one new gap: three metres. Adding one or two scooters gives eleven and fourteen.

Ten lies between the minimum eight and the next possible total eleven. An added van would contribute six metres, which is even larger. We cannot add only a gap or part of a vehicle, so ten is impossible.

methods.title: Build the shortest queue, then extend it
steps: Start with the required van and scooter. Their lengths plus the single gap total 5+1+2=8 metres, so eight is possible. Each extra scooter adds its own two metres and one new gap: three metres. Adding one or two scooters gives eleven and fourteen.

Ten lies between the minimum eight and the next possible total eleven. An added van would contribute six metres, which is even larger. We cannot add only a gap or part of a vehicle, so ten is impossible.

methods.title: Attach one gap to each vehicle
steps: Temporarily give every vehicle a gap after it. A van then contributes six metres and a scooter three. This counts one extra gap at the far end, so subtract one. The length is 6v+3s−1, where v and s are positive integers.

Adding one back to any valid total gives a multiple of three. For ten, adding one gives eleven, which is not divisible by three. The totals eight, eleven, and fourteen pass this test and the construction already shows they are attainable.

wp21-g007.stem: A mentor shares 32 pins among apprentices. Each apprentice receives a different number of pins (a positive integer), and all pins are distributed. What is the largest possible number of apprentices?
wp21-g007.stemRich: A mentor shares 32 pins among apprentices. Each apprentice receives a different number of pins (a positive integer), and all pins are distributed. What is the largest possible number of apprentices?
wp21-g007.stemHtml: A mentor shares 32 pins among apprentices. Each apprentice receives a different number of pins (a positive integer), and all pins are distributed. What is the largest possible number of apprentices?
explanation: To reach as many apprentices as possible, avoid using too many pins on the early recipients. Give one to the first, two to the next, then three, and so on. The running totals are one, three, six, ten, fifteen, twenty-one, and twenty-eight. Seven apprentices can so receive distinct positive amounts.
An eighth would need at least eight pins in addition to the first seven minimum amounts. That would make thirty-six, more than the available thirty-two. We have proved eight is impossible.

Seven is not just an upper bound: use 1,2,3,4,5,6,11. They total thirty-two, are all positive, and are all different. The four pins left after the minimum distribution can safely go to the person who already has the most.

wp21-g009.stem: A training drill begins with 46 repetitions. In each later round, the athlete does half the previous round’s repetitions, then subtracts 1. How many repetitions are done in round 4?

wp21-g009.stemHtml: A training drill begins with 46 repetitions. In each later round, the athlete does half the previous round’s repetitions, then subtracts 1. How many repetitions are done in round 4?
explanation: Round one is already forty-six; do not apply the rule before recording that starting value. Round two is half of forty-six, twenty-three, minus one: twenty-two. Round three is half of twenty-two, eleven, minus one: ten. Round four is half of ten, five, minus one: four.

We apply the rule three times to move from round one to round four. A fourth application would answer round five instead. Also keep the operation order: halve first, then subtract one. Halving forty-five would describe a different rule.

wp21-g010.stem: A charity receives 3 crates on day 1, and twice as many as the previous day on every later day. How many crates are received in total through day n?
wp21-g010.stemRich: A charity receives 3 crates on day 1, and twice as many as the previous day on every later day. How many crates are received in total through day n?
wp21-g010.stemHtml: A charity receives 3 crates on day 1, and twice as many as the previous day on every later day. How many crates are received in total through day n?
explanation: Choose n=3 so the actual sequence is short. The daily counts are three, six, and twelve, for a total of twenty-one. Now test all four formulas at the same chosen n. The proposed expression 3(2^n−1) gives 3(8−1)=21. The alternatives give twenty-seven, twenty-four, and eleven.

Only one formula survives this legal test, so it is the correct choice among the listed answers. A single example does not prove an identity in general, but it can eliminate the wrong answer formulas. Using n=1 may leave accidental ties; three remains easy while separating these choices.

methods.title: Subtract a doubled sum
steps: Let $S=3+6+12+\cdots+3\times2^{n-1}$. Doubling gives $2S=6+12+\cdots+3\times2^n$. Subtract the original sum: all the middle terms cancel, leaving $S=3\times2^n-3=3(2^n-1)$. This proves the formula for every positive integer n.

wp21-g013.stem: A token shows 4 on one side and 9 on the other. It is tossed exactly 6 times. Which total is impossible?
wp21-g013.stemRich: A token shows 4 on one side and 9 on the other. It is tossed exactly 6 times. Which total is impossible?
wp21-g013.stemHtml: A token shows 4 on one side and 9 on the other. It is tossed exactly 6 times. Which total is impossible?
explanation: The smallest total comes from six fours: twenty-four. Replacing one four by a nine adds five. Each further replacement adds another five, so the possible totals are 24,29,34,39,44,49,54.

The choices twenty-four, thirty-nine, and forty-nine all occur in that list. Forty-one does not. Once we move from thirty-nine to forty-four, we have skipped it, and more nines can only increase the total further. We do not need to list the order of every toss, because changing the order does not change the sum.

methods.title: Use a remainder test
steps: If k tosses show nine, the total is 9k+4(6−k)=24+5k. Every possible total so leaves remainder four when divided by five. Forty-one leaves remainder one and cannot work.

The remainder test rules out the impossible choice quickly, but the count k must still be an integer from zero to six when testing possible totals. A remainder alone would not make an out-of-range value such as seventy-four possible.

wp21-g014.stem: At a festival there are dancers, singers, and actors only. There are 3 times as many dancers as singers, and more actors than dancers. There are 70 performers in total. Which dancer count is possible?
wp21-g014.stemRich: At a festival there are dancers, singers, and actors only. There are 3 times as many dancers as singers, and more actors than dancers. There are 70 performers in total. Which dancer count is possible?
wp21-g014.stemHtml: At a festival there are dancers, singers, and actors only. There are 3 times as many dancers as singers, and more actors than dancers. There are 70 performers in total. Which dancer count is possible?
explanation: Try thirty dancers. That forces ten singers, leaving thirty actors. The actors must outnumber the dancers, so equality is not enough: thirty fails. Increasing the dancers above thirty also increases the singers and leaves fewer actors, so thirty-three fails too.

Twenty-eight is not divisible by three, so it cannot be three times a whole number of singers. That leaves twenty-seven. It gives nine singers and thirty-four actors. Both comparisons hold, and the total is seventy.

methods.title: Test a convenient middle choice
steps: Try thirty dancers. That forces ten singers, leaving thirty actors. The actors must outnumber the dancers, so equality is not enough: thirty fails. Increasing the dancers above thirty also increases the singers and leaves fewer actors, so thirty-three fails too.

wp21-g015.stem: Twenty-four boxes contain 86 markers altogether. Every box contains at least 3 markers. Which number cannot be the number of boxes containing exactly 3 markers?
wp21-g015.stemRich: Twenty-four boxes contain 86 markers altogether. Every box contains at least 3 markers. Which number cannot be the number of boxes containing exactly 3 markers?
wp21-g015.stemHtml: Twenty-four boxes contain 86 markers altogether. Every box contains at least 3 markers. Which number cannot be the number of boxes containing exactly 3 markers?
explanation: If ten boxes contain exactly three, they use thirty markers. The fourteen remaining boxes must each have at least four, using fifty-six more. That totals eighty-six exactly, so ten is possible.

If twelve boxes contain exactly three, thirty-six markers are used and fifty remain for twelve boxes. Give eleven boxes four each and the last six. That works. If fifteen boxes contain exactly three, forty-five markers are used and forty-one remain for nine boxes. Give eight boxes four and the last nine. That also works.

If only nine boxes contain exactly three, the other fifteen must all have at least four. The minimum total becomes 9×3+15×4=87, already above eighty-six. This is why nine is impossible: the other boxes cannot quietly contain three as well.

steps: If ten boxes contain exactly three, they use thirty markers. The fourteen remaining boxes must each have at least four, using fifty-six more. That totals eighty-six exactly, so ten is possible.

If twelve boxes contain exactly three, thirty-six markers are used and fifty remain for twelve boxes. Give eleven boxes four each and the last six. That works. If fifteen boxes contain exactly three, forty-five markers are used and forty-one remain for nine boxes. Give eight boxes four and the last nine. That also works.

If only nine boxes contain exactly three, the other fifteen must all have at least four. The minimum total becomes 9×3+15×4=87, already above eighty-six. This is why nine is impossible: the other boxes cannot quietly contain three as well.

methods.title: Count the extra markers
steps: First put three markers in all twenty-four boxes. That uses seventy-two and leaves fourteen extras. Each box we want to move above exactly three needs at least one extra marker. Fourteen extras can move at most fourteen boxes above three, leaving at least ten boxes with exactly three.

Nine would require fifteen boxes above three, but there are only fourteen extras. This quicker explanation uses the same constraint as the answer-testing route. We will return to the full range after the next minimum-and-maximum examples.

wp21-g017.stem: A quiz has between 12 and 20 questions (inclusive). Each of 16 students answers at least \frac14 of the quiz correctly. What are the smallest and largest possible totals of correct answers across the class?

wp21-g017.stemHtml: A quiz has between 12 and 20 questions (inclusive). Each of 16 students answers at least of the quiz correctly. What are the smallest and largest possible totals of correct answers across the class?
explanation: To minimise the correct total, use the shortest quiz, twelve questions, and the smallest allowed correct share, one quarter. That is three correct answers per student. Sixteen students give 16×3=48.

For the maximum, use the longest quiz, twenty questions, and let every student answer all twenty correctly. “At least one quarter” does not limit them to one quarter. Sixteen times twenty gives 320. Both endpoint arrangements are allowed.

wp21-g018.stem: Nine jars stand in a row. The first has 6 beads and the last has 42. Each jar has at least 3 more beads than the jar before it. What is the exact range for the fifth jar?
wp21-g018.stemRich: Nine jars stand in a row. The first has 6 beads and the last has 42. Each jar has at least 3 more beads than the jar before it. What is the exact range for the fifth jar?
wp21-g018.stemHtml: Nine jars stand in a row. The first has 6 beads and the last has 42. Each jar has at least 3 more beads than the jar before it. What is the exact range for the fifth jar?

For the largest count, work backwards from forty-two, leaving three per gap: 42,39,36,33,30. The fifth cannot exceed thirty, or there would not be enough room for the four later increases.

Both endpoints can occur. For eighteen, use 6,9,12,15,18,21,24,27,42. For thirty, use 6,9,12,15,30,33,36,39,42. Intermediate integer values can also be fitted by adjusting the jump into the fifth jar.

methods.title: Count the extra markers
steps: First put three markers in all twenty-four boxes. That uses seventy-two and leaves fourteen extras. Each box we want to move above exactly three needs at least one extra marker. Fourteen extras can move at most fourteen boxes above three, leaving at least ten boxes with exactly three.

Nine would require fifteen boxes above three, but there are only fourteen extras. This quicker explanation uses the same constraint as the answer-testing route. We will return to the full range after the next minimum-and-maximum examples.

methods.title: Test the claimed exact counts
steps: If ten boxes contain exactly three, they use thirty markers. The fourteen remaining boxes must each have at least four, using fifty-six more. That totals eighty-six exactly, so ten is possible.

If twelve boxes contain exactly three, thirty-six markers are used and fifty remain for twelve boxes. Give eleven boxes four each and the last six. That works. If fifteen boxes contain exactly three, forty-five markers are used and forty-one remain for nine boxes. Give eight boxes four and the last nine. That also works.

If only nine boxes contain exactly three, the other fifteen must all have at least four. The minimum total becomes 9×3+15×4=87, already above eighty-six. This is why nine is impossible: the other boxes cannot quietly contain three as well.

methods.title: Prove the whole range, without assuming gaps disappear
steps: There are fourteen markers above the three-per-box baseline. Let r be the number of boxes that receive extras. We must have at least one such box because fourteen extras must go somewhere, and at most fourteen because each needs at least one.

Every integer r from one to fourteen is possible: give one extra to each of r boxes, then put the remaining 14−r extras in one of those boxes. No untouched box changes. Therefore the number with exactly three is 24−r, giving every integer from ten through twenty-three.

This is the reason the feasible counts form an unbroken integer range in this particular problem. We should not assume every minimum-and-maximum problem has no gaps: divisibility or other restrictions can create gaps elsewhere. Here we have supplied a construction for every count. Nine lies below the proven minimum.

wp21-g023.stem: A digital collection starts day 1 with 58 files. During each day the number doubles, and at the end of the day 16 files are deleted. How many files are present on day 3 just before that day’s deletion?
wp21-g023.stemRich: A digital collection starts day 1 with 58 files. During each day the number doubles, and at the end of the day 16 files are deleted. How many files are present on day 3 just before that day’s deletion?
wp21-g023.stemHtml: A digital collection starts day 1 with 58 files. During each day the number doubles, and at the end of the day 16 files are deleted. How many files are present on day 3 just before that day’s deletion?
explanation: Day one starts with fifty-eight. Doubling gives 116, then deleting sixteen leaves one hundred. Day two starts with that one hundred, doubles to two hundred, and ends with 184.

Day three doubles 184 to 368. Stop there: the question asks for the count before the third deletion. Removing sixteen once more would give 352, a real count at a different moment, not the answer requested.
wp21-g023.answerHtml:
Day one starts with fifty-eight. Doubling gives 116, then deleting sixteen leaves one hundred. Day two starts with that one hundred, doubles to two hundred, and ends with 184.

Day three doubles 184 to 368. Stop there: the question asks for the count before the third deletion. Removing sixteen once more would give 352, a real count at a different moment, not the answer requested.

methods.title: Keep before and after in separate columns
steps: Day one starts with fifty-eight. Doubling gives 116, then deleting sixteen leaves one hundred. Day two starts with that one hundred, doubles to two hundred, and ends with 184.

Day three doubles 184 to 368. Stop there: the question asks for the count before the third deletion. Removing sixteen once more would give 352, a real count at a different moment, not the answer requested.

methods.title: Follow the original files and the earlier deletions
steps: Without deletions, the initial fifty-eight files would be multiplied by eight by the third doubling, giving 464. The first deletion of sixteen would have doubled twice by then, contributing a loss of sixty-four. The second would have doubled once, contributing a loss of thirty-two.
Subtract those effects: 464−64−32=368. There is no third-deletion term because our stopping point is before it. This method is longer here, but it is a useful check on the timing.

wp21-g024.stem: Fifty-six lamps stand in a row. In every group of four consecutive lamps, exactly one is blue. Lamp 2 is blue. Which lamp can also be blue?
wp21-g024.stemRich: Fifty-six lamps stand in a row. In every group of four consecutive lamps, exactly one is blue. Lamp 2 is blue. Which lamp can also be blue?
wp21-g024.stemHtml: Fifty-six lamps stand in a row. In every group of four consecutive lamps, exactly one is blue. Lamp 2 is blue. Which lamp can also be blue?
explanation: If every four consecutive lamps contain one blue lamp, compare lamps 1–4 with lamps 2–5. The middle three lamps are shared, so lamp 5 must have the same blue status as lamp 1. Repeating this comparison shows that the pattern repeats every four positions.

Since position two is blue, the blue positions are 2,6,10,14,18,22,26,30,34,38, and so on. Of the listed positions, only thirty-eight appears. We can sketch the short four-lamp cycle rather than drawing all fifty-six lamps.
wp21-g024.answerHtml:
If every four consecutive lamps contain one blue lamp, compare lamps 1–4 with lamps 2–5. The middle three lamps are shared, so lamp 5 must have the same blue status as lamp 1. Repeating this comparison shows that the pattern repeats every four positions.

Since position two is blue, the blue positions are 2,6,10,14,18,22,26,30,34,38, and so on. Of the listed positions, only thirty-eight appears. We can sketch the short four-lamp cycle rather than drawing all fifty-six lamps.

methods.title: Slide the four-lamp window
steps: If every four consecutive lamps contain one blue lamp, compare lamps 1–4 with lamps 2–5. The middle three lamps are shared, so lamp 5 must have the same blue status as lamp 1. Repeating this comparison shows that the pattern repeats every four positions.

Since position two is blue, the blue positions are 2,6,10,14,18,22,26,30,34,38, and so on. Of the listed positions, only thirty-eight appears. We can sketch the short four-lamp cycle rather than drawing all fifty-six lamps.

methods.title: Use the position’s remainder
steps: The blue positions have the form 4k+2. They leave remainder two when divided by four. Thirty-eight is 4×9+2 and fits. Thirty-five, thirty-six, and thirty-seven leave remainders three, zero, and one.

The remainder shortcut comes from the repeating pattern we proved. It is not enough merely to group lamps 1–4, 5–8, and so on; the condition applies to every overlapping group of four, which forces the repeated position.

wp21-g025.stem: Two reminder lights flash together at 07:30. One then flashes every 18 minutes and the other every 24 minutes. Counting 07:30 as the first joint flash, when is their fourth joint flash?
wp21-g025.stemRich: Two reminder lights flash together at 07:30. One then flashes every 18 minutes and the other every 24 minutes. Counting 07:30 as the first joint flash, when is their fourth joint flash?
wp21-g025.stemHtml: Two reminder lights flash together at 07:30. One then flashes every 18 minutes and the other every 24 minutes. Counting 07:30 as the first joint flash, when is their fourth joint flash?
explanation: List multiples of the larger interval to minimise the number of checks: twenty-four, forty-eight, seventy-two. Seventy-two is also a multiple of eighteen, so the lights flash together every seventy-two minutes.

The first joint flash is already counted at 07:30. The second is at 08:42, the third at 09:54, and the fourth at 11:06. Four events have only three intervals between them. Multiplying by four would go one flash too far.
wp21-g025.answerHtml:
List multiples of the larger interval to minimise the number of checks: twenty-four, forty-eight, seventy-two. Seventy-two is also a multiple of eighteen, so the lights flash together every seventy-two minutes.

The first joint flash is already counted at 07:30. The second is at 08:42, the third at 09:54, and the fourth at 11:06. Four events have only three intervals between them. Multiplying by four would go one flash too far.

methods.title: Find the first shared interval
steps: List multiples of the larger interval to minimise the number of checks: twenty-four, forty-eight, seventy-two. Seventy-two is also a multiple of eighteen, so the lights flash together every seventy-two minutes.

The first joint flash is already counted at 07:30. The second is at 08:42, the third at 09:54, and the fourth at 11:06. Four events have only three intervals between them. Multiplying by four would go one flash too far.

methods.title: Use prime factors for the shared interval
steps: $18=2\times3^2$ and $24=2^3\times3$. The least common multiple needs the larger power of each prime: $2^3\times3^2=72$. Three intervals give 216 minutes, or three hours thirty-six minutes. Add that to 07:30 to get 11:06.

wp22-p03.answerHtml: The extra load is 113−80=33 g. Each of those grams removes 4 km, so the total loss is 132 km. Subtract that loss from the original 540 km.

methods.title: Calculate the change

methods.title: Write a range rule
steps: For a load of w grams, range is 540−4(w−80). The subtraction inside the brackets matters: the original 80 g is already included in the 540 km range. Put w=113 into this rule.

wp22-p14.stemHtml: A jar contains 120 spoonfuls of cocoa and costs 18 credits. A bag contains 300 spoonfuls of sugar and costs 12 credits. What is the ingredient cost of a drink using two spoonfuls of cocoa and three of sugar?
explanation: One spoonful of cocoa costs 18:120=0.15 credits, and one spoonful of sugar costs 12:300=0.04. The drink uses two of the first and three of the second.
wp22-p14.answerHtml: One spoonful of cocoa costs 18:120=0.15 credits, and one spoonful of sugar costs 12:300=0.04. The drink uses two of the first and three of the second.

steps: One spoonful of cocoa costs 18:120=0.15 credits, and one spoonful of sugar costs 12:300=0.04. The drink uses two of the first and three of the second.

methods.title: Price a batch of drinks
steps: Make 60 drinks. Their cocoa uses one full jar, costing 18. Their sugar uses 180 spoonfuls, or three fifths of a bag, costing 7.20. The batch costs 25.20, and 25.20:60=0.42 per drink.

wp22-p15.stem: For 6 days, a camper gathers 25 berries a day and eats x of them each day. The saved berries then last 18 days at 5 berries a day. What is x?
wp22-p15.stemRich: For 6 days, a camper gathers 25 berries a day and eats x of them each day. The saved berries then last 18 days at 5 berries a day. What is x?
wp22-p15.stemHtml: For 6 days, a camper gathers 25 berries a day and eats x of them each day. The saved berries then last 18 days at 5 berries a day. What is x?
explanation: The later supply must be 18×5=90 berries. The camper gathers 6×25=150 berries, so 60 are eaten during the first six days. That is 60:6=10 per day.
wp22-p15.answerHtml: The later supply must be 18×5=90 berries. The camper gathers 6×25=150 berries, so 60 are eaten during the first six days. That is 60:6=10 per day.

methods.title: Balance saved and used berries
steps: The later supply must be 18×5=90 berries. The camper gathers 6×25=150 berries, so 60 are eaten during the first six days. That is 60:6=10 per day.

methods.title: Compare one gathering day with later days
steps: Each of the six gathering days supports three of the later days, because 18:6=3. So 15 berries must be saved each gathering day. Of the 25 gathered, the remaining 10 can be eaten.

wp22-p16.stem: An older dog is 6 years older than a younger dog. Their current age ratio is 4:1. What will the older-to-younger ratio be in 2 years?
wp22-p16.stemRich: An older dog is 6 years older than a younger dog. Their current age ratio is 4:1. What will the older-to-younger ratio be in 2 years?
wp22-p16.stemHtml: An older dog is 6 years older than a younger dog. Their current age ratio is 4:1. What will the older-to-younger ratio be in 2 years?
explanation: The ratio gap is three units, and that equals six years. One unit is two years, so their ages are eight and two. In two years they will be ten and four, giving 10:4=5:2.
wp22-p16.answerHtml: The ratio gap is three units, and that equals six years. One unit is two years, so their ages are eight and two. In two years they will be ten and four, giving 10:4=5:2.

methods.title: Use the age gap
steps: The ratio gap is three units, and that equals six years. One unit is two years, so their ages are eight and two. In two years they will be ten and four, giving 10:4=5:2.

methods.title: Write the younger age first
steps: Let the younger dog be y. The older dog is both y+6 and 4y, so 3y=6 and y=2. Add two years to each age separately; the six-year gap stays fixed, but the ratio changes.

wp22-p17.stem: One meter of silk costs x credits and one meter of cotton costs y credits. Their prices add to 17 credits, and silk costs 5 credits more. A shop sells x meters of silk and buys y meters of cotton. What is the difference between the money received and spent?
wp22-p17.stemRich: One meter of silk costs $x$ credits and one meter of cotton costs $y$ credits. Their prices add to 17 credits, and silk costs 5 credits more. A shop sells x meters of silk and buys y meters of cotton. What is the difference between the money received and spent?
wp22-p17.stemHtml: One meter of silk costs credits and one meter of cotton costs credits. Their prices add to 17 credits, and silk costs 5 credits more. A shop sells x meters of silk and buys y meters of cotton. What is the difference between the money received and spent?
explanation: Two prices with sum 17 and difference 5 are 11 and 6. Selling 11 metres at 11 credits brings 121; buying six metres at six credits costs 36. The difference is 85.
wp22-p17.answerHtml: Two prices with sum 17 and difference 5 are 11 and 6. Selling 11 metres at 11 credits brings 121; buying six metres at six credits costs 36. The difference is 85.

methods.title: Find the two prices
steps: Two prices with sum 17 and difference 5 are 11 and 6. Selling 11 metres at 11 credits brings 121; buying six metres at six credits costs 36. The difference is 85.

methods.title: Use the difference of squares
steps: The money received is $x^2$ and the money spent is $y^2$. Factor their difference: $x^2-y^2=(x-y)(x+y)=5\times17=85$. This gets the requested result without finding the two prices separately.

wp22-p18.stemHtml: Four positive numbers are arranged in two rows: a, b above c, d. The row totals are equal, and the column totals are equal. Which of the following statements is necessarily true?
explanation: The row condition is $a+b=c+d$. The column condition is $a+c=b+d$. Subtracting gives $b-c=c-b$, so $b=c$. Substitute that into either equation to get $a=d$.

methods.title: Subtract the two conditions
steps: The row condition is $a+b=c+d$. The column condition is $a+c=b+d$. Subtracting gives $b-c=c-b$, so $b=c$. Substitute that into either equation to get $a=d$.

methods.title: Remove the shared corner
steps: The top row and left column each have the same total as half the whole grid. They share a, so their other entries b and c must match. The remaining opposite pair a and d must then match too. A grid with 3, 7 above 7, 3 shows why the other claims need not hold.

explanation: Each month keeps $\frac34$ of whatever is there at that time. Apply that factor three times: $\frac34\times\frac34\times\frac34=\frac{27}{64}$. We do not subtract three quarters of the original amount, because the supply becomes smaller each month.

wp22-p20.stemHtml: A manual contains 48,000 words and 40 diagrams. A leaflet contains 3,000 words and 15 diagrams. The word-to-diagram ratio of the manual is how many times that of the leaflet?
explanation: The manual has 48,000:40=1,200 words per diagram. The leaflet has 3,000:15=200. Compare those values: 1,200:200=6.
wp22-p20.answerHtml: The manual has 48,000:40=1,200 words per diagram. The leaflet has 3,000:15=200. Compare those values: 1,200:200=6.
