methods.title: Compare the scale factors
steps: The manual has 16 times as many words, but only eight thirds as many diagrams. The ratio so grows by 16 divided by eight thirds, which is 6. This is useful when the raw figures have large common factors.

wp22-p21.stem: A workshop has 42 stools and carts altogether. Each stool has 3 legs and each cart has 4 wheels. The total number of legs and wheels is 146. How many carts are there?
wp22-p21.stemRich: A workshop has 42 stools and carts altogether. Each stool has 3 legs and each cart has 4 wheels. The total number of legs and wheels is 146. How many carts are there?
wp22-p21.stemHtml: A workshop has 42 stools and carts altogether. Each stool has 3 legs and each cart has 4 wheels. The total number of legs and wheels is 146. How many carts are there?
explanation: If all 42 items were stools, there would be 42×3=126 legs. Each cart replaces three legs with four wheels, adding one to the count. The extra 146−126=20 so means 20 carts.
wp22-p21.answerHtml: If all 42 items were stools, there would be 42×3=126 legs. Each cart replaces three legs with four wheels, adding one to the count. The extra 146−126=20 so means 20 carts.

methods.title: Start with all stools
steps: If all 42 items were stools, there would be 42×3=126 legs. Each cart replaces three legs with four wheels, adding one to the count. The extra 146−126=20 so means 20 carts.

methods.title: Use two equations
steps: Let c count carts and s count stools. Then c+s=42 and 4c+3s=146. Subtract three times the first equation from the second; the stool terms cancel and c=20.

wp22-p23.stem: Ada starts work at 09:00 on each of five days. On three of those days she takes an unpaid one-hour break. She finishes at the same time every day and works 32 paid hours in total. When does she finish?

wp22-p23.stemHtml: Ada starts work at 09:00 on each of five days. On three of those days she takes an unpaid one-hour break. She finishes at the same time every day and works 32 paid hours in total. When does she finish?
explanation: She must be at work for 32 paid hours plus three unpaid hours: 35 hours altogether. Split equally over five days, that is seven hours from arrival to departure. Seven hours after 09:00 is 16:00.
wp22-p23.answerHtml: She must be at work for 32 paid hours plus three unpaid hours: 35 hours altogether. Split equally over five days, that is seven hours from arrival to departure. Seven hours after 09:00 is 16:00.

methods.title: Include the unpaid time
steps: She must be at work for 32 paid hours plus three unpaid hours: 35 hours altogether. Split equally over five days, that is seven hours from arrival to departure. Seven hours after 09:00 is 16:00.

methods.title: Check one proposed schedule
steps: Finishing at 16:00 gives seven hours on site each day. Two days contain seven paid hours and three days contain six. The weekly total is 2×7+3×6=32, exactly as required.

wp22-p26.stemRich: Ben borrows some money and spends $\frac25$ of it on rice. He repays his lender with $\frac34$ of that rice at its purchase value. He still owes 8.40 credits. How much did he borrow?
wp22-p26.stemHtml: Ben borrows some money and spends of it on rice. He repays his lender with of that rice at its purchase value. He still owes 8.40 credits. How much did he borrow?
explanation: The rice used to repay the loan is worth $\frac34\times\frac25=\frac3{10}$ of the loan. So seven tenths is still owed. Seven tenths is 8.40; one tenth is 1.20, and the whole loan is 12.

wp22-p27.stem: A tutor changes every score by multiplying it by \frac35 and then adding 24. June’s score goes down. Which of the following is necessarily true of her original score?
wp22-p27.stemRich: A tutor changes every score by multiplying it by $\frac35$ and then adding 24. June’s score goes down. Which of the following is necessarily true of her original score?
wp22-p27.stemHtml: A tutor changes every score by multiplying it by and then adding 24. June’s score goes down. Which of the following is necessarily true of her original score?
explanation: An unchanged score satisfies $\frac35x+24=x$. The missing two fifths must be 24, so x=60. Above 60, the amount removed exceeds 24 and the score goes down. Below 60, the added 24 more than makes up for the reduction.
wp22-p27.answerHtml: An unchanged score satisfies . The missing two fifths must be 24, so x=60. Above 60, the amount removed exceeds 24 and the score goes down. Below 60, the added 24 more than makes up for the reduction.

methods.title: Find the point where nothing changes
steps: An unchanged score satisfies $\frac35x+24=x$. The missing two fifths must be 24, so x=60. Above 60, the amount removed exceeds 24 and the score goes down. Below 60, the added 24 more than makes up for the reduction.

methods.title: Use an inequality
steps: A decrease means $\frac35x+24<x$. Subtract three fifths of x to get $24<\frac25x$. Multiply by the positive number five halves: x>60. At 60 the score stays the same, so the boundary itself is not included.

wp22-p28.stem: A box of beads is split into two piles. One quarter of the first pile is used, and one sixth of the second pile is used. The two remaining piles contain 18 and 25 beads, in an unknown order. How many beads were in the box?
wp22-p28.stemRich: A box of beads is split into two piles. One quarter of the first pile is used, and one sixth of the second pile is used. The two remaining piles contain 18 and 25 beads, in an unknown order. How many beads were in the box?
wp22-p28.stemHtml: A box of beads is split into two piles. One quarter of the first pile is used, and one sixth of the second pile is used. The two remaining piles contain 18 and 25 beads, in an unknown order. How many beads were in the box?
explanation: The first remainder is three quarters of its starting pile, so it must be a multiple of 3. That must be 18, not 25. Its starting size was 18:3×4=24. The second remainder is five sixths, so it began with 25:5×6=30. Total: 54.
wp22-p28.answerHtml: The first remainder is three quarters of its starting pile, so it must be a multiple of 3. That must be 18, not 25. Its starting size was 18:3×4=24. The second remainder is five sixths, so it began with 25:5×6=30. Total: 54.

methods.title: Use whole-number requirements
steps: The first remainder is three quarters of its starting pile, so it must be a multiple of 3. That must be 18, not 25. Its starting size was 18:3×4=24. The second remainder is five sixths, so it began with 25:5×6=30. Total: 54.

methods.title: Test the two assignments
steps: If 18 belongs to the first pile, the originals are 24 and 30, both whole numbers. If 25 belongs to the first pile, it would have started with $\frac{100}{3}$ beads, which is impossible. Only the first assignment works.

wp22-p30.stem: There are n players in a room, where n\ge5. Each starts with 2n tokens. One at a time, a player gives 2 tokens to every player still in the room and leaves. How many tokens does the fifth player have when leaving?
wp22-p30.stemRich: There are $n$ players in a room, where $n\ge5$. Each starts with $2n$ tokens. One at a time, a player gives 2 tokens to every player still in the room and leaves. How many tokens does the fifth player have when leaving?
wp22-p30.stemHtml: There are players in a room, where . Each starts with tokens. One at a time, a player gives 2 tokens to every player still in the room and leaves. How many tokens does the fifth player have when leaving?
explanation: Before leaving, the fifth player receives two tokens from each of the first four leavers: eight tokens. They then give two tokens to each of the n−5 players who remain. Starting with 2n gives 2n+8−2(n−5)=18.
wp22-p30.answerHtml: Before leaving, the fifth player receives two tokens from each of the first four leavers: eight tokens. They then give two tokens to each of the n−5 players who remain. Starting with 2n gives 2n+8−2(n−5)=18.

methods.title: Follow the fifth player
steps: Before leaving, the fifth player receives two tokens from each of the first four leavers: eight tokens. They then give two tokens to each of the n−5 players who remain. Starting with 2n gives 2n+8−2(n−5)=18.

methods.title: Choose a small legal room

wp22-p34.stem: Four years ago, a tree was 3 times as old as a shrub. Today the tree is twice as old as the shrub. How old is the shrub today?
wp22-p34.stemRich: Four years ago, a tree was 3 times as old as a shrub. Today the tree is twice as old as the shrub. How old is the shrub today?
wp22-p34.stemHtml: Four years ago, a tree was 3 times as old as a shrub. Today the tree is twice as old as the shrub. How old is the shrub today?
explanation: Let the shrub be s years old now, so the tree is 2s. Four years ago their ages were s−4 and 2s−4. The earlier comparison gives 2s−4=3(s−4), so s=8.
wp22-p34.answerHtml: Let the shrub be s years old now, so the tree is 2s. Four years ago their ages were s−4 and 2s−4. The earlier comparison gives 2s−4=3(s−4), so s=8.

methods.title: Use the unchanged age gap
steps: Four years ago, write the ages as 3k and k. Today they are 3k+4 and k+4. For the first to be twice the second, 3k+4=2k+8, so k=4. The shrub’s current age is k+4=8.

wp22-g029.stemRich: Six trays hold 42 biscuits. At the same number per tray, how many biscuits fit on 15 trays?
wp22-g029.stemHtml: Six trays hold 42 biscuits. At the same number per tray, how many biscuits fit on 15 trays?
explanation: Forty-two biscuits are shared equally among six trays, so each tray holds seven. Fifteen trays hold fifteen groups of seven, which is 105. Finding the value for one tray is a dependable route whenever a direct multiplier is not immediately comfortable.

methods.title: Scale the whole arrangement
steps: Fifteen trays are two and a half times six trays. Multiply forty-two by the same factor: twice forty-two is eighty-four, and half of forty-two is twenty-one. Together they make 105. We change both quantities by the same factor because the capacity of each tray stays fixed.

wp22-g030.stem: At a constant pace, a student completes 12 exercises in 8 minutes. How many exercises does she complete in 14 minutes?

explanation: Twelve exercises in eight minutes means three exercises in two minutes: divide both numbers by four. methods.title: Use a proportion
steps: Write $\frac{12}{8}=\frac{x}{14}$, keeping exercises above minutes on both sides. Cross multiplication gives 8x=168, so x=21. Equivalently calculate $12\times\frac{14}{8}$ and cancel factors before multiplying. The equal ratios come from the constant pace.

wp22-g032.stemRich: A bakery sells a tart for 58 credits. Making it uses 300 g of pastry at 6 credits per 100 g, 200 g of filling at 9 credits per 100 g, and 4 berries at half a credit each. Ignoring other costs, what is the selling price minus ingredient cost?
wp22-g032.stemHtml: A bakery sells a tart for 58 credits. Making it uses 300 g of pastry at 6 credits per 100 g, 200 g of filling at 9 credits per 100 g, and 4 berries at half a credit each. Ignoring other costs, what is the selling price minus ingredient cost?

wp22-g033.stemHtml: Hire company A charges 3 credits for every minute or part of a minute. Company B charges 14 credits for every 5-minute block or part of a block. What is the difference between the charges for an 11.5-minute hire?
explanation: Company A charges for twelve minutes because the final half-minute starts a new minute. Its charge is twelve times three, or thirty-six. Company B charges for three five-minute blocks, because two blocks cover only ten minutes. Its charge is three times fourteen, or forty-two.

wp22-g035.stem: In a class, boys make up \frac38 of all students. Which could be the difference between the numbers of girls and boys?
wp22-g035.stemRich: In a class, boys make up $\frac38$ of all students. Which could be the difference between the numbers of girls and boys?
wp22-g035.stemHtml: In a class, boys make up of all students. Which could be the difference between the numbers of girls and boys?
explanation: Boys occupy three parts out of eight. Girls occupy the remaining five. The difference is two parts, so it must be twice a whole-number unit count and so even. Only eighteen among the choices is even.

To confirm that eighteen is possible, take nine students per part. Then there are twenty-seven boys and forty-five girls, a difference of eighteen, and twenty-seven is three eighths of the total seventy-two.

wp22-g038.stem: A center plans to put the same number of students in each of 6 rooms. One room becomes a storeroom, so each of the 5 remaining rooms must hold 3 more students. How many students per room were originally planned?

wp22-g038.stemHtml: A center plans to put the same number of students in each of 6 rooms. One room becomes a storeroom, so each of the 5 remaining rooms must hold 3 more students. How many students per room were originally planned?
explanation: Let x be the originally planned number in each room. The original total is 6x. With five rooms, each holds x+3, so the total is also 5(x+3). Set them equal because moving the students does not change how many there are.

wp22-g043.stemRich: A selection program starts with 144 applicants. At the end of each round, $\frac56$ of the applicants who began that round remain. How many remain after two rounds?
wp22-g043.stemHtml: A selection program starts with 144 applicants. At the end of each round, of the applicants who began that round remain. How many remain after two rounds?
explanation: In round one, one sixth of 144 is twenty-four, so five sixths is 120. Those 120 start round two. One sixth of 120 is twenty, so five sixths is one hundred.
The second fraction acts on 120, not again on 144. Each round removes the same fraction of a changing group, so the numbers removed are twenty-four and twenty rather than two identical amounts.

wp22-g045.stem: A grower sends 4 times as many pears to shops as to a market. One quarter of the shop pears and one third of the market pears are rejected. What fraction of all the pears is rejected?
wp22-g045.stemRich: A grower sends 4 times as many pears to shops as to a market. One quarter of the shop pears and one third of the market pears are rejected. What fraction of all the pears is rejected?
wp22-g045.stemHtml: A grower sends 4 times as many pears to shops as to a market. One quarter of the shop pears and one third of the market pears are rejected. What fraction of all the pears is rejected?
explanation: We can choose the scale because only a fraction is requested. Use three market pears and twelve shop pears. The 4:1 ratio holds, and both rejection fractions now produce whole pears.

The shops reject one quarter of twelve, or three. The market rejects one third of three, or one. Four out of the fifteen total pears are rejected. Choosing one market pear would create fractional pears in the working; using three keeps the counting concrete.

We can choose the scale because only a fraction is requested. Use three market pears and twelve shop pears. The 4:1 ratio holds, and both rejection fractions now produce whole pears.

steps: We can choose the scale because only a fraction is requested. Use three market pears and twelve shop pears. The 4:1 ratio holds, and both rejection fractions now produce whole pears.

methods.title: Bound the overall rejection rate
steps: The two group rates are one quarter and one third. Since both groups have positive size, their combined rejection fraction must lie strictly between those rates. It is not their unweighted average because the groups have different sizes.

One fifth is below both rates; one third is the upper endpoint and cannot be reached with the lower-rate group present; five twelfths is above both. Only four fifteenths is strictly between one quarter and one third. The answer choices let a range argument finish the question.

wp22-g046.stem: A maker owns red and blue tiles. She gives away \frac14 of the red tiles and \frac16 of the blue tiles, always giving whole tiles. The remaining color counts are 9 and 20, in an unknown order. How many tiles did she own originally?
wp22-g046.stemRich: A maker owns red and blue tiles. She gives away $\frac14$ of the red tiles and $\frac16$ of the blue tiles, always giving whole tiles. The remaining color counts are 9 and 20, in an unknown order. How many tiles did she own originally?
wp22-g046.stemHtml: A maker owns red and blue tiles. She gives away of the red tiles and of the blue tiles, always giving whole tiles. The remaining color counts are 9 and 20, in an unknown order. How many tiles did she own originally?
explanation: The red remainder is three quarters of its original count, so it must consist of three equal whole-number units. Nine can be divided into three such units; twenty cannot. Thus nine is the red remainder. Each quarter contained three tiles, making twelve red tiles originally.

The twenty blue tiles are five sixths of the original blue count. One sixth is four tiles, so the original blue count was twenty-four. Add twelve and twenty-four to get thirty-six. The whole-tile condition resolves the unknown order of the two remainders.
wp22-g046.answerHtml:
The red remainder is three quarters of its original count, so it must consist of three equal whole-number units. Nine can be divided into three such units; twenty cannot. Thus nine is the red remainder. Each quarter contained three tiles, making twelve red tiles originally.

The twenty blue tiles are five sixths of the original blue count. One sixth is four tiles, so the original blue count was twenty-four. Add twelve and twenty-four to get thirty-six. The whole-tile condition resolves the unknown order of the two remainders.

methods.title: Use a safe size estimate
steps: Twenty-nine tiles remain. Each original group kept between three quarters and five sixths, so the original combined total must be between $29:\frac56=34.8$ and $29:\frac34=38\frac23$. Only thirty-six among the choices fits.

This bound is enough to select the answer without assigning the colours. It uses the fact that both retained fractions are fairly close to one, so doubling or tripling the remaining total would be much too large.

wp22-g047.stem: Club A has 3 times as many members as Club B. Three members move from A to B. Afterwards B has half as many members as A. How many members do the clubs have altogether?
wp22-g047.stemRich: Club A has 3 times as many members as Club B. Three members move from A to B. Afterwards B has half as many members as A. How many members do the clubs have altogether?
wp22-g047.stemHtml: Club A has 3 times as many members as Club B. Three members move from A to B. Afterwards B has half as many members as A. How many members do the clubs have altogether?
explanation: Let B start with b members, so A starts with 3b. After the move, B has b+3 and A has 3b−3. B is then half of A, giving 2(b+3)=3b−3.
Solve: 2b+6=3b−3, so b=9. The original total was four b, or thirty-six. The transfer changes the distribution but keeps that total fixed.
wp22-g047.answerHtml:
Let B start with b members, so A starts with 3b. After the move, B has b+3 and A has 3b−3. B is then half of A, giving 2(b+3)=3b−3.

Solve: 2b+6=3b−3, so b=9. The original total was four b, or thirty-six. The transfer changes the distribution but keeps that total fixed.

steps: Let B start with b members, so A starts with 3b. After the move, B has b+3 and A has 3b−3. B is then half of A, giving 2(b+3)=3b−3.
Solve: 2b+6=3b−3, so b=9. The original total was four b, or thirty-six. The transfer changes the distribution but keeps that total fixed.

methods.title: Use the total’s divisibility
steps: The original 3:1 ratio makes the total a multiple of four. The final 2:1 ratio makes the same total a multiple of three. It must so be divisible by both four and three.

Of the answer choices, only thirty-six has both properties. Confirm with the actual groups: twenty-seven and nine become twenty-four and twelve. The shortcut uses the options to identify the only possible total, and the check shows it really works.

wp22-g048.stem: A freelancer receives a fixed monthly payment plus the same extra amount for each completed task. Ten tasks bring 320 credits; six tasks bring 208 credits. What is the payment per task?
wp22-g048.stemRich: A freelancer receives a fixed monthly payment plus the same extra amount for each completed task. Ten tasks bring 320 credits; six tasks bring 208 credits. What is the payment per task?
wp22-g048.stemHtml: A freelancer receives a fixed monthly payment plus the same extra amount for each completed task. Ten tasks bring 320 credits; six tasks bring 208 credits. What is the payment per task?
explanation: The fixed payment is the same in both months. The difference in money so comes entirely from the four extra tasks. The difference is 320−208=112 credits. Divide by four to get twenty-eight per task.
This is often the quickest route: compare what changed and cancel what stayed the same. We do not need the fixed monthly payment to answer the question, although we can find it afterwards as a check.
wp22-g048.answerHtml:
The fixed payment is the same in both months. The difference in money so comes entirely from the four extra tasks. The difference is 320−208=112 credits. Divide by four to get twenty-eight per task.

wp22-g049.stem: Eight large blocks and twelve small blocks weigh 1,000 g altogether. All large blocks have equal weight, and all small blocks have equal weight. How much do ten large and fifteen small blocks weigh?
wp22-g049.stemRich: Eight large blocks and twelve small blocks weigh 1,000 g altogether. All large blocks have equal weight, and all small blocks have equal weight. How much do ten large and fifteen small blocks weigh?
wp22-g049.stemHtml: Eight large blocks and twelve small blocks weigh 1,000 g altogether. All large blocks have equal weight, and all small blocks have equal weight. How much do ten large and fifteen small blocks weigh?
explanation: Eight becomes ten by multiplying by five quarters. Twelve becomes fifteen by exactly the same factor. Because every part of the collection is scaled equally, the combined weight is scaled by five quarters too.

One quarter of one thousand is 250. Add that quarter to the original thousand to get 1,250 g. We do not need to find the separate weights of the two types of block, which the single equation would not determine.

The requested ratio is thirty-nine divided by twenty-one. Divide both by three to get thirteen sevenths. Reversing the transfer must change both people’s counts; adding nine only to Ari would incorrectly increase the total.

wp23-g054.stemRich: In a survey, 55% of people do not own a bicycle. Of the bicycle owners, 40% own an electric bicycle and the rest own only ordinary bicycles. What percentage of all surveyed people own only ordinary bicycles?
wp23-g054.stemHtml: In a survey, 55% of people do not own a bicycle. Of the bicycle owners, 40% own an electric bicycle and the rest own only ordinary bicycles. What percentage of all surveyed people own only ordinary bicycles?
explanation: Use one hundred people to represent the whole survey. Fifty-five do not own a bicycle, leaving forty-five owners. Forty percent of those forty-five have an electric bicycle: ten percent is four and a half, so forty percent is eighteen.

Ordinary-only owners are the remaining forty-five minus eighteen, or twenty-seven. Since our original sample represents one hundred, twenty-seven people correspond to 27% of the full survey. The forty percent in the question belongs to the smaller forty-five-person group, not to the original hundred.
wp23-g054.answerHtml:
Use one hundred people to represent the whole survey. Fifty-five do not own a bicycle, leaving forty-five owners. Forty percent of those forty-five have an electric bicycle: ten percent is four and a half, so forty percent is eighteen.

Ordinary-only owners are the remaining forty-five minus eighteen, or twenty-seven. Since our original sample represents one hundred, twenty-seven people correspond to 27% of the full survey. wp23-g057.stemRich: A battery has used 72.5% of its original charge. What fraction remains?
wp23-g057.stemHtml: A battery has used 72.5% of its original charge. What fraction remains?
explanation: The remaining charge is 100%−72.5%=27.5%. Write that as 27.5 over 100. Multiply top and bottom by two to remove the decimal: 55 over 200. Reducing by five gives eleven fortieths.
wp23-g057.answerHtml: The remaining charge is 100%−72.5%=27.5%. Write that as 27.5 over 100. Multiply top and bottom by two to remove the decimal: 55 over 200. Reducing by five gives eleven fortieths.

methods.title: Convert the remaining percentage
steps: The remaining charge is 100%−72.5%=27.5%. Write that as 27.5 over 100. Multiply top and bottom by two to remove the decimal: 55 over 200. Reducing by five gives eleven fortieths.

methods.title: Build from familiar fractions
steps: One fortieth is 2.5%, since one twentieth is 5% and halving gives one fortieth. Eleven copies of 2.5% make 27.5%, so eleven fortieths is the answer.
You can also start from one quarter, or ten fortieths, which is 25%. The remaining charge is 2.5 percentage points above that, exactly one more fortieth.

wp23-g058.stemHtml: A display item originally costs 760 credits. Its price is reduced by 75%. What is the new price?
explanation: A 75% reduction leaves 25% of the original price. Twenty-five percent is one quarter. Divide 760 by four: 760 is 720 plus forty, whose quarters are 180 and ten. The final price is 190.
wp23-g058.answerHtml: A 75% reduction leaves 25% of the original price. Twenty-five percent is one quarter. Divide 760 by four: 760 is 720 plus forty, whose quarters are 180 and ten. The final price is 190.

methods.title: Calculate what remains directly
steps: A 75% reduction leaves 25% of the original price. Twenty-five percent is one quarter. Divide 760 by four: 760 is 720 plus forty, whose quarters are 180 and ten. The final price is 190.

methods.title: Calculate and subtract the reduction
steps: Three quarters of 760 is 570, since one quarter is 190 and three quarters is three times that. Subtract the reduction: 760−570=190. This route is correct but takes an extra step compared with finding the complementary 25% directly.

We do not need a decimal for one eleventh. The money increase stays the same, but its percentage shrinks when measured against the larger starting fee.

wp23-g060.stem: A player gives away 25% of her points. She then receives a bonus equal to 30% of the points she has left. Compared with her original score, what is her final score?
wp23-g060.stemRich: A player gives away 25% of her points. She then receives a bonus equal to 30% of the points she has left. Compared with her original score, what is her final score?
wp23-g060.stemHtml: A player gives away 25% of her points. She then receives a bonus equal to 30% of the points she has left. Compared with her original score, what is her final score?
explanation: Represent the original score by one hundred. Giving away twenty-five percent leaves seventy-five. The bonus is thirty percent of those seventy-five points: ten percent is seven and a half, so the bonus is twenty-two and a half.

The final score is seventy-five plus twenty-two and a half, or 97.5. That is 2.5 below the original hundred, so it is a 2.5% decrease. The later thirty-percent bonus uses the reduced score, which is why subtracting twenty-five from thirty gives the wrong result.
wp23-g060.answerHtml:
Represent the original score by one hundred. Giving away twenty-five percent leaves seventy-five. The bonus is thirty percent of those seventy-five points: ten percent is seven and a half, so the bonus is twenty-two and a half.

The final score is seventy-five plus twenty-two and a half, or 97.5. That is 2.5 below the original hundred, so it is a 2.5% decrease. The later thirty-percent bonus uses the reduced score, which is why subtracting twenty-five from thirty gives the wrong result.

methods.title: Use one hundred starting points
steps: Represent the original score by one hundred. Giving away twenty-five percent leaves seventy-five. The bonus is thirty percent of those seventy-five points: ten percent is seven and a half, so the bonus is twenty-two and a half.

The final score is seventy-five plus twenty-two and a half, or 97.5. That is 2.5 below the original hundred, so it is a 2.5% decrease. The later thirty-percent bonus uses the reduced score, which is why subtracting twenty-five from thirty gives the wrong result.

methods.title: Use successive multipliers
steps: Keeping 75% multiplies the original score x by 0.75. Adding 30% of the new score multiplies that result by 1.30. Together the factor is 0.75×1.30=0.975. Thus the final score is 97.5% of x, which is 2.5% below x.
Written as fractions, the factors are $\frac34$ and $\frac{13}{10}$, whose product is $\frac{39}{40}$. One fortieth has been lost, and one fortieth is 2.5%.

wp23-g061.stem: Rae earns 20% more than Sol. Tia earns 16\frac23% less than Rae. What is Tia’s wage divided by Sol’s wage?
wp23-g061.stemRich: Rae earns 20% more than Sol. Tia earns $16\frac23$% less than Rae. What is Tia’s wage divided by Sol’s wage?
wp23-g061.stemHtml: Rae earns 20% more than Sol. Tia earns % less than Rae. What is Tia’s wage divided by Sol’s wage?
explanation: Give Sol a wage of one hundred units. Rae earns 120. Sixteen and two thirds percent is one sixth. One sixth of 120 is twenty, so Tia earns 120−20=100. Her wage divided by Sol’s is one.
wp23-g061.answerHtml: Give Sol a wage of one hundred units. Rae earns 120. Sixteen and two thirds percent is one sixth. One sixth of 120 is twenty, so Tia earns 120−20=100. Her wage divided by Sol’s is one.

methods.title: Use a base of one hundred
steps: Give Sol a wage of one hundred units. Rae earns 120. Sixteen and two thirds percent is one sixth. One sixth of 120 is twenty, so Tia earns 120−20=100. Her wage divided by Sol’s is one.

methods.title: Recognise reciprocal changes
steps: A twenty-percent increase multiplies by $\frac65$. A one-sixth reduction keeps $\frac56$. These factors are reciprocals, so their product is one.

More generally, adding one nth of an amount creates n+1 equal original pieces. Removing one out of those n+1 pieces brings us back to the original. That is why a one-fifth rise and a one-sixth fall cancel even though their percentage figures differ.

wp23-g062.stem: 50% of 15% of x equals 12. What is 22.5% of x?
wp23-g062.stemRich: 50% of 15% of x equals 12. What is 22.5% of x?
wp23-g062.stemHtml: 50% of 15% of x equals 12. What is 22.5% of x?
explanation: Half of fifteen percent is 7.5%. So 7.5% of x is twelve. The requested 22.5% is three times 7.5%, so the corresponding amount is three times twelve, or thirty-six. There is no need to find the full x.
wp23-g062.answerHtml: Half of fifteen percent is 7.5%. So 7.5% of x is twelve. The requested 22.5% is three times 7.5%, so the corresponding amount is three times twelve, or thirty-six. There is no need to find the full x.

methods.title: Compare the requested percentage with the given one
steps: Half of fifteen percent is 7.5%. So 7.5% of x is twelve. The requested 22.5% is three times 7.5%, so the corresponding amount is three times twelve, or thirty-six. There is no need to find the full x.

methods.title: Find x using fractions
steps: Fifty percent of fifteen percent is $\frac12\times\frac3{20}=\frac3{40}$. If three fortieths of x is twelve, one fortieth is four and x=160. Then 22.5% is nine fortieths, giving 9×4=36.

methods.title: Swap percentage factors when that is easier
steps: Fifty percent of fifteen has the same numerical value as fifteen percent of fifty. Both are the product 50×15 divided by one hundred. Here half of fifteen is easier to see, so we use that order. This is the same useful swap that turns 8% of 25 into 25% of 8.

wp23-g063.stem: For x>0, which expression is not equal to 15% of 4x?
wp23-g063.stemRich: For $x>0$, which expression is not equal to 15% of 4x?
wp23-g063.stemHtml: For , which expression is not equal to 15% of 4x?
explanation: The target is 15×4x divided by one hundred, or 60x divided by one hundred. The choices 10% of 6x, 60% of x, and 5% of 12x all produce that same numerator, 60x.

Thirty percent of 4x produces 120x, twice the target. Because x is positive, these values are different. There is no need to reduce every fraction separately: their denominator of one hundred is already common.

steps: The target is 15×4x divided by one hundred, or 60x divided by one hundred. The choices 10% of 6x, 60% of x, and 5% of 12x all produce that same numerator, 60x.

Thirty percent of 4x produces 120x, twice the target. Because x is positive, these values are different. There is no need to reduce every fraction separately: their denominator of one hundred is already common.

methods.title: Keep the product unchanged by opposite scaling
steps: If we triple the base from 4x to 12x, we must divide the percentage by three, from fifteen to five, to keep the same result. If we reduce the base to x, we multiply the percentage by four, to sixty. But doubling the percentage to thirty while leaving the base at 4x doubles the result.

steps: Set x=10. The target is fifteen percent of forty, or six. The three equivalent choices each also give six, while thirty percent of forty gives twelve. This numerical check eliminates the one expression that is not equivalent.

wp23-g064.stemHtml: A workshop uses 80% of its timber on Monday and all the rest on Tuesday. Monday’s use is 36 planks greater than Tuesday’s. How many planks are used on Tuesday?

steps: The use ratio is 80:20=4:1. The three-part difference equals thirty-six, so one part is twelve. Tuesday is that one part. A check gives forty-eight on Monday and twelve on Tuesday, a difference of thirty-six.

wp23-g065.stem: At the end of each hour, 20% of the water then in a tank is removed. After two hours, 128 liters remain. How many liters were there at the start?
wp23-g065.stemRich: At the end of each hour, 20% of the water then in a tank is removed. After two hours, 128 liters remain. How many liters were there at the start?
wp23-g065.stemHtml: At the end of each hour, 20% of the water then in a tank is removed. After two hours, 128 liters remain. How many liters were there at the start?
explanation: Each removal leaves eighty percent. After two removals, the retained fraction is 0.8×0.8=0.64, or sixty-four percent of the original. The actual 128 litres correspond to that sixty-four percent. Each percent is two litres, making the original hundred percent equal to two hundred litres.
Here one hundred is a percentage scale, not an assumed starting number of litres. A final amount is already supplied, so the scale has to be matched to that real amount.
wp23-g065.answerHtml:
Each removal leaves eighty percent. After two removals, the retained fraction is 0.8×0.8=0.64, or sixty-four percent of the original. The actual 128 litres correspond to that sixty-four percent. Each percent is two litres, making the original hundred percent equal to two hundred litres.

Here one hundred is a percentage scale, not an assumed starting number of litres. A final amount is already supplied, so the scale has to be matched to that real amount.

methods.title: Find the fraction retained, then restore the scale
steps: Each removal leaves eighty percent. After two removals, the retained fraction is 0.8×0.8=0.64, or sixty-four percent of the original. The actual 128 litres correspond to that sixty-four percent. Each percent is two litres, making the original hundred percent equal to two hundred litres.
Here one hundred is a percentage scale, not an assumed starting number of litres. A final amount is already supplied, so the scale has to be matched to that real amount.

methods.title: Work backwards one hour at a time
steps: If 128 litres are the eighty percent left at the second removal, the amount just before it was 128:0.8=160. Undo the first removal in the same way: 160:0.8=200. Reversing a twenty-percent loss means dividing by 0.8, not adding twenty percent.

methods.title: Test the offered original amount
steps: Start with two hundred. After the first removal, 160 remain; after the second, 128 remain. This direct replay confirms that two hundred satisfies the full story.

wp24-p01.stem: At a fair, 150 different people each win one prize. Of the winners, 65% live nearby and 55% arrived by train. What is the minimum number who both live nearby and arrived by train?
wp24-p01.stemRich: At a fair, 150 different people each win one prize. Of the winners, 65% live nearby and 55% arrived by train. What is the minimum number who both live nearby and arrived by train?
wp24-p01.stemHtml: At a fair, 150 different people each win one prize. Of the winners, 65% live nearby and 55% arrived by train. What is the minimum number who both live nearby and arrived by train?
explanation: The two group sizes add to 65%+55%=120% of all winners. Only 100% distinct people are available, so at least 20% were counted twice. Twenty percent of 150 is 30.
wp24-p01.answerHtml: The two group sizes add to 65%+55%=120% of all winners. Only 100% distinct people are available, so at least 20% were counted twice. Twenty percent of 150 is 30.

methods.title: Count the unavoidable overlap
steps: The two group sizes add to 65%+55%=120% of all winners. Only 100% distinct people are available, so at least 20% were counted twice. Twenty percent of 150 is 30.

methods.title: Fill the outside space first
steps: At most 35% do not live nearby. Even if all of them arrived by train, the train group still needs another 55%−35%=20% from the nearby group. That is thirty people. This arrangement is possible, so thirty is the true minimum.

wp24-g075.stemHtml: A class has 48 students. Twenty-one work in the greenhouse and eleven work in the orchard. Which could be the number who work in neither place?

So the neither count ranges from sixteen to twenty-seven. Eighteen is the only listed value inside this range. It can occur when the overlap is two: the union is 21+11−2=30, leaving eighteen.

wp24-g077.stem: At lunch, \frac25 of the staff choose soup, \frac14 choose salad, and \frac1{10} choose both. Exactly 8 people choose both. How many choose neither?
wp24-g077.stemRich: At lunch, $\frac25$ of the staff choose soup, $\frac14$ choose salad, and $\frac1{10}$ choose both. Exactly 8 people choose both. How many choose neither?
wp24-g077.stemHtml: At lunch, of the staff choose soup, choose salad, and choose both. Exactly 8 people choose both. How many choose neither?
explanation: One tenth of the staff equals eight, so the full staff total is eighty. Soup is two fifths of eighty, or thirty-two; salad is one quarter, or twenty. Their union is 32+20−8=44. The remaining thirty-six choose neither.
Finding the total first turns the later overlap work into whole-number arithmetic. This can be simpler than subtracting several fractions and then converting the answer.
wp24-g077.answerHtml:
One tenth of the staff equals eight, so the full staff total is eighty. Soup is two fifths of eighty, or thirty-two; salad is one quarter, or twenty. Their union is 32+20−8=44. The remaining thirty-six choose neither.

Finding the total first turns the later overlap work into whole-number arithmetic. This can be simpler than subtracting several fractions and then converting the answer.

wp26-g093.stem: A robot packs x samples in y minutes at a constant rate, where x and y are positive. How many samples will it pack in 4y minutes if its rate becomes 3 times as great?
wp26-g093.stemRich: A robot packs x samples in y minutes at a constant rate, where x and y are positive. How many samples will it pack in 4y minutes if its rate becomes 3 times as great?
wp26-g093.stemHtml: A robot packs x samples in y minutes at a constant rate, where x and y are positive. How many samples will it pack in 4y minutes if its rate becomes 3 times as great?
explanation: The robot originally packs x samples in y minutes. First keep those y minutes unchanged and increase only the rate. Three times the rate means three times as many samples in the same time, so its new output is 3x samples in y minutes.

Now keep that new rate and give the robot four times as long: 4y minutes instead of y. Each block of y minutes contributes another 3x samples. Four such blocks produce 12x samples. Both changes increase the output, so we multiply by both factors. We do not add three and four.

There are three useful relationships hiding in this example. With time fixed, increasing the rate increases the work by the same factor. With rate fixed, increasing the time increases the work by the same factor. With the amount of work fixed, increasing the rate reduces the time by the reciprocal factor. That last relationship is different because we are no longer asking for more work. We are finishing the same job sooner.

For a numerical picture, imagine x is six and y is two. The old robot packs six samples in two minutes. The faster robot packs eighteen in two minutes, and seventy-two in eight minutes. Seventy-two is twelve times six, just as the expression 12x predicts. These convenient values help us picture the relationship; the factor argument works for every positive x and y.

wp26-g095.stem: One inlet fills a tank in 8 hours. An identical inlet has the same rate. A drain empties a full tank in 12 hours. Starting with an empty tank at 09:00, both inlets and the drain run continuously. At what time is the tank full?
wp26-g095.stemRich: One inlet fills a tank in 8 hours. An identical inlet has the same rate. A drain empties a full tank in 12 hours. Starting with an empty tank at 09:00, both inlets and the drain run continuously. At what time is the tank full?
wp26-g095.stemHtml: One inlet fills a tank in 8 hours. An identical inlet has the same rate. A drain empties a full tank in 12 hours. Starting with an empty tank at 09:00, both inlets and the drain run continuously. At what time is the tank full?
explanation: Each inlet adds $\frac18$ of a tank per hour. The second inlet adds another eighth. The drain removes $\frac1{12}$ of a tank per hour, so its contribution has a minus sign. The net rate is $\frac18+\frac18-\frac1{12}=\frac16$ of a tank per hour.

At one sixth of a tank each hour, filling one tank takes six hours. Starting at nine in the morning, six hours later is three in the afternoon, or 15:00. Notice that the requested answer is a clock time. Six hours is the duration, which must still be added to the starting time.

We cannot add eight, eight and twelve. Those are completion times for separate devices, and one device is working against the other two. Converting each device to a fraction of a tank per hour gives quantities that can sensibly be combined.

wp26-g096.stem: Machine A fills one order in 4 hours, while machine B fills the same order in 6 hours. If they work together at their usual constant rates, how many minutes do they need for one order?
wp26-g096.stemRich: Machine A fills one order in 4 hours, while machine B fills the same order in 6 hours. If they work together at their usual constant rates, how many minutes do they need for one order?
wp26-g096.stemHtml: Machine A fills one order in 4 hours, while machine B fills the same order in 6 hours. If they work together at their usual constant rates, how many minutes do they need for one order?
explanation: Use twelve hours, a common multiple of four and six. In twelve hours A completes three orders and B completes two. Together that is five orders in twelve hours. The time remains twelve hours: the machines are working alongside one another, so we add the orders, not the clock times.

One order so takes $\frac{12}{5}$ hours. To turn hours into minutes, multiply by sixty. It is convenient to divide sixty by five first: twelve times twelve is 144 minutes. The fraction of an hour is not a decimal number of minutes.

methods.title: Add the hourly rates
steps: The rates are $\frac14$ and $\frac16$ of an order per hour. Their sum is $\frac5{12}$. Time is one order divided by this rate, giving $\frac{12}{5}$ hours, again 144 minutes.

As a quick sense check, working together must take less than A’s four hours. The answer is two hours twenty-four minutes, which does. Two machines of A’s speed would take two hours; replacing one with the slower B must take longer than two hours. This places the correct time between two and four hours.

wp26-g098.stem: Five identical workers make 30 display boards in 4 hours. How many hours do eight such workers need to make 72 display boards?
wp26-g098.stemRich: Five identical workers make 30 display boards in 4 hours. How many hours do eight such workers need to make 72 display boards?
wp26-g098.stemHtml: Five identical workers make 30 display boards in 4 hours. How many hours do eight such workers need to make 72 display boards?
explanation: We have three quantities to organise: workers, boards, and hours. Put them in that order in two rows. The first row says five workers make thirty boards in four hours. The second says eight workers make seventy-two boards in an unknown number of hours. Every worker has the same constant rate, so changing the team size changes the team’s rate in direct proportion.

Start with the four hours in the first row. If we keep the same five workers but change the work from thirty boards to seventy-two, the time increases by the factor seventy-two divided by thirty. That is twelve fifths. The larger job would take forty-eight fifths of an hour with the original team. We do not have to turn this into a decimal.

Now increase the team from five to eight workers. The job has not changed during this second step. More workers finish that fixed job sooner, so multiply the time by five eighths. The fives cancel, and forty-eight divided by eight is six. Eight workers need six hours.

It helps to say the direction aloud before calculating: more boards means more time; more workers means less time. Both numbers increased, but they push the time in opposite directions. Simply multiplying by both increases would make the extra workers slow the job down, which cannot fit this model.

The order of these two adjustments does not affect the final result. We could first ask how long eight workers need for thirty boards, then enlarge that job to seventy-two boards. Multiplication lets us combine the same two factors in either order. Choosing the order that cancels cleanly keeps the arithmetic short.

methods.title: Scale the workload, then the team
steps: We have three quantities to organise: workers, boards, and hours. Put them in that order in two rows. The first row says five workers make thirty boards in four hours. The second says eight workers make seventy-two boards in an unknown number of hours. Every worker has the same constant rate, so changing the team size changes the team’s rate in direct proportion.

Start with the four hours in the first row. If we keep the same five workers but change the work from thirty boards to seventy-two, the time increases by the factor seventy-two divided by thirty. That is twelve fifths. The larger job would take forty-eight fifths of an hour with the original team. We do not have to turn this into a decimal.

Now increase the team from five to eight workers. The job has not changed during this second step. More workers finish that fixed job sooner, so multiply the time by five eighths. The fives cancel, and forty-eight divided by eight is six. Eight workers need six hours.

It helps to say the direction aloud before calculating: more boards means more time; more workers means less time. Both numbers increased, but they push the time in opposite directions. Multiplication lets us combine the same two factors in either order. Choosing the order that cancels cleanly keeps the arithmetic short.

methods.title: Use the workers–work–time table shortcut
steps: Here is the same relationship in a compact table calculation. Keep work in the middle column: workers, work, time. To find the missing time, multiply the old team size, the new amount of work, and the old time. Divide by the old amount of work and the new team size. For this question that is five times seventy-two times four, divided by thirty times eight.

The numerator uses three known entries that form a V across the two rows. The two remaining known entries form the denominator. This is the table shortcut often called the V method. Its value is that it packages the two scaling steps we have just explained into one calculation. We should still know which quantity is missing and keep the columns in a consistent order.

Cancel before multiplying. Five and thirty reduce to one and six. Seventy-two divided by six gives twelve. Four divided by eight gives one half. Twelve times one half is six. There is no need to multiply everything into a large numerator and denominator first.

If the unknown moved to the work column instead, we would rearrange the same relationship. For example, keeping eight workers and six hours gives thirty times eight times six, divided by five times four, or seventy-two boards. Drawing the same V without checking where the blank sits would be unsafe. The fixed rule underneath the shortcut is that output per worker per hour stays constant.

This is why the words identical and constant matter here. We can exchange five worker-hours for any other five worker-hours because each one produces the same amount. If workers had different rates, we would first express them in equivalent worker units or add their individual rates. The simple team-size table alone would not contain enough information.

methods.title: Count worker-hours
steps: Five workers each work four hours, giving twenty worker-hours. Those twenty worker-hours make thirty boards. Seventy-two boards are twelve fifths of thirty, so the larger job needs forty-eight worker-hours. Eight workers share those forty-eight hours of work, giving six clock hours.

A worker-hour is one worker working for one hour. It measures labour, not the time on the wall clock. Eight people working for six hours contribute forty-eight worker-hours even though only six hours pass. Keeping that distinction clear also helps with questions where the team changes partway through a job.

We can verify the answer using output per worker-hour. Thirty boards in twenty worker-hours is one and a half boards per worker-hour. Eight workers supply eight worker-hours in each clock hour, so their team makes twelve boards each hour. At twelve boards per hour, seventy-two boards take exactly six hours. This check follows the original description directly.

wp26-g101.stem: The combined rate of 3 high-speed scanners is twice the combined rate of 9 standard scanners. Scanners of the same type are identical. How many times as fast is one high-speed scanner as one standard scanner?

Divide by three: F=6S. We multiply the smaller team-rate expression by two to make an equality, rather than doubling the already larger side.

wp26-g102.stem: A machine adds 24 unfinished pieces to a queue each hour. A technician finishes 35 pieces every 75 minutes. There are initially 50 unfinished pieces. At these constant rates, how many unfinished pieces remain after 5 hours?
wp26-g102.stemRich: A machine adds 24 unfinished pieces to a queue each hour. A technician finishes 35 pieces every 75 minutes. There are initially 50 unfinished pieces. At these constant rates, how many unfinished pieces remain after 5 hours?
wp26-g102.stemHtml: A machine adds 24 unfinished pieces to a queue each hour. A technician finishes 35 pieces every 75 minutes. There are initially 50 unfinished pieces. At these constant rates, how many unfinished pieces remain after 5 hours?
explanation: The machine adds five groups of twenty-four, or 120 pieces. The technician’s rate is given for seventy-five minutes, so express the five-hour interval in minutes: five times sixty is three hundred minutes. That is four blocks of seventy-five minutes, during which the technician finishes four times thirty-five, or 140 pieces.

Start with the fifty already waiting, add the 120 arrivals, then remove the 140 finished pieces. The result is thirty. The initial queue is part of the calculation; subtracting the two outputs alone would only tell us how much the queue changes.

The queue shrinks by twenty pieces over the five hours and never runs out, so there is work available throughout. This matters because we assumed the technician could keep working at the stated rate. Here the final queue is still positive, and the constant net decrease makes that assumption consistent.

wp26-g103.stem: Cleaner A covers 360 m² in 3 hours. Cleaner B covers 40 m² in 2 hours. Working together at these constant rates, how many minutes do they need for 140 m²?
wp26-g103.stemRich: Cleaner A covers 360 m² in 3 hours. Cleaner B covers 40 m² in 2 hours. Working together at these constant rates, how many minutes do they need for 140 m²?
wp26-g103.stemHtml: Cleaner A covers 360 m² in 3 hours. Cleaner B covers 40 m² in 2 hours. Working together at these constant rates, how many minutes do they need for 140 m²?
explanation: In six hours A covers 720 square metres, while B covers 120. They so cover 840 square metres together in the same six hours. We add the areas because both cleaners work during that shared interval. We do not add the six hours to another six hours.

The requested area, 140 square metres, is one sixth of 840. With the team unchanged, the time is one sixth of six hours: one hour, or sixty minutes. Dividing both the work and the time by six is an equal-ratio step.

The requested area, 140 square metres, is one sixth of 840. With the team unchanged, the time is one sixth of six hours: one hour, or sixty minutes. Dividing both the work and the time by six is an equal-ratio step.

methods.title: Use hourly rates
steps: A covers 120 square metres per hour and B covers twenty. Together they cover 140 per hour, so the requested 140 takes exactly one hour. The question wants minutes, making the final answer sixty.

methods.title: Use bounds to select the only possible choice
steps: A alone would need seventy minutes for 140 square metres. With B helping, the answer must be less than seventy, eliminating seventy and ninety. Two cleaners as fast as A would need thirty-five minutes. But B is slower than A, so this team needs more than thirty-five minutes.

Of the four offered times, only sixty lies strictly between thirty-five and seventy. These bounds identify the correct choice without finding the exact combined rate. Saying merely that B helps a little would be less precise; the two strict bounds show exactly why the other answers cannot work.

wp26-g104.stem: Ava, Ben and Cleo each work at a constant rate. Together they complete a job in 8 hours. Ava and Ben together complete it in 16 hours. What fraction of the job does Cleo complete in one hour?
wp26-g104.stemRich: Ava, Ben and Cleo each work at a constant rate. Together they complete a job in 8 hours. Ava and Ben together complete it in 16 hours. What fraction of the job does Cleo complete in one hour?
wp26-g104.stemHtml: Ava, Ben and Cleo each work at a constant rate. Together they complete a job in 8 hours. Ava and Ben together complete it in 16 hours. What fraction of the job does Cleo complete in one hour?
explanation: We do not know Ava’s individual rate or Ben’s, and we do not need them. Treat Ava and Ben as one team. In sixteen hours that team completes one job. All three together would complete two jobs in sixteen hours, since they complete one every eight hours.

The difference must be Cleo’s contribution: one job in sixteen hours. In a single hour, Cleo completes one sixteenth of a job. This comparison uses the same time interval for both groups, so subtracting their outputs isolates the extra worker.
wp26-g104.answerHtml:
We do not know Ava’s individual rate or Ben’s, and we do not need them. Treat Ava and Ben as one team. In sixteen hours that team completes one job. All three together would complete two jobs in sixteen hours, since they complete one every eight hours.

The difference must be Cleo’s contribution: one job in sixteen hours. In a single hour, Cleo completes one sixteenth of a job. This comparison uses the same time interval for both groups, so subtracting their outputs isolates the extra worker.

methods.title: Treat the known pair as one team
steps: We do not know Ava’s individual rate or Ben’s, and we do not need them. Treat Ava and Ben as one team. In sixteen hours that team completes one job. All three together would complete two jobs in sixteen hours, since they complete one every eight hours.

The difference must be Cleo’s contribution: one job in sixteen hours. In a single hour, Cleo completes one sixteenth of a job. This comparison uses the same time interval for both groups, so subtracting their outputs isolates the extra worker.

methods.title: Look at the actual eight-hour job
steps: During the eight hours when all three finish the job, Ava and Ben complete half of it. They would need sixteen hours for the whole job. Cleo must complete the other half in those same eight hours. That means a whole job in sixteen hours, or one sixteenth per hour. This also shows that Cleo’s rate equals the combined rate of Ava and Ben.

methods.title: Subtract rates
steps: The all-three rate is $\frac18$ of a job per hour. The pair’s rate is $\frac1{16}$. Subtracting leaves $\frac18-\frac1{16}=\frac1{16}$ for Cleo. This is the same grouping argument written in one fraction calculation.

wp26-g105.stem: Eight identical makers can build one cabinet in 6 hours. Nine such makers can build one bench in 8 hours. How many makers are needed to finish one cabinet and one bench in 24 hours?
wp26-g105.stemRich: Eight identical makers can build one cabinet in 6 hours. Nine such makers can build one bench in 8 hours. How many makers are needed to finish one cabinet and one bench in 24 hours?
wp26-g105.stemHtml: Eight identical makers can build one cabinet in 6 hours. Nine such makers can build one bench in 8 hours. How many makers are needed to finish one cabinet and one bench in 24 hours?
explanation: The cabinet stays the same size, but the available time rises from six hours to twenty-four: four times as long. We so need one quarter as many makers for that cabinet, or two. Each of those two works throughout the twenty-four hours.

The bench’s available time rises from eight to twenty-four hours, three times as long. It needs one third of its original nine makers, or three. The two makers on the cabinet and the three on the bench work during the same twenty-four-hour interval, so five makers in total are enough.

More available time reduces the number of workers for a fixed job. We used that inverse relationship separately for each item because a cabinet and a bench require different amounts of work. We cannot treat them as two identical objects and average their completion times.

This argument also gives a concrete schedule: put two makers on the cabinet and three on the bench for the full twenty-four hours. Both jobs finish at the deadline. The schedule proves that the five-worker answer is achievable, not merely a numerical total.
wp26-g105.answerHtml:
The cabinet stays the same size, but the available time rises from six hours to twenty-four: four times as long. We so need one quarter as many makers for that cabinet, or two. Each of those two works throughout the twenty-four hours.

The bench’s available time rises from eight to twenty-four hours, three times as long. It needs one third of its original nine makers, or three. The two makers on the cabinet and the three on the bench work during the same twenty-four-hour interval, so five makers in total are enough.

This argument also gives a concrete schedule: put two makers on the cabinet and three on the bench for the full twenty-four hours. Both jobs finish at the deadline. The schedule proves that the five-worker answer is achievable, not merely a numerical total.

methods.title: Allocate a team to each item
steps: The cabinet stays the same size, but the available time rises from six hours to twenty-four: four times as long. We so need one quarter as many makers for that cabinet, or two. Each of those two works throughout the twenty-four hours.

The bench’s available time rises from eight to twenty-four hours, three times as long. It needs one third of its original nine makers, or three. The two makers on the cabinet and the three on the bench work during the same twenty-four-hour interval, so five makers in total are enough.

More available time reduces the number of workers for a fixed job. We used that inverse relationship separately for each item because a cabinet and a bench require different amounts of work. We cannot treat them as two identical objects and average their completion times.

This argument also gives a concrete schedule: put two makers on the cabinet and three on the bench for the full twenty-four hours. Both jobs finish at the deadline. The schedule proves that the five-worker answer is achievable, not merely a numerical total.

methods.title: Add the labour required
steps: The cabinet requires eight times six, or forty-eight worker-hours. The bench requires nine times eight, or seventy-two worker-hours. Together they require 120 worker-hours. One maker working for twenty-four hours contributes twenty-four worker-hours. Dividing 120 by twenty-four gives five makers.

This is often the shortest route when the problem combines different jobs. First put every job into the same unit of labour. Then add those amounts and divide by the time available to each worker. There is no need to find a cabinet-per-hour rate and a bench-per-hour rate or try to add unlike items.

Four makers would supply only ninety-six worker-hours by the deadline, which is short of the required 120. Five supply exactly 120, and the separate-team schedule shows how that labour can be used. Six would provide more labour than needed, so six is not the required team size.

Worker-hours describe the ideal constant-rate model stated in the question. We are not adding a setup time or assuming any real-world limit on how many makers can cooperate. Those details would have to be given to change the calculation. Within this model, every worker-hour is interchangeable with another.

methods.title: Use the table shortcut for each job
steps: For the cabinet, keep the columns workers, work, time. The rows are 8, 1, 6 and unknown, 1, 24. Rearranging the constant-rate relationship gives $\frac{8\times1\times6}{1\times24}=2$ makers. For the bench, the same calculation gives $\frac{9\times1\times8}{1\times24}=3$.

The work entry is one in both rows for each calculation because we still want one cabinet or one bench. This is a case where direct inverse scaling is faster than drawing the full table, but the table remains a dependable route. It is especially useful when more than one quantity changes at once.

All three methods describe the same five-person plan from different viewpoints: inverse ratios focus on the extra time, worker-hours focus on the total labour, and the table keeps all three quantities visible. Choose the route you can explain most clearly. With these numbers, the worker-hour addition is particularly compact.

wp26-g105b.stem: A supply of feed is enough for 240 identical animals for 6 days. Each animal eats the same constant amount per day. For how many days would that supply feed 90 animals?
wp26-g105b.stemRich: A supply of feed is enough for 240 identical animals for 6 days. Each animal eats the same constant amount per day. For how many days would that supply feed 90 animals?
wp26-g105b.stemHtml: A supply of feed is enough for 240 identical animals for 6 days. Each animal eats the same constant amount per day. For how many days would that supply feed 90 animals?
explanation: The supply covers 240 animals for six days, so it contains 1,440 animal-days of feed. An animal-day means enough feed for one animal for one day. Ninety animals use ninety animal-days each day. Dividing 1,440 by ninety gives sixteen days.

The amount of feed is fixed. Fewer animals use it more slowly, so it must last longer than the original six days. Animal-days let us calculate that inverse relationship without knowing the weight of any individual meal. We are measuring the supply by what it can support.
wp26-g105b.answerHtml:
The supply covers 240 animals for six days, so it contains 1,440 animal-days of feed. An animal-day means enough feed for one animal for one day. Ninety animals use ninety animal-days each day. Dividing 1,440 by ninety gives sixteen days.

The amount of feed is fixed. Fewer animals use it more slowly, so it must last longer than the original six days. Animal-days let us calculate that inverse relationship without knowing the weight of any individual meal. We are measuring the supply by what it can support.

methods.title: Measure the supply in animal-days
steps: The supply covers 240 animals for six days, so it contains 1,440 animal-days of feed. An animal-day means enough feed for one animal for one day. Ninety animals use ninety animal-days each day. Dividing 1,440 by ninety gives sixteen days.

The amount of feed is fixed. Fewer animals use it more slowly, so it must last longer than the original six days. Animal-days let us calculate that inverse relationship without knowing the weight of any individual meal. We are measuring the supply by what it can support.

methods.title: Choose a convenient daily serving
steps: Suppose each animal eats one unit of feed each day. Then the original group uses 240 units per day, and six days require 1,440 units. The smaller group uses ninety units per day. The same stock lasts 1,440 divided by ninety, or sixteen days.

The one-unit choice is a change of measuring unit, not an extra factual claim about animal diets. We could choose two units per animal and double both the stock and daily use; the number of days would be unchanged. This is why assigning a simple value is legitimate here.

This technique is useful when a question gives only proportional consumption information. A fixed extra loss or a different consumption rate for one group would have to be included separately. Here every animal has the same stated daily need, so the common scale cancels.

methods.title: Use inverse ratios and a benchmark
steps: Halving the group from 240 animals to 120 doubles the duration from six days to twelve. Reducing it further to ninety animals must make the supply last more than twelve days. Ninety is three quarters of 120, so the duration is four thirds of twelve, or sixteen.

The halfway benchmark gives a useful first check: twelve days belongs to 120 animals, not ninety. The exact second ratio then distinguishes sixteen from nearby choices. We use estimation to locate the answer and the ratio to finish it exactly.

The entire adjustment can also be written $6\times\frac{240}{90}=16$. Cancel the common factor thirty in the ratio to get eight thirds, then multiply by six. Keeping the supply fixed is what puts the old animal count above the new count.

explanation: Tripling speed triples the distance covered in the same time. Doubling the time doubles it again. The combined distance factor is 3×2=6, so the new distance is 6d.
wp27-p02.answerHtml: Tripling speed triples the distance covered in the same time. Doubling the time doubles it again. The combined distance factor is 3×2=6, so the new distance is 6d.

methods.title: Use distance equals speed times time
steps: The original speed is $\frac dt$. The new distance is $\frac{3d}{t}\times2t=6d$. The t cancels because both time quantities use the same units.

wp27-g108.stem: A drone climbs along a straight line at 390 kph. After 2 minutes, its horizontal displacement is 12 kilometers. How high above its starting level is it, in kilometers?

wp27-g108.stemHtml: A drone climbs along a straight line at 390 kph. After 2 minutes, its horizontal displacement is 12 kilometers. How high above its starting level is it, in kilometers?
explanation: Two minutes is one thirtieth of an hour. At 390 kilometres per hour, the drone travels thirteen kilometres along its sloping path. Draw a right triangle: twelve is the horizontal side, the unknown height is the vertical side, and thirteen is the sloping side opposite the right angle.
By Pythagoras, the height squared is thirteen squared minus twelve squared: 169−144=25. The height is five kilometres. Thirteen is the length of the flight path, so it is not the requested height.
wp27-g108.answerHtml:
Two minutes is one thirtieth of an hour. At 390 kilometres per hour, the drone travels thirteen kilometres along its sloping path. Draw a right triangle: twelve is the horizontal side, the unknown height is the vertical side, and thirteen is the sloping side opposite the right angle.

By Pythagoras, the height squared is thirteen squared minus twelve squared: 169−144=25. The height is five kilometres. Thirteen is the length of the flight path, so it is not the requested height.

methods.title: Find the sloping distance, then the height
steps: Two minutes is one thirtieth of an hour. At 390 kilometres per hour, the drone travels thirteen kilometres along its sloping path. Draw a right triangle: twelve is the horizontal side, the unknown height is the vertical side, and thirteen is the sloping side opposite the right angle.
By Pythagoras, the height squared is thirteen squared minus twelve squared: 169−144=25. The height is five kilometres. Thirteen is the length of the flight path, so it is not the requested height.

methods.title: Recognise a right-triangle triple

wp27-g109.stem: A shuttle travels from a station to a hotel at 72 kph and returns along the same route at 48 kph, without stopping. What is its average speed for the whole round trip?
wp27-g109.stemRich: A shuttle travels from a station to a hotel at 72 kph and returns along the same route at 48 kph, without stopping. What is its average speed for the whole round trip?
wp27-g109.stemHtml: A shuttle travels from a station to a hotel at 72 kph and returns along the same route at 48 kph, without stopping. What is its average speed for the whole round trip?
explanation: The one-way distance is not given, and its size will cancel. Choose 144 kilometres because both speeds divide it neatly. At seventy-two kilometres per hour the outward trip takes two hours. At forty-eight it takes three hours. The total is 288 kilometres in five hours, giving 57.6 kilometres per hour.

Average speed means total distance divided by total elapsed time. It is the one steady speed that would cover the whole route in the same overall time. It does not usually mean adding the two listed speeds and dividing by two. Here the slower speed lasts three hours while the faster one lasts only two.

This also explains why the answer is below sixty, the midpoint of the two speeds. More time is spent at forty-eight, so that speed has more influence on the time-weighted average. The simple average of sixty would be correct for equal times at the two speeds, but these journeys have equal distances.

wp27-g111.stem: Noor and Eli start at the same time from opposite ends of a path and walk towards one another. Eli walks at 1.75 times Noor’s speed. What fraction of the path does Noor cover before they meet?
wp27-g111.stemRich: Noor and Eli start at the same time from opposite ends of a path and walk towards one another. Eli walks at 1.75 times Noor’s speed. What fraction of the path does Noor cover before they meet?
wp27-g111.stemHtml: Noor and Eli start at the same time from opposite ends of a path and walk towards one another. Eli walks at 1.75 times Noor’s speed. What fraction of the path does Noor cover before they meet?
explanation: Noor’s and Eli’s speed ratio is 1:1.75. Multiply both entries by four to make whole-number units: 4:7. They start together and we stop measuring at the same meeting, so they walk for equal amounts of time. Their distances so have that same ratio, four to seven.

The full path consists of Noor’s four distance units plus Eli’s seven. That makes eleven in all. Noor covers four of those eleven, giving four elevenths. The denominator is eleven because the question asks for Noor’s share of the whole path, not Noor’s distance compared only with Eli’s distance.

Imagine dividing the path into eleven equal strips. Noor walks across four strips from one end while Eli walks across seven from the other. Both arrive at the same dividing point. The strips represent relative distances; we are not claiming they are one metre long. Any common strip length leads to the same fraction.

methods.title: Give the speeds and time convenient values
steps: Let Noor walk at four kilometres per hour and Eli at seven. Those choices have exactly the required speed ratio. Suppose they meet after one hour. Noor has travelled four kilometres and Eli seven, so the starting distance was eleven kilometres. Noor’s four out of eleven gives the same fraction.

methods.title: Use two simple speed benchmarks
steps: Eli is faster, so Noor covers less than half the path. That removes one half and seven elevenths. If Eli were three times as fast as Noor, Noor would cover exactly one quarter. Eli is actually only 1.75 times as fast, so Noor covers more than one quarter.

The required share lies strictly between one quarter and one half. Of the four choices, only four elevenths lies in that interval. This is an answer-elimination method based on meaningful comparison cases; it does not require the exact ratio calculation.

wp27-g112.stem: Two boats leave opposite ends of a canal at the same time. Boat B is 3.5 times as fast as boat A. By the time B has traveled the full length of the canal, what fraction of that length has A traveled?
wp27-g112.stemRich: Two boats leave opposite ends of a canal at the same time. Boat B is 3.5 times as fast as boat A. By the time B has traveled the full length of the canal, what fraction of that length has A traveled?
wp27-g112.stemHtml: Two boats leave opposite ends of a canal at the same time. Boat B is 3.5 times as fast as boat A. By the time B has traveled the full length of the canal, what fraction of that length has A traveled?
explanation: The speed ratio A:B is 1:3.5, or 2:7. Over the same time, A covers two distance units while B covers seven. This time, B’s seven units alone represent the whole canal, because the question ends when B reaches the far end. A so covers two sevenths.

We do not add two and seven to make nine. That would describe their combined distances up to a meeting between them. Here the endpoint is B finishing its own full journey. Drawing the starting points is useful, but identifying when the clock stops is what tells us which distance is the whole.

wp27-g114.stem: Two walkers leave the same gate at the same time in opposite directions along a straight path. Their speeds are 5 and 7 kph. After how many minutes are they 800 meters apart?

wp27-g114.stemHtml: Two walkers leave the same gate at the same time in opposite directions along a straight path. Their speeds are 5 and 7 kph. After how many minutes are they 800 meters apart?
explanation: Every hour, one walker adds five kilometres to one side of the gap and the other adds seven to the other side. Their separation so grows at twelve kilometres per hour. The requested separation is eight hundred metres, or 0.8 kilometres.

Time is distance divided by relative speed: $\frac{0.8}{12}=\frac1{15}$ of an hour. One fifteenth of sixty minutes is four minutes. We add the speeds here because the walkers move away from each other in opposite directions.

wp27-g115.stem: At 08:00 a van leaves Pine for Lake at 60 kph. At 08:30 a car leaves Lake for Pine at 90 kph. The towns are 105 kilometers apart. When do they meet?
wp27-g115.stemRich: At 08:00 a van leaves Pine for Lake at 60 kph. At 08:30 a car leaves Lake for Pine at 90 kph. The towns are 105 kilometers apart. When do they meet?
wp27-g115.stemHtml: At 08:00 a van leaves Pine for Lake at 60 kph. At 08:30 a car leaves Lake for Pine at 90 kph. The towns are 105 kilometers apart. When do they meet?
explanation: During the first half hour only the van moves. At sixty kilometres per hour it covers thirty kilometres. At 08:30, when the car starts, the remaining gap is 105−30=75 kilometres.

From then on they move towards each other, so the gap closes at 60+90=150 kilometres per hour. A seventy-five-kilometre gap takes half an hour to close at that rate. Half an hour after 08:30 is 09:00.

The relative-speed calculation begins when both are moving. Using the original 105-kilometre distance with the combined speed would incorrectly give the car credit for travelling before it actually left.

wp27-g116.stemHtml: Mina walks from home at 3 kph. Twenty minutes later, Owen leaves the same home along the same route and catches Mina 40 minutes after Owen starts. What is Owen’s speed?
explanation: Mina’s twenty-minute head start is one third of an hour. At three kilometres per hour, she gets one kilometre ahead. Owen closes that gap in forty minutes, or two thirds of an hour. Closing one kilometre in two thirds of an hour requires a speed advantage of one and a half kilometres per hour.

That one and a half is the difference between their speeds. Mina is still walking while Owen catches up. Add Mina’s three to get Owen’s speed of four and a half kilometres per hour. Reporting only the speed difference would make Owen slower than Mina, so it could not describe a successful chase.

wp27-g117.stem: Vehicle A travels 9 kilometers in 12 minutes. Vehicle B travels 12 kilometers in 9 minutes. What is the difference between their speeds, in kph?
wp27-g117.stemRich: Vehicle A travels 9 kilometers in 12 minutes. Vehicle B travels 12 kilometers in 9 minutes. What is the difference between their speeds, in kph?
wp27-g117.stemHtml: Vehicle A travels 9 kilometers in 12 minutes. Vehicle B travels 12 kilometers in 9 minutes. What is the difference between their speeds, in kph?
explanation: Twelve minutes fits into an hour five times, so A’s speed is five times nine, or forty-five kilometres per hour. For B, multiply twelve kilometres by sixty and divide by nine: 720 divided by nine is eighty kilometres per hour. The speed difference is 80−45=35.

For the final subtraction, bridge through a round number if helpful: eighty minus forty is forty, then subtract five more to get thirty-five. Or shift both numbers up by five, giving 85−50=35. Adding the same amount to both numbers preserves their difference.
