wp27-g118.stem: A cable carriage normally travels along a 180-meter cable in 12 seconds at a constant speed. On one trip, it travels the first half at twice its normal speed and the second half at half its normal speed. How many seconds does the trip take?
wp27-g118.stemRich: A cable carriage normally travels along a 180-meter cable in 12 seconds at a constant speed. On one trip, it travels the first half at twice its normal speed and the second half at half its normal speed. How many seconds does the trip take?
wp27-g118.stemHtml: A cable carriage normally travels along a 180-meter cable in 12 seconds at a constant speed. On one trip, it travels the first half at twice its normal speed and the second half at half its normal speed. How many seconds does the trip take?
explanation: At the normal speed, each half of the cable takes six seconds. For the first half, doubling the speed halves the time, so that part takes three seconds. For the second half, halving the speed doubles the time, so that part takes twelve seconds. The total is fifteen seconds.

Doubling and halving the speeds do not cancel. They apply to equal distances, not equal time intervals. The slower half adds six seconds compared with normal, while the faster half saves only three. The trip is so three seconds longer overall.

wp27-g119.stem: B is the midpoint of a straight route from A to C. One cyclist rides from A to C at 24 kph. Another takes 20 minutes from A to B, then rides from B to C at 18 kph. Their total journey times are equal. How many kilometers long is AC?
wp27-g119.stemRich: B is the midpoint of a straight route from A to C. One cyclist rides from A to C at 24 kph. Another takes 20 minutes from A to B, then rides from B to C at 18 kph. Their total journey times are equal. How many kilometers long is AC?
wp27-g119.stemHtml: B is the midpoint of a straight route from A to C. One cyclist rides from A to C at 24 kph. Another takes 20 minutes from A to B, then rides from B to C at 18 kph. Their total journey times are equal. How many kilometers long is AC?
explanation: Call each half x kilometres, so the whole route is 2x. The first cyclist’s time is $\frac{2x}{24}=\frac{x}{12}$ hours. The second takes one third of an hour for the first half and $\frac{x}{18}$ hours for the second.

Equal journey times give $\frac{x}{12}=\frac13+\frac{x}{18}$. Multiply by thirty-six to remove the denominators: 3x=12+2x, so x=12. That is one half of the route. The requested whole distance is 2x=24 kilometres.

Choosing x for a half avoids repeatedly writing half of a whole-distance variable. Either choice works, but defining the smaller repeated piece makes the equation easier to read. The final doubling matters because x is not the quantity asked for.

wp27-g120.stem: A train covers a 1,350-kilometer route in 9 hours. A replacement train travels 80% faster. How many hours does the replacement take on the same route?
wp27-g120.stemRich: A train covers a 1,350-kilometer route in 9 hours. A replacement train travels 80% faster. How many hours does the replacement take on the same route?
wp27-g120.stemHtml: A train covers a 1,350-kilometer route in 9 hours. A replacement train travels 80% faster. How many hours does the replacement take on the same route?
explanation: Eighty percent faster means the new speed is 180% of the old speed, a multiplier of 1.8. Because the distance stays the same, divide the old time by 1.8. Nine divided by 1.8 is five hours. Multiplying both parts of that division by ten gives ninety divided by eighteen, which may be easier to calculate.

An eighty-percent increase in speed does not mean an eighty-percent decrease in time. Speed and time multiply to the fixed distance, so their multipliers must multiply to one. The time multiplier here is five ninths.

wp27-g121.stem: Two cyclists start together from the same point of a circular track, riding in the same direction. The track is 600 meters long. Their speeds are 30 and 24 kph. How many minutes pass between consecutive meetings?
wp27-g121.stemRich: Two cyclists start together from the same point of a circular track, riding in the same direction. The track is 600 meters long. Their speeds are 30 and 24 kph. How many minutes pass between consecutive meetings?
wp27-g121.stemHtml: Two cyclists start together from the same point of a circular track, riding in the same direction. The track is 600 meters long. Their speeds are 30 and 24 kph. How many minutes pass between consecutive meetings?
explanation: At the start the cyclists are together. The faster cyclist then moves ahead. Their next meeting occurs when the faster cyclist has gained exactly one complete lap on the slower one. It does not happen merely when the faster cyclist returns to the starting line, because the slower cyclist has moved too.

The speed advantage is thirty minus twenty-four, or six kilometres per hour. That is the rate at which the faster cyclist gains distance. One track lap is six hundred metres, or 0.6 kilometres. Gaining 0.6 kilometres at six kilometres per hour takes one tenth of an hour: six minutes.

We can picture the slower cyclist as standing still while the faster one moves at the relative speed of six kilometres per hour. This does not describe either person’s actual motion on the ground; it describes how their positions change compared with one another. In that relative picture, one complete lap returns the faster rider to the slower rider.

The same reasoning applies after every meeting. At any meeting they are alongside one another again, and the faster rider must gain one more full lap before the next one. With constant speeds the interval repeats every six minutes. The phrase consecutive meetings means there is no other meeting between the pair we are considering.

methods.title: Think about one extra lap
steps: At the start the cyclists are together. The faster cyclist then moves ahead. Their next meeting occurs when the faster cyclist has gained exactly one complete lap on the slower one. It does not happen merely when the faster cyclist returns to the starting line, because the slower cyclist has moved too.

The speed advantage is thirty minus twenty-four, or six kilometres per hour. That is the rate at which the faster cyclist gains distance. One track lap is six hundred metres, or 0.6 kilometres. Gaining 0.6 kilometres at six kilometres per hour takes one tenth of an hour: six minutes.

We can picture the slower cyclist as standing still while the faster one moves at the relative speed of six kilometres per hour. This does not describe either person’s actual motion on the ground; it describes how their positions change compared with one another. In that relative picture, one complete lap returns the faster rider to the slower rider.

The same reasoning applies after every meeting. At any meeting they are alongside one another again, and the faster rider must gain one more full lap before the next one. With constant speeds the interval repeats every six minutes. The phrase consecutive meetings means there is no other meeting between the pair we are considering.

methods.title: Write the extra-distance equation
steps: Let t be the time in hours between meetings. The faster rider covers 30t kilometres and the slower covers 24t. At the next meeting the first distance exceeds the second by one track length, so $30t=24t+0.6$. This gives 6t=0.6 and t=0.1 hour, or six minutes.

The equation makes the relevant distance explicit. We are not saying either rider travels only six hundred metres. In six minutes the faster travels three kilometres, equal to five laps. The slower travels 2.4 kilometres, equal to four laps. Their difference is the one extra lap that causes the meeting.

This whole-lap check is especially clear with these chosen speeds, but it is not necessary for the method that both riders complete an integer number of laps from the starting point at each meeting. What matters is that their travelled distances differ by one circumference. A meeting may occur elsewhere on the track with other speed ratios.

methods.title: Use metres per minute
steps: Thirty kilometres per hour is five hundred metres per minute. Twenty-four kilometres per hour is four hundred metres per minute. Their distance difference grows by one hundred metres each minute. Six hundred metres so takes six minutes.

This unit choice keeps every number whole and avoids converting a fractional hour at the end. It is useful when a track length is given in metres and the choices are in minutes. The important conversion is thirty thousand metres divided by sixty minutes, not thirty divided by sixty while leaving the distance unit unchanged.

If the riders went in opposite directions, their relative speed would be the sum, because both would close the gap from opposite sides. Here they travel in the same direction, so we subtract. The diagram and the words same direction determine the operation, not the fact that the route happens to be circular.

wp28-p18.stemRich: Two eight-sided dice are labeled 1 through 8. You are told only their sum. For how many possible sums is the unordered pair of results uniquely determined?
wp28-p18.stemHtml: Two eight-sided dice are labeled 1 through 8. You are told only their sum. For how many possible sums is the unordered pair of results uniquely determined?
explanation: Sums 2 and 3 force pairs {1,1} and {1,2}. At the high end, 15 and 16 force {7,8} and {8,8}. Every sum from 4 through 14 has at least two unordered pairs, so four sums work.
wp28-p18.answerHtml: Sums 2 and 3 force pairs {1,1} and {1,2}. At the high end, 15 and 16 force {7,8} and {8,8}. Every sum from 4 through 14 has at least two unordered pairs, so four sums work.

methods.title: Look at the extreme sums
steps: Sums 2 and 3 force pairs {1,1} and {1,2}. At the high end, 15 and 16 force {7,8} and {8,8}. Every sum from 4 through 14 has at least two unordered pairs, so four sums work.

methods.title: Use symmetry around the middle
steps: Replacing each result r by 9−r turns sum s into 18−s. The unique low sums 2 and 3 so have unique partners 16 and 15. Starting at sum 4, pairs such as {1,3} and {2,2} create ambiguity; the same pattern extends inward.

wp28-p19.stem: A four-digit code uses no zero. Its first and last digits are equal, and its third digit is twice its second. How many codes are possible?
wp28-p19.stemRich: A four-digit code uses no zero. Its first and last digits are equal, and its third digit is twice its second. How many codes are possible?
wp28-p19.stemHtml: A four-digit code uses no zero. Its first and last digits are equal, and its third digit is twice its second. How many codes are possible?
explanation: The first digit has nine choices and fixes the last. The second can be 1,2,3,4, because doubling it must remain a single nonzero digit. It fixes the third. Total: 9×4=36.
wp28-p19.answerHtml: The first digit has nine choices and fixes the last. The second can be 1,2,3,4, because doubling it must remain a single nonzero digit. It fixes the third. Total: 9×4=36.

methods.title: Count only the free digits
steps: The first digit has nine choices and fixes the last. The second can be 1,2,3,4, because doubling it must remain a single nonzero digit. It fixes the third. Total: 9×4=36.

methods.title: List the middle pairs
steps: The middle digits can be 12,24,36,48. For each middle pair, the matching outside digits can be 11 through 99 in nine ways. Four groups of nine give thirty-six.

wp28-p20.stem: An eight-digit password uses exactly two different digits, each appearing four times. Leading zero is allowed. The sum of its digits must be divisible by 10. How many unordered pairs of digits can be used?
wp28-p20.stemRich: An eight-digit password uses exactly two different digits, each appearing four times. Leading zero is allowed. The sum of its digits must be divisible by 10. How many unordered pairs of digits can be used?
wp28-p20.stemHtml: An eight-digit password uses exactly two different digits, each appearing four times. Leading zero is allowed. The sum of its digits must be divisible by 10. How many unordered pairs of digits can be used?
explanation: If the digits are a and b, the sum is 4(a+b). For this to be divisible by ten, a+b must be divisible by five. Distinct digits from zero to nine can have sums 5,10,15. They give three, four, and two pairs respectively: nine in all.
wp28-p20.answerHtml: If the digits are a and b, the sum is 4(a+b). For this to be divisible by ten, a+b must be divisible by five. Distinct digits from zero to nine can have sums 5,10,15. They give three, four, and two pairs respectively: nine in all.

methods.title: Reduce the divisibility condition
steps: If the digits are a and b, the sum is 4(a+b). For this to be divisible by ten, a+b must be divisible by five. Distinct digits from zero to nine can have sums 5,10,15. They give three, four, and two pairs respectively: nine in all.

methods.title: Match complementary last digits
steps: A digit ending in residue 0 modulo five must pair with the other such digit: {0,5}. Residue one pairs with residue four, giving four pairs from {1,6} and {4,9}. Residue two pairs with residue three, giving four pairs from {2,7} and {3,8}. Total: 1+4+4=9.

wp28-p21.stemRich: A café offers 4 drinks and 6 snacks. One particular drink cannot be paired with two of the snacks. How many allowed drink-and-snack pairs are there?
wp28-p21.stemHtml: A café offers 4 drinks and 6 snacks. One particular drink cannot be paired with two of the snacks. How many allowed drink-and-snack pairs are there?
explanation: Without restrictions there are 4×6=24 pairs. Exactly two are forbidden, so twenty-two remain.
wp28-p21.answerHtml: Without restrictions there are 4×6=24 pairs. Exactly two are forbidden, so twenty-two remain.

methods.title: Subtract the forbidden pairs
steps: Without restrictions there are 4×6=24 pairs. Exactly two are forbidden, so twenty-two remain.

methods.title: Count by drink
steps: The restricted drink has four allowed snacks. Each of the other three drinks has six. Total: 4+3×6=22.

wp28-p22.stem: In how many different ways can a committee of 3 people be chosen from 7 people, if roles are not assigned?
wp28-p22.stemRich: In how many different ways can a committee of 3 people be chosen from 7 people, if roles are not assigned?
wp28-p22.stemHtml: In how many different ways can a committee of 3 people be chosen from 7 people, if roles are not assigned?
explanation: Choosing first, second, and third gives 7×6×5=210 ordered selections. Each committee appears in 3!=6 orders, so divide by six to get thirty-five.
wp28-p22.answerHtml: Choosing first, second, and third gives 7×6×5=210 ordered selections. Each committee appears in 3!=6 orders, so divide by six to get thirty-five.

methods.title: Remove the order from a sequential selection
steps: Choosing first, second, and third gives 7×6×5=210 ordered selections. Each committee appears in 3!=6 orders, so divide by six to get thirty-five.

methods.title: Split by one named person
steps: If that person is included, choose two of the other six in fifteen ways. If excluded, choose three of the other six in twenty ways. Fifteen plus twenty is thirty-five.

wp28-p23.stem: Five different books are arranged on a shelf. Two named books must stay together, in either order. How many arrangements are possible?
wp28-p23.stemRich: Five different books are arranged on a shelf. Two named books must stay together, in either order. How many arrangements are possible?
wp28-p23.stemHtml: Five different books are arranged on a shelf. Two named books must stay together, in either order. How many arrangements are possible?
explanation: The joined pair plus the other three books make four objects, which can be arranged in 4!=24 ways. Inside the pair there are two orders, so multiply by two to get forty-eight.
wp28-p23.answerHtml: The joined pair plus the other three books make four objects, which can be arranged in 4!=24 ways. Inside the pair there are two orders, so multiply by two to get forty-eight.

methods.title: Treat the pair as one block
steps: The joined pair plus the other three books make four objects, which can be arranged in 4!=24 ways. Inside the pair there are two orders, so multiply by two to get forty-eight.

methods.title: Choose the pair’s starting position
steps: The adjacent pair can start in positions 1,2,3,4. It has two internal orders. The other three books can be ordered in six ways. The product is 4×2×6=48.

wp28-p24.stem: How many three-digit even numbers can be formed from 1,2,3,4,5 without repeating a digit?
wp28-p24.stemRich: How many three-digit even numbers can be formed from 1,2,3,4,5 without repeating a digit?
wp28-p24.stemHtml: How many three-digit even numbers can be formed from 1,2,3,4,5 without repeating a digit?
explanation: An even number ends in 2 or 4, giving two choices. Four digits then remain for the hundreds position and three for the tens. Total: 2×4×3=24.
wp28-p24.answerHtml: An even number ends in 2 or 4, giving two choices. Four digits then remain for the hundreds position and three for the tens. Total: 2×4×3=24.

methods.title: Choose the restricted last digit first
steps: An even number ends in 2 or 4, giving two choices. Four digits then remain for the hundreds position and three for the tens. Total: 2×4×3=24.

methods.title: Use symmetry between final digits
steps: There are 5×4×3=60 three-digit numbers without repetition. Each of the five digits appears equally often at the end. Two of them are even, so two fifths of sixty, or twenty-four, are even.

wp28-p25.stemRich: How many different arrangements are there of the letters in LEVEL?
wp28-p25.stemHtml: How many different arrangements are there of the letters in LEVEL?
explanation: Five distinct positions would have 5!=120 orders. Swapping the two Ls or the two Es does not create a new word, so divide by 2! twice: 120:4=30.
wp28-p25.answerHtml: Five distinct positions would have 5!=120 orders. Swapping the two Ls or the two Es does not create a new word, so divide by 2! twice: 120:4=30.

methods.title: Divide out repeated-letter swaps
steps: Five distinct positions would have 5!=120 orders. Swapping the two Ls or the two Es does not create a new word, so divide by 2! twice: 120:4=30.

methods.title: Choose letter positions
steps: Choose two of the five places for L in ten ways. Of the remaining three places, choose two for E in three ways. V fills the last place. Total: 10×3=30.

wp28-p26.stemRich: Eight people sit around a round table. Arrangements differing only by rotation count as the same; clockwise and counterclockwise orders count as different. How many arrangements are possible?
wp28-p26.stemHtml: Eight people sit around a round table. Arrangements differing only by rotation count as the same; clockwise and counterclockwise orders count as different. How many arrangements are possible?
explanation: Choose one named person and keep their seat fixed to remove rotational duplicates. The other seven can be ordered around them in 7!=5,040 ways.
wp28-p26.answerHtml: Choose one named person and keep their seat fixed to remove rotational duplicates. The other seven can be ordered around them in 7!=5,040 ways.

methods.title: Fix one person as an anchor
steps: Choose one named person and keep their seat fixed to remove rotational duplicates. The other seven can be ordered around them in 7!=5,040 ways.

methods.title: Divide line arrangements by rotations
steps: Eight numbered seats would give 8!=40,320 assignments. Each circular order appears once for each of eight rotations, so divide by eight: 40,320:8=5,040. Reflections are not divided out because the question counts them separately.

wp28-p27.stem: A class of 6 students is split into two named teams, Cedar and Maple, with 3 students on each. How many splits are possible?
wp28-p27.stemRich: A class of 6 students is split into two named teams, Cedar and Maple, with 3 students on each. How many splits are possible?
wp28-p27.stemHtml: A class of 6 students is split into two named teams, Cedar and Maple, with 3 students on each. How many splits are possible?
explanation: Choose three of the six for Cedar in 6×5×4:6=20 ways. Everyone else must join Maple. Because the teams have names, swapping all their members produces a different split.
wp28-p27.answerHtml: Choose three of the six for Cedar in 6×5×4:6=20 ways. Everyone else must join Maple. Because the teams have names, swapping all their members produces a different split.

methods.title: Choose Cedar, then Maple is fixed
steps: Choose three of the six for Cedar in 6×5×4:6=20 ways. Everyone else must join Maple. Because the teams have names, swapping all their members produces a different split.

methods.title: Start with all student orders
steps: Arrange the six students in 6!=720 ways, put the first three in Cedar and the rest in Maple. Internal orders within each team do not matter, so divide by 3!×3!=36. That leaves twenty splits.

wp28-g124.stem: How many three-digit numbers can be made from the digits 2, 4, 6 and 8 if the hundreds digit is smaller than the tens digit and the tens digit is smaller than the units digit?
wp28-g124.stemRich: How many three-digit numbers can be made from the digits 2, 4, 6 and 8 if the hundreds digit is smaller than the tens digit and the tens digit is smaller than the units digit?
wp28-g124.stemHtml: How many three-digit numbers can be made from the digits 2, 4, 6 and 8 if the hundreds digit is smaller than the tens digit and the tens digit is smaller than the units digit?
explanation: If the first digit is two, the possibilities are 246, 248 and 268. If the first digit is four, the only possibility is 468. Starting with six or eight leaves too few larger digits to finish. There are four numbers. The strict increases also mean no digit can repeat.
wp28-g124.answerHtml: If the first digit is two, the possibilities are 246, 248 and 268. If the first digit is four, the only possibility is 468. Starting with six or eight leaves too few larger digits to finish. There are four numbers. The strict increases also mean no digit can repeat.

methods.title: List in an organised order
steps: If the first digit is two, the possibilities are 246, 248 and 268. If the first digit is four, the only possibility is 468. Starting with six or eight leaves too few larger digits to finish. There are four numbers. The strict increases also mean no digit can repeat.

methods.title: Choose the digit left out
steps: Any three of the four digits have exactly one increasing order. Choosing the three digits is so the same as choosing which one digit to leave out. There are four choices for that omitted digit, so there are four numbers. We do not multiply by six orders because five of those orders would violate the condition.

wp28-g125.stem: A café offers 4 sandwich fillings and 6 drinks. A meal contains one filling and one drink. How many different meals are possible?
wp28-g125.stemRich: A café offers 4 sandwich fillings and 6 drinks. A meal contains one filling and one drink. How many different meals are possible?
wp28-g125.stemHtml: A café offers 4 sandwich fillings and 6 drinks. A meal contains one filling and one drink. How many different meals are possible?
explanation: Choose the filling first: four options. For each filling, all six drinks remain available. That gives six meals for the first filling, another six for the second, another six for the third, and another six for the fourth. Four times six is twenty-four.
Adding four and six would count individual menu items, not combinations of one of each. A complete meal requires both a filling choice and a drink choice, which is why the choices multiply.

Choose the filling first: four options. For each filling, all six drinks remain available. That gives six meals for the first filling, another six for the second, another six for the third, and another six for the fourth. Four times six is twenty-four.

methods.title: Multiply the choices at the two stages
steps: Choose the filling first: four options. For each filling, all six drinks remain available. That gives six meals for the first filling, another six for the second, another six for the third, and another six for the fourth. Four times six is twenty-four.
Adding four and six would count individual menu items, not combinations of one of each. A complete meal requires both a filling choice and a drink choice, which is why the choices multiply.

methods.title: Draw a rectangular choice table
steps: Use four rows, one per filling, and six columns, one per drink. Every cell represents exactly one meal. No two cells describe the same filling-and-drink combination, and every possible meal has a cell. The table has twenty-four cells. This is a visual explanation of the multiplication rule.

wp28-g126.stem: A two-character access code uses decimal digits from 0 to 9. The sum of its two digits must be 12. How many codes are possible?
wp28-g126.stemRich: A two-character access code uses decimal digits from 0 to 9. The sum of its two digits must be 12. How many codes are possible?
wp28-g126.stemHtml: A two-character access code uses decimal digits from 0 to 9. The sum of its two digits must be 12. How many codes are possible?
explanation: The first digit can be three through nine. A smaller first digit would require a second digit above nine. Once the first digit is fixed, the second must be twelve minus it, so only one choice remains. Seven first-digit options times one completion gives seven codes.
wp28-g126.answerHtml: The first digit can be three through nine. A smaller first digit would require a second digit above nine. Once the first digit is fixed, the second must be twelve minus it, so only one choice remains. Seven first-digit options times one completion gives seven codes.

methods.title: Choose the first digit, then complete the sum
steps: The first digit can be three through nine. A smaller first digit would require a second digit above nine. Once the first digit is fixed, the second must be twelve minus it, so only one choice remains. Seven first-digit options times one completion gives seven codes.

methods.title: List all the codes
steps: The codes are 39, 48, 57, 66, 75, 84 and 93. Reversed unequal digits give different codes because position matters. The repeated code 66 is allowed because the question does not require distinct digits. There are seven in all.

wp28-g128.stem: A lock code has three positions, each filled with one of the symbols A, B, C, D, E or F. Symbols may repeat. How many codes are possible?
wp28-g128.stemRich: A lock code has three positions, each filled with one of the symbols A, B, C, D, E or F. Symbols may repeat. How many codes are possible?
wp28-g128.stemHtml: A lock code has three positions, each filled with one of the symbols A, B, C, D, E or F. Symbols may repeat. How many codes are possible?
explanation: There are six options for the first position. Because repetition is allowed, choosing a symbol does not remove it from the pool. The second position again has six options, and so does the third. Multiply: six times six times six is 216. Codes such as AAA and ABA are included.
wp28-g128.answerHtml: There are six options for the first position. Because repetition is allowed, choosing a symbol does not remove it from the pool. The second position again has six options, and so does the third. Multiply: six times six times six is 216. Codes such as AAA and ABA are included.

methods.title: Keep the pool unchanged
steps: There are six options for the first position. Because repetition is allowed, choosing a symbol does not remove it from the pool. The second position again has six options, and so does the third. Multiply: six times six times six is 216. Codes such as AAA and ABA are included.

methods.title: Group codes by their first two symbols
steps: There are thirty-six possible two-symbol beginnings. Each beginning can be completed with any of six final symbols. That gives thirty-six groups of six, or 216. This view makes clear that the same six endings are available after every beginning.

wp28-g129.stem: A lock code has three positions filled with symbols chosen from A, B, C, D, E and F. No symbol may appear twice. How many codes are possible?
wp28-g129.stemRich: A lock code has three positions filled with symbols chosen from A, B, C, D, E and F. No symbol may appear twice. How many codes are possible?
wp28-g129.stemHtml: A lock code has three positions filled with symbols chosen from A, B, C, D, E and F. No symbol may appear twice. How many codes are possible?
explanation: The first position has six choices. Once one is used, five remain for the second position. Once two are used, four remain for the third. Multiply six, five and four to get 120. The declining counts come directly from the no-repeat condition.

Compare this with the previous code question: the available symbols are the same, but the pool now shrinks after every choice. That one wording change turns six times six times six into six times five times four.

Compare this with the previous code question: the available symbols are the same, but the pool now shrinks after every choice. That one wording change turns six times six times six into six times five times four.

methods.title: Remove each used symbol

Compare this with the previous code question: the available symbols are the same, but the pool now shrinks after every choice. That one wording change turns six times six times six into six times five times four.

methods.title: Choose an unordered group, then order it
steps: There are $\frac{6\times5\times4}{3\times2\times1}=20$ groups of three distinct symbols. Each group can be arranged in six orders. Twenty groups times six orders gives 120 codes. Dividing by six alone would count groups, not the ordered codes requested.

wp28-g130.stem: In how many different ways can 6 distinct framed photographs be placed in a row?
wp28-g130.stemRich: In how many different ways can 6 distinct framed photographs be placed in a row?
wp28-g130.stemHtml: In how many different ways can 6 distinct framed photographs be placed in a row?
explanation: Choose any of the six photographs for the first position. Five remain for the second, then four, three, two and finally one. Their product is 720. The final factor of one matters conceptually even though it does not change the product: the last photograph is forced.

This descending product is called six factorial, written with an exclamation mark. It is a short name for a multiplication, not a new mysterious operation. Six factorial means six times five times four times three times two times one.
wp28-g130.answerHtml:
Choose any of the six photographs for the first position. Five remain for the second, then four, three, two and finally one. Their product is 720. The final factor of one matters conceptually even though it does not change the product: the last photograph is forced.

This descending product is called six factorial, written with an exclamation mark. It is a short name for a multiplication, not a new mysterious operation. Six factorial means six times five times four times three times two times one.

methods.title: Fill the row one position at a time
steps: Choose any of the six photographs for the first position. Five remain for the second, then four, three, two and finally one. Their product is 720. The final factor of one matters conceptually even though it does not change the product: the last photograph is forced.

This descending product is called six factorial, written with an exclamation mark. It is a short name for a multiplication, not a new mysterious operation. Six factorial means six times five times four times three times two times one.

methods.title: Insert the sixth photograph into a row of five
steps: Five distinct photographs have 120 row orders. In any such order there are six places to insert the sixth photograph: before the first, after the last, or one of four gaps between neighbours. Every final six-photo row has exactly one underlying five-photo row and one insertion position. Thus 120×6=720.

wp28-g132.stem: Five islands are connected so that every pair has exactly one two-way ferry route. How many routes are there?
wp28-g132.stemRich: Five islands are connected so that every pair has exactly one two-way ferry route. How many routes are there?
wp28-g132.stemHtml: Five islands are connected so that every pair has exactly one two-way ferry route. How many routes are there?
explanation: Choose the first island in five ways and a different second island in four ways. That gives twenty ordered selections. But A to B and B to A describe the same two-way route. Every route has been counted exactly twice, so divide by two to get ten.
The division by two comes from that specific duplication. If the question counted separate one-way services in each direction, the ordered selections would be distinct and we would keep twenty.
wp28-g132.answerHtml:
Choose the first island in five ways and a different second island in four ways. That gives twenty ordered selections. But A to B and B to A describe the same two-way route. Every route has been counted exactly twice, so divide by two to get ten.

The division by two comes from that specific duplication. If the question counted separate one-way services in each direction, the ordered selections would be distinct and we would keep twenty.

methods.title: Count ordered pairs and remove the duplication
steps: Choose the first island in five ways and a different second island in four ways. That gives twenty ordered selections. But A to B and B to A describe the same two-way route. Every route has been counted exactly twice, so divide by two to get ten.
The division by two comes from that specific duplication. If the question counted separate one-way services in each direction, the ordered selections would be distinct and we would keep twenty.

methods.title: Add only routes to later islands
steps: Label the islands A through E. A connects to four later islands. B adds three new routes to C, D and E; its route to A is already counted. C adds two, D adds one, and E adds none. The total 4+3+2+1 is ten. This organised count never duplicates a route.

wp28-g133.stem: How many diagonals does a seven-sided polygon have?
wp28-g133.stemRich: How many diagonals does a seven-sided polygon have?
wp28-g133.stemHtml: How many diagonals does a seven-sided polygon have?
explanation: From one vertex, a diagonal cannot end at that same vertex or either of its two neighbours. Four of the other six vertices remain available. Seven vertices each give four diagonal endpoints, but every diagonal is counted from both ends. Divide 7×4 by two to get fourteen.
wp28-g133.answerHtml: From one vertex, a diagonal cannot end at that same vertex or either of its two neighbours. Four of the other six vertices remain available. Seven vertices each give four diagonal endpoints, but every diagonal is counted from both ends. Divide 7×4 by two to get fourteen.

methods.title: Count diagonals from each vertex
steps: From one vertex, a diagonal cannot end at that same vertex or either of its two neighbours. Four of the other six vertices remain available. Seven vertices each give four diagonal endpoints, but every diagonal is counted from both ends. Divide 7×4 by two to get fourteen.

methods.title: Count all vertex pairs, then remove the sides
steps: Any pair of vertices defines a segment. Seven times six divided by two gives twenty-one such segments. Seven are sides of the polygon, leaving fourteen diagonals. This is often easier to picture because it separates the pair-counting rule from the definition of a diagonal.

wp28-g135.stem: A shop offers 5 drinks and 4 snacks. A customer chooses one of each. If the drink is cocoa, the snack must be a biscuit; with any other drink, any snack is allowed. How many choices are possible?
wp28-g135.stemRich: A shop offers 5 drinks and 4 snacks. A customer chooses one of each. If the drink is cocoa, the snack must be a biscuit; with any other drink, any snack is allowed. How many choices are possible?
wp28-g135.stemHtml: A shop offers 5 drinks and 4 snacks. A customer chooses one of each. If the drink is cocoa, the snack must be a biscuit; with any other drink, any snack is allowed. How many choices are possible?
explanation: If the customer chooses cocoa, the biscuit is forced: one possible pair. If the customer chooses another drink, there are four drink options and four snack options, giving sixteen pairs. These two cases cannot happen together, so add them: one plus sixteen is seventeen.

The condition works in one direction. Cocoa requires the biscuit, but the biscuit is still allowed with any of the other drinks. Excluding those biscuit pairs would impose a restriction the question did not give.

wp28-g138.stem: Eight children are split between two teachers, Maya and Alex, with four children assigned to each. How many different assignments are possible?
wp28-g138.stemRich: Eight children are split between two teachers, Maya and Alex, with four children assigned to each. How many different assignments are possible?
wp28-g138.stemHtml: Eight children are split between two teachers, Maya and Alex, with four children assigned to each. How many different assignments are possible?
explanation: Choose four of the eight children for Maya. An ordered selection would have $8\times7\times6\times5$ possibilities. But each group of four appears in $4\times3\times2\times1=24$ selection orders. Divide by those twenty-four orders to get seventy groups.

After Maya’s four are chosen, Alex’s four are fixed. We do not need a second independent choice for Alex. We also do not divide by another two: the teachers have different names, so exchanging the two groups creates a different assignment.

The word group means the order inside the group is irrelevant. Naming the teachers does not make the children’s internal selection order relevant; it only distinguishes which group goes to which teacher. These are two separate issues, and keeping them separate prevents an extra division or multiplication.

methods.title: Fix one child and count both possible teachers
steps: Choose one particular child. If that child goes to Maya, select three companions from the other seven: $\frac{7\times6\times5}{3\times2\times1}=35$. If the child goes to Alex, there are another thirty-five assignments by the same reasoning. The cases are disjoint and cover every assignment, so there are seventy.

If the two groups had no labels and the question only asked for a partition into two unnamed groups, exchanging the groups would not create a new partition. Then the answer would be $70:2=35$. The original question names the teachers, so seventy is the correct count here.

wp28-g139.stem: In how many different ways can a committee of 7 people be chosen from 8 people?
wp28-g139.stemRich: In how many different ways can a committee of 7 people be chosen from 8 people?
wp28-g139.stemHtml: In how many different ways can a committee of 7 people be chosen from 8 people?
explanation: Every seven-person committee leaves exactly one of the eight people out. Choose that omitted person instead of listing the seven included people. There are eight possible omissions, and each gives a different committee. Therefore there are eight committees.

This is a one-to-one match: once we know who is out, we know everyone who is in. Conversely, every allowed committee tells us exactly who was left out. That is why counting the smaller complementary choice gives the full answer.

wp28-g140.stem: What is the ratio of the number of row arrangements of 7 distinct objects to the number of row arrangements of 5 distinct objects?
wp28-g140.stemRich: What is the ratio of the number of row arrangements of 7 distinct objects to the number of row arrangements of 5 distinct objects?
wp28-g140.stemHtml: What is the ratio of the number of row arrangements of 7 distinct objects to the number of row arrangements of 5 distinct objects?
explanation: The counts are 7! and 5!. Write the larger factorial as $7\times6\times5!$. The common 5! is a whole nonzero factor in the numerator and denominator, so it cancels. The ratio is seven times six, or forty-two.
There is no advantage in calculating 5,040 and 120 first unless you already know them. Factoring out the smaller factorial keeps the calculation short and makes the cancellation visible.

wp28-g141.stem: How many three-digit numbers have a hundreds digit and a units digit whose sum is 7?
wp28-g141.stemRich: How many three-digit numbers have a hundreds digit and a units digit whose sum is 7?
wp28-g141.stemHtml: How many three-digit numbers have a hundreds digit and a units digit whose sum is 7?
explanation: The hundreds digit cannot be zero and cannot exceed seven, so it has seven choices: one through seven. The tens digit is unrestricted and has all ten choices from zero to nine. Once the hundreds digit is chosen, the units digit is forced to complete a sum of seven. That final position so has one choice, giving 7×10×1=70.

For example, a hundreds digit of two forces a units digit of five. The tens digit can still be anything, giving 205, 215, 225 and so on through 295. There are ten numbers in that one hundreds-digit case. A different hundreds digit creates another disjoint set of ten.

A digit appearing in several possible values across the whole problem does not mean it has all those values available after an earlier choice has been made. The units digit can be six in one number and five in another, but once the first digit is fixed, exactly one of them is allowed. This is what a dependent choice means.

wp28-g142.stem: The digits 3, 4, 7 and 8 are placed once each in a square: A and B on the top row, C and D on the bottom row. B must be even, and C×D must be even. How many arrangements are possible?
wp28-g142.stemRich: The digits 3, 4, 7 and 8 are placed once each in a square: A and B on the top row, C and D on the bottom row. B must be even, and C×D must be even. How many arrangements are possible?
wp28-g142.stemHtml: The digits 3, 4, 7 and 8 are placed once each in a square: A and B on the top row, C and D on the bottom row. B must be even, and C×D must be even. How many arrangements are possible?
explanation: B is even, so it uses either four or eight. The bottom product must be even, which means at least one bottom entry must be even. Since there are only two even digits in total, the remaining even digit must be on the bottom row. A must so be odd.

Choose B in two ways, A in two ways, then place the two remaining digits in C and D in two orders. The product 2×2×2 is eight. Once we have enforced those top-row choices, the bottom product automatically has its required even factor.

The positions form a square, but the multiplication rule still works. Choice stages need not be a physical line. We can choose the most restricted position first, then count the remaining possibilities in whatever order is easiest.

wp28-g143.stem: In a chess event, each pair of players plays exactly one game. There are 45 games altogether. How many players take part?
wp28-g143.stemRich: In a chess event, each pair of players plays exactly one game. There are 45 games altogether. How many players take part?
wp28-g143.stemHtml: In a chess event, each pair of players plays exactly one game. There are 45 games altogether. How many players take part?
explanation: With n players, each can face n−1 others. The product n(n−1) counts every game twice, once from each player’s side. The actual game count is so $\frac{n(n-1)}2$. Set that equal to forty-five and multiply by two: n(n−1)=90.

We need two consecutive positive integers whose product is ninety. Nine times ten is ninety, so n is ten, the larger of the consecutive pair. The smaller number nine represents each player’s opponents. Ten players each face nine opponents, and ninety player-appearances make forty-five games.
wp28-g143.answerHtml:
With n players, each can face n−1 others. The product n(n−1) counts every game twice, once from each player’s side. The actual game count is so . Set that equal to forty-five and multiply by two: n(n−1)=90.

We need two consecutive positive integers whose product is ninety. Nine times ten is ninety, so n is ten, the larger of the consecutive pair. The smaller number nine represents each player’s opponents. Ten players each face nine opponents, and ninety player-appearances make forty-five games.

methods.title: Reverse the pair-count formula
steps: With n players, each can face n−1 others. The product n(n−1) counts every game twice, once from each player’s side. The actual game count is so $\frac{n(n-1)}2$. Set that equal to forty-five and multiply by two: n(n−1)=90.

We need two consecutive positive integers whose product is ninety. Nine times ten is ninety, so n is ten, the larger of the consecutive pair. The smaller number nine represents each player’s opponents. Ten players each face nine opponents, and ninety player-appearances make forty-five games.

methods.title: Test the offered player counts
steps: Nine players would give nine times eight divided by two, or thirty-six games. That is too few. Eight would give even fewer, so that option is also out. Ten players give ten times nine divided by two, or forty-five, which fits. Twelve give sixty-six, too many.

The number of games rises whenever we add a player, because the newcomer plays every existing player. That makes it safe to use a too-small answer to eliminate all smaller offered counts. We still check the candidate that matches rather than assuming the next one must work.

methods.title: Build the tournament one player at a time
steps: One player alone produces no games. Adding a second creates one game. Adding a third creates two new games, one against each existing player. Adding a fourth creates three more. The total grows by one, then two, then three, and so on.

The running totals are one game for two players, three for three, six for four, ten for five, fifteen for six, twenty-one for seven, twenty-eight for eight, thirty-six for nine, and forty-five for ten. This organised addition reaches the required total without using an equation.

Be careful with the final added number. The last addition is nine games, but it comes from the tenth player, who faces the nine already there. Reporting nine players because the last added number was nine would miss that extra person.

The table is a useful explanation of why the pair formula works. Its additions are the numbers one through n−1. Pairing the ends of that sequence gives the same total n(n−1) divided by two. For a small event, the running totals can be a quick route; for a large one, the compact formula saves writing.

wp29-g154.stemHtml: A fair six-sided dice is rolled twice independently. What is the probability that the two results add to 8?
explanation: The successful pairs are (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3) and (6,2). There are five. All six first results can pair with all six second results, so there are thirty-six equally likely ordered pairs. Five out of thirty-six gives the probability.
The pair (2,6) is different from (6,2) because the first and second rolls are distinct positions. The pair (4,4) is listed once, not twice: reversing it does not create a different ordered pair.

wp29-g157.stemHtml: A bag contains 4 red counters and 4 yellow counters. Two are drawn uniformly at random without replacement. What is the probability that their colors differ?
explanation: The first counter can have either colour. After it is removed, seven counters remain. Exactly four have the opposite colour, whichever colour came first. The required second draw so has probability four sevenths.

methods.title: Split success into first try or second try
steps: Finding the prize on the first try has probability $\frac17$. Missing first and finding it second has probability $\frac67\times\frac16=\frac17$. Those success cases cannot both occur, so add them: two sevenths.
The second-try probability of one sixth applies only after a first miss. Adding one seventh and one sixth without the miss factor would mix an unconditional probability with a conditional one.

wp29-g161.stemHtml: Lina chooses one of the 26 English letters uniformly at random. Independently, Noah chooses one of the four letters in NOAH uniformly at random. What is the probability that they choose the same letter?

wp29-g162.stem: A workshop has r groups, each containing s participants with different ages. One participant is selected uniformly from each group, independently across groups. What is the probability that the oldest participant is selected from every group?
wp29-g162.stemRich: A workshop has r groups, each containing s participants with different ages. One participant is selected uniformly from each group, independently across groups. What is the probability that the oldest participant is selected from every group?
wp29-g162.stemHtml: A workshop has r groups, each containing s participants with different ages. One participant is selected uniformly from each group, independently across groups. What is the probability that the oldest participant is selected from every group?
explanation: Each group has exactly one oldest participant among s people, so its success probability is $\frac1s$. We need success in all r independent groups. Multiply r copies of that fraction: $(\frac1s)^r=\frac1{s^r}=s^{-r}$.

The base comes from the number of people available in each group. The exponent comes from how many group selections must all succeed. Keeping those roles separate helps avoid reversing r and s. The different-age condition guarantees one oldest person per group.

steps: Take three groups of two people. Each group has a one-half chance of selecting its older member, so all three succeed with probability one eighth. The proposed form s to the power negative r gives two to the power negative three, which is one eighth.

wp29-g163.stemHtml: Factory A makes 800 buttons a day, including 40 blue buttons. Factory B makes 400 buttons a day, including 110 blue buttons. One button is chosen uniformly from their combined daily output. What is the probability that it is not blue?
explanation: Factory A makes 760 non-blue buttons and B makes 290. There are 1,050 non-blue buttons among 1,200 buttons altogether. Divide 1,050 by 1,200 and simplify to seven eighths. The selection is from the combined output, so every individual button has equal weight.
wp29-g163.answerHtml: Factory A makes 760 non-blue buttons and B makes 290. There are 1,050 non-blue buttons among 1,200 buttons altogether. Divide 1,050 by 1,200 and simplify to seven eighths. The selection is from the combined output, so every individual button has equal weight.

methods.title: Count the non-blue output
steps: Factory A makes 760 non-blue buttons and B makes 290. There are 1,050 non-blue buttons among 1,200 buttons altogether. Divide 1,050 by 1,200 and simplify to seven eighths. The selection is from the combined output, so every individual button has equal weight.

methods.title: Subtract the blue share
steps: The two factories make forty plus 110, or 150 blue buttons. That is one eighth of the 1,200-button total. The non-blue probability is one minus one eighth, or seven eighths. This complement calculation uses the smaller counts and is quicker.

methods.title: Use weighted factory probabilities
steps: A random button comes from A with probability $\frac23$ and from B with probability $\frac13$, because their outputs are eight hundred and four hundred. The non-blue probabilities within those factories are $\frac{19}{20}$ and $\frac{29}{40}$. The weighted result is $\frac23\times\frac{19}{20}+\frac13\times\frac{29}{40}=\frac78$. An unweighted average would incorrectly treat the two factories as equally likely.

wp29-g164.stem: A music app offers five genres. Each day, Tia chooses uniformly from the four genres she did not choose the previous day. On Monday she chose jazz. What is the probability that she chooses folk on Wednesday?
wp29-g164.stemRich: A music app offers five genres. Each day, Tia chooses uniformly from the four genres she did not choose the previous day. On Monday she chose jazz. What is the probability that she chooses folk on Wednesday?
wp29-g164.stemHtml: A music app offers five genres. Each day, Tia chooses uniformly from the four genres she did not choose the previous day. On Monday she chose jazz. What is the probability that she chooses folk on Wednesday?
explanation: Monday’s jazz choice is already given, so it contributes no probability factor. On Tuesday, four genres are available: folk and three others. If Tia chooses folk on Tuesday, Wednesday folk is forbidden. She must so choose one of the other three Tuesday options, with probability three quarters.

After any of those three Tuesday choices, folk is one of four allowed Wednesday genres. Its probability is one quarter. Multiplying gives three sixteenths. The restriction only concerns the immediately previous day, so jazz is allowed again on Wednesday.
wp29-g164.answerHtml:
Monday’s jazz choice is already given, so it contributes no probability factor. On Tuesday, four genres are available: folk and three others. If Tia chooses folk on Tuesday, Wednesday folk is forbidden. She must so choose one of the other three Tuesday options, with probability three quarters.

After any of those three Tuesday choices, folk is one of four allowed Wednesday genres. Its probability is one quarter. Multiplying gives three sixteenths. The restriction only concerns the immediately previous day, so jazz is allowed again on Wednesday.

methods.title: Choose a Tuesday genre that keeps folk available
steps: Monday’s jazz choice is already given, so it contributes no probability factor. On Tuesday, four genres are available: folk and three others. If Tia chooses folk on Tuesday, Wednesday folk is forbidden. She must so choose one of the other three Tuesday options, with probability three quarters.

After any of those three Tuesday choices, folk is one of four allowed Wednesday genres. Its probability is one quarter. Multiplying gives three sixteenths. The restriction only concerns the immediately previous day, so jazz is allowed again on Wednesday.

methods.title: Count the two-day paths
steps: There are four possible Tuesday genres and, after each, four Wednesday genres. That gives sixteen equally likely two-day paths. Exactly three paths end in Wednesday folk: one through each Tuesday genre other than jazz and folk. Three successful paths out of sixteen gives three sixteenths.

methods.title: Condition on the excluded Tuesday case
steps: Tuesday folk happens with probability $\frac14$ and then Wednesday folk has probability zero. The other Tuesday cases have probability $\frac34$ and then Wednesday folk has probability $\frac14$. Thus $\frac14\times0+\frac34\times\frac14=\frac3{16}$. Writing the zero branch makes the dependence explicit.

wp29-g165.stem: A jar contains 6 red sweets and 1 blue sweet. All seven are drawn in a uniformly random order without replacement. What is the probability that the fifth sweet drawn is blue?
wp29-g165.stemRich: A jar contains 6 red sweets and 1 blue sweet. All seven are drawn in a uniformly random order without replacement. What is the probability that the fifth sweet drawn is blue?
wp29-g165.stemHtml: A jar contains 6 red sweets and 1 blue sweet. All seven are drawn in a uniformly random order without replacement. What is the probability that the fifth sweet drawn is blue?
explanation: For the fifth sweet to be blue, the first four must be red. Their successive probabilities are $\frac67$, $\frac56$, $\frac45$ and $\frac34$. Three sweets then remain, one blue, so the fifth draw is blue with probability $\frac13$.

Multiply those conditional probabilities: $\frac67\times\frac56\times\frac45\times\frac34\times\frac13=\frac17$. The middle factors cancel. We do not use the original counts at every stage because the sweets are not replaced.

The last two draws need no further condition. Once the single blue sweet has appeared fifth, the requested event is complete. Including extra probability factors for the remaining red sweets would multiply by one anyway, but they are unnecessary.

methods.title: Follow the required colour sequence
steps: For the fifth sweet to be blue, the first four must be red. Their successive probabilities are $\frac67$, $\frac56$, $\frac45$ and $\frac34$. Three sweets then remain, one blue, so the fifth draw is blue with probability $\frac13$.

Multiply those conditional probabilities: $\frac67\times\frac56\times\frac45\times\frac34\times\frac13=\frac17$. The middle factors cancel. We do not use the original counts at every stage because the sweets are not replaced.

The last two draws need no further condition. Once the single blue sweet has appeared fifth, the requested event is complete. Including extra probability factors for the remaining red sweets would multiply by one anyway, but they are unnecessary.

methods.title: Use symmetry of positions
steps: Imagine the full random order laid out face down. The single blue sweet is equally likely to occupy any of the seven positions. There is nothing special about the fifth position, so its probability is one seventh. The same answer would hold for first, third or last.

This is a particularly useful shortcut because it avoids following all the earlier draws. We do not need to know which red sweet appears in which earlier position. The only feature relevant to the question is the position of the unique blue sweet.

The equal-position argument does not say every colour pattern is equally likely in every urn problem. It works here because a uniformly random ordering makes each individual sweet equally likely to occupy each position. With one blue sweet, counting its position is enough.

methods.title: Count full orders of labelled sweets
steps: Label the red sweets to distinguish all seven objects. There are 7! equally likely full orders. Fix the blue sweet in position five, and arrange the other six in 6! orders. The ratio $\frac{6!}{7!}=\frac17$ confirms the symmetry argument. Labelling identical-colour objects is legitimate because each underlying individual sweet is equally likely at each draw.

geo33-g094.stem: AB is tangent to a circle with center O and radius 4 cm. Given: OA=OB and angle AOB is 90°. What is the area inside triangle AOB but outside the circle (in cm²)?
geo33-g094.stemRich: AB is tangent to a circle with center O and radius 4 cm. Given: $OA=OB$ and angle AOB is 90°. What is the area inside triangle AOB but outside the circle (in cm²)?
geo33-g094.stemHtml: AB is tangent to a circle with center O and radius 4 cm. Given: and angle AOB is 90°. What is the area inside triangle AOB but outside the circle (in cm²)?
explanation: Draw radius OC to the contact point. It is perpendicular to AB and bisects the vertex angle of the right isosceles triangle. Both small triangles are right and isosceles, so AC=CB=OC=4. The triangle has area 8×4 divided by 2=16. The sector is a quarter of 16π, or 4π. Subtract to obtain 16−4π.
geo33-g094.answerHtml: Draw radius OC to the contact point. It is perpendicular to AB and bisects the vertex angle of the right isosceles triangle. Both small triangles are right and isosceles, so AC=CB=OC=4. The triangle has area 8×4 divided by 2=16. The sector is a quarter of 16π, or 4π. Subtract to obtain 16−4π.

methods.title: Subtract a quarter disk from the triangle
steps: Draw radius OC to the contact point. It is perpendicular to AB and bisects the vertex angle of the right isosceles triangle. Both small triangles are right and isosceles, so AC=CB=OC=4. The triangle has area 8×4 divided by 2=16. The sector is a quarter of 16π, or 4π. Subtract to obtain 16−4π.

methods.title: Eliminate choices using a justified area bound
steps: The shaded area is positive and smaller than the whole triangle,16. Since 3<π<4, 8−4π is negative, 8π−8 is greater than 16, and 32−4π is greater than 16. Only 16−4π can be the shaded area. The bound follows from containment, not from estimating the drawing.

methods.title: Find the equal legs instead of the base
steps: The altitude OC=4 splits the right isosceles triangle into two 45°–45°–90° triangles. Hence OA=OB=4√2. Their included angle is 90°, giving area one half of (4√2)²=16. Subtract the 90° sector area 4π.

Given: $OE=EC=12$ cm. What is the area of the shaded region between CD, CE and the minor arc DE (in cm²)?
geo33-g095.stemHtml: ABC is a right triangle whose sides AB and AC are tangent to a circle with center O at B and D, respectively. B, O, E and C lie on one straight line, and E is on the circle. Given: cm. What is the area of the shaded region between CD, CE and the minor arc DE (in cm²)?
explanation: OD=12 and OC=24. Radius OD is perpendicular to tangent DC. Thus ODC is a30°–60°–90° triangle, with DC=12√3 and central angle DOC=60°. Its area is 72√3. The 60° sector has area one sixth of 144π=24π. Their difference is 72√3−24π.
geo33-g095.answerHtml: OD=12 and OC=24. Radius OD is perpendicular to tangent DC. Thus ODC is a30°–60°–90° triangle, with DC=12√3 and central angle DOC=60°. Its area is 72√3. The 60° sector has area one sixth of 144π=24π. Their difference is 72√3−24π.

methods.title: Subtract the 60° sector from a special right triangle
steps: OD=12 and OC=24. Radius OD is perpendicular to tangent DC. Thus ODC is a30°–60°–90° triangle, with DC=12√3 and central angle DOC=60°. Its area is 72√3. The 60° sector has area one sixth of 144π=24π. Their difference is 72√3−24π.

methods.title: Find the tangent using the Pythagorean theorem
steps: DC²=OC²−OD²=24²−12²=432, so DC=12√3. Half of OD×DC is 72√3. Since OD is half the hypotenuse, the angle at C is 30° and the sector angle is 60°, giving the same sector area 24π.

geo33-g096.stem: A semicircle has center O and radius r. A and B lie on its curved boundary, and angle OAB is 60°. What is the ratio of the perimeter of the semicircle to the perimeter of triangle AOB?
geo33-g096.stemRich: A semicircle has center O and radius r. A and B lie on its curved boundary, and angle OAB is 60°. What is the ratio of the perimeter of the semicircle to the perimeter of triangle AOB?
geo33-g096.stemHtml: A semicircle has center O and radius r. A and B lie on its curved boundary, and angle OAB is 60°. What is the ratio of the perimeter of the semicircle to the perimeter of triangle AOB?
explanation: OA=OB=r, so the two base angles of triangle AOB are equal. Both are 60°, making the triangle equilateral with perimeter 3r. The semicircle boundary contains a half circumference πr and diameter 2r, totaling(π+2)r. Divide by 3r and cancel the positive radius to obtain(π+2):3.
geo33-g096.answerHtml: OA=OB=r, so the two base angles of triangle AOB are equal. Both are 60°, making the triangle equilateral with perimeter 3r. The semicircle boundary contains a half circumference πr and diameter 2r, totaling(π+2)r. Divide by 3r and cancel the positive radius to obtain(π+2):3.

methods.title: Write both perimeters in terms of the radius
steps: OA=OB=r, so the two base angles of triangle AOB are equal. Both are 60°, making the triangle equilateral with perimeter 3r. The semicircle boundary contains a half circumference πr and diameter 2r, totaling(π+2)r. Divide by 3r and cancel the positive radius to obtain(π+2):3.

methods.title: Substitute a convenient radius and eliminate expressions
steps: Choose r=2. The triangle perimeter is 6 and the semicircle perimeter is 2π+4, giving (π+2):3. At r=2 the other expressions give π:3, twice the required ratio, or half the required ratio. All three are eliminated.

methods.title: Use scale invariance as an initial filter
steps: Enlarging the whole figure multiplies both perimeters by the same factor, so their ratio cannot depend on r. This eliminates the two expressions with an uncancelled r. The semicircle perimeter includes its diameter, so π:3 omits a required part. The remaining expression is (π+2):3.

geo33-g097.stem: Square ABCD is circumscribed about a circle, and square EFGH is inscribed in the circle. What is the ratio of the area of EFGH to the area of ABCD?
geo33-g097.stemRich: Square ABCD is circumscribed about a circle, and square EFGH is inscribed in the circle. What is the ratio of the area of EFGH to the area of ABCD?
geo33-g097.stemHtml: Square ABCD is circumscribed about a circle, and square EFGH is inscribed in the circle. What is the ratio of the area of EFGH to the area of ABCD?
explanation: Let the circle radius be r. The outer square has side 2r and area 4r². The inner square has diagonal 2r and area (2r)² divided by 2=2r². Its area is half the outer area.
geo33-g097.answerHtml: Let the circle radius be r. The outer square has side 2r and area 4r². The inner square has diagonal 2r and area (2r)² divided by 2=2r². Its area is half the outer area.

methods.title: Use the common diameter
steps: Let the circle radius be r. The outer square has side 2r and area 4r². The inner square has diagonal 2r and area (2r)² divided by 2=2r². Its area is half the outer area.

methods.title: Partition into equal right triangles
steps: Join the center to the four vertices of the inner square. It becomes four congruent right isosceles triangles. The four corner regions between the squares are congruent to those triangles. The inner square therefore contains four of eight equal-area pieces, or half the total.

methods.title: Choose a numerical radius
steps: Choose radius 3. The outer side is 6 and area 36. The inner diagonal is 6 and its area is 18. The ratio 18:36 is 1:2, so the requested fraction is 1:2.

geo33-g098.stem: A circle with center O has radius 9 cm. A, G, F, E and D lie on the same arc in that order. Given: angle ABF is 26°, angle FCD is 49°, and angle GOE is 90°. What is the sum of the lengths of the highlighted minor arcs AG and ED (in cm)?
geo33-g098.stemRich: A circle with center O has radius 9 cm. A, G, F, E and D lie on the same arc in that order. Given: angle ABF is 26°, angle FCD is 49°, and angle GOE is 90°. What is the sum of the lengths of the highlighted minor arcs AG and ED (in cm)?
geo33-g098.stemHtml: A circle with center O has radius 9 cm. A, G, F, E and D lie on the same arc in that order. Given: angle ABF is 26°, angle FCD is 49°, and angle GOE is 90°. What is the sum of the lengths of the highlighted minor arcs AG and ED (in cm)?
explanation: Inscribed angles ABF and FCD intercept arcs AF and FD, whose measures are 52° and 98°. Together arc AD measures 150°. Removing central arc GE of 90° leaves arcs AG and ED totaling 60°. Their length is 60:360 of 18π, or 3π.

geo33-g099.stemHtml: Two congruent circles with centers O and P have radius 4 cm and intersect at A and B. The minor arc AB is one quarter of the circumference of each circle. What is the area of the union of the two disks (in cm²)?
explanation: The 90° minor arcs give angles AOB=APB=90°. OA=AP=PB=BO=4, so OAPB is a square with area 16. Outside this square, the union consists of two 270° sectors, each with area 12π. The total is 24π+16.
geo33-g099.answerHtml: The 90° minor arcs give angles AOB=APB=90°. OA=AP=PB=BO=4, so OAPB is a square with area 16. Outside this square, the union consists of two 270° sectors, each with area 12π. The total is 24π+16.

methods.title: Partition the union into two major sectors and a square
steps: The 90° minor arcs give angles AOB=APB=90°. OA=AP=PB=BO=4, so OAPB is a square with area 16. Outside this square, the union consists of two 270° sectors, each with area 12π. The total is 24π+16.

methods.title: Add the disks and subtract their overlap once
steps: The overlap consists of two 90° sectors minus square OAPB. Its area is 8π−16. The sum of the two disk areas is 32π, so the union area is 32π−(8π−16)=24π+16.

methods.title: Use a bound to eliminate two choices, then calculate the square
steps: The union is larger than one whole disk plus a half of the other:24π. Both expressions beginning with 12π are smaller than 24π. To distinguish 24π+8 from 24π+16, calculate the central square’s area 4²=16. Estimation alone does not settle these two remaining choices.

explanation: The distance between the parallel tangents is the diameter 6, so AB=6. The circle area is 9π. Hence 6×BC=9π and BC=3π:2.
geo33-g100.answerHtml: The distance between the parallel tangents is the diameter 6, so AB=6. The circle area is 9π. Hence 6×BC=9π and BC=3π:2.

methods.title: Set the two areas equal
steps: The distance between the parallel tangents is the diameter 6, so AB=6. The circle area is 9π. Hence 6×BC=9π and BC=3π:2.

methods.title: Use an exact upper bound to eliminate choices
steps: The circle is strictly inside a6-by 6 circumscribed square, so its area is less than 36. A rectangle of equal area and height 6 must have width less than 6. Since π>3, each of 3π,6π and 2π exceeds 6. Only 3π:2 remains.

methods.title: Use the general rectangle-width relation
steps: For a circle of radius r, the tangent rectangle has height 2r. Equal areas give width=πr² divided by 2r=πr:2. Substituting r=3 gives 3π:2.

explanation: Let the small radius be r. The large diameter is 2r+6, so its radius is r+3. The area difference gives π(r+3)²−πr²=21π. Cancel π and expand:6r+9=21, so r=2.
geo33-g101.answerHtml: Let the small radius be r. The large diameter is 2r+6, so its radius is r+3. The area difference gives π(r+3)²−πr²=21π. Cancel π and expand:6r+9=21, so r=2.

methods.title: Express both radii with one variable
steps: Let the small radius be r. The large diameter is 2r+6, so its radius is r+3. The area difference gives π(r+3)²−πr²=21π. Cancel π and expand:6r+9=21, so r=2.

methods.title: Use a difference of squares
steps: The radii differ by 3. Since R²−r²=21, factor to get(R−r)(R+r)=21. Thus R+r=7. Combining sum 7 and difference 3 gives R=5 and r=2.

methods.title: Test numerical choices from the middle of their values
steps: Test r=2: the large radius is 5, and the area difference is (25−4)π=21π, so it fits. The difference equals (6r+9)π and increases as r increases, so no other listed radius can give the same area.

methods.title: Recognise an equilateral triangle

methods.title: Find the altitude of the isosceles triangle
steps: OB=OC=6 and the included angle is 60°. Its equal base angles are 60°, so BC=6. The altitude halves the base to 3 and has length 3√3. Half of 6×3√3 is 9√3.

geo33-g088.stem: Two congruent circles with centers O and M are externally tangent. Each has radius 4 cm. MA and MB are tangent to the circle with center O at A and B. What is the smaller angle AOB?
geo33-g088.stemRich: Two congruent circles with centers O and M are externally tangent. Each has radius 4 cm. MA and MB are tangent to the circle with center O at A and B. What is the smaller angle AOB?
geo33-g088.stemHtml: Two congruent circles with centers O and M are externally tangent. Each has radius 4 cm. MA and MB are tangent to the circle with center O at A and B. What is the smaller angle AOB?
explanation: OM is the sum of the two radii,8. OA=4 and is perpendicular to MA, so right triangle OAM has a leg half its hypotenuse. The angle at M is 30° and angle AOM 60°. Symmetry doubles the latter, giving angle AOB 120°.
geo33-g088.answerHtml: OM is the sum of the two radii,8. OA=4 and is perpendicular to MA, so right triangle OAM has a leg half its hypotenuse. The angle at M is 30° and angle AOM 60°. Symmetry doubles the latter, giving angle AOB 120°.

methods.title: Use the line joining the centers
steps: OM is the sum of the two radii,8. OA=4 and is perpendicular to MA, so right triangle OAM has a leg half its hypotenuse. The angle at M is 30° and angle AOM 60°. Symmetry doubles the latter, giving angle AOB 120°.

methods.title: Use the tangent kite after finding the angle at M
steps: The two matching right triangles make angle AMB=60°. In kite OAMB, the two contact angles are 90°. Its angle at O is 360°−90°−90°−60°=120°.

geo33-g089.stem: The circumference of the smaller circle is 8\pi cm, and the shaded area inside the larger circle but outside the smaller one is 65\pi cm². Between which two values is the circumference of the larger circle (in cm)?
geo33-g089.stemRich: The circumference of the smaller circle is $8\pi$ cm, and the shaded area inside the larger circle but outside the smaller one is $65\pi$ cm². Between which two values is the circumference of the larger circle (in cm)?
geo33-g089.stemHtml: The circumference of the smaller circle is cm, and the shaded area inside the larger circle but outside the smaller one is cm². Between which two values is the circumference of the larger circle (in cm)?
explanation: The small radius is 4 and its area 16π. Adding the shaded 65π gives the large area 81π, so its radius is 9 and circumference 18π. Using π≈3.14 gives about 56.52, between 56 and 57.
geo33-g089.answerHtml: The small radius is 4 and its area 16π. Adding the shaded 65π gives the large area 81π, so its radius is 9 and circumference 18π. Using π≈3.14 gives about 56.52, between 56 and 57.

methods.title: Find both radii through the areas
steps: The small radius is 4 and its area 16π. Adding the shaded 65π gives the large area 81π, so its radius is 9 and circumference 18π. Using π≈3.14 gives about 56.52, between 56 and 57.

methods.title: Use the circumference–area relationship
steps: For a circle, area equals circumference squared divided by 4π. The smaller circumference 8π gives 16π area. Thus the larger circumference squared is 4π×81π=324π², giving 18π and the same interval.

geo33-g090.stem: The sides of triangle ABC are 7 cm, 24 cm and 25 cm. What is the circumference of the circle circumscribed about the triangle (in cm)?
geo33-g090.stemRich: The sides of triangle ABC are 7 cm, 24 cm and 25 cm. What is the circumference of the circle circumscribed about the triangle (in cm)?
geo33-g090.stemHtml: The sides of triangle ABC are 7 cm, 24 cm and 25 cm. What is the circumference of the circle circumscribed about the triangle (in cm)?
explanation: 7²+24²=49+576=625=25², so the triangle is right. In its circumscribed circle, the hypotenuse 25 is a diameter. Circumference equals π times diameter, giving 25π.
geo33-g090.answerHtml: 7²+24²=49+576=625=25², so the triangle is right. In its circumscribed circle, the hypotenuse 25 is a diameter. Circumference equals π times diameter, giving 25π.

methods.title: Recognise the right triangle and its diameter
steps: 7²+24²=49+576=625=25², so the triangle is right. In its circumscribed circle, the hypotenuse 25 is a diameter. Circumference equals π times diameter, giving 25π.

methods.title: Use the midpoint of the hypotenuse as the center
steps: In a right triangle the midpoint of the hypotenuse is equally distant from all three vertices. Its distance is half of 25, or 12.5. Therefore the circumscribed circle has circumference 2π×12.5=25π.

geo33-g091.stemRich: A circle has radius $\sqrt{30}$ cm. Its central angles alternate between α and β, with six angles of each kind, as in the accompanying figure. One α-sector and one β-sector are shaded. What is their total area (in cm²)?
geo33-g091.stemHtml: A circle has radius cm. Its central angles alternate between α and β, with six angles of each kind, as in the accompanying figure. One α-sector and one β-sector are shaded. What is their total area (in cm²)?
explanation: The full turn gives 6α+6β=360°, so α+β=60°. The two shaded sectors cover one sixth of the circle. Its area is 30π, so the shaded total is 5π.
geo33-g091.answerHtml: The full turn gives 6α+6β=360°, so α+β=60°. The two shaded sectors cover one sixth of the circle. Its area is 30π, so the shaded total is 5π.

methods.title: Find the sum of the two needed angles
steps: The full turn gives 6α+6β=360°, so α+β=60°. The two shaded sectors cover one sixth of the circle. Its area is 30π, so the shaded total is 5π.

methods.title: Group the sectors into six identical area sums
steps: Each α-sector has the same area as every other α-sector; likewise for β. Six pairs cover the entire disk. One α-sector plus one β-sector therefore has one sixth of the total area 30π, giving 5π, even though the shaded sectors are separated.

geo33-g092.stem: Three circles with centers A, B and C are externally tangent to one another. Their radii are 2 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm, respectively. What is the length of the highlighted arc of the circle with center A (in cm)?
geo33-g092.stemRich: Three circles with centers A, B and C are externally tangent to one another. Their radii are 2 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm, respectively. What is the length of the highlighted arc of the circle with center A (in cm)?
geo33-g092.stemHtml: Three circles with centers A, B and C are externally tangent to one another. Their radii are 2 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm, respectively. What is the length of the highlighted arc of the circle with center A (in cm)?
explanation: The center distances are AB=2+4=6, AC=2+6=8 and BC=4+6=10. Thus angle A is 90°. The short arc between the two contact points is one quarter of the small circle, so the highlighted major arc is three quarters of circumference 4π, giving 3π.
geo33-g092.answerHtml: The center distances are AB=2+4=6, AC=2+6=8 and BC=4+6=10. Thus angle A is 90°. The short arc between the two contact points is one quarter of the small circle, so the highlighted major arc is three quarters of circumference 4π, giving 3π.

methods.title: Join the centers and recognise a right triangle
steps: The center distances are AB=2+4=6, AC=2+6=8 and BC=4+6=10. Thus angle A is 90°. The short arc between the two contact points is one quarter of the small circle, so the highlighted major arc is three quarters of circumference 4π, giving 3π.

geo33-advanced-p02.stemHtml: AD is a diameter. B, C, F and G divide one semicircular arc AD into five equal arcs, and E is the midpoint of arc AB. What is angle ADE?

methods.title: Find the fraction of a full circumference

geo33-advanced-p03.stem: A circle with center O has radius 6 cm. OACD is a square, C lies on the circle, and ray OA meets the circle at B. What is AB (in cm)?
geo33-advanced-p03.stemRich: A circle with center O has radius 6 cm. OACD is a square, C lies on the circle, and ray OA meets the circle at B. What is AB (in cm)?
geo33-advanced-p03.stemHtml: A circle with center O has radius 6 cm. OACD is a square, C lies on the circle, and ray OA meets the circle at B. What is AB (in cm)?
explanation: OC is both a radius of length 6 and a square diagonal. Thus OA=6 divided by √2=3√2. Since OB=6, AB=OB−OA=6−3√2.
geo33-advanced-p03.answerHtml: OC is both a radius of length 6 and a square diagonal. Thus OA=6 divided by √2=3√2. Since OB=6, AB=OB−OA=6−3√2.

methods.title: Use the square diagonal
steps: OC is both a radius of length 6 and a square diagonal. Thus OA=6 divided by √2=3√2. Since OB=6, AB=OB−OA=6−3√2.

methods.title: Use the Pythagorean theorem in the square
steps: Let the square side be s. Its diagonal satisfies 2s²=6², so s²=18 and s=3√2. Subtract this side from radius OB to obtain 6−3√2.
