beats.title: The Language of Algebra

lines.say: Welcome to your very first algebra lesson.
Algebra is about a quarter of the quantitative section — roughly 5 questions out of 20.
But honestly? It's way bigger than that.
Word problems, geometry — almost every time, you end up building an equation and solving it.
Moving terms across, isolating an unknown — that's algebra. And it runs through the whole section.
It's the language every quantitative question is written in.
So we start with definitions — a shared vocabulary.
Because when a question says "prime" or "even," you need to know exactly what that allows… and what it rules out.
Let's go.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Integers

lines.say: First word: integer.

lines.label: The word 'Integer' pops up at the top

lines.say: An integer is a whole number — it splits into whole units of one.
No fractions. No decimals. Nothing after the decimal point.

lines.label: A clean number line from −4 to 4 appears

lines.say: Here's the integer line. One, two, three — sure.
But it doesn't stop at zero.
Negative three? Integer. The minus sign just tells you which side of zero you're on.
And zero is an integer too. Sounds a bit strange — say it out loud anyway.

lines.label: Three test numbers appear in a row: −12, 0.6, ½

lines.say: Quick test. Integer or not?

lines.draw: Tick ✓ under −12; cross ✗ under 0.6 and under ½

lines.say: Negative twelve — integer. Zero point six and one half sit between the marks. Not integers.
Exam habit: "integer" lets in negatives and zero.
Don't quietly upgrade it to "positive integer." That's adding information the question never gave you — and there's a wrong answer waiting for it.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Integers" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Fractions

lines.say: Next: fractions.

lines.label: The word 'Fraction' pops up at the top

lines.say: A fraction is a number that isn't whole — one number divided by another. And the denominator is never zero.
Now kill this myth: a fraction does NOT have to be smaller than one.
Nine quarters.
Four quarters fill one whole. Another four fill a second. One quarter left over.
Two and a quarter. Bigger than one — still a fraction. We call it improper, but there's nothing wrong with it.

lines.label: ½ and 0.5 appear side by side

lines.say: Fractions come in two spellings: ordinary fractions and decimals.

lines.draw: Draw an equals sign between ½ and 0.5

lines.say: One half and zero point five — same number, same point on the line.
On the exam you'll mostly see ordinary fractions. Decimals show up less — but they show up, and we'll train both.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Fractions" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Natural numbers

lines.say: Natural numbers.
In this course, natural numbers are the positive counting numbers.
One, two, three — and on forever.
Truth is, the exam rarely uses this term. What it loves is a different phrase.
Positive integer.

lines.draw: Draw a double arrow linking 'Natural numbers' and 'Positive integer'

lines.say: Same set. Whole numbers, above zero. Not negative, and not zero.
Some books sneak zero into the natural numbers. If a question ever defines it differently — the question wins.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Natural numbers" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Positive & negative

lines.say: Positive and negative.
Positive means greater than zero. That's it.
It does NOT mean integer.
Two thirds — positive. Three point two — positive.
Negative means below zero — with exactly the same freedom.
Negative seven. Negative one fifth. Both negative.
One more word to watch.
Nonnegative means zero OR positive. That little line lets zero in.
Read the word in front of you — not the example in your head.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Positive & negative" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Opposites

lines.say: Opposite numbers.

lines.label: The word 'Opposites' pops up at the top

lines.say: Two opposites sit the same distance from zero — on opposite sides.

lines.label: A clean number line from −8 to 8 appears

lines.draw: Put dots on 7 and −7, and draw an arc from each one to 0

lines.say: Seven and negative seven. Mirror images across zero.
Add them — you land exactly on zero. That's the test: opposites add up to zero.
Fractions work the same way.
Now the trap that runs all course long.
"Negative x" means the opposite of x. It does NOT mean "a negative number."
If x is negative four, then negative x is positive four.
And zero? It's its own opposite. Flip its sign — nothing changes.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Opposites" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Consecutive numbers

lines.say: Consecutive numbers.
Consecutive numbers are integers that follow each other — each one exactly 1 more than the one before.

lines.draw: Draw a "+1" hop between each pair

lines.say: Zero, one, two, three.

lines.draw: Draw a "+1" hop between each pair

lines.say: And negatives count too. Negative two, negative one, zero — a gap of exactly one each time.
Two conditions, always: integers, and a difference of exactly one.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Consecutive numbers" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Remainders

lines.say: Remainders.

lines.label: The word 'Remainder' pops up at the top

lines.say: The remainder is what's left over when a division doesn't come out whole.
Ten divided by three.

lines.draw: Under it write "3 · 3 = 9", then "10 − 9 = 1", and circle the 1

lines.say: Three fits in whole up to nine — three times. Then one is left.
Three can't fit into that one. So one is the remainder.
Twelve divided by five. Five fits twice — up to ten. Two left over. Remainder two.
Notice: the remainder is always smaller than the number you divide by. If it isn't, another group still fits.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Remainders" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Even & odd

lines.say: Even and odd.
An even number is an integer that divides by two with no remainder. Every even number can be written as two k.
Odd is two k plus one — one more than an even number.

lines.label: Four numbers appear in a row: 8, 9, −8, −9

lines.draw: Write "E" under 8 and −8, and "O" under 9 and −9

lines.say: Eight — even. Nine — odd.
Negative eight? Still even — it's two times negative four. Negative nine: odd.
The sign has nothing to do with it.

lines.draw: Draw a big ✗ next to ½

lines.say: One half? It's not even — but that doesn't make it odd. It's neither.
Even and odd only exist for integers.
So when a question says n is odd, you just learned two things: n is an integer — and it's in the odd group.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Even & odd" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Zero

lines.say: Zero gets its own slide. It's the exam's favourite troublemaker.

lines.label: A clean number line from −4 to 4 appears

lines.draw: Circle 0; write "+" over the right side and "−" over the left side

lines.say: Right of zero — positive. Left of zero — negative.
Zero itself? Neither positive nor negative. It's the only number like that.
And zero is even. Zero divided by two is zero — no remainder.
Here's a trick to remember it. Is one thousand three hundred fifty-eight even? Everyone says yes — it ends in eight.
Four fifty-six? Even — it ends in six. And three fifty? Even too. It ends in zero.
Zero is an even digit… and an even number.

lines.label: The summary line appears: zero is an integer, even, neither + nor −

lines.say: Lock it in. Zero is an integer, zero is even, and zero is neither positive nor negative.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Zero" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Primes

lines.say: Prime numbers. Just a first taste — there's a full chapter on these later.

lines.label: The word 'Prime' pops up at the top

lines.say: A prime is a positive integer with exactly two different divisors: one, and itself.
Put differently — you can't break it into a product of smaller whole numbers.
Fifteen? Three times five. It breaks. Not prime — we call that composite.
Five? Five times one doesn't count — you're still holding the five.
And two plus three is a sum, not a product. So five is prime.
Here are the first few.
Two edges the exam loves. Zero and one are NOT prime. One has only one divisor.
And two IS prime — the only even prime. Every bigger even number also divides by two.
Which means every prime except two is odd.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Primes" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Reciprocals

lines.say: One more idea — and people mix it up with opposites constantly.

lines.label: The word 'Reciprocals' pops up at the top

lines.say: A number times its reciprocal gives one.

lines.draw: Draw a flip arrow from 3/5 to 5/3, then write "= 1"

lines.say: For a fraction — just flip it.
Whole numbers too. Eight is eight over one, so its reciprocal is one eighth.
Keep the sign: the reciprocal of negative two is negative one half.
Nothing times zero gives you one. So zero has no reciprocal.
Can't remember which is which?

lines.label: The summary line appears: opposites sum to 0, reciprocals multiply to 1

lines.say: Check the result. Opposites add to zero. Reciprocals multiply to one.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Reciprocals" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: $1$ is not prime · $2$ is the only even prime

lines.say: Let's lock it all in.
"Integer" lets in negatives and zero.
"Nonzero" still allows negatives. And "positive" still allows fractions.

lines.label: '1 is not prime · 2 is the only even prime' appears

lines.say: Most of this you already knew. The surprises — zero is even, one isn't prime — are exactly where the traps are.
Five questions next. Don't rush them. Miss one? Go find the word you skipped.
Next lessons: the real basics — addition, subtraction, multiplication, division.
Then, step by step, the bigger techniques: equations, powers, roots — and question types you never met at school. See you there.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Addition & Subtraction

lines.say: Addition and subtraction. The base of the base.
Remember — there's no calculator on this exam.
Good news: the numbers are rarely big. Most of this you'll do in your head.
But when a longer calculation does show up, you want a method that never fails.
Let's build it.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Signed numbers

lines.say: Signed numbers — a fancy name for numbers with a plus or a minus attached.
Rule number one: a sign always belongs to the number right after it.

lines.draw: Circle "−14" together with its minus sign

lines.say: That minus belongs to the fourteen.
A plus and a minus side by side — different signs — collapse into one minus.

lines.label: A clean number line from −15 to 15 appears

lines.draw: Dot at 9, arrow 14 steps to the left, landing dot at −5

lines.say: Start at nine. Move fourteen to the left. Sail past zero… and land on negative five.

lines.draw: Back on the top line, write "= −5"

lines.say: Shortcut: different signs? Take the difference — fourteen minus nine is five — and the bigger one decides the sign.
Fourteen was the negative one. So: negative five.

lines.draw: On the number line, arrow from −9 moving 14 to the right, landing on 5; write "= 5"

lines.say: Flip it. Start at negative nine, move fourteen to the right. Positive five.
Same difference, five — but this time the bigger one is positive.
What you must NEVER do: strip the signs, add nine and fourteen, and stick a sign on at the end.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Signed numbers" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Same signs

lines.say: Now two signs that match.

lines.draw: Circle the two minus signs and write "+" above them

lines.say: Two of the same sign side by side — minus, minus — become a plus.
Subtracting negative four is adding four. Ten.
And plus, plus? That's just a plus. Ignore the extra plus sign.
So the rule: same signs side by side — write plus. Different signs — write minus.
Careful — turning it into a plus does NOT guarantee a positive answer. You still calculate.
Negative six plus four: negative two.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Same signs" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Two negatives

lines.say: Now both numbers are negative.
They push in the same direction. Eight to the left of zero… then six more to the left.
So ignore the minus for a second. Eight plus six is fourteen.
Both were negative — put the minus back. Negative fourteen.
Same move, written as a subtraction. Same answer.
Now a warning about a slogan: "two minuses make a plus."
Here we've got two minus signs — and the answer is firmly negative.
That slogan belongs to specific operations. Name the operation first — THEN reach for a sign rule.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Two negatives" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Any order

lines.say: In addition and subtraction, the order doesn't matter — as long as every sign travels with its number.

lines.draw: Underline 12 and +3 in one colour, −7 and −5 in another

lines.say: Gather the positives: twelve and three — fifteen.
Gather the negatives: seven and five — twelve.
Fifteen minus twelve: three.
Move the seven and leave its minus behind? You've changed the problem.
Easier trick: put the bigger number first. Negative nine plus fourteen is fourteen minus nine. Five.
Bigger minus smaller — and the answer takes the sign of the bigger one.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Any order" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Column addition

lines.say: Column addition — for when the numbers get longer.
Job one is alignment. Ones under ones, tens under tens, hundreds under hundreds.
Think graph paper: room for exactly one digit per square.
And we always start from the right.
Seven plus five is twelve. But there's only room for one digit.

lines.draw: Under the ones column write 2; write a small 1 above the tens column

lines.say: Write the two. Carry the one to the tens — and that one is really one ten.
Tens: six plus eight plus the carried one — fifteen.

lines.draw: Under the tens write 5; write a small 1 above the hundreds column

lines.say: Write five, carry one.
Hundreds: four plus two plus one. Seven.
Seven hundred fifty-two.
Now — every single time — sense-check it.
About five hundred plus about three hundred — around eight hundred. Our answer fits.
Seventy-five would be absurd. Seven thousand would be absurd. Estimating catches place-value slips for free.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Column addition" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — 467 + 285, stacked in columns with the answer line drawn

beats.title: Column subtraction

lines.say: Column subtraction. Same alignment. Right to left.
Ones: three minus six. Can't do it — we can't write a negative in the middle of a number.
So the three turns to its neighbour and says: lend me a ten.
Usually that's easy — the neighbour hands over a ten and drops by one.
But the neighbour is zero. It's got nothing.
Zero says: don't worry, I've got you. And goes to the seven.

lines.draw: Cross out the 7 and write 6 above it

lines.say: Seven lends a hundred — and drops to six.

lines.draw: Cross out the 0 and write 10 above it; then cross out the 10 and write 9

lines.say: Now zero has ten tens. It passes one ten down to the three — and keeps nine.

lines.draw: Write a small 1 in front of the 3, making 13

lines.say: The three is now thirteen.
Pause. We added nothing. Six hundreds, nine tens, thirteen ones — still seven hundred three.
Thirteen minus six: seven.
Nine minus eight: one.
Six minus two: four. Four hundred seventeen.
Check it: add back what you subtracted. Four seventeen plus two eighty-six — seven hundred three.
If you'd gotten five seventeen, this check exposes the hundred you forgot to reduce.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Column subtraction" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — 703 − 286, stacked in columns with the answer line drawn

beats.title: Round numbers

lines.say: You don't always need columns.
Three ninety-eight is sitting right next to four hundred.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow moving 2 from the 57 over to the 398

lines.say: Move two across.
Four hundred plus fifty-five: four fifty-five. The total never changed.
Subtraction: take away a round two hundred instead.
But that's two too many — so give two back.
Four hundred four.
Subtract too much, and the result's too small — so you fix it by adding.
If the fix isn't instantly obvious, go back to columns. A shortcut only counts if you can say why it works.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Round numbers" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Name the operation first, then the sign rule.
Align the columns. Track every carry and every borrow.
Estimate to check the size of your answer.

lines.say: Let's lock it in.
Same signs side by side — plus. Different signs — minus.

lines.label: 'Name the operation first, then the sign rule.' appears
'Align the columns. Track every carry and every borrow.' appears
'Estimate to check the size of your answer.' appears

lines.say: This is stuff you need to handle with your eyes closed. If it's still slow — practise until it isn't.
Five questions next — no video between them. Take your time, then check the written solutions.
Next up: multiplication and division. See you there.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Multiplication & Division

lines.say: Multiplication and division.
We're still in the foundations — the base of the base.
Everything later is built on this. So let's make it bulletproof.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Sign rules

lines.say: Before you multiply or divide anything — look at the signs.
Same signs — both positive or both negative — give a positive.
Ignore the minuses for a second. Four sevens: twenty-eight.
Same signs — positive twenty-eight.
Different signs — one positive, one negative — give a negative.
Same twenty-eight — but only one minus. Negative twenty-eight.

lines.draw: Next to both rules, write "× and :"

lines.say: And division follows the exact same rules.
Working method: split the job in two. Decide the sign. Then do the numbers.
And don't confuse this with adding negatives — that's a completely different rule.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Sign rules" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Zero

lines.say: Zero plays by its own rules.
Anything times zero is zero. Three, negative four, a million — times zero, it's zero.
Zero divided by nine. Picture it: zero cakes, shared between nine people.
Everyone gets… nothing. Zero.
Now flip it. Nine cakes — shared between zero people.
There's nobody to share with. It makes no sense.

lines.draw: Draw a big ✗ next to it

lines.say: Dividing by zero is undefined. It has no meaning at all.
That's why questions always make sure a denominator can't be zero — look for the condition that guarantees it.
And a fraction bar? It's just division in a different coat.
Twenty-four over six is twenty-four divided by six. Four.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Zero" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Long multiplication

lines.say: For bigger numbers: long multiplication. Stack them, lined up on the right — just like column addition.
Take the bottom number's rightmost digit — the seven — and run it across the top number.
Seven times six: forty-two.

lines.draw: Under the line write 2 in the ones place; write a small 4 above the 4

lines.say: Write two, carry four.
Seven times four: twenty-eight. Plus the carried four: thirty-two.
Careful — the carried digit gets ADDED, not multiplied.

lines.draw: Write 2 in the tens place; write a small 3 above the 2

lines.say: Write two, carry three.
Seven times two: fourteen. Plus three: seventeen.
First row: one thousand seven hundred twenty-two.
Now the three. But it sits in the tens place — it's really thirty.

lines.draw: Start the second row: write a 0 in the ones place

lines.say: So this row starts one place to the left. That zero isn't decoration — it records that we're multiplying by tens.
Three times two forty-six: seven thirty-eight. With the zero: seven thousand three hundred eighty.

lines.draw: Draw a line under both rows and add them: 9102

lines.say: Add the rows: nine thousand one hundred two.
Sense-check: two-fifty times forty is ten thousand. Both our numbers are a little smaller. Right where it should be.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Long multiplication" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — 246 × 37, stacked in columns with the first line drawn

beats.title: Splitting a factor

lines.say: Long multiplication works. But multiplication can also be done by splitting — and on this exam, that's usually the faster way.
Remember when we called it "times"? Seventeen times eight means seventeen eights.
So split the seventeen.
Ten eights, plus seven eights.
Ten eights: eighty. Seven eights: fifty-six.
Add them: one hundred thirty-six.
That's the distributive law — the eight multiplies both pieces.
On this exam it's usually a one-digit number times a two-digit number — and splitting is the way we'll work, much more than long multiplication.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Splitting a factor" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Long division

lines.say: Long division. Different layout — and this time we start from the LEFT.
Seven into three? Doesn't fit. So take two digits: thirty-two.
Seven into thirty-two goes four times. Five times would be thirty-five — too much.

lines.draw: Write 4 above the 2; write 28 under 32 and subtract, leaving 4

lines.say: Four sevens are twenty-eight. Subtract: four left over.

lines.draw: Bring the 7 down next to the 4, making 47

lines.say: Bring down the next digit. Forty-seven.

lines.draw: Write 6 on top; write 42 under 47 and subtract, leaving 5

lines.say: Seven into forty-seven: six times, forty-two. Remainder five.

lines.draw: Bring the 6 down, making 56; write 8 on top; write 56 and subtract, leaving 0

lines.say: Bring down the six: fifty-six. Seven into fifty-six — exactly eight. Nothing left.
Four hundred sixty-eight.

lines.label: The cycle appears: Divide → multiply → subtract → bring down

lines.say: That's the whole engine, on repeat.
Check it by multiplying back. It rebuilds the number exactly.
And notice — you can't run this without your times table. How else do you know seven goes into forty-seven six times?

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Long division" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — 3276 ÷ 7 in a long-division frame (divisor outside, space for the quotient on top)

beats.title: Smart division

lines.say: Long division works. But on this exam, there's a faster way.
Remember this: on the psychometric, calculations are always SIMPLE.
Not always EASY — you might have to think hard. But the arithmetic itself? Simple.
They're not testing whether you're a pocket calculator. They're testing understanding.
So split the number into chunks that eight divides easily.
Seven eights are fifty-six — so seventy eights are five hundred sixty.
Five seventy-six is five-sixty plus sixteen.
Five-sixty over eight: seventy. Sixteen over eight: two. Seventy-two.
Notice what we split: the number being divided. Never the divisor.
Twelve over two-plus-four is NOT twelve over two plus twelve over four. We'll hit that hard later.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Smart division" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Many negatives

lines.say: One last sign trick: what about a whole pile of factors?

lines.draw: Draw a bracket joining (−2) and (−3), and write "+" under it

lines.say: Every pair of negatives cancels into a positive.
Three negatives — two pair up, one is left over.
So the product is negative. Negative thirty.

lines.draw: Bracket the negatives in two pairs, then write "= +30"

lines.say: Add a fourth negative — everything pairs off. Positive thirty.
So just count the negative factors. Even — positive. Odd — negative.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Many negatives" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Signs first · split to multiply · split to divide

lines.say: One last thing — and I'm serious about this one.
No calculator. Every small step lives in your times table. It has to be perfect, up to ten times ten.
You don't need twelve times twelve. If you know up to ten, you can build the rest.
Twelve nines: ten nines plus two nines. One hundred eight.

lines.label: 'Signs first · split to multiply · split to divide' appears

lines.say: Five questions next. Written or mental — whatever's clearest. Just make sure you could explain any shortcut you use.
Then: order of operations.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: What Is a Fraction?

lines.say: Fractions. Another piece of the algebra foundations.
You'll need them for equations and expressions — and for word problems and geometry too.
So before any rules, let's get what a fraction actually IS.
Let's start.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Part of a whole

items.t: Equal parts of the same whole

lines.say: A fraction is a part of a whole.

lines.label: A pizza cut into 4 equal slices appears, 1 slice shaded

lines.say: Here's a whole pizza cut into four slices. One is shaded.
One out of four. We write it one over four — one quarter.
Read that fraction bar as "out of."

lines.label: 'Equal parts of the same whole' appears

lines.say: And one word is essential: EQUAL.
One giant slice and three tiny ones? Then one slice is NOT a quarter.
Whenever we cut a whole, we cut it into equal parts.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Part of a whole" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Parts of a fraction

items.t: Numerator — how many pieces we have
Denominator — how many equal pieces make one whole

lines.label: A pizza appears with 3 of 4 slices shaded

lines.say: Now shade three of the four slices.
Three quarters. Three copies of one quarter.

lines.label: 'Numerator — how many pieces we have' appears
'Denominator — how many equal pieces make one whole' appears

lines.say: The number on top is the numerator. It counts the pieces we have.
The number underneath is the denominator. It tells you how many equal pieces make one whole.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow from each label to its number

lines.say: Watch the trap: the denominator is NOT the unshaded pieces.
There's one unshaded slice here — and the denominator is still four.
Top: numerator. Bottom: denominator.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Parts of a fraction" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Improper & mixed

lines.say: Who says we can only count pieces from one whole?

lines.label: Two pizzas appear, cut in quarters: the first fully shaded, the second 3/4 shaded

lines.say: Seven quarter-slices. The first four fill a whole pizza. Three more go into the next one.
Seven quarters — the numerator is bigger than the denominator. That's an improper fraction.
"Improper" is just a name. It's bigger than one — and it's perfectly correct.
Same amount: one whole and three quarters. That's a mixed number — a whole number AND a fraction.
And that "and" means PLUS. One plus three quarters. Never times.
When top and bottom are equal, the fraction is exactly one. Eight quarters? Exactly two.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Improper & mixed" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Improper → mixed

lines.say: Improper to mixed: how many times does the denominator fit into the numerator? Four into fifteen?
Four fits in whole up to twelve — three times. That's the whole part.
Three left over. The remainder goes on top.
The denominator stays four. Three and three quarters.
Why does this work? Because a fraction bar IS division. Fifteen over four is fifteen divided by four.
And that's why a denominator can never be zero.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Improper → mixed" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Mixed → improper

lines.say: And back the other way: mixed number to improper fraction.
Count everything in fifths.
Each whole holds five fifths. Two wholes: ten fifths.
Plus the three extra fifths.
Thirteen fifths.
The rule: whole number times denominator, plus numerator — over the SAME denominator.
The pieces didn't change size, so the denominator stays five.
Check it by going back: five into thirteen — two times, three left over. Two and three fifths.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Mixed → improper" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Expanding

lines.say: Take half a pizza.

lines.label: Three pizzas appear: 1/2, 2/4 and 4/8 shaded — the same half each time

lines.say: Cut every slice in two. Then again.
Same shaded half — two quarters, then four eighths.
The amount never changed. Top and bottom both changed — by the same factor.
That's expanding: multiply the numerator AND the denominator by the same number.

lines.draw: Write "×4" on top and bottom, then "= 12/20"

lines.say: Three fifths, times four on top and bottom: twelve twentieths.
Change only one of them? You've changed the amount. Two quarters is a half — but two halves is a whole.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Expanding" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Reducing

lines.say: Reducing is the same move backwards: DIVIDE top and bottom by the same number.
Picture the pizza: erase some of the cut lines. Fewer, bigger slices — the same shaded amount.
Eighteen and twenty-four — both divide by six.

lines.draw: Write ":6" on top and bottom, then "= 3/4"

lines.say: Three quarters.
Didn't spot the six? No problem — go in stages.
Divide by two: nine twelfths. Divide by three: three quarters. Same place.
You're done when top and bottom share no common factor except one.
And an unreduced fraction isn't wrong. Sometimes you WANT the bigger denominator — to match another fraction.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Reducing" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Bigger or smaller?

lines.say: What happens when we change the numbers?

lines.label: Two pizzas appear: 1/4 shaded and 3/4 shaded

lines.say: Grow the numerator — more pieces — and the fraction grows.
One quarter, three quarters. More pizza. Easy.

lines.label: Two more pizzas appear: 1/4 shaded and 1/6 shaded

lines.say: Now the tricky one. Grow the denominator — and the fraction SHRINKS.
Same pizza, cut into six instead of four. Every slice gets smaller.
One sixth is less than one quarter — even though six is bigger than four.
Think of cakes shared between people. The numerator is the cakes. The denominator is the people.
More cakes — everyone gets more. More people — everyone gets less.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Bigger or smaller?" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: What cancelling means

lines.say: You'll hear "cancel" constantly. Here's what it really means.
Divide the WHOLE top and the WHOLE bottom by the same number.
Both are six times something. Divide both by six: five sevenths.
But look at this one. Now the top is six PLUS five.

lines.draw: Draw a big ✗ over the 6 on top

lines.say: That six isn't a factor of the whole top. You can NOT cancel it.
Ask yourself: does it multiply the ENTIRE top and the ENTIRE bottom? If not — hands off.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "What cancelling means" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Numerator: how many pieces · Denominator: how many make a whole
Bigger numerator $\to$ bigger · Bigger denominator $\to$ smaller
Same factor on top and bottom $\to$ same value
Cancel factors — never terms in a sum

lines.say: Let's lock it in.

lines.label: 'Numerator: how many pieces · Denominator: how many make a whole' appears
'Bigger numerator → bigger · Bigger denominator → smaller' appears
'Same factor on top and bottom → same value' appears
'Cancel factors — never terms in a sum' appears

lines.say: This lesson is the foundation for every fraction you'll meet — in algebra, word problems and geometry.
Five questions next. Before you calculate, say what the numbers are counting.
Next: multiplying and dividing fractions.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Multiplying & Dividing Fractions

lines.say: Multiplying and dividing fractions.
Good news: multiplying is the EASIEST fraction operation. Easier than adding.
And we'll use the reducing skills from the last lesson. If those still feel shaky — go back and practise first.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Multiplying

lines.say: What does three quarters OF two fifths even mean? Let's see it.

lines.label: A 4 × 5 grid appears: 2 columns shaded, 3 rows shaded, overlap in dark blue

lines.say: Two columns out of five: two fifths. Then three rows out of four: three quarters of that.

lines.draw: Circle the dark overlap and count the 6 small squares

lines.say: The overlap: six little pieces, out of twenty in the whole.
So: top times top, bottom times bottom. Six twentieths — reduce to three tenths.
No common denominator needed. That's only for adding.
Two sevenths times three fifths: six thirty-fifths.
Two fractions below one, multiplied — the answer is SMALLER. You're taking a part of a part.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Multiplying" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Cancel first

lines.say: We could multiply fourteen by twenty-five… and fifteen by twenty-one… and then reduce some monster fraction.
Or: cancel FIRST.
Fourteen and twenty-one share a seven.
Two and three.
Twenty-five and fifteen share a five.
Five and three.
Ten ninths.
Straight down or diagonally across — it doesn't matter. Once you multiply, all the tops are one product and all the bottoms are another.
But ONLY with multiplication. A plus or a minus in there? No cancelling.
Didn't spot it early? No problem — you can still reduce at the end.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Cancel first" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Whole numbers

lines.say: A whole number has no denominator… or does it?
Six is six over one. Six cakes for one person — six.
Now it's a normal fraction times a fraction.

lines.draw: Cross out 6 and 12; write 1 and 2; then write "= 7/2"

lines.say: Six and twelve cancel to one and two. Seven halves.
Seven halves is bigger than one — improper. You can also write it as three and a half.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Whole numbers" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Use the reciprocal

lines.say: Now the rule. To divide by a fraction — multiply by its reciprocal.
Keep the first fraction. Change divide to times. Flip the second.
Three quarters times five halves.
Fifteen eighths.
Which one do you flip? Only the one AFTER the division sign. Never the first.
Remember the name: multiply by the reciprocal. First you change to multiply — THEN you flip. So the flip lands on the second one.
Dividing by a whole number? Same rule. Five is five over one — flip it to one fifth.
Five sixths times one fifth: one sixth.
And you can never divide by zero — so zero has no reciprocal.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Use the reciprocal" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Stacked fractions

lines.say: Looks scary. It isn't.
Find the main fraction bar — the longest one, level with where the equals sign would sit.

lines.draw: Trace over the long main bar

lines.say: So it's five sixths DIVIDED BY ten ninths.
Rewrite it on one line. Now it's plain division.
Multiply by the reciprocal.

lines.draw: Cancel 5 with 10 (1 and 2) and 9 with 6 (3 and 2); write "= 3/4"

lines.say: Five and ten: one and two. Nine and six: three and two. Three quarters.
There's an old trick with arcs — the "ears" method. Here it is, just so you've seen it.
Outer numbers on top: five times nine. Inner numbers underneath: six times ten.
Same answer. But people swap what goes on top all the time — so my advice: skip it.
Multiply by the reciprocal and you'll never get confused.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Stacked fractions" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Whole over a fraction

lines.say: One more stacked one — with a whole number on top.
Which bar is the main one? The longer one — level with the equals sign.

lines.draw: Trace over the long main bar

lines.say: So it's two divided by three quarters.
Turn the two into a fraction: two over one.
Multiply by the reciprocal: two over one times four thirds. Eight thirds.
Three goes into eight twice, two left over — two and two thirds. If the answers show eight thirds, you're already done.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Whole over a fraction" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Mixed numbers

lines.say: Mixed numbers need one extra step: turn them into improper fractions first.
One and two thirds is five thirds.
Five thirds times three fifths… everything cancels. One! They're reciprocals.
DON'T multiply the whole parts and the fraction parts separately. A mixed number is a sum — that shortcut breaks it.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Mixed numbers" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: What division means

lines.say: Why does dividing by a fraction make the answer BIGGER? Let's see what it means.
How many eighths fit into three quarters?

lines.label: A pizza cut into eighths appears, 6 slices shaded (= 3/4)

lines.say: Three quarters is six eighths.
Six eighths fit. So the answer is six.
Divide by a small fraction and the answer gets BIGGER.
That's not weird — you're counting how many little pieces fit.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "What division means" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Divide $\to$ keep, change, flip the second.

lines.say: Let's lock it in.

lines.label: The multiplication rule appears: a/b · c/d = ac/bd
'Divide → keep, change, flip the second.' appears

lines.say: Five questions next. Cancel before you multiply — and know which factor you removed.
Next: adding and subtracting fractions. Different operation — different rule.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Adding & Subtracting Fractions

lines.say: Adding and subtracting fractions.
Still the foundations — so this has to become automatic.
And watch out: the rule here is DIFFERENT from multiplying.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Same denominator

lines.label: A bar cut into 7 equal parts appears, 2 shaded

lines.say: Two sevenths.

lines.label: A second bar appears, 3 of 7 shaded

lines.say: Plus three sevenths.

lines.label: A third bar appears, 5 of 7 shaded

lines.say: Put them together: five sevenths.
The pieces are all sevenths. We add HOW MANY pieces — the numerators.
The denominator stays seven. The pieces didn't change size.
Two apples plus three apples is five apples.
Subtraction works the same way: six sevenths minus two sevenths — four sevenths.
But what if one bar were cut into eighths and the other into sixths? The pieces don't line up — you can't just add them.
For that, you need a common denominator.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Same denominator" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Expand just one

lines.say: Tenths and fifths. Different denominators — so we make them match.
Can five reach ten? Yes — times two. So only ONE fraction has to change.

lines.draw: Write "×2" on top and bottom of 1/5, then "= 2/10"

lines.say: One fifth becomes two tenths. Top AND bottom — times two. That keeps its value.
Three tenths stays exactly as it is. Three plus two: five tenths.
And five tenths reduces to one half.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Expand just one" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Expand both

lines.say: Halves and thirds. Different-sized pieces.

lines.label: Two pizzas appear: 1/2 shaded and 1/3 shaded

lines.say: You can't just count "two pieces" — they're different sizes.
Can two become three? No. So BOTH fractions change.
Stuck finding a denominator? Just multiply them: two times three — six. Cut both pizzas into sixths.

lines.label: The same pizzas appear cut into sixths: 3/6 and 2/6 shaded

lines.draw: Under the new pies write "3/6" and "2/6"

lines.say: The half becomes three sixths. The third becomes two sixths.

lines.draw: On 1/2 write "×3" on top and bottom; on 1/3 write "×2" on top and bottom

lines.say: Times three — top AND bottom. Times two — top and bottom. Change only the bottoms and you've changed the amounts.
Now we can count: five sixths.
That's all a common denominator is — naming both amounts in the same-sized piece.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Expand both" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Common denominator

lines.say: Eight and twelve. We could multiply them: ninety-six. That works — but it's big.
Faster: take the BIGGER denominator and run through its multiples.
Twelve — does eight go in? No. Twenty-four — yes. Both eight and twelve fit.

lines.draw: Write "×3" on top and bottom of 3/8, and "×2" on top and bottom of 5/12

lines.say: Eight needs times three. Twelve needs times two. Top and bottom.
Nine twenty-fourths plus ten twenty-fourths: nineteen twenty-fourths.
Used ninety-six anyway? Totally fine — you'd just reduce at the end.
Don't spend longer hunting for the denominator than it takes to calculate.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Common denominator" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Subtracting

lines.say: Subtraction — exactly the same steps.
Common denominator of six and four. Multiples of six: six — no. Twelve — yes.
Six times two: ten twelfths. Four times three: three twelfths.
Ten minus three: seven twelfths.
Tidy habit: write the sign between the expanded fractions before you combine them. It kills sign errors.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Subtracting" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Whole & mixed numbers

lines.say: A whole number can wear any denominator you like.
Two is ten fifths. Minus three fifths: seven fifths.
Mixed numbers? Turn them into improper fractions first. No special borrowing rules needed.
Three and one sixth: nineteen sixths. One and three quarters: seven quarters.
In twelfths: thirty-eight minus twenty-one — seventeen twelfths.
One and five twelfths.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Whole & mixed numbers" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: $+\ \ -$ $\to$ common denominator, then add the tops
$\times$ $\to$ top times top, bottom times bottom

lines.say: All four operations, side by side.

lines.label: '+ −  →  common denominator, then add the tops' appears
'×  →  top times top, bottom times bottom' appears

lines.say: Most fraction mistakes come from using the right rule in the wrong place.
So before you calculate, name the operation. Then say the rule.
Five questions next. Then: decimal fractions.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Decimal Fractions

lines.say: Decimal fractions.
Honestly? Pure decimal questions are rare on the exam.
But decimals sneak into other questions — a motion problem, a percentage, a stray zero point two five in an equation.
So you need to handle them smoothly. Let's go.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Place value

lines.say: Until now, fractions had a numerator and a denominator. A decimal point is just another way to write the same fraction.
Left of the point: the whole numbers — ones, tens, hundreds. Right of the point: the fraction part — tenths, hundredths, thousandths.
Three point zero seven: three ones, zero tenths, seven hundredths.

lines.draw: Circle the 0 in the tenths box

lines.say: That zero isn't decoration. It pushes the seven into the hundredths place.

lines.draw: Under each one write its fraction: 4/10, 7/100, 6/1000

lines.say: Zero point four: four tenths. Zero point zero seven: seven hundredths. Zero point zero zero six: six thousandths.
Same fraction, two ways to write it.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Place value" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Decimal → fraction

lines.say: Decimal to fraction is the easy direction.
Start with the denominator: count the digits after the point. Two digits — two zeros. A hundred.
The numerator is simply the number after the point: thirty-six. Thirty-six hundredths.

lines.draw: Write ":4" on top and bottom, then "= 9/25"

lines.say: Reduce by four: nine twenty-fifths.
The denominator is always a one with zeros — ten, a hundred, a thousand. One zero for each decimal place.
Three decimal places — thousandths. One thousand one hundred twenty-five thousandths… reduces to nine eighths.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Decimal → fraction" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Fraction → decimal

lines.say: Fraction to decimal is a little harder.
The trick: get the denominator to ten, a hundred or a thousand — a one with zeros.
Fifty ends in a zero too — but it's not a one with zeros. We need a hundred.

lines.draw: Write "×2" on top and bottom, then "= 14/100"

lines.say: Fifty times two is a hundred. So the top gets times two as well: fourteen hundredths.
Now go backwards: two zeros, two places after the point. Zero point one four.
Sometimes you go DOWN instead of up.

lines.draw: Write ":3" on top and bottom, then "= 1/10 = 0.1"

lines.say: No need to reach a hundred. Divide top and bottom by three: one tenth. Zero point one.

lines.label: A row of must-know values appears: ½ = 0.5, ¼ = 0.25, ¾ = 0.75, ⅕ = 0.2, ⅛ = 0.125

lines.say: And know these five by heart. They show up everywhere.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Fraction → decimal" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Trailing zeros

lines.say: A zero at the far right of a decimal changes nothing.
Turn each one into a fraction: five tenths, fifty hundredths, five hundred thousandths. The zeros cancel with the denominator — same fraction every time.
Bottom line: zeros at the end? Just cross them out.

lines.draw: Circle the 0 right after the point in 0.05

lines.say: But a zero squeezed in right after the point? That changes everything — five hundredths is ten times smaller.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Trailing zeros" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Adding & subtracting

lines.say: Adding and subtracting decimals is exactly like column addition.
Ones over ones — and the easiest way to see it: decimal point directly over decimal point.

lines.draw: Under the hundredths write 3; carry a small 1 above the tenths

lines.say: Seven plus six: thirteen hundredths. Write three, carry one.

lines.draw: Under the tenths write 3; carry a small 1 above the ones

lines.say: Four plus eight plus one: thirteen tenths. Write three, carry one.

lines.draw: Under the ones write 4, and bring the point straight down

lines.say: Three plus zero plus one: four. The point drops straight down.
Four point three three.

lines.label: 5.20 − 1.78 appears in columns on the right

lines.say: Subtraction? Same idea. Five point two — write it as five point two zero, so every column has a digit.

lines.draw: Solve 5.20 − 1.78 in the columns, borrowing as usual: 3.42

lines.say: Zero minus eight — borrow, like always. Three point four two.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Adding & subtracting" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — 3.47 + 0.86, stacked with the points lined up

beats.title: Multiplying

lines.say: Multiplying decimals: ignore the points and multiply as usual.
Fourteen times six: eighty-four.
Now where does the point go? Count the digits after the point in BOTH numbers together: one, plus one — two.
Two places from the right: zero point eight four.
Quick tip — you can skip counting and just estimate. One and a bit, times a bit over a half: under one. So 0.84, never 8.4.
Three times four: twelve. Decimal places: two plus one — three. But twelve only has two digits…
So add a zero in front. Zero point zero one two.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Multiplying" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: ×10 and ÷10

lines.say: Multiplying or dividing by ten just moves the decimal point.

lines.draw: Write "= 0.47" and draw a hop arrow moving the point one place right

lines.say: Times ten — the number has to grow, so the point moves one place to the RIGHT.
Times a hundred — two zeros, two places. One zero, one place; two zeros, two places.

lines.draw: Write "= 0.047" and draw three hops to the left

lines.say: Dividing? The number shrinks — the point moves LEFT. One place for every zero.
Forty-seven divided by a thousand: three places left. Zero point zero four seven.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "×10 and ÷10" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Dividing

lines.say: Dividing decimals: write it as a fraction — then expand until both are whole numbers.

lines.draw: Rewrite it as a fraction: 4.8 over 0.06

lines.say: Four point eight over zero point zero six.

lines.draw: Write "×100" on top and bottom, then "= 480/6 = 80"

lines.say: Times a hundred, top AND bottom — both points jump two places. Four eighty over six: eighty.
Now a smarter move. Times a hundred works — but you only need WHOLE numbers, not the biggest ones.

lines.draw: Write it as 0.75/1.5, then "×4" on top and bottom: "= 3/6 = 1/2"

lines.say: One point five times four is six. Zero point seven five times four is three. Three over six: one half. Much easier than seventy-five over a hundred fifty.
Or switch to ordinary fractions: three quarters divided by three halves — also one half.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Dividing" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Comparing decimals

lines.say: One more skill: which decimal is bigger? The longer one LOOKS bigger. Don't fall for it.
Trailing zeros change nothing — so give them the same number of places: zero point six eight zero.

lines.draw: Underline the tenths (6 and 6), then the hundredths (8 and 0); write ">" between them

lines.say: Compare left to right. Tenths: a tie. Hundredths: eight beats zero. Zero point six eight is bigger.
Ones: a tie. Tenths: zero against nine. Two point nine wins.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Comparing decimals" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Decimal places = zeros in the denominator
Multiply: count the decimal places — or estimate
Divide: expand until both are whole

lines.say: Let's lock it in.

lines.label: 'Decimal places = zeros in the denominator' appears
'Multiply: count the decimal places — or estimate' appears
'Divide: expand until both are whole' appears

lines.say: Some fractions never end. One third is zero point three three three — forever. Zero point three three is only an approximation.
On the exam, you'll mostly need adding, subtracting, and expanding by ten to clear a decimal. Multiplying decimals is rare.
Five questions next — then twenty mixed fraction questions.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Comparing Fractions

lines.say: Now things get properly psychometric.
We've learned the fraction techniques — adding, subtracting, multiplying, dividing.
Now: the questions that actually show up on the exam. We'll start from the basics and build up to real exam questions.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Benchmark ½

lines.say: First technique: estimate the size.
Five thirteenths or eight fifteenths? No idea what either one is. But compare each one to one half.
Half of thirteen is six and a half. Five is less — so five thirteenths is a bit below one half.
Half of fifteen is seven and a half. Eight is more — a bit above one half.
One is below a half, one is above. Done.
Think cakes: five cakes for thirteen kids is less than five for ten — and five for ten is exactly a half.
My tip: work from the denominator to the numerator. Halve the bottom — then check the top.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Benchmark ½" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Same top or bottom

lines.say: Second technique: compare tops and bottoms.
Same denominator — same number of kids. More cakes, more for everyone. Seven elevenths.
Same numerator — the same cakes. Which group would you rather be in? The one with fewer kids — fewer people fighting over the cake.
Same top — the SMALLER bottom wins. Five elevenths. That's the one people flip.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Same top or bottom" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Make them match

lines.say: Sometimes neither the tops nor the bottoms match. But you can MAKE them match — by expanding.
Look: five can become fifteen.

lines.draw: Write "×3" on top and bottom of 5/11, then "= 15/33"

lines.say: Times three, top and bottom: fifteen thirty-thirds.
Now both have fifteen on top. Fifteen cakes — for thirty-three kids, or for thirty-four?
Fewer kids, bigger share. Five elevenths is bigger.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Make them match" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Cross-multiply

lines.say: Can't get from eight to eleven, can't match the tops either. We could build a common denominator of eighty-eight…
Instead: cross-multiplication. The best and most important technique for comparing fractions.

lines.draw: Draw a diagonal arrow from the 11 up to the 5; write "55" above 5/8

lines.say: Eleven times five — fifty-five. Write it ABOVE the first fraction.

lines.draw: Draw a diagonal arrow from the 8 up to the 7; write "56" above 7/11

lines.say: Eight times seven — fifty-six. Above the second fraction.
This is critical: each product goes above ITS numerator. Write them underneath and you'll get the answer backwards.
Fifty-five, fifty-six. The second is bigger — seven elevenths.
Big numbers? Don't panic — it still works. It's secretly a common denominator, comparing the tops.
One method that always works beats five you half-remember.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Cross-multiply" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: To decimals

lines.say: Another option: turn them into decimals. But you need to know your decimals well.
One fifth is zero point two — so two fifths is zero point four.
One eighth is zero point one two five — so three eighths is zero point three seven five.
Zero point four is bigger.
But remember what always works?
Cross-multiply: eight times two, sixteen. Five times three, fifteen. Same answer — and much simpler.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "To decimals" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Distance from 1

lines.say: Fractions close to one? Cross-multiplying gets clumsy. Ask what's MISSING to make a whole.
Eight ninths is missing one ninth.
Eleven twelfths is missing one twelfth.
One cake for twelve people is smaller than one cake for nine. So eleven twelfths is missing less…
…which makes it bigger. Missing less means bigger.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Distance from 1" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Roots? Square it

lines.say: Roots make comparing awkward. So get rid of them: square the whole fraction.
We'll learn roots properly later — and then cross-multiplying handles these too. For now, just know: squaring a root cancels it. Root ten squared is ten.
Three squared, nine — over ten. Two squared, four — over five.
Now it's easy. Cross-multiply: forty-five against forty. Or distance from one: a tenth missing against a fifth missing.
The bigger one stays bigger after squaring. Three over root ten wins.
Warning: square the numerator AND the denominator. Squaring only the root changes the whole comparison.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Roots? Square it" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Plug in numbers

items.t: Pick LEGAL values · eliminate three choices · two survive? plug in again

lines.say: Now a more psychometric technique: plugging in numbers.
Letters look scary. But x is a fraction, y is bigger than one — so pick legal values.
x is one half. y is two.
Two over one and a half — expand by two — four thirds.
One and a half over two and a half — three fifths.
Cross-multiply again: five times four, twenty — three times three, nine. The first is bigger.
But now think instead of calculating. Four thirds: top bigger than bottom — more than one. Three fifths: less than one.
So the first is bigger.

lines.label: The plug-in rules appear in one line

lines.say: On a real question: pick legal values, knock out three choices — and if two survive, plug in a different kind of number.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Plug in numbers" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — x between 0 and 1, y > 1; y/(y−x) ? (y−x)/(y+x)

beats.title: Flip them

lines.say: One bonus trick for the creative ones: flip them.

lines.draw: Under each fraction write its reciprocal: 19/3, 25/4, 31/5

lines.say: Nineteen thirds, twenty-five quarters, thirty-one fifths.
Six and a third. Six and a quarter. Six and a fifth. Easy to order.
Six and a third is the biggest… but we flipped. Flipping positive numbers reverses the order.
So three nineteenths is the SMALLEST.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Flip them" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Cross-multiply: always works — products above the numerators
Also: benchmark ½ · match tops or bottoms · distance from 1 · square roots away

lines.say: Let's sum it up.

lines.label: 'Cross-multiply: always works — products above the numerators' appears

lines.say: Cross-multiplication is the method I recommend most. It always works, it's simple, and it eats everything.

lines.label: 'Also: benchmark ½ · match tops or bottoms · distance from 1 · square roots away' appears

lines.say: The others are shortcuts for when the numbers invite them.
Even with letters and scary expressions — cross-multiplication will do the job. We'll see it again and again.
Next: real exam-style questions. Try each one first — then watch its solution.

beats.title: Expressions — Fundamentals

lines.say: Algebraic expressions. Numbers and letters, working together.
Collecting terms, opening brackets, taking out a common factor.
Most of this you remember from school — so let's review it fast and make it airtight.
And then: the three short multiplication formulas. Those are gold on this exam.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Terms & coefficients

lines.say: Start with a single term.
Five x. The five is the coefficient — it means five TIMES x.
Five times x, five x — same thing.

lines.label: x and −x appear side by side

lines.draw: Under x write "1 · x"; under −x write "−1 · x"

lines.say: A plain x has a hidden coefficient of one. Negative x? Negative one.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Terms & coefficients" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Like terms

lines.say: You can only add and subtract terms from the same family — same letters, same powers.
x and y? Different families. x and x squared? Also different families.

lines.draw: Underline 5x and −2x in one colour, 6y and −2y in another, −3x² and 7x² in a third

lines.say: Let's colour the families. And remember — every minus sign travels with the term after it.
Five x minus two x: three x. Picture it: you had five x, someone took two of them — three are left.
Six y minus two y: four y.
Negative three x squared plus seven x squared: four x squared.
Four x squared plus three x plus four y. Three families — and they stay separate.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Like terms" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Multiplying terms

lines.say: Multiplication is different. Here, ANY terms can be multiplied together.
In a product the order doesn't matter. So gather numbers with numbers, letters with letters.
Three times four times two… and a, a, b.
Twenty-four. Two a's make a squared. Twenty-four a squared b.
You could also write twenty-four b a squared. We usually put the powers first — but either way is correct.
Don't mix them up. Two a PLUS three a is five a. Two a TIMES three a is six a squared.
The operation sign decides the rule.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Multiplying terms" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Opening brackets

lines.say: Nothing written between the number and the bracket? That means times.
The outside number multiplies EVERY term inside.

lines.draw: Draw arrows from the 4 to the x and to the 3; write "= 4x + 12"

lines.say: Four times x, four times three. Four x plus twelve.

lines.draw: Draw arrows from the −3 to each term; write "= −6x + 15"

lines.say: Negative three times two x: negative six x.
Negative three times negative five: PLUS fifteen.
Keep each sign glued to its number — and the signs take care of themselves.
We wrote every step to explain it. In practice, once you get it, jump straight from the brackets to the answer.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Opening brackets" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Minus before brackets

lines.say: A lonely minus in front of a bracket is really times negative one.
So it flips the sign of EVERY term inside. Minus B. And minus minus C — plus C.
A plus in front of the bracket? Nothing changes. Just drop the brackets.
The minus flips everything — not just the first term. That's exactly where students lose points.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Minus before brackets" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Two brackets

lines.say: Two brackets: every term in the first meets every term in the second.

lines.draw: Draw the four arcs: x to x, x to 3, 4 to x, 4 to 3

lines.say: x times x, x times three. Then four times x, four times three.
x squared, plus three x, plus four x, plus twelve.
Then collect the family: three x plus four x — seven x.
With practice you'll jump straight to the last line. For now, write all four products.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Two brackets" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Common factor

lines.say: Taking out a common factor. A super important technique — as important as adding fractions.
First: what's a factor? A building block in MULTIPLICATION. Six is two times three. Eight is two times four — or two times two times two.
Taking out a common factor is opening brackets — in reverse.
What goes into both six x and fifteen? Three.
Three goes outside. Three times what gives six x? Two x. Three times what gives fifteen? Five.

lines.draw: Draw check arrows from the 3 to each term inside

lines.say: Check by opening: three times two x, six x. Three times five, fifteen. It works.
Now with letters. Break each term into its building blocks: two times a times a. Two times three times a. Two times four.
Is a common? It's in the first two terms — but not in the eight. So a can't come out.
Two is in all three. That's our common factor.
Two out front. What's left: a squared, minus three a — the minus stays — plus four.

lines.draw: Draw check arrows from the 2 to each term inside

lines.say: Check by opening: two a squared, minus six a, plus eight. It works.
The common factor can be a number, a letter — even a whole bracket.
So why put things BACK into brackets? Because in fractions you can't cancel across a plus.
Factor it into a product — and suddenly you CAN cancel. You'll see it again and again.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Common factor" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: (a + b)²

lines.say: Now the short multiplication formulas. They show up a LOT on the exam — know them cold.
You don't HAVE to use them — you can always open the brackets. The formulas just save you time and mess.
a plus b, squared: the first squared, plus two times the first times the second, plus the second squared.
Don't forget the middle term! It is NOT just a squared plus b squared.
Test it: three plus two, squared — twenty-five. Just squaring each one gives thirteen.
The middle term is the missing twelve.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "(a + b)²" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: (a − b)²

lines.say: Same formula — with a minus.
The minus lands ONLY on the middle term. b squared stays positive — negative b times negative b.
With a plus, everything is plus. With a minus, the minus is only on two a b.
Five minus three, squared: four. The formula: twenty-five minus thirty plus nine — four. It checks out.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "(a − b)²" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Sum × difference

lines.say: Third formula: a difference times a sum.

lines.draw: Under it write "+ab − ab" and cross both out

lines.say: Open it and the two middle terms cancel each other out.
What's left: the first squared minus the second squared.
It's called the difference of squares — and it works in both directions.
Careful: a squared PLUS b squared doesn't break apart like this. That minus is essential.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Sum × difference" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Formulas backward

lines.say: You have to recognise the formulas backwards too.
First term: x squared — that's x, squared. Last term: thirty-six — that's six squared.
Now check the middle: two times x times six — twelve x. It matches!
So it's x plus six, squared.
Nine x squared minus twenty-five: three x, squared, minus five squared. Difference of squares.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Formulas backward" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

A minus before a bracket flips every sign
Expand to combine · Factor to cancel

beats.title: Working with Expressions

lines.say: Expressions — exam style.
Some algebra questions just hand you an expression and ask what it equals.
Most of the time you won't even reach a number. You'll simplify, factor, cancel — and match a choice.
Let's see what these questions look like, and where the traps are.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: What's an expression?

lines.say: First — what IS an expression?
An expression is a string of numbers and letters. Something equals a question mark.
An equation is different: one thing equals ANOTHER thing. Two sides.

lines.draw: Circle the "= ?" in the first line

lines.say: That little question mark is how you spot an expression.
And it matters — some moves are legal in an equation but NOT in an expression.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "What's an expression?" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: No cancelling!

lines.say: Here's the most common mistake with expressions.
Two fractions — common denominator, like we learned. It's a times b.
The first fraction needs times a, top and bottom. The second needs times b.
a squared plus b squared, over a b.
And now many students just wipe away the denominator. NO.

lines.draw: Draw a big ✗ next to the ab

lines.say: In an equation — later on — you can clear a denominator from both sides.
In an expression there's only one side. The denominator stays.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "No cancelling!" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: The main fraction bar

lines.say: Order of operations still rules expressions.

lines.label: The stacked fraction 12 over 1 over (1/3 + 1/6) appears

lines.say: A fraction bar, on a fraction bar, on a fraction bar. Scary? It's just layers.
Find the MAIN bar — the longest one. Everything above it is the top. Everything below it is the bottom.

lines.draw: Number the layers 1, 2, 3 — from the innermost outward

lines.say: Then work from the innermost layer outward. Never all the bars at once.
Crowded? Rewrite it in one line with brackets and division signs.
This exact one is Question 1 — so try it yourself first.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The main fraction bar" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Opposite brackets

lines.say: First, opposite numbers: a pair that differs only by the minus. Fifteen and negative fifteen.
They add to zero. And multiplying by negative one jumps you to the opposite.
Now a pattern the exam LOVES.
a minus b, over b minus a. Same two letters — opposite order.
Let's plug in: a equals seven, b equals two.
Top: five. Bottom: negative five. Same number, opposite signs — negative one.

lines.label: The rule appears: (a − b)/(b − a) = −1, when a ≠ b

lines.say: And it's ALWAYS negative one. Any numbers you like — because a minus b is the opposite of b minus a.
You could prove it by taking a minus out of the bracket. But honestly? Trust it. It's always negative one.
One condition: a can't equal b. Otherwise it's zero over zero — undefined.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Opposite brackets" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: A repeated bracket

lines.say: Lots of letters doesn't mean lots of work.
Look — a plus b appears in both parts. It's a common factor. Treat it as ONE object.
Take it out front. What's left: u minus four, plus u plus four.
Minus four and plus four cancel.
u plus u: two u. So it's a plus b, times two u.
Tip: if it helps, call the repeated bracket K on your paper. Swap it back at the end.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "A repeated bracket" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Plug in numbers

items.t: 1 · Only an expression ($=\ ?$) — not an equation.
2 · Pick legal, easy values — obey every condition.
3 · Eliminate three choices — don't stop at the first match.
4 · Two still match? Plug in different numbers.

lines.say: Letters scaring you? In an expression, you can plug in numbers.
Only when it's something equals question mark. Two sides? Not this method.
Pick easy, legal numbers. Nothing says the letters must differ? Then they can all be one.
The catch: you're NOT hunting for the right answer. You're knocking out three wrong ones.
The first choice that matches might not be the only one.

lines.label: Rule 4 appears: a tie? new numbers

lines.say: Two still match? Plug in different numbers and test just those two.
It's a great safety net. But what you can solve with algebra — solve with algebra.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Plug in numbers" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Pick your method

lines.say: In the questions coming up, you'll see more than one route.
Small numbers? Just calculate.
Spot a structure? Factoring can turn a scary expression into one line.
Stuck? Plugging in can knock out wrong choices without any algebra.

lines.draw: Draw a bracket around all three and write "which is safest & fastest?"

lines.say: The longest solution isn't the smartest. The shortcut isn't always better. Pick what's safe AND fast for these numbers.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Pick your method" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

Repeated bracket? Take it out front

beats.title: Equations — Fundamentals

lines.say: Equations. One of the most basic techniques in all of algebra.
You'll use it in algebra questions, in word problems, in geometry.
Sooner or later, almost every question turns into an equation you have to solve.
Solving means one thing: find the value of the unknown. Let's go.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Isolate x

lines.say: Two sides, and an equals sign in the middle. Whatever's on the left has the same value as whatever's on the right.
Our job: get x alone on one side.
The golden rule — whatever you do to one side, you do to the other. That keeps the balance.
The plus seven is in the way. So subtract seven — from BOTH sides.

lines.draw: Under it write "−7" on both sides, then "4x = 24"

lines.say: Seven minus seven cancels. Thirty-one minus seven: twenty-four. Four x equals twenty-four.
But we want ONE x, not four. So divide both sides by four.
x equals six.
Check it in the original: four times six is twenty-four, plus seven — thirty-one. It works.
"Move it across and flip the sign" is just shorthand for doing the same thing to both sides.
And x doesn't have to end up on the left. Put it wherever it comes out positive — that's usually easier.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Isolate x" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Every x works

lines.say: Not every equation gives you one neat answer.
Open the bracket: two x plus six. And the right side? Two x plus six. The exact same thing.

lines.draw: Cross out 2x on both sides; write "6 = 6"

lines.say: Take two x off both sides: six equals six. Always true.
x disappeared. It doesn't matter what you plug in — the two sides are always equal.
That's called infinitely many solutions. x can be any number.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Every x works" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: No solution

lines.say: Now the opposite situation.
Open the bracket: two x plus six equals two x plus nine.

lines.draw: Cross out 2x on both sides; write "6 = 9" and a big ✗

lines.say: Take two x off both sides: six equals nine.
We know that's false. That's a contradiction.
No matter which x you try, you'll hit that contradiction. So this equation has NO solution.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "No solution" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: x in the denominator

lines.say: Equations with fractions. The method: a common denominator on both sides — then cancel it.
But when x is in the bottom, write the restriction FIRST.
If x were three, the bottom would be zero. Not allowed. So x can't be three.
Give the right side the same denominator: two is two times x minus three, over x minus three.
Same denominator on both sides of an equation — cancel it. Algebraically, we just multiplied both sides by x minus three.
Open it: two x minus six. Collect: x equals eight.
Eight isn't three — it's allowed. And ten over five is two. It checks.
If an answer ever makes a denominator zero — throw it out, even if it looks right.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "x in the denominator" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Fractions & brackets

lines.say: Brackets first. The three multiplies EVERYTHING inside.
Three x minus six — not three x minus two. Then plus five.
Collect: three x minus one equals two x plus eight.
x terms to one side, numbers to the other: x equals nine.
Now a plain number under the fraction. Same method: common denominator.
Five is twenty quarters. Same denominator on both sides — cancel it. The four divided the WHOLE top, so we get x plus three equals twenty. Not x plus twelve!
x equals seventeen.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Fractions & brackets" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Don't divide by x

lines.say: Here's a trap that costs people points.
It's tempting to divide both sides by x. But what if x is zero? You can't divide by zero.
Divide by x and you silently lose a solution.
Instead: a product equals zero when one of the factors is zero.
So either x is zero, or x minus five is zero.
Two solutions: zero and five. Keep them both.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Don't divide by x" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Recap

$x$ cancels and it's false $\to$ no solution
Never divide by something that could be $0$
$x$ in the denominator $\to$ write the restriction first
