beats.title: Systems of Equations

lines.say: Last lesson: one equation. Now: a system — two equations, sometimes even more.
These show up mainly in algebra questions.
The difficulty here is technical, not conceptual. So let's master the techniques.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Two equations

lines.say: Two unknowns, two equations. We need values that make BOTH true at the same time.
The first one alone has endless pairs. The second one narrows it down to one.

lines.draw: Next to them write "2 unknowns, 2 equations ✓"

lines.say: Rule of thumb: as many equations as unknowns — and you can solve it.
Two main methods: substitution, and elimination. Same answer either way.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Two equations" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Substitution

lines.say: Method one: isolate a letter in one equation, and plug it into the other.
From the first: y equals eleven minus x.
Put that WHOLE expression into the second equation, in place of y. The brackets matter — the minus hits both terms.
Two x minus eleven plus x equals seven. Three x is eighteen. x is six.
Back to y equals eleven minus x: y is five.
Tip: if they ask for x, isolate y. It disappears — and you're left with exactly the letter you want.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Substitution" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Elimination

lines.say: Method two — often faster: add or subtract the equations.
Look — plus y and minus y. Opposites.
Add the two equations, left to left, right to right.
The y's cancel. Three x equals eighteen. x is six.
Same answer as substitution. Of course.
Same sign instead of opposite signs? Then subtract — and keep the whole second equation in brackets.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Elimination" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Match coefficients

lines.say: Nothing cancels yet. So we MAKE it cancel.
Multiply whole equations until one letter has the same coefficient.

lines.draw: Write "×3" next to the first and "×2" next to the second

lines.say: First equation times three, second times two.
Every term gets multiplied — including the right side. Six x plus nine y is fifty-seven. Six x plus four y is thirty-two.
Now subtract: six x minus six x is gone. Five y equals twenty-five. y is five.
Back into the first: two x plus fifteen is nineteen. x is two.
Which letter should you match? The one they DON'T ask for — so it cancels and leaves the one you want.
Choose the smallest multipliers you can. Less arithmetic, fewer mistakes.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Match coefficients" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Ask what they want

items.t: You may not need $x$ and $y$ separately.

lines.say: One more thing before the questions.
Sometimes the question doesn't want x or y at all — it wants a combination, like x plus y.

lines.label: 'You may not need x and y separately.' appears

lines.say: Then adding or subtracting the equations can hand you that combination directly.
So always circle what they ask for — before you start solving.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Ask what they want" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

Multiply WHOLE equations to match coefficients

beats.title: Solving Equations Smarter

lines.say: Now we solve equations the way the exam wants them solved.
Not just "find x" — but spotting the traps and the shortcuts.
Dividing by an unknown, counting solutions, and calculating what they ask for — without finding every letter.
Let's go.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Dividing by x

lines.say: Looks obvious, right? y equals x.
Cancel x squared on both sides — done. Or is it?
You can divide both sides by something — as long as it isn't zero.
And nobody told us x isn't zero.
Put x equals zero: zero equals zero. True for ANY y.
So the safe move: everything to one side, then factor.
A product equals zero when at least one factor is zero.
Either x is zero — or x equals y. Two branches. Dividing would have killed one of them.
If the question says x isn't zero, cancel away. If it doesn't — split into cases.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Dividing by x" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Product equals zero

lines.say: Power two and up? Don't divide. Take out a common factor.
x squared is common. What's left: x squared minus nine.
Now it's a product equal to zero — so one factor must be zero.
x squared is zero: x is zero. That's one.
x squared is nine: three — or negative three.

lines.draw: Circle the three values and write "3 solutions"

lines.say: Three different solutions: zero, three, negative three.
And notice — dividing by x squared at the start would have erased the zero.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Product equals zero" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Squares: two roots

lines.say: Something squared is sixteen. What could that something be?
Four — or negative four. Both square to sixteen.
So split into two cases.
x minus six is four: x is ten. x minus six is negative four: x is two.
Two solutions.
Careful: the root symbol on its own — root of sixteen — is just four. But when YOU take a root to solve an equation, you get plus AND minus.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Squares: two roots" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: One equation, two unknowns

items.t: One equation, two unknowns $\to$ no values…
Necessarily true = true in EVERY allowed case

lines.say: One equation, two unknowns. Can we solve it?

lines.label: 'One equation, two unknowns → no values…' appears

lines.say: No. We can't find the value of each letter.
But we CAN find how they relate — which one is bigger, and by how much.

lines.label: 'Necessarily true = true in EVERY allowed case' appears

lines.say: That's exactly what "necessarily true" questions test. It has to hold in every case — and one legal counterexample kills a choice.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "One eq, two unknowns" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Build the expression

items.t: Asked for an expression? Don't find each letter.
Add, subtract — or divide — the equations

lines.say: Sometimes they don't ask for x or y. They ask for an expression.

lines.label: 'Asked for an expression? Don't find each letter.' appears

lines.say: Then don't calculate every unknown separately. Calculate the expression directly.

lines.label: 'Add, subtract — or divide — the equations' appears

lines.say: Adding the equations, subtracting them, sometimes dividing them — look for the short route straight to what they want.
How do you know which one? Practice. You'll start to recognise the patterns.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Build the expression" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Hidden formula

lines.say: A rarer type — but worth knowing: a short multiplication formula hiding inside the question.

lines.label: The formula (x − y)² = x² + y² − 2xy appears

lines.say: See x minus y, x squared plus y squared, and x times y together? That's this formula.

lines.draw: Circle x − y, x² + y² and xy in the formula

lines.say: Notice I wrote the two x y at the end — just so the x squared plus y squared sit together.
Find the right formula, plug in what you know, and isolate what they ask for. Know two pieces — get the third.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Hidden formula" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Break it apart

items.t: Big equation? Break it into the small ones.

lines.say: The last type: lots of equations that look scary.

lines.label: 'Big equation? Break it into the small ones.' appears

lines.say: You could isolate and substitute letter by letter — but it takes ages.

lines.label: 2a = a + a and 3b = b + b + b appear

lines.say: Instead, split the big equation into pieces — and swap in the small equations one at a time.
Once you know the trick, these become simple. You'll see it in question seven.

beats.title: Exponent Laws

lines.say: Powers and roots. We start with the powers.
First the basic laws — then psychometric questions.
These show up a lot on the exam. Not just in algebra — inside geometry questions too.
So the laws have to be fluent. Automatic. Let's build them.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: What a power is

lines.say: A power is just a short way to write repeated multiplication.
Four cubed means three fours, multiplied together.
Sixty-four.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow to the 4 and an arrow to the 3

lines.say: The number at the bottom is the base. The small one up top is the exponent.
And it is NOT four times three. The exponent counts how many copies of the base you multiply.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "What a power is" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Exponent 1 and 0

lines.say: Any number to the power of one is itself. One copy of the base — that's it.
Any nonzero number to the power of zero is ONE. Sounds strange — so here's why.
A number over itself is one. But subtracting the exponents gives five to the zero. So five to the zero has to be one.
Negative base, fraction base — doesn't matter. The whole bracket to the zero: one.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Exponent 1 and 0" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Bases 1 and 0

items.t: Zero to a negative power is undefined.

lines.say: One to any power is one. One times one times one — a million times — still one.
Zero to a POSITIVE power is zero. Zero times anything is zero.

lines.label: 'Zero to a negative power is undefined.' appears

lines.say: A negative exponent means dividing by zero — undefined. Zero to the zero? Not defined in this course either.
You'll probably never meet those. Just know they're off-limits.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Bases 1 and 0" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Negative exponents

lines.say: A negative exponent does NOT make the number negative.
It tells you: flip it.
Flip the fraction, and the minus in the exponent disappears.
Five cubed over two cubed: a hundred twenty-five eighths. Positive.
A whole number? It's two over one — flip it. One over two cubed. One eighth.
The minus in the exponent means "flip". A minus in the base decides the sign. Keep them apart.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Negative exponents" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Multiplying powers

lines.say: Same base, multiplied — ADD the exponents.
Why? Three squared is two threes. Three to the fourth is four more. That's six threes.
Three to the sixth. The base stays three.
But this is a PLUS. The rule is for multiplying only. Nine plus eighty-one is ninety — nowhere near three to the sixth.
Same base AND a multiplication sign. Check both before you add exponents.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Multiplying powers" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Dividing powers

lines.say: Same base, divided — SUBTRACT the exponents. Top minus bottom.

lines.draw: Cross out three 5s on top against the three 5s on the bottom

lines.say: Seven fives on top, three on the bottom. Cancel three pairs.
Four fives are left. Five to the fourth.
More on the bottom? The leftovers stay downstairs: one over five cubed — or five to the minus three.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Dividing powers" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Power of a power

lines.say: A power raised to a power — MULTIPLY the exponents.
Two cubed, four times over. Four groups of three twos.
Twelve twos. Two to the twelfth.
Careful — this one isn't a power of a power. It's multiplying: add. Two to the seventh.
Brackets around a power: multiply. Two powers side by side: add. Students mix these up — you won't.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Power of a power" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Same exponent

lines.say: Different bases, same exponent? You can put them under ONE exponent.
Why? Two cubed times three cubed is three twos and three threes. Multiplication lets us reorder them into three pairs of two times three.
Two times three, cubed — or two cubed times three cubed. Same thing: two sixteen. You'll use this a LOT.
Division works the same way. The exponent goes on top and bottom.

lines.label: The trap appears: (a + b)² ≠ a² + b²

lines.say: But NOT over a plus or a minus. The square of a sum has a middle term — we learned that.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Same exponent" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Negative bases

lines.say: A negative base to an EVEN power: the minuses pair off. Positive eighty-one.
An ODD power: one minus is left over. Negative twenty-seven.
No brackets? The power comes first — the minus comes after. Three squared is nine, then the minus: negative nine.
Brackets decide what the base is. Plugging in a negative number yourself? Always put it in brackets.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Negative bases" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: When aᵇ = 1

lines.say: A rule the exam loves. When is a to the b equal to one?
Option one: a is one. Then b can be anything.
Option two: a is negative one — but then b must be even.
Option three: b is zero. Then a doesn't matter — anything nonzero to the zero is one.
When a question says a to the b equals one — check all three.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "When aᵇ = 1" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: 2⁴ = 4²

lines.say: Usually, swapping the base and the exponent changes the answer.
Two to the fourth: sixteen. Four squared: sixteen.
This pair — two and four — is the one special case. It's not a rule. It's an exception.
Any other pair of different numbers? One side is always bigger. Just remember two and four.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "2⁴ = 4²" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Splitting exponents

lines.say: The multiplication rule works backwards too.
A sum in the exponent splits into a product: two to the n, times two cubed. Eight times two to the n.
Eight copies of two to the n, minus one copy. Seven copies.
We never subtracted exponents across a minus sign. We split first, then took a common factor.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Splitting exponents" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: The rules table

lines.say: Here's the table to know by heart.

lines.label: Rules 3–4 appear: aᵐaⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ · aᵐ/aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ

lines.say: Multiply: add. Divide: subtract. Power of a power: multiply.
And know your small squares and cubes. Sixty-four is eight squared — and four cubed — and two to the sixth.
Ten core questions next. Match the right law to the right structure first. Speed comes later.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The rules table" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Roots — Fundamentals

lines.say: Roots. The partner of powers.
Same deal as last lesson: a short set of rules — and they have to be automatic.
At the end there's a table to learn by heart. Then fifteen questions.
Let's go.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: What a root is

items.t: Inside a square root: never negative.

lines.say: A square root asks one question: which number, squared, gives what's inside?
Seven squared is forty-nine. So the root of forty-nine is seven.
But wait — negative seven squared is also forty-nine.
The root sign always means the NON-negative answer. So root forty-nine is just seven.
Solving an equation is different: x squared equals forty-nine has TWO solutions. Seven and negative seven.

lines.label: 'Inside a square root: never negative' appears

lines.say: And the number inside a square root can't be negative. Zero is fine — root zero is zero.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "What a root is" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Root of a square

lines.say: Root of negative eight, squared. Careful.
Negative eight squared is sixty-four. Root sixty-four: positive eight.
So the root of a square does NOT always give back what you started with.
Root of x squared is the absolute value of x — its distance from zero. Never negative.
If the question tells you x is positive, then it's just x. If it doesn't — keep the absolute value.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Root of a square" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Pull out squares

lines.say: Simplifying a root: hunt for a perfect square hiding inside.
Seventy-two is thirty-six times two. And thirty-six is a perfect square.
Root thirty-six is six. The two stays inside. Six root two.
That's exact — not an approximation.
Two hundred is a hundred times two. Ten root two.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Pull out squares" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Adding roots

lines.say: Roots add like letters. Three x plus two x is five x — three root five plus two root five is five root five.
But root five plus root three? Different roots. They don't combine.
These LOOK different. Simplify first.
Root seventy-two is six root two. Root thirty-two is four root two. Same root — ten root two.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Adding roots" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Multiply & divide

lines.say: Multiplying or dividing? Roots can go under ONE root.
Root seventy-five over root three: root of seventy-five over three — root twenty-five. Five.
Keep the conditions in mind: nothing negative under a square root, and no zero on the bottom.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Multiply & divide" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Odd & even roots

items.t: Even root of a negative number: no real value.

lines.say: Cube roots are different. Negative four cubed is negative sixty-four — so the cube root of negative sixty-four is negative four.
Odd roots accept negatives. Even roots don't.

lines.label: 'Even root of a negative: no real value' appears

lines.say: Square root, fourth root, sixth root of a negative number? It doesn't exist here.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Odd & even roots" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Roots as powers

lines.say: A root is just a fractional power. Square root: power one half. Cube root: power one third.
Square a to the one half and you get a to the one — back to a. That's why it works.
This lets you use every exponent law from last lesson on roots too.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Roots as powers" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Not for sums

lines.say: The big trap. A root does NOT split over a plus.
Check with numbers: a nine, b sixteen.
Root of twenty-five is five. Three plus four is seven. Not equal.
Products and quotients split. Sums and differences don't.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Not for sums" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: The rules table

lines.say: Here's the table to learn by heart.
Read the conditions — they're part of every rule.
Now fifteen questions, no videos in between. Simplify first, then combine.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The rules table" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Exponents & Roots — Techniques

lines.say: Expressions and equations with powers and roots.
Now we move from the rules to the techniques the exam actually tests.
Let's start with one that's very important on the psychometric: dividing by a root.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Dividing roots

lines.say: Root forty-eight over root three. Two ways — both by the root rules.
Way one: put them under the same root.
Forty-eight over three is sixteen. Root sixteen: four.
Way two: split the top.

lines.draw: Below, write "√48 = √16 · √3"; cross out √3 top and bottom; write "= √16 = 4"

lines.say: Root forty-eight is root sixteen times root three. Now cancel root three, top and bottom. Four again.
Same answer, of course. Personally? I prefer splitting.
When a question has several roots and different terms to cancel, splitting is usually the easier road.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Dividing roots" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Number over a root

items.t: Shortcut: ① ignore the root  ② put the root on the answer

lines.say: Now a whole number over a root. The six isn't under a root — so how do we cancel?
Actually, you could put it under one: six is root thirty-six. Root thirty-six over root three — one big root. That works.
But it's easier to split the six: six is two times three.
And three is root three times root three.
Because root three times root three is root three squared — and the square cancels the root.

lines.draw: Cross out one √3 on top and the √3 on the bottom; write "= 2√3"

lines.say: Cancel. Two root three.
Another one. Twenty could be ten times two — or four times five.
There's a five underneath, so choose four times five. Then five is root five times root five.
Cancel root five with root five: four root five.
This comes up a LOT — especially in geometry, with the special right triangles, where you divide by root two or root three.
So here's the one-second shortcut.

lines.label: The shortcut appears: 1) ignore the root  2) add the root to the answer

lines.say: Pretend the root isn't there: six over three is two. Then put the root back on the answer: two root three. Done — zero mistakes.
Twenty over root five: no root — twenty over five is four. Add the root: four root five. Simple — worth mastering.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Number over a root" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Same prime base

lines.say: Powers with different bases? Turn every base into the SAME base.
And go for the smallest base possible — break everything down to its primes.
Eight is two cubed. Two cubed to the fourth — multiply the exponents: two to the twelfth.
Sixteen is two to the fourth. To the third: two to the twelfth.
They're equal — and we never calculated a big number.
Smallest base, always. Two, not four. Not eight. Otherwise you get stuck with big numbers later.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Same prime base" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Negative exponents

lines.say: One more thing you'll need with these answers.
A negative exponent means: flip the base.
The reciprocal of two is one half. One half cubed — one over two cubed. The minus is gone.
So a factor with a negative exponent really lives on the bottom of the fraction.
Why does that matter? The same answer can show up in the choices written either way. Recognise both.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Negative exponents" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Adding roots: split

lines.say: Adding and subtracting roots. Method one: split into factors.
Root eight is root four times root two. Root eighteen is root nine times root two.
Why nine and two — and not six and three? Because root nine comes out as a whole number. Always split so one part comes out whole.
Two root two plus three root two. Just like two x plus three x: five root two.
Root twelve is two root three. Root forty-eight as root four times root twelve — two root twelve. Stuck! Root three and root twelve are apples and bananas.
Try another split. Six times eight? Nothing comes out whole. Two times twenty-four? Same problem.
Sixteen times three — root sixteen is four. Four root three. Now it matches: six root three.
It works — but it took trial and error. Four times twelve or six times eight is what most people see; sixteen times three isn't obvious to everyone.
That's why there's a second method — especially if algebra isn't your strongest area.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Adding roots: split" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Adding roots: factor

lines.say: Method two: take out a common factor. Most of us are good at that.
Ignore the roots for a second. Eight and eighteen — common factor two.
Take out root two. Left inside: root four plus root nine.
Quick check: root two times root four is root eight, root two times root nine is root eighteen. We're fine.
Two plus three is five. Five root two — same answer as before.
Common factor twelve. Inside: one plus root four — three. Three root twelve.
And root twelve is easy to split: two root three. Six root three — same as before, and no trial and error.
Use whichever method feels easier. You'll always land in the same place.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Adding roots: factor" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Power equations

lines.say: An exponential equation: the unknown sits up in the exponent.
The method: make the bases equal — then make the exponents equal.
Twenty-seven is three cubed. Now both sides have base three.
Same base, so the exponents must be equal. Two x minus one equals three. x is two.
One restriction: this works for a positive base that isn't one. One to any power is one — that tells you nothing.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Power equations" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Root equations

lines.say: An equation with a root? Get rid of the root: square both sides.
The square cancels the root.
But first — a root is never negative. So the other side can't be negative either.
So x has to be at least one.
And squaring can sneak in fake solutions.

lines.draw: Write "square → solve → check in the ORIGINAL"

lines.say: So after you solve, plug every answer back into the ORIGINAL equation. Throw out anything that fails.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Root equations" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Number over a root: ignore it, then put it back
Add roots: split into factors, or take a common factor
Power equation: equal bases $\to$ equal exponents
Root equation: square both sides, then check

beats.title: Advanced Exponents & Roots

lines.say: Advanced exponents and roots.
No new rules here — these questions combine the ones you already know.
The hard part is choosing the right form. Let's see how.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Translate first

items.t: Claim about every value $\to$ a counterexample

lines.say: Before any arithmetic — translate.
A big power? Break the base into primes. Equal bases start cancelling.
A root inside a root? Turn it into a fractional exponent.

lines.label: 'Claim about every value → a counterexample' appears

lines.say: A claim about every value? One legal counterexample kills it.
Don't compute giant numbers just because you can.
Testing a claim? Try the boundary values the question allows: zero, one, negative one, a fraction.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Translate first" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Laws + identities

lines.say: Some questions hide a multiplication formula inside an exponent question.
Once an exponent law gives you x plus y, this formula hands you x squared plus y squared — directly.
No need to find x and y separately. If the expression they ask for is already determined — just build it.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Laws + identities" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

items.t: Route 1: the math — exponent and root laws
Check that the choices differ first

lines.label: 'Route 1: the math — exponent and root laws' appears

lines.say: Route one: the math. Apply the laws step by step.
Route two: plug in numbers. With powers, one is your best friend — one to any power stays one.

lines.label: 'Check that the choices differ first' appears

lines.say: But before you trust one substitution, check the choices give different values. If they tie — change the numbers. Don't guess.
Keep fractions exact. And use whichever route you can run fastest.

beats.title: Inequalities

lines.say: Inequalities.
An inequality is almost exactly like an equation.
One difference — and one tip that'll save you on the exam. Let's go.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Four signs

lines.say: In an equation, the two sides are equal. In an inequality, they don't have to be.
One side can be bigger than the other. Or they can be equal — depending on the sign.

lines.label: The four signs appear: a < b, a > b, a ≤ b, a ≥ b

lines.say: Four signs. Less than. Greater than. Less than or equal. Greater than or equal.
x less than or equal to five: x can be five itself — or anything smaller.
Five. Four and a half. Three. Negative seven. All fine.

lines.label: A number line from −8 to 6 appears

lines.say: On the exam, the sign almost always points like the number line: smaller on the left, bigger on the right.

lines.draw: Put dots on −8 and −3, and write "−8 < −3" above them

lines.say: Negative eight is less than negative three — it's farther left.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Four signs" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Same moves

lines.say: Here's the good news: you solve an inequality exactly like an equation.
Move terms across, add, subtract, multiply, divide — as long as you do it to both sides.
Take five from both sides.
x is less than nine. The sign didn't move.
Keep the inequality sign on every line you write. Don't let it disappear halfway.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Same moves" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: A minus flips it

lines.say: Now the one difference.
When you multiply or divide by a NEGATIVE number — the sign flips.
Negative twelve is less than negative four. True — it's farther left.
Divide both sides by negative four: three and one. And look — now it's GREATER than. The sign flipped.
Mathematically that's correct. But on the exam, I recommend you don't multiply by a minus at all.
Under time pressure it's exactly the thing that trips you up.

lines.draw: Move each number to the other side: write "4 < 12"

lines.say: Instead, move the terms across — like in an equation. Negative four goes left and becomes four. Negative twelve goes right and becomes twelve.
Divide by four: one is less than three. Same answer — three greater than one — but the sign never had to flip.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "A minus flips it" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT SLIDE → x to the plus side]

beats.title: x to the plus side

lines.say: Let's solve one — and use that tip.
I want to isolate x. But I don't want x to end up negative.
So instead of moving the 3x to the left, I move the x to the right — where there are MORE x's.
x goes right, thirteen goes left.
Negative eight is less than two x.
Divide by two — a positive number, so nothing flips. x is greater than negative four.
Done the other way, you'd get a negative x, divide by a minus, flip the sign — and complicate your life.
So: move x to the side where it stays positive.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "x to the plus side" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Every x works

lines.say: Just like equations, some inequalities have infinitely many solutions.
Open the brackets.
Twelve minus eight x minus five… less than nine minus eight x.

lines.draw: Cross out −8x on both sides, then write "7 < 9"

lines.say: Minus eight x on both sides — they cancel. Left with seven less than nine.
Is seven less than nine? Always. x disappeared — it doesn't matter at all.
So every value of x satisfies the inequality.
And if x disappears and you're left with something FALSE — like five less than three — then no x works.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Every x works" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Same moves as an equation — on both sides
$\times$ or $:$ by a negative $\to$ flip the sign
Tip: move x to the side where it stays positive
x disappears: true $\to$ every x · false $\to$ no x

lines.say: Move terms, add, subtract, multiply, divide — all allowed, on both sides.
Just watch the minus. Keep x positive and you'll almost never need to flip.

beats.title: Absolute Value

lines.say: Absolute value.
It shows up in expressions, in equations and in inequalities on the exam.
One idea runs the whole topic. Let's get it.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Distance from zero

lines.say: Absolute value is the distance of a number from zero.

lines.label: A clean number line from −8 to 8 appears

lines.draw: Draw an arc from 0 to 5 and write "5 units"

lines.say: Five is five units away from zero.

lines.draw: Draw an arc from 0 to −7 and write "7 units"

lines.say: Negative seven? The number is negative — but its distance from zero is seven units.
And a distance can't be negative. The way to my friend's house isn't minus three kilometres. It's three kilometres.
We write it with two straight bars, one on each side.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Distance from zero" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Plus or minus inside

lines.say: So what do the bars do?
A positive number stays exactly the same. Six is six units from zero.
A negative number becomes the same number — positive. Negative nine is nine units away.

lines.draw: Circle the minus sign in −9 and cross it out

lines.say: In practice? The minus just drops off.
And zero? Zero isn't far from zero at all. It's right there. The absolute value of zero is zero.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Plus or minus inside" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Whole expression

lines.say: Now the trap. What if there's a whole expression inside the bars?
The absolute value belongs to the WHOLE expression — not to each number inside it.
Calculate the inside first. Five minus eleven is negative six. Its absolute value: six.

lines.draw: Below, write "5 + 11 = 16" and cross it out

lines.say: What you must NOT do: turn the eleven positive first and add. That's sixteen — a different number.
Inside first. Then the bars.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Whole expression" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: The rules

lines.say: Three rules.
Rule one — the most important one, it's really the definition. An absolute value is never negative.
It can be zero. It can be positive. See bars — think: zero or positive.
Rule two: for a product, you can take the bars on the whole thing or on each factor. Same result.
Rule three is for a sum — and honestly? If you don't memorise this one, that's fine. Plugging in will get you through.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The rules" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: When is it equal?

lines.say: Still, let's see why rule three works.

lines.draw: Under each, write "= 7" and put "=" between them

lines.say: Same signs: negative two plus negative five is negative seven — absolute value seven. Separately: two plus five, seven. Equal.

lines.draw: Under each, write "= 3" and "= 7", and put "<" between them

lines.say: Different signs: negative two plus five is three. Separately: two plus five, seven.
Taking each one separately makes everything positive — the biggest possible total. A mixed sign inside eats some of it.
So: same signs — equal. Different signs — smaller.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The rules" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Sign clues

lines.say: Now the understanding questions. These come up again and again on the exam.
Compare a number with its own absolute value — and you instantly know its sign.
The absolute value is bigger than the number? Then the number is negative. The absolute value of negative five is five — bigger.
They're equal? The number is positive — or zero. Don't forget the zero.

lines.draw: Draw a big ✗ next to the third clue

lines.say: The number bigger than its absolute value? Can't happen. A positive number would be equal, and a negative one is smaller.

lines.label: The rule behind it appears: |x| = x when x ≥ 0, |x| = −x when x < 0

lines.say: Behind all three: for a negative x, the absolute value is negative x — and negative x is positive.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Sign clues" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Equations

lines.say: An equation with an absolute value? Split it into two cases.
The inside equals the right side — or the inside equals MINUS the right side.
Why both? Because if x plus three were negative eight, the bars would still turn it into eight.
First case: x is five. Second case: x is negative eleven. Two solutions.
Quick sign check before any algebra: the right side is zero? One case only. The right side is negative? No solution at all — bars can't give a negative.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Equations" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Inequalities

lines.say: Absolute value in an inequality. This part is a bit trickier — it's like the second-degree inequalities from before.
The range of x is always symmetric. And it depends on which side the absolute value sits.

lines.label: A number line from −4 to 8 appears

lines.say: Why? Take the absolute value of x bigger than five: the number itself — ignoring its sign — must be six, seven, eight… or negative six, negative seven, negative eight. The minus disappears in the bars.
So when the absolute value is on the BIG side, the range is OPEN — two separate cases.

lines.draw: Write "x − 2 > 4 or x − 2 < −4", then "x > 6 or x < −2"; shade both outer parts

lines.say: Bigger than the number, or smaller than its minus. x above six — or below negative two.
The absolute value on the SMALL side? The number itself must stay small — four, three, two, one, and the same on the negative side. The range is CLOSED — trapped in the middle.

lines.draw: Write "−4 < x − 2 < 4", then "−2 < x < 6"; shade from −2 to 6 on the line

lines.say: Put the four on the right, and minus four on the left. Add two: x is between negative two and six.
Small side: closed, between. Big side: open, outside. Exactly like second-degree inequalities.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Inequalities" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Plug in

beats.title: Prime Numbers

lines.say: Prime numbers.
This topic shows up on the exam a lot — questions on primes, on factors, on divisors.
So let's start from the base: what a prime actually is.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: What a prime is

lines.label: The word 'Prime' pops up at the top

lines.say: A prime is a natural number — positive and whole — bigger than one…
…that you can't write as a product of two smaller natural numbers.
Sounds weird? It's what you remember from school: it only divides by itself and by one.
Thirteen? You can't break it. Prime.
Fourteen? Two times seven. It breaks — not prime.
Same with ten — two times five. Eight — two times four, or two times two times two. Six — two times three. They all break.
The primes are the small numbers you never meet as an answer inside the times table.
Seven, five, three, two — none of them break either. All prime.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "What a prime is" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: 1 and 2

lines.say: Two special cases.
One is NOT prime. It has only one divisor — you can't break it into anything.

lines.label: '2 is the only even prime' appears

lines.say: Two IS prime — it's two times one, so it divides only by itself and one.
And it's the only even one. Every other even number divides by two as well — twenty, eighteen… not prime.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "1 and 2" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Know them by heart

lines.say: You don't need to know primes forever — there are infinitely many.
But up to forty? Know them by heart.
Two, three, five, seven, eleven, thirteen, seventeen, nineteen, twenty-three, twenty-nine, thirty-one, thirty-seven.
If a question asks for the primes between thirty and forty — run through them.

lines.draw: Next to 31 and 37, tick them; write "32–36, 38, 39 ✗"

lines.say: Thirty-one yes. Thirty-two, three, four, five, six — no. Thirty-seven yes. Thirty-eight, thirty-nine — no.
One more worth knowing: the largest two-digit prime is ninety-seven.
Know these — instead of trying to calculate them in the middle of a question.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Know them by heart" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Divisor = factor

lines.say: Two words that mean exactly the same thing: divisor and factor.
A factor of a number divides it with no remainder.

lines.draw: Next to it write "4 is a factor of 20"

lines.say: Twenty divides by four — so four is a factor of twenty. A divisor of twenty.

lines.draw: Next to it write "6 is a factor of 30"

lines.say: Thirty divides by six — six is a factor of thirty.
The word "divisor" confuses a lot of students. Every time you see it — replace it with "factor". Same thing.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Divisor = factor" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Prime factors

lines.say: A prime factor is a factor that is also a prime.
Twelve breaks into two times two times three. Those are its prime factors: two and three.
But twelve also divides by four, by six, by twelve. Where do they come from?

lines.draw: Under 4 write "2·2"; under 6 write "2·3"; under 12 write "2·2·3"

lines.say: Every one of them is a combination of the prime factors. Four is two times two. Six is two times three. Twelve is all of them.
A number divides by all its prime factors — and by every combination of them.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Prime factors" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Break it down

lines.say: Every number that isn't prime is built from primes. Always.
Take one hundred twenty-six. Start with a divisor you recognise.

lines.draw: Draw a factor tree: 126 → 2 and 63; 63 → 3 and 21; 21 → 3 and 7; circle the primes

lines.say: Two times sixty-three. Sixty-three is three times twenty-one. Twenty-one is three times seven.
Stop only when every leaf is a prime. Twenty-one isn't a leaf yet — seven is.
So one hundred twenty-six is two, times three squared, times seven.
Start with six times twenty-one instead? Same primes at the end. Always.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Break it down" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Is it a divisor?

lines.say: Now: is a number a divisor? Check its ingredients.
Eighteen needs one two and two threes — all in stock. It divides.
Twelve needs TWO twos. One twenty-six has only one. Twelve does not divide it.
If a prime is missing — or there aren't enough copies — you can't build it out of the number.
And watch for disguised factors: a six contains a two and a three. Ten squared is two squared times five squared. Unpack them first.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Is it a divisor?" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

Know the primes up to $40$ — and $97$
A number divides by every combination of its prime factors

beats.title: Factor Tools

lines.say: Factor tools.
There's a question type many students find hard: "the greatest divisor".
It comes in two versions. Let's make both of them simple.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Greatest common

lines.say: Version one: the greatest COMMON divisor of two numbers.
Replace "divisor" with "factor": the biggest common factor. Taking out a common factor — you already know how.
Seventy-two and ninety. What's in BOTH of them?

lines.draw: Circle one 2 and the 3² in both lines

lines.say: One two — ninety has only one. Two threes — both have them. The five? Only in ninety. Out.
Two times three squared: eighteen.
In practice it's exactly like taking out a common factor. No need to multiply the big numbers out.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Greatest common" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Greatest guaranteed

lines.say: Version two: the greatest GUARANTEED divisor. Now there's one number — and we don't know it.
The biggest factor of any number is the number itself. But if it isn't given — what factor can we be SURE is inside?
It divides by two and by five? Then it definitely divides by ten. They share nothing.
Two and six? Does it have to divide by twelve? No — six divides by two AND by six. The two is already inside the six.
So: break the numbers into primes, and a prime that appears in both — offset it. Count it once.
Seventy-two and ninety: three twos, two threes — shared, count once — and a five. Three hundred sixty.
That's the least common multiple — the greatest guaranteed divisor.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Greatest guaranteed" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Break & build

items.t: Break apart: split a number into factor pairs
Build: multiply the pieces you're given

lines.say: This is the heart of the whole topic.
With primes we can take any number apart — and put numbers together.

lines.label: 'Break apart: split into factor pairs' appears
'Build: multiply the pieces you're given' appears

lines.say: Many questions dress it up with a long story. Underneath, they're just asking: can you break it — or can you build it?

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Break & build" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Symmetric divisors

lines.say: Most numbers split into divisors in pairs.
Ten: one and ten, two and five. Twelve: one and twelve, two and six, three and four.
Pairs — so an even number of divisors.

lines.draw: Circle the 3 in 9 and the 5 in 25

lines.say: But a prime squared? Nine: one, three, nine. The three sits in the middle — three times three has no partner.
Twenty-five: one, five, twenty-five. Same thing.
So a number with exactly three divisors must be a prime squared. Spot that and you save a lot of time.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Symmetric divisors" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Counting divisors

lines.say: One more tool: counting ALL the divisors.
A divisor chooses how many twos and how many fives it takes.
Twos: zero, one, two or three — four options. Fives: zero, one or two — three options.
Four times three: twelve divisors. Each exponent plus one, multiplied.
Only on a real prime factorization, with distinct primes.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Counting divisors" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

Greatest guaranteed divisor: all the primes, shared ones once

lines.say: Let's lock it in.

lines.label: 'Greatest common divisor: what's in both → take out a common factor' appears
'Greatest guaranteed divisor: all the primes, shared ones counted once' appears

lines.say: In my eyes, breaking and building numbers is the most important lesson in the whole primes topic.
The factor tools card comes right after this video. Then five questions.

beats.title: Division & Remainder

lines.say: Division and remainder.
First: divisibility signs — little clues that tell you if a number divides, without calculating.
Then: remainders. The part that trips people up.
Only small, simple divisors — exactly what the exam needs. Let's go.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: By 2, 5 and 10

items.t: Divisible by $2$: the last digit is even
Divisible by $5$: the last digit is $0$ or $5$
Divisible by $10$: the last digit is $0$

lines.say: Start with the obvious ones — the ones you already know.

lines.label: 'Divisible by 2: the last digit is even' appears

lines.say: Three seventy-six ends in six. Even. Divisible by two.

lines.label: 'Divisible by 5: the last digit is 0 or 5' appears

lines.draw: Circle the 0 in 330 and the 5 in 2,745

lines.say: Three thirty ends in zero. Two thousand seven forty-five ends in five. Both divide by five.

lines.label: 'Divisible by 10: the last digit is 0' appears

lines.say: And ten? Ends in zero. That's it.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "By 2, 5 and 10" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: By 3 and 9

items.t: Divisible by $3$: the digit sum divides by $3$
Divisible by $9$: the digit sum divides by $9$

lines.say: Now the new ones.

lines.label: 'Divisible by 3: the digit sum divides by 3' appears

lines.say: Add the digits. Four plus one is five, plus seven — twelve.
Twelve divides by three — so the whole number, four seventeen, divides by three.

lines.label: 'Divisible by 9: the digit sum divides by 9' appears

lines.say: Nine — exactly the same idea. Seven plus six is thirteen, plus five — eighteen. Eighteen divides by nine. So does seven sixty-five.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "By 3 and 9" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: By 4 and 8

items.t: Divisible by $4$: check the last two digits
Divisible by $8$: check the last three digits

lines.say: Four and eight are a bit trickier.

lines.label: 'Divisible by 4: check the last two digits' appears

lines.say: Look only at the last two digits: twenty-four. Twenty-four divides by four — so the whole number does.
Why? Split it: three thousand five hundred, plus twenty-four. A hundred divides by four — so every hundred, every thousand does too.
Only the tens and the ones are left to check.

lines.label: 'Divisible by 8: check the last three digits' appears

lines.say: Eight: the same idea with the last three digits. Three-twenty divides by eight — forty eights. A thousand divides by eight, so the thousands don't matter.
Honestly? Division by eight is rare on the exam. When it shows up, the numbers are friendly — three-twenty, four-eighty, six-forty.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "By 4 and 8" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: By 6, by 15

lines.say: Six is a strange bird. It has no sign of its own.
But six is two times three. So a number that divides by two AND by three divides by six.
One sixty-two: even — two ✓. Digit sum nine — three ✓. So it divides by six.
Use the same trick for any bigger number that isn't in the table. Fifteen is three times five.
Three thirty: ends in zero — five ✓. Digit sum six — three ✓. Divisible by fifteen.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "By 6, by 15" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: By 11

items.t: Way 1: first two digits $-$ last digit
Way 2: outer digits $-$ middle digit $\to 0$ or $11$

lines.say: Eleven — the hardest one.
Two-digit? No wisdom needed: forty-four, sixty-six, seventy-seven, eighty-eight.
Three-digit? Two techniques.

lines.label: 'Way 1: first two digits minus the last digit' appears

lines.say: Take the left two digits — seventy-one — and subtract the last digit, five. Sixty-six. Divides by eleven — so seven fifteen does.

lines.label: 'Way 2: outer digits minus the middle digit → 0 or 11' appears

lines.say: Or: add the two outside digits and subtract the middle. Seven plus five, minus one — eleven.
One thirty-two: one plus two, minus three — zero. Zero or eleven? It divides.
Most exam numbers are simple — one twenty-one, one thirty-two. But be ready.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "By 11" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Divisibility stories

items.t: $\frac{1}{4}$ of the zebras wear pyjamas. Of those, $\frac{1}{5}$ love to sleep late.

lines.say: Why do we need all this? For divisibility stories — word problems solved with these signs.

lines.label: The story appears: 1/4 of the zebras wear pyjamas; of those, 1/5 love to sleep late

lines.say: How many zebras could there be? We can't know exactly — twenty? forty? a hundred?
But we CAN know what's impossible. There's no such thing as a quarter of a zebra.
So the number must divide by four — and by five.
"What could it be?" really means: eliminate what it can't be.
You'll do exactly this in the first question after the lesson.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Divisibility stories" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: What a remainder is

lines.say: Now: remainders.
A remainder is what's left when you divide one number by another.
Fifty-three divided by seven.
Seven fits in whole up to forty-nine — seven times.
Then four are left. Four is the remainder.

lines.label: N = dq + r, with 0 ≤ r < d, appears

lines.say: Number equals divisor times quotient, plus remainder. And the remainder is always smaller than the divisor.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "What a remainder is" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: The remainder trap

lines.say: Here's where students go wrong.
What's the remainder of four divided by seven?
Four. NOT three. It's not the difference between them.
Picture a shop. Every bottle costs seven shekels.
Thirty shekels: seven, fourteen, twenty-one, twenty-eight — four bottles. Two shekels stay in your hand. That's the remainder.
Now walk in with four shekels. Not enough for a single bottle. Zero bottles — and four shekels still in your hand.
The remainder is what's left in your hand after buying as many as you can.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The remainder trap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Biggest remainder

lines.say: What's the remainder of x divided by five? We don't know x — so let's try.

lines.label: A row of x values appears: 1 to 6

lines.draw: Under each write its remainder when divided by 5: 1, 2, 3, 4, 0, 1

lines.say: One shekel, a five-shekel can: remainder one. Two: two. Three: three. Four: four.
Five? Divides exactly — no remainder. Six? Back to one.
So the biggest remainder is always one less than what you divide by. One more — and it divides again.
Divide by ten? The biggest remainder is nine.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Biggest remainder" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Algebraic form

lines.say: A number with a known remainder can be written algebraically.
Divides by six with remainder two? Call it six k plus two — k is a whole number.

lines.draw: Underline 6k and write "÷6 ✓"; circle the 2 and write "remainder"

lines.say: Six k always divides by six. The two on the end is the remainder.

lines.draw: Draw a "+6" hop between each pair

lines.say: Plug in k: two, eight, fourteen, twenty, twenty-six. Each one six more than the last.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Algebraic form" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Combine remainders

lines.say: One quick bonus.

lines.label: a leaves 4, b leaves 5, dividing by 7, appears

lines.say: Their sum? Add the remainders: nine. Nine divided by seven leaves two.
Their product? Multiply the remainders: twenty. Twenty divided by seven leaves six.
The complete sevens never matter. Only the leftovers do.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Combine remainders" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: $4$: last two digits · $8$: last three digits

lines.say: Honestly? There's not much to memorise here.
Two, five and ten you knew. Three and nine — one idea.

lines.label: '4: last two digits · 8: last three digits' appears

lines.say: Eleven is the odd one out — a little practice and you've got it.
Now four questions. Come in focused — remainders are the part that confuses people.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Integers

lines.say: Positive or negative?
Some algebra questions don't ask for a number at all. They ask: is this expression positive, negative — or can't you tell?
Good news: this topic is usually easy. It rests on the basic sign rules.
Let's run through it.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Sign rules

items.t: $ab>0$: same sign  ·  $ab<0$: opposite signs  ·  $ab=0$: a zero

lines.say: Multiplication first.
Same sign — plus times plus, or minus times minus — the result is always positive.
Different signs — plus times minus, in any order — the result is negative.

lines.label: The product rules appear: ab > 0, ab < 0, ab = 0

lines.say: Careful: a positive product does NOT mean both are positive. They could both be negative.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Sign rules" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Count the minuses

lines.say: One nuance that saves time.
The plus signs don't affect the sign of the result. Only the minuses do.
Count the minuses: one, two, three. An odd number.
So the whole thing is negative.

lines.draw: Tick the minus signs 1 to 4, then write "> 0"

lines.say: Four minuses — an even number. Positive.
Why? Minus times minus is plus. Every two minuses cancel into a plus and stop mattering.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Count the minuses" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Dividing

lines.say: Division? Exactly the same as multiplication. Nothing more to remember.
Same signs — positive. Plus four.
Different signs — negative. Minus four.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Dividing" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Always positive

lines.say: Two facts you'll use in every sign question.
A number to an even power is never negative — whatever the sign of the base.
An absolute value is zero or positive. And if y isn't zero — it's strictly positive.
And a minus in front of a letter doesn't mean negative. It means the opposite. If x is minus seven, minus x is plus seven.
In the question coming up: find the pieces that are surely positive — then the piece that decides the sign.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Always positive" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Count only the minuses: odd $\to\ -$, even $\to\ +$
Even powers and $|x|$ are never negative

lines.say: Let's lock it in.

lines.label: 'Count only the minuses: odd → −, even → +' appears
'Even powers and |x| are never negative' appears

lines.say: A light topic. Basic rules — pretty simple questions on the exam.
Next question — then consecutive numbers.

beats.title: The Number Line

lines.say: Ranges on the number line.
You know the number line — zero, positives to the right, negatives to the left.
Today it becomes a weapon: it tells you what multiplying, dividing, powers and roots do to a number — without calculating.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Four ranges

lines.say: The rough split you know: positives and negatives, with zero as the border.

lines.label: A number line from −2 to 2 appears

lines.say: But we cut it finer — into four ranges.

lines.draw: Shade and label the four ranges: "< −1", "−1 to 0", "0 to 1", "> 1"

lines.say: Numbers below negative one. Negative fractions. Positive fractions. Numbers above one.

lines.label: The four ranges appear as inequalities

lines.say: Why not just positive and negative? Because numbers in these ranges behave differently when you raise them to a power or multiply them.
And here's the key: every number inside one range reacts the same way. One half or one quarter — multiply a positive fraction, and it always behaves the same.
Watch the borders too: negative one, zero and one. A power of one is always one, and zero has no reciprocal.
So step one in every question: which range are we allowed to be in? If they only say x is positive, it could be below one or above one.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Four ranges" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Mirror image

lines.say: Second big idea: the number line is symmetric.

lines.label: A number line from −40 to 40 appears

lines.say: The negatives are a mirror image of the positives. Usually it's easier to look at the positive side — then mirror it.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow from 12 out to 36, and a mirrored arrow from −12 out to −36

lines.say: Twelve times three moves out to thirty-six. Negative twelve times three moves out to negative thirty-six. Both move AWAY from zero — the mirror image.

lines.draw: Draw arrows from 12 in to 4, and from −12 in to −4

lines.say: Times a third: twelve drops to four. Negative twelve goes to negative four — and negative four is BIGGER than negative twelve.
Both moved toward zero. On the negative side, closer to zero means bigger.
So here's the tip: instead of plugging in negatives and risking a mistake, look at the positive side and mirror the picture.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Mirror image" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Multiply & divide

lines.say: How do multiplying and dividing move a positive number?
Multiply by something bigger than one — you grow. Eight times three is twenty-four.
Divide by something bigger than one — you shrink. Twelve divided by three is four.
Multiply by a fraction — you shrink too. You're only taking a third.
Divide by a fraction — it flips: dividing by a third is multiplying by three. Thirty-six.
One is the dividing line. And for negatives? The same moves — mirrored: away from zero, or toward zero.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Multiply & divide" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Hierarchy

lines.say: Now: hierarchy.
A number that lives in a range further right is ALWAYS bigger — whatever power or root you apply to it.
The only exceptions: the exceptional powers — we'll see them in a moment.

lines.label: The fifth root of 9/8 and the square root of 5/6 appear

lines.say: Which is bigger? Calculating those roots is a nightmare. Don't.
Nine eighths isn't really a fraction — the top beats the bottom, so it's more than one. Five sixths is a real fraction, less than one.
A root of a number above one stays above one. A root of a positive fraction stays a positive fraction.
So the fifth root of nine eighths lives in the bigger family — it's bigger. Ignore the roots; look at the number itself.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Hierarchy" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Exceptional powers

lines.say: One catch: exceptional powers. They move a number into a different range — so deal with them FIRST.

lines.draw: Write "= 9" and draw an arrow jumping from the negative side to the positive side

lines.say: Exception one: a negative number to an even power. Negative three squared is nine — it jumped to the positive side.
Exception two: a negative exponent. Flip it and drop the minus: five halves squared. The base was a fraction — now it's above one!
So if another choice is a positive fraction, this one wins immediately — it moved to the bigger family.
And read the brackets: negative three squared WITH brackets is nine. Without brackets, it's negative nine.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Exceptional powers" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Same operation

lines.say: When two numbers get exactly the same operation — just ignore the operation.
Whoever was bigger without it is bigger with it — once any exceptional power is handled.
Exceptional power here — a minus in the exponent. Handle it first.
One seventh cubed against one sixth cubed. Now both have the same power — ignore it.
Who's bigger: one sixth or one seventh? One sixth. So six to the minus three is bigger. No calculating.
But careful — this works for the same operation on positive numbers. Squaring negatives, or taking reciprocals, can flip the order.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Same operation" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Strong on strong

lines.say: Last tool of this lesson — our own slogan: strong on strong, weak on weak.

lines.label: 0 < a < b and 0 < c < d → ac < bd appears

lines.say: Comparing two products? Match the big factors against each other, and the small ones against each other.

lines.draw: Draw a line from a to b and from c to d, and write "weak" and "strong" over them

lines.say: a loses to b. c loses to d. Weak times weak loses to strong times strong.
If one side has a stronger factor AND a weaker factor, this alone doesn't settle it — and signs need care.
You'll use this right away in the next question.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Strong on strong" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Higher range $\to$ bigger, whatever the root
Exceptional powers first: even power of a negative, negative exponent
Same operation? Ignore it · Strong on strong, weak on weak

lines.say: Let's lock it in.

lines.label: 'Higher range → bigger, whatever the root' appears
'Same operation? Ignore it · Strong on strong' appears

lines.say: This understanding — how numbers grow, shrink and jump ranges — is what makes these questions fast.

beats.title: Exercises with Letters

lines.say: Exercises with letters.
Sometimes a calculation shows up on the exam — but instead of 32 plus 57, it's written in letters.
Each letter stands for a digit. Our job: crack the code.
On the psychometric these puzzles are small — and there's a clear technique. Let's go.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: The 4 steps

lines.say: Here's the technique. Four steps, every time.
One: write the exercise vertically. Suddenly you can see things.

lines.label: Step 2 appears: check the ones digit

lines.say: Two: check the ones digit.

lines.label: Step 3 appears: check the leftmost digit

lines.say: Three: check the leftmost digit.
Four: plug in numbers and see what fits.

lines.draw: Draw a big bracket around the four steps

lines.say: Let's run it on an example — and on the way, see what the letters mean.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The 4 steps" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: What letters mean

lines.say: First — what does AB mean?
AB is a two-digit number: A in the tens, B in the ones. Like twenty-three.
It is NOT A times B. These aren't unknowns like in equations.
Think of it as a number written in another language — a different symbol for 2, a different symbol for 3. Still just 23.
The same letter always means the same digit.
Different letters? Read the question. Usually it says "different digits" — then AB can't be 22 or 33.
If it doesn't say so, repeats are allowed.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "What letters mean" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: The 4 steps in action

items.t: $A, B, C, D$ are different digits. $\ \overline{AB}+\overline{AD}=\overline{CDB}$. $\ A+C+D=\ ?$

lines.say: A, B, C and D are different digits. AB plus AD equals CDB.
Step one — vertical. It's already on the board.
Step two: the ones. B plus D gives B.
B plus something equals B. That something must be zero — five plus zero is five. So D is zero.
Step three: the leftmost digits. A plus A gives CD — and D is zero.
Ten, twenty, thirty…? Two digits add up to eighteen at most. Only ten works.
Five plus five is ten. A is five, C is one.
Notice the carry: the one from that ten went into the hundreds. Carries are part of the equation.
Five plus one plus zero: six.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Worked example" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — A, B, C, D are different digits. AB + AD = CDB. A + C + D = ?; the same exercise written vertically

beats.title: Leading digit

items.t: More digits in the sum $\to$ leading digit is $1$

lines.say: Two rules about the leftmost digit.
One: a leftmost digit is never zero. We don't write oh-eight. It's not a phone area code — it's just eight.

lines.label: 'More digits in the sum → leading digit is 1' appears

lines.say: Two — and this one is gold: if a sum has more digits than the numbers you added, its leading digit is one.
Why? The biggest two-digit sum is ninety-nine plus ninety-nine — one ninety-eight.
You can pass a hundred. You can never reach two hundred.
So two two-digit numbers giving three digits? The hundreds digit is one. Always.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Leading digit" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Special digits

items.t: $5\times$ even $\to$ ends in $0$ · $5\times$ odd $\to$ ends in $5$
$6\times$ even $\to$ keeps the same ones digit

lines.say: Now the special digits.

lines.draw: Circle the ones digit of 25 and of 36

lines.say: Multiply them by themselves — the ones digit doesn't change. Five times five: twenty-five. Six times six: thirty-six.
No other digit does that. Check it yourself.
And the obvious ones: zero times any number is zero. One times any number is the number itself.
Five times an even number ends in zero: ten, twenty, thirty. Five times an odd number ends in five: fifteen, thirty-five.
And a less famous one: six times an even digit keeps that digit. Six times two, twelve. Six times four, twenty-four. Six times eight, forty-eight.
Why care? They save you substitutions. You'll use this in a question very soon.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Special digits" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Plug in numbers

lines.say: Here's the truth: every letter question can be solved by plugging in numbers.
A computer would just try every option. We're not computers — so first we look for shortcuts, then we plug in.

lines.label: 'AB − BA is always divisible by — ?' appears

lines.say: Example: AB minus BA is always divisible by — what? There's no result to work from. So plug in.
AB is fifty-one. Fifty-one minus fifteen: thirty-six. Divisible by six, by nine, by four.
Take the next number, fifty-two. Fifty-two minus twenty-five: twenty-seven. Not by six, not by four. Only nine survives both.
Worth remembering — it comes back on the exam. AB minus BA: always divisible by nine. AB plus BA: always divisible by eleven.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Plug in numbers" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Minus → plus

lines.say: A small tip: any subtraction can be flipped into an addition. It's often easier to see.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow from the first line to the second

lines.say: AA minus BB equals BB becomes BB plus BB equals AA.
Now it's easy to see: B can be one, two, three or four.
Not five — fifty-five plus fifty-five is already more than a hundred.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Minus → plus" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Algebraic form

lines.say: Another tool: the algebraic form of a number.
Twenty-seven is ten times two, plus seven. Five thirty-eight: a hundred times five, ten times three, plus eight.

lines.label: AB = 10A + B and ABC = 100A + 10B + C appear

lines.say: Same with letters. AB is ten A plus B. ABC is a hundred A, plus ten B, plus C.
Let's prove the nine rule. Ten A plus B, minus ten B plus A. Nine A minus nine B — nine times A minus B.
Nine times anything is divisible by nine. Done — without knowing A or B.
Some strong students prefer this route. My advice? Most of the time, plugging in two numbers is faster.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Algebraic form" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: 1 · Vertical   2 · Ones digit   3 · Leftmost digit   4 · Plug in
Sum with more digits $\to$ leading digit $1$

lines.say: Let's lock it in.
Our technique: vertical, ones digit, leftmost digit — then plug in.
Plugging in works in almost every algebra topic — and in geometry too.
One habit: a matching last digit isn't a full proof. Check the size as well.
Three questions next. Try each one — then watch its solution.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Defining a New Operation

lines.say: Defining a new operation.
It's a question type you never met at school — it's new on the psychometric.
But everything you need to solve it, you already know: substitution, brackets, powers, fractions, isolating an unknown.
Let's see what a new operation actually is.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: A new symbol

lines.say: Honestly? You've met new operations before. Nobody just called them that.
As a little kid, what's four dot six? You'd have no idea.
Not because you can't multiply — because nobody told you what the dot means.
Once someone explained: the dot means times — easy. Twenty-four.
Same with the plus sign. Until someone told you it means "and", it was just a mark.
And this one really was a new operation: a small two up high.
Somebody told you: multiply the number by itself. Now you read it instantly.
Square roots — same story. A symbol, a definition, and then you can solve.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "A new symbol" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: The heart

lines.say: Now I'll teach you a brand-new operation. The heart.
What's six heart two? Right now — impossible. I haven't told you what the heart does.

lines.label: The definition appears: a ♥ b = 3(a + b)

lines.say: So let's define it. a heart b means: add a and b, then multiply the sum by three.
a is whatever sits before the heart. b is whatever sits after it.
Six goes into a, two goes into b. Six plus two is eight. Times three: twenty-four.

lines.draw: Next to it write "6 · 3 + 2 = 20" and cross it out

lines.say: Follow the whole recipe. Six times three, plus two, is twenty — that's a different rule.
That's all a new operation is: a definition — and then you follow it.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The heart" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Exam symbols

lines.say: On the exam they rarely play with hearts and stars.
Most of the time the symbol is a dollar sign. Sometimes a hash, sometimes a special bracket.
In the questions in this course you'll see a diamond. Same idea, exactly.
Whatever the symbol — read its definition first. Then substitute.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Exam symbols" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Operation first

lines.say: Where does a new operation sit in the order of operations?
Before everything — before powers, times, divide. Only brackets beat it.
Let's say the diamond squares its input.
Can I just add three and four first, and do one diamond on seven? No!
Each diamond first: nine, and sixteen. Then add: twenty-five.
The diamond of seven is forty-nine — a totally different number.
Not sure what comes first? Pretend the operation is a square. What would you do with a square? Do exactly that.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Operation first" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Nested: inside out

lines.say: An operation inside an operation? Start from the inner brackets and work outwards — like any expression.

lines.label: The star appears: a ⋆ b = 2a + b²

lines.say: A new operation — star. Two times the first, plus the square of the second.
Inner brackets first. Two star three: four plus nine — thirteen.
Put thirteen in its place. Thirteen star one: twenty-six plus one — twenty-seven.
The result of the inside becomes the input of the outside.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Nested: inside out" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Find the operation

lines.say: Another type: they don't give you the definition at all.
They took three, did the operation, and got twenty-four. That's all you know.
The operation could be infinitely many things.
For example: eight x. Eight times three is twenty-four. Just one possibility off the top of my head.
So the question asks which definition CANNOT be it.
Your move: go through the choices. Put three in each — the one that doesn't give twenty-four is the answer.
On the exam, the moment you find it: mark it and move on. Don't waste time on the rest.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Find the operation" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Order can matter

lines.say: One more thing about the star.
Three star four: six plus sixteen, twenty-two. Four star three: eight plus nine, seventeen.
Swap the inputs — a different answer. Never assume a new operation behaves like plus.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Order can matter" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Unknown input

lines.say: And if an input is unknown? Replace the operation with its definition — and it's an ordinary equation.
Two x plus four equals eighteen. Two x is fourteen. x is seven.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Unknown input" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

The operation comes first — only brackets beat it
Find the operation? Test each choice

lines.say: Nothing complicated here — just follow the recipe faithfully.
