beats.title: Algebraic Understanding

lines.say: That's it — we've reached the last topic in algebra.
Algebraic understanding.
These are algebra questions that don't belong naturally to any topic we've learned — or that mix a few topics together.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: No fixed recipe

items.t: 3 · Psychometric thinking: plug in numbers or answers

lines.say: Three kinds of solution show up in this topic.
Sometimes the solution is algebra.
Sometimes it's understanding — seeing what the givens really say.

lines.label: '3 · Psychometric thinking: plug in numbers or answers' appears

lines.say: And sometimes we HAVE to use a psychometric tool: plugging in numbers, or plugging in the answers.

lines.draw: Put a box around the three numbers

lines.say: Now the honest truth: it's a fairly small part of the exam — and the questions don't repeat themselves.
There's no repeating principle I can hand you that solves them all.
But this lesson, and the practice after it, give you tools that open your head for questions like these.
As usual — let's start with example questions.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "No fixed recipe" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Must, can, cannot

items.t: Must be true — every allowed case
Can be true — at least one allowed case
Cannot be true — no allowed case at all

lines.say: Before any tool — read what they actually ask.

lines.label: 'Must be true: every allowed case' appears

lines.say: Must be true? It has to hold in every single case the givens allow.

lines.label: 'Can be true: at least one allowed case' appears

lines.say: Can be true? One legal example is enough.

lines.label: 'Cannot be true: no allowed case' appears

lines.say: Cannot be true? Now you need to rule out every legal example.

lines.draw: Write "must" / "can" / "cannot" in a corner of the slide and circle one

lines.say: These directions flip easily when you're rushing. So write the word down before you touch the choices.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Must, can, cannot" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Extreme cases

lines.label: The integer gaps appear: a > b > c integers → a ≥ b + 1, c ≤ b − 1

lines.say: Integers leave gaps. If a is bigger than b, it's bigger by at least one.
Chain two gaps and a is at least two above c.
Those gaps let you find the biggest or smallest possible value — without listing every case.
And check strictness: an integer sum strictly less than twelve is at most eleven.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Extreme cases" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Scaling

lines.say: One variable gets multiplied — what happens to the other?
Start from one and one. The new a is sixteen, so x squared is sixteen cubed — four thousand ninety-six. x is sixty-four.
Positive, because the question says so.
You'll see the full two-way treatment of this idea in question two.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Scaling" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Connect topics

lines.say: Last idea: sometimes the key is a structure from a DIFFERENT topic.

lines.label: 'a² + b² = c² → a right triangle' appears

lines.say: A sum of squares can be Pythagoras in disguise — algebra becomes geometry.
A cycle of ratios cancels to one.
But the connection must come from the givens. Lengths must be positive; cancelling needs nonzero values. Check before you use it.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Connect topics" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

Integers leave gaps — use them for max and min

beats.title: Consecutive Integers

lines.say: Consecutive numbers.
Questions about them usually have more than one way in. Learn all three — then pick the one that feels easiest.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: What they are

lines.say: Consecutive numbers are integers with a gap of exactly one.
Zero, one, two, three, four.
They can be negative too: minus two, minus one, zero.

lines.label: Consecutive evens appear: n − 2, n, n + 2

lines.say: Consecutive EVEN numbers — or consecutive odd — have a gap of two.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "What they are" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Way 1 · Algebra

items.t: $a,\ a+1,\ a+2 \qquad b-1,\ b,\ b+1 \qquad c-2,\ c-1,\ c$

lines.say: Way one: write them with algebra.
Two consecutive numbers a and b, with b bigger. Say a is two, b is three.

lines.label: b = a + 1 and a = b − 1 appear

lines.say: b is one more than a. Or: a is b minus one.
Three of them? Write all three with ONE letter.

lines.label: Three ways to write three in a row appear

lines.draw: Box the middle version: b − 1, b, b + 1

lines.say: From the first, from the middle, or from the last. The middle one is often the neatest.
Heads-up: "bigger than zero" doesn't mean they start at one. a could be seventeen.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Way 1 · Algebra" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Way 2 · Plug in

lines.say: Way two: plug in numbers.
One, two, three. Or two, three, four — anything legal.
I prefer the smallest numbers. Less arithmetic.
And you're allowed to plug in whenever the question is an expression equals question mark.
It's usually the recommended way. It comes back in almost every topic.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Way 2 · Plug in" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Way 3 · Differences

lines.say: Way three: understand the differences.

lines.draw: Draw hops: "1" from a to b, "1" from b to c, "2" from a to c

lines.say: a to b — a gap of one. b to c — one. So a to c — two.
But watch the SIGN of each difference.

lines.label: b − a = 1 and a − b = −1 appear

lines.say: Bigger minus smaller: plus one. Smaller minus bigger: minus one.
This way suits students who are stronger in algebra.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Way 3 · Differences" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: 2 · Plug in the smallest legal numbers

lines.say: Three ways.

lines.label: '1 · Algebra: a, a+1, a+2 — or b−1, b, b+1' appears
'2 · Plug in the smallest numbers' appears

lines.say: Plugging in is usually the recommended one. Simple, fast, no fighting with letters.
Two questions next — try them, then watch the solutions.

beats.title: Even & Odd

lines.say: Even and odd.
How do operations on even and odd numbers decide whether the result is even or odd?
Let's go.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Even numbers

lines.say: An even number is an integer — it must be an integer — that divides by two with no remainder.
Six, fourteen, forty-two, six eighty-four. Finding even numbers is never the problem.
One nuance that matters: zero is even.
It's an integer, and zero divided by two is zero, no remainder.
But honestly, the definition doesn't help people REMEMBER it. So here's a tip.
How did you know six eighty-four is even? You didn't divide. You looked at the last digit — four.
And seven thousand three twenty? Even — it ends in zero. So zero is an even digit. Zero is even.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Even numbers" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Adding & subtracting

lines.draw: Next to each line write an example: 6 + 10 = 16, 9 + 13 = 22, 6 + 9 = 15

lines.say: Six plus ten: sixteen. Nine plus thirteen: twenty-two. Six plus nine: fifteen.
Why is odd plus odd even? Each odd number is "even plus one". The two extra ones join into a two.
Subtraction? Exactly the same: thirteen minus nine is four.
And what IS odd? Just what the name says: an integer that isn't even. One, three, five, seven.
Not "divides by one" — everything divides by one. Odd means: an integer that's not even.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Adding & subtracting" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Multiplying

lines.draw: Next to each line write an example: 4 · 2 = 8, 3 · 5 = 15, 2 · 3 = 6

lines.say: Four times two: eight. Three times five: fifteen. Two times three: six.
Why show examples? Because you don't need to memorise these tables.
Forgot one? Plug in the smallest numbers — one for odd, two for even. One quick plug-in and you know.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Multiplying" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Count the odd terms

lines.say: In adding and subtracting, even numbers don't affect the parity at all.
Only the odd ones matter.
Ignore the evens. The odd ones: nine, thirteen, seven — three of them, an odd count.
Two of them pair up into an even. One odd is left over — so the total is odd.
Here only two odds. They pair up — the total is even.
On the exam it won't be plain numbers — it'll be letters. But the principle stays.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Count the odd terms" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: One even factor

lines.say: In multiplication — one even factor is enough to make the whole product even.
Three terms. I don't care what they equal.

lines.draw: Under 8·11 write "E"; under 7·12 write "E"; under 9·5 write "O"

lines.say: Eight is there — even. Twelve is there — even. Nine times five: odd times odd — odd.
And in a sum, the evens don't matter. One odd term — the whole thing is odd.
Careful with brackets: six times the whole bracket — even. But six x plus three — odd.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "One even factor" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Dividing

items.t: Even $:$ even $\to$ odd, even or fraction

lines.say: Division rules are a bit more complex. Remember — you can almost always make a fraction.
Fifteen over five: three, odd. Five over three: a fraction.
Ten over five: two, even. Fourteen over three: a fraction.
Odd over even — always a fraction. Every even number has a two inside, and an odd number doesn't divide by two.
Even over even: six over two is three — odd. Twenty over two is ten — even. Ten over six — a fraction. Anything.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Dividing" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Three plug-ins

lines.say: Here's the key difference.
For adding and multiplying, ONE plug-in was enough. Two times three is six — even. Done.
With division I plug in three times — to see every result that can come out.
Keep them close: one, two, three. Not two, then six, then ten.
That way you cover the cases — instead of memorising those rules.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Three plug-ins" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Powers keep parity

items.t: Powers don't change parity — you may delete them

lines.say: Even times even is even. Odd times odd is odd. So what happens with a power?
Two to any power — always even.
Three to any power — always odd.
A power doesn't change parity. So in a parity question — you're allowed to delete the powers.
One catch: that's for positive whole exponents. Anything to the zero is one — odd.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Powers keep parity" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Plug in: 2 for even · 1 or 3 for odd
Delete powers — they don't change parity

lines.say: Summary.

lines.label: 'Plug in: 2 for even, 1 or 3 for odd' appears
'Delete powers — they don't change parity' appears

lines.say: Even-and-odd question? Plug in numbers. Don't overcomplicate it.
You can even plug in zero for even sometimes — but I'd avoid it. It can wipe things out and confuse you.
Three questions next.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Powers on the Number Line

lines.say: The number-line method.
Last lesson: the ranges, and what multiplying and dividing do. Now: what POWERS do in each range.
It looks a little strange at first. Practise it a bit — and it becomes the fastest tool you have.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.
beats.canvas: Massive title — "Powers on the Number Line"

beats.title: The arrows

lines.say: Draw the number line with the four ranges.

lines.label: A number line from −2 to 2 appears

lines.say: Each range gets an arrow. The arrow tells you where the number moves as the power gets bigger.
Above one: the arrow points right.
Positive fractions: left.
Negative fractions: right.
Below negative one: left — for odd powers.
Right means bigger. Left means smaller. The bigger the power, the further you travel along the arrow.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The arrows" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Above one

lines.say: Above one, the arrow points right. Every extra power pushes the number further right — bigger.

lines.draw: Label them x, x², x³ and draw a right arrow under them

lines.say: Three, nine, twenty-seven. Bigger and bigger.
And a square root is a power of one half — so it sits between one and x.
At x equals one exactly? They're all equal. That's why the border matters.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Above one" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Between 0 and 1

lines.say: A positive fraction: the arrow points LEFT. A bigger power makes it smaller.

lines.draw: Label them x³, x², x, √x (x = 1/4) and draw a left arrow

lines.say: One quarter squared: one sixteenth. Cubed: one sixty-fourth. Smaller and smaller.
Bigger power — further left — smaller number. The root goes the other way: the square root of a quarter is a half.
In the exam there'll be letters, not fractions. That's exactly where the arrow saves you.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Between 0 and 1" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Negative fractions

lines.say: Negative fractions: the arrow points right. Bigger odd power — further right — bigger.

lines.draw: Mark −1/2 and −1/8 on an imagined line and draw a right arrow

lines.say: Negative one half cubed is negative one eighth. That's to the RIGHT of negative one half.
Even powers are different — they turn positive. And every positive beats every negative.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Negative fractions" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Below −1

lines.say: Below negative one: odd powers move LEFT — they grow in size but stay negative.
Negative three cubed is negative twenty-seven. Smaller than negative three.
Even powers jump to the positive side — treat them separately.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Below −1" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Three steps

items.t: 1 · Exceptions — a negative base with an even power jumps positive
3 · Draw the line and the arrows — then read off the answer

lines.say: In a question that compares powers, work in three steps.
Step one: look for exceptions. A negative number to an even power becomes positive — it changes sides.
Step two: the root gets in the way. Turn it into a power, so you can compare exponents.
Step three: draw the line and its arrows, and read the answer straight off.
And a negative exponent? The arrow method already includes it — keep it as a power of minus one. No need to flip.
You'll do this exact routine in the next question.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Three steps" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Finding the range

lines.say: Sometimes it's the other way around: they give you the order — and YOU find the range.
Take it in two parts. Left part first: x is less than x cubed.

lines.draw: Under the left part write "power ↑ → number ↑"

lines.say: The power went up, and the number went up. That fits the ranges where the arrow points right: above one, and negative fractions.

lines.label: The four ranges appear as candidates

lines.say: So cross out below negative one and positive fractions.
Now the right part: x cubed is less than x squared. Above one, x cubed would be BIGGER than x squared.
So cross out above one. What's left: negative fractions.
Why? x squared is the exception — it turns positive, and a positive beats the negative x cubed.
These reverse questions are rarer — but they show up. And you can always check by plugging in a number from the range.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Finding the range" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Arrow right = bigger power, bigger number · Arrow left = smaller

lines.say: Let's lock it in.

lines.label: A number line from −2 to 2 appears

lines.draw: Circle the arrow for negative fractions

lines.say: Plugging in numbers always works — but it takes time. Understanding what each range does can solve these in seconds.

beats.title: Systems of Inequalities

lines.say: Systems of inequalities.
Now it gets more interesting — more than one inequality at once.
Some of these questions are simple. Some can eat your time. I'll show you every type — and how to crack each one.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Solve each, overlap

lines.say: Two inequalities, or one double inequality — same rule.
Solve each one separately. Then find where they overlap.
First one: take two from both sides — x less than seven.
Second one: divide by three — x greater than three.

lines.label: A number line from 0 to 10 appears

lines.draw: Shade left of 7 in one colour, right of 3 in another; circle the overlap 3 to 7

lines.say: One range points left of seven. The other points right of three. Where do they overlap?
Between three and seven. That overlap is the answer.
Strict signs — so three and seven themselves are out. If x must be an integer: four, five, six.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Solve each, overlap" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: No overlap

lines.say: Sometimes there's no solution at all.
x has to be greater than seven — AND less than two.

lines.label: A number line from 0 to 10 appears

lines.draw: Shade right of 7 and left of 2; write "no overlap"

lines.say: Look at the line. One range is on the right, the other on the left. They never meet.
And it's AND, not OR. x has to satisfy both at the same time. Impossible.
So there's no solution. Mathematically it's called the empty set — you'll rarely see that symbol on the exam.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "No overlap" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Test the choices

lines.say: A very common exam type: trial and error.
Mathematically these are hard. With plugging in, they're simple — and they often show up early in the section.
First: can x be negative?
A negative number to an odd power is negative. And a negative number can't be bigger than twenty. So x is positive.
That already kills any negative choices. Now just plug in.
Two to the fourth is sixteen — less than twenty. Two to the fifth is thirty-two — more. It works. Mark it.
Only one answer is right on this exam — so once one works, you can move on.
Just for the exercise: three to the fourth is eighty-one — already past twenty. No good.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Test the choices" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — x⁴ < 20 < x⁵, x an integer

beats.title: Chain them

lines.say: Two inequalities that share a side? Chain them.
Here x is less than something — and something is less than x.
So: two y minus one, less than x, less than y plus one.
Now the trick: ignore the middle. If the left is less than x, and x is less than the right — the left is less than the right.

lines.draw: Cross out the x, then write "2y − 1 < y + 1"

lines.say: x is gone. A simple inequality with one unknown.
y to the left, one to the right: y less than two.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Chain them" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: x² inequalities

items.t: $x^2<a \Rightarrow -\sqrt a<x<\sqrt a \qquad x^2>a \Rightarrow x>\sqrt a$ or $x<-\sqrt a$

lines.say: Second-degree inequalities. Rare on the exam — but worth knowing.
First, get rid of the fractions. Cross-multiply.
Two times the left top, three times the right top.
Open the brackets, x's left, numbers right: four x squared less than thirty-six. x squared less than nine.

lines.label: The rule appears: x² on the small side → between the roots; on the big side → outside them

lines.say: The rule: x squared on the SMALL side — x is trapped between the roots. On the BIG side — it's outside them.
Root of nine is three. So x is between negative three and three.
Why? Take x positive: one, one and a half, two — squared, all under nine. Four? Sixteen. Too big.
And squaring kills the minus. Negative two squared is four — fine. Negative four squared is sixteen — too big. It's symmetric.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "x² inequalities" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Plus an equation

lines.say: An equation AND an inequality. We use substitution — just like with two equations.
z is x plus y. So put x plus y where z is.
Now it's a double inequality — and we know how to split those.
First part: x less than x plus y. Cancel the x — y is greater than zero.
Second part: x plus y less than y. Cancel the y — x is less than zero.
y positive, x negative. So their product is negative. And about z itself? We know nothing.

beats.title: Products of Consecutive Integers

lines.say: Special products.
Products of consecutive numbers — or consecutive EVEN numbers — follow some very handy rules.
Let's meet them.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Two in a row

lines.say: Two consecutive numbers: one is always even, one is always odd.
They can't both be even, or both odd. So their product is always even.
Two, six, twelve, twenty. Always even.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Two in a row" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Three and four

items.t: Three in a row $\to$ divides by $6$
Four in a row $\to$ divides by $24$

lines.label: 'Three in a row → divides by 6' appears

lines.say: Three in a row: at least one is even — and one of them divides by three. So the product divides by six.
One times two times three: six. Three times four times five: sixty. Divides by six.

lines.label: 'Four in a row → divides by 24' appears

lines.say: Four in a row: always divides by twenty-four. Check yourself with other numbers — it always works.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Three and four" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Just plug in

lines.say: That's already a pile of rules — and there are more coming. They start to get messy.
So here's the move: don't memorise them. Plug in the smallest numbers you can.
Whatever the smallest product comes out to — that's what the product always divides by.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Just plug in" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Even products

lines.say: Now even numbers.
Two even numbers: the smallest is two times two — four. So the product always divides by four.
Proof: each even number is two times something. Together — four times something. But two times two is quicker.
Three evens: two, two, two — eight.
Two CONSECUTIVE evens: two times four — eight. One of them always has a four inside.
Never plug in zero here. It wipes everything out.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Even products" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Hidden products

lines.say: On the exam, the consecutive numbers hide inside an expression.
x squared minus one: the neighbours on both sides of x. If x is odd — two consecutive evens.
x cubed minus x: three in a row.
You'll see both in the next two questions.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Hidden products" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Plug in the smallest numbers — the product is the divisor

lines.say: The whole lesson in one line:

lines.label: 'Plug in the smallest numbers — the product tells you the divisor' appears

lines.say: Three in a row? One, two, three. Four in a row? One, two, three, four. Two evens? Two times two. Two consecutive evens? Two times four.
No rules to memorise. Plug in — and these questions get much easier.

beats.title: Operation Patterns

lines.say: Last time we saw what a new operation is — with the basic questions.
Now: the more advanced types. Still not complicated — just a little different.
Once you've seen each type, nothing on the exam will surprise you.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Operation on an expression

lines.say: Type one: the operation works on an expression, not a single letter.
Careful: twenty is NOT t. Twenty is four t — the whole input.
Four t is twenty, so t is five.
Now use the rule: t plus five — ten.
Put twenty straight into t? You'd be calculating F of eighty.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Expression input" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Conditions

items.t: Odd $x \to$ one rule $\quad$ Even $x \to$ another rule

lines.say: Type two: conditions.

lines.label: 'Odd x → one rule · Even x → another rule' appears

lines.say: Before you apply anything, check the input: odd or even?
And check again at every step — the output of one step is the input of the next, and its parity can change.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Conditions" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Circular rules

lines.say: Type three: a circular operation — the operation appears inside its own definition.
You go into a loop: each value needs the one before it.
So keep substituting — down and down — until you reach the start value they gave you.

lines.draw: Draw a down arrow, then an up arrow

lines.say: Then climb back up with real numbers.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Circular rules" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Isolate the operation

items.t: $\blacklozenge(x)$ on both sides $\to$ treat it as the unknown

lines.say: Type four — very rare on the exam: the operation sits on both sides of an equation.

lines.label: '◆(x) on both sides → treat it as the unknown' appears

lines.say: Isolate it exactly like you'd isolate x. Once it's alone, it's a basic question again.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Isolate the operation" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

items.t: Skip it $\to$ solve the rest $\to$ come back $\to$ plug in

lines.say: Type five: "which is necessarily true" — with the operation inside every answer choice.

lines.label: 'Skip it · solve the rest · come back · plug in' appears

lines.say: Here's my tip: skip it. Solve the whole rest of the section first.
Why? You have to apply the operation many times in every choice. It can eat your time.
Come back at the end — and plug in numbers. It's much faster than opening everything.

Half of seventeen is eight and a half. Nine is more. Above one half.
So: seven fifteenths, then one half, then nine seventeenths. Choice one.

beats.title: Complete to one, then cancel

lines.say: Three brackets, each one minus a fraction.
Don't hunt for common denominators. Complete to one in your head.
One minus a half: a half. One minus a third: two thirds. One minus a quarter: three quarters.
Now multiply — but cancel first.
The two on the bottom cancels the two on top. Same for the three.
All that's left: one on top, four on the bottom. One quarter. Choice one.
Everything in the middle collapsed. That's called a telescoping product — you'll see it again.

Two ways to solve this one — fractions, or decimals. Pick your favourite.

beats.title: Method 1 · Fractions

lines.say: Multiplication and division share a level — so we go left to right.
Method one: switch to ordinary fractions.
Four point five is nine halves. Zero point two is two tenths — one fifth.
Dividing by thirty is multiplying by one thirtieth.
Nine and thirty share a three: three and ten. Three over two times five times ten — three hundredths.
The choices are decimals, so: zero point zero three. Choice one.

beats.title: Method 2 · Decimals

lines.say: Method two: stay in decimals the whole way.
Ignore the points: forty-five times two, ninety. Two decimal places in total — zero point nine zero. Zero point nine.
Now zero point nine divided by thirty. Ninety hundredths divided by thirty: three hundredths.
Zero point zero three. Same answer.
Watch the traps: zero point three and zero point zero nine are each one decimal hop away.

S on top, S on the bottom — cancel it.
P over Q, plus R over Q.
Same denominator — add the tops. P plus R, over Q. Choice one.

lines.say: Question seven — a hard one.

beats.title: Method 1 · Plug in twice

lines.say: Let's plug in. x over y is one half: x equals one, y equals two.
Choice one: is two less than one? No.
Choice two: is one less than two? Yes. Can we circle it? No — when you plug in, you must eliminate three.
Choice three: one times two is two — not one.
Choice four: two over one is two — more than one. Yes.
Two choices survive. Don't guess! We need another substitution — a DIFFERENT kind of number.
A positive ratio can also come from two negatives.
x is negative one, y is negative two. Still one half.
Choice two: is negative one less than negative two? No — negative one is closer to zero, so it's bigger. Out.
Choice four survives both. That's the answer.

beats.title: Method 2 · Why it works

lines.say: So why is choice four always true?
A positive ratio means the signs match — both positive, or both negative.
Either way, the bottom is bigger in absolute value — further from zero than the top.
That's why "x is less than y" only works when they're positive, and "y is less than x" only when they're negative. Possible — not necessary.
But flip any positive fraction smaller than one — you get something bigger than one. Always.
So y over x is always more than one. Choice four — in every case.

Tops: q minus p, against q plus p. Adding beats subtracting.

Semi-final two: choices three and four share the bottom — q minus p. q is bigger than p, so that's positive too.

lines.say: Last question of the set — a hard one.
Three fractions to put in order — three ways to do it.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Same tops

lines.say: Big, awkward bottoms. But look at the tops: five, four, three. Tiny.
So let's make the TOPS equal. Five, four and three all go into sixty.
Five twenty-sixths times twelve: sixty over three-twelve. Four twenty-firsts times fifteen: sixty over three-fifteen. Three sixteenths times twenty: sixty over three-twenty.
Same tops. Now the SMALLEST bottom wins.
Five twenty-sixths is the biggest. Three sixteenths is the smallest.
Smallest to biggest: three sixteenths, four twenty-firsts, five twenty-sixths. Choice one.

beats.title: Method 2 · Cross-multiply

lines.say: Cross-multiplication works too. Don't compare every pair — take two fractions, then use the choices.
Three sixteenths against four twenty-firsts: sixty-three against sixty-four. Three sixteenths is smaller.
Any choice that says otherwise is out: two and four.
One more comparison between what's left: four twenty-firsts against five twenty-sixths. A hundred four, a hundred five — four twenty-firsts is smaller.

lines.draw: Cross out choice 3 and circle choice 1

lines.say: Choice three says the opposite. Choice one.

beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — question q-099 with its four answer choices — "Given: the three fractions 5/26, 4/21, 3/16. Which of the following inequalities is correct?"

beats.title: Method 3 · Flip them

lines.say: And for the creative ones: flip them.
Twenty-six fifths: five and a fifth. Twenty-one quarters: five and a quarter. Sixteen thirds: five and a third.
Five and a third is the biggest flip — so three sixteenths is the smallest original.
Flipping reverses the order. Choice one, a third time.

lines.say: First expression question — real exam style.
You've tried it. Now let's solve it.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Expand both

lines.say: Two squares. Two short multiplication formulas.
a plus b, squared: a squared plus two a b plus b squared.
Now the second one. And here's where students fall — that minus in front.

lines.draw: Write "− ( a² − 2ab + b² )" — keep the brackets

lines.say: Put the whole expansion in brackets. Don't try to save a step.

lines.draw: Open the brackets: write "− a² + 2ab − b²"

lines.say: The minus flips every sign: minus a squared, PLUS two a b, minus b squared.

lines.draw: Cross out a² with −a², and b² with −b²

lines.say: a squared cancels. b squared cancels.
Small nuance: equal terms added and subtracted CANCEL out. REDUCING is different — that's top and bottom of a fraction.
Two a b plus two a b — four a b. Choice four.
A few extra seconds on the brackets beats a fast wrong answer.

lines.draw: Next to the choices write their values: −1, −7, 0, 48

m minus two times m plus two: m squared minus two squared. m squared minus four.

beats.title: Expression Questions II

lines.say: First guided question.
Layers of fractions — let's peel them.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Inside out

lines.say: Fraction on a fraction on a fraction. The main bar is the long one — twelve over everything else.
So we need the bottom first. And inside the bottom — the deepest layer.
One third is two sixths. Plus one sixth: three sixths. One half.
Next layer up: one divided by a half. Multiply by the reciprocal — two.
And the main bar: twelve divided by two. Six. Choice two.
Deepest level first, then climb out floor by floor. Never all the bars at once.
A side tip about the exam: there are no visual traps in the choices. When an answer equals a choice NUMBER — say the answer is three — it sits in slot three.

beats.title: Expression Questions II

lines.say: Question two.
Remember the pattern the exam loves? Here it is.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Opposite brackets

lines.say: Look at the fraction: p minus q, over q minus p. Same letters, opposite order — the pattern the exam loves.
Let's just pick two numbers and plug in: p equals seven, q equals two.
Five over negative five. The same number — one positive, one negative. Negative one.
And that's the rule: swap the order of the two terms and it's ALWAYS negative one — whatever numbers you plug in. p isn't equal to q, so we're safe from zero over zero.
So seven minus negative one. Minus a negative — plus. Eight.
Choice two.
Watch the trap: six is what you get if you treat that fraction as PLUS one.

lines.say: Question three.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Common factor

lines.say: c plus d appears in both parts. That's our common factor.
Take it out front. Inside: t minus three, plus t plus three.
Minus three and plus three cancel.
t plus t: two t. Two t, times c plus d.
Choice one.

beats.title: Method 2 · Plug in

lines.say: Letters scary? In an expression you can plug in numbers.
Why ones? You could use one, two, three — or ten, thirteen, seventy-two. Nothing says the letters must be different, so pick the easiest: all ones.
c plus d is two. One minus three is negative two. Two times negative two, plus two times four. Four.
Choice one: two times one times two — four. A match! But here's the catch: DON'T circle it yet.
When you plug in, you're not hunting for the right answer. You're knocking out wrong ones.

lines.draw: Next to choices 2, 3 and 4 write "6", "0", "3" and cross them out

lines.say: Choice two: six. Choice three: zero. Choice four: three. All out.
Three knocked out — NOW choice one.

beats.title: Expression Questions II

lines.say: Question four.
Four letters, two squares. This one actually appeared on an exam — and it scares everyone.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Plug in ones

lines.say: Strong algebra students might expand this. It takes a minute or more.
For the rest of us: it's an expression. Plug in numbers.
Nothing says the letters must be different — so make them all one.
One plus one plus one plus one: four. Squared — sixteen. One plus one minus one minus one: zero. Sixteen minus zero — sixteen.

lines.draw: Next to choice 1 write "2" and cross it out

lines.say: Choice one: one plus one — two. Out.
Choice two: four times two times two — sixteen. A match! But DON'T circle it yet.

lines.draw: Next to choices 3 and 4 write "0" and "2", and cross them out

lines.say: Choice three: zero. Choice four: two. Both out.
NOW we've eliminated three. Choice two.
And if two choices had both given sixteen? Change one number — make d two — and test only those two.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Question 4" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — question q-138 with its four answer choices — "What is the value of the expression: {(a + b + c + d)}^{2} − {(a + b − c − d)}^{2} = ?"

beats.title: Method 2 · Plug in again

lines.say: Want proof it wasn't luck? Same question, different simple numbers: zero, one, two, three.
Zero plus one plus two plus three: six. Squared — thirty-six. Zero plus one minus two minus three: negative four. Squared — sixteen. Twenty.

lines.draw: Next to the choices write their values: 1, 20, −12, 13

lines.say: Choice one: zero plus one — one. Choice two: four times one times five — twenty. Choice three: two times zero minus six — negative twelve. Choice four: four plus nine — thirteen.
Choice two again. Any legal numbers — same winner.
So when may you plug in? Only in an EXPRESSION — something equals a question mark. Two sides? Not allowed.
Eliminate three — never grab the first match. A tie? New numbers.
It's a safety net. What you can solve with algebra, solve with algebra.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Question 4" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Method 3 · Two blocks

lines.say: For the algebra fans: it's really just two blocks.

lines.draw: Write "A = a + b, B = c + d"

lines.say: Call a plus b, A. Call c plus d, B.
Then it's A plus B squared, minus A minus B squared. That always collapses to four A B.

lines.draw: Write "= 4(a + b)(c + d)" and circle choice 2

lines.say: Swap the blocks back: four, times a plus b, times c plus d. Choice two.
Know the algebra? Great. Don't? Plugging in got you there just as surely.

beats.title: Advanced Expressions

lines.say: Advanced expressions — question five.
Four different ways to crack it. Each one teaches you something.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Just calculate

lines.say: Method one: simply calculate. The numbers aren't big.
And squares like these you should know by heart.
Eighteen squared: three hundred twenty-four. Minus eighteen: three hundred six.
Seventeen squared: two hundred eighty-nine. Plus seventeen: also three hundred six.
Three oh six minus three oh six: zero. Choice two.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Question 5" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — question q-125 with its four answer choices — "({18}^{2} − 18) − ({17}^{2} + 17) = ?"

beats.title: Method 2 · Units digit

lines.say: But even the calculation can be shortened — with psychometric thinking: the units digit.
Eighteen squared ends in four — eight times eight is sixty-four. Seventeen squared ends in nine.

lines.draw: Under the first bracket write "…4 − …8 → ends in 6"

lines.say: Ends in four, minus eighteen: it ends in six.

lines.draw: Under the second bracket write "…9 + …7 → ends in 6"

lines.say: Ends in nine, plus seventeen: also ends in six.
Six minus six — the answer ends in zero.
Only one choice ends in zero. Choice two.
This works because all four choices end in different digits. If they didn't, we'd need another method.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Question 5" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — question q-125 with its four answer choices — "({18}^{2} − 18) − ({17}^{2} + 17) = ?"

beats.title: Method 3 · Common factor

lines.say: Method three: pull out a common factor. Yes — you can do that with plain numbers too.
Eighteen squared minus eighteen: take out eighteen. Eighteen times seventeen.
Seventeen squared plus seventeen: take out seventeen. Seventeen times eighteen.
Same product both times — order doesn't matter in multiplication. So: zero.
Choice two.

beats.title: Method 4 · Say it in words

lines.say: And the fastest way — no pen needed.
Eighteen squared is eighteen eighteens. Take one eighteen away: seventeen eighteens.
Seventeen squared is seventeen seventeens. Add one seventeen: eighteen seventeens.
Seventeen eighteens minus eighteen seventeens — exactly the same thing.
Zero. Pick whichever route you like on the exam — they're all correct.

beats.title: Advanced Expressions

lines.say: Question six.
Lots of brackets, lots of minus signs. Stay calm.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Drop the brackets

lines.say: The whole question is about one thing: when does a minus sign affect a bracket?
Not sure? Always test with numbers.
Ten minus one, in brackets, minus one: nine minus one, eight. Without the brackets: also eight.
So a minus AFTER a bracket doesn't touch it. Only a minus right in FRONT of a bracket flips the signs inside.
Look: every minus here comes after a bracket. Nothing sits in front of one.
So we can simply drop all the brackets.

lines.draw: Write "= p − q − r − s + q"

lines.say: P minus q, minus r, minus s, plus q.
Minus q and plus q cancel out.

lines.draw: Write "= p − r − s" and circle choice 2

lines.say: P minus r minus s. Choice two.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Question 6" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — question q-126 with its four answer choices — "\{[(p−q)−r]−s+q\}= ?"

beats.title: Method 2 · Plug in

lines.say: Not sure about the signs? Plug in numbers. But choose smartly.
We usually plug in ones — but not here. We subtract q, r and s from p, so p equal to them gives a negative answer. And the choices would come out the same.
So: p is a round, bigger number — ten. And q, r, s are different: two, three, four. Second letter, two; third, three.

lines.draw: Next to the choices write their values: 11, 3, 9, 17

lines.say: The choices give eleven, three, nine and seventeen. All different — one substitution is enough.

lines.draw: Work the question from the inside out: 10 − 2 = 8, 8 − 3 = 5, 5 − 4 = 1, 1 + 2 = 3

lines.say: Innermost bracket first: ten minus two, eight. Minus three, five. Minus four, one. Plus two — three.
Three. Choice two.
Which route? Here the direct method is much shorter. Plugging in always works for expressions with letters — it's your default backup when you're stuck.

lines.say: Question seven.
We don't know how to factor this yet — so let the answers do the work.

beats.title: Method 1 · Open the choices

lines.draw: Next to choice 1 write "x² + x + 24x + 24 = x² + 25x + 24"

lines.say: Choice one: x times x, x squared. x times one, x. Twenty-four times x, twenty-four x. Twenty-four times one, twenty-four.
x squared plus twenty-five x plus twenty-four. The x squared matches, the twenty-four matches — but twenty-five x doesn't.
Now notice: every choice starts with x times x — x squared.

lines.draw: Next to each choice, multiply the two numbers: 24, 24, 24, 24

So the only thing that decides it is the middle term: we need eleven x.

lines.say: Twenty-four plus one: twenty-five x. Twelve plus two: fourteen x. Eight plus three: eleven x. Six plus four: ten x.
Eleven x — choice three.

lines.say: Question nine.
Two people, two claims. Who's right?

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Add the fractions

lines.say: Daniel says: A plus B, over A, equals one plus B over A.
Can we cancel the A? There's a plus in there… let's not guess. Work backwards from the side we know how to handle.

lines.draw: Under Daniel's claim write "1 + B/A = A/A + B/A = (A + B)/A ✓"

lines.say: One plus B over A: a whole plus a fraction. Write one as A over A — same denominator — add the tops. A plus B, over A. Daniel is right.
So "only Maya" and "both wrong" are out.
Maya says: A, over A plus B, equals one plus A over B.

lines.draw: Under Maya's claim write "1 + A/B = B/B + A/B = (B + A)/B ✗"

lines.say: Same move: one is B over B. B plus A, over B. That's not what she started with.
Maya is wrong. Only Daniel is right — choice one.

beats.title: Method 2 · Split the fraction

lines.say: Could we shorten that? Yes — by splitting a fraction over a plus.
We said you can't cancel across a plus. But you CAN give each term on top its own copy of the bottom.

lines.draw: Under Daniel's claim write "(A + B)/A = A/A + B/A = 1 + B/A"

lines.say: A over A is one. Plus B over A. Done.
Maya's side has only ONE term on top — there's nothing to split. A over the whole bottom.
You already know this from geometry: one-eighty plus alpha, over two, is ninety plus alpha over two.
Split correctly and the question becomes simple. Only Daniel — choice one.

Three algebra routes — and one plug-in.

beats.title: Method 1 · Open the brackets

lines.say: The minus sits in front of the second bracket only. So only the second bracket flips.

lines.draw: On top write "p − q − q + p"

Two p minus two q. Take out the common factor: two, times p minus q.

beats.title: Method 2 · Opposite brackets

lines.say: Here's a sharper route. Split the top over the bottom.
The first part: identical numbers. One.
The second part: q minus p over p minus q — the same numbers, reversed. Swap the order and you always get opposites: five minus two is three, two minus five is minus three. Minus one.

Take a minus out of the second one: q minus p is minus, p minus q. Open it and check — same thing.

lines.draw: On top write "(p − q) + (p − q) = 2(p − q)"

lines.say: Minus a minus: plus. So it's p minus q, plus p minus q. The same object twice — like two basketballs. Two of them.

lines.draw: Cancel (p − q); write "= 2" and circle choice 2

lines.say: Two, times p minus q, over p minus q. Cancel. Two — choice two.
Route one is the standard. Routes two and three are the sharper ones.

So pick p bigger than q, and not one or two: p is three, q is two.
Choices: one, two, six, four. All different.

beats.title: Simplify each choice

lines.say: We're hunting for the expression where a vanishes.

lines.say: First, look at the conditions: x is not two, and not four.
Why? Because either one would make a denominator zero — and dividing by zero is undefined.
Now the method: a common denominator for both sides. Here it's x minus four, times x minus two.
Left side: three times x minus two on top. Right side: one times x minus four on top.

Open the bracket: three x minus six equals x minus four.
x terms left, numbers right: two x equals two. x equals one.
One isn't two and isn't four — allowed. Choice one.

lines.say: Two equations, two unknowns — as many equations as unknowns, so we can solve it.

beats.title: Method 1 · Match the y's

lines.say: They want x. So let's make the y's match — and cancel them.
We could match the x's instead — times three and times two, making six x. But they want x, so match the y's.
The first equation has one y, the second has two. Multiply the first equation by two.
Every term: four x plus two y equals thirty-eight.

Negative x equals negative seven. x is seven.

Look at the coefficients: three and seven, then seven and three. Mirror images.
Add the two equations. Three x plus seven x: ten x. Seven y plus three y: ten y. Twenty-three plus twenty-seven: fifty.

The square of a difference.

lines.say: Advanced equations — question eight.
One unknown, two fractions. Two clean ways to finish it.

beats.title: Method 1 · Common denominator

lines.say: Fractions of x on both sides. Clear them all at once.
Thirds and fifths — the common denominator is fifteen.
Multiply every term by fifteen. But leave twenty-two times fifteen as it is — don't calculate it.
Two fifths of x times fifteen: six x. One third of x times fifteen: five x.
Move the six x across: eleven x.
Here's why we didn't multiply: twenty-two and eleven cancel. Two times fifteen — thirty.
Thirty. Choice four.

lines.say: Or: gather the x terms first.
Move two fifths of x across. A third plus two fifths — five fifteenths plus six fifteenths: eleven fifteenths.
Stop and look. Eleven fifteenths of x is twenty-two. A bit less than all of x.
So x must be close to twenty-two — and a bit MORE than it.
Fifteen and twenty-two are too small. A part of them can't be twenty-two. Out.

lines.say: Forty-five? A part of it could be twenty-two — but it's far too big. We want something close to twenty-two.
Thirty survives. Estimation finished the job.
Want the full maths? Divide by eleven fifteenths — multiply by the reciprocal. Twenty-two and eleven cancel: thirty.
Two mathematical routes — a common denominator, or adding the fractions. Both are excellent. Pick whichever feels natural.

beats.title: Method 2 · Two quick tools

lines.say: Two tools that make this instant.
Tool one: to isolate a letter, multiply across the diagonal and divide by the one left.

lines.draw: Next to choices 1 and 2 write "diagonal ÷ leftover ✓"

lines.say: a equals b c over d. d equals b c over a. Both fine.

Same with the two and the three: one third equals two sixths. Diagonal partners can swap.
Choice three swaps a and d — diagonal partners. Fine.
Choice four moves three letters around — a drops to the bottom, c and d both shift. That's not a diagonal swap. Choice four.

The hard part here is the words. Turn them into algebra — and it's almost done.

beats.title: Translate, then expand

lines.say: Two integers. Call them a and b.
The sum of their squares: a squared plus b squared.
Equals the square of their sum: a plus b, all squared.
First short multiplication formula.

lines.draw: Cross out a² and b² on both sides; write "0 = 2ab"

lines.say: The squares cancel. Zero equals two a b.
When is a product zero? Only when one of the factors is zero.

lines.say: Question twelve.
Three equations, three unknowns. There's always a shortcut — let's find it.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Add, then subtract

lines.say: Lots of equations, lots of unknowns — that's a signal. There's almost always a short route.
The clues: what they ask for — and which letters are missing from the answers. And most of these are solved by adding, subtracting, or both.
They only ask for x. So get rid of y and z.
Look at y: plus three y in the first, minus three y in the second.
Add them — the y's vanish. Five x plus three z equals thirty-one.
The third equation has three z too: four x plus three z equals twenty-six.
Subtract — the z's vanish. x equals five.
Five. Choice two.
No solving for y, no solving for z. Find the shortcut — don't work hard.

lines.say: Question thirteen.
One of the last questions in a section. Think before you calculate.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Add the equations

lines.say: Two equations, four letters — and they want x plus y.
To get x plus y, we need x and y with the SAME coefficient.

lines.label: A quick example appears: x + 2y = 5 vs 2x + 2y = 5

lines.say: Look: x plus two y equals five — no way to get x plus y. But two x plus two y equals five? Divide by two: x plus y is two and a half. We still don't know x or y — but we know their sum.
Clue from the choices: every one has a plus b. So — add the equations.
The x coefficients: one and a quarter plus two and three quarters. Four.
The y coefficients: two and a third plus one and two thirds. Four again.
Four x plus four y equals two a plus two b.

lines.draw: Write "4(x + y) = 2(a + b) → x + y = (a + b)/2"

lines.say: Take out the fours and the twos. x plus y is a plus b, over two.
Choice two. Solve for x and y separately? You'd burn precious minutes.

Two equations, five letters. Read the clues — then plug in.

beats.title: Method 1 · Get rid of c

lines.say: Clues: they ask about a and b. The answers use x and z. And c? It's gone.
So our job is to make c disappear.
The first equation has one c, the second has five. Multiply the first by five.
Five a plus five b plus five c equals five x.

lines.draw: Subtract the second equation; write "4a + 2b = 5x − z"

lines.say: Now subtract the second. The c's cancel. Five a minus a — four a. Five b minus three b — two b.
Exactly the expression they asked for: five x minus z.
Choice three.

beats.title: Method 2 · Plug in

lines.say: Lots of letters? Plug in numbers. Make a, b and c all one.
One plus one plus one: x is three. One plus three plus five: z is nine.
The target: four plus two — six. We're hunting for six.

lines.draw: Next to the choices write: negative, negative, 6, negative

lines.say: Choice one: three minus forty-five — negative. Choice two: six minus thirty-six — negative. Choice four: nine minus eighteen — negative.
Only choice three can make six: fifteen minus nine. Choice three.
Two approaches — the maths and the plug-in. In this question, both are excellent.

lines.say: Advanced equations B — question fifteen.
A word problem hiding a short multiplication formula.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Difference of squares

lines.say: Translate. Call the numbers a and b.
Their difference is four. The difference of their squares is seventy-two.
That second one is the third short multiplication formula.
a minus b, times a plus b.
And we know a minus b is four.
Divide by four: the sum is eighteen. Choice two.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Question 15" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — question q-178 with its four answer choices — "The difference between two integers is 4. The difference between the squares of the numbers is 72. What is their sum?"

beats.title: Method 2 · Plug in

lines.say: Or hunt for the numbers. Two integers, four apart.
Where to start? Eight and four gives sixty-four minus sixteen — the squares are too small. We need a bigger square.
Nine and five: eighty-one minus twenty-five — fifty-six. Too small.
Ten and six: sixty-four. Closer.
Eleven and seven: seventy-two. There it is.
Eleven plus seven — eighteen. Choice two.
Both routes work. I'd pick the formula — but the plug-in is great too.

beats.title: Method 3 · Start from the choices

lines.say: You can also plug in using the answers.
A sum of twenty and a difference of four: take away four, halve it — eight and twelve. Squares: eighty. Not seventy-two.
Eighteen: eighteen minus four is fourteen, halve it — seven and eleven. Seventy-two!
Choice two, a third way.

lines.say: Question sixteen.
Three ratios, four letters. We'll see four different ways to crack it.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Substitute

lines.say: Write each letter in terms of the next one.
x over y is two, so x is two y.
y is six z. So x is twelve z.
z is three w. So x is thirty-six w.
x over w: thirty-six. Choice three.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Question 16" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — question q-179 with its four answer choices — "Given: x, y, z, w ≠ 0. x/y = 2, y/z = 6, z/w = 3. x/w = ?"

beats.title: Method 2 · Plug in

lines.say: Plug in. Start at the end: w equals one.
z over w is three, so z is three. y is six times that — eighteen. x is twice that — thirty-six.
Thirty-six over one. Choice three.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Question 16" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — question q-179 with its four answer choices — "Given: x, y, z, w ≠ 0. x/y = 2, y/z = 6, z/w = 3. x/w = ?"

beats.title: Method 3 · Two brainwaves

lines.say: Brainwave one: you're allowed to MULTIPLY equations.

lines.draw: Write "(x/y)·(y/z)·(z/w) = x/w" and cancel y and z

lines.say: Multiply the three ratios. The y's cancel, the z's cancel. What's left: x over w.
Two times six times three: thirty-six. One line.
Brainwave two: each letter is bigger than the next — so x is bigger than w, and x over w is bigger than one.
That kills one thirty-sixth and three elevenths straight away.
Here two choices survive, so this trick narrows it down — the multiplication settles it. Choice three.
A wide range of routes — and honestly, they're all excellent. Whichever one you found is a great way.

lines.say: Question seventeen.
One equation, two unknowns — and every answer is written with m.

beats.title: Method 1 · Write n with m

lines.say: One equation, two unknowns — we can't find them. But we can write one using the other.
The answers only use m. So get rid of n.
m times n is one — so n is one over m.
m divided by one over m: multiply by the reciprocal. m times m.
m squared. Choice four.
Prefer the arcs for dividing fractions? Outer product over inner product — m times m over one. Same answer.

beats.title: Method 2 · Plug in

lines.say: Careful with the plug-in here. m and n both equal to one works — but then EVERY choice is one.
We need values whose product is one — without being one. Take m equals two, n equals one half.

lines.draw: Next to the choices write their values: 1/4, 1/2, 2, 4

lines.say: A quarter, a half, two, four. All different. One substitution is enough.
Two divided by a half: four.
Four — choice four.
Two routes. Here the maths was short, so it's the better choice — but plugging in is perfectly fine too.

lines.say: Question eighteen.
A tough one. The trick: look at what they're asking.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Square both sides

lines.say: One equation, two unknowns. And the answers mix x and y — so isolating one letter won't help.
If the answers had only x, we'd isolate y and substitute. Only y? Isolate x. But with both — we don't know which route, and the wrong one burns time.
So use the clue in the question. They want x squared and y squared. The given equation has no squares.
So — square both sides.
Careful on the right. Many students write nine y squared plus one — wrong. The WHOLE three y plus one gets squared — that's a short multiplication formula.
Four x squared equals nine y squared, plus six y, plus one.
Move the nine y squared across. That's exactly double what they asked for.
Divide by two: three y plus a half.
Choice two.

beats.title: Method 2 · Plug in

lines.say: Plug-in is easier here. Find x and y that fit the equation.
y equals one: two x is four, so x is two.

lines.draw: Next to the choices write their values: 1, 3.5, 7, 6

lines.say: Check the choices are all different: one, three and a half, seven, six. Good.
The expression: two times four, minus four and a half — three and a half.
Choice two. For most students, this route is the one to pick.

lines.say: Question nineteen.
True for EVERY x and y. So the coefficients must match.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Match coefficients

lines.say: Expand the left side with the first formula.
a squared x squared, plus two a b x y, plus b squared y squared.
It equals the right side for every x and y. So matching terms need matching coefficients.
x squared: a squared is four. a is two or negative two.
y squared: b squared is nine. b is three or negative three.
x y: two a b is negative twelve. So a b is negative six — opposite signs.
Two and negative three, or negative two and three. Either way, the gap is five.
Choice two.

beats.title: Method 2 · Spot the formula

lines.say: Shortcut: the right side IS a short multiplication formula.
Four x squared, minus twelve x y, plus nine y squared: two x minus three y, squared.
So a is two, b is negative three. Two minus negative three — five.
Choice two. The full method matters, though — some coefficient questions hide a second option you must not miss.

beats.title: Two squares that add to zero

lines.say: First, clear the fraction. Multiply everything by three.
Three a squared plus three b squared equals b squared.
Move b squared across: three a squared plus two b squared equals zero.
Looks strange. You might want to say: impossible — or 'can't be determined.'
Not so fast. A square is never negative… but it CAN be zero.
Something at least zero, plus something at least zero, equals zero. The only way: both are zero.
So a is zero. Choice three.
An understanding question — not a technical one.

beats.title: Exponents & Roots Questions

lines.say: Question one.
Powers everywhere — nine, eight, three, four. Let's make them talk to each other.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Smallest prime base

lines.say: Different bases. So break every base down to its primes — the smallest base possible.
Nine is three squared. Three squared to the sixth: multiply the exponents — three to the twelfth.
Eight is two cubed. Times negative two: two to the minus six.
On the bottom, three to the eighth stays. Four is two squared: two to the minus four.
Now subtract exponents, top minus bottom. Threes: twelve minus eight — three to the fourth.
Twos: minus six, minus minus four. Minus minus is plus — minus two. Two to the minus two.
Three to the fourth times two to the minus two. Choice one.
Careful — this could also show up in the choices as three to the fourth over two squared. The negative exponent just moves it to the bottom.

beats.title: Method 2 · Pair the families

lines.say: A quick second look: pair up the families.
Nines with threes, eights with fours.
Nine to the sixth is three to the twelfth, over three to the eighth: three to the fourth. Eight over four is two — to the minus two.
Same answer. Choice one.

lines.say: Question two.
A fraction full of roots. We need to add and subtract them first — then cancel.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Split into factors

lines.say: We can't cancel yet — there's adding and subtracting. So first, simplify every root.
Root twenty-seven: root nine times root three. Why nine? Because it comes out whole. Three root three.
Top: three root three plus three root three — six root three.
Root forty-eight: sixteen times three — four root three. Root twelve: four times three — two root three.
Bottom: four root three minus two root three — two root three. Like four x minus two x.
Root three cancels. Six over two: three. Choice three.
Notice — the answer three sits in choice three. The exam often places a number like that in its own position. Never choose on that alone — but don't be surprised by it.

beats.title: Method 2 · Common factor

lines.say: Now with a common factor.
The top is root twenty-seven plus root twenty-seven. Like x plus x: two root twenty-seven.
Bottom: forty-eight and twelve share a three. Take out root three — inside, root sixteen minus root four. Four minus two: two. Two root three.
The twos cancel. Root twenty-seven over root three: root nine. Three.
Same answer — choice three. Pick whichever method feels easier.

lines.say: Question three.
The unknown is up in the exponent. You know the method — equal bases.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Equal bases

lines.say: An exponential equation. Step one: make the bases equal.
Four and one eighth — both are powers of two.
Four is two squared. Times two x: two to the four x.
One eighth? Quick tip: ignore that it's a fraction — eight is two cubed. And because it's a fraction, add a minus.
Two to the minus three. Multiply exponents: minus three times four — minus twelve. Minus three times minus two x — plus six x.
Same base on both sides. So the exponents are equal.
Move the four x across: twelve equals two x. x is six. Choice three.
And always go to the SMALLEST base. Two — not four, not eight.

beats.title: Method 2 · Check the answer

lines.say: Want to be sure? Plug six back in.
Left: four to the twelfth — two to the twenty-fourth. Right: one eighth to the minus eight — eight to the eighth — also two to the twenty-fourth.
They match. Six it is.

lines.say: Question four.
A root equation. One move gets rid of the root.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Square both sides

lines.say: Don't overthink it. Square both sides.
The square cancels the root.
Left: just x minus seven. Right: three squared is nine.
Move the seven across: x is sixteen.
Check in the original: root nine is three. It works. Choice four.

lines.say: Question five.
x outside a root, x inside a root. Watch the easy way.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Square both sides

lines.say: A lot of students rush to push the numbers INSIDE the roots. That works — but it's easier to just square both sides.
Left side squared: x squared, times root five squared — which is just five. Five x squared.
Right side: five squared is twenty-five, root x squared is x. Twenty-five x.
Now step by step. Divide both sides by five.
x squared equals five x.
Now divide by x — allowed, because the question tells us x isn't zero.
x is five. Choice two.
Check: five root five on both sides. Perfect.

beats.title: Advanced Powers A

lines.say: Advanced powers — question one.
Two routes: the exponent laws first, then plugging in a number.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Exponent laws

lines.say: Numerator first. Every factor inside a bracket gets the power.
Three to the fourth, x to the fourth. Five cubed, x cubed. Don't multiply them out.
Now the bottom. Fifteen is three times five — split it first.

lines.draw: Under the denominator write "(3 · 5 · x²)³ = 3³ · 5³ · x⁶"

lines.say: Each factor gets the cube. And x squared, cubed — multiply the powers: x to the sixth.
Now cancel. Five cubed on top, five cubed underneath — gone.

lines.draw: Cross out 5³ on top and on the bottom

lines.say: Three to the fourth over three cubed — one three is left.

lines.draw: Cross out 3³ and leave one 3 on top

lines.say: x to the fourth times x cubed is x to the seventh. Over x to the sixth — one x is left.
So the big fraction is three x. Times one third x…
…the threes cancel. x squared. Choice four.

lines.draw: Under a⁻² write "1/a²"; under d⁻⁵ write "1/d⁵"

lines.say: a to the minus two is one over a squared. d to the minus five is one over d to the fifth.

beats.title: Method 2 · Switch floors

lines.say: Here's the shortcut. A negative exponent just switches floors.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow taking a⁻² down to the bottom, and write "a²" there

lines.say: a to the minus two lives upstairs. It moves downstairs — and becomes a squared.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow taking d⁻⁵ up to the top, and write "d⁵" there

lines.say: d to the minus five lives downstairs. It moves upstairs: d to the fifth.
b cubed and c to the fourth have positive powers. They stay where they are.
So: b cubed and d to the fifth on top. a squared and c to the fourth underneath.
Choice one. And careful with choice four — it moves the wrong letters.

solve-q-290.title: Let x be real and y be an integer, with x ≠ 1 and x^(y+2) = 1. Which claim must be true?

beats.title: Advanced Powers A

lines.say: Question three.
Tricky one — both the given and the answer choices need care.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: When is a power 1?

lines.say: The given: x to the power y plus two equals one.
A power that equals one — that should ring a bell. We know exactly when that happens.
Option one: the base is one. Any exponent works.
Option two: the base is negative one — with an even exponent.
Option three: the exponent is zero. Any base works — except zero. Zero to the zero is undefined.
Now the extra given: x is not one.
So option one is gone.
What's left? Either x is negative one and y plus two is even — or y plus two is zero, so y is negative two.

lines.draw: Next to the options write "x = −1" and "y = −2"

lines.say: Now the choices. Each one is an "or" statement. It fails if one legal case makes both parts false.
Choice one: x is zero, or y isn't negative two. Take x equals five, y equals negative two — five to the zero is one, legal. But x isn't zero, and y IS negative two. Both parts false.
Choice three: x is zero, or y isn't zero. Take x negative one, y zero — negative one squared is one, legal. Both parts false again.
Choice four: x is zero? Zero to any power is never one. Out.

lines.draw: Cross out choice 4 and circle choice 2

lines.say: Choice two covers both cases that survive: y is negative two, or x is negative one. Choice two.

beats.title: Method 1 · Substitute

lines.say: Two equations, two unknowns. We want y — so we get rid of x.
The second equation says x is y squared. Put that into the first one.
y squared, to the power y — equals y to the power y squared.
Power of a power: multiply. y to the two y.
Same base on both sides — so the exponents must be equal.
Two y equals y squared.
y is bigger than one, so it isn't zero — we can divide by y. y equals two.
Choice two. Honestly — quite long.

It starts as an exponent equation — and ends as a multiplication-formula question.

beats.title: Exponents, then a formula

lines.say: First given: five to the x times five to the y.
Same base, multiplying — add the exponents.
And a hundred twenty-five is five cubed.
Same base — compare the exponents. x plus y is three.
Second given: two x y is four.
Put them together and you've built the first multiplication formula.
x plus y is three — so three squared. And two x y is four.
Nine minus four: five. Choice one.

Two ways: the math route, then plugging in a number.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Count the copies

lines.say: Two to the y, plus two to the y, plus two to the y, plus two to the y.
You can't add exponents across a plus sign. But look — it's the same term, four times.
Just like y plus y is two y — four copies of two to the y is four times two to the y.
And four is two squared.
Same base, multiplying — add the exponents: two to the y plus two.

lines.draw: Write "x = y + 2 → x − y = 2" and circle choice 2

lines.say: Same base on both sides: x is y plus two. So x minus y is two. Choice two.

lines.say: Now the psychometric way. It's an equation — so plug a number into one letter, then work out the other.
Plug into y — it shows up four times.
y is one: two plus two plus two plus two — eight.
Two to the what is eight? Two cubed. x is three.
Three minus one: two. The choices are plain numbers, so one substitution is enough. Choice two.

lines.say: Advanced powers B — question seven.
Three different roots. First job: make them all the same kind.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Match the roots, then merge

lines.say: Look at the roots. Square roots on top, a square root underneath — and one eighth root.
Before anything else, make every root the same order.
Turn the root into a power. The base stays two. The power goes on top, the root goes underneath: four over eight.
Little memory trick: the power is up in the sky, the root is down in the ground.
Four eighths is a half. Two to the half — that's just root two.
Shortcut: you're allowed to cancel the root's index with the power. Divide both by four — square root of two to the one.
Now the whole top is square roots. Multiply them under ONE root.
Root of a half, times forty, times two.

lines.draw: Cancel the ½ with the 2; write "= √40"

lines.say: A half and a two cancel. Root forty on top.
Some students spot it even earlier — root a half and root two cancel straight away. Same result.
Same order on top and bottom — divide first, then take the root. Forty over ten is four. Root four: two.
Two. Choice two.

solve-q-295.title: Which of the following numbers is the largest?

beats.title: Advanced Powers B

lines.say: Question eight.
Which one is biggest? Here we estimate — using perfect squares.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Estimate each choice

lines.say: We don't know these exactly. But we can estimate.
Choice one: root thirty-nine. Root thirty-six is exactly six. So this is a little more than six.
Choice two: two pi. Pi is about three point one four. Twice that: about six point two eight.
Both of these sit around six and a bit. Let's see if anything beats them.
Choice three. Root twenty-three: root twenty-five is five, so just under five — about four point eight. Root five is about two point two.
Together: about seven. That beats choices one and two.
Now choice four: three root five. Two ways.
Way one: root five is about two point two, times three — about six point seven.
Way two: bring the three inside the root. A number goes in squared — nine times five, root forty-five.
Root forty-five is less than root forty-nine, which is seven. So it's under seven.

lines.draw: Cross out choice 4 and circle choice 3

lines.say: About seven wins. Choice three.
Notice: choices one and two are too close to split by estimating — and we didn't need to. Choice three beat them both.

lines.say: Question nine.
Two fractions with roots. Two ways to add them.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Match the denominators

lines.say: Adding fractions — we need the same denominator.
Method one: rewrite the second fraction so it matches the first.
Four is two times two — and two is root two times root two. So four is two, root two, root two.
Cancel one root two. The second fraction becomes one over two root two.
Little tip: flip it and you know this one. Four over root two — ignore the root, four over two is two, put the root back: two root two. Now flip back: one over two root two.
Now the denominators match. Three plus one: four over two root two. That's two over root two.
Two over root two — ignore the root, two over two is one, put the root back: root two.
Root two. Choice two.

beats.title: Method 2 · Multiply the denominators

lines.say: Method two: the most basic common denominator — multiply the two denominators.
Two root two times four: eight root two.
First fraction times four on top: twelve. Second fraction times two root two on top: root two times two root two is four.
Sixteen over eight root two. That's two over root two — root two again.
Same answer. Pick the method you like.

lines.say: Question ten.
A root inside a root. Two ways: algebra, then plugging in.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Inside the root

lines.say: First step: bring the x inside the inner root.
How does a factor go into a root? Raised to the root's index. Square root — so x goes in as x squared.
X squared times x: x cubed. So inside we have root of x cubed.
Now it's a root of a root. Just like a power of a power — multiply the indices. Two times two: a fourth root.
Fourth root of x cubed. Choice four.

beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — question q-297 with its four answer choices — "\sqrt{x · \sqrt{x}} = ?"

beats.title: Method 2 · Plug in

lines.say: Plug in a number. One is easy — but every choice would give one. Useless.
We need a number whose roots come out clean. The lesson's favourite is four — but here four gives root eight at the end. Not clean.
So take sixteen. Its roots come out whole.
Choice one: sixteen. Choice two: root sixteen, four. Choice three: cube root of sixteen — not a whole number. Choice four: fourth root of sixteen cubed — eight.
Now the question: root sixteen is four. Sixteen times four: sixty-four. Root sixty-four: eight.
Eight — choice four.
Know both routes. Here too, plugging in is shorter for most students.

lines.say: Question eleven.
Getting rid of that denominator isn't obvious — until you see the formula.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Difference of squares

lines.say: The choices have no denominator. So we need to get rid of it.
No common factor on top. So what can we do? Spot the third multiplication formula.
a minus b is root a plus root b, times root a minus root b.
Check: root a times root a is a. Root b times minus root b is minus b. The middle terms cancel.
We're used to this formula with squares. It works just as well with square roots.
Now the root a minus root b cancels with the denominator.
What's left: root a plus root b. Choice four.

beats.title: Method 2 · Plug in

lines.say: Plug in. a and b have to be different — so not both one.
Pick numbers with clean roots: one and four. And plug in smart — a is four, b is one, so the top stays positive.
Check the choices: two minus one is one. Zero. Four plus one is five. Two plus one is three. All different — one substitution is enough.
The question: four minus one is three. Root four minus root one: two minus one, one. Three over one: three.
Three — choice four. The plug-in is the easy route for most students.

beats.title: Advanced Powers B

lines.say: Question twelve.
How many solutions? We'll solve it — and count.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Open the brackets

lines.say: To count the solutions, we have to solve it.
Open the brackets. Root x times root x.
Root x times root x is x. So x minus three root x is zero — x equals three root x.
When does a number equal three times its own root?
Zero works: zero equals zero. Nine works: nine equals three times three.
Exactly two solutions. Choice two.
Faster: it was already a product equal to zero — each factor can be zero.
But never divide both sides by root x. That throws away x equals zero — and leaves you with only one solution. Wrong answer.
