lines.say: Question thirteen.
A system of equations — with roots. Two ways: exact, then estimating.

beats.title: Method 1 · Add, then split the roots

lines.say: They want x. So we need to get rid of y.
Add the equations — y cancels. Three x equals root one-oh-eight plus root twenty-seven.

lines.draw: Next to it write "≠ √135" and cross it out

lines.say: What you must NOT do: add them into root one-thirty-five. That's wrong.
To add roots, we need a common root. Split each one into a number times a root.
Does a hundred and eight split into something with a clean root? Thirty-six times three. So six root three.
Twenty-seven: nine times three. Three root three. Same root three — good.
Six root three plus three root three: nine root three. Divide by three: three root three.
Choice two.

beats.title: Method 2 · Estimate

lines.say: Can't split the roots? Estimate instead.
Root one-oh-eight: root one hundred is ten, root one-twenty-one is eleven — about ten point four. Root twenty-seven: just over five, about five point two.
Three x is about fifteen point six. So x is about five point two.
Root fifteen: under four — out. Three root three: three times one point seven three, about five point two. Root thirty: about five point five. Nine root three: way too big.
Careful — this one's tighter than usual. Five point two and five point five are close, so keep one decimal place.
Five point two matches. Choice two. Know the exact method — but estimating is a solid backup.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Flip, then square

lines.say: Simplify the left side. A negative power flips the fraction.
One over x to the half, equals four.
A power of a half is a square root. One over root x equals four.
Multiply by root x: one equals four root x. Divide by four: root x is a quarter.
Square both sides: x is one sixteenth.

lines.say: The short, elegant route: isolate x by raising both sides to a power.
Power of a power — we multiply. Minus a half times what gives one? Minus two.
It's always the reciprocal of the power. So raise both sides to minus two.
Left side: just x. Right side: four to the minus two — one over sixteen.
Straight to the answer. Choice four.

Sixteen to the minus a half: one over root sixteen — one quarter.
We wanted four. We got a quarter. Wrong — but look: it's exactly the reciprocal.
The minus sign flips things. So the right answer is the reciprocal of sixteen.
One sixteenth. Choice four.

lines.say: Advanced inequalities — question nine.
Two ways in: the math, then a psychometric shortcut.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Solve it

lines.say: x is a positive integer. How many values fit between these two fractions?
First — simplify. Forty eightieths is one half.
Seventy eightieths reduces by ten: seven eighths.
A double inequality is really two inequalities. Split it into a left part and a right part.

lines.draw: Write "1/2 < x/(x+1)" and "x/(x+1) < 7/8" on two lines

lines.say: Now we want to multiply by x plus one — an unknown. Careful!
Multiply by a negative and the sign flips. So ask: is x plus one positive?
x is a positive integer — so x plus one is positive too. No flip.
Cross-multiply: x plus one is less than two x. So x is bigger than one.
Second one: eight x is less than seven x plus seven. So x is less than seven.
Bigger than one, smaller than seven, positive integers: two, three, four, five, six.
Five values. Choice two.

beats.title: Method 2 · Spot the pattern

lines.say: Now the psychometric flash of insight.
After simplifying, look closely: in x over x plus one, the bottom is one more than the top. Consecutive numbers.
One half and seven eighths are built exactly the same way: one over two, seven over eight.
So just try values. x equals one gives one half — equal, not bigger. Out.
Two: two thirds. Three: three quarters. Then four fifths, five sixths, six sevenths — all fit.
Seven gives seven eighths — equal again, not smaller. Out.
Five values — choice two.
The shortcut is faster. But the technique from method one — check the sign before you multiply by an unknown — you'll need again and again.

a is less than one.

lines.say: Question four.
This time the absolute value is on the BIG side. And watch the word CANNOT.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Big side: open range

lines.say: The absolute value is on the BIG side. So the range is open — two separate cases.
Either the inside is bigger than six — x is bigger than three.
Or the inside is smaller than negative six — x is smaller than negative nine.
They ask what x CANNOT be. So find the one that fits neither range.
Six — above three, fine. Eight — above three, fine. Negative ten — below negative nine, fine.
Two? It's not above three, and it's not below negative nine. It's stuck in the forbidden middle. Choice three.
Check: two plus three is five — and five is not bigger than six.

lines.say: Last question.
They ask what an expression equals. You know what that means — plug in.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Plug in

lines.say: It's an expression — so we're allowed to plug in a number. x just has to be negative.
Take x equals negative three. Why negative three? No reason — any negative number works.
Two times negative three is negative six. Over three: negative two. Five minus two — three.

lines.draw: Next to the choices write their values: 7, 3, 3, 8

lines.say: Now the choices at x equals negative three. Seven — no. Three — yes. Negative x is… three. Yes too! Five minus x is eight — no.
Two survive. With other numbers, one plug-in would have killed three choices. Here negative three happens to make negative x equal three.
So plug in again — a different negative.
x equals negative one: five plus negative two over one. Three again.

lines.draw: Next to choice 3 write "−x = 1 ✗" and circle choice 2

lines.say: But negative x is now one. Out. Choice two.

beats.title: Method 2 · Replace |x|

lines.say: The algebra is short too.
x is negative, so its absolute value is negative x.
Two x over negative x — the x's cancel. Negative two, whatever the negative number is.
Five minus two: three. And that's why choices with an x in them can't be right — the x disappears. Choice two.

lines.say: Advanced absolute value — question six.
Most absolute-value questions on the exam are UNDERSTANDING questions. This is one of them.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Understand the givens

lines.say: Two approaches today: understanding first, then plugging in numbers.
Given one: the absolute value of b equals a. Same distance from zero.
Given two: but b and a are NOT equal.

lines.draw: Under the question write "|b| = a → a ≥ 0"

lines.say: An absolute value is never negative — so a is zero or positive.
Could a be zero? Then b is zero too — and they'd be equal. Not allowed.
So a is positive, and b is the negative number the same distance from zero.

lines.draw: Draw a number line: b left of 0, a right of 0, same distance

lines.say: Given three: three c equals a. So c is a third of a.
a positive — so c is positive too, but smaller. It sits between zero and a.
Biggest: a. Smallest: b. In the middle: c.
b, then c, then a. Choice four.

beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — question q-363 with its four answer choices — "Given: |b| = a, b ≠ a, and 3\,c = a. Which of the following statements necessarily follows?"

beats.title: Method 2 · Plug in

lines.say: Now plug in numbers that obey every given.
Try a three, b three. The absolute value of b is a — fine.
But they have to be different. Bad substitution — so change it.
b negative three. Absolute value three, equals a — and they're different. Now both givens work.
Three c equals three — c is one.
Negative three, one, three: b, c, a. Choice four again.
Which way is better? I prefer understanding — but plugging in is an excellent backup.

lines.say: Question seven.
Another understanding question — one step harder.

beats.title: Method 1 · Put it on the number line

lines.say: Let's place the givens on the number line.

lines.draw: Draw a number line: p and q left of 0 (p further), r and s right of 0 (s further)

lines.say: p and q are negative — p is further from zero. r and s are positive — s is further.
Notice: every answer uses absolute value. Absolute value means distance from zero.
So the question is really: who is further from zero?
Two positives — s is always further than r. We don't know by how much, but always.
Same for the negatives: p is always further than q.
But a negative against a positive? The givens say nothing about that.

lines.draw: Next to choice 1 write "p = −2, s = 2 → equal"

lines.say: Choice one: p against s. p could be negative two and s two — equal. Or p could be negative twenty — bigger. Not necessarily.
Choice two: q against s — again negative versus positive. q could be negative twenty. Out.
Choice three: r against p — positive versus negative. r could be twenty. Out.
Three out — on the exam, mark the fourth and move on.
Here we'll check it anyway: q and p are both negative, same side of zero. p is further. Always. Choice four.

lines.say: Question eight.
This one is a genuinely high-level analysis question. Take it slowly.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Analyse the givens

lines.say: Given one: d is less than c, which is less than b. We don't know any signs yet.
Given two: the absolute value of b is LESS than the absolute value of c.
Look at that. Without bars, b is bigger than c. With bars, c suddenly jumps above b.

lines.draw: Under the question write "c < b but |c| > |b| → c < 0"

lines.say: Only a negative number changes when you put bars on it. So c must be negative.
d is even smaller than c — so d is negative too, and further from zero.
And b? The givens can't pin it down. b could be negative, closer to zero than c — or b could be positive, as long as it's closer to zero than c.
Example: c negative two, d negative three — b could be negative one, or b could be one.
They want the statement that is NOT necessarily true.
Choice one: b is not equal to its absolute value. That claims b must be negative.
But b could be positive — then b equals its absolute value. Not necessarily true!
That's our answer — choice one. On the exam, mark it and move on.
Let's check the others anyway — all must be always true.
Choice two: c and d are both negative, d further left. So d is further from zero. Always true.
Choice three: d is further from zero than c, and c is further than b. So d is further than b. Always.
Choice four: d is negative — so d is not equal to its absolute value. Always true.
Choice one it is.

beats.title: Advanced Absolute Value

lines.say: Question nine.
Unlike the last ones, this is a TECHNIQUE question — and the wording is new.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Test each choice

lines.say: Read the question carefully: POSSIBLE, but NOT NECESSARILY correct.
So anything that's never true — out. Anything that's always true — out.
We want the one that's sometimes true, sometimes not.
Choice one looks like the given — brackets instead of bars, and a square.
The technical way: square both sides of the given. Two squared is four. And the absolute value of a plus b, squared, is exactly the same as a plus b in brackets, squared — both are positive.
So choice one is always true. Out.
And a much simpler way to see it: absolute value behaves like an even power. What's true with bars is true with a square.
Choice two: the absolute value of a times b.
You can split bars over multiplication: the absolute value of a b IS the absolute value of a times the absolute value of b.
Always EQUAL — never less. Never true. Out.
Choice three: take out the common factor three inside the bars.
Split the bars: three times the absolute value of a plus b.
So it says: something is less than three times itself. That something is positive — divide it away: one is less than three. Always true. Out.
Three out — on the exam, mark four. Here, let's see why it's right.
That's a rule: the absolute value of a sum is less than or EQUAL to the sum of absolute values.
Same signs — three and one: four equals four. Equal, not less.
Opposite signs — five and negative two: three against seven. Less!
Sometimes true, sometimes not. Choice four.
Know that rule, and you can mark this one instantly.

lines.say: Question ten.
Two equations, two unknowns, absolute values. Three ways to solve it.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Full algebra

lines.say: Method one: full algebra.
The first equation divides by three: absolute x plus two absolute y equals nine.
They want x — so we need to get rid of y. Subtract the equations.
Two absolute y cancels. Absolute x minus x equals six.
Move the x across: absolute x equals six plus x.
An absolute-value equation has two options: the sides are equal, or one is the opposite of the other.
Option one: x equals six plus x. Zero equals six. False — no solution here.
Option two: x equals minus six minus x. Two x is negative six. x is negative three.
Choice two.

beats.title: Method 2 · Algebra, then plug in

lines.say: Method two: same algebra — until we reach the absolute-value equation.
Then, instead of solving it — plug in the answers. They're all numbers.
x equals two: absolute two is two. Six plus two is eight. No.
x equals negative three: absolute value three. Six plus negative three: three. Yes!
Much quicker at that stage than finishing the algebra.

Check the first equation: six plus three is nine. Not twenty-seven. Out.
Choice two, x is negative three. Negative three plus two absolute y equals three — absolute y is three.
First equation: nine plus eighteen — twenty-seven. It works!
Choice two. My picks: the shortened algebra, or plugging in the answers right away.

lines.say: Question eleven.
One equation, two unknowns, absolute values — three approaches.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Equal or opposite

lines.say: An absolute-value equation: either the insides are equal, or one is the opposite of the other.
Option one: equal. Move terms across — y equals x.
Option two: opposite. Open the bracket, move terms — x equals negative y.
So x equals y, or x equals negative y.
Choice one, x equals y — only partly true. x could be negative y. Not necessarily.
Choice two: equal or opposite — either way, same absolute value. Always true. Choice two.

beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — question q-368 with its four answer choices — "Given: |x + 3\,y| = |3\,x + y|. Which of the following statements necessarily follows?"

beats.title: Method 2 · Square both sides

lines.say: Some students get rid of the bars by squaring both sides. After squaring, the bars mean nothing.
Open with the first shortcut formula.
Six x y on both sides — cancel it.
Move terms and divide by eight: y squared equals x squared.
Remember: absolute value and an even power are basically the same. True with squares — true with bars.
Absolute x equals absolute y. Choice two.

beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — question q-368 with its four answer choices — "Given: |x + 3\,y| = |3\,x + y|. Which of the following statements necessarily follows?"

beats.title: Method 3 · Plug in

lines.say: Plugging in here isn't obvious — but it's the shortest.
Equal numbers — x one, y one. Four on both sides. Works.
So x less than y — no. y less than x — no. Choices three and four are out.
One and two both survive. The answers hint: equal, or equal in absolute value. Let's split them.
Opposite numbers: one and negative one. Absolute two equals absolute two. Works!

lines.draw: Cross out choice 1 and circle choice 2

lines.say: So they don't have to be equal. Choice two.
Three approaches. The third is hardest to spot — but shortest. Pick what suits you.

beats.title: Method 1 · Two symmetric bands

lines.say: We've seen absolute-value inequalities before. A double one has an elegant route.

lines.draw: Draw a number line: shade 11 to 13 and −13 to −11

lines.say: Two x plus one, in bars. If it's positive, it's between eleven and thirteen. If negative — symmetrically, between negative thirteen and negative eleven.
Positive band first. The unknown is in the middle — work on all three parts.
Subtract one: ten to twelve. Halve: x between five and six.
Peek at the choices — it isn't there. So on to the negative band.
Negative thirteen to negative eleven. Subtract one, halve: x between negative seven and negative six.
Choice two.
Six to seven is the bait — that's what you get if you forget to subtract the one.

lines.say: Question thirteen — the last one.
Find the most precise domain. Two approaches.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Two cases

lines.say: As usual with absolute value — two cases.
Case one: x is positive or zero. Then the bars do nothing.
x plus x is less than fourteen. Two x under fourteen — x under seven.
Case two: x is negative.
Then the bars turn it into its opposite. Negative five plus five — zero. Negative one plus one — zero. Always zero.
Zero is less than fourteen — always true. Every negative number works.
So: every negative number, and positives only below seven.
x less than seven. Choice four.

lines.say: Prime questions — number one.
The trick: draw it on a number line.

beats.title: Number line

lines.say: First — which primes are near twenty? Write out the whole numbers.

lines.label: A number line from 10 to 32 appears

lines.draw: Circle the primes on the line: 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, 29, 31

lines.say: Eleven, thirteen, seventeen, nineteen… then twenty-three, twenty-nine, thirty-one.
Between x and twenty: exactly two primes. So seventeen and nineteen are in — thirteen must stay out.
x can't be thirteen or below — then there'd be three primes. And x isn't prime anyway.
So x is fourteen, fifteen or sixteen.
Between twenty and y: exactly two primes — twenty-three and twenty-nine. Thirty-one must stay out.

lines.draw: Shade 30 on the right, and cross out 31

lines.say: So y is thirty or thirty-one — and thirty-one is prime. Not allowed. y is thirty.
We want the SMALLEST product. Take the smallest x and the smallest y.
Fourteen times thirty: four hundred twenty. Choice four.
If they'd asked for the largest — take the largest x: sixteen times thirty.

beats.title: Advanced Primes

lines.say: Advanced primes. First question.
It looks brutal. It isn't — if you spot the idea.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: The only even prime

lines.say: Two primes, and a sum. Which choice can NOT be their sum?
Trial and error? Split twenty-five into two primes, then twenty-seven… that takes forever.
On the psychometric there's almost always one simple idea. Once it clicks, the answer falls out.
Look at the choices. Every single one is odd.
When is a sum odd? Even plus even — even. Odd plus odd — even.
Only one even and one odd give an odd sum.
And the primes are almost all odd — except one. Two. The only even prime.
So one of the primes MUST be two. Take two off each choice and check what's left.
Twenty-five: two plus twenty-three. Twenty-three is prime. Possible.
Twenty-seven: two plus twenty-five. Twenty-five is five times five — not prime.
So twenty-seven can't be the sum. On the exam — mark it and move on.
In the lesson we check the rest. Thirty-three: two plus thirty-one — prime. Forty-five: two plus forty-three — prime.
The whole question was one fact: two is the only even prime. The exam loves it.

beats.title: Method 1 · Break into primes

lines.say: The idea: break every number into its prime factors.
Ten is two times five. Fifteen is three times five. Seven is prime.
Exactly two of them divide by a. Which prime shows up in exactly two?
Five. So a equals five.
Second group. Twenty-two: two times eleven. Fifteen: three times five. Thirty: two, three and five.
Only ONE of these divides by b. Two appears twice. Three — twice. Five — twice. Eleven — only once.
So b is eleven.
Five times eleven: fifty-five. Choice three. This is the recommended route.

beats.title: Method 1 · Understanding

lines.say: This is a factors question. What is y actually built from?

lines.draw: Under y write "a … d times, b … c times"

lines.say: y contains the prime a — d times. And the prime b — c times.
Does y divide by a? Of course. By b? Of course. By c or d? No — those primes aren't in y at all.
First look at the choices — what can we kill fast?
Choice two, c. Out immediately. c only shows up as an exponent — it's how MANY times a appears, not a factor of y.
Choice four, d to the b. y has no factor d. Out.
Choice one: b to the d. y has b only c times — and d is bigger than c. Not enough b's.
Three are out — on the exam, mark the fourth.
In the lesson — why it works. a to the c: y has a d times, and c is less than d. Enough. b to the a: y has b c times, and a is less than c. Enough. Choice three.

beats.title: Test each statement

lines.say: First, the given. x divides by fifteen — so x must contain the primes three and five.
x is a times b times c. So at least one of them brings the three, and at least one brings the five.
Statement one: at least one of them divides by five. Someone had to bring the five. True for sure.
Maybe one number brings both — fifteen, one, two. Maybe they split the job — three, five, one. Either way, someone holds the five.
Statement two: it's possible that exactly one divides by fifteen. Sure — fifteen, one and two.
Possible. Out.
Statement three: if a and b don't divide by three — who brought the three? c must have.

Numbers: one, five, three — c squared is nine. Or one, five, six — thirty-six. Both divide by nine.
Three statements out — on the exam you mark the fourth. This is probably the last question in the section anyway.
In the lesson, let's learn from statement four. Notice the word: DIFFERENT prime divisors.
Square x, and the same primes just appear twice as often. No NEW prime shows up.
So the number of different prime divisors stays exactly the same — never greater. Choice four.

beats.title: Method 1 · Prime squared

Two different primes multiplied — like six — give four: one, two, three and six.
Three divisors? A prime squared. Four has one, two and four — only one prime built it.

Primes up to twelve: two, three, five, seven, eleven. Five of them.

lines.say: Question eleven.
A hard one. And it's a test of working smart, not just working hard.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Start with the simple choices

lines.say: We have to add one of the choices to the givens — and see which one forces f to be positive.
But don't just start at the top of the list.
Choice one says e is positive. Then d, which is smaller, could be positive, zero or negative. Three cases to check. Slow.
Look for a choice with just ONE case.
Choice two: e is negative. d is smaller than e — so d is negative too. One case only.
Choice three: d is positive. e is bigger — so e is positive too. Also one case.
The exam is testing whether you work efficiently. So start with two or three.
Choice two. d and e are both negative. But the sum of all three is positive — that's given.
So f has to make up for them. f must be positive — bigger than the two negatives together.
That's exactly what they asked for. Choice two.
Start smart, and you usually reach the answer much faster.

beats.title: Method 1 · Pure parity

lines.say: Two rules to remember. One: a power doesn't change parity. Odd to any power stays odd, even stays even.
Two: adding or subtracting behave the same. Plus an even or minus an even — same parity effect.
Now look at the two brackets. Both are built from the same a.

lines.draw: Under (a − 6) write "a ± even" and under (a + 5) write "a ± odd"

lines.say: Once we shifted a by an even number — six. Once by an odd number — five.
So the two brackets MUST have different parities. If one is even, the other is odd.
The powers change nothing. So x is always even plus odd — always odd.
Choice three.

You're never allowed to do that in a regular equation. In an odd-even question, it's legal.
Without the powers: a minus six plus a plus five — two a minus one.
Two a is always even, whatever a is. Even minus one — always odd.

lines.say: Question fifteen.
Looks scary. It isn't — if you know one rule about odd products.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Factor by factor

lines.say: Start with the left side: two m plus one.
Two m is always even — two times anything is even. Plus one: always odd.
Does it matter if m is even or odd? No — the left side is odd either way.

lines.draw: Under 2m + 1 write "always odd" and cross out choice 1

lines.say: So m isn't necessarily odd. Choice one out.
The left side is odd — so the right side is odd too.
Now the rule: a product is odd ONLY if every factor is odd. One even factor brings a two in — and the product turns even.
So each factor here is odd. Go one by one — and remember, powers don't matter for parity.

lines.draw: Next to (p + 1)² write "p + 1 odd → p even" and cross out choice 2

lines.say: p plus one is odd — so p is even. Choice two out.

lines.draw: Next to q⁵ write "q odd" and circle choice 3

lines.say: q to the fifth is odd — so q is odd. That's our answer. On the exam, mark it and move on.

lines.draw: Next to (r − 1)² write "r − 1 odd → r even" and cross out choice 4

lines.say: In the lesson: r minus one is odd — so r is even. Choice four out.
Master that one rule — an odd product means every factor is odd — and this question is quick.

beats.title: Advanced Integers

lines.say: Last question of the set.
Parity with division. The math — then plugging in, with a warning.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Count the 2s

lines.say: Three of these are always whole numbers. One isn't necessarily. Let's hunt with the math.
Every even number contains the factor two at least once. So write m as two k.
Choice one: m times n plus one squared, over eight.
n is odd — so n plus one is even. Another factor two. Squared — at least two twos.
Two k times four t squared — eight k t squared. The top contains the whole eight. Always whole. Out.
Shortcut by understanding: count the twos. One from m, two from the square — three twos on top, three in the eight. It cancels.
Choice two: m squared times n squared over eight.
Two k squared is four k squared. n is odd — no twos at all. Only two twos on top — but eight needs three.
A third two MIGHT come from k — but not necessarily.
Choice two. On the exam, mark it. In the lesson, let's see what the others teach us.
Choice three: formula one minus formula two. The squares cancel — only two m n minus negative two m n: four m n. You should know this one by heart by now.
Four m n over eight — and m is two k. Eight k n over eight. Always whole. Out.
Choice four: n is odd, so n minus one and n plus one are consecutive EVEN numbers.
One of them divides by two — and the other by four. The product of two consecutive evens always divides by eight. Out.

beats.title: Method 2 · Plug in — carefully

lines.say: Plugging in here is risky: you could pick numbers where all four come out whole.
So pick the RIGHT numbers — the smallest. m equals two — not four, not six. n equals one.
Choice one: two times two squared — eight. Over eight — one. Whole. Does that mean always whole? No — we just can't eliminate it. Keep going.
Choice two: four times one, over eight — one half. Not whole!
We found one that's not necessarily whole. Mark it — no need to check the rest on the exam.
The math is the recommended route — it solves every question like this for sure. Plugging in is the fallback; sometimes it's shorter, sometimes you get stuck plugging and plugging.

lines.say: First number-line question.
Strong on strong, weak on weak — let's use it.

beats.title: Strong on strong

lines.say: Everything is above one, and the order is given: a, then b, then c, then d.
We're hunting for the statement that is NOT correct.
Choice one: a times b against c times d. a and b are the weaklings; c and d are the strongest two.

lines.draw: Draw lines pairing a with c and b with d

lines.say: Weak against strong, weak against strong — strong wins. Correct.
Choice two: a times c against b times d. Match strong with strong: b beats a, d beats c.

lines.draw: Draw lines pairing a with b and c with d

lines.say: Both weaklings are on the left. Correct.
Choice three: b against c times a. Forget a for a second — c already beats b.
And multiplying c by a, a number above one? That's like giving c an energy drink. It only gets stronger.

lines.draw: Next to choice 3 write "c > b, × a > 1"

lines.say: Correct.
Three out — so it's choice four. But let's check it.
a times d against c. d already beats c — and times a, it gets even stronger. So a times d can't be less than c.
Choice four is never true. That's our answer.

t to the minus one. Choice four.

lines.say: Advanced number line. First question.
Two ways to crack it — understanding, then plugging in.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Understanding

lines.say: Three unknowns — and all of them live in one zone: numbers bigger than one.
What does multiplying do in that zone? It makes things BIGGER.
Now look at the choices. Every one is a product of three letters.

lines.draw: Under each choice write it as three letters: b·c·c, a·b·b, b·a·a, b·b·b

lines.say: b c squared is b times c times c. a b squared is a, b, b. And so on — three factors each time.
When is a product of three factors from this zone the smallest? When every factor is as small as possible.
The smallest letter is a. So the smallest product would be a times a times a.

lines.draw: Write "a·a·a" next to the stem and cross it out

lines.say: But a cubed isn't in the choices. So find the next closest thing.
Two a's and one b — b a squared. b is the next letter up from a.
That's the smallest. Choice three.

beats.title: Method 2 · Plug in

lines.say: Now the psychometric route: plug in simple numbers.
a is two, b is three, c is four. They ask for the smallest — one substitution is enough.
Choice one: three times four squared — three times sixteen, forty-eight.

lines.draw: Next to choice 2 write "2 · 9 = 18" and cross out choice 1

lines.say: Choice two: two times three squared — eighteen. Already smaller than forty-eight. Choice one is out.

lines.draw: Next to choice 3 write "3 · 4 = 12" and cross out choice 2

lines.say: Choice three: three times two squared — twelve. Smaller again. Choice two is out.

lines.draw: Next to choice 4 write "27"; circle choice 3

lines.say: Choice four: three cubed, twenty-seven. Twelve is clearly the smallest. Choice three.
Two approaches, both short. Use whichever you like.

beats.title: Advanced Number Line

lines.say: Question four.
Lots of rules in one question — multiplying by a fraction, dividing by a fraction, and a new comparison trick.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Place them, then test

lines.say: Before anything else — put the givens on the number line.

lines.label: A number line from 0 to 2 appears

lines.draw: Mark p and q between 0 and 1, and r and s after 1

lines.say: p and q are positive fractions, between zero and one. r and s are bigger than one.
They want the one that's NOT necessarily true. Three are always true — we hunt for the fourth.
Choice one: q times s is less than s. s is bigger than one, q is a positive fraction.
What does multiplying by a positive fraction do? It pulls the number toward zero — it shrinks it.

lines.draw: Next to choice 1 write "s = 4, q = ½ → 2 < 4"

lines.say: Try it: s is four, q is a half — you get two. Smaller. Or divide both sides by s, positive: q is less than one. True.
Always true. Out.
Choice two: r minus q against s minus p. That's a distance against a distance.
s is further right than r, and p is further left than q — the second gap is bigger. Always.

lines.draw: Under choice 2 write "r + p < s + q"

lines.say: Or move the minuses across: r plus p against s plus q. Strong against strong, weak against weak.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow r ↔ s and write "right"; draw an arrow p ↔ q and write "right"

lines.say: Strong: s beats r — right side. Weak: q beats p — right side again. Right side wins twice — always true.
Choice three: r is less than r over p. Dividing by a positive fraction pushes AWAY from zero — it enlarges.

lines.draw: Next to choice 3 write "r = 2, p = ½ → 4 > 2"

lines.say: Two divided by a half is four. Bigger. Or multiply across by p, then divide by r: p is less than one. True.
Three always-true choices gone. On the exam: mark the fourth and move on.
In the lesson, let's check it. r plus q against s plus p.
Strong: s beats r — right side. Weak: q beats p — LEFT side. One win each — no decision.

lines.draw: Next to choice 4 write "r = 1.1, q = 0.9 | s = 1.2, p = 0.1"

lines.say: So make it fail: r close to s, and q much bigger than p. r is one point one, q zero point nine; s one point two, p zero point one.
Left: two. Right: one point three. The claim breaks. Not necessarily true — choice four.

lines.say: Question five.
A hard one — it's all about what multiplying does on the negative side.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Understanding

lines.say: a is a negative fraction. b and c are positive fractions. Which is the LARGEST?
First move: can signs knock anything out?
Negative times positive times positive — negative. a c — negative. a b — negative. a itself — negative.
All four are negative. Signs don't help. So we go deeper.
These are products of fractions — and multiplying by a fraction pulls you toward zero.
On the positive side, closer to zero means SMALLER. On the negative side it's the mirror image: closer to zero means BIGGER.

lines.label: A number line from −1 to 1 appears

lines.draw: Draw an arrow on the negative side pointing toward 0 and write "bigger"

lines.say: Three fractions multiplied — that's the product pulled closest to zero.
On the negative side, closest to zero is the biggest. a b c — choice one.

beats.title: Method 2 · Plug in

lines.say: That idea isn't obvious, so let's see it with numbers.
a is negative a half, b is a quarter, c is a half.
a b c: negative one sixteenth. a c: negative a quarter. a b: negative an eighth. a: negative a half.

lines.label: A number line from −1 to 0 appears

lines.say: Negative a half is halfway to minus one. A quarter is halfway back to zero. An eighth, halfway again. A sixteenth — closest of all.
Negative one sixteenth is the largest. Choice one.
Lock it in: multiplying by a fraction always pulls toward zero. On the positive side that shrinks you. On the negative side it grows you.

beats.title: Method 1 · The axis

lines.say: x to the sixth is less than x to the fifth. Where does x live?

lines.label: A number line from −2 to 2 appears

lines.say: This is about how powers behave — so we use the axis.
Remember the exception: a negative number to an EVEN power turns positive.

lines.draw: Over the negative side write "x⁶ > 0, x⁵ < 0"

lines.say: If x were negative, x to the sixth would be positive and x to the fifth negative. A positive can't be less than a negative.
So x is positive. Both negative ranges are out.

lines.draw: Over the part above 1 write "power ↑ → bigger"; over 0 to 1 write "power ↑ → smaller"

lines.say: Above one: the higher the power, the bigger the number. Between zero and one: the higher the power, the SMALLER. A fraction times a fraction times a fraction…

lines.draw: Cross out choice 1 and circle choice 2

lines.say: We need the higher power to be smaller — that only happens for positive fractions. Choice two.

A positive fraction — take a half. A sixty-fourth against a thirty-second. Yes, smaller.

lines.say: Question seven.
Hard — and we'll solve it three ways: the axis, plugging in, and a clever shortcut.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · The axis

lines.say: x is a negative fraction, between minus one and zero. Put four expressions in order.
They're all powers — the fifth root is a power too. So: the axis.

lines.label: A number line from −1 to 0 appears

lines.say: In this range, as long as the powers are ODD, a bigger power gives a bigger number.

lines.draw: Next to the stem write "5, 1, ⅕, −5 — all odd ✓"

lines.say: Fifth power — odd. x itself — power one, odd. Fifth root — an odd root. Minus five — odd. The rule holds.
So the biggest is the one with the biggest power: x to the fifth. It must be last in the chain.
Choice two doesn't end with x to the fifth, and choice four doesn't either. Both out.
And the smallest power, minus five, gives the smallest number — it must come first.

lines.draw: Cross out choice 3 and circle choice 1

lines.say: Choice three starts with the root. Only choice one starts with x to the minus five. Choice one.

beats.title: Method 2 · Plug in

lines.say: Plugging in? Negative a half usually works — but not here. The fifth root of a half, with no calculator? No thanks.
So choose smart: a negative fraction with a clean fifth root.
Negative one over thirty-two. Its fifth root is negative a half.

lines.draw: Next to the stem write "x⁵ ≈ 0⁻, x = −1/32, ⁵√x = −½, x⁻⁵ = (−32)⁵"

lines.say: x to the fifth: a tiny negative, practically zero — no need to calculate. The fifth root: negative a half.
x to the minus five flips it: negative thirty-two, to the fifth. Hugely negative — by far the smallest.

lines.draw: Circle x⁻⁵ at the start of choice 1

lines.say: So the chain must START with x to the minus five. Only choice one does.
Choice one.

beats.title: Method 3 · The shortcut

lines.say: The clever route. With odd powers and no sign tricks, the powers must go in one steady direction.

lines.draw: Under each choice write its powers: (−5, ⅕, 1, 5), (1, ⅕, 5, −5), (⅕, −5, 1, 5), (5, −5, ⅕, 1)

lines.say: Write x as x to the one, and the root as x to the one fifth. Now just read the powers.
Choice one: minus five, a fifth, one, five — always going up. Possible.
Choice two goes down then up. Choice three — down then up. Choice four — down then up. None can happen.
Only choice one is steady. The recommended route is still the axis — but this one's fun.

lines.say: x is a positive fraction. Which expression is the largest?

lines.label: A number line from 0 to 1 appears

lines.draw: Next to choice 1 write "between 0 and x"

lines.say: Choice two: the tenth root. If the power shrinks it, the root does the opposite — it grows it. But it can't pass one.

lines.draw: Next to choice 2 write "between x and 1"

Choice four: ten divided by x. Dividing by a fraction pushes away from zero — it's MORE than ten.

lines.say: Plug in? A half to the tenth power, the tenth root of a half… no calculator. Stuck?
Here's the trick: the ten doesn't really matter. What matters is whether each operation shrinks or grows. So replace every ten with a two.
Now pick x with a nice square root: a quarter.

lines.draw: Next to the choices write "1/16, ½, ½, 8"

Eight is the biggest. Choice four. Understanding is still the strongest route here.

solve-q-501.title: Given: {a}^{2} < a < c \cdot  b < b < c. Which of the following statements is POSSIBLE but NOT necessarily correct?

beats.title: Advanced Number Line

lines.say: Last question of the set.
A long chain of letters — decode it first, then read the choices.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Decode, then test

lines.say: Before the choices — decode the chain.
Start with a squared less than a. A negative a is impossible: its square would be positive and bigger.

lines.draw: Under a² < a write "a = positive fraction"

lines.say: So a is positive — and squaring made it smaller. That only happens to positive fractions.
a is positive, so everything bigger in the chain is positive too. Now: c b is less than b.

lines.draw: Under cb < b write "÷ b → c < 1"

lines.say: b is positive — divide both sides by it: c is less than one.

lines.label: A number line from 0 to 1 appears

lines.draw: Mark a, then b, then c on the line, all before 1

lines.say: So all of them are positive fractions: a the smallest, c the biggest.
Now the question: POSSIBLE but not necessarily. Always-true is out. Never-true is out.
Choice one: a times b against a plus b. A product of fractions shrinks; a sum grows. Always true.
Choice two: divide by a — a b against c. a b is smaller than b, and b is smaller than c. Always true.
Or strong on strong: a squared against a — a wins. b against c — c wins. The right side wins twice.
Choice three: a plus c less than one. Two fractions — small ones add to less than one, big ones to more.
a zero point one, b zero point three, c zero point five: zero point six. But a zero point three, b zero point five, c zero point nine — the chain still holds — and the sum is one point two.
Sometimes true, sometimes not. That's our answer — choice three.
In the lesson, choice four too: a product of two fractions above one? Never. Out.
That's the number line done. Great work.

lines.say: Question nine.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Algebraic form

lines.say: Method one: the math. x is a two-digit number — tens digit T, units digit U.
The condition: x equals its units digit cubed, plus the sum of its digits.
Cancel U from both sides. Move T across.
Nine T equals U cubed. So U cubed is a multiple of nine — U is three, six or nine.
U six: two sixteen — T would be twenty-four, not a digit. U nine: even bigger. U three: twenty-seven equals nine T.
T is three. The tens digit is three — choice three.

When the cube sits on the tens digit, big choices die instantly. Here it sits on the units — so use nine T equals U cubed.
Five: forty-five — not a cube. Two: eighteen — no. Four: thirty-six — no.
Three: twenty-seven — three cubed! T is three, U is three. Thirty-three.
Check: three cubed, plus three, plus three — thirty-three. Choice three.

lines.say: Advanced operations — question ten.
Two ways: the standard way, and a psychometric shortcut.

beats.title: Method 1 · Inside out

lines.say: A brand-new operation — but only numbers here, no unknowns.
The diamond appears twice. So we'll run the operation twice.
Always start with the inner one.

lines.draw: Under the inner diamond write "x = 1, y = 2, z = 2"

lines.say: Inner diamond: x is one, y is two, z is two.
The rule: each number to the power of the product of the other two.
One to the fourth: one. Two to the power one-times-two: four. Two to the power one-times-two again: four. Nine.

lines.draw: Write "◆(1, 1, 9)" next to the outer diamond

lines.say: Now the outer diamond: one, one, nine.
One to any power is one. One again. Nine to the power one-times-one: nine.
One plus one plus nine: eleven. Choice three.

beats.title: Method 1 · Three calculations

lines.say: Two definitions: the diamond and the hash.
The diamond appears twice inside the brackets — left and right. Then the hash acts on both results.
So three calculations. Start with the left diamond.
Nine squared: eighty-one. Minus two times nine times six: minus a hundred eight. Plus six squared: thirty-six. Nine.
Right diamond: sixty-four, minus ninety-six, plus thirty-six. Four.
Now the hash on nine and four: eighty-one, plus two times nine times four — seventy-two — plus sixteen.
One hundred sixty-nine. Choice three.

lines.say: For students who see the algebra: same two letters, just swapped.
Top of the definition: x minus y, squared. Swap the letters — a minus b and b minus a are opposites, and squared they're equal.
So the top part cancels completely.
The bottom of the definition is x squared times y — the powers differ, so it doesn't cancel fully. But both versions contain a and b.
What's left must be a over b or b over a — the same power on both letters.

lines.say: Question fifteen.
A hard one. We'll go choice by choice — technically and by understanding.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Choice by choice

lines.say: The operation takes a number and gives one over it — the reciprocal.
They ask what's NECESSARILY true for every positive a and b. We test each choice.
Choice one: one over a is less than one?
Technically: multiply both sides by a — it's positive, no flip — and you get one less than a. True only when a is above one.
Two, three, four — yes: a half, a third, a quarter. But a equals one gives exactly one. And a could be a half — then one over a is two. Not always true.
On to the second claim.
One over a, divided by one over b: b over a — not a over b. A negative power flips floors.
Choice three: one over a less than one over a plus two?
Both positive, so cross-multiply without flipping: a plus two less than a. Two less than zero — never true.
Or by understanding: a bigger denominator makes a SMALLER fraction. a equals four: one quarter is not less than one sixth.
Three out — in the exam, mark choice four and move on.

lines.draw: Next to choice 4 write "(1/a)·a = 1 = (1/b)·b ✓" and circle choice 4

lines.say: Here in the lesson we check it: a number times its reciprocal is one. One equals one — always true. Choice four.

beats.title: Understanding Questions

lines.say: Question one.
It's really a maximum-minimum question in disguise. Three ways to solve it.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Find the maximum

lines.say: Three integers, c below b below a. And a plus b is less than twelve.
They ask what b plus c CANNOT be. So let's find the biggest b plus c can ever be.
a and b are integers, so a plus b is at most eleven.
Now compare. a plus b is the two biggest numbers. b plus c is the two smallest. The difference is a against c.
c is at least one below b, and b is at least one below a — so c is at least two below a.
So b plus c is at most nine.
Ten goes past the maximum. It can't happen. Choice three.

beats.title: Method 2 · Plug in the maximum

lines.say: Second way: plug in numbers that make b plus c as big as possible.
We want b as big as it can be — then c can be big too.
Six and five: eleven, still under twelve. That's the biggest b we can get.
Push a up to seven and b drops to four — worse. So the biggest c is four, and the biggest b plus c is nine.
Again — ten is out of reach. Choice three.

lines.draw: Next to choice 3 write "b = 6, c = 4, a ≥ 7 → a + b ≥ 13 ✗"

lines.say: Ten: b has to be bigger than c, so the smallest b is six, with c four. Then a is at least seven — and a plus b is at least thirteen. Too big.
Some of you already see it's impossible. The simplest move is still to knock out choice four too.

lines.draw: Next to choice 4 write "(1, 0, −10) ✓" and cross it out

lines.say: Negative ten: b zero, c negative ten, a one. Everything holds.
The only impossible one: choice three. Three methods, all excellent — pick the one that's comfortable for you.

solve-q-578.title: Given: 0 < a and 0 < x, and {x}^{2} = {a}^{3}. If a is increased by a factor of 9, then x increases by a factor of —

beats.title: Understanding Questions

lines.say: Question two.
A hard one — and this time we start with the psychometric solution.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Plug in 1 and 1

lines.say: x squared equals a cubed, both positive. a gets multiplied by nine. What happens to x?
Plug in two numbers that satisfy the equation. The simplest pair: one and one.
Didn't spot it? Put a equal one: x squared is one, so x is plus or minus one. x is positive — so x is one.
Now multiply a by nine. The new a is nine. Nine cubed: seven hundred twenty-nine.
x squared is seven twenty-nine, so x is twenty-seven. Positive again.
x went from one to twenty-seven. It grew twenty-seven times. Choice three.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Question 2" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — question q-578 with its four answer choices — "Given: 0 < a and 0 < x, and {x}^{2} = {a}^{3}. If a is increased by a factor of 9, then x increases by a factor of —"

beats.title: Method 2 · Scale factor k

lines.say: Now the mathematical solution.
Multiply a by nine. The right side becomes nine a, all cubed.
To keep the equation balanced, x must grow too. By how much? Call it k.
Open the brackets with the power rules: k squared x squared equals nine cubed a cubed.

lines.draw: Cross out x² and a³ (they are equal)

lines.say: But x squared equals a cubed — so they cancel.
k squared is seven twenty-nine, so k is twenty-seven. Choice three.
Strong algebra students see it in their head: the right side grows nine cubed times — seven twenty-nine. What squared gives seven twenty-nine? Twenty-seven.
For most students, though, plugging in is the simpler route here.

solve-q-579.title: Given: a, b and c are three integers, distinct and positive, and \frac{{c}^{2}}{ab} = \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{a}. Which of the following statements is

beats.title: Understanding Questions

lines.say: Question three.
A hard one. It needs a flash of insight that connects two worlds.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Pythagoras in disguise

lines.say: Step one: simplify the equation.
Common denominator a times b: a over b times a, b over a times b.
Both sides are over a b — so c squared equals a squared plus b squared.
Now what? This is the insight: Pythagoras. Leg squared plus leg squared equals hypotenuse squared.
a, b and c are positive — so they can be the sides of a right triangle. Legs a and b, hypotenuse c.
Read the question carefully: which statement is NOT NECESSARILY correct?
Anything that's always true — we eliminate. We're hunting for the one that can fail.

lines.draw: Next to choice 1 write "always ✓" and cross it out

lines.say: Choice one: c is less than a plus b. Two sides of a triangle are always longer than the third. Out.
Choice two: c is less than six. Now we have to connect letters to numbers.
Back to the givens: a, b, c are integers. So they're not just any Pythagoras numbers — they're a Pythagorean triple. The smallest: three, four, five.
Three, four, five: c is five, less than six. But then comes five, twelve, thirteen — or the expansion six, eight, ten. c is thirteen, or ten.
Sometimes true, sometimes not — so it's not necessarily correct. Choice two. If you saw that — excellent, it's not simple at all.
If not, eliminate the rest.
Choices three and four: a leg is always shorter than the hypotenuse. Always true — out.
A seriously tough one. I hope it gives you tools for similar questions.

solve-q-580.title: A plant's growth rate is determined by a formula: it increases the more sunlight (S) the plant receives and the more water (W) it gets, and decreases

beats.title: Understanding Questions

lines.say: Last question of algebra.
No calculation at all — just understanding.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Check each variable

lines.say: Go back to the rule they defined.

lines.draw: Under the question write "S↑ → ↑, W↑ → ↑, D↑ → ↓"

lines.say: More sunlight — the rate goes up. More water — up. More weeds — down.
Now test each expression against all three.
Choice one: S to the power W, over D.
In a fraction, a bigger top gives a bigger result, a bigger bottom a smaller one.

lines.draw: Next to choice 1 write "S ✓ W ✓ D ✓" and cross it out

lines.say: S grows — the top grows. W grows — S times itself more times, and S is above one — the top grows. D grows — the bottom grows, the result shrinks. It fits. Out.

lines.draw: Next to choice 2 write "✓" and cross it out

lines.say: Choice two: S times W, minus D. Both positive, multiplied — bigger S or W, bigger result. Minus D — more weeds, smaller result. Out.

lines.draw: Next to choice 3 write "✓" and cross it out

lines.say: Choice three: S minus D plus W. S and W add, D subtracts. We've already seen minus D works. Out.
Three eliminated — you can mark the fourth. But let's check it anyway.

lines.draw: Next to choice 4 write "D↑ → ↑ ✗" and circle choice 4

lines.say: S times W times D. S and W are fine. The problem is D: more weeds makes the rate BIGGER. That's the opposite of the rule. Choice four.
That's the last question in algebraic understanding — and in algebra.

beats.title: Fast Calculation

lines.say: No calculator on this exam — and no time to waste.
Fast calculation isn't doing the long method faster.
It's spotting an easier calculation that gives exactly the same answer.
Every trick today comes with a reason. A trick you understand is a trick you can rebuild under pressure.
Let's build the toolkit.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT SLIDE → Move to a round number]

beats.title: Move to a round number

lines.say: Four ninety-eight is hugging five hundred. It's two short.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow taking 2 from the 76 over to the 498

lines.say: So move two across.
Five hundred plus seventy-four: five seventy-four.
The total didn't change — we added two to one part and took two from the other.
Careful: don't add two to BOTH. That inflates the sum by four. For addition, you shift in opposite directions.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Move to a round number" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Shift both numbers

lines.say: Subtraction wants the opposite move.
Add the same amount to BOTH numbers — and the gap between them doesn't change.
Four eighty-seven plus thirteen is a round five hundred. So add thirteen to both.
Nine sixteen minus five hundred: four sixteen.
Picture both ends on a number line sliding right together. The distance stays put.
Lock in the contrast. A SUM survives when you move an amount between the parts. A DIFFERENCE survives when you shift both parts together.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Shift both numbers" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Split a factor

lines.say: Fifteen is ten plus five.
Times ten is instant — three sixty.
Times five? Just half of that — one eighty.
Add them: five hundred forty.
Other splits worth owning: twelve is ten plus two, nineteen is twenty minus one, ninety-eight is a hundred minus two.
Pick the split that keeps the pieces small enough to hold in your head.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Split a factor" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Double & halve

lines.say: Here's a beautiful one. Double one factor, halve the other — and the product doesn't move.

lines.draw: Halve the 16 and double the 35: write "= 8 × 70"

lines.say: Sixteen halves to eight. Thirty-five doubles to seventy.
Again: four times one-forty.
Five hundred sixty.
Every step is the same number — we're just moving a factor of two from one side to the other.
Stop the moment it gets easy. There's no prize for halving all the way down to one.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Double & halve" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: ×25 and ×125

lines.say: Twenty-five is a quarter of a hundred.
So times twenty-five means times a hundred, divided by four.
Divide first and the numbers stay tiny. Forty-four over four is eleven.
Eleven hundred.
One size up: a hundred twenty-five is an eighth of a thousand.
Twenty-four over eight is three. Three thousand.
This comes from the real value of those numbers — not from shuffling decimal points around.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "×25 and ×125" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Near a round number

lines.say: Ninety-seven is almost a hundred.
A hundred forty-twos is instant: forty-two hundred.
But that's three copies too many. Three forty-twos is one twenty-six.
Take it off in two small bites: minus a hundred, then minus twenty-six.
Four thousand seventy-four.
Rounded up? The easy product is too big — subtract. Rounded down? Too small — add.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Near a round number" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Friendly pairs

lines.say: Multiplication doesn't care about order.
So hunt for the pair that makes a round number.

lines.draw: Draw an arc linking the 8 and the 125

lines.say: Eight times a hundred twenty-five: a clean thousand.
Thirty-seven thousand. The answer just falls out.
Pairs to watch for: four and twenty-five, two and fifty, five and twenty.
This freedom belongs to multiplication. Mixed with division? Keep track of what's on top and what's underneath.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Friendly pairs" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Cancel first

lines.say: Big products on top, big products underneath — and we're not calculating a single one of them.
Forty-eight and twelve both take a twelve.

lines.draw: Cross out 48 and write 4; cross out 12 and write 1

lines.say: Four on top, one underneath.
Thirty-five and fourteen both take a seven.

lines.draw: Cross out 35 and write 5; cross out 14 and write 2

lines.say: Five on top, two underneath.
Four times five is twenty. Over two: ten.
This works because top and bottom are PRODUCTS. If the top were forty-eight PLUS thirty-five — no cancelling.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Cancel first" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Around a centre

lines.say: Forty-eight and fifty-two: two below fifty, two above fifty.
When two numbers sit evenly around a centre, the product is the centre squared minus the gap squared.
Fifty squared: twenty-five hundred. Two squared: four. Two thousand four hundred ninety-six.
We'll prove this properly in the expressions lesson — it's the difference of squares.
But the gaps must be equal. Forty-eight and fifty-three? Not evenly around fifty. It doesn't apply.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Around a centre" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Squares ending in 5

lines.say: A number ending in five, squared.
Take the front part — six — and multiply it by the next whole number — seven.
Forty-two.
Then stick twenty-five on the end.
Four thousand two hundred twenty-five.
Works for a hundred fifteen too: eleven times twelve is a hundred thirty-two — then twenty-five. Thirteen thousand two hundred twenty-five.
Careful — it's a squaring pattern only. Not a rule for any two numbers ending in five.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Squares ending in 5" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Swap a percentage

lines.say: Percentages get their own chapter later — but here's a gem for now.
Twenty-four percent of seventy-five… equals seventy-five percent of twenty-four.

lines.draw: Draw a swap arrow between 24 and 75, and write "= 75% of 24"

lines.say: Both are the same product over a hundred, so you're allowed to swap.
Seventy-five percent is three quarters. Three quarters of twenty-four?
Eighteen. Instant.
Scope: you're swapping factors in a multiplication. Not the base of a percentage change.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Swap a percentage" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Estimate

lines.say: An estimate needs a job: catch a misplaced zero, or kill answer choices.
Forty-nine twenty-ones is near a thousand.
But "near a thousand" won't separate two choices that are ten apart. So tighten it.
Forty-nine twenties: nine eighty. Plus one more forty-nine: one thousand twenty-nine.
Use exactly as much precision as the decision needs. One choice left? Stop. Several left? Go exact.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Estimate" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

lines.say: The goal isn't to force every calculation through your favourite trick.
Nothing looks easier? A solid written calculation is still a great answer.
Seven questions next. Write down the route you chose — not just the answer.

beats.title: How to Approach Word Problems

lines.say: Welcome to word problems.
A short story — a queue, a shop, a tank, a journey — and a question about it.
We're not going to memorise a trick for every story. We're going to learn to see what's underneath.
And we start with the most down-to-earth tool there is: trial and error.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Stories to structure

items.t: A picture · a table · a short list · an equation

lines.say: Every story hides a structure you can work with.

lines.label: 'A picture · a table · a short list · an equation' appears

lines.say: Sometimes it's a total split into parts. Sometimes a ratio. Sometimes just a short list of cases.
Your first job is to turn the words into one of these.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Stories to structure" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Trial & error: 3 types

items.t: 3 · Patterns — step by step, or plug in

lines.say: This first chapter is trial and error. It comes in three types.
Type one: general problems. No hint what to try first — you simply try.
Type two: minimum and maximum. A little understanding tells you which way to push — fewer tries.
Type three: patterns. Mostly trial, hardly any error.

lines.draw: Number the three types 1, 2, 3 in the margin

lines.say: One lesson for each — each followed by real questions.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Trial & error: 3 types" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Possible vs must

items.t: Possible $\to$ one example is enough · Must $\to$ every allowed case

lines.say: One distinction you'll use all chapter.
Two positive integers add to fourteen. Pick one — the other is fixed. You're not guessing both.

lines.label: 'Possible → one example · Must → every case' appears

lines.say: What's possible? One legal example proves it. What must happen? A few examples aren't enough — you need a reason, or a counterexample.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Possible vs must" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Try it first

lines.say: How to use this chapter.
Every guided question comes BEFORE its video. Give it a real try on paper.
Stuck? Write what you do know — a row of boxes, the first two cases. That's often enough.
Then watch the solution: same question, same numbers. Compare your working with mine.
Let's start with type one.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Try it first" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: General Problems

lines.say: General problems — the first type of trial and error.
The name says it all: we try, and we err. Then we try again.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Try and err

items.t: Sometimes the first try works · sometimes it takes a few

lines.say: Trial and error. Try, get it wrong, try again.
What makes a problem a general problem? It depends on luck.
Nothing in the question tells you "try this first". You read it — and the only way forward is to try.

lines.label: 'Sometimes the first try works · sometimes it takes a few' appears

lines.say: Sometimes you'll hit it on the first try. Sometimes it takes a few. Both are fine.
That's exactly how you're expected to solve these.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Try and err" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Draw the story

items.t: Draw it $\to$ follow it $\to$ split into routes when it branches
Or: test the answer choices one by one

lines.say: So how do you try? You draw the story — and follow it.

lines.label: 'Draw it → follow it → split into routes' appears

lines.say: When the story can go two ways, split it into two routes. Follow one to the end.

lines.label: 'Or: test the answer choices one by one' appears

lines.say: And often the fastest try of all: take the answer choices, and test each one against the story.

lines.draw: Draw a small fork next to "split into routes"

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Draw the story" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Keep an order

items.t: Items of $4$ and $7$: no $7$s, one $7$, two $7$s, $\ldots$

lines.say: Trying isn't random guessing. Keep your tries in order.

lines.label: 'Items of 4 and 7: no 7s, one 7, two 7s, …' appears

lines.say: Say a total is made of four-unit and seven-unit items. Start with no sevens. Then one. Then two.
For each, ask: can fours make up the rest?

lines.draw: Write an arrow → next to "no 7s, one 7, two 7s"

lines.say: Once the sevens alone pass the total, stop. Your list is complete — for a reason, not because you ran out of ideas.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Keep an order" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Every condition

lines.say: A try has to pass EVERY condition — including the question itself.
Right total but wrong number of objects? It fails.
A negative count of cars? Not allowed.
And make sure you're answering what they asked: possible, impossible, the least, the most.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Every condition" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

lines.say: General problems: no shortcut — try and err, and a bit of luck.

beats.title: Minimum & Maximum

lines.say: The second type of trial and error: minimum and maximum.
Here, a bit of understanding saves you a lot of tries.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Ranges

items.t: Know which way to push $\to$ fewer tries

lines.say: Minimum-maximum questions are about ranges. What's the smallest possible value? The largest?
Unlike general problems, you're not trying blindly.
You can work out which way to push — which direction takes you to the minimum, and which to the maximum.

lines.label: 'Know which way to push → fewer tries' appears

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Ranges" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: A recurring motif

lines.say: By the way — minimum and maximum isn't only this lesson.
It comes back all over the quantitative section: in geometry, in overlap problems later on, in lots of question types.
So the thinking you build here pays off again and again.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "A recurring motif" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Bold words

lines.say: On the exam, some words are printed in bold. Use them.
They're there so you don't mix up the largest with the smallest.
Read the bold word before you start pushing in any direction.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Bold words" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Squeeze the others

items.t: Three different positive integers, total $26$. Largest one as large as possible?

lines.label: 'Three different positive integers, total 26. Largest as LARGE as possible?' appears

lines.say: We want one number as large as possible. So push the other two DOWN — as small as they're allowed.
Positive, and different: one and two.
That leaves twenty-three for the largest.
Nothing bigger fits — the other two need at least three between them. And one, two, twenty-three really works. Maximum: twenty-three.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Squeeze the others" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Balance the group

items.t: Same total $26$. Largest one as small as possible?

lines.label: 'Same total 26. Largest as SMALL as possible?' appears

lines.say: Now flip it: the smallest possible LARGEST number. Now we push the other way — keep the numbers close together.
If the largest were nine, the most we could reach is nine plus eight plus seven — twenty-four. Too small.
So the largest must be at least ten — and seven, nine, ten works. Minimum: ten.
Same total, opposite questions, opposite directions.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Balance the group" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Max of one part $\to$ squeeze the others · Min of the largest $\to$ balance

lines.label: 'Max of one part → squeeze the others · Min of the largest → balance' appears

lines.say: Maximum of one part: squeeze everything else down. Minimum of the largest: balance the group.
And always show both halves: nothing better fits — and your value really works.
Now a real question of this type.

beats.title: Patterns

lines.say: The last type of trial and error: patterns.
Here we barely think and barely err. It's mostly trial — careful trial.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Step by step

items.t: Start $52$. Each cycle: halve, then remove $2$.

lines.say: The first kind: step by step — item by item.
The simplest, best way to solve these: write the items one at a time, exactly as the rule says, until you reach what they ask.

lines.label: 'Start 52. Each cycle: halve, then remove 2' appears
A row appears: Start 52 · Cycle 1 · Cycle 2 · Cycle 3

lines.say: Half of fifty-two is twenty-six, minus two: twenty-four. Then twelve minus two: ten. Then five minus two: three.
On the exam you don't need boxes. Just write one, two, three — and the numbers.

beats.title: Sequences

items.t: Forget school formulas for arithmetic and geometric sequences
Plug in a number $\to$ check every answer

lines.say: The second kind: sequences. Rarer — but worth knowing.
You're given a formula with n — for a general term, or for the sum up to some point.

lines.label: 'Forget school formulas for arithmetic / geometric sequences' appears

lines.say: If you remember arithmetic or geometric sequence formulas from school — leave them. They're not relevant here.
You could solve it by understanding — but very few students manage that.

lines.label: 'Plug in a number → check every answer' appears

lines.say: The simple, reliable way: plug in a number, and check the answers.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Sequences" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Plug in n = 3

items.t: $n=3$: small enough to calculate, big enough to separate

lines.say: Which number do we plug in? Usually three.

lines.label: 'n = 3: small enough to calculate, big enough to separate' appears

lines.say: Why not one? It's shorter to calculate…
But the exam is often built so that n equals one leaves you with two possible answers.
Three is small enough to calculate easily, and big enough to tell the answers apart.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Plug in n = 3" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Keep the rule order

items.t: Halve, then subtract — not the other way round

lines.say: Two traps with step-by-step questions.

lines.label: 'Halve, then subtract — not the other way' appears

lines.say: Order matters. Fifty-two minus two, then halved, is twenty-five — a different rule.
And don't assume a pattern from one difference. The drops aren't equal — apply the rule every single time.

beats.title: Smart Trial & Error

lines.say: Trial and error — the advanced level.
No formula, no equation. You try, you miss, you try again.
Looks like luck? It isn't. There are techniques that get you there much faster.

beats.title: Why it matters

lines.say: First — why does the exam love these questions so much?
At school you were spoon-fed. Here's the question bank. Learn these exact questions.
At university, nobody hands you the formula. You go and figure it out yourself.
These questions test exactly that: when there's no equation — do you freeze, or do you start?
Try, check, adjust. And by the way — you'll use this all through the quantitative section.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Why it matters" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Work in order

lines.say: Here's a classic setup.
Four tickets, each one costs six or eleven. Which totals are possible?
Don't try random mixes. Work in order — start from the minimum.
All cheap: twenty-four.
Now swap ONE cheap ticket for an expensive one.
Eleven instead of six — that's plus five. Twenty-nine. No need to recalculate everything.

lines.label: The totals appear in a row: 24, 29, 34, 39, 44

lines.say: Every swap adds exactly five. Twenty-four, twenty-nine, thirty-four, thirty-nine, forty-four.
And notice: we only care HOW MANY of each ticket — not which one was bought first.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Work in order" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: The skip

lines.say: Thirty-six sits between twenty-four and forty-four. So it's possible — right?
No! From thirty-four we jump straight to thirty-nine. Thirty-six gets skipped.
That's the skip. When two values swap, the totals move in fixed jumps — and some numbers get jumped over.
So the moment you jump past an answer choice — you can stop. That's your 'impossible'.
Being inside the range is NOT enough.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The skip" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Constant step

lines.say: A constant step hides a mathematical pattern.

lines.draw: Under each total write its remainder when divided by 5: 4, 4, 4, 4, 4

lines.say: Divide each total by five: the remainder is always four.
See the pattern, and you barely need to try. Just look for the choice that breaks it.

lines.draw: Next to the list write "36 → remainder 1 ✗"

lines.say: Thirty-six leaves remainder one. It breaks the pattern — impossible.
Same test another way: subtract twenty-four — you need zero, five, ten, fifteen or twenty.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Constant step" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

items.t: Work in order — start from the minimum.
Constant step? Watch for the skip.
See the pattern — test by remainder.
Numbers in the answers? Plug them in.

lines.say: Trial and error, part two: minimum and maximum.
Understand min and max — and you need far fewer tries.

beats.title: Max one, min the rest

items.t: To maximise one — give all the others the minimum.
To minimise one — give all the others the maximum.

lines.say: Here's the key idea of this whole lesson.

lines.label: 'To maximise one — give all the others the minimum.' appears

lines.say: Want one thing as big as possible? Give everything else the least you're allowed.

lines.label: 'To minimise one — give all the others the maximum.' appears

lines.say: And the reverse for a minimum.
Two lines. They'll solve most of the questions in this lesson.

beats.title: At least

items.t: At least $\frac14$ of 28 members get a large pack.

lines.label: The example appears: at least ¼ of 28 members get a large pack

lines.say: At least a quarter of twenty-eight members get a large pack. The minimum number of large packs?
A quarter of twenty-eight: seven. So at least seven.
Six is not enough — even if it would look cheaper.
And 'at least' means seven, eight, nine, all the way up. For a MAXIMUM, don't stop at seven.

items.t: 2 · Build one real example that reaches it.

lines.say: Found a minimum or a maximum? Two jobs.

lines.label: '1 · Show you can't go further.' appears

lines.say: First: show nothing more extreme can work.

lines.label: '2 · Build one real example that reaches it.' appears

lines.say: Then: build a real example that actually hits it.
A bound you can't actually reach isn't the answer.

beats.title: Patterns & Cycles

lines.say: Trial and error, part three: patterns.
No formulas from school. No arithmetic or geometric sequences.
We write it out, term by term — with a little psychometric thinking to shorten it.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Term by term

items.t: Write it out — neatly, one term at a time.

lines.say: Pattern questions: a sequence with a fixed rule.
We don't build a formula. We understand what they want, write the terms one by one, and stop when we get there.

lines.label: 'Write it out — neatly, one term at a time.' appears

lines.say: The most important thing here? Work in order.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Term by term" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Watch the edges

items.t: Start of the first step?   End of the last step?

lines.say: Inside the sequence, the rule just repeats. No problem there.
The trouble is always at the edges.

lines.label: 'Start of the first step? End of the last step?' appears

lines.say: Does the start include the first step? Does the end include the last one?
Ask yourself both, every time.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Watch the edges" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Repeating cycles

lines.say: Some patterns repeat in a fixed cycle.
One marked, three not — over and over.
Positions one, five, nine… You don't need to draw all of it.
A fixed cycle means a mathematical pattern: every marked position leaves the same remainder.
Find that remainder — and just check the answers.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Repeating cycles" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Meeting times

items.t: Every 12 min and every 15 min — together at 8:00

lines.say: Two things repeating at different rates. When do they meet again?

lines.label: 'Every 12 minutes and every 15 minutes — together at 8:00' appears

lines.say: Listing every time works — but it's slow. They meet at a common multiple.
The easy way: take the BIGGER number and jump along its multiples.
Fifteen, thirty, forty-five, sixty. Twelve divides sixty. They meet every sixty minutes.
Why the bigger one? Fewer jumps.
Eight o'clock is the first meeting — so the third is ten o'clock. Only two jumps. Watch that edge!

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Meeting times" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

lines.label: Eight objects appear in a row

lines.say: Eight objects in a row.

lines.draw: Mark each gap between neighbours with a small tick

lines.say: How many gaps between them? Seven — not eight.
Items and gaps are different counts. Decide which one the question is about.
