beats.title: From Words to Equations

lines.say: Word problems. A brand-new topic.
About five of the twenty questions in a section are word problems — a quarter.
In practice it's even more. Plenty of algebra and geometry questions are word problems in disguise.
The question is written in words. Your job: work out what it means in maths.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Three stages

items.t: 1 · Translate the words into an equation

lines.say: How do we solve a word problem? Three stages.

lines.label: Stage 1 appears: translate the words into an equation

lines.say: Stage one: translate the words into an equation. This is where the understanding happens — the hardest part.
Stage two: solve it. That's pure technique — your algebra. Don't lose points here.

lines.label: Stage 3 appears: answer the question they asked

lines.say: Stage three: answer the question. Careful — solving the equation doesn't always finish the job.
You might find x equals eight — and they ask for x minus one. Or two x.
It's not a trick. It's a concentration check. Always look again at what they asked.
And not every word problem needs an equation. Some you'll solve by trial and error, or by testing the answers. Today: translating.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Three stages" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Step by step

items.t: A number is multiplied by 4, and then 18 is added. The result is 6 times the original number. What is twice the number?

lines.say: Lots of words. Don't panic. Piece by piece.
"A number" — we don't know it. Call it x.
"Multiplied by four" — four x. "And then eighteen is added" — plus eighteen.
"The result is" — that's our equals sign. "Six times the original number" — six x.
Read it back: a number, times four, plus eighteen, equals six times the number. Almost word for word. Every equation is just a sentence.
Stage two — technique. Take four x from both sides.
Eighteen equals two x. x is nine.
Stage three! Did they ask for the number? No — twice the number.
Eighteen. That's the answer — not nine.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Step by step" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — the "multiplied by 4, then 18 is added" sentence

beats.title: More and less

lines.say: Now the phrases — and how each one becomes maths.

lines.label: 'A is 6 more than B:  A = B + 6' appears

lines.say: A is six more than B. Start with B, add six — you reach A. A equals B plus six.

lines.label: 'A is 9 less than B:  A = B − 9' appears

lines.say: A is nine less than B. Start with B, take away nine. A equals B minus nine.

lines.draw: Under the second line write "B = A + 9"

lines.say: Same fact, the other way round: B is A plus nine. Both are right — just write it the right way.
Quick check: if B is twenty, A is eleven. Not negative eleven.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "More and less" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Times and twice

lines.label: 'A is three times B:  A = 3B' appears

lines.say: A is three times B: A equals three B.
Don't mix up three TIMES as much with three MORE.
If B is seven: three times is twenty-one. Three more would be ten.
And "twice" or "double" — always times two. Just like "half" is always divided by two.
Three times, four times — those get their own number. Twice is only ever two.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Times and twice" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Fractions of a whole

lines.say: "Of" means times. Two fifths of n is two fifths times n.

lines.label: 'One quarter less than n:  3/4 n' appears

lines.say: One quarter less than n: take all of n, remove a quarter of it — three quarters of n are left.
The quarter is a quarter OF n. n is the whole.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Fractions of a whole" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: The difference

items.t: The difference between A and B is 12:  $|A-B|=12$

lines.label: 'The difference between A and B is 12:  |A − B| = 12' appears

lines.say: "The difference between A and B is twelve."
We don't always know which one is bigger. That's why it's written with absolute-value bars — a difference is always positive.

lines.draw: Under it write "A − B = 12  or  B − A = 12"

lines.say: If A is bigger, A minus B is twelve. If B is bigger, B minus A is twelve.
When the story tells you who's bigger — the older person, say — just write bigger minus smaller.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The difference" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Makes up · costs as

items.t: 3 notebooks cost the same as 5 pens:  $3N=5P$

lines.label: 'A is 2/3 of B:  A = 2/3 B' appears

lines.say: Sometimes you'll meet awkward wording: "A makes up two thirds of B". Just swap it for "is": A is two thirds of B.

lines.label: '3 notebooks cost the same as 5 pens:  3N = 5P' appears

lines.say: "Costs the same as" — that's an equals sign.
Three notebooks: three N. Five pens: five P. Three N equals five P.

lines.draw: Circle "the same as" and write "=" above it

lines.say: "As", "the same as", "equal to" — all equals signs. Write it the way you hear it.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Makes up · costs as" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Ratio as units

items.t: The ratio of A to B is $2:3$

lines.label: 'The ratio of A to B is 2 : 3' appears

lines.say: One more: a ratio. The ratio of A to B is two to three.
For every two A, there are three B.
So we write them as two x and three x.
Ratios get a full lesson of their own soon — this is just the translation.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Ratio as units" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

items.t: Work step by step — one phrase at a time
Translate $\to$ solve $\to$ answer what they asked

lines.say: Let's sum up this short lesson.

lines.label: 'Work step by step — one phrase at a time' appears

lines.say: The biggest tip: work step by step. Long question, lots of words? Don't panic.

lines.label: 'Translate → solve → answer what they asked' appears

lines.say: And go over the phrase table — the memory card right after this video. Make every phrasing automatic.
This is only the start of word problems. Lots more types ahead.

beats.title: Equal Ratios

lines.say: Equal ratios. A short lesson — and one of the most important in the whole course.
This technique follows you everywhere: word problems, geometry, algebra.
Let's learn it on an easy example.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: The ratio table

items.t: 6 packs hold 42 cards. How many cards are in 15 packs?

lines.label: The example appears: 6 packs hold 42 cards — how many in 15 packs?

lines.say: Six packs hold forty-two cards. How many in fifteen packs?
Plenty of you will just do it in your head. Great — but let's learn the technique on an easy one.

lines.label: A ratio table appears: Packs | Cards — 6 | 42 and 15 | ?

lines.say: Put the data in a ratio table. One column for packs, one for cards.
The ratio between six and forty-two must be the same as the ratio between fifteen and the missing number. Same packs, same cards in each.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow from 6 to 42 and write "×7"

lines.say: Across: six to forty-two — times seven.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow from 15 to the ? and write "×7 = 105"

lines.say: Equal ratios — so fifteen gets the same times seven. One hundred and five.
Could we go down instead? Six to fifteen is times two and a half. Not whole — so here, across is the easy way.
When across or down is a whole number, that's all you need.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The ratio table" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Triangle value

items.t: A student solves 15 exercises every 6 minutes. How many does he solve in 8 minutes?

lines.label: The example appears: 15 exercises in 6 minutes — how many in 8 minutes?

lines.say: Now a harder one. Fifteen exercises in six minutes. How many in eight?

lines.label: A ratio table appears: Minutes | Exercises — 6 | 15 and 8 | ?

lines.say: Across: six to fifteen — times two and a half. Down: six to eight — not whole either.
So we use the triangle value.

lines.draw: Draw a diagonal line from 8 to 15

lines.say: Multiply along the diagonal: eight times fifteen.
Then divide by what's left: six. Diagonal times, divide by the rest. The three numbers make a triangle — hence the name.

lines.draw: Cancel 15 and 6 by 3 (5 and 2), then write "= 8 × 5 : 2 = 20"

lines.say: Cancel first: fifteen and six share a three. Eight times five over two. Twenty.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Triangle value" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Cross-multiply

lines.say: Same question, a second way: cross-multiplication.
When ratios are equal, the diagonal products are equal.
Six x equals eight times fifteen.
A hundred and twenty. x is twenty. Same answer.
Triangle value or cross-multiplying — pick whichever feels natural.
I prefer the triangle value: it writes the answer straight away, without isolating x.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Cross-multiply" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

items.t: Across or down is a whole number? Use that multiplier.
Not whole? Triangle value: diagonal $\times$, then $:$ the rest.

We'll use this so often — geometry, word problems, algebra — that it will become automatic.

beats.title: Read, Organise, Calculate

lines.say: Some word problems are really reading-comprehension tests.
No tricky equation. Just: do you understand what you're reading?

beats.title: Reading, not algebra

items.t: Don't solve it all at once — step by step.

lines.say: Sometimes the wording is hard to follow. Sometimes they just pile on information to see if you panic.
Some students see a wall of text and skip the question. Don't.

lines.label: 'Don't solve it all at once — step by step.' appears

lines.say: Same technique as always: one step at a time. The calculations themselves are simple.

beats.title: Label every cost

items.t: Price per kilogram $\ne$ price per gram  ·  A fixed fee is paid once

lines.say: In a business question, separate the money coming in from the money going out.
Something sells for sixty-four, the ingredients cost thirty-seven — the profit is twenty-seven.

lines.label: 'Price per kilogram ≠ price per gram · A fixed fee is paid once' appears

lines.say: Watch the units: a price for a kilogram isn't a price for a gram. And a fixed fee is paid once — a per-item fee gets multiplied.
Write a small label next to every number. That's what stops them getting mixed up.

items.t: Lots of text? Don't skip it — work step by step.
Every word counts — especially "or part of".

beats.title: Ratios

lines.say: An important lesson: ratios.
Ratios show up across the whole quantitative section — side ratios in geometry, rates in work and motion problems.
So let's really understand what a ratio is.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT SLIDE → What a ratio tells you]

beats.title: What a ratio tells you

lines.say: In everyday talk, "he's tall compared to me" only says he's taller. Not by how much.
In maths, a ratio tells you exactly how many times.

lines.label: A bar picture appears: blue 3 units, orange 5 units

lines.say: The ratio of blue to orange is three to five. For every three blue, there are five orange.
So there's more orange — and not just more: five thirds as much. One and two thirds times.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "What a ratio tells you" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT SLIDE → A ratio is a fraction]

beats.title: A ratio is a fraction

lines.say: A ratio is just a fraction written with a colon. Three to five is three fifths — three divided by five.
Read it in order: the first name goes with the first number. Blue three, orange five.
And don't worry about being tricked on the order — the exam avoids that wording. When it does appear, it's obvious which is which: the older child gets the bigger number.
And because it's a fraction, you can expand it or reduce it. Twelve to twenty is three to five.
Usually we write a ratio fully reduced — like a fraction.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "A ratio is a fraction" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: No amounts!

lines.say: The big one:
From a ratio alone, you can't know the amounts. Three and five? Six and ten? Thirty and fifty? Only the relationship.
You'll know the amounts only when they give you an actual number — a total, a difference, or one of the groups.
That's why we write the amounts with x: three x and five x.

lines.draw: Write "3x/5x = 3/5" and cross out both x's

lines.say: Cancel the x and the ratio is still three to five — but now we can build equations with it.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "No amounts!" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Part of a whole

items.t: Blue is $\frac38$ of all the items

lines.say: The same idea hides in different wording.

lines.label: 'Blue is 3/8 of all the items' appears

lines.say: Blue is three eighths of all the items. Three out of eight.
So blue is three x — and ALL of them is eight x.
Orange is whatever's left: five x.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Part of a whole" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Fractions in a ratio

lines.say: Sometimes the ratio has a fraction or a decimal: one and a half to two.
Expand by two to get whole numbers: three to four. Three x and four x — much easier to work with.
Tip: give the plain x to the smaller one. Then you never have to divide.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Fractions in a ratio" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Reversed: "costs as"

items.t: 3 notebooks cost the same as 5 pens

lines.label: '3 notebooks cost the same as 5 pens' appears

lines.say: This one doesn't look like a ratio — but it is. And it's reversed.
Three N equals five P. Which one is more expensive?
Pick a number both sides can reach — fifteen.
Three notebooks make fifteen if each costs five. Five pens make fifteen if each costs three.
So notebook to pen is five to three — the opposite of the numbers in the sentence. Fewer notebooks match more pens, so each notebook costs more.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Reversed: "costs as"" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Units and divisibility

lines.say: When you're counting people, x is a whole number. And that tells you a lot.
The difference is three x — so it divides by three. The total is seven x — it divides by seven.
And the groups themselves: the first divides by two, the second by five.
A class of twenty? Impossible with two to five. Twenty-one? Sure — six and fifteen.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Units and divisibility" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

The units tell you what divides by what

But also algebra. And geometry — say, an area that's the difference of two other areas. You build an expression for it, then calculate.
Even in charts, sometimes.

beats.title: Choose x wisely

items.t: Let $x$ = the thing they ask for
At the end: did they ask for $x$ — or $2x$, or $x-1$?

lines.label: 'Let x = the thing they ask for' appears

lines.say: A tip: in most cases, let x be exactly what the question asks for.
Not always — but most questions are built so that the missing value is your x, and solving it IS the answer.

beats.title: Before and after

lines.say: When things change, write the new amounts before you write the equation.

lines.label: A before/after table appears for two boxes: x and x + 10, move 4

lines.draw: In the After column write "x + 4" and "x + 6"

lines.say: After: x plus four, and x plus six. Those are the amounts the equation uses.
Moved between groups? The total stays the same. Removed? The total drops. Added from outside? It grows.

wp-039.title: Give It to the Little Guy

beats.title: Give It to the Little Guy

lines.say: A technique that sounds funny — and saves points, even for strong students.
We call it: give it to the little guy.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.
beats.canvas: Massive title — "Give It to the Little Guy"
beats.bigTitle: Give It to the Little Guy

beats.title: Equal sides

items.t: Two stacks: 8 blocks and 4 blocks. One is twice the other.

lines.say: An equation has an equals sign. The two sides have to be the same amount.

lines.label: 'Two stacks: 8 blocks and 4 blocks. One is twice the other.' appears

lines.say: Eight and four. Eight is double four.
To make them equal — which one do you double?
The small one. Doubling the eight only pushes them further apart.
So when one thing is twice another, the times two goes on the SMALLER side. Give it to the little guy.
Lots of students double the bigger one — because "it's the double". That's exactly backwards.

beats.title: Ages: gaps stay

items.t: Today: 12 and 18  ·  Four years ago: 8 and 14

lines.say: Ages are where this bites most.

lines.label: 'Today: 12 and 18 · Four years ago: 8 and 14' appears

lines.say: Everyone gets older by the same number of years. So the gap between two people never changes — six years now, six years then.
But the ratio does change. Twelve to eighteen isn't eight to fourteen.
So: before you write the equation, write a row for EACH time in the story. Now — and then.

Stronger in maths? You'll probably reach for the equation. Finding it hard? Testing the answers is a great route.
Practise both, and see which comes more naturally to you.

lines.label: The example appears: 50 shekels is enough for 4 bottles, but not for 5

Enough for four: four bottles cost fifty or less. So one bottle is at most twelve and a half.
Not enough for five: five bottles cost more than fifty. So a bottle costs more than ten.
Just like an equation — only we built inequalities, and we'll eliminate the choices that don't fit.

beats.title: Calculating Percentages

lines.say: Percentages. A brand-new topic.
And honestly? You already know more than you think.
Everybody knows fifty percent off means half price.
Today we make that gut feeling precise — and fast.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: What a percent is

lines.say: A percentage is just a way to describe a part of something. Exactly like a fraction.
One hundred percent is the whole.
So one percent is one hundredth.

lines.draw: Circle the % sign and draw a fraction bar next to it

lines.say: Look at the percent sign itself: a little circle, a slash, a little circle. It's literally a fraction sign — something over a hundred.
Thirty-seven percent: thirty-seven hundredths.
And it's not a count until you know the whole. Thirty-seven percent of a hundred tickets is thirty-seven. Of two hundred tickets — seventy-four.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "What a percent is" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Percent ↔ fraction

lines.say: Percent to fraction: put it over a hundred.
Fifty over a hundred. Reduce — one half. Half price, exactly as you'd expect.
Twenty percent: twenty hundredths — one fifth.
Fraction to percent: the other way round. Expand until the bottom is a hundred — then the top IS the percent.

lines.draw: Write "×25" on top and bottom, then "= 75/100 = 75%"

lines.say: Four times twenty-five is a hundred. Three times twenty-five: seventy-five. Seventy-five percent.

lines.draw: Write "×20" on top and bottom, then "= 40/100 = 40%"

lines.say: Five times twenty: a hundred. Two times twenty: forty percent.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Percent ↔ fraction" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Fractions to know

lines.say: Some conversions you must know by heart for this exam.
A half: fifty. A quarter: twenty-five. Almost everyone knows those.
What people forget: one eighth is twelve and a half percent.
Here's how to remember it. A quarter is half of a half — and twenty-five is half of fifty. An eighth is half of a quarter — half of twenty-five: twelve and a half.
And as decimal fractions it's exactly the same: zero point five, zero point two five, zero point one two five.
A tenth: ten percent. A fifth is two tenths: twenty. A twentieth is half a tenth: five.
A third: thirty-three and a third. A sixth is half a third: sixteen and two thirds. Can't halve it precisely? Half of thirty-two is sixteen — so it's sixteen and a bit.
Then build the families. Three eighths: thirty-seven and a half. Five eighths: sixty-two and a half. Three fifths: sixty. Seven twentieths: seven fives — thirty-five.
On the exam you'll see twelve point five AND twelve and a half. Get used to both.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Fractions to know" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: The percent equation

lines.say: Method one: the percent equation. Translate the words into math.
Percent means over a hundred. "Of" means times.
Sixty-five over a hundred, times eighty.
Cancel twenty: four fifths of sixty-five. Fifty-two.
Unknown percent? Same translation.
A over a hundred, times sixty, is twenty-one. Multiply by a hundred: sixty A is twenty-one hundred. A is thirty-five.
And the exam version — a letter inside the percent.
Both sides are over a hundred — multiply it away. And keep those brackets!
Cancel twenty: three times twenty plus x equals two times eighty minus x. Sixty plus three x equals a hundred sixty minus two x. Five x is a hundred. x is twenty.
The hard part is building the equation. After that it's just algebra — shaky there? Go back to the equations lessons.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The percent equation" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Equal ratios

lines.say: Method two: equal ratios — the triple value. Perfect for quick calculations.
Percents on one side, amounts on the other.
Multiply across the diagonal, divide by what's left. Sixty-five times eighty, over a hundred: fifty-two.
Now the real power. Fifteen percent of some number is forty-two. What's thirty-five percent of it?
Divide both sides by three: five percent is fourteen. Seven of those: ninety-eight.
Notice — we never found the whole. That's the advantage: you calculate straight what they ask for.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Equal ratios" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: The 10% method

lines.say: Method three: ten percent. Always easy — just divide by ten.
Ten percent of two thirty: twenty-three. Ten percent of sixty-six: six point six — the point just hops one place left.
Thirty percent? Three ten-percent chunks: sixty-nine.
Thirty-five percent: split it. Thirty percent is sixty-nine. Five percent is half of ten percent: eleven and a half. Together: eighty and a half.
For mental math this is the fastest route there is. Numbers not round? Use the ratio table. Truly stuck? The equation.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The 10% method" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: More tools

lines.say: A few extra tools.
Swap them: sixteen percent of twenty-five equals twenty-five percent of sixteen — a quarter of sixteen. Four.
Whole missing? Thirty percent is fifty-four, so ten percent is eighteen — and the whole is a hundred eighty.
And a change is measured against where it started. Eighty up to a hundred: twenty out of eighty. Twenty-five percent.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "More tools" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Percent of a Percent

lines.say: Percent questions on the exam come in two types.
Type one: straight calculation — what we just did.
Type two: a percent of a percent — and the whole isn't even given.
That's today.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Plug in 100

items.t: A price rises $25\%$, then falls by $20\%$ of the new price. What is the overall change?

lines.say: No starting price. From school, your instinct is: call it x. With percents on percents, that gets messy fast.
So on the psychometric we plug in a hundred. Any number works — a hundred is simply the fastest.
Start at a hundred.
Up twenty-five percent: a hundred twenty-five.
Now careful. The twenty percent is of the NEW price. The hundred is history — the whole is now a hundred twenty-five.
Twenty percent of one twenty-five: twenty-five. Back down to a hundred.
Back where we started! Not because twenty equals twenty-five — because the second percent sits on a bigger base.
And here's the beauty of a hundred: whatever you get in numbers — that's your answer in percent.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Plug in 100" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — A price rises 25%, then falls 20% of the new price — overall change?

beats.title: Two losses

items.t: A stock of material loses $25\%$, then $20\%$ of what remains. What percent was lost in total?

lines.say: Same trick. A hundred units.

lines.label: A chain of three boxes appears: Start → After 25% loss → After 20% more

lines.say: Lose twenty-five percent: seventy-five left.
Twenty percent of what remains — of seventy-five. Ten percent is seven and a half; twenty percent is fifteen. Sixty left.
A hundred down to sixty: we lost forty. Forty percent.
Not forty-five! The second twenty percent came out of a smaller amount.
Shortcut: think about what STAYS. Lose twenty-five percent — keep seventy-five. Lose twenty percent of that — keep eighty percent of seventy-five: sixty. Straight there.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Two losses" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — Loses 25%, then 20% of what remains — total loss?

beats.title: Who is the 100?

items.t: Lena earns $25\%$ more than Noor. Ari earns $40\%$ less than Lena. By what percent is Ari's pay lower than Noor's?

lines.say: Three people. We'll plug in a hundred — but into WHO?
Here's the rule: the whole always comes right after "of" — or after "than".
But this question has several "thans". Lena than Noor. Ari than Lena. Ari than Noor.

lines.draw: Underline "than Noor's" in the last sentence

lines.say: The one that decides is the "than" in the QUESTION itself — lower than Noor's. So Noor is our hundred.
Noor: a hundred. Lena, twenty-five percent more: a hundred twenty-five. Ari, forty percent less than Lena: keep sixty percent of one twenty-five — seventy-five.
Seventy-five against a hundred: twenty-five percent lower.
And again — the number we found is the percent. That's why we choose a hundred.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Who is the 100?" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — Lena 25% more than Noor; Ari 40% less than Lena; Ari vs Noor?

beats.title: When 100 fails

items.t: Rise $20\%$, then add a fixed $15$ credits

lines.say: One warning. A hundred works when EVERYTHING in the story is a percentage.

lines.label: 'Rise 20%, then add a fixed 15 credits' appears

lines.say: Add a fixed fifteen credits, and the answer changes with the real starting price. From a hundred: thirty-five percent up. From two hundred: twenty-seven and a half.
So when there's a fixed amount, use a letter — or the number they gave you.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "When 100 fails" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Working backwards

lines.say: Going backwards? Ninety-six isn't the whole — it's what STAYED.
Ninety-six is eighty percent. Ten percent is twelve. The original: a hundred twenty.
Don't just add twenty percent of ninety-six — that twenty percent was taken from the original, not from ninety-six.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Working backwards" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

Each new percent sits on the new amount

beats.title: Overlapping Groups

lines.say: Overlap problems.
Two groups — and some members belong to BOTH.
They come in two flavours on the exam. Let's learn both.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Four regions

lines.say: Two groups: students who play music, and students who play sport.
Some play both. That shared part is the overlap.

lines.label: Two overlapping circles appear inside a rectangle: Music only · Both · Sport only · Neither

lines.say: The middle sits inside both circles — music AND sport. We call it "both".
Inside the music circle but outside sport: music only.
Inside sport, outside music: sport only.
And outside both circles — students who do neither.
Four regions. Every student lands in exactly one of them.
Careful: "music students" means the WHOLE music circle — music only plus both. Not just music only.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Four regions" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Two question types

items.t: Type 1 · Range: the smallest and largest possible overlap
Type 2 · Exact: enough data to fill every region

lines.say: On the exam, overlap questions come in two types.
Type one: a piece of data is missing, so the overlap isn't fixed. We find its range — minimum and maximum.
Type two: we get enough data to know every region exactly.
One lesson for each. First — a picture that makes ranges obvious.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Two question types" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Pizza: at least one?

lines.say: You've all ordered pizza. Eight slices.

lines.label: The setup appears: 8 slices, mushrooms on 5, tomatoes on 4
Two pizzas appear, each with 5 mushroom slices shaded

lines.say: Mushrooms go on five slices — the shaded ones.
Pizza one: put all four tomato toppings on mushroom slices.

lines.draw: On the left pizza, write T on four shaded slices

lines.say: Four slices with both. That's the most — there are only four tomato toppings.
Pizza two: someone hates mushrooms. Tomatoes go on the plain slices first.

lines.draw: On the right pizza, write T on the three unshaded slices

lines.say: Three used — one tomato left. And no plain slice is left.

lines.draw: Write the last T on a shaded slice

lines.say: It MUST go on a mushroom slice. At least one slice has both — no way around it.
And a topping is a topping: you can't put tomatoes on the same slice twice.
So: at least one, at most four. That's a range.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Pizza: at least one?" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Count each once

lines.say: One line ties all four regions together.
Add both circles — the middle got counted twice. Subtract it once.
Then add the ones outside both circles.
Everyone counted exactly once. That's the whole formula.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Count each once" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

items.t: Four regions: A only · both · B only · neither
A full group = its only-region + both
Two types: range questions · exact questions

beats.title: Overlap Ranges

lines.say: Range questions.
A piece of data is missing — so the overlap isn't one number.
Our job: the biggest it could be, and the smallest it MUST be.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Missing data → range

lines.say: In a range question we can't find the exact overlap.
What we CAN find: the maximum possible — and the minimum that must be.

lines.label: The example appears: 12 students · 8 play music · 7 play sport

lines.say: Twelve students. Eight play music, seven play sport.
How many could do both? Let's hand things out and see.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Missing data → range" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT SLIDE → Place them one by one]

beats.title: Place them one by one

lines.label: Twelve boxes appear, the first 8 shaded as music players

lines.say: Twelve students. The eight shaded ones play music.
Minimum first: we DON'T want sport on music students — so sport goes to the others first.

lines.draw: Write S in the 4 unshaded boxes

lines.say: Four used. Three sport players left — and everyone left plays music.

lines.draw: Write S in 3 of the shaded boxes

lines.say: No choice: three must do both. Minimum — three.

lines.label: A second row of twelve boxes appears

lines.say: Now the maximum: give every sport player to a music student.
Seven both. Can't go higher — there are only seven sport players.
So the overlap is somewhere from three to seven.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Place them one by one" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Max = smaller group

lines.say: Now the technique — no drawing needed.
Put the small group inside the big one. That's the maximum.
Eight and seven: seven. Nothing to calculate.
Equal groups? Five and five — the maximum is five.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Max = smaller group" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Min = the excess

lines.say: The minimum: how far do the two groups go over the total?
Eight plus seven is fifteen.
But there are only twelve students.
Three too many. Those three have no choice — they must be both.
Picture fifteen items for twelve students: three students end up holding two.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Min = the excess" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: When min is 0

lines.say: What if the groups don't go over the total?
Five music, seven sport, twelve students. Five plus seven — exactly twelve.
Hand everything to different students. Nobody has to do both.
Minimum zero. Not minus anything.
If the sum doesn't pass the total, no overlap is forced.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "When min is 0" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Spot the wording

items.t: "at least" → the minimum that must be
"could be" · choices like "between 3 and 9" → a range

lines.say: How do you recognise a range question?
"At most" — think MORE. That's the maximum.
"At least" — think LESS. The minimum that must be.

lines.label: 'could be' and ranges in the choices appear

lines.say: "What could be" — no single answer. And sometimes the choices themselves give it away.
Spot the words — then go straight to max and min.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Spot the wording" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Worked example

items.t: 65% have property A · 55% have property B

lines.say: Let's run both rules on one example.
Max: the smaller group — fifty-five percent.
Min: sixty-five plus fifty-five is a hundred twenty. Twenty percent over — so at least twenty percent have both.
Or reason it out: thirty-five percent don't have A. Give them B first.
Fifty-five minus thirty-five: twenty percent left, and they must double up. Same answer.
Formula or logic — use whichever feels natural. Most students find the formula — sum minus total — the easiest.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Worked example" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Fractions too

lines.say: Fractions work the same way. The whole is one.
Two thirds plus a half is seven sixths — a sixth too many. At least a sixth are in both.
And the maximum? The smaller group — a half.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Fractions too" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Exact Overlap

lines.say: Exact overlap.
Now the question gives us every piece we need.
And one method will handle all of them: the squares method.

beats.title: One more fact

lines.label: The club appears: 18 members · 10 Spanish · 9 French · 4 speak neither

lines.say: Eighteen members. Ten speak Spanish, nine speak French — and exactly four speak neither.
That last fact is what makes it exact.
Four are outside both groups. So the other fourteen speak at least one language.
Ten of them speak Spanish. The other four speak no Spanish — so they MUST be French only.
French is nine. Four are French only — so five speak both.
Five. No choice about it.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "One more fact" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: The squares method

lines.say: With bigger numbers, use the squares method.

lines.label: A strip of four boxes appears: Neither · Spanish only · Both · French only

lines.say: One long strip, four boxes: neither, Spanish only, both, French only.

lines.draw: Draw a bracket over 'Spanish only' + 'Both' and write 10

lines.say: The Spanish bracket covers two boxes: Spanish only and both.

lines.draw: Draw a bracket under 'Both' + 'French only' and write 9

lines.say: French covers both and French only. The two brackets MUST share the middle box — that's the overlap.
All four boxes together make the total — eighteen.
Now it's sudoku. Neither is four.
Four plus the whole Spanish bracket, ten, is fourteen. Eighteen total — so French only is four.
French is nine: four only, so five both. Spanish only: ten minus five, five.
Check: five, five, four, four — eighteen.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The squares method" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Given both → neither

lines.say: Same club — but this time they tell us both, and ask for neither.

lines.label: The data appears: 18 members · 10 Spanish · 9 French · 5 speak both

lines.say: Both is five.
French is nine — five both, so four French only.
We want neither — so keep moving left.
The Spanish bracket is ten, plus four — fourteen. Eighteen total: neither is four.
We never needed Spanish only. Fill only the boxes on your path.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Given both → neither" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Start from any box

lines.say: You can start from whichever box the question hands you.

lines.label: The data appears: 18 members · 10 Spanish · 9 French · 4 French only

lines.say: French only is four — so both is nine minus four, five.
Spanish only: ten minus five. Then five plus five plus four is fourteen — neither is four.
Same diagram, different starting box. That's why the strip is so powerful.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Start from any box" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Fractions of overlap

items.t: The overlap is $\frac15$ of group A and $\frac13$ of group B

lines.say: Now a question that scares a lot of students.

lines.label: The overlap is 1/5 of group A and 1/3 of group B

lines.say: The overlap is a fifth of group A — and a third of group B. How many times bigger is A only than B only?
Call the overlap x. You could even call it one.

lines.draw: Write 5x over the A bracket, then 4x in 'A only'

lines.say: It's a fifth of A — so A is five x. Take away the overlap: A only is four x.

lines.draw: Write 3x under the B bracket, then 2x in 'B only'

lines.say: It's a third of B — so B is three x. B only is two x.
Four x against two x — twice as big. A ratio of two to one.
Scary wording. Simple once it's in the boxes.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Fractions of overlap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Union ≠ population

items.t: "distinct items in either collection" = the union → neither is 0

lines.say: One reading trap.

lines.label: 'distinct items in either collection' = the union

lines.say: When they say two collections show forty DIFFERENT items between them, forty is everyone in at least one.
Not every item in the world — just the ones in the collections.
Inside that total, neither is zero. We'll use this in a guided question.

The two brackets share the middle box

beats.title: Averages

lines.say: Averages.
On the exam you'll usually just see the word "average" — it means the arithmetic mean.
An average is a number that describes the middle of a group of numbers.
Let's see exactly what "the middle" means.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: The middle

lines.say: Start with the easy case: a symmetric group.
Twelve and twenty-eight. Where's the middle?
Twenty. Eight below it, eight above it.

lines.draw: Pair 4 with 16 and 8 with 12 using two arcs; write "→ 10"

lines.say: Four with sixteen, eight with twelve. Each pair's middle is ten. So the average is ten.
When the numbers are symmetric, the average is simply the middle. No calculation needed.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The middle" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Adding the average

items.t: Add or remove a number equal to the average → the average stays the same.

lines.say: Four, six, eight. The average is six — and notice, six is also one of the numbers.
Now add another six. What's the average?
Still six. A number equal to the average sits right on the middle — not left, not right.
That's our first rule: add or remove numbers equal to the average, and the average doesn't move.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Adding the average" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Towers of blocks

lines.say: Now the harder case — a group that isn't symmetric.
Five towers of blocks: three, eight, four, ten, five.
Before we calculate — let's box the average in.

lines.draw: Circle the tallest tower (10) and the shortest (3)

lines.say: If we move blocks from tall towers to short ones, no tower can end up taller than ten, or shorter than three.
So the average is always between the smallest and the largest number. And when the numbers aren't all equal, it can't even equal the smallest or the largest — it sits strictly between them.

lines.label: The same blocks, shared equally: five towers of 6

lines.say: Now share the blocks out evenly… every tower is six.
Six is the average. We didn't add or remove a single block — we just shared them equally.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Towers of blocks" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: The formula

lines.say: So what did we actually do?

lines.label: average = sum ÷ number of values appears

lines.say: We took all the blocks — the sum — and shared them among the towers — the number of values.
Thirty blocks, five towers. Six.
That's the formula you know from school — and now you know why it works.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The formula" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: One value changes

lines.say: A quick extra. Five scores, and one of them goes up by ten.
The total goes up by ten. Shared over five scores —
— the average goes up by two. We never needed the original scores.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "One value changes" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Symmetric? The average is the middle.
Adding the average doesn't change it.
Always between the smallest and the largest.

beats.title: Sum from the Average

lines.say: Sum from the average.
One small algebra move — and it solves a huge number of exam questions.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Turn it around

lines.say: Average equals sum divided by the number of values.
Eight divided by two is four — so eight is two times four.
Same thing here: multiply both sides by the number of values.
Sum equals the number of values times the average.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Turn it around" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Each as the average

lines.say: Why does this matter? Because often you don't know the individual numbers.
Seven values with an average of nine. What are they? No idea.
But you don't need them. Treat every one of them as if it were nine.
The sum is sixty-three. Some are bigger, some smaller — doesn't matter. Together, they make sixty-three.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Each as the average" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: What one can be

items.t: 8 students solve 6 puzzles a day, on average. What can NOT be the number one student solves?

lines.say: Here's how that shows up in a question.

lines.label: The example appears: 8 students solve 6 puzzles a day on average

lines.say: Eight students, six puzzles a day on average. What can't one student — Sapir — solve?
Treat each as six: together they solve forty-eight puzzles.
Sapir could solve ten — the others make up the rest. She could even solve all forty-eight.
But forty-nine? Impossible. That's more than the whole class solves together.
Number of values and the average given? Multiply. That's the sum.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "What one can be" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: A new member

items.t: 4 values, average 20; add a value of 30

lines.say: One more, quickly. Four values average twenty. Add a new value of thirty.
The old sum is eighty. Add thirty: a hundred ten. Now divide by five values, not four. Twenty-two.
Update both parts — the sum and the number of values.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "A new member" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Treat every value as the average.

lines.label: 'Treat every value as the average.' appears

lines.say: Now let's use it on real exam questions.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Weighted Averages

lines.say: Weighted averages.
So far the average sat exactly in the middle. Now some values count more than others.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Different weights

items.t: Matriculation: a 5-unit math exam counts 5 times as much as a 1-unit exam

lines.say: A weighted average is an average where the values have different importance — different weights.
You know it from your matriculation grades: a five-unit exam counts five times as much as a one-unit exam.
The heavier value pulls the average toward itself.
And watch out: on the exam it'll just say "average" — you have to notice it's weighted.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Different weights" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Repeated copies

items.t: Score 70 with weight 3; score 90 with weight 1

lines.label: 'Score 70 with weight 3; score 90 with weight 1' appears

lines.say: Seventy with weight three, ninety with weight one.
Weight three means: treat it as if it appeared three times.
Seventy, seventy, seventy — and ninety.
Three hundred. And divide by four — not by two. We now have four copies.
Seventy-five: closer to seventy, because seventy weighs more.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Repeated copies" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: The formula

lines.say: That's exactly the weighted-average formula.
Each value times its weight — and divide by the sum of the weights.
More values? Each one times its own weight. Same idea.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The formula" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: The see-saw

lines.say: Now the psychometric picture: the average is a balance point — a see-saw.

lines.label: A number line appears with 70 (weight 3), 75 (mean) and 90 (weight 1)

lines.say: The heavy side pulls the pivot toward it. The average moves closer to the bigger weight.
Seventy-five is five from seventy, fifteen from ninety.
Three weights times five — equals one weight times fifteen. Balanced.
The distances are the weights — flipped. Three times the weight means three times closer.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The see-saw" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Split the gap

lines.say: So you can find the average without the formula.

lines.label: 70 and 90, weights 3 and 1, appear on an axis

lines.say: The gap is twenty. The distances must be one to three — four parts.

lines.draw: Split the gap into 4 parts of 5; mark the mean one part above 70

lines.say: Twenty over four: parts of five. One part from seventy: seventy-five.
On the exam, draw exactly this: an axis, the two values above, the weights below.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Split the gap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Groups as weights

lines.say: When you combine groups, the size of each group is its weight.
Six to nine is two to three. Reduce the weights first — it doesn't change the average.
Sixty-two. Not sixty — the bigger group pulls harder.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Groups as weights" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Divide by the sum of the weights
Closer to the heavier group: distances = weights, flipped

lines.label: 'Divide by the sum of the weights' appears
'Closer to the heavier group — distances are the weights flipped' appears

lines.say: Formula or ratios — both work. With a little practice, ratios are much faster.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Work, Rate and Time

lines.say: Rate problems. Another classic type in the quantitative section.
Workers, machines, pumps — anything that gets a job done over time.
Let's start with the one formula behind all of it.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: The formula

lines.say: Here it is.
Rate is what you manage to do in ONE unit of time — say, in one hour.
Multiply it by the number of hours you work — and you get all the work you got done.
Three quantities. They give you two — you find the third.
Not sure what to divide by what? Use the triangle. Cover the one you want.

lines.draw: Box "Work"; beside it write "= rate × time"

lines.say: Want the work? Cover it — rate times time.

lines.draw: Box "Time"; beside it write "= work : rate"

lines.say: Want the time? Cover it — work divided by rate.

lines.draw: Box "Rate"; beside it write "= work : time"

lines.say: And the rate: work divided by time.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The formula" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT SLIDE → Rate has a time unit]

beats.title: Rate has a time unit

items.t: A machine prints 18 labels in 3 minutes.

lines.say: Let's pick apart one sentence.

lines.label: 'A machine prints 18 labels in 3 minutes' appears

lines.say: The work? Eighteen labels — everything it did. The time? Three minutes.
The rate? Work over time. Eighteen over three…
…six. But careful — it's not "six". It's six labels PER MINUTE.
Six labels is nobody's rate. Six labels per minute — that's a rate.
A rate is always a fraction: work over time. Even six over one is still a fraction.
This is where most students trip: work is everything you did. Rate is what you do in ONE unit of time.
And eighteen in three minutes is the same rate as six in one. Same fraction, different spelling.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Rate has a time unit" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Work = rate × time

lines.say: Now use the formula forwards.
Six labels a minute, for seven minutes: forty-two labels.
And backwards — the triangle again.

lines.draw: Below write "42 : 7 = 6 per minute" and "42 : 6 = 7 minutes"

lines.say: Forty-two labels in seven minutes: six per minute. Forty-two at six per minute: seven minutes.
Not three formulas to memorise. One multiplication, read three ways.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Work = rate × time" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Three relationships

lines.say: This next part sounds obvious. But it's exactly what the harder questions lean on.
Time is fixed — say sixty minutes. Work faster, get more done.
Two hot dogs a minute for sixty minutes: a hundred twenty. Four a minute: two hundred forty. Twice as fast, twice the work.

lines.label: 'Rate fixed: time × ½ → work × ½ (direct)' appears

lines.say: Rate is fixed — two a minute. Half the time? Half the work.

lines.draw: Next to it write "60 min → 120 · 30 min → 60"

lines.say: Sixty minutes: a hundred twenty. Thirty minutes: only sixty.
Now the one that flips. The work is fixed — a hundred twenty hot dogs, that's the job.

lines.draw: Next to it write "2/min → 60 min · 4/min → 30 min"

lines.say: Two a minute: sixty minutes. Four a minute — twice as fast — only thirty minutes.
Work fixed means inverse. Faster rate, less time. Keep this in the back of your mind — team questions use it.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Three relationships" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: One job = 1

items.t: One job in 5 hours $\to$ $\frac15$ of the job per hour

lines.say: Sometimes they never tell you how big the job is.

lines.label: 'One job in 5 hours → 1/5 of the job per hour' appears

lines.say: No problem. Call the whole job one. Five hours for one job — one fifth of the job each hour.
Another worker takes eight hours: one eighth per hour.
Fractions feel awkward? Pick a convenient job size instead — forty units: eight per hour and five per hour. Same relationship.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "One job = 1" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Rate = work in ONE time unit — always a fraction
Time or rate fixed $\to$ direct · Work fixed $\to$ inverse

beats.title: Working Together

lines.say: Working together — combined rate.
Usually two workers, sometimes more. And usually at different rates.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Add the rates

items.t: 4 per minute $+$ 7 per minute $=$ 11 per minute

lines.say: When workers work together, they have one combined rate.

lines.label: '4 per minute + 7 per minute = 11 per minute' appears

lines.say: One makes four items a minute, the other seven.
Together: eleven a minute. To get a combined rate — just add the rates.
Add RATES. Never add completion times: four hours and seven hours together is NOT eleven hours.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Add the rates" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Working against you

items.t: Fill rate $-$ drain rate $=$ net rate
9 litres in, 4 litres out — every minute

lines.say: Sometimes one worker works against the others.
I wash dishes — someone else keeps making them dirty. A pump fills a tank — a drain lets water out.

lines.label: 'Fill rate − drain rate = net rate' appears

lines.say: Whoever works against you gets a minus.

lines.label: '9 litres in, 4 litres out — every minute' appears

lines.say: Nine in, four out: the tank gains five litres a minute.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Working against you" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Match the times

items.t: To add, the times must match

lines.say: One more thing before you add.

lines.label: 'To add, the times must match' appears

lines.say: Adding is easy when both workers are measured over the same time.
If one does a job in three hours and the other in two — first stretch both to a common time. Then add.
You'll see exactly how in the next two questions.

beats.title: Team Questions

lines.say: Team questions — also called workers questions.
They're considered hard. Not because of the arithmetic — because they need real understanding.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Spot a team question

items.t: Identical, constant rate + a group of workers

lines.say: Last time, each worker had a different rate. Here — every worker has the SAME rate.

lines.label: 'Identical, constant rate + a group of workers' appears

lines.say: Two giveaways. The words "identical and constant rate" — they work like robots, same speed, never tired.
And a group — usually more than two workers.
See both? It's a team question.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Spot a team question" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Team rate

items.t: Team rate $=$ workers $\times$ one worker's rate

lines.label: 'Team rate = workers × one worker's rate' appears

lines.say: One worker packs three cartons an hour. Five identical workers?
Fifteen an hour.
Now remember the three relationships. Fixed job, double the team — half the time. Fixed time, double the team — double the output.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Team rate" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: The table

lines.say: Every team question goes into a table.

lines.label: An empty table appears: Team, Work, Time

lines.say: Three columns: team, work, time. And the work always sits in the MIDDLE.
How to remember the order? Team questions need more time — so the row ends with Time: Team, Work, Time.
Row one: what they tell you. Row two: what they ask about.
Then two ways to solve: ratios — or the V method. You'll see both in the next question.

lines.say: The last type: work time.

beats.title: What work time is

items.t: Work time $=$ time $\times$ number of workers

lines.say: Work time is how long ONE worker would need to do the whole job alone.

lines.label: 'Work time = time × number of workers' appears

lines.say: Three workers, each working four hours.
Only four hours pass on the clock. But there are twelve hours of work in there.
So one worker alone would need twelve hours.
Think like the boss paying salaries: you pay every worker, for every hour.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "What work time is" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Jobs in phases

items.t: 6 workers for 5 days, then 4 workers for 3 days

lines.say: It really shines when the team changes halfway.

lines.label: '6 workers for 5 days, then 4 workers for 3 days' appears

lines.say: Each phase on its own: thirty worker-days, then twelve. Forty-two in total.
One worker alone: forty-two days.
Don't average six and four workers — each team size belongs to its own stretch of time.

lines.say: One quick warning.
Pages per hour plus pages per hour — fine. Pages per hour plus pages per minute — convert first.

beats.title: Distance, Speed and Time

lines.say: Motion problems.
Here's the secret: a motion problem is just a work problem.
Instead of cracking seeds, you're covering distance.
Same logic, new names. Let's go.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Motion is work

lines.say: In work problems, you cracked twenty seeds an hour.
In motion, you cover twenty kilometres an hour.

lines.draw: Draw an equals sign between the two lines

lines.say: Exactly the same idea. You'll keep seeing the parallels.
A few things ARE different — and that's what this lesson is about.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Motion is work" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: The formula

lines.say: The formula: distance equals time times speed.

lines.label: The motion triangle appears: distance on top, speed and time below

lines.say: Eighteen kilometres an hour for two hours?
Eighteen times two: thirty-six kilometres.
Need the time? Distance divided by speed. Need the speed? Distance divided by time.

lines.draw: Beside the triangle write "t = d : v" and "v = d : t"

lines.say: Forget which is which? Cover the one you want with your finger — the triangle shows the rest.
Know it cold? Great. Need the triangle? It's right here.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The formula" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Units

items.t: $1$ km $=1{,}000$ m · $1$ hour $=60$ minutes · $1$ minute $=60$ seconds

lines.say: Motion questions love to mix units. Your job: work in the SAME units, always.
Kilometres per hour: how many kilometres in ONE hour.
Metres per second: how many metres in ONE second.
And careful with decimals of an hour. One point two five hours is one hour fifteen minutes — not twenty-five.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Units" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Forget 3.6

items.t: A walker moves at $5$ metres per second. How many km does he cover in half an hour?

lines.say: Some books teach: metres per second to kilometres per hour — multiply by three point six.
Forget it. It almost never appears on the exam — and nobody remembers whether to multiply or divide.
Instead: identical ratios. Watch.

lines.label: The example appears: 5 metres per second — how many km in half an hour?
A time–distance table appears with two blank rows

lines.draw: Write "×60" beside the rows and fill in 300 m

lines.say: One second to one minute: times sixty. So the distance times sixty too — three hundred metres.

lines.draw: Write "×30" and fill in 9,000 m = 9 km

lines.say: One minute to thirty minutes: times thirty. Nine thousand metres — nine kilometres.
Easy — and you never have to memorise a conversion factor.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Forget 3.6" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Draw a sketch

items.t: Distance in the formula $=$ the path actually travelled

lines.say: Some motion questions sneak in geometry — Pythagoras.
A plane climbing at an angle. One person walking north, another walking west.
The moment the directions differ — draw it.
In fact, in every motion problem: draw. The sketch shows you what the question is really asking.
The distance in the formula is the real path — the sloping flight path, the whole round trip.

beats.title: Average Speed

lines.say: Average speed.
Honestly? Rare on the exam.
But the idea behind it shows up in disguise — so let's understand it properly.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: What it means

items.t: Average speed $=$ one constant speed for the same trip

lines.say: Picture my hand crossing this page.
Slow at first. Then fast. Slow again. Fast — and stop.
My speed kept changing.

lines.label: 'Average speed = one constant speed for the same trip' appears

lines.say: Average speed is the ONE constant speed that would cover the same trip in the same time.
The exam may never say 'average speed'. It may say: 'if it had moved at a constant speed…'. Same thing.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "What it means" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: The formula

lines.label: The formula appears: total distance over total time

lines.say: Total distance, divided by total time. That's the whole thing.
I don't care how fast you went at the start, or in the middle, or at the end.
Only: how far in total — and how long in total.
Stops count as time too, if the trip includes them.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The formula" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Not the average

items.t: Average speed $\ne$ the average of the speeds

lines.say: And here's the big one.

lines.label: 'Average speed ≠ the average of the speeds' appears

lines.say: Average speed is NOT the average of the speeds. At least, not necessarily.
Go one way fast and come back slow — the slow leg takes MORE time.
So the average speed sits closer to the slower speed.
Remember weighted averages? The bigger group pulls the average toward itself. Here, the longer time does the pulling.
We won't use an averages formula for this. Total distance over total time — and if the distance is missing, pick a friendly number.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Not the average" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

lines.say: Ratios run through the whole quantitative section — and in motion, they're gold.

items.t: Same speed: time and distance — direct

lines.label: 'Same speed: time and distance are direct' appears

beats.title: Relative Speed

lines.say: Relative speed.
How fast two moving things get closer — or farther apart.

beats.title: What it is

items.t: Relative speed $=$ how fast the gap changes

lines.say: Relative speed is the rate at which two bodies approach each other — or move away from each other.

lines.label: 'Relative speed = how fast the gap changes' appears

items.t: Toward each other: add the speeds

lines.draw: Draw two arrows pointing at each other above the sum

items.t: The distance that matters: the gap at the start

lines.label: 'The distance that matters: the gap at the start' appears

Not the whole way they travel. Not where they end up. Just that starting gap.
One of them leaves earlier? First work out that head start — that's your gap.
