beats.title: Counting Possibilities

lines.say: Counting possibilities — combinatorics.
The name comes from the word "combination". And combinations are simply possibilities.
In these questions we find how many ways there are to arrange something — or to choose something.
Always according to the data the question gives us. Let's start.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: What is counting?

items.t: How many ways to arrange? How many ways to choose?

lines.say: Every question in this topic asks one thing: how many possibilities?

lines.label: 'How many ways to arrange? How many ways to choose?' appears

lines.say: Arrange — like people in a row. Choose — like a meal, a code, a committee.
And the answer is always one number: how many different results there are.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "What is counting?" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Different results

items.t: A row: swap two people → a new row
A committee: same people → the same committee
A code: $AB$ and $BA$ are different codes

lines.say: Before calculating anything — decide what counts as a different result.
In a row, swapping two people changes the order. That's a new result.
In a committee with no roles, the same people picked in a different order — still the same committee.
In a code, AB and BA are different — the positions are different.

lines.draw: Tick the row and the code; put a ✗ next to the committee

lines.say: Order matters for rows and codes. Not for groups. We'll use this all topic long.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Different results" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Type 1: list it

items.t: Trial and error: list $\to$ check $\to$ count

lines.say: The first type: trial and error — just like many other question types on the exam.

lines.label: 'Trial and error: list · check · count' appears

lines.say: There's no formula here. You simply write the options, check which fit, and count them.
One tip: list in an organised order — smallest first — so nothing is missed and nothing repeats.
The next question is exactly this type. Try it by listing.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Type 1: list it" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Ask first: what makes two results different?
Small question? List it — in order.

lines.say: Most counting questions won't need a full list. For those, we use a technique — next lesson.
First, try the question.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Multiply the Choices

lines.say: In most counting questions on the exam we won't list and count.
We use a technique that gets us to the answer fast: multiplying the possibilities.
Let's understand how it works.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Stages of choice

lines.say: Find how many options there are at every stage of choice — then multiply.
A stage of choice is simply a moment where you have to pick something.
An outfit: first pick a shirt — four options. Then trousers — three options.
Write the options for each stage, multiply: twelve outfits.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Stages of choice" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Why we multiply

lines.say: Why multiply and not add? Picture it.
Pick the first shirt. It goes with each of the three trousers — three different outfits.
Pick the second shirt — again three outfits. The third shirt, three more. The fourth, three more.
Three plus three plus three plus three. Four times three. That's why we multiply.
Adding four plus three would count clothes, not outfits.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Why we multiply" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Order doesn't matter

lines.say: Does it matter which stage we write first? No.
Pick the trousers first. Each pair goes with all four shirts. Four plus four plus four.
Three times four, or four times three — in multiplication the order doesn't matter. Twelve either way.
So with two things to choose, write them in whatever order you like.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Order doesn't matter" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Dependent choices

items.t: The options at stage $2$ depend on stage $1$

lines.say: In some questions a choice depends on what you picked before.
You can't just pick freely — check what was chosen, and only then see what's allowed.
Sometimes the later choice is forced. Then that stage contributes one option — a factor of one.
Work in stages. Imagine you already picked the first one — then ask what's really left.
This is exactly where people slip. You'll see it in the third question.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Dependent choices" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Count the options at each stage — then multiply
The order of the stages does not matter
Dependent stage? Imagine the first pick, then count

lines.say: Two questions next. Work in stages.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: With or Without Repetition

lines.say: With or without repetition.
Many questions have us choose from a pool — digits, letters, books, people.
And one detail changes everything. Let's see it.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: The pool

items.t: Did the item leave the pool — or can I pick it again?

lines.say: Build a number, and you always pick its digits from a pool — zero to nine, or whatever the question allows.
So after every pick, ask one question.
That's the whole difference between with and without repetition.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The pool" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: With repetition

items.t: With repetition: the item goes back into the pool

lines.label: 'With repetition: the item goes back into the pool' appears

lines.say: With repetition, the item you picked goes right back into the pool. You can pick it again.
So every stage has the same number of options.
Careful: "a three-digit number" does not mean different digits. Four four four is a three-digit number.
Codes too: a symbol can repeat — unless the question forbids it.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "With repetition" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Without repetition

items.t: Without repetition: the item leaves the pool

lines.label: 'Without repetition: the item leaves the pool' appears

lines.say: Without repetition, once you pick something, it's out. It doesn't come back.
So the pool shrinks — one option fewer at every stage.

lines.draw: Under the line write "− 1 each stage"

lines.say: Read the question carefully: may I pick it again or not? The next two questions are twins — only this detail changes.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Without repetition" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: A row: n!

lines.say: Arranging items in a row is a special case of choosing without repetition.
Once an item is placed first, you can't place it again — you pick only from what's left.

lines.label: 'n items in a row: n! ways' appears

lines.say: Five items in a row: five factorial. Eight items: eight factorial. What's factorial? Right now.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "A row: n!" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Factorial

lines.say: The exclamation mark is called factorial.
It means: multiply the number by every whole number below it, one less each time, down to one.
Five times four is twenty, times three sixty, times two one hundred twenty.
A hundred factorial — a hundred times ninety-nine times ninety-eight, all the way down to one.
We need it for rows — and later for choosing groups.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Factorial" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: With repetition: the pool stays the same

lines.say: Three questions next: a code with repeats, a code without, and a row.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Two-Way Connections

lines.say: Mutual action.
An action between two things at the same time. It creates a doubling — let's see why.
It's quite common on the exam, so understand it well.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Mutual action

lines.say: A handshake, a two-way route, a game between two teams — it happens between two at the same time.
When A shakes B's hand, B shakes A's hand. That's one handshake — not two.

lines.draw: Draw a double-headed arrow between A and B

lines.say: But when we count in stages — first one, then the other — we count it twice.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Mutual action" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Count, then halve

items.t: First end: $n$ options $\times$ second end: $n-1$ options

lines.say: So here's the method: count as usual — as if nothing special were happening.
Pick the first end, then the second end. Then — at the very end — divide by two, to cancel the doubling.
Every link was counted from both of its ends — that's the two we divide by.
But with roles, A-then-B and B-then-A really are different results. Then we keep the full count.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Count, then halve" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Where it hides

lines.say: Learn to spot it — so it jumps out at you in the exam.
Handshakes: when one shakes, the other shakes back at the same moment.
Paths between every two houses: this path, from here to there, is the same path coming back.
A game between two teams: when one plays the other, the other plays the first.
And diagonals — the diagonal from this vertex to that one is the same diagonal back.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Where it hides" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Diagonals

items.t: Diagonal: joins two vertices that are not next to each other

lines.say: That last one leads to a rare question type — but it does show up: counting the diagonals of a polygon.
Four ways to count them:
You'll see all four on the diagonal question coming up.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Diagonals" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Mutual action: count as usual, then divide by $2$

lines.say: Two questions next.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Add or Subtract Cases

lines.say: Adding or subtracting possibilities.
Here we can't get the total in one calculation. We have to split into cases.
Sometimes we add the cases — sometimes we subtract.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Rare and hard

items.t: Rare $\cdot$ hard $\cdot$ near the end of the section

lines.say: First thing to know: these questions are very rare on the exam.
They're considered very hard. Maybe one question every few years — and if it comes, it's near the end of the section.
So don't panic. But know the idea.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Rare and hard" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Adding cases

lines.say: Adding possibilities: split the calculation into separate cases.
Usually two cases, sometimes three. Count each one — then add.
The cases must not overlap — every result belongs to exactly one case. Otherwise you count it twice.
A small case heading — like "the special item" and "not the special item" — keeps the split clean.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Adding cases" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Subtracting

lines.say: Subtracting possibilities is even rarer.
Here the question forbids a certain arrangement or choice.
Count everything as if nothing were forbidden. Count the forbidden ones. Subtract.
It's worth it when the forbidden set is small and easy to count. And count both the same way — ordered with ordered.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Subtracting" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Adding: separate cases, count each, add

lines.say: Two questions next — one of each.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Choosing a Group

lines.say: Choosing without order mattering.
Until now, the order we picked in mattered — a row changes when you swap people.
Now: questions where the order of picking changes nothing.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Order doesn't matter

lines.say: Choosing a group — first, know these are edge questions. Very hard, and very rare.
We pick a smaller group from a bigger one. Four children out of ten, say.
Picked Danny first and Yossi second — or Yossi first? They're both in the group either way.

lines.label: The six orders of A, B, C appear

lines.draw: Bracket all six and write "= 1 group"

lines.say: Six different picking orders — one and the same group. That's a doubling we must remove.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Order doesn't matter" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Divide by k!

lines.say: How? Count as usual — as if order mattered. Then divide by the internal arrangements.
The internal arrangements are all the ways to line up the chosen members — k factorial, for k chosen.
Three chosen? Divide by three factorial, six. Four chosen? Divide by twenty-four.
Choose the usual way, then divide by the factorial of how many you chose.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Divide by k!" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: n−1 out of n

lines.say: The second type is actually more common — and very simple: choosing n minus one out of n.

lines.label: 'Choose n−1 out of n → n ways' appears

lines.say: Choose all but one — and the answer is simply the total.

lines.draw: Next to it write "pick who stays OUT"

lines.say: Why? Instead of choosing nine, choose the one who stays out. Ten people — ten choices.
That's why it's called complementary choice. The same idea: choosing eight of ten means choosing the two who stay out.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "n−1 out of n" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

lines.say: Two questions next — one of each.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Factorial Expressions

lines.say: Let's use that question for a quick extension.
Sometimes a factorial question is pure algebra — letters, no story, nothing to count.
Here's how to handle it.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Stop early

lines.say: Remember the trick: seven factorial is seven times six times five factorial.
Same idea with letters. n plus two, factorial.
Take the first factor, then the next one down — and stop the moment you reach n factorial.
You only expand as far as you need to match something else in the expression.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Stop early" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Plug in first

lines.say: What is n factorial times n plus two factorial?
One way — psychometric thinking — is to just plug in a number.
Take n equals two. Two factorial times four factorial: two times twenty-four. Forty-eight.
Then check which answer also gives forty-eight at n equals two.
Remember: a factorial takes whole numbers zero and up — and zero factorial is one. Plug in legal values only.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Plug in first" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: The math

lines.say: Now let's go deeper — the math, so we really understand factorials.
Replace n plus two factorial with n plus two, times n plus one, times n factorial.
Now there are two copies of n factorial.
n factorial times n factorial is n factorial squared.
Check with n equals two: four times three times four. Forty-eight. It matches.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The math" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.

beats.title: Not one factorial

lines.say: One trap to kill.
A product of factorials is NOT one big factorial.
Plug in n equals two: forty-eight on the left, seven hundred twenty on the right. Nowhere near.
We cancel identical products — we don't add exclamation marks together.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Not one factorial" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Expand only until you match, then cancel
Letters? Plug in a small legal value

lines.say: Let's lock it in.
A factorial is a number times the factorial just below it.

lines.label: 'Letters? Plug in a small legal value' appears

lines.say: Plugging in is fast. The math tells you why. Use both.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Forced Digits

lines.say: That idea from the last question deserves a closer look.
When one choice forces another — the forced position gets exactly one option.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: All digits the same

items.t: Four-digit numbers whose digits are all the same: how many?

lines.say: Four-digit numbers whose digits are all identical. How many?
First digit: nine options. Anything but zero.
Second digit — nine options too? Well, it could be one in one-one-one-one, two in two-two-two-two…
But that's not really true. Once the first digit is chosen, the rest MUST match it.

lines.draw: Above the other three positions write "1", "1", "1"

lines.say: Pick five first — the rest are five, five, five. One option each.
Nine numbers: one-one-one-one, two-two-two-two, up to nine-nine-nine-nine. Not nine to the fourth.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "All digits the same" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — Four-digit numbers whose digits are all the same: how many?

beats.title: First = last

items.t: Four-digit palindromes (first = last, second = third): how many?

lines.say: One more. The first digit equals the last, and the middle two match each other.
First digit: nine. Second digit: no restriction at all — ten, including zero.
Third must copy the second. Fourth must copy the first. One option each.
Choosing the first digit really chooses two digits at once.
Ninety. And one-zero-zero-one counts — so don't drop zero from the middle.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "First = last" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — Four-digit palindromes (first digit = last, second = third): how many?

beats.title: Recap

items.t: A free position keeps all its options — zero too

lines.say: Lock it in.

lines.label: 'A free position keeps all its options — zero too' appears

lines.say: Count each genuinely free choice once. Give every forced position a one.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Probability

lines.say: Probability.
In the last topic we counted possibilities. Now we ask: what's the chance something actually happens?
Good news — on the psychometric, this is a pretty simple topic. Let's build it.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Wanted over possible

items.t: Count outcomes that are equally likely — one face, one counter, one ordered pair.

lines.say: In everyday language we say: my chances of passing this exam are high.
High? How high? Very? A little? That's not a measurement.
In maths, probability gives the chance an actual number.

lines.label: The formula appears: probability = wanted ÷ possible

lines.say: Probability is always a fraction. On top: the outcomes we want. Underneath: all the possible outcomes.

lines.draw: Circle "wanted" and write "what I want to happen"; circle "possible" and write "everything that can happen"

lines.say: Wanted — what I want to happen. Possible — every result that can happen.
One quick condition: we count outcomes that are equally likely. One die face, one counter, one ordered pair of dice.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Wanted over possible" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Between 0 and 1

lines.say: Now look what that fraction can do.
If every possible result is a good one, the top equals the bottom. That's one — the maximum.
If no result is good, the top is zero. Zero over anything is zero — the minimum.
So a probability can never be one and a half, or two and a third. Always between zero and one.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Between 0 and 1" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Possible first

items.t: Tip: write the POSSIBLE (bottom) first — then find the WANTED (top).

lines.say: Here's my tip for every probability question.

lines.label: The tip appears: count the possible first, then the wanted

lines.draw: Number the steps: "1" next to possible, "2" next to wanted

lines.say: Always write the denominator first — everything that can happen. Only then look for what you want.
It keeps you from getting confused. You'll see it in every question that follows.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Possible first" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Probability

lines.say: Now the two edges: zero and one.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Certain & impossible

items.t: A bag holds only green counters.

lines.label: The bag appears: only green counters

lines.say: A bag with only green counters. What's the chance of drawing red?
There are no red counters at all.
The possible — some number, it doesn't even matter how many. The wanted — zero. Zero over anything is zero.
Impossible means probability zero.
And green? Every counter is good. Top equals bottom — one. Certain.
Got an answer above one or below zero? You made a mistake. Go back and check the counting.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Certain & impossible" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Probability

lines.say: Until now: the chance of one event. Now — several events.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: And · Or

items.t: AND — both must happen $\to$ multiply the probabilities
OR — either one is enough $\to$ add the probabilities

lines.say: When there are several events, there are two kinds of connection.
One: I want the first event to happen AND the second one too. "And" — we multiply.
Two: I want the first event OR the second. "Or" — we add.
By the way — "or" questions are much rarer on the exam. They're also the harder ones.
Most of what you'll see is "and". Let's practise it.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "And · Or" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Probability

lines.say: We finish probability with a nuance that comes up again and again: the sum of two dice.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Dice symmetry

lines.say: Two dice: the sums go from two — one plus one — up to twelve — six plus six.
Picture one red die and one blue die. Red one, blue two — and red two, blue one — are two different results.

lines.label: A table of sums appears: sum / number of ways

lines.say: Sum two: only one plus one. One way.
Sum three: one-two or two-one. Two ways.
Sum four: red one, blue three. Red two, blue two. Red three, blue one. Three ways.
Don't flip the two-two — it's the same result. Count it once.
Five: four ways. Six: five ways. Seven: six ways.
By the way — opposite faces of a die always add to seven: six and one, five and two, four and three.
Then back down: five, four, three, two, one.

lines.label: The bar chart of ways appears

lines.say: Symmetric around seven! Seven is the top — six ways — and it drops evenly on both sides.
So two sums the same distance from seven always have the same probability.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Dice symmetry" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Two dice: sums are symmetric around 7

lines.say: Let's lock in probability.
That's the whole toolkit. Next question — the symmetry in action.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Trial & Error Questions

lines.say: First question: a crystal game.
No clever trick here — we draw, and we follow.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Draw and follow

lines.say: General problem. No hint what to hit first — so we just follow the game.

lines.label: A row of boxes appears: Start 2 · Break 1 · Break 2 · Break 3

lines.say: We start with two large crystals.
Break one: there are no small crystals yet — so it has to hit a large one.
One large disappears, four small appear. One large plus four small: five.
Now the road splits. Let's take one road: hit the other large crystal.
It turns into four more small ones. Eight small crystals.
Break three: only small ones left. One disappears.

lines.draw: Under Break 3 write 7, then circle choice 4

lines.say: Seven — and seven is in the choices. Lucky on the first road. That's this type: sometimes the first try just works.

beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — question wp21-g004 with its four answer choices — "A game begins with 2 large crystals. Breaking a large crystal replaces it with 4 small crystals. Breaking a small crystal removes it. After exactly 3 breaks, which crystal count is possible?"

beats.title: Method 2 · The other road

lines.say: What if we'd taken the other road?

lines.label: A second row appears: Start 2 · Break 1 5 · Break 2 · Break 3

lines.say: Same first break: five. But now hit a small crystal instead.
One large, three small: four.
Break three: hit the large one — three small plus four new small: seven again.
Or hit a small one — one large, two small: three.
Three isn't in the choices. If this had been your first road, you'd simply try again. Try — and err.
Every road ends at seven or three. The only one on the list: seven. Choice four.

beats.title: Method 3 · Net change

lines.say: One more way to check it — the net change.
A large break: lose one, gain four — net plus three. A small break: minus one.
Two large breaks and one small: two, plus three, plus three, minus one. Seven.

solve-wp21-g005.title: A queue contains at least one delivery van of length 5 m and at least one scooter of length 2 m. There is a 1 m gap between consecutive vehicles and n

beats.title: Trial & Error Questions

lines.say: Question two: a queue of vehicles.
They ask what CANNOT be — so every length we can build gets crossed out.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Build and test

lines.say: Again, no shortcut. We build queues and test the answers.
At least one of each type — so we have no choice: start with one van and one scooter.
Van five metres, gap one, scooter two. Eight.
Eight is possible — and they want the impossible one. Out.
Quick-calculation tip: group the numbers into convenient chunks instead of adding one by one. Here, glue each extra vehicle to its gap. Scooter plus gap: three. Van plus gap: six.
Add a scooter: eight plus three, eleven. Possible.
Fourteen: eight plus three plus three. Possible too.
Now ten. From eight, even the smallest addition — a scooter and its gap — jumps straight to eleven. We fly past ten.
Ten can't be built. That's our answer.
Had you started from the other end of the choices, you'd have found ten first — then it's worth checking the others, just to be sure.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Question 2" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — question wp21-g005 with its four answer choices — "A queue contains at least one delivery van of length 5 m and at least one scooter of length 2 m. There is a 1 m gap between consecutive vehicles and no gap counted at either end. Which total queue length is impossible?"

beats.title: Method 2 · Count the gaps

lines.say: A shorter check.
Give every vehicle the gap after it: van six, scooter three. But the last vehicle has no gap after it — minus one.
So the length plus one is always a multiple of three.
Ten plus one is eleven — not a multiple of three. Ten is impossible. Choice four.

lines.say: A survey question — a percent of a percent.
Try it first. Then let's solve it together.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Plug in 100

lines.say: The whole is the survey. So: a hundred people.

lines.draw: Above "55%" write "55" and next to it "owners 45"

lines.say: Fifty-five don't own a bicycle. So forty-five do.
Now forty percent — of whom? Of the owners. Of forty-five.
Ten percent of forty-five: four and a half. Forty percent: eighteen electric.
The rest own only ordinary bicycles: forty-five minus eighteen — twenty-seven. We started from a hundred, so that's twenty-seven percent. Choice four.
Or skip the subtraction: sixty percent of forty-five — twenty-seven directly.
Notice what I did: I wrote the numbers right on top of the question. Do exactly that in the exam.

lines.say: Second way: a percent tree. More visual — but more writing.

lines.say: Split the survey: fifty-five percent no bicycle — the other branch, forty-five percent owners.
Now split the owners. And here's the classic mistake: every time you go down a branch, that group becomes the new hundred percent.
Forty percent electric — so sixty percent ordinary, of the owners. Branches always add up to a hundred.
To get a bottom branch, multiply along the path: sixty percent of forty-five percent. Ten percent of forty-five is four and a half — times six, twenty-seven. Twenty-seven percent.
Visual, yes. But once you've practised it, plugging in a hundred is faster.

lines.say: Let's start with algebra. She has x points.
She gives away twenty-five percent OF x. A percent never stands alone — always attach its whole. And x minus twenty-five percent of x? Take the complement: seventy-five percent of x.
Then a bonus of thirty percent — of what she has LEFT. Keep all of it and add thirty percent: one point three times.

Bonus: thirty percent of seventy-five — not thirty points! Ten percent is seven and a half; thirty is twenty-two and a half. Total: ninety-seven and a half.

Seven and a half percent of x is twelve.

lines.say: Kilometres per hour — but the times are in minutes. Convert to hours first.

beats.title: Method 1 · List and check

lines.say: No formula needed. We simply check.
We only have the digits two, four, six and eight — and each digit must be bigger than the one before.
Start with two in front. Two four six: four is bigger than two, six bigger than four. Works.
Two four eight. Two six eight. Both work.
Four in front: only four six eight.

beats.title: Advanced Counting

lines.say: Question sixteen.
Three ways to solve this one.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · The mutual-action formula

lines.say: Each pair of players plays once. Does that remind you of something? Mutual action.
Two teams playing each other, two people shaking hands — it's the same action seen from both sides.
Choose the first player: n options. The opponent: n minus one.
But when red plays black, black is playing red at the same time — same game, counted twice. So divide by two.
Here we go backwards: they give the games and ask for the players.
Multiply by two: n times n minus one is ninety.
n and n minus one are consecutive. Which consecutive numbers multiply to ninety?
Ten and nine. So ten players. Choice two.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Question 16" highlighted; the full question is already on the canvas as typed text.
beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — question wp28-g143 with its four answer choices — "In a chess event, each pair of players plays exactly one game. There are 45 games altogether. How many players take part?"

beats.title: Method 2 · Test the answers

lines.say: The psychometric way: plug in the answers — still with the mutual-action formula.
Twelve players: twelve times eleven over two — sixty-six. Too many.

lines.draw: Next to 10 write "10·9/2 = 45 ✓" and circle choice 2

lines.say: Ten players: ten times nine over two — forty-five. That's it.
By the way, you can start from the middle to save a test: nine gives thirty-six — too few — so eight is out too.
But with numbers this friendly, just test them.

beats.title: Method 3 · A growing sequence

lines.say: A less-known way — but it really shows what mutual action means.

lines.label: A table appears: players 2 to 10, with 'new games' and 'total' to fill

lines.say: One player alone? No games. Two players: one game.

lines.draw: Fill the rows: new games 1, 2, 3 … 9 and totals 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, 36, 45

lines.say: A third player adds two games — one against each player already there. Total three.
A fourth adds three: total six. Every newcomer plays everyone who was there before.
Keep going… the tenth player adds nine games. Total forty-five.

lines.draw: Circle the 10 in the last row

lines.say: Careful: the last added number is nine, but it comes from the TENTH player. Ten players. Choice two.
On the exam, just write one plus two plus three… across the page. Whatever's comfortable for you.

beats.title: Advanced Counting

lines.say: Last question of the set.
Medium-plus, maybe even hard. Two ways in.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Trial and error

lines.say: Label the heights one to seven — seven the tallest.
Now build rows of six, always tallest to shortest. Work in order: only change the right end.
Seven, six, five, four, three, two. Then swap the two for a one.
Keep moving the gap one place left each time…
No more options. Seven rows.
Worried you missed one? Six is fewer than we've already found. Forty-two — or seven hundred twenty, six factorial — would need dozens more rows, and our list ran out of options.
Seven. Choice two.

beats.title: Method 2 · Choose who stays out

lines.say: There's a smarter way — a flash of insight: the complementary event.
You're the teacher. Instead of choosing six students and arranging them…
…choose the ONE who stays in place.
"You stay — everyone else, come here." And they line up tallest to shortest. Only one way.
Any of the seven students can be the one left out. Seven options.

solve-wp29-g150.title: A box contains 28 tokens, all either gold or silver. A uniformly random token is gold with probability \frac37. How many silver tokens are in the box?

beats.title: Probability Questions

lines.say: Question four.
First, one new idea: the complementary probability.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Complement first

lines.say: All the probabilities together always make one.
If my chance of passing an exam is two thirds, my chance of failing is one third. Pass or fail — there's no third option.
A coin: heads one half, tails one half. Together — one.
Now the question. Gold has probability three sevenths.
So silver completes it to one: four sevenths.
And what is that probability? Silver tokens out of all twenty-eight tokens.
x silver out of twenty-eight equals four sevenths.
Cross-multiply: seven x equals four times twenty-eight. x is sixteen.
Sixteen silver tokens. Choice three.

lines.say: Or find the gold first.
Three sevenths of twenty-eight: twelve gold. Twenty-eight minus twelve — sixteen silver.
Careful: twelve is the gold count. They asked for silver.

beats.title: Spell out the pairs

lines.say: Let's lay it out so we can see it. When is the sum eight?
First die two — second must be six. Three — five. Four — four. Five — three. Six — two.
Five options. Two dice give six times six — thirty-six possibilities. Five out of thirty-six — we could stop here.

lines.say: Question eight.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: The past doesn't matter

lines.say: At first glance it looks like Rosa should get heads now. Six tails in a row — heads has to come!
And Sam? Seven heads in a row — what are the chances?
It only looks that way. What happened in the past doesn't affect the future.
The coin doesn't know what came before. Every toss: heads one half, tails one half.
Think of a roulette table. People wait for five reds in a row — then bet on black. It means nothing. Still one half.
And someone who just walked up to the table doesn't know the history. The chance can't be different for them.
The chances are equal. Choice three.
This one is rare on the exam — but when it shows up, it's meant to trick you.

lines.say: Advanced probability — question thirteen.

beats.title: Method 1 · Lina first

lines.say: Start with the regular math. Let Lina choose first.
Twenty-six letters. Which ones are good for us? Only the four letters of NOAH.
So Lina picks a good letter with probability four out of twenty-six.
Now Noah. Is every one of his letters good? No! Only the letter Lina already chose.
Say Lina picked O. Now Noah must pick O — one letter out of his four.
One quarter. And it doesn't matter which of the four Lina picked — Noah always needs that one.
Lina AND Noah — an "and" connection means multiply.
Cancel the fours: one twenty-sixth.
Choice three. And careful — four twenty-sixths is only Lina's step. It's sitting there as a trap.

lines.say: Now a small psychometric flash. Faster — almost no calculation.
The order doesn't matter. They just need the same letter. So let Noah go first.
Which of Noah's letters are good for us? All of them! Every letter of NOAH is also in Lina's alphabet.
Four out of four. Probability one. Noah's choice doesn't interest us at all.
Say he picks H. Now Lina must pick H — one letter out of twenty-six.
One twenty-sixth. That's already the answer. Choice three.

But in every group, only ONE person is the oldest.

lines.draw: Next to the question write "one group: 1/s"

lines.say: So in each group, the chance of picking the oldest is one out of s.
We want the oldest from this group AND this one AND this one — all r groups.
"And" means multiply. One over s, r times: one over s, to the power r.
Is that in the choices? Not in that form. They added some exponent technique.
A fraction to a power: one to the r is just one, and s to the r goes underneath. One over s to the r — and a negative exponent flips it: s to the minus r.
Choice one.

beats.title: Method 2 · Plug in

lines.say: The psychometric way: the choices have letters — so plug in easy numbers.
Try one group with one person? He's automatically the oldest.
But look at the choices: with ones, every choice becomes one. Useless.
Two and two? Check the choices first: three of them come out one quarter. Useless again.
So here's the rule: when you plug in, check the choices FIRST — make sure they're all different. You'd have to plug into them anyway.

lines.draw: Write "r = 2, s = 3" and next to the choices write 1/9, 1/8, 1/6, 2/3

lines.say: Two groups, three people each: one ninth, one eighth, one sixth, two thirds. All different — good numbers.
Now the question: one third in the first group, one third in the second. Multiply — one ninth.
One ninth — choice one. Plugging in makes a letters question a numbers question.

lines.say: Question fifteen.
Wanted over total — then a shortcut with the complement.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Wanted over total

lines.say: Probability: what we want, over everything there is.
She chooses from the COMBINED output. Picture one big basket with both factories poured in.
Eight hundred plus four hundred: twelve hundred buttons. That's the bottom.
What do we want? NOT blue.
Factory A: seven sixty not blue. Factory B: two ninety not blue.
Ten fifty out of twelve hundred. Reduce however you like — seven eighths.
Choice two.

Factory B makes 400 buttons a day, including 110 blue buttons. One button is chosen uniformly from their combined daily output. What is the probability that it is not blue?"

beats.title: Method 2 · Complement

lines.say: Now let's shorten the calculation with the complementary probability.
Same basket, twelve hundred buttons. But instead of counting the not-blue ones — count the blue ones.
Forty plus one-ten: one fifty. One fifty out of twelve hundred — one eighth. That's easy.
But one eighth is the chance of BLUE. Blue and not blue must add up to one.
So not blue is seven eighths. Choice two.
It's like percentages: sometimes the complement is simpler — then subtract it from the whole.
And one eighth is choice three — the blue trap. Answer the question they asked.

lines.say: Question sixteen.
A hard one — and the key word is dependence.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Day by day

lines.say: Monday she chose jazz. We want folk on Wednesday.
Do we calculate anything for Monday? No. It's given — it already happened. Its probability is one.
Now Tuesday. She can't repeat jazz, so she has four options.
But wait — are all four good for us? No! If she picks folk on Tuesday, she can't pick folk on Wednesday.
So three good options out of four: three quarters. Two neighbouring days depend on each other.
Wednesday. Jazz is back in the pool — it's not the day before anymore. Folk is allowed.
Four allowed genres, we want folk: one quarter.
Tuesday AND Wednesday — multiply. Three sixteenths. Choice one.
What matters here: one stage's choice changes the next stage's options. Take the dependence into account.

lines.say: Last question of the set.
First the calculation — then symmetry solves it in seconds.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Method 1 · Multiply

lines.say: For the fifth sweet to be blue, the first four must all be red.
First sweet red: six red out of seven.
Second red: five out of six. Third: four out of five. Fourth: three out of four.
Now three sweets are left — two red, one blue. We want the blue one.
One out of three.
Red AND red AND red AND red AND blue — multiply. But before you calculate, look how it cancels.

lines.draw: Cancel the diagonal pairs and write "= 1/7"

lines.say: Six with six, five with five, four with four, three with three. One seventh.
Choice one.

beats.canvas: Pre-loaded — question wp29-g165 with its four answer choices — "A jar contains 6 red sweets and 1 blue sweet. All seven are drawn in a uniformly random order without replacement. What is the probability that the fifth sweet drawn is blue?"

beats.title: Method 2 · Symmetry

lines.say: Now the flash — no calculation. Symmetry.
In Denmark there's the "law of Jante" — nobody is better than anybody else. Everyone's equal.
Easy question first: what's the chance the FIRST sweet is blue? One out of seven. Everyone knows that.
Why? One of the seven must come out first — and no sweet has priority over another.
The last one? Same logic. One of them must stay last. All equal — one out of seven.

lines.draw: Next to the question write "any position: 1/7"

lines.say: And the fifth? One of the seven must be fifth. The blue has the same chance as every other sweet.
One seventh — choice one. First, fifth, last — it doesn't matter.
Symmetry comes back in hard questions: three players, who wins round three? All equal.

lines.say: AB is tangent to a circle with center O, radius 4. OA equals OB, and angle AOB is 90. What's the shaded area?
Shaded areas — we met them in quadrilaterals. The most common way to solve them: subtract areas.
And it's one of the principles that keeps coming back in edge circle questions.
So first — a scheme. What minus what gives the shaded part?
If we know the area of triangle AOB, and the area of the sector inside it — subtract them. That's our scheme.
Now the givens. OA equals OB, and the angle at O is 90.

lines.draw: Write 45° at A and at B

lines.say: So AOB isn't just a right triangle — it's right AND isosceles. A silver triangle. The base angles: 45 each.
AB is tangent. We learned an automatic construction: a point of tangency — draw a radius to it.

lines.draw: Draw OC to the point of tangency and mark the right angle at C

lines.say: Call the point C. The radius is perpendicular to the tangent.
AOB is isosceles, and OC is the height to its base — so it's also an angle bisector and a median.

lines.draw: Write 4 on OC, 4 on AC and 4 on CB

lines.say: The radius is 4, so OC is 4. And OCB is a silver triangle too — so CB is 4, and AC is 4.

lines.say: We have everything. Start with the triangle.
The best way: base AB times the height, over 2.
Plenty of students say: I have a hypotenuse in a silver triangle — find the legs, multiply, divide by 2.
I ask — why? You already have a base and a height. Don't work for nothing — there's no time on the psychometric.
Base 8 times height 4, over 2 — 16.
But wait. We can stop here and look at the answers. They often help.
The shaded area must be 16 minus some sector — something with pi.
8 pi minus 8? The pi is in the wrong place — that's circle minus triangle. Out, for sure.
8 minus 4 pi — pi is in the right place, but the triangle is 16, not 8. Out.
32 minus 4 pi — same argument. We need 16 minus something. Out.
Only 16 minus 4 pi is left. Choice four.
We started with math and switched halfway to psychometric thinking. On the exam — mark it and move on.

lines.say: We're in a lesson, so let's also calculate the sector.
The whole circle: pi r squared — 16 pi.
The sector is part of it — the part is set by the central angle. 90 degrees.
Some know by heart that 90 is a quarter — wonderful. If not: 90 over 360 — a quarter. A quarter of 16 pi — 4 pi.
16 minus 4 pi. The answer we found is really right.
Choice four.

lines.say: One more approach — fully psychometric: estimating sizes.
Maybe you plug in the givens and don't know how to go on. Maybe you run out of time — it's one of the last questions.
What do we know? The triangle is 16. The shaded part is inside it — so less than 16.
And by eye — even less than half. Now the answers.
8 pi — pi is 3.14, so 8 pi is about 25. Minus 8 — about 17. More than the whole triangle? Impossible. Out.
8 minus 4 pi — negative. They do that a lot: hide a negative answer behind letters. An area can't be negative. Out.
32 minus 4 pi — about 32 minus 12.5 — about 19. Too big. Out.
16 minus 4 pi — about 3.4. The only one possible — and by eye it's about a quarter of the triangle.
Choice four.
Which approach? Up to you. Me — math, then shorten with partial calculation. It's safer.
The problem with estimating: sometimes it rules out only one or two answers. But when there's no choice — a great card up your sleeve.

lines.say: ABC is a right triangle, tangent to the circle at B and D. OE and EC are both 12. What's the shaded area?
Again shaded areas. We need a scheme: what minus what.
The problem — here the scheme isn't trivial. The big triangle minus something? Triangle BDC minus something? Not clear.
What do we do in these cases? Work with the givens, plug them in — and hope the solution shows itself.
B is a point of tangency, and it's already marked 90 — the radius is perpendicular to the tangent.
D is a point of tangency too. But careful: BD is NOT a radius, so there's no 90 there.

lines.draw: Draw the radius OD and mark the right angle at D

lines.say: Draw a radius to the point of tangency and mark 90. The most basic construction there is.
The radius is 12 — OE is a radius, so OD is 12 too.
And now it's clear: the shaded area is triangle ODC minus the sector. Like the last question.

lines.say: Triangle ODC: right angle at D. One leg, OD, is 12. The hypotenuse OC is 12 plus 12 — 24.
We need the other leg, DC. Pythagoras? Probably... but there's no need.
Spot the special triangle: the hypotenuse is exactly twice a leg. That only happens in a golden triangle.

lines.draw: Write 30° at C and 60° at O

lines.say: Opposite the short leg — 30. Opposite DC — 60.
The long leg is root 3 times the short one: 12 root 3.
Leg times leg over 2: 72 root 3.
Calculate the sector? We saw we can shorten — look for 72 root 3 minus something.
Choices 2 and 4 don't have 72 root 3 — out.
But here the trick doesn't finish the job: two answers start with 72 root 3.
Some students start from the sector instead. Let's use both.

lines.say: The sector: part of the circle. The whole circle — pi times 12 squared — 144 pi.
Which part? The angle at O is 60 — 60 out of 360 is a sixth. A sixth of 144 pi — 24 pi.
72 root 3 minus 12 pi — wrong sector. Out.
Only 72 root 3 minus 24 pi has both parts right.
Choice three.
By the way — starting from the sector alone, 24 pi leaves two answers too. Together they settle it.

lines.say: A sample question — medium.
An inscribed–circumscribed question. We'll solve it three ways.

beats.title: Method 1 · The math way

lines.say: A semicircle with center O and radius r. Angle OAB is 60. The perimeter of the semicircle divided by the perimeter of triangle AOB?
Questions like this — we call them inscribed–circumscribed. Common in edge circle questions.
What do we do? Write the inscribed shape — and the other shape — with the circle's radius.

lines.draw: Write r on OA and on OB

lines.say: OA and OB are radii — r and r. So the triangle is at least isosceles: base angles equal.

lines.draw: Write 60° at B and at O

lines.say: Angle A is 60, so B is 60 — and an isosceles triangle with a 60 is equilateral. AB is r too.
Triangle perimeter: 3r.
Now the semicircle. Many students take half the circumference — only partly right.
It has two parts: the arc — half of 2 pi r, that's pi r — and the diameter at the bottom, 2r.
Take r out as a common factor, then cancel it: pi plus 2, over 3.
Choice one.

lines.say: The recommended way for most students: plug in a number. It saves the algebra mistakes.
The usual choice is r equals 1. But look at the answers first — two of them contain r.
With r equal 1, multiplying or dividing by r changes nothing — three answers come out the same. It doesn't settle this one.
So pick r equals 2 instead.
Triangle: 2, 2, 2 — 6. Semicircle: arc 2 pi, diameter 4.
2 pi plus 4 over 6 — that's pi plus 2 over 3. Now put r equals 2 in every answer.
Pi over 3 — no diameter, too small. With r in the top — double. With r in the bottom — half. All out.
Choice one.

items.t: Perimeter ÷ perimeter or area ÷ area: $r$ must cancel.

lines.say: Third way: estimating sizes. Say the radius is 1 again.
The arc from A to B is longer than the chord AB — the shortest path between two points is the straight line. So it's 1-plus.

lines.draw: Write 1+ on each of the three arcs

lines.say: Same for the other two arcs. The curved part is 3-plus. Add the diameter, 2: the semicircle is 5-plus.
The triangle is 3. So we want around 5-plus over 3.
Pi over 3 — about 1. Out.
The answers with r — an interesting distractor. Try r equals 2 and 3 — the ratio would keep changing.

lines.label: Ratio of perimeters (or areas): r must cancel appears

lines.say: But if we enlarge or shrink the whole figure, the ratio doesn't change. So when they ask perimeter over perimeter, or area over area — the radius must cancel.
Any answer with r is a distractor — out at first glance. Unless it's area over perimeter — then an r can stay.
Pi plus 2 over 3 — 5-plus over 3. Choice one.
Full math — fine. Plug in a number — recommended for everyone. Estimating — only when there's no choice.

lines.say: Square ABCD is circumscribed about the circle, and square EFGH is inscribed in it. Area of EFGH over area of ABCD?
We'll start with the psychometric way: plug in a number. No need to write both areas with r.

lines.draw: Write r = 1 and draw the diameter across the circle

lines.say: Let the radius be 1. The side of the outer square — BC — equals the diameter. So it's 2.
Area: side squared — 4.
Now the inner square. Many students go through silver triangles: 1, 1, so the side is root 2, then square it.
Possible — but a bit long. A square's area is also diagonal times diagonal over 2.
Its diagonals are diameters of the circle — each is 2.
2 times 2 over 2 — 2.
Inner over outer: 2 over 4 — a half.
Choice three. That's the standard, recommended way.

These two triangles are identical — each is half of a little square, cut by its diagonal. And the same everywhere.
4 out of 8 — a half. The big square is twice the small one.

lines.say: The third and last: triangle, circle, triangle — but only equilateral triangles.
Here it's different: the outer triangle isn't twice the inner one — it's FOUR times.
And the outer side is twice the inner side.
We didn't prove it — you can sit down and prove it. The key: in an equilateral triangle, the center is twice as far from a vertex as from a side.
Careful: a length factor is not an area factor. Root 2 for sides means 2 for areas; 2 for sides means 4 for areas.

To calculate an arc length we first need a central angle.
But there's no central angle on arc AG, or on arc ED. So — a construction. A pretty natural one: I must have a central angle.

lines.draw: Draw the radii OA and OD

lines.say: Draw radius AO and radius OD.
Now what? Angle B is 26. Which arc does it stand on? AG plus GF — the whole arc AF.
An inscribed angle doesn't help directly — I need central angles. But the central angle on the same arc is twice as big.

lines.draw: Draw the radius OF and write 52° at O between A and F

lines.say: Another radius — OF. Angle AOF: twice 26 — 52.

lines.draw: Write 98° at O between F and D

lines.say: Angle C is 49. It stands on arc FD. The central angle — twice: 98.
Lots of givens. Lots of mess. We have to find our way through it.

Finding each one alone — impossible. But the sum — possible.
Their sum is the whole big angle AOD — 52 plus 98, 150 —

How is it split? Maybe 30 and 30, maybe 20 and 40 — I don't know, and it doesn't matter.
Slide the middle part left or right — the sum of the two stays 60.

Radius 9: circumference 2 pi times 9 — 18 pi.

Shaded areas — but until now we subtracted. That doesn't look like the case here.
Some students think: a circle plus the bold part. But how do you calculate that part? Not clear.
In cases like this — go to the givens and see what information you can squeeze out of them.
The arc is a quarter of the circumference. What did we learn? A quarter of the circumference means a central angle of 90.

lines.say: Now I see how to calculate the shaded area.
It's the right Pac-man, plus the square, plus the left Pac-man.
Each Pac-man is a sector. One whole circle: pi times 4 squared — 16 pi.
We want three quarters of it — the quarter we don't want. 12 pi.
The square: 4 squared — 16. Total: twice 12 pi, plus 16.
24 pi plus 16 — choice one. Complicated — and done.

lines.say: Students ask: what about estimating sizes? Here it's hard to finish — but easy to rule out two answers.
One circle — clearly 16 pi. And the shaded part is more than one circle.
Not just more: one circle is 16 pi, the other half circle is 8 pi — plus the piece in the middle. So more than 24 pi.
12 pi plus 8 and 12 pi plus 16 — far too small.
What about the other two? Both are 24 pi — plus 16, plus 8. Too close. We're in trouble.
We raised our chances to 50 percent. But solving 100 percent by estimating — hard.
If you really must gamble — it looks big by eye, so the bigger one. But again — a gamble.

lines.say: Radius 3. AD and BC are tangent to the circle at E and F. The rectangle's area equals the circle's area. What's BC?
The rectangle is tangent to the circle at E and F — so EF is a diameter.
Radius 3, diameter 6. And the diameter equals the rectangle's height, AB.
Rectangle area: AB times BC — 6 BC. It equals the circle: pi r squared — 9 pi.
Isolate BC: divide by 6 — 3 pi over 2.
Choice four. The math solution — honestly, not bad.

lines.say: Now the psychometric way — estimating sizes.
The diameter is 6. And BC is shorter than the diameter — the rectangle has the circle's area, but it's shorter than the square around the circle.
So BC is less than 6. Now the answers.
3 pi — 3 times 3-plus — 9-plus. Too big.
6 pi — 18-plus. Way too big.
2 pi — 6-plus. Just too big as well.
Three answers out — mark the fourth with certainty. No need to even calculate it: 3 pi over 2 is about 4.7. Choice four.

lines.say: A small circle inside a big one, tangent at A. AB and AC are diameters, CB is 6. The shaded area is 21 pi. The small radius?
How do we calculate the shaded area? Big circle minus small circle.
No radius is given. Call the big one R, the small one r.
We need one unknown — write R with r. Easier than the other way round: adding is easier than subtracting.

lines.draw: Write r and r on AC, and 6 on CB

lines.say: The big diameter AB is 2r plus 6.
The radius is half of that: r plus 3.
Pi multiplies everything — divide it out. Open the brackets: r squared plus 6r plus 9, minus r squared. The squares cancel. 6r is 12 — r is 2.
Choice three.

lines.say: Now the psychometric way: plugging in answers. They're all round numbers — easy to plug in.
Where to start? From the middle.
Why? Start from the smallest and it fails — every answer is bigger, you learned nothing. Start in the middle: if it's too big, go down; too small, go up. Two tries are always enough.
Here the answers aren't in order: 3, 4, 2, 1. Order the values — 1, 2, 3, 4 — the middle values are 2 and 3.
Try 3. Small diameter 6, big diameter 6 plus 6 — 12, big radius 6. 36 pi minus 9 pi — 27 pi.
Not 21 pi — too big. So 3 is out, and 4 is out too: we need a smaller radius.
Try 2. Small diameter 4, big diameter 10, big radius 5. 25 pi minus 4 pi — 21 pi. It fits!
Choice three. Solved two ways — pick the one that suits you.

An arc length — so first a central angle.
AB equals AC, so angle B equals angle C. Together they're 180 minus 2 alpha.
Each one is half of that: 90 minus alpha.
Notice — angle B is an inscribed angle, standing on the bold arc. The central angle is twice as big.
180 minus 2 alpha.
Did you notice we divided by 2, then multiplied by 2? Spot that early, and you write 180 minus 2 alpha straight away.

lines.say: An arc is the part of the circumference set by the central angle, out of 360.
180 minus 2 alpha over 360, times 2 pi r.
Lots of letters. Glance at the answers and continue smartly: they all have pi r in front — so shape ours like that.
Cancel the 2 against 360: 180 below.
Every answer has a 1 in the bracket. Split the fraction: 180 over 180, minus 2 alpha over 180.
That's 1 minus alpha over 90.
Choice four. The math solution — it got tangled at the end with not-simple algebra.

lines.say: Whenever there are unknowns, we can plug in a number — and turn it into a simpler question.
Which value? A convenient special case. What's more convenient than 60 degrees?

lines.draw: Write 60° at A, B and C

lines.say: Make the triangle equilateral: angle A is 60, so 2 alpha is 60 — alpha is 30. Each base angle is 60.
The central angle is then 120. And r isn't given either — plug in 1.
Circumference 2 pi. A third of it: 2 pi over 3.
Now put alpha 30 and r 1 into every answer — and rule out anything that isn't 2 pi over 3.
30 over 30 is 1. 1 minus 1 — 0. Out.
30 over 60 — a half. Pi over 2. Out.
30 over 180 — a sixth. 1 minus a sixth — 5 sixths pi. Out.
30 over 90 — a third. 1 minus a third — 2 thirds pi. It fits — and all three others are out. Choice four.
Two solutions: full math — or psychometric, plugging in numbers.
That's it for circles. On to the summary.

items.t: Central angle $=2\times$ inscribed angle on the same arc
Tangent $\perp$ radius $\cdot$ area $\pi r^2$ $\cdot$ circumference $2\pi r$

lines.say: So OB is 6. And the whole triangle has sides of 6.
The area of an equilateral triangle — remember: a, 2, 3, 4.
a squared, root 3, over 4.
6 squared is 36. 36 over 4 — 9. 9 root 3.
Choice one.

lines.say: Isosceles triangle ABC inside a circle with centre O. AB equals AC, angle A is 40. What is angle ABO?
First, the mathematical solution.
Angle BAC is an inscribed angle on arc BC. Angle BOC is a central angle — on the same arc.
The central angle is double the inscribed angle on the same arc. 80 degrees.

lines.draw: Mark OB and OC as equal

lines.say: OB and OC are radii — isosceles again.
This time the top angle is 80 — not 60, so it's not equilateral. The base angles: 180 minus 80, halved — 50 each.

lines.draw: Draw the radius from O to A

lines.say: Draw a radius from the centre O to vertex A.
An isosceles triangle is symmetric — so the radius splits angle A in two equal parts.
20 and 20. No need to prove it — this isn't a high-school exam. It's an easy question at the start of the section.

lines.draw: Mark OA and OB as equal

lines.say: Now look at triangle AOB. Again — equal radii, so it's isosceles. Equal base angles.
So the question mark is 20 too. Choice two.
This way is shorter, with less calculation — I prefer it.

items.t: Radius $\perp$ tangent at the tangent point

lines.say: Two congruent circles, centres O and M, touching each other. MA and MB are tangent to circle O. What is angle AOB?
Only the radius — 4. How do we get an angle? Start from the givens and see what they give.
Two tangents from the same point M: they're equal — and with the radii they make a kite.
We don't have the kite yet. We need a helper line — one of the most common: a radius to the tangent point.

lines.draw: Draw OA and OB with right-angle marks at A and B

lines.label: Radius ⟂ tangent at the tangent point appears

lines.say: A radius to the tangent point is perpendicular to the tangent. 90 at A, 90 at B.

lines.draw: Write 4 on OA and on OB

lines.say: Now there's a kite. 90 and 90 — the other two angles share 180. Still not enough.

lines.say: The small circle has circumference 8 pi. The shaded ring is 65 pi. What is the circumference of the large circle?
First given: circumference 8 pi. From a circumference, can we find the radius? Yes.
2 pi r equals 8 pi. Cancel pi: two radii — the diameter — is 8. The radius is 4.
Its area: pi r squared — 16 pi. That's the white circle.

items.t: Every triangle has exactly one circumscribed circle

lines.say: The sides of triangle ABC are 7, 24 and 25. What is the circumference of the circumscribed circle?
But there's no circle here at all! To solve it we need two rules.

lines.label: Every triangle has exactly one circumscribed circle appears

lines.say: One: every triangle can be circumscribed — there's a circle through all three vertices.
Two: there's only one such circle, with one radius. True for every triangle.

lines.say: Draw the circle around the triangle. The right angle is an inscribed angle.
An inscribed angle on a diameter is 90. And the other way round: a 90 inscribed angle must stand on a diameter.
So the hypotenuse — 25 — is the diameter.
No need to halve it to 12.5 and double again: 2 pi r is diameter times pi. 25 pi.
Choice three. A really interesting question.

Count them: six alphas and six betas — all around, 360.
One equation, two unknowns — we can't get alpha or beta alone. But we can get their sum.
Divide by 6 — or take out a common factor of 6. Alpha plus beta — 60.
Could be 20 and 40, could be 10 and 50. Doesn't matter.

beats.title: Advanced Circles

lines.say: Circles — the advanced level.
In the last lessons we learned the basic rules and practised basic and more advanced questions.
Honestly — you already have the tools for most circle questions on the psychometric.
Now: harder questions. Edge questions from the end of the section.

beats.title: What's ahead

items.t: Inscribed $\cdot$ circumscribed: write it all with $r$
Partial calculation $\cdot$ plug in numbers $\cdot$ estimate

lines.say: We'll meet a few principles that keep coming back in these questions.

lines.label: Shaded areas: what minus what appears

lines.say: Shaded-area questions — build a scheme: which shape minus which shape.

lines.label: Inscribed / circumscribed: write everything with r appears

lines.say: Shapes inside circles and circles inside shapes — write everything with the radius.
And psychometric thinking: partial calculation, plugging in numbers, and estimating sizes.
With these we solve much faster — sometimes even when we're not sure of the full solution.
Let's start.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "What's ahead" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Sectors and Arcs

lines.say: Sectors and arcs.
First let's understand what a sector is and what an arc is.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: A sector

items.t: Sector $=$ two radii $+$ the arc between them

lines.label: A circle cut into four with one sector shaded appears

lines.say: A sector is the part of the circle enclosed between two radii and the arc between them.

lines.draw: Trace the two radii and the arc of the shaded part

lines.say: Two radii — and the arc that forms between them. This whole area is called a sector.
It's a bit like a slice of pizza.

lines.label: Sector = two radii + the arc between them

beats.loads: Sidebar with "A sector" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Sector area

lines.say: The area of the sector equals the sector's share of the whole circle.
First — there's a formula. We have a central angle — the central angle of the sector, α.
Take α over 360, times the area of the circle — times π r squared. That's the formula for a sector's area.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Sector area" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Skip the formula

items.t: Which fraction of the circle is it?

lines.say: I recommend — pretty much across the board — NOT using this formula.
Unless someone really doesn't get it any other way and needs the formula to understand.

lines.label: Which fraction of the circle is it?

lines.say: I much prefer — and strongly recommend — solving sector and arc questions by understanding, not with the formula.
Let's see what I mean.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Skip the formula" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Quarters and eighths

lines.label: A circle cut into eight with one slice shaded appears

lines.say: Take a circle and split it into four parts. This sector is a quarter of the circle.
If it's a quarter, its angle is 90 — 360 divided by 4.
Instead of knowing α is 90 and plugging 90 over 360 times π into the formula — all I need to understand is: this sector is a quarter of the circle.
If I know the area of the circle, I just divide it by 4 — and I know the area of the sector.

lines.draw: Draw the second line that halves the quarter

lines.say: Now split the circle into 8. This sector — a real pizza slice, family-size pizza — is an eighth of the circle.
Its central angle is 45 — exactly half of 90. Good and important to know. But what really interests me: it's an eighth of the circle.
Radius 6 — the circle is 36π. A quarter: 9π. An eighth: 9π over 2. Divide — done.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Quarters and eighths" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Fifths

lines.say: One more example.

lines.label: A circle cut into five equal sectors, one shaded, appears

lines.say: We split this circle into 5 parts — 5 equal sectors.

lines.draw: Write 72° at the centre of the shaded sector

lines.say: The angle — I know how to find it: 360 divided by 5 is 72.
But what really interests me: this sector is a fifth of the circle.
Once I know the circle's area — just our formula — I divide by 5. Say the circle is 25π: the sector is 5π. Simple.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Fifths" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Arc length

v.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="184.5 44.5 271.0 271.0" role="img" aria-label="Circle"><title>Circle</title><circle cx="320.000" cy="180.000" r="109.500" fill="none" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><circle cx="320.000" cy="180.000" r="3.2" fill="#203344"/><text x="305.000" y="195.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">O</text><path d="M 320.000 70.500 A 109.500 109.500 0 0 0 225.170 125.250" fill="none" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="7"/></svg>

lines.label: A circle with a highlighted arc appears

lines.say: Arc. An arc is simply part of the circle — we remember that from the vocabulary.
The length of the arc is also the arc's share of the whole circle.
There's a formula here too: α over 360 — this time times the circumference.
Before it was times the area, because we wanted an area. Now it's times the circumference, because we want a length.
But here too — my advice: leave the formula. Let's solve it by understanding.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Arc length" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Sixths and thirds

lines.label: A circle in six parts with one arc highlighted appears

lines.say: I split the circle into 6 equal parts. The arc is 1/6 of the circle.
Find the circumference with the formula I know — and divide by 6.
The angle here, by the way, is 60. Why? 360 divided by 6.
Radius 9: the circumference is 18π. A sixth of it: 3π.

lines.draw: Extend the highlighted arc to two sixths and write 120°

lines.say: Split the circle into 3 — the arc is a third. Find the circumference, divide by 3: 6π. The angle, of course, is 120 — 360 divided by 3.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Sixths and thirds" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Two fifths

lines.say: A slightly more complicated one.

lines.label: A circle in five parts with an arc over two parts appears

lines.say: Again I split the circle into 5, so every angle is 72.
But I marked an arc that covers two of those angles.
That's fine — it's simply two fifths of the circle. One fifth here, and another fifth here — together two fifths.
If each angle is 72, then 72 plus 72 is 144. That's all.
So: there are formulas, and they'd work — but it's much simpler to see which part of the circle it is. A third, a quarter, a fifth, a sixth — and calculate.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Two fifths" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Angles to know

lines.say: Angles worth remembering for sectors and arcs:
90 is a quarter. 45 an eighth — why? Half of 90, and half of a quarter is an eighth. 60 is a sixth.
40 is a ninth: 360 divided by 9 is 40. 36 is a tenth: 360 divided by 10. 72 — a fifth.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Angles to know" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Build bigger ones

items.t: The exam checks understanding — not pocket calculators

lines.say: And we can stretch these angles.
90 is a quarter — so 270, three times 90, is three quarters of the circle.
144 is twice 72. 72 is a fifth — so 144 is two fifths.
120 is a third. You can just know it — but it's also 60 times 2, a sixth times 2. Or 40 times 3, a ninth times 3.

lines.label: The exam checks understanding — not calculators

lines.say: Remember these and you'll get arcs and sectors in seconds, without the formula.
On the psychometric, these are the angles you'll get. Nobody will give you 23 and a half degrees.
They check whether you understand that 60 degrees is a sixth of the circle. That's what they check.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Build bigger ones" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Arc vs perimeter

lines.say: One last distinction from the course. An arc is only the curved edge.

lines.draw: Trace the two radii of the shaded sector

lines.say: The perimeter of a sector is the curved edge plus the two radii.
Radius 9, 60 degrees: the arc is 3π — the perimeter is 3π plus 18. Read what they're asking for.
Let's go to examples.

lines.say: A circle with centre O has radius 6. The highlighted arc AB is 3π long. What is α?
Here too I could plug into the arc-length formula: α over 360 times 2π r equals 3π, and so on.
And if that confused you a little — excellent. You don't need it.
I know the highlighted arc is 3π. I know the radius is 6. Let's find the whole circumference.
The circumference: 2π r — 2π times 6 — 12π.

lines.say: So the whole circle is 12π, and the highlighted arc is 3π.
3π out of 12π — that's a quarter. 3 out of 12.
And if the highlighted arc is a quarter of the circle — the angle is a quarter of the circle too.
A quarter of 360 — 90. Found it.
Choice four.

lines.say: A circle with centre O, radius 6. Two shaded sectors: 60 degrees and 90 degrees. What is their total area?
Here too I could plug into the formula. I'll save myself that — I have a 60 and a 90.
90 degrees — we know that's a quarter.
60 degrees — a sixth.
Together: a quarter plus a sixth. In twelfths: 3 twelfths plus 2 twelfths — 5 twelfths.
So the shaded part is 5/12 of the circle's area.

lines.say: Let's find the area of the circle.
π r squared — π times 6 squared, the radius is 6 — 36π.
I don't need the whole circle. Only 5/12 of it.
36 divided by 12 is 3, times 5 — 15π.
Choice two.
Or separately: a sixth of 36π is 6π, a quarter is 9π — 15π. Same thing.
So once again: no formulas for arcs and sectors. Just see which part of the circle it is — it solves much faster.

lines.say: Circles.
Before we go through the rules — the theorems — let's get to know the lines and the angles we have in a circle.

items.t: Circle $=$ the round line $\cdot$ on the exam, "area of a circle" $=$ the area inside

lines.label: A circle with centre O appears

lines.say: This is a circle — the line we see here, going all the way around.
By the way, just for general knowledge — most people don't know the difference.

lines.draw: Trace the round line with your finger

lines.say: The circle is the round line itself — the boundary.
Everything inside — the whole flat shape, like a wooden disk — strictly speaking, that's the disk.

lines.label: Circle = the round line · on the exam, 'area of a circle' = the area inside

lines.say: On the exam they just say 'the area of a circle' for the inside, and 'circumference' for the distance around. Fine — as long as we know which is which.

items.t: All radii of one circle are equal: $r$

lines.label: A circle with several radii from O appears

lines.say: Radius. A radius is a straight line joining the centre of the circle to any point on the circle.
Here's one radius. Here's another. And another.
All the radii of one specific circle are equal.
Spin the radius around — it's the same radius turning, the same length in every direction.

lines.draw: Write r on two of the radii

lines.say: We usually mark the radius with the letter r.

lines.label: All radii of one circle are equal: r

items.t: Chord: both ends on the circle

lines.label: A circle with two chords, AB and CD, appears

lines.say: Chord. A chord is a straight line joining two points on the circle.
Mark two points on the circle, join them — that's a chord. Two more points, join them — also a chord.
We can draw infinitely many chords in a circle. And notice — they're not equal in length.

lines.draw: Draw one more very short chord near the edge

lines.say: A long chord, a short chord, and here — a very short chord.

lines.label: Chord: both ends on the circle

lines.label: A diameter AB through O appears

lines.say: The longest chord we can draw in a circle is the one that cuts it right through the middle.
It passes exactly through the centre — and a chord like that is called a diameter.
It splits the circle into two halves — two semicircles. And it's the longest chord there is.
Its length is 2r — because it's made of two radii.
Diameter 14? The radius is 7. Always switch to r before you use a formula.

items.t: Inscribed angle: vertex ON the circle, between two chords

lines.label: A circle with an angle at C between two chords appears

lines.say: An inscribed angle is an angle between two chords.
Its vertex sits on the circle — that's why it's called inscribed. And it sits exactly between two chords.
Careful: if we just drew two lines and stopped somewhere inside the circle, the vertex would be inside — or outside.
Then it's NOT an inscribed angle. An inscribed angle has its vertex on the circle.

lines.label: Inscribed angle: vertex on the circle, between two chords

lines.label: A circle with an angle at O between two radii appears

Its vertex is at the centre of the circle, and it's between two radii. A radius here — and a radius here.

items.t: Short arc $=$ minor arc $\cdot$ long arc $=$ major arc

lines.label: A circle with the highlighted arc AB and its chord appears

lines.say: An arc is some part of the circle.
Mark a piece of the circle, highlight it — that's an arc.
An arc can be short — or very long. Almost the whole circle.
The chord AB splits the circle into two arcs: the highlighted one on top —

lines.draw: Trace the long bottom arc from A to B

lines.say: — and another, bigger arc here, around the bottom.
Even though it's more than half the circle — it's still an arc. People often think an arc is always something short. Not true.

lines.label: Short arc = minor arc · long arc = major arc

items.t: The angle rests on the arc you can see from its vertex

lines.label: A central angle and an inscribed angle on the same arc appear

lines.say: We can close off this arc with two radii — that's a central angle closing off the arc.
And with an inscribed angle: take a point on the circle and close off the arc with two chords.
When an angle closes off an arc like this, we say the angle rests on the arc. In English: it intercepts the arc.
What does that mean? Imagine I'm standing inside the central angle.

lines.draw: Draw two short 'walls' along OA and OB

lines.say: These radii are walls — tall walls. The part of the circle I can see from here is the highlighted arc.

lines.draw: Draw two short 'walls' along CA and CB

lines.say: Same for the inscribed angle: I stand at C, the chords are walls — all I can see is the highlighted arc.

lines.label: The angle rests on the arc you can see from its vertex

lines.say: So this central angle and this inscribed angle both rest on the same highlighted arc.
That's it for the vocabulary. Next lesson — the rules.

lines.say: Here, here, here — every inscribed angle I draw on this arc is half of the central angle.
Inscribed angles that rest on the same arc — or on equal arcs — are equal to each other.
Why? It comes straight from the first rule. If each one is half of the same central angle — they're equal to each other.

lines.say: The central angle on a diameter is simply a straight line — 180 degrees.
And half of 180 is 90.
A very, very important theorem for the exam. Honestly — these first three rules are used all the time in circle questions.
