lines.label: A quadrilateral ABCD with all four vertices on the circle appears

lines.say: In a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle, opposite angles add up to 180.
First — what's an inscribed quadrilateral? All four of its vertices are on the circle.
If even one vertex were inside the circle or outside it — it's no longer inscribed. We need all four on the circle.
Opposite angles add up to 180: this angle and the one facing it — together 180.
Same for the other pair: left plus right — 180.

lines.say: Important — if I know this angle is 70, I know the one opposite is 110.

lines.say: Let's prove it.
Draw two radii from the centre — to this vertex and to this vertex.

lines.draw: Write 2α at O on the side facing A

lines.say: Here we get a central angle — call it 2α. The angle at A rests on the same arc — so it's half: α.

lines.draw: Write 2β for the other central angle

lines.say: Same from the other side. The other central angle — 2β. The angle at C rests on that arc — so it's β.
And look: 2α plus 2β is a whole circle.
Divide by 2 — α plus β is 180. Two opposite angles add up to 180. Proved.

beats.title: One rule behind it all

items.t: Inscribed quadrilateral $\rightarrow$ opposite angles add to $180°$

lines.say: To sum up angles in a circle — there's really one important rule:
An inscribed angle is half of the central angle. All the other rules come from it:
All inscribed angles on the same arc are equal. On a diameter — 90. Inscribed quadrilateral — opposite angles 180.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "One rule behind it all" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Equal chords

items.t: Equal chords $\rightarrow$ equal central angles $\rightarrow$ equal arcs

lines.say: One more fact from the course that we'll use later:

lines.label: Equal chords → equal central angles → equal arcs

lines.say: In the same circle, equal chords cut off equal arcs — and equal central angles.
Join each chord's ends to the centre: two triangles, radius, radius, equal chord — identical triangles. So the central angles are equal.
And it works backwards too: equal arcs — equal chords.
Now let's solve a sample question.

items.t: AOCB is not inscribed — O is not on the circle

lines.say: A, B and C are on a circle with centre O. Angle AOC is 112. What is angle ABC?
We just learned about inscribed quadrilaterals. But notice — AOCB is NOT an inscribed quadrilateral.
O isn't on the circle. For it to be inscribed, O would have to be somewhere on the circle.
So I can't say these angles add up to 180.
180 minus 112 — 68 — is exactly the trap. Cross it out.
By the way, you can see it with your eyes: the angle at B is much bigger than 90. Of course it isn't 68.

lines.say: So how do we solve it? First way: inscribed is half of the central angle on the same arc.

lines.draw: Mark a point D on the long arc and draw DA and DC

lines.say: Let's draw an inscribed angle that rests on the same arc as the 112.
It's half of the central angle — 56.
Now I've made an inscribed quadrilateral: ABCD — all four vertices on the circle.
In an inscribed quadrilateral, opposite angles add up to 180. So 180 minus 56 — 124.
Choice three.

lines.say: Another way. It's a bit harder — not hard to understand, but some students find it hard to see.

lines.draw: Shade the reflex angle at O and write 248°

lines.say: If this angle is 112, the angle that completes it to 360 is 248.
And that 248 is ALSO a central angle. A very big one, wide open — but still a central angle.

lines.draw: Trace the long arc from A around to C

lines.say: It rests on this long arc — all the way around.
Now stand at B, between the two walls BA and BC. What part of the circle do you see? All of this long arc.
So angle ABC is the inscribed angle of the 248.
Half of 248 — 124. Same answer. Choice three.
And 56? That's half of the wrong arc — the one B sits on.

lines.say: A tangent is a straight line that just brushes past the circle. It touches it at one point.

lines.draw: Draw a line that cuts through the circle

lines.say: If it were a little further in, it would pass through the circle — cut it at two points — and the part inside would be a chord.

lines.draw: Draw a line outside the circle

lines.say: If it passed outside, it wouldn't touch the circle at all. Just a line.

lines.draw: Mark D and write 'point of tangency'

lines.say: Our tangent just brushes the circle at one point. That point is called the point of tangency.

lines.label: The circle with its two tangents appears

lines.say: The radius is perpendicular to the tangent at the point of tangency.
A very, very important rule.

lines.draw: Draw radius OD and mark the right angle

lines.say: The tangent touches the circle here. When I draw a radius to the point of tangency, I get 90 degrees between the tangent and the radius.

lines.label: Radius to the point of tangency ⊥ tangent

lines.say: This rule is used very often on the exam.
Every time you see a circle question with tangents — don't think too much. Auxiliary line: draw the radius to the point of tangency.

lines.say: Two tangents that come out of the same point are equal to each other — and with the radii to the points of tangency, they make a kite.

lines.say: From this point P I draw two tangents to the circle. These two tangents are equal in length.

lines.say: Now I also draw radii to the points of tangency — and I get a kite.
Why a kite? Two pairs of equal sides: the equal radii, and the two equal tangents.

Always, automatically. It should be Pavlov — anyone who doesn't know who Pavlov is, look him up.

lines.say: Area and circumference of a circle.
Two very basic formulas — we use them a lot in psychometric questions.

lines.say: Here are the formulas.
The area of a circle is π r squared.
The circumference is 2π r.
This sign here is a letter called pi. And the radius — we know what that is. The radius of the circle, given or not.
Only the area has r squared. Area in square centimetres; circumference — a length, in centimetres.

items.t: $C=3$ diameters $+$ a bit $=$ a bit more than $6r$

lines.say: So what is pi? Let's really see.

lines.label: The circumference peeled off and laid next to diameters appears

lines.say: Take a circle and peel off its circumference — lay it out as a straight line.
Here I've marked the diameter. How many times does the diameter fit into the circumference?

lines.draw: Count the three d's along the strip

lines.say: Three times — and a little extra.

lines.label: C = 3 diameters + a bit = a bit more than 6r

lines.say: Three diameters are 6r. So the circumference is a bit more than 6r.
And the formula says the circumference is 2π r. So 2π is a bit more than 6 — π is a bit more than 3.

beats.title: π is a number

items.t: $\pi$ is a fixed number — not an unknown like $x$

lines.say: π is about 3.14. Why 'about'? It keeps going: 3.141592 and so on.
Doesn't really interest us. 3.14 is enough — even 3.1 is enough for the exam.
All we need to know about π: it's a bit more than 3.

lines.label: π is a fixed number — not an unknown like x

lines.say: π is a number. A constant. Not an unknown like x, y or z in equations.
It's just not a round number — the decimals keep going. So we mark it with the letter π.
I could write 3.14 times r squared, or 6.28 times r. Why 6.28? 2 times 3.14.
To keep it simple they gave it a special sign — pi. Easier to calculate, easier to see in the formula.
And if the answers have π in them — keep the π. Don't swap it for 3.14.

lines.say: Simple examples.

lines.label: A circle with radius r appears

lines.say: Say the radius is 6.
Its area is π r squared: π times 6 squared — 36π. That's the area of the circle.
Its circumference is 2π r: 2π times 6 — 12π.
I put 6 in place of the radius and found the area. Put 6 in place of the radius and found the circumference.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "From the radius" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Back from C

lines.say: Another example. I don't know the radius — but I'm given that the circumference is 22π. Find the radius.
If the circumference is 22π, put it into the circumference formula: 2π r equals 22π.
Divide by 2π: here I get r, and here — 11.
The radius is 11. I used the formula backwards: instead of radius → circumference, circumference → radius.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Back from C" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Back from the area

lines.say: Now I'm given a circle whose area is 121π.
Again I don't know the radius. The area is 121π — just put it into the formula: π r squared equals 121π.
Divide by π: r squared is 121. Take the root of both sides: r is 11.
Notice: minus 11 isn't relevant. A radius is a length — it's positive, never negative.
So: from the radius we find the area and the circumference — and from the area or the circumference we find the radius.
Let's see a psychometric question.

beats.title: Write it as an equation

lines.say: A circle's area in square centimetres is three times its circumference in centimetres. What is its radius?
What I need to do is simply work from the data.
Ignore the square centimetres and the centimetres — ignore the units.
Just think of it as: the circle's area is three times its circumference.
Its area: π r squared. Equals three times the circumference: three times 2π r.

beats.title: Divide, then check

lines.say: Divide by π: r squared equals 6r.
Divide by r — r is a radius, it isn't zero — and r is 6.
Choice three.
Let's really check.
Radius 6: the area is 36π, the circumference is 12π. And 36π really is three times 12π.
A quick shortcut from the course: area over circumference is r over 2. If that's 3 — r is 6.

lines.say: The two axes are perpendicular to each other, and they meet at one point.
That point is called the origin. Its x is 0 and its y is 0.
Every point has an x value and a y value — and they decide where the point is.

lines.draw: Mark 5 and 7 on the x-axis, and −2 and −3 on the y-axis

lines.say: A point can sit right on an axis — say 5 or 7 on x, or −2, −3 on y.
But once we have both axes, we can move across AND up — so a point can be anywhere in the plane.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The origin" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: (x, y): x first

lines.say: How do we write where a point is?
The value of A is made of its x value and its y value, inside brackets.

lines.label: x always first · y always second

lines.say: x always comes first, y always second. Always.
So (4, 3) and (3, 4) are two different points.

lines.say: Here's A. We don't have its values — we need to find them.
How? From A, I drop a perpendicular to each axis.

lines.draw: Draw a dashed line from A down to the x-axis and write 4

lines.say: Down to the x-axis: it cuts the x-axis at 4. So the x of A is 4.

lines.draw: Draw a dashed line from A across to the y-axis and write 3

lines.say: Across to the y-axis: it cuts it at 3. So the y of A is 3.
Notice — I wrote the 4 first and the 3 second. x first, y second. A is (4, 3).

lines.draw: Drop dashed lines from C to both axes and write −3 and −3

lines.say: Perpendicular to the x-axis — minus 3. Perpendicular to the y-axis — minus 3.
C is (−3, −3). Left and down.
So let's sum up: every point has two values, an x and a y. We find them where the perpendiculars cut the x-axis and the y-axis.
And the notation is always A(x, y) — x on the left, y on the right.

beats.title: On an axis

lines.say: One small thing the course adds.

lines.label: On the x-axis: y = 0 · on the y-axis: x = 0

lines.say: A point on the x-axis has y equal to 0 — for example (6, 0). A point on the y-axis has x equal to 0 — like (0, −4).
That's really the very basics. I assume most of you know this lesson already.
But for whoever doesn't, it was important for me to show how we find the value of a point.
From here we move on — to questions and more insights on the coordinate plane.

lines.say: We learned how to mark and find the values of points.
Now it's time to find the length of a segment.
A reminder: a segment is a line bounded by two points — so it has a definite length.

Here both are 3. And here I subtract the x values.
These two points are on the same side of the axis — no minus here.
From the y-axis to S is 7. From the y-axis to R is 2. What's left between them — 5.
Same side — subtract. Opposite sides — add.

From minus 4 to 6: 4 units up to the y-axis, 6 more after it. 10.
The classic mistake is 6 minus 4 — 2. The ends are on opposite sides of zero. A quick sketch prevents it.
Most students have no problem with these — once you do it once, you get it.

beats.title: No crossing: parallel

items.t: A line that never cuts an axis is parallel to it
A line parallel to neither axis cuts each axis exactly once

lines.say: Two facts that sometimes come up with no drawing at all.

lines.label: A line that never cuts an axis is parallel to it

lines.draw: Draw a horizontal line above the x-axis

lines.say: This line will never cut the x-axis. So if a question says: a line that does not cut the x-axis — I know it's parallel to the x-axis.

lines.label: A line parallel to neither axis cuts each axis exactly once

lines.draw: Draw a slanted line through both axes

lines.say: And if a line isn't parallel to either axis — it definitely cuts each of them, once. And keeps going to infinity.
Careful: this is about a whole line. A short segment can stop before it reaches the axis.

The horizontal leg: from x = −1 to x = 4 — 5.
The vertical leg: from y = 0 up to 12 — 12.

beats.title: No formula needed

items.t: Parallel $\rightarrow$ subtract or add $\cdot$ slanted $\rightarrow$ right triangle $+$ Pythagoras

lines.say: Now, God forbid, if someone here remembers the distance formula from analytic geometry —
Forget it. Or don't — if you need it for school. But we really don't need it.
By the way, if you dig into that formula, you'll see it's exactly what we did. It's just Pythagoras.

lines.label: Parallel → subtract or add · slanted → right triangle + Pythagoras

lines.say: So: parallel to an axis — subtract the values, or add the two parts. Slanted — close a right triangle, Pythagoras. Easy.

For the perimeter I need the length of each of the three sides. Let's start.
BC — the simplest. B and C have the same y, minus 5, so BC is parallel to the x-axis.

lines.draw: Split BC at the y-axis; write 8 on the left part and 13 on the right

lines.say: I'll split it into two parts: from B to the y-axis, and from the y-axis to C.
B is at minus 8 — so that part is 8. C is at 13 — so that part is 13.

lines.draw: Draw a perpendicular from A down to BC; call its foot H

lines.say: Now how long are the two parts of the base?

lines.draw: Write 12 on BH and 9 on HC

lines.say: The x of A is 4, so H is also at 4. From B at minus 8 to H at 4 — 8 plus 4, 12. And from H to C — 13 minus 4, 9.
On the left: 12 and 12 — a right isosceles triangle. The silver triangle: a, a, a root 2. So AB is 12 root 2.
On the right: 9 and 12. That's 3, 4, 5 times 3 — so AC is 15.

lines.say: Perimeter: 21 plus 15 plus 12 root 2 — 36 plus 12 root 2.
Don't add the altitude — it's a helper line inside, not part of the boundary.
Choice one.
So what did we have here? Supposedly analytic geometry — a coordinate plane.
But really, the solution is Pythagoras. I need the triples, and the silver and golden triangles.
Whoever isn't solid on those — really go back to Pythagoras and the special triangles.

beats.title: Circles on the Plane

lines.say: Sometimes a psychometric question has a coordinate plane — with a circle.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Radius first

items.t: In a circle: find the radius first
How? Lines parallel to the axes $\rightarrow$ a triangle or a square

lines.label: In a circle: find the radius first

lines.say: With a circle, the most important thing for me to find is the radius.
With the radius I then find the circumference, the area, a sector, an arc — whatever's needed.
And if the radius isn't given — which is likely — I'll need to find it.

lines.label: How? Lines parallel to the axes → a triangle or a square

lines.say: How? Draw lines parallel to the axes, and close either a triangle or a square.
Let's see the different ways a circle can show up on the coordinate plane.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Radius first" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

items.t: Tangent to both axes: centre $(r,\ r)$

lines.label: A circle tangent to both axes, centre C, appears

lines.say: Here's a circle tangent to both axes.
When it's tangent — what did we say we do? Draw radii to the points of tangency. They're parallel to the axes.

lines.draw: Draw the two radii to the axes and mark the right angles

lines.say: One radius here, another there — and a square forms.
Now if I have the value of the centre — say (4, 4) — I know right away the radius is 4.

lines.label: Tangent to both axes: centre (r, r)

lines.say: By the way — if the circle is tangent to both x and y, the centre must have the same x and y. Because the radii are equal: (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3) and so on.

lines.say: A circle with centre (−4, 4) is tangent to both axes too. The values aren't equal — but without the signs, they are.

lines.label: A circle with centre C on the x-axis and a point P appears

lines.say: Another circle — its centre is on one of the axes, here the x-axis.
Sometimes the circle sits a bit further along the x-axis.
Then say I have the value of the centre, and the value of this point on the circle, where it cuts the x-axis.
To find the radius, I subtract the x of the centre from the x of the point.
8 minus 6 — the radius is 2. Not 6! 6 is where the centre is, not the radius.

lines.label: A circle centred at the origin with a point A appears

lines.say: The truth is, the most common circle questions on the coordinate plane — are when the centre is at the origin.
Most likely I'll be given a point on the circle, and asked for an area, a circumference, something like that.
For that I need the radius. How do I find it?
I draw a radius to the point. Now it's a slanted line — and we already know how to find the length of a slanted line.

lines.draw: Drop a perpendicular from A to the x-axis; write 5 and 12

lines.say: Close a triangle: the x of the point is 5, so this leg is 5. The height of the point is 12.
5, 12, 13 — that's the radius.

lines.label: The circle centred at the origin appears

lines.say: And now the circumference and the area — this we already know.
Circumference 26 pi. Area 169 pi.
But look what I did: I drew a radius, closed a right triangle, found the radius — and from there, whatever they ask.

lines.say: Let's see an example of a psychometric question with a circle.

lines.say: A circle centred at the origin, radius 10. A is a point on the circle whose y value is 5. What is alpha?

lines.draw: Write 5 next to the y of A

lines.say: The y of A is 5 — so the height of A is 5.
Its x? Not given. But I don't really need it.

lines.draw: Drop a perpendicular from A to the x-axis; call its foot H

lines.say: What do I do with a circle? As usual — first I drop a perpendicular and close a right triangle.
What do I know about this triangle? This leg — the height of A — is 5. And the hypotenuse is the radius, 10.

beats.title: Half the hypotenuse

fig.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="148.0 -6.0 401.1 358.0" role="img" aria-label="Coordinate plane"><title>Coordinate plane</title><line x1="174.000" y1="180.000" x2="466.000" y2="180.000" stroke="#71818d" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M459.0 176.0 L466.0 180.0 L459.0 184.0" fill="none" stroke="#71818d" stroke-width="1.8"/><text x="480.000" y="166.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18">x</text><line x1="320.000" y1="326.000" x2="320.000" y2="34.000" stroke="#71818d" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M316.0 41.0 L320.0 34.0 L324.0 41.0" fill="none" stroke="#71818d" stroke-width="1.8"/><text x="306.000" y="20.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18">y</text><text x="307.000" y="197.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="15">O</text><circle cx="320.000" cy="180.000" r="132.727" fill="none" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="320.000" y1="180.000" x2="434.945" y2="113.636" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="320.000" y1="180.000" x2="452.727" y2="180.000" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5"/><circle cx="434.945" cy="113.636" r="3.2" fill="#087f83"/><text x="479.945" y="96.636" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18">A (x, 5)</text><path d="M 355.836 180.000 A 35.836 35.836 0 0 0 351.035 162.082" fill="none" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2"/><text x="360.000" y="169.282" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#087f83" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18">α</text><text x="379.727" y="202.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">10</text></svg>

lines.say: Now I have a right triangle with a leg and a hypotenuse. I could do Pythagoras and find the other leg.
But I don't really need Pythagoras. Why?
A right triangle where a leg is half the hypotenuse. When does that happen?
Only in the golden triangle — 30, 60, 90.
And the short leg sits opposite the 30.
So our alpha is 30.
Choice two.

lines.say: First the whole circle: 100 pi.
30 out of 360 is a twelfth. 90 holds three 30s — three, three, three, three — 12. Or just 360 divided by 30.
So the sector is 100 pi over 12 — 25 pi over 3.
A circle on the coordinate plane isn't very complicated. Just remember — always close a Pythagoras triangle.

lines.say: E is the origin. ABCD is a right trapezoid. AE equals EB. What's the area of the trapezoid?
We need the area of a trapezoid. It's really a quadrilaterals question, presented on a coordinate system.
The area of a trapezoid: sum of the bases, times the height, over 2.
What we need to do: pull the data out of the system.
Start with AD — the top base. We have points A and D.
The y of A is 4, and the y of D is 4. So AD is parallel to the x-axis.
So its length is simply the difference between the x's: 8 minus 3 — 5.
Top base — done.

Here they're more than similar: the hypotenuses are equal — so they're congruent.
The top triangle: E is the origin, zero-zero. A is at 3, 4. So we moved 3 to the right, and climbed 4 floors.

BC: 3, plus 3, plus 5 under AD — 11.
The height DC: 4 up plus 4 down — 8.
Into the formula: 5 plus 11 is 16. Times 8, over 2 — cancel the 2: 16 times 4 — 64.
Choice one.
By the way — 40 is a trap. That's only the 5-by-8 rectangle, without the triangle on the left.

How do we find the radius and the height? From the rectangle.

lines.say: The sides are parallel to the axes, and we're given two opposite corners.
In this case it's always easy to find the rectangle's dimensions.
The bottom side is parallel to the x-axis — so y is fixed along it. The right side is parallel to the y-axis — so x is fixed along it.
So the bottom-right corner is 3, 1.
The x-difference: from minus 2 to 3 — 5. That's the width — and it's the radius, because we turn around the side itself.
The y-difference: from floor 1 to floor 9 — we climbed 8. That's the height.

Here: half a circle, minus the triangle.
For the semicircle we need the radius. The radius is OA.
We learned: to find a slanted segment on the axes — build a right triangle with it as the hypotenuse.

lines.say: O is zero-zero, A is 6, 6. We moved 6 right and climbed 6.
Legs 6 and 6 — a silver triangle.

lines.say: The whole circle: pi r squared. Careful — square the 6 AND the root 2: 36 times 2 — 72 pi.
Half a circle — 36 pi.
Now — don't rush to the triangle. We can think psychometrically: partial calculation.
The answer must be 36 pi minus something. Any other answer is out.
6 root 2 minus 3 pi — no 36 pi. Out.
36 pi minus something — possible.
18 pi minus 6 — the wrong number in front of pi. 36 root 2 minus 6 pi — pi in the wrong place. Both out.
So it's definitely choice two. Partial calculation really shortens the solution.
On the exam: mark it and move on. This is probably the last question — go back over the section if you have time.

We need a base and the height to it. Take OB as the base.
OB is a radius — 6 root 2.
The height: the triangle is obtuse, so it's an outside height — the distance from A to the y-axis.

lines.draw: Draw the horizontal distance from A to the y-axis and write 6

lines.say: And that distance is exactly how far we moved right in x — 6.
6 root 2 times 6, over 2 — 18 root 2.
36 pi minus 18 root 2 — choice two.
And if you found the triangle first? Then it's something with pi, minus 18 root 2 — partial calculation works from that side too. Only choice two.

lines.say: Now by estimating sizes. Honestly — here it's a bit weak. Better to calculate with partial calculation.
But some students get here with no time, or can't even find the radius. So we work with what we can.
First — check the answers. Are they far enough apart to rule some out?
Choice one: 6 root 2 is a bit under 9. 3 pi is a bit over 9. So it's negative! An area can't be negative — out, with no calculating.
In the Hebrew version we compared the top dark piece with a square. Here that's not reliable: the top piece is an eighth of the circle — 9 pi, about 28 — smaller than the 6-by-6 square.
So use two quick bounds instead.
The semicircle: 36 pi is more than 36 times 3 — 108.
The triangle: base 6 root 2 is less than 9, height 6 — less than 27. So the shaded area is more than 81.
18 pi minus 6 is about 50. 36 root 2 minus 6 pi is about 32. Both too small. Choice two.
Two approaches: full math with the partial-calculation shortcut, or estimating. The recommended one: math with partial calculation.

lines.say: ABCDEF is a regular hexagon. CD lies on the x-axis, and B is on the y-axis. What's the dark area?
We need a way to express the dark area. There are many options —
— the simplest: the dark area equals, in area, 5 equilateral triangles with the hexagon's side.
Remember how we split a regular hexagon? Into 3 rhombi.

lines.draw: Draw the three rhombi inside the hexagon

lines.say: Draw a rhombus's long diagonal — two triangles of equal area. Draw the short diagonals — equal-area triangles too, all equilateral.
So the white corner triangle AFE has the same area as one equilateral triangle — even though it's not equilateral itself.
It's our 30-30-120 triangle — its area is a squared root 3 over 4, exactly like the equilateral.
So the dark area is 5 times a squared root 3 over 4 — a is the hexagon's side.

lines.say: The lines are parallel. What does that tell us?
Their slope is equal. And if the slope is equal — the triangles are similar.
So this is really a similarity question on the coordinate system.
The ratio of the legs: 4 is two fifths of 10. So here too, the y-leg is two fifths of 5 — 2.
Or simply: the x-leg was halved, 10 to 5 — so the y-leg is halved too, 4 to 2.
Almost done. From floor 7 I go down 2 floors — floor 5.
B is zero, 5. Choice three. A similarity question on the axes.
If you prefer an equation: y equals two fifths x plus b; plug in A: 7 equals 2 plus b, so b is 5. Same answer.

beats.title: Go through the choices

lines.say: Which of the following cannot be the number of points a straight line shares with the y-axis?
To solve it — sketch a coordinate system.
Go through the answers. An answer that's impossible — mark it. Any answer that's possible — cross it out.

lines.draw: Sketch a slanted line crossing the y-axis once

lines.say: One point: a standard slanted line. One shared point with the y-axis. Possible —
— out.

lines.draw: Sketch a vertical line to the right of the y-axis

lines.say: Zero points: a line parallel to the y-axis. A line is endless — if its distance from the axis is always the same, they never meet.
Parallel lines never meet. Zero is possible — out.
Infinitely many: only in one situation — when the line lies right on top of the y-axis. Then every point is shared.
Possible — out.
And 3 is impossible. Choice two. To cross an axis more than once you need a parabola, or some other curve — not a straight line.

beats.title: Three situations

items.t: 1. Parallel to one axis $\rightarrow$ perpendicular to the other — they never meet
2. Doesn't cross an axis $\rightarrow$ parallel to it · a slanted line crosses both
3. Lying on an axis $\rightarrow$ infinitely many shared points

lines.say: To solve these questions, understand three situations.

lines.label: Parallel to one axis → perpendicular to the other appears

lines.say: One: parallel–perpendicular. A line parallel to one axis is necessarily perpendicular to the other.

lines.label: Doesn't cross an axis → parallel to it appears

lines.say: Two: crossing or not. If a line doesn't cross the y-axis — it must be parallel to it, and perpendicular to the x-axis.
But a line that does cross an axis doesn't have to be perpendicular to it — it can be slanted, and then it crosses both axes.

lines.label: Lying on an axis → infinitely many points appears

lines.say: Three: coinciding lines. A line can lie right on an axis — infinitely many shared points.

lines.say: Line a doesn't meet the y-axis. Line b doesn't meet the x-axis. Which must be true?
Go through the claims. Start with choice one.
If 4, minus 3 is on a — then 4, 7 is on a too?
a has no shared point with the y-axis. What do we learn? It must be parallel to it.
So draw a vertical line through 4, minus 3.

lines.label: a: every point with x = 4 appears

lines.say: Every point on it has x equal to 4: 4, 7 — 4, zero — 4, a hundred. So 4, 7 is on a.
That's the right answer. On the exam — mark it and move on.

Choice two: minus 4, minus 3? The x changed — it's off the vertical line x equals 4. Wrong.
Now b. It has no shared point with the x-axis — it can't be slanted. It must be parallel to the x-axis.

Keeping a coordinate isn't enough — keep the right one: x on a vertical line, y on a horizontal line.

lines.say: A line passes through minus 2, 4. It's perpendicular to neither axis. Which point cannot be on it?
To understand it — sketch a coordinate system.
The line passes through minus 2, 4. It's not perpendicular to the x-axis — so a vertical line is impossible.
And it's not perpendicular to the y-axis — so a horizontal line is impossible too.
Go through the answers. Which point can't be on the line?
Minus 2, 9. Same x — notice! If we join the points, the line is perpendicular to the x-axis. Not allowed.
So this point is impossible — choice one. On the exam: mark and move on.
In the lesson, the others: 3, 7 — join it, a slanted line, neither vertical nor horizontal. Possible. Same for 1, minus 4 and 4, minus 2.

lines.say: Any point with y equal to 4 — the line would be perpendicular to the y-axis. Any point with x equal to minus 2 — perpendicular to the x-axis.
Only minus 2, 9 has that pattern. Choice one.

items.t: Through the origin: $x:y$ is the same for every point

lines.say: Now the more complicated part of the lesson — a line that passes through the origin.
It's not really complicated — it can even be an easy question. But very often the questions here are not simple.

lines.label: A line through the origin with several points appears
Through the origin: x : y is the same for every point

lines.say: When a line passes through the origin, the ratio between the x and the y of all its points is always constant.

lines.draw: Draw the stairs from O: 2 across, 3 up, three times

lines.say: Go right 2 and up 3 — I reach a point on the line. Again right 2, up 3 — another. The same stairs we saw before.
(2, 3), (4, 6), (6, 9) — the ratio between x and y stays the same every time.

lines.say: Line AB passes through the origin. A is (−2a, −2b) — so a and b are positive, because A is in the negative region.
Which of these cannot be the coordinates of point B?
B is somewhere on this line — we don't know exactly where. And notice, everything here is in letters, in unknowns.
Some of you will see right away: the ratio is constant. But let's build a helper drawing.

lines.draw: Close a right triangle under A; write 2a and 2b on its legs

lines.say: I close a triangle for A. Its legs: 2a and 2b — from the values of A.

lines.draw: Close a right triangle under B; write x and y on its legs

lines.say: And a triangle for B. x and y — I don't know them. That's what they're asking.
Two similar triangles: a 90 degree angle, and because the lines are parallel, these angles are equal.
Similar — so x over y equals 2a over 2b. That's a over b.
So I plug each answer in for x and y and check: is it equal to a over b? If not — that's the one we're looking for.

lines.say: Choice 1: a cubed over b cubed. Is it equal to a over b?
Not only don't I know — I can say it's NOT equal. It's given that a is not equal to b.
If a ≠ b, once I raise them to a power I can't cancel down to a over b.
So that's the answer — the one that can't be the coordinates of B. Choice one.

3a over 3b: cancel the 3 — a over b. Equal. Cross it out.
1 over b divided by 1 over a — a fraction divided by a fraction: multiply by the reciprocal. a over b. Also possible.
a over 2, b over 2 — the halves cancel. a over b. Cross it out.

lines.say: So what's important to understand? A line through the origin — its points make similar triangles, one inside the other.
So the ratio of x to y must be the same at every point. Build that equation, and check the choices.

lines.label: a → a³: × a² · b → b³: × b²

lines.say: The course puts it one more way: cubing multiplies a by a squared, and b by b squared — two different multipliers. Off the line.
With numbers: a = 2, b = 3. The line is 2 to 3. The cubes — 8 to 27. Not the same.
Not an easy question. Whoever needs to — rewind and watch it again, slowly.
An edge question, like we sometimes get at the end of the section. And we're strong students — we can handle it.

beats.title: Coordinates in Questions

lines.say: We're almost there — the very end of geometry. The coordinate system.
Last lesson we learned the basics. Now — psychometric questions at a higher level.

beats.title: Two kinds of questions

items.t: Kind 1: ordinary geometry — the data sit on the axes
Kind 2: understanding lines — parallel, crossing, fixed coordinates

lines.say: In general, coordinate questions come in two main kinds.

lines.label: Kind 1: ordinary geometry on the axes appears

lines.say: Kind one: standard geometry questions, like everything we learned so far — lines, triangles, all the way to 3D and similarity.
The data just appear on the coordinate system. Our job: pull the data out of it.
Kind two: understanding the coordinate system itself. Lines, parallel lines, lines that cross.
We'll practise both. Let's start.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Two kinds of questions" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Lines and Angles

lines.say: Welcome to geometry.
In the quantitative section, about 5 questions out of 20 are geometry — a quarter of the section.
And the questions are mostly built on the rules of geometry. Master the rules, and you'll solve most of them.
There are also insight questions — the ones that need a spark — but they're rarer.
Let's start with definitions.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Lines and segments

v.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="79.3 137.0 481.4 72.2" role="img" aria-label="A line through A and B"><title>A line through A and B</title><line x1="105.294" y1="180.000" x2="534.706" y2="180.000" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><circle cx="234.118" cy="180.000" r="3.2" fill="#203344"/><circle cx="405.882" cy="180.000" r="3.2" fill="#203344"/><text x="234.118" y="163.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">A</text><text x="405.882" y="163.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">B</text></svg>

lines.label: A line through two points A and B appears

lines.say: A line is a straight line that passes through two points.
Here are two points — and we've drawn a line through them.
There's a rule, an axiom: through two points passes exactly one straight line.
Any other line you draw through the two points can't be straight — it has to be curved, or broken.
Pretty obvious.

lines.draw: Draw an arrowhead at each end of the line

lines.say: A line is infinite. It keeps going forever, at both ends.

lines.draw: Thicken the part between A and B

lines.say: When we want to cut a line off, we call it a segment.
A segment is a straight line bounded between two points. It doesn't continue.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Lines and segments" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Angles at a point

v.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="137.6 25.9 364.9 308.3" role="img" aria-label="Angles at a point"><title>Angles at a point</title><line x1="163.571" y1="180.000" x2="476.429" y2="180.000" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="230.276" y1="308.139" x2="409.724" y2="51.861" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/></svg>

lines.say: Intersecting lines: two straight lines that have one point of intersection.
They cross each other at some point.

lines.draw: Draw a full circle around the point and write 360°

lines.say: Around that point, a kind of circle of angles forms — four angles.
And a whole circle of angles is 360 degrees. That's its size.
A full circle: 360 degrees.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Angles at a point" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Right angle

lines.label: Two perpendicular lines with a right-angle mark appear

lines.say: A right angle is an angle of exactly 90 degrees.
A right angle is made by two lines that are perpendicular to each other.

lines.draw: Point to the little square mark

lines.say: We mark 90 degrees like this — with a little square.
On the psychometric exam, in almost every case, there's also a dot in the middle of the square.

lines.draw: Write 90° in each of the four angles

lines.say: Notice: 90 is exactly a quarter of 360. A full circle is 360 — here we have a quarter, a quarter, a quarter, a quarter. 90, 90, 90, 90.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Right angle" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Acute/obtuse/straight

lines.label: Two crossing lines appear, with the two angles marked

lines.say: An acute angle is an angle smaller than 90 degrees.
Imagine a line here making 90 degrees — this angle is smaller, so it's called acute.
An obtuse angle is an angle bigger than 90 degrees.
By the way — if there's an acute angle here, you can already see an obtuse angle right next to it. And the other way around.
A straight angle is equal to 180 degrees. It's really just a straight line.

lines.draw: On the straight line, mark a vertex and draw a half-circle arc over the whole line

lines.say: Here's a straight line — put a vertex on it — and this whole angle is 180.
Because a full circle is 360, and this is half of it. Half of 360 is 180 — on this side, and on the other side too.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Acute/obtuse/straight" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Adjacent angles

v.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="137.6 12.2 364.9 193.8" role="img" aria-label="Angles at a point"><title>Angles at a point</title><line x1="320.000" y1="180.000" x2="476.429" y2="180.000" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="320.000" y1="180.000" x2="386.110" y2="38.228" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="320.000" y1="180.000" x2="163.571" y2="180.000" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><path d="M 351.286 180.000 A 31.286 31.286 0 0 0 333.222 151.646" fill="none" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2"/><text x="364.856" y="151.423" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#087f83" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18">65°</text><path d="M 333.222 151.646 A 31.286 31.286 0 0 0 288.714 180.000" fill="none" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2"/><text x="291.423" y="135.144" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#087f83" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18">x</text></svg>

lines.label: Two adjacent angles on a straight line appear: 65° and x

lines.say: Adjacent angles: two neighbouring angles formed where two lines cross — and together they add up to 180.
Look at this straight line. The angle on it is 180 — a straight angle sits on one straight line.
So here we have an obtuse angle, here an acute angle — and together they complete the straight line. So they add up to 180.
Here the acute one is 65, so x is 180 minus 65: 115.
Two adjacent angles: one is acute, one is obtuse, and together they're 180.
There's one very special case: they're not obtuse and acute — they're both right angles. And then too, 90 plus 90 is 180.

beats.title: Vertical angles

v.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="137.6 53.5 364.9 253.1" role="img" aria-label="Angles at a point"><title>Angles at a point</title><line x1="163.571" y1="180.000" x2="476.429" y2="180.000" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="200.169" y1="280.550" x2="439.831" y2="79.450" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><path d="M 351.286 180.000 A 31.286 31.286 0 0 0 343.966 159.890" fill="none" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2"/><text x="369.978" y="161.809" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#087f83" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18">40°</text><path d="M 343.966 159.890 A 31.286 31.286 0 0 0 288.714 180.000" fill="none" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 288.714 180.000 A 31.286 31.286 0 0 0 296.034 200.110" fill="none" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

lines.label: Two crossing lines appear, with one angle marked 40°

lines.say: Vertical angles: two angles facing each other vertex to vertex, where two lines cross.
Vertical angles are equal to each other.
Why are they equal? Let's think. This one is 40, and this is a straight line.

lines.draw: In the large angle next to the 40°, write 140°

lines.say: So the angle next to it has to be 140 — it completes it to 180.
And that 140 also completes the angle on its other side to 180 — because now we're looking at this straight line.

lines.draw: In the small angle opposite the 40°, write 40°

lines.say: If the 140 completes both of them to 180, those two angles must be equal. 40 and 40.

lines.draw: In the large angle opposite the 140°, write 140°

lines.say: And the angle facing the 140 — vertical to it — is also 140.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Vertical angles" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Angle bisector

v.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="294.0 5.2 208.4 200.8" role="img" aria-label="Angles at a point"><title>Angles at a point</title><line x1="320.000" y1="180.000" x2="476.429" y2="180.000" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="320.000" y1="180.000" x2="446.553" y2="88.054" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="320.000" y1="180.000" x2="368.339" y2="31.228" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><path d="M 351.286 180.000 A 31.286 31.286 0 0 0 345.311 161.611" fill="none" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2"/><text x="370.583" y="163.565" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#087f83" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18">α</text><path d="M 345.311 161.611 A 31.286 31.286 0 0 0 329.668 150.246" fill="none" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2"/><text x="351.262" y="136.972" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#087f83" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18">α</text></svg>

lines.label: An angle split into two equal parts, α and α, appears

lines.say: An angle bisector is a line that leaves the vertex of an angle and splits it into two equal angles.
It passes exactly through the middle — so we call both halves alpha and alpha.
So if the whole angle is 72 degrees, each half is 36.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Angle bisector" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Naming angles

v.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="184.1 50.1 268.8 211.8" role="img" aria-label="Angle BAC has vertex A"><title>Angle BAC has vertex A</title><line x1="234.118" y1="222.941" x2="405.882" y2="222.941" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="234.118" y1="222.941" x2="320.000" y2="94.118" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><path d="M 259.882 222.941 A 25.765 25.765 0 0 0 248.409 201.504" fill="none" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2"/><text x="272.735" y="202.274" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#087f83" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18">α</text><text x="216.118" y="235.941" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">A</text><text x="420.882" y="222.941" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">B</text><text x="320.000" y="76.118" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">C</text></svg>

lines.say: This is a good opportunity to talk a little about angles.
I marked this angle with alpha. That's a Greek letter — it's common to mark angles with Greek letters.
Alpha, beta, gamma, delta. Students sometimes mix up the names — it doesn't really matter.
We can use other letters too, but on the psychometric these are usually the ones you'll meet.
This arc marks the angle. There's another way to mark an angle:
Angle BAC. The sign itself is the two rays — the two lines.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow from B to A to C on the figure

lines.say: What does BAC mean? Start at B, move to A, continue to C. The angle made from B, through A, to C — and A is the vertex.
So we can mark an angle with a Greek letter, with the angle sign, or simply give it a number in degrees — 30 degrees is also a way.

beats.title: Parallel lines

v.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="122.2 89.6 395.5 185.1" role="img" aria-label="Constant perpendicular separation of parallel lines"><title>Constant perpendicular separation of parallel lines</title><line x1="148.235" y1="128.471" x2="491.765" y2="128.471" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="148.235" y1="231.529" x2="491.765" y2="231.529" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="234.118" y1="231.529" x2="234.118" y2="128.471" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="405.882" y1="231.529" x2="405.882" y2="128.471" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="234.118" y1="219.506" x2="246.141" y2="219.506" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="1.7"/><line x1="246.141" y1="219.506" x2="246.141" y2="231.529" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="1.7"/><line x1="405.882" y1="219.506" x2="417.906" y2="219.506" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="1.7"/><line x1="417.906" y1="219.506" x2="417.906" y2="231.529" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="1.7"/><text x="320.000" y="115.588" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">a</text><text x="320.000" y="248.706" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">b</text></svg>

lines.label: Two parallel lines a and b appear, with two perpendicular connectors

lines.say: Parallel lines are lines whose distance from each other is constant.
There's some distance here — and a distance is always a line perpendicular to both of them.

lines.draw: Write '=' between the two perpendicular connectors

lines.say: So here the distance is constant, and here too — and as they keep going, along their whole length, that distance stays the same.
Which means they never meet. They never cross each other. They just keep going side by side at the same distance.

beats.title: Small and large angles

lines.label: Parallel lines a and b cut by a transversal appear

lines.say: Parallel lines and a transversal. When two parallel lines are cut by a line, we get small angles and large angles.

lines.draw: Number the eight angles 1 to 8 — even numbers in the small angles, odd numbers in the large ones

lines.say: Look: the even numbers — 2, 4, 6 and 8 — are small angles. The odd numbers — 1, 3, 5 and 7 — are large angles.
Here's what we know: all the small angles are equal to each other. 2 equals 4 — they're vertical angles.
But not only 2 and 4. 6 equals 8 too. All the small angles are equal.
And all the large angles are equal to each other. 1 and 3 are vertical, 5 and 7 are vertical — and 1 equals 5, and 3 equals 7. All four are equal.
One more thing we know: a small angle plus a large angle is 180.
Why? Here they're adjacent angles — and adjacent angles complete to 180.
And if we took this large angle with that small angle down there — also 180, because that small angle equals this one.

lines.draw: In red, mark all the small angles; in blue, mark all the large angles

lines.say: Really, at each crossing of the transversal with one of the lines, we get small angles and large angles.

lines.draw: Circle the whole group of angles at the top crossing and draw an arrow down to the bottom crossing

lines.say: Take this whole circle of angles — as if we cut it out and moved it down. It's exactly the same angles.
So all the red ones are equal, and all the blue ones are equal.

beats.title: Look for the Z

v.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="61.7 32.3 498.4 295.3" role="img" aria-label="Two parallel lines cut by a transversal"><title>Two parallel lines cut by a transversal</title><line x1="105.867" y1="121.600" x2="534.133" y2="121.600" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="105.867" y1="238.400" x2="534.133" y2="238.400" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="234.808" y1="301.667" x2="405.192" y2="58.333" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><text x="93.700" y="121.600" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">a</text><text x="93.700" y="238.400" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">b</text><path d="M 392.525 121.600 A 31.633 31.633 0 0 0 379.036 95.687" fill="none" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2"/><text x="407.082" y="97.555" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#087f83" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18">α</text><path d="M 247.475 238.400 A 31.633 31.633 0 0 0 260.964 264.313" fill="none" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2"/><text x="232.918" y="262.445" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#087f83" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18">α</text><line x1="174.000" y1="121.600" x2="360.892" y2="121.600" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="5"/><line x1="360.892" y1="121.600" x2="279.108" y2="238.400" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="5"/><line x1="279.108" y1="238.400" x2="466.000" y2="238.400" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="5"/></svg>

lines.label: Parallel lines with a Z shape and its two equal angles appear

lines.say: In psychometric questions, whenever you meet two parallel lines — always look for this Z.
The Z will help you know which angles are equal.

lines.draw: Circle the two angles inside the corners of the Z

lines.say: The Z holds two angles inside it. The angle here and the angle here — the two angles in the corners of the Z — are equal.
In school these have names: alternate, corresponding, co-interior and so on. We don't really need them.
What interests us is small and large. But the Z shows you right away what equals what.
Once I know this one equals that one, it's easy to continue from it to the rest of the angles here — and from the bottom angle to the rest of the angles below.
So every time you see parallel lines: mark the Z, find the two equal angles trapped inside it, and carry on from there — which angle equals which, which angle completes which to 180.

Parallel lines: all small angles equal · all large angles equal · small $+$ large $=180°$
Parallel lines? Look for the Z.

Based on the information in the figure — what is the value of x?
Look at the two parallel lines and the line cutting them. Ignore the extra line for now.
When two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, the small angles are equal.

lines.say: We're given two pairs of parallel lines: line a is parallel to b, and c is parallel to d.
Based on this information and the information in the figure — what is the value of x?
There are several ways to solve it: with quadrilateral rules — if you noticed a parallelogram here — with triangle rules, or with the rules of lines.
We haven't learned quadrilaterals and triangles yet, so we'll solve it with line rules only. If you know them and solved it differently — completely fine.
How do we find x? If we find the angles next to it, we can get it by completing to 180.
Start with the first given: line a is parallel to b, and line c cuts both of them.

lines.draw: Highlight lines a, b and c

lines.say: To see it simply, we'll ignore the rest of the figure.
Remember: a line cutting two parallel lines makes 8 angles. 4 acute angles — all equal. 4 obtuse angles — all equal. And an acute plus an obtuse is 180.

lines.draw: At the lower crossing of line c, write 83° in the acute angle next to x

lines.say: The angle we want here is also 83 — all the acute ones are equal.
Back to the question. Another given: lines c and d are parallel, and there's a line cutting them.

lines.draw: Highlight lines c, d and the diagonal

lines.say: Again, ignore the rest. 8 angles, 4 acute ones — all equal. So this angle is 54.

lines.draw: At the lower vertex, write 54° in the other acute angle next to x

lines.say: Back to the question — and now we can build an equation. The angles together make a straight angle: 180.
83 plus 54: add the tens — 80 plus 50 is 130. 3 and 4 is 7. 137.
137 plus something is 180. 180 minus 137 — 43.
Choice two.

lines.say: In the accompanying figure, four lines meet at one point. Based on the figure — which expression equals theta?
What's hard about this question? All the information is given with unknowns — not with numbers.
And that's the main way psychometric geometry questions get harder: working with unknowns instead of numbers.
We'll solve it three ways: the full mathematical way, the psychometric way — plugging in numbers instead of the unknowns — and a flash of insight, for those who see it.
Full math first. Where do we start? We need theta, and there are lots of unknowns.
Our base has to be some anchor: either a full angle — 360 degrees — or a straight angle — 180.

lines.draw: In the angle next to p, write 180° − p

lines.say: Start with p, the first given. If this angle is p, the angle next to it is 180 minus p.

lines.draw: In the angle next to q, write 180° − q

lines.say: Move on to q. The angle next to it is 180 minus q.

lines.draw: In the angle next to r, write 180° − r

lines.say: Same for r: 180 minus r.
Now we have to notice that these four angles together make a straight angle — so their sum is 180.
Once we see that, we've almost finished the question.

lines.label: The equation appears: (180° − p) + (180° − q) + (180° − r) + θ = 180°

lines.say: It's important to be careful with the parentheses. A plus in front doesn't affect the parentheses — but if there were a minus here, it would affect both terms inside.
In this case we can simply drop the parentheses, because it's all addition.

lines.draw: Cross out one 180° on each side of the equation

lines.say: 180 and 180 cancel.
We want theta, so we keep it on the left. Move minus p across as plus — and minus q, and minus r. So on the right we have p plus q plus r.
The two 180s left make 360 together — move it across: minus 360.
So theta equals p plus q plus r minus 360.
Choice three.
Once it was clear what to do, the solution was simple. The question is how you spot it in advance — and on the last question of the section, that's not simple.

lines.say: Method two: plugging in numbers.
There's a way to turn these questions into simpler ones. They made the question harder by putting unknowns instead of numbers.
So we'll put things back the way they were: numbers instead of unknowns. That turns the question into an easy one.
If there were a number instead of p — which number? Whatever's comfortable. But it looks obtuse, so plug in an obtuse angle. And don't make it hard for yourself — use round angles.
It looks like about 150 degrees. So I chose p = 150. 160 or 140 would be completely fine too.

lines.draw: Write 150° by p, and 30° in the angle next to it

lines.say: If p is 150, the angle next to it is 30. Numbers roll easily — with numbers I complete automatically. With unknowns it's a bit less natural.
Now q. We could choose something else — but we get to pick the case that's easiest for us. So 150 again.
Why? Afterwards we'll plug these values into the answers. It's much easier to use the same angle everywhere than to remember: p was 150, q was something else… That could confuse us.

lines.draw: Write 150° by q and by r, and 30° next to each

lines.say: So q is 150 — its neighbour is 30. And r is 150 — its neighbour is 30.
30, 30 and 30 make 90. So theta, in this case, is 90 degrees.
What now? To the answers. Plug in 150 for p, q and r — and look for 90, in the case we chose.
Any answer that fits, we can't eliminate. We're hoping to eliminate three answers.

lines.draw: Next to choice 1 write 150 and cross it out

lines.say: Choice one: 150 minus 150 is 0, plus 150 — 150. Eliminated. We need 90.

lines.draw: Next to choice 2 write 270 and cross it out

lines.say: Choice two: three times 150 is 450, minus 180. Some students already see it's too big — no need to calculate. If you do: 450 minus 200 is 250, plus 20 — 270. Eliminated.
Choice three: 450 minus 360 — exactly 90. But we can't mark it yet. That's the disadvantage of plugging in: we have to eliminate three answers.

lines.draw: Next to choice 4 write −150 and cross it out

lines.say: Choice four: 150 minus 150 is 0, minus 150 — negative. Eliminated.
Three answers eliminated — mark choice three.

lines.say: Now the third solution: a flash of insight.
Some students — usually very strong students — look at the question and understand in advance that the answer is choice three. How?

lines.draw: Trace the arcs of p, q and r around the point, and shade θ

lines.say: They see that p plus q plus r is 360 degrees — plus something more: theta. Theta is counted twice here.
So if I add p, q and r and subtract 360 from that sum — I'm left with theta.
That's a bit hard for most of us to see, so let's see it as an equation.
On one side: p plus q plus r. On the other side — what does it equal? 360 gets us to here, and there's another piece: theta.
To isolate theta, move the 360 across: theta equals p plus q plus r minus 360. Choice three.
So we've seen three ways. Which one do we choose?
The shortest way is the insight. But the vast majority of students don't see it on the exam, in such a short time.
It's the last question — you're under pressure near the end of the section. If you saw it — wonderful, that's the shortest way. There's almost no work here.
For most students that leaves two options: mathematical work, or psychometric work with plugging in.
If you're very strong in geometry and algebra, the mathematical work is completely fine.
For most students, it's much, much simpler to solve this question by plugging in numbers.
It turns the question from a very high level into a low one. The completions are almost immediate — and the answer is certain.

fig.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="105.5 108.9 412.3 142.2" role="img" aria-label="Parallel lines and a bent transversal"><title>Parallel lines and a bent transversal</title><line x1="148.235" y1="134.912" x2="491.765" y2="134.912" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="148.235" y1="225.088" x2="491.765" y2="225.088" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="320.000" y1="134.912" x2="358.850" y2="165.265" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="320.000" y1="225.088" x2="358.850" y2="165.265" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><text x="137.500" y="134.912" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">a</text><text x="137.500" y="225.088" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">b</text><path d="M 343.687 153.418 A 30.059 30.059 0 0 0 350.059 134.912" fill="none" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2"/><text x="365.474" y="150.570" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#087f83" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18">38°</text><path d="M 350.059 225.088 A 30.059 30.059 0 0 0 336.371 199.879" fill="none" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2"/><text x="362.266" y="202.140" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#087f83" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18">57°</text><path d="M 341.931 152.046 A 21.471 21.471 0 0 0 347.156 183.271" fill="none" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2"/><text x="319.886" y="171.785" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#087f83" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18">x</text></svg>

lines.say: Given: two parallel lines — a is parallel to b.
Based on the information in the figure — what is the value of x?
It seems like a fairly simple question. The figure is simple — two parallel lines. And the angles are given as numbers, not unknowns.
So what makes it a hard question?
The difficulty is the broken line connecting the two lines.
If there were a straight line cutting both lines, we'd know how to deal with it. But here there's a broken line —
— and we're looking for the angle between its two parts: the upper part and the lower part. It's not really clear where to start.
To solve this question, we need an auxiliary construction.
What's an auxiliary construction? Something we add to the figure that helps us solve the question — that makes it possible to solve. It's a thinking addition.
Several auxiliary constructions here would solve it with triangle rules, which we haven't learned yet.
For example: if we extended this line so it cuts line b too, not only line a — we'd get two acute angles, and could solve it with the triangle rules: an exterior angle.
Another option: the same thing with the lower line — extend it upwards. Here too we get a triangle.
Another way: draw a line perpendicular to both parallel lines. We'd get two triangles, find each angle from the angle sum in a triangle — and x completes the sum to 180.
If you solved it one of those ways — completely fine.
We want to solve it with line rules only. So we need a different construction.

lines.draw: Draw a line through the bend, parallel to a and b

lines.say: Here's the construction: a line through the bend, parallel to line a and to line b.
If these lines are parallel, the acute angles here are equal.

lines.draw: Write 38° in the upper part of x

lines.say: So this angle equals 38.

lines.draw: Write 57° in the lower part of x

lines.say: And if these lines are parallel, the acute angle 57 equals the angle here. So this angle is also 57.
So x equals 38 plus 57: 95 degrees.
Choice four.
Once you know how to add the auxiliary construction, this question becomes a simpler one.
The difficulty here is a thinking difficulty: which construction to add — and realising that you need to add one at all.
That's it for lines and angles.

lines.say: Way one: plug in numbers.
We could plug a number into the octagon's side — but then to get AE we'd divide by root 2. We'd rather multiply.
So plug in AE. What's simpler than 1?

lines.draw: Write 1 on AE and on CE

lines.say: AE is 1, so CE is 1 — a silver triangle. AC, the hypotenuse, is root 2 times bigger: root 2.

lines.draw: Write √2 on the square's side and 1 on the bottom corner leg

lines.say: AC is an octagon side — so all sides are root 2, and so is the square's side. And the corner triangle at the bottom: leg 1.
Lina: BE is from E down to B — root 2 plus 1. Twice AE is 2.
1 plus 1.4 against 2 — BE is bigger. Lina is right.
Eliminate every answer that says otherwise: 'only Noam' and 'neither'.
Noam: triangle ACE — 1 plus 1 plus root 2: 2 plus root 2. CD: 1, plus root 2, plus 1 — also 2 plus root 2.
Equal — Noam is right too.
Both are correct. Choice four.

lines.say: Way two: estimate — and know the octagon.

lines.draw: Mark AE and the bottom corner leg of BE

lines.say: Lina compares 2AE with BE. One AE is the same as the bottom leg on BE — the silver-triangle legs are equal.
Cancel them. What's left? One AE — against the square's side.
And you can see which is bigger.
Some of you will say: we learned never to rely on the drawing!

lines.label: Regular polygon → the drawing is accurate appears

lines.say: True — but every rule has an exception. In regular polygon questions the drawing is accurate: it can't be drawn any other way.
Don't see it? Measure with your fingers — something is left over. And it's no guess: the square's side is a hypotenuse, AE is a leg.
Lina is right.
Noam: here we just need to know which piece cancels which.
CE is on both sides — cancel it. AE is the same as the leg on the left of CD. AC is an octagon side — the same as the middle of CD.
Everything cancels — Noam is right too. Choice four.

lines.say: A regular octagon cut by two vertical segments. The white rectangle is 8 plus 8 root 2. What is the shaded area?

Now we're almost done. What's the difference between white and grey?
The four triangles together equal the white square — they cancel.
The two grey rectangles equal the two white rectangles.

beats.title: The formula

lines.say: The sum of the interior angles of a polygon is 1,620. How many sides?
Two ways: the math way, and an understanding way through an anchor.
The formula: the angle sum is 180 times n minus 2 — n is the number of sides.
We could open the brackets — but we want the smallest numbers possible. Simplify first.
Both divide by 10.
Is 162 divisible by 18? Hard to see — but both are even. Divide by 2.
81 divides by 9 — times table. n minus 2 is 9, so n is 11.
Choice two. The standard way — through the formula.

beats.title: An anchor · +180 per side

lines.say: Another way — through an anchor.
Which angle sums do we know by heart? Triangle 180, quadrilateral 360 —
— and you should know: pentagon 540, hexagon 720, octagon 1,080.
1,620 we don't know. But the octagon is close — and 1,620 is bigger, so more than 8 sides.
Now the pattern: every extra side adds 180. Triangle 180, quadrilateral 360, pentagon 540 — always plus 180.
From the octagon, add 180: 1,260 — nine sides. Easy way: add 200, take away 20.
Again: 1,440 — ten sides. Again: 1,620 — eleven sides.
Eleven sides. Choice two.

lines.say: A sample question — hard.
Two ways: the math way — and the understanding way.

beats.title: The math way

lines.say: A is the angle sum of a 12-sided polygon, B of a 17-sided polygon. B minus A equals the angle sum of which polygon?
Express B with the formula: 180 times 17 minus 2 — 180 times 15.
A: 180 times 10.
We won't calculate each one and subtract. We take out a common factor — easier arithmetic.
180 times 15 minus 10 — 5 times 180: 900.
Which polygon has 900? 5 triangles' worth — plus 2: seven sides. A heptagon.
Choice three.

beats.title: The understanding way

lines.say: Now the understanding way.
What's the difference between B and A in sides? 17 minus 12 — 5 extra sides.
Every side adds 180. Five sides — 5 times 180: 900.
900 is 5 times 180 — a polygon with 5 plus 2 sides. A heptagon.
Choice three. Very simple — once you understand the plus 180.
That's it for polygons: the regular pentagon, hexagon and octagon — and general polygons.

lines.say: Polygons.
A polygon is a closed shape with 3 sides or more.
There really aren't many rules here — let's go through them.

lines.say: The sum of the angles in a polygon depends on the number of sides.
A triangle and a quadrilateral have different sums — and the more sides we add, the bigger the sum.
The formula: 180 times n minus 2. n is the number of sides.
Here n is 5. 5 minus 2 is 3. 3 times 180 — 540.
Let's check it on something we know — a quadrilateral.
4 minus 2 is 2. 2 times 180 is 360 — and the angles of a quadrilateral really do add up to 360.

lines.say: There's another way — if the formula gets you tangled, or it just doesn't come to you in the moment.
Split the polygon into triangles.

lines.label: The heptagon appears, cut into triangles from vertex A

lines.say: Every triangle has 180 inside it. So just add them up.
1, 2, 3, 4, 5 triangles.
5 times 180 — 900. That's the angle sum of the heptagon.
Remember — that's exactly what we did in the quadrilateral: one diagonal, two triangles, 180 plus 180, 360.
7 sides, 5 triangles. Always n minus 2 — that's where the formula comes from.

beats.title: +1 side = +180°

v.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="170.6 30.5 298.8 275.3" role="img" aria-label="Regular 5-sided polygon"><title>Regular 5-sided polygon</title><polygon points="320.000,72.647 217.901,146.826 256.900,266.850 383.100,266.850 422.099,146.826" fill="none" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><text x="320.000" y="56.544" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">A</text><text x="202.586" y="141.850" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">B</text><text x="247.434" y="279.878" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">C</text><text x="392.566" y="279.878" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">D</text><text x="437.414" y="141.850" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">E</text></svg>

lines.say: When you add one more side to a polygon — the angle sum grows by 180.

lines.draw: Draw a small triangle on side CD, then cross out CD

lines.say: Watch. I added 2 sides — but I erased the side that was here. So now I have 6 sides.
What really happened? I added one more triangle.
One more triangle — one more 180.
Pentagon 540. Hexagon 720. Heptagon 900. Octagon 1080. Every extra side — plus 180.

items.t: Regular $=$ all sides equal AND all angles equal

lines.say: A regular polygon is a polygon where ALL the sides and ALL the angles are equal.

lines.label: A regular hexagon and a folded hexagon appear

lines.say: For example, a regular hexagon: 6 sides — 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 — all the sides equal, and all the angles equal.
Why do we stress that the angles are equal too? Because of this.
I can take two sides and fold them inward — and I get a hexagon where all the sides are still equal.
These two sides are exactly those two sides. But it's no longer a regular hexagon.

lines.label: Regular = all sides equal AND all angles equal appears

lines.say: A regular polygon is symmetric — it looks the same from every direction.

beats.title: On a circle

v.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="170.6 30.5 298.8 282.9" role="img" aria-label="Regular 5-sided polygon"><title>Regular 5-sided polygon</title><polygon points="320.000,72.647 217.901,146.826 256.900,266.850 383.100,266.850 422.099,146.826" fill="none" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><text x="320.000" y="56.544" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">A</text><text x="202.586" y="141.850" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">B</text><text x="247.434" y="279.878" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">C</text><text x="392.566" y="279.878" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">D</text><text x="437.414" y="141.850" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">E</text><circle cx="320.000" cy="180.000" r="107.353" fill="none" stroke="#bb6821" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="212.6" y1="72.6" x2="427.4" y2="287.4" stroke="none"/></svg>

lines.say: Every regular polygon can be inscribed in a circle.

lines.label: A regular pentagon inside a circle appears

lines.say: We draw a circle around the regular polygon — and all its vertices sit on the circumference.
The point in the middle is the centre of the circle.
By the way, a circle can also be drawn inside every regular polygon — less interesting for us right now.

lines.label: Regular ⇒ fits in a circle appears

lines.say: Careful — it only works one way. If a polygon fits in a circle, that does NOT mean it's regular.

lines.label: Fits in a circle ⇏ regular appears

lines.say: I could move this vertex along the circle and stretch a side — still on the circle, not regular.
And the folded hexagon from before? It can't be inscribed in a circle — so it's definitely not regular.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "On a circle" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: One angle

lines.say: The size of one angle in a regular polygon.
The angle sum we already know how to find: 180 times n minus 2.
But I want just one angle.
The polygon is regular — all the angles are equal. So I just divide by the number of angles.
n sides — n angles. So: the angle sum, divided by n.
Pentagon: 540 divided by 5 — 108.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "One angle" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: The formula sheet

lines.say: Now let's open the brackets.
180n minus 360, over n.
Now split the fraction — the opposite of a common denominator.
180n over n — the n cancels. We get 180 minus 360 over n.
Why am I showing you this? Because this is the formula on the psychometric formula sheet. Know it when you see it.
Most students actually remember the first one — it's more intuitive: the angle sum divided by the number of angles.
It's exactly the same formula. Just simplified.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The formula sheet" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Three to know

lines.say: Here's a table of the three regular polygons that show up most on the exam.

lines.label: A table appears: pentagon, hexagon, octagon — angle sum, each angle, central angle

lines.say: Pentagon, hexagon, octagon. 5, 6 and 8 sides. These are angles worth remembering.
The central angle is the angle in the middle — at the centre of the circle, when we draw radii to the vertices.
In a hexagon, 6 radii give 6 angles — one opposite each side. 360 over 6 — 60.
360 over 8 — 45. 360 over 5 — 72. Just like arcs and sectors: a fifth, a sixth, an eighth of a circle.

lines.label: Tip: central angle 360°/n, then complete to 180° appears

lines.say: The angle itself is sometimes hard to remember. The hexagon — almost everyone remembers: 60 and 120.
Pentagon and octagon — less. So here's a tip. The central angle is easy: octagon, 360 over 8 is 45 — half of 90.
The polygon's angle simply completes it to 180. 45 plus what is 180? 135.
72 — to get to 180 I need another 108. And 60 plus 120.
Don't remember the angle? Fine. Find the central angle in seconds and complete it to 180.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Three to know" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

lines.say: In a regular polygon, the diagonals divide the polygon's angle into equal angles.

lines.label: A regular pentagon with the two diagonals from A appears

lines.say: From this vertex I drew two diagonals. In a pentagon, that's all I can draw — more sides, more diagonals.

lines.draw: Mark the three angles at A as equal

lines.say: The diagonals split the pentagon's angle into 3 angles — and they're equal.
Why? As we learned about 2 minutes ago — every regular polygon can be inscribed in a circle.
Look at this angle: its vertex is on the circle — it's an inscribed angle. And it rests on this arc.
The polygon is regular — so all the arcs are equal.

lines.label: Equal arcs → equal inscribed angles appears

lines.say: Inscribed angles on equal arcs are equal. So the diagonals cut the angle into equal angles.
Here: 108 divided by 3 — 36 each.

lines.say: The exception is the hexagon.

lines.label: A regular hexagon with its six radii appears

lines.say: A regular hexagon is made of 6 EQUILATERAL triangles.
Actually it's not really an exception — it's just more regular than the other regular ones.
It also splits into isosceles triangles — radius and radius.

lines.draw: Write 60° at the centre in one triangle

lines.say: But in the hexagon, the head angle is 360 over 6 — 60 degrees. So the triangle is equilateral.
Very important to know this split of the hexagon into equilateral triangles.
We'll use it for areas — and for angles — later on.
