beats.title: Recap

items.t: Angle sum: $180°(n-2)$ — or split into triangles
Diagonals from one vertex $\rightarrow$ equal angles (inscribed angles on equal arcs)
Radii $\rightarrow$ $n$ congruent isosceles triangles · hexagon: 6 equilateral

lines.say: That's polygons — there really aren't many rules. Let's review.

lines.label: Angle sum: 180°(n − 2) — or split into triangles appears

lines.say: Angle sum: remember 180 times n minus 2 — or just split into triangles. A pentagon: 1, 2, 3 triangles, 3 times 180.

lines.label: Diagonals from one vertex → equal angles (inscribed angles) appears

lines.say: The diagonals split the angle into equal angles — because they're inscribed angles in the circle.

lines.label: Radii → n congruent isosceles triangles · hexagon: 6 equilateral appears

lines.say: And every regular polygon splits into isosceles triangles — again because of the circle: they're radii.
The regular hexagon is the special case: equilateral triangles, not just isosceles.
That's polygons. Let's move on.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Polygon Areas

lines.say: Let's move on to the area of polygons.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: No formula

lines.say: The truth is — there's no formula for the area of a polygon.

lines.label: Triangle: side × height to that side ÷ 2 — the only one appears

lines.say: Except for one exception — the triangle. Side times the height to that side, over 2.
For other polygons we don't really have a formula.
Not even for a quadrilateral! Sure, we know the special ones — square, rectangle, parallelogram, trapezoid, kite.
But for just any quadrilateral — there's no formula.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "No formula" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Split into shapes

items.t: Split it into shapes you know
Draw a line $\rightarrow$ triangles, rectangles, squares, trapezoids
Or: a bigger shape minus the missing pieces

lines.say: So how do we find the area of a polygon?

lines.label: Split it into shapes you know appears

lines.say: We break it into pieces — shapes we DO know.
Once we know the area of each piece, we know the area of the whole polygon.

lines.label: A line → triangles, rectangles, squares, trapezoids appears

lines.say: A diagonal, a height — whatever gives you a base and a matching height.

lines.label: Or: a big shape minus the missing pieces appears

lines.say: And sometimes it's easier the other way: surround it with a big shape and subtract what's missing.
Let's see some examples.

lines.say: According to the data in the figure, what is the area of the pentagon?
I see a pentagon. It isn't regular — there are a few right angles here, but it isn't regular.
To find its area I need to split it into shapes I know and can find the area of.
So I draw a line here — connect these two vertices — and I get a right triangle.
The area of a right triangle is simply the product of the legs over 2. 12 times 5 over 2 — 30.
What's left here is a trapezoid. But I don't know its area —
— for a trapezoid I need both bases and the height. I have the top base, I have the height — no bottom base.
How do I find it? Let's start working with what we have.
Right triangle, 5 and 12 — a Pythagorean triple: 5, 12, 13. So AD is 13.

lines.say: A regular hexagon has side length 8. What is its area?
A hexagon — I don't know how to find its area. But I DO know I can split it into equilateral triangles.

lines.draw: Draw the three long diagonals through the centre

lines.say: I draw the diagonals — 6 equilateral triangles, each with side 8.
And an equilateral triangle — that I know how to do.
The formula: a, 2, 3, 4. a squared, times root 3, over 4.
My a is 8. 8 squared — 64. Over 4 — cancel: 16. 16 root 3.

16 root 3 is right there in the choices — but that's the area of ONE triangle.

draw the diagonals, split it into 6 equilateral triangles, find one — and multiply by 6.

lines.say: A regular octagon has side length 5. What is its area?
Every time they ask us for the area of an octagon, we always split it the same way.

lines.draw: Draw two horizontal and two vertical lines through the corners of the flat sides

lines.say: A rectangle cut off the top, a rectangle off the side — and we get these shapes.
A square in the middle. 4 triangles. And 4 rectangles.
The octagon is regular — so it's symmetric: all the triangles are equal, all the rectangles are equal.

lines.draw: Mark the right angle and the two equal legs in one corner triangle

lines.say: And each triangle has a 90 degree angle and two equal legs — a silver triangle, 45-45-90.
Its hypotenuse is a side of the octagon — 5. So we can find its legs.

lines.say: The square in the middle: side 5 — 25. That's clear.
The four triangles together — they're equal to the square.
If we took them and put them inside the square, they'd make exactly the square.
And that's true in EVERY regular octagon — always. Each triangle is exactly a quarter of the square.
So each one is 25 over 4.

The other side I don't know. But it's the leg of the corner triangle.
Hypotenuse 5, and it's a silver triangle — from the hypotenuse to the leg, divide by root 2.

lines.draw: Write 5√2/2 on the short side of one rectangle

lines.say: 5 over root 2 — 5 root 2 over 2.
So one rectangle is 5 times 5 root 2 over 2 — 25 root 2 over 2.
Four of them — 50 root 2.

Total: 50 plus 50 root 2.
Choice two.
Notice — there's a pattern here that's ALWAYS true in a regular octagon.
The area of a regular octagon is always 2a squared plus 2a squared root 2. a is the octagon's side.
So instead of remembering a formula: the square in the middle is just the side squared — 25.
Take it twice — 50. Then write the same number again, this time with root 2. 50 plus 50 root 2.
Side 3: the square is 9, twice — 18. 18 plus 18 root 2. Side 7: 49, twice — 98. 98 plus 98 root 2.

lines.say: ABCDE is a regular pentagon. What is angle ADB?
Why several ways? Because we can cut a polygon into shapes we know — triangles, quadrilaterals — and work with diagonals.
Way one: through triangle DCB.
Regular polygon — all sides equal. So DC equals CB. The triangle is isosceles.
What do we know about angle C? The angle sum of a pentagon is 540. Five equal angles —
— 540 divided by 5: every angle is 108. Know this by heart!
So C is 108. And so are A, B, E — and the whole angle at D.
Isosceles triangle, vertex angle 108. The two base angles together: 72. Each one — 36.
Same thing on the other side: triangle DEA — sides DE and EA equal, vertex 108.
So angle EDA is 36 too.
The whole angle at D is 108. Take away 36 and 36 — the middle piece is 36.
Choice one. A simple way — through the triangle.

items.t: In a regular pentagon, one diagonal cuts off a triangle and leaves an isosceles trapezoid.

lines.say: Way two: through the trapezoid.
ABDE is a trapezoid. If you didn't know — now you do:

lines.label: One diagonal → isosceles trapezoid + triangle appears

lines.say: In every regular pentagon, one diagonal gives an isosceles trapezoid and a triangle.
Angles A and E — the trapezoid's top base angles — are 108 each: pentagon angles.
The legs are equal, so it's isosceles — and the bottom base angles are equal too.
Top angle plus bottom angle on the same leg: 180. So the bottom angle EDB is 72.
EDB is 72. The small angle EDA we found: 36. What's left for the middle — 36.
Same answer. Choice one.

items.t: Inscribed angles on equal chords are equal.

lines.say: Way three: through the diagonals.
In a regular polygon the diagonals are symmetric. From D we can draw only two: to B and to A. D to C and D to E are sides.
The diagonals from one vertex split its angle into EQUAL pieces. Let's prove it once.

lines.draw: Draw the circle through all five vertices

lines.say: Every regular polygon can be inscribed in a circle.
The three small angles at D rest on the chords BC, AB and AE — sides of the pentagon. Equal chords.

lines.label: Equal chords → equal inscribed angles appears

lines.say: Inscribed angles on equal chords are equal. Call each one x.

lines.draw: Write x in each of the three pieces at D

lines.say: Three x together: the whole angle at D — 108.
108 divided by 3? Split it into something easy: 90 plus 18. 90 over 3 is 30, 18 over 3 is 6. 36.
The middle angle is x — 36. Choice one.
Three ways: the triangle, the trapezoid, the diagonals. These are the common ways for questions like this.

items.t: A radius to a vertex bisects the angle.

lines.say: A regular octagon inscribed in a circle with center O and radius r. Which statement is not true?
How do we solve these? Statement by statement.
Anything definitely true — eliminate. After three are out, the one left is the false one.
Angle AOB equals angle GOH. Both are central angles in a regular polygon — and central angles are equal.
There's even a formula: 360 over the number of sides. 360 over 8 — 45 each.
True — out.
Next: the circumference of the circle is greater than the perimeter of the octagon.
Less obvious. How do I get from the radius to the side? Don't. We only need to decide which is bigger.

lines.draw: Trace the arc AB and the side AB

lines.say: Look at side AB and arc AB. The side is the shortest path from A to B. The arc — a detour.
Arc BC is longer than side BC too. And so on, all the way around.
So the circumference is greater. True — out. By the way, that's true for every regular polygon in a circle.
Angle BCO equals angle OCD. Look at triangles OBC and OCD.
Radius, radius, radius — both isosceles, same legs. The bases BC and CD are equal sides of the octagon. The triangles are congruent — so the angles are equal.

lines.label: Radius to a vertex bisects the angle appears

lines.say: Another way to see it — a very important principle: a radius to a vertex always cuts the angle into two equal halves.
Three answers out. On the exam — mark choice two and move on. No time to prove it.

lines.say: We're in a lesson — so let's check: the perimeter of the octagon is 8r.
The eight radii against the eight sides. Work inside one central triangle: OCD.
The central angle: 45. The two base angles: 135 over 2 — 67 and a half each.

lines.draw: Write 45° at O and 67.5° at C and at D

lines.say: Remember: the larger angle faces the longer side.
The side of the octagon faces 45. The radius faces 67 and a half. So the radius is longer than the side.
One side shorter than one radius — eight sides shorter than eight radii.
So the perimeter is less than 8r, not equal. That's the false statement. Choice two.

lines.say: Let me use this question to teach a principle that comes back on the exam.
When does the sum of the radii equal the perimeter of the regular polygon? Pause and think.
The regular hexagon! It splits into six equilateral triangles — the radius equals the side. Six radii, six sides — equal.
The hexagon is the balance point.
Go up to seven sides: seven radii. The whole circumference is 2 pi r — about 6.28 radii — and the polygon is even less. So seven radii are bigger.
Eight sides — the same. That's our question.
Go down — it flips. In a pentagon the side faces 72 and the radius faces 54: the perimeter is bigger than five radii. True for the square too.
Some questions this understanding solves in seconds — no calculation at all. Choice two.

lines.say: ABCDEF is a regular hexagon. The perimeter of triangle ACE is 30. What is the perimeter of the hexagon?
First, the math solution. We need to see that ACE is equilateral. Let's prove it once — from now on, you know it.
The angle sum of a hexagon is 720 — each angle 720 over 6: 120. Know it by heart.
Triangle ABC: isosceles — hexagon sides. The base angles together: 60. Each one: 30.

lines.draw: Write 30° at A and at C inside triangle ABC

lines.say: Same in triangle AFE, and in triangle CDE: 30 and 30.
The angle of the triangle at A: 120, minus 30, minus 30 — 60. Same at C and at E.
All angles 60: equilateral. Proved.
Or by symmetry: all three corner triangles are congruent, so the three diagonals are equal.
The perimeter is 30, so each side of the triangle is 10.

lines.draw: Write 10 on AC, CE and EA

lines.say: Now from the triangle's side to the hexagon's side. Work in triangle ABC.

lines.draw: Drop the altitude from B to AC; mark H

lines.say: Isosceles — so the altitude is also a median and an angle bisector.

lines.draw: Write 60° and 60° at B, 5 and 5 on AH and HC

lines.say: It splits 120 into 60 and 60, and 10 into 5 and 5.
60, 90 — the angle at A is 30. That's not just a right triangle: it's a golden triangle.
5 faces 60 — it's the long leg. To the short leg: divide by root 3. To the hypotenuse: double. AB is 10 over root 3.
Six sides: 60 over root 3. Ignore the root, 60 over 3 is 20, attach the root — 20 root 3.
Choice four. That's the math solution.

lines.say: Now the psychometric solution — estimating the size.
The hexagon's perimeter MUST be bigger than the triangle's. Why?
In triangle AFE: AF plus FE is greater than AE — two sides are always greater than the third.
Same in the other two corner triangles. So the hexagon's perimeter is greater than 30.
Now to the answers — on the exam they usually help us.
17 root 3: 17 times 1.7 — about 29. Less than 30 — out.
It's close — if you want to be sure: root 3 is less than 1.75, and 17 times 1.75 is 29.75. Still under 30.
17 root 2: about 17 times 1.4 — around 24. Out.
20 root 2 — 20 times 1.4 isn't hard, but here's a trick: multiply by something easy, 1.5. 20 times 1.5 is 30.
Root 2 is less than 1.5, so 20 root 2 is less than 30. Out.
And 20 root 3: root 3 is more than 1.5, so it's more than 30. Possible.
Three out — choice four.

A regular hexagon connects to golden and equilateral triangles. So guess a root 3 answer.

items.t: Either diagonal cuts the rhombus in half $\Rightarrow$ equal areas

lines.say: In the standard partition, a triangle is equilateral — exactly one sixth of the hexagon.
The corner triangle is not equilateral — this side is clearly longer than that one. But it's ALSO one sixth.
Why? Look at a rhombus.

lines.draw: Draw both diagonals in one rhombus

lines.say: The short diagonal: two equilateral triangles. The long diagonal: two corner triangles.

lines.label: Either diagonal cuts the rhombus in half appears

lines.say: Either way, each triangle is half the rhombus. So they have the same area.

lines.say: And three corner triangles are three sixths — half the hexagon. The triangle in the middle is the other half.

lines.say: A regular hexagon with side 6. What is the sum of the areas of triangles ABC, CDE and EFA — the shaded area?
The full way: drop an altitude in a corner triangle and work with 30, 60, 90.

lines.draw: Drop the altitude from B to AC

lines.say: The legs are 6, the vertex is 120 — the altitude makes two golden triangles with hypotenuse 6.
Short leg: 3 — that's the height. Long leg: 3 root 3 — so the base is 6 root 3.
Base times height over 2: 9 root 3. Times three triangles.
27 root 3. It works — but it's long.
Choice one.

lines.say: Now the understanding way.
Each shaded triangle is one sixth of the hexagon — the same area as an equilateral triangle with side 6.
So: three times 6 squared root 3 over 4.
36 over 4 is 9. Three times 9 root 3 — 27 root 3.
Choice one. No altitudes, no golden triangles.

lines.say: Squares on four sides of a regular hexagon. Maya: the square perimeters are three times the hexagon's. Daniel: the square areas are bigger than the hexagon's.
Is Maya right? Is Daniel? Both, or neither?
The full solution — but instead of x, we plug in a number. The hexagon side is also the square side. Let it be 2.
One square: 4 sides of 2 — perimeter 8. Four squares: 32.
The hexagon: 6 sides of 2 — 12.
Three times 12 is 36 — not 32. Maya is wrong.
So we can already eliminate two answers: 'both correct' and 'only Maya'.
Why do this first? If we're out of time, at least we've doubled our chances.
Now Daniel. One square: 2 squared, 4. Four squares: 16.
The hexagon: six equilateral triangles with side 2. Six times 2 squared root 3 over 4 — 6 root 3.
16 or 6 root 3? No need to calculate — just estimate. 6 times 2 is 12, and root 3 is less than 2. So 6 root 3 is less than 12 — less than 16.
Daniel is right.
Only Daniel — choice three. The full, standard solution.

items.t: Same sides: the square always has the most area.

lines.say: Another solution — geometric understanding.
Maya first. No x, no numbers — just count sides.
Each square has 4 sides — four squares: 16. The hexagon has 6. All the same length.
16 isn't three times 6. Maya is wrong.
Daniel is the trickier part. We need to cut the hexagon in a smart way:

lines.draw: Split the hexagon into three rhombi

lines.say: Into three rhombi. Now: which is bigger — one rhombus or one square?
Both have all sides equal. What's different? In the square every angle is 90. In the rhombus this angle is sharper.
Squeeze the angle — the opening shrinks and shrinks, down to zero. Straighten it towards 90 — the area grows.
Same perimeter — but the square always has more area. It uses its sides in the best way.
So three squares are already bigger than the three rhombi — the hexagon. And we have four squares.
Daniel is right, Maya is wrong. Choice three.

lines.say: Area questions that a long calculation solves — and a psychometric trick solves in seconds.
And angle questions full of letters — where plugging in numbers saves us.
For almost every question we'll see two ways: the full math solution, and the psychometric one.
Let's start with a sample question.

beats.title: Advanced Quadrilaterals I

lines.say: A sample question — medium level.
Four statements. One of them is not necessarily true.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Statement by statement

lines.say: Which of the following statements is not necessarily true?
What do we do? Go statement by statement.
Anything that's definitely true — eliminate. And hope to be left with one statement.
Statement one: every rectangle is a parallelogram.
What does that mean? Every rectangle has ALL the properties of a parallelogram. Not every parallelogram is a rectangle — that's a different claim.
Let's check. A parallelogram: opposite sides equal and parallel — the rectangle has that. Opposite angles equal, adjacent angles add to 180 — the rectangle has that too.
So every rectangle really is a parallelogram. The reverse isn't true: not every parallelogram has four right angles.
It's necessarily true — and we're asked what's NOT necessarily true. Eliminate.
Statement two: every rhombus is a kite.
What's a kite? Two isosceles triangles on a shared base — the short diagonal.
A rhombus: all sides equal. But look — its diagonal also makes two isosceles triangles on a shared base.
So a rhombus has every property of a kite. Not every kite is a rhombus — by the way, a kite with all sides equal IS a rhombus.
True — eliminate.
Statement three: every square is a rectangle.
A square is an upgraded rectangle. Opposite sides equal? In a square ALL sides are equal — upgraded. All angles 90? Yes.
So every square is a rectangle. Not every rectangle is a square — its sides needn't all be equal.
Eliminate.
Three answers out — on the exam, mark choice four without checking.
We're in a lesson, so let's check it anyway: every parallelogram has perpendicular diagonals.
Perpendicular diagonals — that's a rhombus property. Not every parallelogram has it: take a rectangle 8 by 3 — its diagonals are not perpendicular.
So the statement is not necessarily true. Choice four.

Two ways: the math way — and the psychometric way.

beats.title: Method 1 · The math way

lines.say: ABCD is a rectangle, E is on AD. Triangle ABE has area 5, triangle ECD has area 13. What's the area of the shaded triangle EBC?
Method one: the full math solution.
ABE is a right triangle — every angle in a rectangle is 90. Its area: leg times leg over 2.
But neither leg is given. So we define letters.

lines.draw: Write h on AB and x on AE

lines.say: AB is the rectangle's height — call it h. AE is part of the length — call it x.
x times h over 2 is 5. Multiply by 2: xh is 10.
Triangle ECD: again a right triangle, same height h. ED is another piece of the length — not x. A new unknown: y.
yh over 2 is 13, so yh is 26.
Now the shaded triangle EBC. Its base, BC, is x plus y.

lines.draw: Draw the height from E down to BC

lines.say: Its height? Drop it from E — it's exactly the rectangle's height, h.
Open the brackets: xh plus yh over 2. That's 10 plus 26 over 2 — 36 over 2 — 18.
Choice two. A long, tiring solution, by the way.
But this base matters. We won't always see the psychometric shortcut — and then we have an anchor to work with.

items.t: A diagonal splits a rectangle into two triangles of equal area.

lines.say: Now the psychometric solution: symmetry. A very important tool in geometry — especially in quadrilaterals.

lines.draw: Draw the height from E to BC and call its foot F

lines.say: Drop a height from E to BC. We get a left rectangle — ABFE.
Triangle ABE is 5. Notice: the white triangle and the shaded triangle next to it are equal?

lines.label: A diagonal splits a rectangle into two equal areas appears

lines.say: A diagonal in a rectangle splits it into two equal-area triangles. Totally clear.

lines.draw: Write 5 in the left shaded part

lines.say: So this shaded piece is 5 too.

lines.draw: Write 13 in the right shaded part

lines.say: The right rectangle: ECD is 13. Again a rectangle, again a diagonal — the shaded piece is 13.
The shaded triangle equals the sum of the white ones: 5 plus 13 — 18.
Choice two. Much, much shorter — and now it's clear why this question is rated easy-plus.
This principle is very important. Next, we'll stretch it to more questions.

lines.draw: Draw the height from E and mark the two halves

lines.say: Here too the white areas always add up to the shaded one. Why? As we proved — drop a height, and each shaded piece equals its white twin.

items.t: Bases add up to the length $\cdot$ each height $=$ the rectangle height

lines.label: Several triangles on the base of a rectangle appear

lines.say: It's true here as well. It doesn't matter how many triangles are inside the rectangle —

lines.label: Bases add up to the length · height = rectangle's height appears

lines.say: — as long as their bases add up to the rectangle's length, and their heights equal the rectangle's height.
Always: the shaded areas add up to the white areas — and both are half of the rectangle.
One condition: the triangles can't overlap, and each top vertex must sit on the opposite side.

lines.say: By the way — this isn't only true in a rectangle.

lines.label: A parallelogram with a diagonal appears

lines.say: It's true in the whole parallelogram family: parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus, square.
A diagonal in a parallelogram splits it into two equal-area triangles. No doubt.

lines.label: A triangle on the full base of a parallelogram appears

lines.say: And this one? Harder to see with symmetry. But draw a line parallel to the sides —

lines.draw: Draw a line from E parallel to the slanted sides

lines.say: — and it splits into two parallelograms, left and right. In each one, white equals shaded.

lines.label: Same base · same height → ½ appears

lines.say: So in total the shaded part is half the parallelogram. Same base, same height — no matter how many triangles.

lines.say: A slightly more advanced one.

lines.label: A rectangle with its base split into four equal parts and one triangle appears

lines.say: The base is split into four equal pieces. The shaded triangle stands on one piece, with its top on the upper side.
What part of the rectangle is it?

lines.draw: Draw the diagonal and shade the lower half lightly

lines.say: A triangle on the whole base would be half the rectangle.
Ours stands on a quarter of the base, with the same height — so it's a quarter of that half.
A quarter of a half — an eighth of the whole rectangle.
The symmetry principle is very important — some psychometric questions fall apart with it. Let's see another one.

lines.say: A sample question — fairly hard.
Which extra data is enough? Symmetry does the work.

lines.say: ABCD is a rectangle. AE is twice ED, and BG is twice GC. Which additional data is enough to find the shaded area?
Not the clearest wording. What do they want?
Which piece of data — if they gave it to us — would be enough to calculate the shaded area.

lines.draw: Write 2 : 1 on AD and on BC

lines.say: Let's see what's in the figure: E splits AD, 2 to 1. G splits BC the same way, 2 to 1.
So E sits right above G — EG is parallel to AB. It cuts the rectangle into a left rectangle and a right one.
And F? Nobody told us where F is on AB. Remember that.

beats.title: The area of ECD

lines.say: Start with the data that works: the area of ECD.
They don't say how big — call it s. Could be 10, 100 — any number.
We already learned symmetry: EC is a diagonal of the right rectangle. So the shaded triangle EGC is s too.
The right rectangle is s plus s — 2s.
The left rectangle: same height, twice the base — 2 to 1. So it's twice as big: 4s.
And the shaded triangle FEG? Its base is EG — the full side — and its tip F is on the opposite side. Symmetry again: half the left rectangle — 2s.
Total shaded: s plus 2s — 3s. Given ECD, we can find the shaded area.
Some students see it even faster: the rectangle is 6s, the shaded part is half of it — and ECD is a sixth.
On the exam — we understood this, we mark choice four and run.

lines.say: We're in a lesson — so let's see why the other answers fail.
The area of AFE. Say it's s. Can we find the whole shaded area?
Try symmetry: AFE is half of a small upper rectangle. But the lower rectangle — how big is it?
We can't know — we don't know where F is.
If they told us F was the midpoint of AB, we'd know the upper and lower parts match. They didn't.
So even with a number — 5, 10, 20 — we can't find the shaded area. We don't know the ratio AF to FB.
Eliminate.
The area of FBG — exactly the same problem. We don't know the upper rectangle, because we don't know where F is.
Eliminate.
None of the data is sufficient? We already saw that one IS enough — ECD.
Choice four.

lines.say: A sample question — medium level.
Two approaches again: the full math, and the ratio principle.

beats.title: Method 1 · The math way

fig.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="79.3 17.4 481.3 325.1" role="img" aria-label="Area ratio across a trapezoid diagonal"><title>Area ratio across a trapezoid diagonal</title><polygon points="255.111,66.444 125.333,293.556 514.667,293.556 384.889,66.444" fill="none" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><text x="241.111" y="50.444" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">A</text><text x="111.333" y="309.556" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">B</text><text x="528.667" y="309.556" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">C</text><text x="398.889" y="50.444" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">D</text><polygon points="255.111,66.444 125.333,293.556 384.889,66.444" fill="#d5f1ed" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><text x="320.000" y="43.444" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">4</text><text x="320.000" y="316.556" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">12</text><text x="238.889" y="147.556" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="17">14 cm²</text></svg>

lines.say: ABCD is an isosceles trapezoid. AD is 4, BC is 12, and the shaded triangle ABD has area 14. What's the trapezoid's area?
Full math solution first. The shaded area is a triangle — an obtuse one.
Area of a triangle: base times height over 2. The only base we have is AD — 4.

lines.draw: Extend AD and drop the height from B to the extension

lines.say: Where's the height to AD? In an obtuse triangle the height is outside. Extend AD, and drop the shortest distance from B.
4h over 2 is 14 — so h is 7.
Notice: this height to AD is also the trapezoid's height — the distance between the two parallel lines.
Trapezoid area: sum of the bases times the height over 2. 4 plus 12 is 16, times 7 over 2 — 8 times 7 — 56.
Choice three. Not too bad — but there's a much shorter psychometric solution.

beats.title: Method 2 · Ratios

fig.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="79.3 17.4 481.3 325.1" role="img" aria-label="Area ratio across a trapezoid diagonal"><title>Area ratio across a trapezoid diagonal</title><polygon points="255.111,66.444 125.333,293.556 514.667,293.556 384.889,66.444" fill="none" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><text x="241.111" y="50.444" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">A</text><text x="111.333" y="309.556" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">B</text><text x="528.667" y="309.556" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">C</text><text x="398.889" y="50.444" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">D</text><polygon points="255.111,66.444 125.333,293.556 384.889,66.444" fill="#d5f1ed" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><text x="320.000" y="43.444" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">4</text><text x="320.000" y="316.556" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">12</text><text x="238.889" y="147.556" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="17">14 cm²</text></svg>

items.t: Same height $\Rightarrow$ area ratio $=$ base ratio

lines.say: The psychometric solution rests on a ratio principle.
Some students notice: the shaded triangle and the white triangle have the same height — the trapezoid's height.
In the white one it's easy to see. In the shaded one — it's the outside height we saw.

lines.label: Same height → area ratio = base ratio appears

lines.say: Same height — so the ratio of the areas is set by the ratio of the bases.
Shaded base: 4. White base: 12. Three times bigger — so the area is three times bigger: 42.

lines.draw: Split BC into 4, 4, 4 and join the points to D

lines.say: Let's see it. Split BC into three pieces of 4. Now every triangle here has the same base — 4 — and the same height.

lines.draw: Write 14 in each of the four triangles

lines.say: So they all have the same area: 14, 14, 14, and the shaded 14.
The whole trapezoid: 14 plus 42 — 56. Careful: 42 alone is only the white triangle — that's a trap answer.
Choice three. Same height — the area ratio follows the base ratio. Base three times bigger, area three times bigger.
Much shorter — you barely write anything. You just see it.

A shaded shape with no formula — two main approaches.

beats.title: Approach 1 · Subtract areas

lines.say: A rectangle made of 35 congruent squares, each side 1. What's the shaded area?
What is the shaded shape? A trapezoid? Let's count sides.
1, 2, 3, 4, 5 — a pentagon. We never learned a pentagon area formula.
We call these shaded-area questions. There are two main approaches.
One: take the area you know — the rectangle — and subtract the white areas. Two: break the shaded area into familiar shapes.
Approach one — subtracting areas. It's the main one, and the most common.
The rectangle: 35 squares — area 35.
Four white triangles, all right triangles. Area: leg times leg over 2.
Upper left: legs 1 and 2. 1 times 2 over 2 — 1.
Upper right: legs 6 and 2 — 6.
The two lower ones: legs 2 and 3 — 3 each.
All the white together: 13. 35 minus 13 — 22.
Choice one.

lines.say: Next idea: completions.
Many students look and say: whole squares I can count. And two half-squares complete each other into one.

lines.draw: Shade the full squares inside the middle 3-by-3 block

lines.say: Here, the middle 3-by-3 block is 9 whole squares — easy to count.
But careful: the sloping sides here cut squares into pieces that don't match — thirds, two-thirds, odd slivers.
Pairing pieces by eye would be a guess. Only pair pieces that truly complete each other.
So in this figure completions alone don't settle it cleanly. The next approach handles the slopes exactly.

lines.say: Quadrilateral ABCD: angle A is alpha, angle B is 110, angle C is beta. DE bisects angle D. What's angle AED?
What's hard here? We go through the quadrilateral to find angle D, split it in two, then work in triangle ADE.
And all of it with letters — in under a minute, when it's second-to-last in the section.
Full solution first. The angles of any quadrilateral add up to 360.
Isolate D: 360 minus 110 is 250. D equals 250 minus alpha minus beta.
DE bisects it. Half of 250 is 125 — minus half alpha, minus half beta.

lines.draw: Write 125 − α/2 − β/2 at D in triangle AED

lines.say: Put it in the drawing — hardly any room.
Now triangle AED: the angles add up to 180.
180 minus 125 — 55. Notice: already choices one and four are out — the number must be 55, not 110.
Beta: there's minus beta over 2 inside the brackets — the minus flips it: plus beta over 2.
Choice three has minus beta over 2 — eliminate.
And alpha: minus alpha plus half alpha — minus half alpha.
55 minus alpha over 2 plus beta over 2. Choice two. Long and pretty tiring.

lines.say: The psychometric solution: plug in numbers.
Pick some alpha, some beta. Plug them into the drawing AND into the answers. Find the answer that matches.
That turns a complex question into a simple one — numbers are much easier to work with.
Alpha looks obtuse — I'll take 100. Beta — 70. You can pick others, as long as the drawing still works.
Angle D: 100 plus 70 plus 110 is 280. 360 minus 280 — 80. Bisected — 40 and 40.
Now the question mark is a joke: 100 plus 40 is 140. To 180 — 40 degrees.
Now plug alpha 100 and beta 70 into every answer — and eliminate anything that isn't 40.
The drawback of plugging in: to be sure, we have to eliminate the other answers.
Choice one: 110 plus 50 minus 35 — 125. Out. Choice two: 55 minus 50 plus 35 — 40. It fits!
Still — don't mark it yet. If you're out of time, it's a very reasonable guess.
Choice three: 55 plus 50 minus 35 — 70. Out. Choice four: 110 minus 50 plus 35 — 95. Out.
Choice two.
Two approaches. If you're strong in algebra and do it in under a minute — great, solve it fully.
For most students the full algebra is hard — especially at the end of a section under time pressure. Plugging in is a wonderful solution for that.

lines.say: Rectangle ABCD is made of six congruent rectangles. Its perimeter is 50. What's its area?
The main difficulty: realise there's a fixed ratio between the length and the width of each small rectangle.
That ratio comes from the way the six rectangles are put together.

lines.draw: Write x on the short sides of the four middle rectangles

lines.say: Call the width of a small rectangle x. They're all the same — so each of the four stacked ones is x high.

lines.draw: Write 4x on the long side of a standing rectangle

lines.say: Look at a standing rectangle: its long side covers four x's. So the long side is 4x.
We found the ratio: 1 to 4.

lines.draw: Write x, 4x, x along AB and 4x along BC

lines.say: Now label everything: the height is 4x. Across the width: x, then 4x, then x — 6x.
Perimeter: 4x plus 4x plus 6x plus 6x — 20x. It's 50, so x is 2.5.
Careful — nobody asked for x. It's not even in the answers. We were asked for the area.
Area: base times height. 4x is 10, 6x is 15. 10 times 15 — 150.
Choice one.
A shortcut from the course: 6x to 4x is 3 to 2. Half the perimeter is 25 — five parts, so one part is 5: sides 15 and 10. Same 150.
And that's it for quadrilaterals.

lines.say: What does that tell us? Together the two angles are 144.
Could be 72 and 72. Could be 100 and 44. No problem.
But neither one can be 144 — or more than 144.
If alpha is 144, beta is zero. Beta has to be a real angle — so 144 is impossible.

lines.say: Let's check the other answers too.
Alpha 16: beta is 128. Together 144 — possible.
Alpha 64: beta 80 — fine.
Alpha 128 — some students think: wait, the angle looks acute. It can't be 128.
But on the exam, drawings don't have to be accurate. An angle can be drawn acute and still be obtuse.
Alpha 128, beta 16 — also possible.
The only impossible value: 144. Choice one.

items.t: Parallelogram: opposite sides are parallel and equal

lines.say: ABCD is a parallelogram. What is its perimeter?
To get the perimeter of a quadrilateral, add its sides: AB plus BC plus CD plus AD.

lines.label: Parallelogram: opposite sides are parallel and equal appears

lines.say: ABCD is a parallelogram — so opposite sides are parallel and equal.
AB is 7 — so CD is 7 too.
Now BC and AD. We don't know them. We do know part of AD: AE is 3. That will probably help.

In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal — so angle D is 64 too.
Adjacent angles add up to 180. So angle A is 180 minus 64 — 116.
All of angle C: opposite angles are equal, or adjacent angles add to 180. Either way — 116.
Angle ECD: 116 minus 58 — 58. So CE is an angle bisector.

lines.say: Now look at triangle EDC. Two angles are known — we can find the third.
Angles in a triangle add up to 180. 64 plus 58 is 122. 180 minus 122 — 58.

lines.draw: Trace the Z: BC, CE, ED

lines.say: By the way — ED is parallel to BC, so there's a Z here. Alternate angles are equal: angle CED is 58 right away.
Either way — angle E is 58.

lines.draw: Mark the angles at C and E in triangle EDC as equal

lines.say: Equal angles — so the sides opposite them are equal. The triangle is isosceles.
CD is 7 — so ED is 7 too.

items.t: Rectangle: the diagonals bisect each other and are equal

lines.say: ABCD is a rectangle. The perimeter of triangle EBC is 25. What is the area of triangle ABE?
Where do we start? We have a rectangle and the perimeter of a triangle.
We'll probably need a rectangle property — about the diagonals.

lines.label: Rectangle: the diagonals bisect each other and are equal appears

lines.say: In a rectangle the diagonals bisect each other and are equal.

lines.draw: Mark AE, EC, EB and ED as equal

lines.say: So AE, EC, ED and EB are all equal.
The perimeter of EBC is 25: EB plus 12 plus EC.
So EB and EC together are 13. They're equal — 6.5 each.

lines.draw: Write 6.5 on EB and on EC

items.t: A median splits a triangle into two equal areas

lines.say: Now the area of ABE. There are several ways — and it's important to know all of them.
On the exam, pick the first one that jumps out. But now we're at the basics — learn them all.
Way one: the median. Look at triangle ABC.

lines.label: A median splits a triangle into two equal areas appears

lines.say: We've learned: a median splits a triangle into two triangles of equal area.

lines.draw: Draw the height from B to line AC (outside for triangle EBC)

lines.say: Why? BE is the median to AC: AE equals EC. Same base — and the same height from B, even when it falls outside.
Triangle ABC is easy: 5 times 12 over 2 — 30. ABE is half of it: 15.
Choice three.

items.t: The diagonals split a rectangle into 4 equal areas

lines.label: The diagonals split a rectangle into 4 equal areas appears

lines.say: Way two: the diagonals of a rectangle always split it into four triangles of equal area.
By the way — that's true across the whole parallelogram family: rectangle, rhombus, square.

lines.draw: Write S₁ in the left and right triangles, S₂ in the top and bottom

lines.say: Why? The top triangle is congruent to the bottom one. The left is congruent to the right. And we just saw S1 equals S2.
So one triangle is the rectangle divided by 4: 5 times 12 is 60, over 4 — 15. Choice three.

lines.say: And a third way — the most basic one: base times height.

lines.draw: Draw the height from E to AB

lines.say: We need the height from E to AB. Slide BC over — it's the height of both side triangles together. So one triangle's height is half of 12 — 6.
5 times 6 over 2 — 15. Choice three.

beats.title: Two area formulas

fig.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="196.3 11.6 247.4 336.9" role="img" aria-label="A rhombus made from two equilateral triangles"><title>A rhombus made from two equilateral triangles</title><polygon points="320.000,57.563 249.311,180.000 320.000,302.437 390.689,180.000" fill="none" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><text x="320.000" y="37.563" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">A</text><text x="228.311" y="180.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">B</text><text x="320.000" y="322.437" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">C</text><text x="411.689" y="180.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">D</text><line x1="249.311" y1="180.000" x2="390.689" y2="180.000" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5"/><path d="M 268.161 180.000 A 18.850 18.850 0 0 0 258.736 163.675" fill="none" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2"/><text x="274.206" y="165.627" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#087f83" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18">60°</text><text x="320.000" y="202.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">6</text></svg>

lines.say: ABCD is a rhombus. The diagonal BD is 6, and angle ABD is 60. What is the area of the rhombus?
We learned two formulas for the area of a rhombus.
Side times the height to it — a rhombus is a parallelogram with all sides equal, so it works like a parallelogram.
Or: the product of the diagonals over 2. Any quadrilateral with perpendicular diagonals — its area is the product of the diagonals over 2.
A diagonal is given here — so we'll probably use the diagonal formula. That's way one.

lines.draw: Draw diagonal AC; write O where the diagonals meet

lines.say: Remember: in a rhombus the diagonals bisect each other. Draw AC —

lines.draw: Write 3 on BO and 3 on OD

lines.say: — it cuts BD into 3 and 3.

lines.draw: Mark the right angle at O

lines.say: And the diagonals are perpendicular — the angle at O is 90.
A special triangle forms here: right-angled, with a 60 — a golden triangle.
In a golden triangle there's a fixed ratio between the short leg, the long leg and the hypotenuse.
3 is opposite the 30 — it's the short leg. For the long leg, multiply by root 3.
AO is 3 root 3.

beats.title: Diagonals ÷ 2

fig.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="196.3 11.6 247.4 336.9" role="img" aria-label="A rhombus made from two equilateral triangles"><title>A rhombus made from two equilateral triangles</title><polygon points="320.000,57.563 249.311,180.000 320.000,302.437 390.689,180.000" fill="none" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><text x="320.000" y="37.563" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">A</text><text x="228.311" y="180.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">B</text><text x="320.000" y="322.437" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">C</text><text x="411.689" y="180.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">D</text><line x1="249.311" y1="180.000" x2="390.689" y2="180.000" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5"/><path d="M 268.161 180.000 A 18.850 18.850 0 0 0 258.736 163.675" fill="none" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2"/><text x="274.206" y="165.627" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#087f83" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18">60°</text><text x="320.000" y="202.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">6</text></svg>

lines.say: The diagonals bisect each other — so the bottom part is 3 root 3 too.
Everything's ready: product of the diagonals over 2. BD is 6. AC is 3 root 3 plus 3 root 3 — 6 root 3.
6 times 6 root 3 over 2. Cancel the 6 with the 2 — 3. 3 times 6 root 3 — 18 root 3.
Choice four.

lines.say: Notice: once you've found all the inner pieces, you can get the area in different ways.
Some students take the golden triangle we found — base 3, height 3 root 3 — and multiply by 4.
Some take the top triangle BDA: base 6, height 3 root 3 — twice.
Some take the right-hand triangle ADC: base 6 root 3, height 3 — twice too.
Lots of ways — at this stage, get to know them all.

lines.say: One more way. Well done if you spotted this one.
Some notice the 60 degrees and say: wait — that's a hint.

lines.draw: Mark AB and AD as equal

lines.say: In a rhombus all the sides are equal. AB equals AD — so the angle opposite AD is 60 too. The triangle is at least isosceles.

lines.draw: Write 60° at D and at A in triangle ABD

lines.say: An isosceles triangle with two 60s — together 120 — so the top angle is 60 as well.
Worth remembering: an isosceles triangle with two 60-degree angles is always equilateral.

lines.draw: Write 6 on AB, AD, BC and CD

lines.say: BD is 6 — so AB and AD are 6. And all the sides of a rhombus are equal: DC and BC are 6 too.
So what do we have? Two equilateral triangles.
Area of one equilateral triangle: side squared times root 3 over 4. Twice: 2 times 36 root 3 over 4 — 18 root 3.
That's the shorter, psychometric way. Choice four.

items.t: Square: all sides equal · all angles $90°$

lines.say: ABCD is a square. O is a point inside it, and triangle AOD is equilateral. What is angle OBC?
Where do we start? Probably with the square.

lines.label: Square: all sides equal · all angles 90° appears

lines.say: A square has lots of properties. All sides equal. All angles equal — 90 each.
The diagonals too: they bisect each other, they're equal, perpendicular, and they bisect the angles.
We need to decide which properties matter here — and which don't.
There are no diagonals. O is inside — but it's not where the diagonals meet. So we probably won't need the diagonal properties.

lines.draw: Mark all four sides of the square with one tick

lines.say: What we will need: all sides are equal. Mark them all with the same tick.

lines.draw: Write 90° at A and at B

lines.say: All angles are 90. Mark the ones next to the angle we want — A and B. We may need them.

lines.say: Done with the square. Next given: AOD is equilateral.

lines.draw: Mark AO and DO with the same tick

lines.say: In an equilateral triangle all sides are equal: DA, OD, AO. AD already has a tick — so DO and AO get the same tick.
That's the catch in this question: the sides of the triangle equal the sides of the square.

lines.draw: Write 60° at A inside triangle AOD

lines.say: And all its angles are 60.
Now look at the triangle that holds the angle at B: ABO.
ABO is isosceles: AB equals AO. If we hadn't marked the sides, we might not have noticed.

lines.draw: Write α at B and at O inside triangle ABO

lines.say: Equal sides — equal angles opposite them. Angle ABO and angle AOB — call both alpha.
The top angle: 90 minus 60 — 30. We're almost done.
Angles in the highlighted triangle add up to 180: 30 plus alpha plus alpha.
180 minus 30 — 150 equals 2 alpha. One alpha — 75.

lines.say: Careful! 75 is angle ABO — and 75 is one of the answers.
But the question asks for angle OBC.
Together they fill the square's corner at B — 90. So 90 minus 75 — 15.
Choice three. Stop one step too early — and you'd circle the trap.

lines.say: ABCD is a kite. What is its area?
As we learned: the area of a kite is the product of the diagonals over 2.
Here we're given part of the long diagonal — OC. We need AO.
And part of the short diagonal, BD: BO. We need OD.
Let's recall what a kite is: a quadrilateral made of two isosceles triangles.

lines.draw: Mark AB and AD as equal; mark CB and CD as equal

lines.say: Triangle ABD is isosceles — AD equals AB. And triangle DCB — BC equals DC.

items.t: Isosceles: the height is also a median and an angle bisector

lines.label: Isosceles: the height is also a median and a bisector appears

lines.say: In an isosceles triangle the height is also a median and an angle bisector.

lines.draw: Mark the right angle at O

lines.say: So the main diagonal AC is perpendicular to the secondary diagonal BD —
— it bisects the angles, and it's a median: BO equals OD. The main diagonal bisects the secondary one. BO is 12 — so OD is 12.
Careful — not the other way round. In a kite, AO is not equal to OC.

lines.say: The diagonals are perpendicular — so triangle ADO is right-angled.
We know the hypotenuse, 13, and a leg, 12. The Pythagorean triple 5, 12, 13 — the other leg is 5.
That's everything. Now the area.
AC is 5 plus 15 — 20. BD is 12 plus 12 — 24. Over 2.
You could do 20 times 24 first — better to cancel first: 24 over 2 is 12. 20 times 12 — 240.
Choice one.

lines.say: Notice: once we've found all the pieces, there are more ways to get the area.
Some take triangle ABD — base 24, height 5 — and triangle CBD — base 24, height 15 — and add.
Some take four right triangles: two small ones, 12 by 5 over 2, twice. Two big ones, 12 by 15 over 2, twice.
Lots of ways — all 240.

We need the sum of the sides. Three sides are given — we need the fourth.
Start with the first given: AB equals AD. So triangle ABD is isosceles.

lines.draw: Write 30° at D in triangle ABD

lines.say: In an isosceles triangle the base angles are equal. Angle ABD is 30 — so this one is 30 too.
30, 30 — the top angle A: 180 minus 60 — 120.

lines.say: In every trapezoid, the angles on the same leg add up to 180.

lines.draw: Write 60° at B, and 30° for angle DBC

lines.say: A is 120 — so all of angle B is 60. The bottom part, DBC, is 30.

lines.draw: Trace the Z: AD, DB, BC

lines.say: Another way to see it — our familiar Z. The bases are parallel, so the Z angles are equal.

lines.label: Isosceles trapezoid: equal base angles appears

lines.say: The trapezoid is isosceles: the bottom base angles are equal, the top base angles are equal.
Either way angle C is 60: equal to B — 30 plus 30 — or it completes A to 180.

lines.draw: Mark the right angle at D in triangle BCD

lines.say: Not just a right triangle — a golden triangle.
Its short leg is opposite the 30: CD. The trapezoid is isosceles — so CD equals AB: 5.
When we know the short leg, the hypotenuse is easy — exactly twice the short leg. BC is 10.
Almost done. The perimeter: 5 plus 5 plus 5 plus 10 — 25.
Choice four.

beats.title: Quadrilaterals

lines.say: Quadrilaterals.
So far we've finished lines, angles and triangles.
Now we're entering the kingdom of quadrilaterals.
Let's start with a general quadrilateral. What is it?

lines.say: A quadrilateral is a closed shape with 4 sides.
Four sides — 1, 2, 3, 4 — and they close up. That's a quadrilateral.
The sides don't have to be equal. The angles don't have to be right angles.
If the question doesn't say so — don't add it yourself.

lines.say: The sum of the angles in a quadrilateral. Let's draw a diagonal that cuts it.
We've really split the quadrilateral into two triangles.
We know the angles in a triangle add up to 180. So 180 here — and 180 here.
Now make the diagonal disappear for a second.
Two corners are whole triangle angles. The other two are each made of a piece from both triangles.
So all the pieces together are exactly the four angles of the quadrilateral.
The angles in a quadrilateral add up to 360.
That's almost the only rule we have for a general quadrilateral — at least the only one that matters for the exam.

lines.say: So which kinds of quadrilaterals are there? What do you remember from school?
There's the ordinary quadrilateral — and then:
The square. A perfect quadrilateral — all the sides equal. Completely symmetric.
Take a square and stretch it a little — you get a rectangle.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow from the square to the rectangle

lines.say: Take a rectangle and step on it — squash it a bit sideways — you get a parallelogram.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow from the rectangle to the parallelogram

lines.say: Shorten the parallelogram until all its sides are equal — it becomes a rhombus.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow from the parallelogram down to the rhombus

lines.say: You can also squash a square a bit and get a rhombus.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow from the square to the rhombus

lines.say: Turn it a little — standing on a corner, like on playing cards. Now it really looks like a rhombus.
Squash the rhombus a bit from above — and you get a kite.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow from the rhombus to the kite

lines.say: And take a rectangle, move its sides a little — you get a trapezoid. A bit of a strange shape.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow from the rectangle to the trapezoid

lines.say: Those are all our quadrilaterals — and how one turns into another.
The names carry information. When a question names the shape — underline it.
From here: a lesson on each one. We start with the square — the easiest to understand, because we all know what a square is.

lines.draw: Shade one of the four small triangles

lines.say: Look what formed here — a silver triangle.
Right-angled — the diagonals are perpendicular. And isosceles — the half-diagonals are equal.
So the square is made of 4 silver triangles.
Actually it's also made of 2 silver triangles — depends how you look. Here: a 90° angle and two equal legs.
That's why the diagonal is the side times root 2 — the 45-45-90 ratio.
Keep crossing it with more diagonals and you can split the square into endless silver triangles.

lines.say: The area of the square equals its side — squared. That's why we call it 'squared'.
Side a — the area is a squared.

lines.draw: Count the squares along one side: write 6

lines.say: Say each little square is 1 square centimetre. The side here: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. It's 6.
So the area is 6 squared — 36. And really, there are 36 little squares here.

lines.say: Another way to find the area of a square — less known, less used: with the diagonals.

lines.label: Square ABCD with both diagonals appears

lines.say: The product of the diagonals over 2. The diagonals are equal — so it's d squared over 2.
Why does it work? Say the diagonal is 12.

lines.draw: Write 6 on two half-diagonals of one small triangle

lines.say: Then half the diagonal is 6.
Now I can find the area of this triangle: legs times legs over 2 — 18.
Times 4 — the whole square. 72. And 12 squared over 2 is also 72.
Do it with a letter d, and you get d squared over 2 every time.

beats.title: Square: all yes

items.t: Sides equal? · Diagonals equal? · Perpendicular? · Bisect the angles?

lines.say: That's the square. The simplest quadrilateral — the perfect one.
We always define the square as 'yes'.

lines.label: Sides equal? Diagonals equal? Perpendicular? Bisect the angles? appears

lines.say: Why yes? The diagonals equal? Yes. Perpendicular? Yes. Sides equal? Yes. Bisect the square's angles? Yes.
Everything is yes. It's simply a perfect quadrilateral.
Let's see a question.

lines.say: The diagonal of a square is 12 centimetres. What is its area?
In principle I could draw the square, put 12 on the diagonal, and start Pythagoras to find the side —
— and then square the side.
But there's no reason to.
The area of a square is the product of the diagonals over 2. 12 times 12 over 2.
Choice four.

lines.say: Just to see the long way once: call the side s.
Pythagoras in the half-square: s squared plus s squared is 144. So s squared is 72.
But s squared already IS the area. Stop there — don't find s and square it back.
144? That's the diagonal squared — someone forgot to divide by 2.
36? That's half the diagonal squared.
72. Choice four.

lines.draw: Draw matching ticks on opposite sides

lines.say: Opposite sides are equal — this equals this, and this equals this.

lines.draw: Draw right-angle marks at the four corners

lines.say: All the angles are 90 degrees — we didn't touch the angles.

lines.draw: Draw parallel arrows on opposite sides

lines.say: And of course opposite sides are parallel.
Adjacent sides? Not necessarily equal. If they are — it's a square.

items.t: NOT perpendicular · DON'T bisect the angles

lines.label: Rectangle ABCD with both diagonals appears

lines.say: The diagonals of the rectangle.
First — they're equal to each other. The rectangle is symmetric.

lines.draw: Draw equal ticks on all four half-diagonals

lines.say: They also bisect each other — and every half is equal. This equals this equals this equals this.
Now pay attention.

lines.label: Not perpendicular · don't bisect the angles appears

lines.say: The diagonals are NOT perpendicular. You can actually see it here.
And they don't bisect the rectangle's angles — unlike the square.
In the square they were perpendicular and bisected the angles. Here — neither.

lines.say: The area of a rectangle — we find it like the square.
In the square we did side squared. Here the length isn't equal to the width.
So: length times width. Or base times height — depends how you look at it.

lines.draw: Write 8 on AB and 3 on BC

lines.say: Length 8, width 3.
8 times 3 — 24. Three rows of 8 unit squares. No dividing by 2 — it's the whole rectangle.
Let's see a sample question.

The last angle left is 60.

lines.say: What do we know about the angles?
Opposite angles are equal: A equals C, and B equals D.
And two adjacent angles add up to 180 — wherever they are.
D and C are adjacent — sum 180. A and D — 180. B plus C — 180. A plus B — 180.

lines.say: Let's see why.

lines.draw: Extend AD and BC into long parallel lines

lines.say: The sides are parallel — so let's draw them as parallel lines.
These sides are parallel too — draw them as lines as well.
Remember: two parallel lines and a transversal make small angles and large angles.
And it's the same crossing in every corner of the parallelogram.

lines.draw: Write β in the two large angles and α in the two small angles

lines.say: So all the large ones are equal — call them beta. All the small ones are equal — alpha.
There's the first rule: opposite angles are equal.
And a small angle plus a large angle is 180. Adjacent angles add up to 180.

lines.say: The diagonals of the parallelogram.
They're NOT equal. You can see it here — a longer diagonal and a shorter one.

lines.draw: Draw matching ticks on the two halves of each diagonal

lines.say: What DO we know? They bisect each other. This part equals this one, and this equals this.

lines.label: Bisect each other — nothing more appears

lines.say: They also don't bisect the parallelogram's angles, even though sometimes it looks like it.
And they're not perpendicular.
Not sure? Exaggerate: a very wide, very low parallelogram. Draw a diagonal — you'll see right away it doesn't bisect the angle.

a times h. The HEIGHT — perpendicular to the base. Not the sloping side.

items.t: Same base, same height → same area

lines.say: Why? Let's understand.

lines.label: The parallelogram with a rectangle on the same base appears

lines.say: Say we don't know the area of a parallelogram — but we DO know the area of a rectangle.
Draw a rectangle on the same base as the parallelogram.

lines.draw: Shade the triangle that's in the rectangle but not in the parallelogram

lines.say: The difference: this triangle is in the rectangle...

lines.draw: Shade the triangle on the other side

lines.say: ...and this one is in the parallelogram but not in the rectangle.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow moving the first triangle onto the second

lines.say: Cut the triangle out of the rectangle and move it into the parallelogram.
The area of the parallelogram equals the area of the rectangle.

lines.label: Same base, same height → same area appears

lines.say: And the rectangle's area is base times height. So a times h is the area of the parallelogram.
Let's solve an example.

x is 180 minus 3 alpha minus 3 beta.
We already know alpha plus beta is 45 — so 3 alpha plus 3 beta is 135. But let's write it.
180 minus 3 times alpha-plus-beta: 180 minus 135. 45.
We don't know what alpha is, or beta. We never found them.
But the angle x — that's 45.

lines.say: ABCD is a parallelogram. AE is perpendicular to BC.
AD is 17, CD is 13, EC is 12. What is the area of the parallelogram?
Notice: the moment a perpendicular is dropped — a right triangle forms here.
And that takes us straight back to Pythagoras.
That's usually how it goes: when we need missing sides, we use Pythagoras — a lot.
Let's put the data in a more convenient way.
Opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal. If DC is 13 — AB is also 13.

lines.draw: Write 17 under the whole of BC

lines.say: If AD is 17 — then all of BC is 17.
And if BC is 17 — what's left, BE, has to be 5.

5, 12, 13 — a Pythagorean triple!
So the height AE is 12.
Area of a parallelogram: base times height. 17 times 12 — 204.
Choice three.
Watch the traps: 13 times 17 is 221 — that uses the sloping side, not the height. The base is all of BC, 17.

lines.draw: Draw equal ticks on all four sides

lines.say: A rhombus is a quadrilateral with all sides equal.

lines.draw: Mark the opposite angles as equal

lines.say: About the angles: opposite angles are equal too.
A rhombus is really a perfected parallelogram:
like a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal and parallel — and on top of that, all the sides are equal.
Remember? In the quadrilaterals lesson we shortened a parallelogram until we got a rhombus.

lines.say: Instead of remembering all the rhombus properties — sides, angles, diagonals —
just remember its shape. And remember that it's symmetric.

lines.label: Rhombus ABCD with both diagonals appears

lines.draw: Trace the vertical diagonal in colour

lines.say: This diagonal is a line of symmetry. The right side is exactly equal to the left side —
the triangle on the right is congruent to the triangle on the left.
So the sides up here are equal, and down here too. Right equals left. This angle equals this one.

lines.draw: Trace the horizontal diagonal in another colour

lines.say: And it's not only symmetric right-to-left — it's also symmetric top-to-bottom.
The top triangle is congruent to the bottom one. Top angle equals bottom angle.

lines.label: Symmetric: right = left, top = bottom appears

lines.say: Bottom line: all the sides equal, opposite angles equal, diagonals perpendicular, bisecting the angles and each other.

lines.label: Rhombus ABCD with both diagonals appears

lines.say: The area of a rhombus: the product of the diagonals over 2.
How did we get it? Given two diagonals, take half of one and half of the other.

lines.draw: Shade one small right triangle; write its legs as half-diagonals

lines.say: Those are the legs of this right triangle. Its area: legs times legs over 2.
Then just times 4 — the whole rhombus. What you end up with: diagonal times diagonal, over 2.
Diagonals 10 and 6? 10 times 6 over 2 — 30.
And a rhombus is also a parallelogram — so base times height works too, if that's what you're given.
Let's solve a sample question.

beats.title: Two equations

fig.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="210.8 -0.8 218.3 361.5" role="img" aria-label="A rhombus whose diagonals have a known sum and difference"><title>A rhombus whose diagonals have a known sum and difference</title><polygon points="320.000,45.231 263.846,180.000 320.000,314.769 376.154,180.000" fill="none" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><text x="320.000" y="25.231" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">A</text><text x="242.846" y="180.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">B</text><text x="320.000" y="334.769" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">C</text><text x="397.154" y="180.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">D</text><line x1="320.000" y1="45.231" x2="320.000" y2="314.769" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="263.846" y1="180.000" x2="376.154" y2="180.000" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5"/></svg>

lines.say: The sum of the diagonals of a rhombus is 34. The absolute difference between them is 14.
Why 'absolute'? So we don't get tangled up — big minus small or small minus big. A length can't be negative.
What is the perimeter?
Let's build two equations with two unknowns. Call the diagonals a and b — a is the bigger one.
a plus b is 34. a minus b is 14.
Add them: plus b, minus b — cancels. 2a is 48, so a is 24. The bigger diagonal.
And b: 24 minus what gives 14? Minus 10. b is 10.

lines.say: The diagonals bisect each other.

lines.draw: Write 12 and 12 on the halves of the long diagonal

lines.say: So I split 24 into 12 and 12.

lines.draw: Write 5 and 5 on the halves of the short diagonal

lines.say: And 10 into 5 and 5.
I need the perimeter — so I need the side.
Again — a right triangle here. 5, 12 —
— 13. A Pythagorean triple.
Once I know one side — all the others are 13 too.
4 sides together — 52.
Choice one.

lines.say: That's the rhombus.
One tip to sum up — instead of remembering all its rules, remember one thing:
a rhombus is a symmetric shape. Right equals left, and top equals bottom.
That way you can always see the angles, the sides — everything you need.

lines.draw: Draw matching ticks on the two lower sides

lines.say: So the bottom part is like the bottom of a rhombus — these sides are equal.

lines.draw: Draw a second kind of tick on the two upper sides

lines.label: Kite ABCD with both diagonals appears

lines.say: The diagonals of the kite. They're not equal.
We call them the main diagonal and the secondary diagonal.
The main one is the kite's line of symmetry. It joins the two head angles.
It makes two triangles — right and left — that are congruent.

lines.draw: Trace BD in another colour; write 'secondary'

lines.say: The secondary one does NOT split the kite symmetrically. One triangle here, another there — not the same.

lines.label: Kite ABCD with both diagonals appears

lines.say: The area of a kite: the product of the diagonals over 2.
Quite like the rhombus — the diagonals are perpendicular, so right triangles form.
But here the triangles aren't equal, so I can't just take one and multiply.
What I CAN do once the diagonals are given: find the area of the whole right-hand triangle, ADC.
Its base is the main diagonal. Its height — half of the secondary one.
Base times height over 2 — and times 2 for the whole kite.
Bottom line: the product of the diagonals over 2. Exactly like the rhombus, and like the square.
Let's see a sample question.

lines.say: Kite ABCD: AB equals AD, and CB equals CD.
Angle ABD is 45. Angle DBC is 60. And DC is 6. What is the perimeter of the kite?
Let's see — triangle BDC.
It's isosceles: in a kite, these two sides are equal. This is 6, and this is 6.

lines.draw: Write 60° at D in triangle BDC

lines.say: And there's a 60 here. An isosceles triangle with a 60 angle — has to be equilateral.
If this is 60 and it equals that one — then that's 60 too. 60, 60, 60.
Equilateral — so BD is 6 as well.

lines.say: At the top: this angle is 45 — so angle ADB is 45 too. It's isosceles.
What's left: A is 90.
We got a silver triangle! 45, 45, 90.
From the hypotenuse to a leg — divide by root 2. Ignore the root: 6 divided by 2 is 3. Attach the root: 3 root 2.

lines.say: Now the perimeter: 6 plus 6 is 12.
Wait — do I need to continue? Look at the choices.
Only two choices start with 12. Here the trick narrows it down, but doesn't settle it.
So another tip: some choices have root 2, some have root 3.
The moment I see I'm in a silver triangle — the answer will most likely contain root 2.
If the hypotenuse is a whole number, the leg has a root 2 — and the other way round.
Root 3 belongs to the golden triangle. Not here.
And if I add it all up to the end: 12 plus 6 root 2.
Choice four.

lines.say: A trapezoid has 4 sides.

lines.draw: Trace the top and bottom sides; write 'bases'

lines.say: The bottom side and the top side — we call them bases.

lines.draw: Trace the two slanted sides; write 'legs'

lines.say: The sides on the sides — we call them legs.

lines.draw: Draw parallel arrows on the two bases

lines.say: In a trapezoid the bases are parallel to each other. Notice — they're NOT equal. But they're parallel.
The legs are NOT parallel to each other. If they were, we'd have a parallelogram.
So the definition of a trapezoid: the legs aren't parallel.

beats.title: Why: two copies

v.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="49.0 84.0 542.0 192.0" role="img" aria-label="Two equal trapezoids form a parallelogram"><title>Two equal trapezoids form a parallelogram</title><polygon points="75.000,250.000 355.000,250.000 285.000,110.000 145.000,110.000" fill="#d5f1ed" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><polygon points="355.000,250.000 495.000,250.000 565.000,110.000 285.000,110.000" fill="#fff0db" stroke="#bb6821" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><line x1="145.000" y1="250.000" x2="145.000" y2="110.000" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="7 5"/><line x1="145.000" y1="239.500" x2="155.500" y2="239.500" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="1.7"/><line x1="155.500" y1="239.500" x2="155.500" y2="250.000" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="1.7"/><text x="125.000" y="180.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">h</text></svg>

lines.say: There are many ways to prove and explain it. Here's one that's very simple and clear to me.

lines.label: Two trapezoids, one flipped, joined into a parallelogram appear

lines.say: Take the trapezoid. Copy it, flip it, and attach it on the right.
What we got: two trapezoids, one upside down — and together, one very big parallelogram.

lines.draw: Write a + b under the whole bottom

lines.say: The base of the parallelogram: a plus b.
The area of a parallelogram: base times height — so a plus b, times h.
But our trapezoid is only half of the parallelogram.
So the trapezoid is a plus b, times h, over 2.
In the exam, you're not going to start proving formulas.
What matters: memorise it. Sum of the bases, times the height, over 2.

items.t: Equal legs · equal base angles · equal diagonals

lines.say: An isosceles trapezoid — a trapezoid whose legs are equal. Just like its name.

lines.draw: Draw equal ticks on the two legs

lines.say: Left side equals right side.
It's symmetric — a bit like an isosceles triangle. If we continued the legs up, they'd close into an isosceles triangle.

lines.draw: Write β at both bottom corners

lines.say: Its base angles are equal: beta equals beta.

lines.draw: Write α at both top corners

lines.say: And since each leg's angles add up to 180 — alpha equals alpha too.
The diagonals: here they're equal to each other —

lines.draw: Draw matching ticks on the two upper pieces and on the two lower pieces

lines.say: — and they cut each other into matching pieces: the top parts are equal, and the bottom parts are equal.

lines.draw: Draw a leg perpendicular to the bases, with right-angle marks top and bottom

Nothing else special about it.

lines.say: ABCD is an isosceles trapezoid with area 54.
Triangle DEC — the triangle here on the right — has area 6. The height DE is 6.
What is AD — the top base?
Triangle DEC has area 6. So we can find EC with the area formula — legs times legs over 2.
6 times EC over 2 equals 6. EC is 2.
Now a tip for every trapezoid question you'll ever meet: always drop the heights. Both of them.

lines.draw: Draw the height from A down to F

lines.say: One height is already given. I just drop the second one.
It's an isosceles trapezoid — symmetric, right equals left. So BF is also 2.

lines.draw: Write x on AD and on FE

lines.say: Call FE and AD x. It's the same thing.

lines.say: Watch out — a common mistake.
What formed in the middle is NOT a square. True, in the drawing it looks like one.
But on the psychometric, drawings don't have to be accurate. x doesn't equal 6.
It's a rectangle. I don't know that the short base equals the height.
I know the triangle on the right has area 6 — so the one on the left also has area 6. The trapezoid is symmetric.
The whole trapezoid is 54. So what's left in the middle — the rectangle — is 42.
Rectangle: length times width. 6x equals 42. x is 7.
We found AD. Choice two.

lines.say: Now notice — if I hadn't spotted that:
a lot of students see a trapezoid, they need an area, there's a trapezoid formula — so they use the trapezoid formula.
Look how much longer it is. Forget the 6, 42, 6 for a moment.
Sum of the bases: x plus x plus 4. Times 6, the height. Over 2. Equals 54.
That's 6x plus 12 equals 54. 6x is 42. x is 7.
Same answer — much longer.
We saved all that just by understanding: if this is 6, that's 6 too — the middle has to be 42. Symmetric.
And the area of a rectangle — the simplest thing there is.

lines.say: A solid sphere, radius 5, diameter AB. Cut P is perpendicular to AB, 6 from B. Cut Q is perpendicular to AB, 8 from A.
Which cut gives the greater total surface area of the two pieces?
Again — a min–max question in geometry.
Let's understand what the total surface area of the two pieces is. Look at cut P.
The surface of the two pieces is the sphere's surface — plus the two flat faces the cut created.

lines.label: Total = sphere surface + 2 cut disks appears

lines.say: And for Q it's the same: the sphere, plus its two flat faces.
The sphere's surface is the same in both cases — it's the same sphere.
So we need to decide which flat faces are bigger — if either.

items.t: Closer to the center $\rightarrow$ bigger cut

lines.say: This extends a principle we all know from circles: chords. Picture a circle for a moment.
The longest chord in a circle is the one through the center — the diameter.
Move away from the diameter — the chord gets shorter. Further still — shorter still. Almost down to 0.

lines.label: Closer to the center → bigger cut appears

lines.say: Back to the sphere. When is the cut face biggest? When we cut right through the center.
The farther from the center, the smaller the faces.
So how far from the center is each cut?
Radius 5. Cut P is 6 from B — 1 past the center. Cut Q is 8 from A — 3 past the center.
Cut P is closer to the center — bigger faces, bigger total surface.
Cut P — choice two.

lines.say: ABCD and EFGH are parallelograms. AB and EF are 3, BC and FG are 6. Angle ABC is 75, angle EFG is 45.
Which statement is definitely NOT true?
Start with AC greater than AB. AC is a diagonal of the first parallelogram, AB is a side.
What do we know about the third side of a triangle when two sides are given? It has a range.
Less than the sum — 9. More than the difference — 3. So AC is between 3 and 9.
It can't be 3 — it's definitely more than 3. And AB is 3. So AC greater than AB is definitely true.
We're asked what's definitely NOT true — so it's out.
There's another way we learned: an anchor. A 60 degree angle would send us straight to an equilateral triangle.
Here the angle is 75 — no ready-made anchor. The triangle inequality settles it anyway.

items.t: Same sides: bigger angle $\rightarrow$ bigger opening

lines.say: Next: AC greater than EG. AC is the diagonal of the first parallelogram, EG of the second.
Notice: the sides are identical. AB equals EF — 3. BC equals FG — 6.
What's different is the angle: 75 against 45.

lines.say: With identical sides — the smaller the angle, the shorter the side facing it. The bigger the angle, the longer.
That's the angle-opening principle: a bigger angle makes a bigger opening.
So AC is clearly longer than EG. Definitely true — so it's out too.

Equal areas? Definitely not. Definitely false — that's our answer.
Choice one.

Same sides — only the angles differ, and not by much. So make the gap huge.
Push 75 up to 80 — close to 90. Pull 45 down to 30.
Now it's obvious by eye: the first area is bigger than the second.
As the angle approaches 90, the parallelogram becomes a rectangle — the maximum area: 6 times 3, 18.
As it approaches 0, the height shrinks and shrinks — the area is just a hair above 0.
And after exaggerating, look at AC and EG again: the bigger the angle, the longer the diagonal — you see it by eye.

lines.say: How would we solve it on the exam?
Proving that equal areas is impossible is harder than crossing out the last claim: equal perimeters.
Same sides — obviously the same perimeter.
So on the exam: out with two, out with three, a glance at four — out — and mark one without checking.
That was a challenging one.

lines.say: KLM is a right triangle — angle L is 90. N is on KL, and MN bisects angle KML. Which statement must be true?
Start with the given: angle KMN equals angle NML — both are marked x.
Take the claim about angle LKM — call it alpha — against angle MNL — call it beta.

lines.draw: Write α at K and β at N, inside angle MNL

lines.say: The claim: alpha is bigger than beta.
Some students look and see right away it's wrong — an angle-opening principle: the higher the vertex, the more acute the angle —
— as long as both angles stand on the same segment. Here both look down at ML.
We met this in circles: a central angle and an inscribed angle on the same chord. There, it's exactly half.
Here we don't know what part alpha is of beta — but the higher it is, the more acute.
Didn't see it? Exaggerate: raise K higher and higher — the angle at K gets sharper by eye.
Or picture yourself at M, facing a building: floor N, then floor K. The higher floor you look at, the bigger your angle —
— and the angle up there, completing it to 90, is smaller.
The more mathematical way: look at triangle KMN. Beta is an exterior angle of it.
An exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior angles not next to it: beta equals alpha plus x.
So beta is bigger than alpha. Alpha bigger than beta — impossible.
