lines.say: Next: KM less than MN.
Here too some students just see it: KM is bigger than MN — not the other way round. Why?
What's the shortest distance from M to line KL? The perpendicular — ML. The crosswalk again.
Going from M to N is already a diagonal — and from M to K, an even longer one.
The bigger the angle at M, the longer the diagonal.
Or the building: you're at M, talking to a friend on floor N — or on floor K. The higher floor is farther. Floor 100 — farther still.
The more mathematical way: triangle MLN is a right triangle — legs ML and NL, hypotenuse MN.
Triangle MLK shares the same leg ML — but KL is longer than NL. A bigger leg — a bigger hypotenuse.
So KM is bigger than MN. KM less than MN — out.

lines.say: Next: the angle at K — alpha — against x.
Honestly, here we can't know. They can be equal. Alpha can be bigger, as in the drawing — and x can be bigger too.
On the exam I recommend plugging in numbers. Say alpha is 80.
80, 90 — angle M is 10, so x is 5. Alpha is bigger.
But alpha could be 10 — a sharper angle. The drawing doesn't have to be accurate.
10, 90 — angle M is 80, so x is 40. Now x is bigger.
Didn't get it? Exaggerate: raise K — alpha gets sharper while x grows.
Not necessarily true — out.
On the psychometric: three out — mark the fourth.
Choice three. In the lesson, of course, we'll check it.

items.t: Same angle, farther from the vertex $\rightarrow$ bigger opening

lines.say: KN against NL. Plenty of students look and say: KN faces angle x, NL faces angle x — equal angles, equal segments.
But draw one more line from M to KL — it also faces an angle x. Is it equal to both? No.
There's another angle-opening principle: how close you are to the vertex.

lines.label: Same angle, farther from the vertex → bigger opening appears

lines.say: The closer to the vertex, the shorter the distance you cover. The farther away — the bigger the opening.
KN is farther from vertex M than NL — the diagonals are longer. So KN is longer.
Another way is a mathematical proof. Drop a perpendicular from N to KM — call it E.

lines.draw: Draw NE perpendicular to KM and mark the right angle at E

lines.say: Triangles MEN and MLN: same angles — and a shared side, MN. They're congruent.
So NE equals NL.
Now look at triangle KEN — a right triangle. NE is a leg, KN is the hypotenuse.
The hypotenuse is longer than a leg — so KN is longer than NL. It's right.
A complex question — and thanks to it we learned quite a few principles.

beats.title: Equal perimeters

items.t: Same perimeter: more sides $\rightarrow$ closer to a circle $\rightarrow$ more area

lines.say: A square and a regular octagon, compared under different conditions. Which statement is false?
Start with equal perimeters: if the shapes have the same perimeter, the octagon has the bigger area.
Remember shape efficiency from the lesson: two regular shapes with the same perimeter —
— the more efficient one, the one closer to a circle, encloses more area.

lines.label: Same perimeter: more sides → closer to a circle → more area appears

lines.say: The more sides a shape has, the more efficient it is — more area with the same perimeter.
The octagon is clearly more efficient — closer to a circle. So with the same perimeter it really encloses more.
True — so it's out. We're asked which is false.

beats.title: Equal areas

items.t: Same area: the square needs more boundary

lines.say: Next: if the areas are equal, the square has the bigger perimeter.
Same shape-efficiency idea — just reversed.
We already know the octagon is more efficient. If both enclose the same area — the octagon needs less perimeter to do it.

lines.label: Same area: the square needs more boundary appears

lines.say: The square, to enclose the same area, needs more perimeter. True — out too.

items.t: Same circle: more sides $\rightarrow$ more area

lines.say: Next: both inscribed in the same circle — the octagon has the bigger area.
Which shape gets closer to the circle? The more sides, the closer the area gets to the circle's.
A circle is like a regular polygon with infinitely many sides.

lines.label: Same circle: more sides → more area appears

lines.say: You can see it here: the square sits inside the octagon — on every other vertex.
The octagon has the advantage of all the pieces outside the square. Clearly the octagon's area is bigger.
True — out as well.
On the exam, three out — mark the fourth and move on.
Choice two.

items.t: Two octagon sides $>$ one square side

lines.say: In the lesson we check it too: in the same circle, the square has the bigger perimeter?
The same principle we saw for the area holds for the perimeter.
Inscribed in a circle, a shape's perimeter is always less than the circle's — and gets closer to it the more sides it has.

lines.label: Two octagon sides > one square side appears

lines.say: Look: each side of the square is replaced by two octagon sides. Two sides of a triangle are longer than the third.
So the octagon's perimeter is bigger — the claim is false.
If you've mastered shape efficiency, this question was easy — even though it's one of the last in the section.

lines.say: A solid block is cut into two pieces by one straight plane. Which CANNOT be the total number of faces of the two pieces?
What we have here is a trial-and-error question in geometry.
We cut the block and see which number of faces we can't reach.
The obvious cut: right through the middle, parallel to a face.

lines.draw: Draw a cut through the middle, parallel to the front face

lines.say: We get two boxes. Each box has 6 faces — we doubled the faces.
6 and 6 — 12 faces. So 12 is possible.

lines.say: Normally we'd keep experimenting now and cross out two more answers.
But some students stop here and already see the answer — a psychometric min–max insight.
They notice the answers have a minimum and a maximum — and the problem is probably at the edges.
Here the edges are 10 and 15. Reach one edge — and you can be quite sure the other is the answer.
It's a tricky insight — few students think of it, especially in an exam.
If you can — wonderful. If not, and you're short on time, remember: in min–max questions the problem is usually at the edges.
Not always — usually.

lines.say: Let's go on with standard trial and error. Another cut: a diagonal one.

lines.draw: Draw a diagonal cut through two opposite edges of the block

lines.say: We get two triangular prisms. Each prism has 5 faces.
Together — 10 faces. 10 is out.
And there's our edge: we reached 10 — so the insight points to 15.
A less obvious cut, to reach 11: cut off a corner.

lines.draw: Cut off one corner of the block

lines.say: The corner is a triangular pyramid: 3 faces plus a base — 4.
And the block now has 7 faces, not 6: the 6 it had, plus the new one.
7 plus 4 — 11. There are other ways to reach 11 — we showed one.
Three out — mark the fourth.
15 — choice two.

beats.title: Why not 15

lines.say: Want a proof? Each original face ends up in at most two pieces — at most 12 faces.
Plus the two new cut faces — 14 at most. 15 is impossible.
So — a trial-and-error question in geometry.

lines.say: A rectangle tightly holds two rows of n equal circles, radius r, each tangent to its neighbors.
How many tangency points are there between the circles and the sides of the rectangle?
Start with understanding. The rectangle has 4 sides: the bottom, the top, and the two short sides.
Check how many tangency points each side has with the circles. Start with the bottom.
Each circle in the bottom row touches the bottom once. n circles — n tangency points.
And by symmetry the same for the top: the top row — n points.
Now the right side. Here the number doesn't depend on n: the two end circles touch it — 2 points. The left side too — 2.
Altogether: 2n plus 4. Careful — with one row it would be 2n plus 2. Here there are two rows.
Choice four. That was the understanding approach.

beats.title: Plugging in

fig.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="125.5 41.7 388.9 276.6" role="img" aria-label="Two rows of congruent tangent circles in a tight rectangle"><title>Two rows of congruent tangent circles in a tight rectangle</title><polygon points="151.538,292.308 488.462,292.308 488.462,67.692 151.538,67.692" fill="none" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><circle cx="207.692" cy="236.154" r="56.154" fill="#e8eefb" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5"/><circle cx="207.692" cy="123.846" r="56.154" fill="#e8eefb" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5"/><circle cx="320.000" cy="236.154" r="56.154" fill="#e8eefb" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5"/><circle cx="320.000" cy="123.846" r="56.154" fill="#e8eefb" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5"/><circle cx="432.308" cy="236.154" r="56.154" fill="#e8eefb" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5"/><circle cx="432.308" cy="123.846" r="56.154" fill="#e8eefb" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5"/></svg>

lines.say: Now let's solve it by plugging in. You can plug in any number for n — usually small ones.
But in questions like this, plugging in 1 or 2 usually gives two or more matching answers.
Look — n equals 2 gives 8 for two different answers.
So plug in 3: small enough to count easily — and usually only one answer fits.

lines.draw: Sketch two rows of 3 circles in a rectangle and mark the tangency points

lines.say: Count: 3 on the top, 3 at the bottom, 2 on each short side — 10.
Plug 3 into the answers. Anything that isn't 10 — out.
2n plus 2 — 8, out. 4n — 12, out. n squared plus 2 — 11, out. 2n plus 4 — 10.
Choice four.
That's it — we've finished geometric understanding, and in fact we've finished geometry altogether.
Let's go to the summary of this topic.

items.t: End of the section + 'none must be true' → suspicious!
Flexible drawing: can I change it and keep every given?

lines.say: PQRS is a trapezoid — PS parallel to QR. ST is perpendicular to QR. Which statement must be true?
We need to decide who's bigger: triangle STR, or trapezoid PQTS.
At first glance — easy. We can see the trapezoid is bigger than the triangle.
But notice: this is a high-difficulty question. It sits at the end of the section.
And among the answers there's 'none of the other statements must be true'.

lines.label: End of section + 'none must be true' → suspicious! appears

lines.say: All these facts should make me suspect: this question isn't as innocent as it looks.
We call these flexible-drawing questions.

lines.label: Flexible drawing: can I change it and keep every given? appears

lines.say: Here we ask: do we have enough givens to rely on the drawing?
If the drawing is fixed — usually we can tell. If it's flexible — sometimes we can tell which area is bigger, and sometimes not.

lines.say: So how do we start? We exaggerate the drawing — and check that every given still holds.
Look at the legs PQ and SR. Right now they look about equal — but nobody said the trapezoid is isosceles.
By the way — if it were isosceles, the trapezoid would clearly be bigger than the triangle.
But leg SR could be much longer than it looks.

lines.draw: Extend QR far to the right and redraw SR to the new R

lines.say: For example: stretch the base QR — really stretch it to the right. The leg gets much longer.
Drawn like this, it's pretty clear the triangle is bigger than the trapezoid.
Did we break a given? PS is still parallel to QR — still a trapezoid. ST is still perpendicular to QR.
Every given survived. So the drawing CAN look like this — and then the triangle is the bigger one.

lines.say: So who's bigger? We can't know. What does it depend on?
The trapezoid's area: the sum of the bases, times the height, over 2.
The triangle's area: its base TR, times the same height, over 2.

lines.label: Same height → compare TR with PS + QT appears

lines.say: If TR equals the sum of the trapezoid's bases — the areas are equal.
If TR is bigger than that sum — the triangle is bigger. And the other way round.
Here we don't have enough givens to decide.

Ava: one equals two. Noah: two equals three. Mia: one plus three equals two plus four.
At first glance all the regions look almost equal — about a quarter of the circle each.
So we check: is this drawing flexible? Look at the givens.
AB is a diameter — the longest chord in the circle. It splits the circle into two equal halves.
But CD — why didn't they call it a diameter? It could look like one.

lines.label: AB: diameter ✓ · CD: only a chord! appears

lines.say: They didn't say it. They only said the chords are perpendicular.
So we can exaggerate — the drawing is flexible. CD can sit lower, almost at B, or higher.
It's still perpendicular to AB, and it's still a chord.

I $+$ IV $=$ half the disk III $=$ IV $\Rightarrow$ I $+$ III $=$ half

lines.say: Ava says area one equals area two. We can see it's true — in the first picture and in the exaggerated one.

lines.label: Diameter = line of symmetry: I = II, IV = III appears

lines.say: A diameter is a line of symmetry: what's on one side of it equals what's on the other. Ava is right.
Noah: two equals three.
Look at the exaggerated picture: two and three aren't equal. Before, they only looked equal.
Not necessarily true — Noah is out.
Mia: one plus three equals two plus four. That's true.

lines.label: I + IV = half the disk, III = IV → I + III = half appears

lines.say: One equals two, three equals four. One and four together are half the circle — so one and three together are half too.
And two and four together — also half. So Mia is right.

lines.say: ABCD is a parallelogram with diagonal AC. Angle BAC is 45. Beta — angle ABC — is between 0 and 80.
Alpha is angle CAD. What's the exact range of alpha?
Notice: every answer gives alpha a minimum and a maximum.
So what we have here is a min–max question in geometry. How do we solve it? We check the edges.
What does that mean? First we need the link between alpha and beta.
Vertices A and B of a parallelogram complete each other to 180 — adjacent angles.
So the bigger beta gets, the smaller alpha gets. And the smaller beta gets — the bigger alpha.

lines.say: They gave beta a range: less than 80 — and obviously more than 0.
Check the edge. What happens as beta approaches 80? We don't plug in 79.999 forever — we plug in 80.
80 plus 45 is 125. So alpha is 55.
But understand: beta can't actually be 80 — it has to be smaller.
A little smaller beta — a little bigger alpha. So alpha must be MORE than 55.
You can see it by exaggerating the drawing too: push beta up toward 80 — alpha shrinks toward 55, but never gets there.
Now the answers: choices one and three let alpha go below 55 — out.
Choices two and four start at 55 — they fit.

lines.say: We checked beta at its maximum and found alpha's minimum.
Now: what happens when beta is at its minimum? It approaches 0 — check it at 0.
0 plus 45 plus something is 180. That something is 135.
But beta is more than 0 — it can't really be 0. So alpha must be a little less than 135.
Exaggerate again: beta shrinks toward 0, alpha grows toward 135.
Choice two says 'less than or equal' — alpha could equal 55 or 135. That would need beta to be exactly 80 or 0 — impossible.
Choice four.

Alpha is less than beta, less than gamma, less than 90. Which statement cannot be true?
Another min–max question in geometry. We can solve it by geometric understanding from the drawing —
— but it's easier if we first make the drawing match the givens.
The rule: the more acute the angle, the more slanted the segment — and the longer it is.

lines.label: More acute angle → longer crossing appears

lines.say: Here the drawing already agrees: YZ at alpha is the most slanted, UV at gamma the steepest.
But always check! If all three angles looked equal — we'd redraw them: make alpha the sharpest, beta a bit less sharp, and leave gamma.
Think of a crosswalk between line a and line b. Straight across is the shortest. The more diagonal you cross — the longer the walk.
Why? Every crossing is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with the same height between the lines. More slant — longer hypotenuse.

lines.say: We're asked which statement is definitely NOT true.
WX less than YZ. Alpha is more acute than beta — so YZ is more slanted and longer. Always true.
Once the drawing matches the givens, you don't even need to think — you see it by eye.
It's always true — so it's out.
VX greater than WX. Here it's not so clear. VX is the distance between the lower endpoints — and nobody fixed where the segments sit.
I can move them apart, or closer. VX can be smaller than WX, equal to it, or bigger.
It's possible: not necessarily true, and not necessarily false. We're asked what's definitely false — so it's out.
UV greater than WX. Gamma is bigger than beta — so UV is steeper, and shorter.
UV is ALWAYS shorter than WX. UV greater than WX — never.
Choice three.
In the lesson we check the last one too: UV less than YZ — gamma is steeper than alpha, so it's always true.
So — another min–max question, and fixing the drawing made it a lot simpler.

lines.say: The opening of an angle.

lines.label: The farther the vertex from the segment, the smaller the angle appears
The same segment with the vertex nearer and farther appears

lines.say: Here's a segment, and here's the vertex. The distance — that's the perpendicular from the vertex down to the line.
If I move the vertex away — and away again — the angle gets smaller and smaller. It closes.
Move it really far, and it's almost completely closed.
And the closer I bring the vertex to the segment, the more it opens — until it almost reaches 180.

lines.draw: Write α < β < γ, from farthest to nearest

lines.say: So the farther away, the smaller: α is less than β, less than γ.

items.t: Vertex fixed, segment longer $\rightarrow$ the angle opens: $\alpha<\beta$

lines.say: Now the vertex stays at a fixed distance. I don't move it.

lines.label: A fixed vertex P, segment AB and the longer segment AC appear

lines.say: Instead, I change the segment the angle rests on. I make it longer.
Now the angle rests on the whole of this longer segment — so it grew. β is bigger than α.
You can even see it by eye: α sits inside β. It's contained in it. Very easy to see.

items.t: Farther from the arc $\rightarrow$ smaller angle: $\alpha<\beta<\gamma$

lines.say: Angles in a circle.

lines.label: A circle with an arc and three vertices, farther and farther away, appears

lines.say: Here's an arc, and an angle resting on it — γ.
If I take the vertex and move it away, I get angle β. It's smaller.
Move it even farther — I get α.

lines.label: Farther from the arc → smaller angle: α < β < γ appears

lines.say: Here too: the farther the vertex from the arc, the smaller the angle.
One warning from the course: moving along the circle itself doesn't change it — on the same arc, inscribed angles are equal.

lines.say: More on angles in a circle: an angle resting on a diameter.

lines.label: A diameter AB, a vertex inside the circle and a vertex outside appear

lines.say: Circle, diameter marked.
Why? If the vertex were on the circle, it's an inscribed angle on a diameter. That's 90 degrees.

lines.label: Inside: more than 90° · outside: less than 90° appears

lines.say: Vertex inside the circle — it's closer, it opens: β is more than 90.
Vertex outside the circle — farther away, it closes: α is less than 90.
90 is exactly in the middle — only ON the circle.

lines.say: A triangle with sides 9, 12 and 16. Angle α is opposite the 16. Which statement must be true?
Before I read the answers, let's look at what's given: α, 9, 12, 16.
Some fairly strong students will look and say: 9, 12, 15 — that's a right triangle! 3, 4, 5.
But it's not 15 — it's 16.

lines.label: The choices compare α with 90° → the anchor is 90° appears

lines.say: If you don't see that — look at the choices. α is compared with 90: less than 90, more than 90, equal to 90.
So the anchor is 90. I ask myself: if α were 90, what would happen?
If α were 90, it's a right triangle: 9, 12, 15. The triple 3, 4, 5 — times 3.

lines.label: 15 → 16: the side opposite α grew appears

lines.say: But this side isn't 15. It's 16 — it's bigger.
Remember the start of the lesson: a vertex, and the segment opposite it gets longer — the angle opens.
Think of the 9 and the 12 as two rods joined at α. To push their ends from 15 apart to 16 apart — you open the angle.
So α opened a bit past 90. It's greater than 90.
Choice two.

lines.say: A check from the course: 16 squared is 256. 9 squared plus 12 squared is 225.
The opposite side's square is bigger — the angle is more than 90.
Careful: '16 is the longest side' only tells you α is the biggest angle — not that it's more than 90. The anchor is what decides.
That's it for minimum–maximum — and that's the last of the geometry theory.
What can I wish you? That you do as well in the other topics as you do in geometry — and I'm waiting for you there too.
So — go up and succeed. Now: a few diagrams that can change.

lines.say: How do we test a claim? First way: change the shape — but keep every given condition.
Second: calculate a bound — a minimum, a maximum.
Third: build a counterexample. One allowed case where the claim fails — and 'must be true' is out.

lines.say: Two concentric circles, radii r and 1.4r. Liam: the outer circumference is 1.4 times the inner. Maya: the ring is bigger than the inner disk.
We need to decide: Liam, Maya, both, or neither.
Start with the math solution — circle rules, no similarity.
Circumference: 2 pi r. Outer radius 1.4r — times 2 pi: 2.8 pi r.
Inner radius r — 2 pi r. 2.8 is really 1.4 times 2. Liam is right.
So the answers that say otherwise — 'neither' and 'Maya only' — are out.
Now it's either Liam only, or both of them.

fig.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="166.2 26.2 307.5 307.5" role="img" aria-label="Concentric circles with radii in the ratio five to seven"><title>Concentric circles with radii in the ratio five to seven</title><circle cx="320.000" cy="180.000" r="127.750" fill="#d5f1ed" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><circle cx="320.000" cy="180.000" r="91.250" fill="white" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="320.000" y1="180.000" x2="320.000" y2="271.250" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="320.000" y1="180.000" x2="447.750" y2="180.000" stroke="#bb6821" stroke-width="2.5"/><circle cx="320.000" cy="180.000" r="3.2" fill="#203344"/><text x="304.000" y="225.625" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">r</text><text x="393.000" y="160.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">1.4r</text></svg>

lines.say: Maya: the ring is bigger than the white disk.
Shaded areas — a scheme: big circle minus small circle.
Big circle: pi times 1.4r squared. Small: pi r squared.
1.4 squared is 1.96. Minus 1 — the ring is 0.96 pi r squared.
And the white disk is pi r squared — 1. So 0.96 is LESS than 1.
Careful — this is close! With 1.5 the ring would be bigger. With 1.4, it isn't. Maya is wrong.
Choice three.

lines.say: Now the shorter way — with similarity.
First: similar shapes aren't only triangles. Circles are similar. Squares. Regular hexagons. Every regular shape.
Liam: in similar shapes the length ratio is kept. Radius times 1.4 — circumference times 1.4. Nothing to calculate. Liam is right.
Maya: from a length ratio to an area ratio — square it.
1 to 1.4 isn't comfortable — we don't like decimals. Expand it: 5 to 7. Same ratio.
Square it: 25 to 49. The small disk — 25 units. The big one — 49 units.
The ring: 49 minus 25 — 24 units. Less than 25. Maya is wrong.
Choice three.
Questions like this — much shorter with similarity.

lines.say: D and F are the midpoints of AB and AC. The trapezoid DBCF has area 15. What's the area of triangle ADF?
Step one: understand the given — D and F are midpoints.
DF is called a midpoint segment. One of its properties: it's always parallel to the third side.

lines.draw: Write α at D and α at B

lines.say: And then the top triangle is similar to the big one. Angle D is alpha — so angle B is alpha. Parallel lines.

lines.draw: Write β at F and β at C

lines.say: Angle F is beta — so angle C is beta.
The top triangle is similar to the big one.

lines.draw: Write x on AD and x on DB

lines.say: Call AD x. A midpoint — so DB is x, and all of AB is 2x. Ratio 1 to 2.

lines.draw: Write y on DF and 2y on BC

lines.say: So if DF is y, BC is 2y.

lines.draw: Drop the height from A; write h to DF and 2h to BC

lines.say: We need heights. The small triangle's height — h. The big one's — 2h. So the trapezoid's height is h.
Trapezoid: sum of the bases times the height over 2 — equals 15.
Times 2: 3yh is 30. Divide by 3: yh is 10. Keep it.
Triangle ADF: base y, height h, over 2 — 10 over 2 is 5.
Choice two.

lines.say: Now the psychometric way: length ratio squared equals area ratio.
Midpoint segment — length ratio 1 to 2. Square it: 1 to 4.
Small triangle — 1 unit. Big triangle — 4 units.
The trapezoid is big minus small: 3 units. And it's 15.
So one unit is 5 — and the small triangle is one unit. 5.
Choice two. Much shorter — and no unknowns.

lines.say: One more way — a property of the midpoint segment worth knowing.

lines.draw: Mark M, the midpoint of BC, and join D, F and M

lines.say: Two midpoints of sides? Find the midpoint of the third side by eye — and join all three.
What you always, always get: four identical triangles.
Another way to see it: three parallelograms — and a diagonal cuts each one into two equal triangles.
The trapezoid is three of these identical triangles. So each is 5 — and the top one too.
Choice two.
Which is best? If you know this rule — it's the shortest. If not — length ratio, area ratio.
And if you know neither — the full math with unknowns is always there.

lines.say: Two regular hexagons: areas 72 root 3 and 24 root 3. What's the ratio of their perimeters?
Start with math. A regular hexagon — six equilateral triangles. One triangle's area, times 6.
Call the first side a. a squared root 3 over 4, times 6, equals 72 root 3.
Cancel the 6, cancel root 3: a squared over 4 is 12 — a squared is 48. a is root 48 — 4 root 3.
Same for the second, side b: b squared over 4 is 4, b squared is 16, b is 4.

lines.say: Now with similarity. Two regular shapes from the same family — necessarily similar.
From the givens we get the area ratio. From the area ratio — the length ratio. And perimeter IS a length ratio.
72 root 3 is three times 24 root 3. Area ratio 3 to 1.
From length to area — we square. So from area back to length — we take the root.
Root 3 to root 1 — root 3 to 1. That's the perimeter ratio.
Choice four. Much, much shorter — all we did was go back from area ratio to length ratio.

lines.say: A sphere contains a smaller ball. The small ball's diameter is two thirds of the big sphere's radius. Difference of volumes over the small volume?
What are they asking? The small ball's volume — and the big one minus the small one.
First: two spheres are two similar 3D shapes.
So: length ratio cubed equals volume ratio.
What's the length ratio? The small diameter is two thirds of the big radius.
A diameter is two small radii — so the small radius is one third of the big radius. Ratio 1 to 3.
Careful — compare radius with radius, not diameter with radius.

lines.say: For the volume ratio — cube it. 1 cubed is 1, 3 cubed is 27. But we're not done.
Small ball — 1 unit. Big sphere — 27 units.
The difference: 27 minus 1 — 26 units. Difference over the small ball: 26 to 1.
Choice three.
Watch out for 27 to 1 — that's the whole sphere, before subtracting.

lines.say: A cone tank, radius r, height h. A cone cup: radius r over 3, height h over 4. How many cups fill the tank?
Full math with 3D: find both volumes and divide.
Cone: base area times height over 3. Pi r squared, times h, over 3.
The cup: pi times r over 3 squared — r squared over 9 — times h over 4. Over 3.
Save some work: both have the same denominator, 3. Just compare the numerators.
pi r squared h — and pi r squared h over 36. The tank is 36 times bigger.
Choice one.

lines.say: Now the psychometric way — partial similarity.
The cones aren't similar: the height was divided by 4, the radius by 3. Different changes.
But the bases are both circles — similar. And the heights are lines — similar.
So we look at how each part affects the volume.
The height is a line. Length ratio kept — height 4 times bigger, volume 4 times bigger.
The radius is 3 times bigger. Circles are similar — area ratio is the square: 9.
Total: times 4, times 9 — times 36.
Choice one.
Height changes the volume by the same factor. Radius changes it by the square.

lines.say: Triangle ABC. ED is parallel to AB. BD is 4, DC is 8, AE is 5. What's AC?
Step one: prove that the small triangle EDC is similar to the big triangle ABC.
How do we prove triangles are similar? On the psychometric, one rule is enough — angle, angle.
Two equal angles — and the triangles are similar.

lines.draw: Write α at A and α at E

lines.say: Call angle A alpha. ED is parallel to AB — so angle E is also alpha. Parallel lines, equal acute angles.

lines.draw: Write β at B and β at D

lines.say: Angle B — beta. Same argument: angle D is also beta.
And angle C? Shared by both triangles, of course.
Equal angles — similar triangles. The small EDC is similar to the big ABC.
From here — two ways. Let's start with the full math solution.

lines.say: To compare the triangles I need matching sides. Opposite equal angles — matching sides.
Opposite alpha in the small triangle: DC — 8. Opposite alpha in the big one: the whole side BC — 4 plus 8, 12.
Opposite beta in the small triangle: EC. We don't know it — call it x.
Opposite beta in the big triangle: AC. That's x plus 5.
Work in a fixed order: small triangle over big triangle.
DC over BC equals EC over AC. 8 over 12 equals x over x plus 5.
Cross-multiply. 12x equals 8x plus 40.
Gather the x's on the side with more x: 4x is 40, x is 10. That's EC.
They asked for AC: 10 plus 5 — 15.
Choice one.

In the small triangle, the ratio between the sides is 8 to x. In the big one: 12 to x plus 5.
By the way — swap the x and the 12 in the first equation, and you get exactly this one.
Solve it — the same x equals 10. Either way, both are correct.

lines.say: Now the psychometric way — through the parts of the sides.
The part BD matches the part DC. DC is exactly twice BD: 4 and 8 — a 1 to 2 ratio.
So the part AE matches the part EC — and EC must also be exactly twice AE.
AE is 5 — so EC is 10, and all of AC is 15. Much, much shorter.
You can also work across: AE is 5 and BD is 4 — times 1.25.
So EC is also DC times 1.25: 8 times 1.25 — 10. Same answer.
Which way is better? Here, clearly — the psychometric one. Significantly shorter.
Choice one.

items.t: All angles equal $\Rightarrow$ all three triangles similar

lines.say: ABC is a right triangle, right angle at C. DECF is a square, AF is 3, the square's side is x. What's BE?
First, understand: this object hides three similar triangles.
The big one ABC, the small top one ADF, and the small bottom one DBE.

lines.draw: Write 90° at C and α at A

lines.say: Let's prove it. In the big triangle: C is 90. Call angle A alpha.
So angle B is 90 minus alpha — completing to 180.

lines.draw: Write 90° at E and at F

lines.say: Bottom triangle DBE: angle E is 90 — the square's angle is 90, so the angle next to it is 90 too. Same for F.

lines.draw: Write α at angle BDE and 90° − α at angle ADF

lines.say: In DBE: 90, 90 minus alpha — so angle D is alpha. In the top one: 90 and alpha — the rest is 90 minus alpha.

lines.label: All angles equal → all three similar appears

lines.say: All the angles are equal — all three triangles are similar.

lines.draw: Write x on all four sides of the square

lines.say: A square — all sides are x.
We could compare the big triangle with a small one — or the two small ones.
Personally, I think the two small triangles give a simpler solution.
Opposite 90 minus alpha in the top triangle: AF — 3. In the bottom one: DE — x.
Opposite alpha in the top triangle: DF — x. In the bottom one: BE — what we're looking for.
Top triangle over bottom triangle, in a fixed order.
Plug in: 3 over x equals x over BE.
Looking for one of the four? Multiply diagonally, divide by the one left.
x times x — x squared — divided by 3.
Choice one.

lines.say: Now the psychometric way — plug in numbers.
Our automatic choice is usually 1. But is 1 convenient here?
x equals 1 means the legs of the top triangle are 3 and 1 — not a triangle we know. Not silver, not golden.
Simplest: plug in 3 — and create the most convenient special case. Silver triangles.

lines.draw: Write 3 on all four sides of the square

lines.say: x equals 3: now the top triangle's legs are 3 and 3. A silver triangle.
The two small triangles aren't just similar — they're identical, a 1 to 1 ratio.
So BE is 3 as well.
Now plug 3 into the answers. Which gives 3?
x squared over 3 — 9 over 3, really 3. Stays. x over 3 — 1, out. 3x — 9, out. x squared — 9, out.
Remember: plugging in only rules answers out. After three are out, one is left.
Choice one.
So — full math or plugging in? Pick what's comfortable.
Here, since we know the object has similar triangles and we can make a fast special case — I'd plug in 3.

items.t: Plugged-in angles only show what matches what — never real values

lines.say: Right triangle ABC, right angle at A. AD is perpendicular to BC, BD is 9, DC is 16. What's AD?
Again — a similarity object with three similar triangles: the left ABD, the right ADC, and the big ABC.
Until now we wrote alpha, then 90 minus alpha. Most students find it easier with a number.

lines.draw: Write 20° at C and 70° at B

lines.say: C is acute — plug in, say, 20 degrees. A is 90, so B is 70.

lines.draw: Write 20° and 70° at the two angles at A

lines.say: Left triangle ABD is also right-angled: 90 and 70 — so the angle at the top is 20. On the right: 90 and 20 — the top angle is 70.
20, 70, 90 in the big one, in the right one, in the left one. Equal angles — similar triangles.
A small warning: we may plug in angles only to see what matches what. Opposite equal angles — matching sides.
We may NOT plug in, say, 45 and 45, and then decide the triangle is silver — BD is 9, so AD is 9… and so is DC? Contradiction.

lines.say: Why is it hard? We have two numbers: 9 and 16. But an equation — fraction equals fraction — has four parts. We need three numbers.
Let's see how to handle it.
To find AD, compare triangles that contain AD — the left one and the right one.
This time I'll work inside the same triangle.
Left triangle: opposite 70 — the long leg, AD. Opposite 20 — the short leg, BD.
Right triangle: opposite 70 — the long leg, DC, 16. Opposite 20 — the short leg, AD.
Long leg over short leg — in both triangles.
AD appears twice — that's why two numbers are enough. One unknown.
Cross-multiply: AD squared is 144. Take the root: 12.
Choice three.

items.t: Congruent: same shape AND same size

lines.say: So first — what is similarity?

lines.label: Two triangles appear: the same shape, one bigger than the other

lines.say: Two shapes are similar when it's the same shape — just a different size.
I took a triangle and enlarged it. Same shape. One is bigger than the other.
And if the two shapes are exactly the same size?

lines.label: Congruent: same shape AND same size

lines.say: Then they're not just similar — they're congruent. The exact same shape.

beats.title: Matching lines

items.t: NOT diameter $\leftrightarrow$ chord — not the same kind of line
Linear ratio $=$ the ratio between two matching lines

lines.say: Linear ratio. What's a linear ratio?
When I have two similar shapes, I have matching lines between them.
Matching lines — the same kind of line.
Take two circles — they really are similar: a small circle and a big circle, the same shape.
If I compare a radius, what matches it in the other circle is the radius. Circumference with circumference.
What I can't do: take a diameter in one circle and a chord in the other. Not the same kind of line.

lines.label: Linear ratio = the ratio between two matching lines

lines.say: The linear ratio is the ratio between two matching lines.

beats.title: The linear ratio

v.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="36.0 46.0 568.0 276.0" role="img" aria-label="Two similar triangles with corresponding vertices A–D, B–E, C–F"><title>Two similar triangles with corresponding vertices A–D, B–E, C–F</title><polygon points="80.000,270.000 240.000,270.000 120.000,150.000" fill="#d5f1ed" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><polygon points="320.000,270.000 560.000,270.000 380.000,90.000" fill="#e8eefb" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><text x="68.000" y="286.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">A</text><text x="252.000" y="286.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">B</text><text x="120.000" y="132.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">C</text><text x="308.000" y="286.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">D</text><text x="572.000" y="286.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">E</text><text x="380.000" y="72.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">F</text><text x="160.000" y="296.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">4</text><text x="440.000" y="296.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">6</text></svg>

lines.label: The two similar triangles appear, with bases 4 and 6

lines.say: Here are two similar triangles. I took the small one and enlarged it.
The base here is 4, and the matching base there is 6.
These are matching lines — it's the same side of the triangle.
Right now we're not proving it — we're looking. Later we'll learn how to know what matches what.
So the linear ratio, small to large, is 4 to 6 — 2 to 3.
And that ratio is ALWAYS the same — for every pair of matching lines.

lines.draw: Write 8 on the left side of the small triangle and 12 on its partner

lines.say: I don't know the other sides. But whatever they are — the big one is one and a half times the small one.
If this side is 8, its partner is 12. If this one is 2, its partner is 3.

beats.title: Angles stay the same

v.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="36.0 46.0 568.0 276.0" role="img" aria-label="Two similar triangles with corresponding vertices A–D, B–E, C–F"><title>Two similar triangles with corresponding vertices A–D, B–E, C–F</title><polygon points="80.000,270.000 240.000,270.000 120.000,150.000" fill="#d5f1ed" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><polygon points="320.000,270.000 560.000,270.000 380.000,90.000" fill="#e8eefb" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><text x="68.000" y="286.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">A</text><text x="252.000" y="286.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">B</text><text x="120.000" y="132.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">C</text><text x="308.000" y="286.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">D</text><text x="572.000" y="286.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">E</text><text x="380.000" y="72.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">F</text><text x="160.000" y="296.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">4</text><text x="440.000" y="296.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">6</text></svg>

items.t: Angles: equal $\cdot$ lengths: one fixed ratio

lines.say: What's important to notice:

lines.draw: Mark the equal angles: A and D, B and E, C and F

lines.say: The angles of the two triangles don't change. They're identical.
This angle is equal to this one. The top angle — equal.

lines.label: Angles equal · lengths in one ratio

lines.say: The lengths grow — the angles stay. We'll use this later, in similar triangles.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Angles stay the same" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Not only sides

items.t: Heights $\cdot$ medians $\cdot$ diagonals $\cdot$ perimeters $\cdot$ even differences of sides

lines.say: Notice: the linear ratio isn't only between sides.
Not only the sides of the triangles — any pair of matching lines.

lines.label: Heights · medians · diagonals · perimeters · even differences

lines.say: Heights, medians, diagonals — even differences between sides. Side minus side — that matches too.
For example, two squares — squares are similar: a small one, a big one, the same shape.
If the big square's diagonal is twice the small one's — then its side is twice as long too.
And differences: sides 8 and 5, difference 3. Double the shape — 16 and 10, difference 6. Doubled too.
One ratio between one pair of matching lines — it holds for all of them.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Not only sides" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Area ratio

lines.say: Now — the area ratio.
In similar shapes, the ratio of the areas equals the linear ratio SQUARED.
If the linear ratio is 1 to 2 or 1 to 3 — the area ratio is that, squared.
Let's see why — or at least, let's see it.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Area ratio" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: A grid of squares

lines.label: A small square with side 2 and a big square with side 6 appear

lines.say: A small square with side 2. And a big square with side 6 — three times as long.
The linear ratio: 1 to 3.

lines.draw: Draw the grid: 3 small squares across and 3 rows up

lines.say: How many small squares fit inside the big one? 3 across, 3 rows.
1, 2, 3 … 9. Nine small squares.
So the linear ratio 1 to 3 — squared: 1 squared stays 1, 3 squared is 9. Area ratio 1 to 9.
Nine times the area — not three times.

lines.say: Another example — not with a square.

lines.label: A right triangle with legs 1, 2 and a bigger one with legs 4, 8 appear

lines.say: A right triangle with legs 1 and 2. A bigger one: legs 4 and 8.
The vertical leg grew 4 times. The horizontal leg — 4 times too. From 2 to 8.
These two are similar. Linear ratio 1 to 4.

lines.draw: Write the areas: 1 in the small one, 16 in the big one

lines.say: The areas: half of 1 times 2 — 1. Half of 4 times 8 — 16.
Sixteen small triangles fit inside the big one.
Exactly by the rule: 1 squared is 1, 4 squared is 16.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Triangles too" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Square both parts

lines.say: So remember — this is a very, very important rule.
Plenty of similarity questions are about exactly this: area ratio and linear ratio.
The ratio doesn't need a 1 in it. Linear 2 to 3 — square both parts — areas 4 to 9.
And backwards: areas 25 to 49 — take the root of both — the linear ratio is 5 to 7.
Have the linear ratio? Square it — you've got the area ratio.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Square both parts" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Circles

v.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="177.2 37.2 285.6 285.6" role="img" aria-label="Two equal disks with their diameters partitioning the diameter of a larger disk"><title>Two equal disks with their diameters partitioning the diameter of a larger disk</title><circle cx="320.000" cy="180.000" r="116.800" fill="#e8eefb" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><circle cx="261.600" cy="180.000" r="58.400" fill="#d5f1ed" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5"/><circle cx="378.400" cy="180.000" r="58.400" fill="white" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="203.200" y1="180.000" x2="436.800" y2="180.000" stroke="#bb6821" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="7 5"/></svg>

lines.say: Let's look at a circle.

lines.label: A big circle with two small circles on its diameter appears

lines.say: I take a circle — and enlarge it.

lines.draw: Mark the small circle's diameter, then the big circle's diameter

lines.say: Look at the small circle's diameter. The big circle's diameter is exactly twice as long.
So the linear ratio here is 1 to 2.
So the area ratio is 1 to 4. The small circle's area is exactly a quarter of the big circle's.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Circles" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: The man with glasses

v.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="177.2 37.2 285.6 285.6" role="img" aria-label="Two equal disks with their diameters partitioning the diameter of a larger disk"><title>Two equal disks with their diameters partitioning the diameter of a larger disk</title><circle cx="320.000" cy="180.000" r="116.800" fill="#e8eefb" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><circle cx="261.600" cy="180.000" r="58.400" fill="#d5f1ed" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5"/><circle cx="378.400" cy="180.000" r="58.400" fill="white" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="203.200" y1="180.000" x2="436.800" y2="180.000" stroke="#bb6821" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="7 5"/><text x="261.600" y="180.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">3 units</text><text x="378.400" y="180.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">3 units</text></svg>

lines.say: Why did I shade the small circles inside — and add another one?
This is a shape worth knowing. It repeats itself a LOT in the psychometric exam.

lines.label: The same figure appears, with 3 units in each small circle

lines.say: Say the area of this small circle is 3 units. The other one — the same circle — 3 as well.

lines.draw: Write 12 next to the big circle

lines.say: The big circle is 4 times bigger — 12.
The two small circles together: 6. So the big circle needs 6 more.

lines.draw: Write 3 in the top leftover and 3 in the bottom leftover

lines.say: Those 6 split into the top leftover and the bottom leftover — 3 each.
Meaning: the area of one small circle equals the area of this 'Batman' up here.
I call this shape the man with glasses — like Kenny from South Park, with a pair of binoculars.
Some questions ask: which is bigger — this area or the leftover? Instead of calculating and subtracting —
I just know: the white top leftover is exactly one small circle. We'll meet this again.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The man with glasses" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Similar $=$ same shape, other size $\cdot$ congruent $=$ same size too
Linear ratio: the same for every pair of matching lines

lines.say: Let's sum up the lesson.

lines.label: Similar = same shape, other size · congruent = same size too

lines.say: Similar shapes: the same shape, a different size. Exactly the same size — congruent.

lines.label: Linear ratio: the same for every pair of matching lines

lines.say: The linear ratio: between matching lines of the two shapes — always the same one.
And the area ratio is always the linear ratio squared.
That's our base for similarity. From here: similarity in regular shapes, then in non-regular ones.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Recap" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Similarity in Regular Shapes

lines.say: Similarity in regular shapes.
Regular shapes are ALWAYS similar.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Always similar

items.t: Always similar: circles $\cdot$ squares $\cdot$ equilateral triangles $\cdot$ regular hexagons…
Same number of sides! A regular pentagon is not similar to a regular hexagon.

lines.say: Why? Because they're regular — it's always the same shape.
Think of a circle. Every circle in the world looks exactly the same — just in different sizes.

lines.label: Circles · squares · equilateral triangles · regular hexagons…

lines.say: Same with squares. Same with equilateral triangles, regular hexagons.

lines.label: Same number of sides! A pentagon is not similar to a hexagon

lines.say: Just keep the number of sides the same: a regular pentagon and a regular hexagon — not similar.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Always similar" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Equilateral triangles

v.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="4.0 14.2 492.0 333.8" role="img"><title>Equilateral triangles, side ratio 1:3</title><polygon points="30,300 130,300 80,213.4" fill="#d5f1ed" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><polygon points="170,300 270,300 220,213.4" fill="#d5f1ed" stroke="none"/><line x1="220" y1="213.4" x2="420" y2="213.4" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="270" y1="126.8" x2="370" y2="126.8" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="270" y1="300" x2="370" y2="126.8" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="370" y1="300" x2="420" y2="213.4" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="370" y1="300" x2="270" y2="126.8" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="270" y1="300" x2="220" y2="213.4" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="1.8"/><polygon points="170,300 470,300 320,40.2" fill="none" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><text x="80" y="322" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">a</text><text x="320" y="322" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">3a</text></svg>

lines.say: First example: the equilateral triangle.
All equilateral triangles in the world are similar. All angles equal, all sides equal.

lines.label: A small equilateral triangle and one 3 times bigger appear

lines.say: The big one is really just an enlarged picture of the small one — side a, and side 3a.
How many small triangles fit into the big one?

lines.draw: Count the small triangles inside the big one: 1 to 9

lines.say: 1, 2, 3 … 9. Exactly what we learned last lesson.
Linear ratio 1 to 3 — the perimeter too. Area ratio 1 to 9. It works.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Equilateral triangles" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Squares

lines.say: Squares — also similar. The big square is just a slightly bigger version of the small one.
And the areas? Splitting it into pieces here would be hard — so we won't.
We just work with the method: linear ratio, and the area ratio — squared.
Linear ratio 4 to 7. Area ratio: 4 squared is 16, 7 squared is 49.
So if this square is 16 square centimetres — that one is 49. If it's 32 — 98. Exactly double. And so on.
Bottom line: 16 ratio units against 49 ratio units.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Squares" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Regular hexagons

lines.say: A regular hexagon — also a regular shape. So all regular hexagons are similar.
A small hexagon, a big hexagon. Linear ratio 3 to 5.
What's the area ratio? Try to think before I reveal it.
9 to 25. 3 squared is 9, 5 squared is 25.
No need to split each hexagon into six equilateral triangles. Similarity already did the work.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Regular hexagons" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT SLIDE → Circles: C is a line]

beats.title: Circles: C is a line

lines.say: Circles — we talked about them. Every circle is the same circle, just in another size.
Here the linear ratio is 2 to 5. The area ratio — as usual — 4 to 25.
But notice. Say they ask me: the small circle's circumference is 8 — what's the big one's?
Circumference is a line. So I stay with the linear ratio.
Small circumference 8 — the big one is 20. Two and a half times, like the radius.
I treat the circumference as a line — because that's what it is. Only for areas do we square.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Circles: C is a line" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

Regular — so we have similarity here.
We were just talking about perimeter.

The perimeter here: 8 sides — 8s.
And there: 4s plus 4s plus … eight times — 32s.

The answer, of course: 4. Choice three.

lines.say: AB is a diameter of a circle with radius 7. Four identical small circles sit on AB — their diameters fill it from A to B.
What's the sum of the circumferences of the four small circles?
Honestly, it bugs me that the radius is 7. Not convenient.
From A to B is 14. For one small circle's radius — 14 over 8, 7 quarters. An annoying number. A fraction.
Then 2π r with r equals 7 quarters… I can. I can even do it with algebra. But it's just annoying.
Lucky for us — we don't need to go there. We're in the similarity lesson.

lines.say: The small circles are similar to the big circle.
If I find the linear ratio between them — I'll find their circumference. Because circumference is a line.

lines.draw: Write r on a small radius and 4r on the big radius

lines.say: Small radius r. The big radius — four small diameters — 4r.
Linear ratio 1 to 4. Circumference is a line — so the circumferences are 1 to 4 too.
One small circumference is exactly a quarter of the big one.
And four of them together? Exactly the big circle's circumference.

items.t: Circles on a diameter: their circumferences add up to the big one

lines.say: The big circle's circumference — easy. I have the radius, I have the formula.
2π r: 2π times 7 — 14π. And that's also the sum of the small circumferences.
Choice three. See how easy that was with similarity — instead of radius 7 quarters, multiplying, the formula…

lines.label: Circles on a diameter: sum of circumferences = big circumference

lines.say: By the way — this object: a big circle with circles on its diameter.
The big circumference ALWAYS equals the sum of the small ones — no matter how many, even if they're different sizes.
Careful — only circumferences. The four small disks together cover just a quarter of the big AREA.

What's the ratio of the small disk to the area inside the big circle but outside the small one?
We can already see the linear ratio: the small diameter AC is a third of the big diameter AB.
Linear ratio 1 to 3. The area ratio — squared — 1 to 9.

lines.say: But they didn't ask for the small disk against the big disk.
They asked for the small disk against what's LEFT — outside it.
A small tip about answers: usually they don't confuse me — they help me.
In a harder question, the common mistake usually won't even be in the choices. It's a hint: read the question again.
But in a very easy question — the common-mistake answer CAN be there. Like here: 1 to 9 is choice 2. Don't fall for it.

lines.draw: Write 1 in the small disk and 9 next to the big circle

lines.say: Say the small disk is 1 unit. The big disk is 9.
The leftover isn't the whole big disk. It's the big disk minus the small one: 9 minus 1 — 8.
Small disk to leftover: 1 to 8.
Choice four.

beats.title: Similar Triangles and Rectangles

lines.say: Similarity in shapes that aren't regular.
Last lesson we did regular shapes — circles, squares, regular polygons. There the similarity is easy to see.
Now: shapes that aren't regular. The similarity is a bit harder to see — or rather, to know what matches what.
Let's start with triangles.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Two angles are enough

items.t: Similar triangles $=$ all the angles are equal
Two equal angles are enough — the third completes to $180°$

lines.label: Similar triangles: all angles equal appears

lines.say: Similar triangles are triangles whose angles are all equal.

lines.label: Two equal angles are enough appears

lines.say: By the way — it's enough that two angles are equal. If two are equal, the third obviously is too.
It has to complete to 180.
So if you see a 90 and an α in both triangles — that's all you need. They're similar.

items.t: Matching sides $=$ opposite the same angle

lines.label: Two similar right triangles appear, one turned

lines.say: Here are two similar triangles.

lines.draw: Mark the equal angles in both triangles

lines.say: Why similar? 90 and 90. The same α, the same β.
In similar triangles, the matching sides are the sides that sit opposite the same angles.

lines.label: Matching sides: opposite the same angle appears

lines.say: In a regular polygon there's no question of matching — every side is the same side.
In a triangle the sides are different: a short leg, a long leg, a hypotenuse.
So I have to be careful to compare the matching lines. How do I know which one matches?
I look at which angle the side is opposite.

lines.say: I strongly, strongly recommend this in similarity questions — and I'm telling you from years of experience.
Students always tried to work with ratios and division, the way they were taught in all kinds of places — and got tangled up.
Make a little table: small triangle, big triangle. Write the matching sides one opposite the other.

lines.draw: Draw a two-column table: small | big

lines.say: 6 is opposite α here — what's opposite α in the other triangle? 9. So 6 goes with 9.
8 is opposite β — opposite β over there: 12. And the hypotenuse, 10, goes with the hypotenuse, 15.
Every row, the same multiplier: times one and a half.
Once you have the table, it's very easy to see what matches what — and to find what's missing.

items.t: Use the angles — not left and right

lines.label: The two triangles appear, one of them turned

lines.say: Here it was easy — we just looked.
But notice: even if I took the triangle and turned it 90 degrees, or 180, or a little —
you'd still know which side matches. You just look at which angle the side is opposite.

lines.label: Use the angles, not left and right appears

lines.say: Not where it sits on the page. The angle.

beats.title: Ratios inside

items.t: A fraction is just a ratio: $4:5=8:10$

lines.say: Notice: the ratio between two sides in the SAME triangle is also equal in both triangles.
It's not only 'every side in the big one is one and a half times the small one'. Look —
6 over 8 — three quarters. 9 over 12 — also three quarters. Exactly the same.
Same with another pair: 8 over 10 — four fifths. 12 over 15 — four fifths.

lines.label: A fraction is a ratio: 4 : 5 = 8 : 10 appears

lines.say: Until now we wrote ratios with a colon, 1 to 2. A fraction is exactly the same thing.
I write it as a fraction because it's easier to see — fractions you know how to reduce.

beats.title: Parallel to the base

lines.say: Now: how does similarity of triangles usually show up on the exam?
Type one — a line parallel to the base.

lines.label: Triangle ABC with DE parallel to BC appears

lines.say: I draw a line inside the triangle, parallel to the base. DE parallel to BC.

lines.draw: Mark α at B and β at C; mark α at D and β at E

lines.say: Parallel lines — so the angle at D equals the angle at B, and the angle at E equals the angle at C.
Small triangle ADE, big triangle ABC. Same angles — similar.
This type is a bit confusing. Here's why.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow from DE to BC

lines.say: BC is opposite the angle at A. In the small triangle, opposite that angle — DE. So DE matches BC.
Now AE. The common mistake: students say AE matches EC.
But EC isn't a side of either triangle at all! It's a leg of the trapezoid.

lines.label: AE ↔ AC, AD ↔ AB, DE ↔ BC appears

lines.say: AE is opposite β in the small triangle. Opposite β in the big one — the WHOLE side AC.
And the same way, AD matches the whole AB.
Once you catch this, you won't make the mistake. Always check which angle you're opposite.

lines.say: Type two — 'diagonal similarity': an altitude to the hypotenuse.

lines.label: A right triangle with the altitude to the hypotenuse appears

lines.say: I draw a line that's NOT parallel to the base — but the angles still match, crossed over.

lines.draw: Mark the right angles at A and at D; mark the shared angle at B

lines.say: 90 and 90. The angle at B is shared. Two equal angles — the third completes to 180. Similar.
Why do I call it 'altitude to the hypotenuse'? I could draw some slanted line in any triangle —
but on the psychometric that's very unlikely. In most cases it will appear only in a right triangle.
The table. Small triangle ABD, whole triangle CBA.

lines.label: AB ↔ CB, BD ↔ BA, AD ↔ CA appears

lines.say: The hypotenuse of the small one, AB, matches the hypotenuse of the whole one, CB.
And here's what's different: the matching sides sit in different places in the drawing.
AB is a hypotenuse in the small triangle — but a leg in the big one. So again: opposite which angle?
With 6, 8, 10: the factor is 6 to 10, three fifths — so BD is 3.6 and AD is 4.8.

v.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="145.9 35.7 348.3 290.6" role="img" aria-label="Two similar triangles between parallel lines in an hourglass arrangement"><title>Two similar triangles between parallel lines in an hourglass arrangement</title><polygon points="236.571,75.714 403.429,75.714 320.000,159.143" fill="#d5f1ed" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><polygon points="320.000,159.143 194.857,284.286 445.143,284.286" fill="#e8eefb" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><text x="219.571" y="61.714" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">A</text><text x="420.429" y="61.714" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">B</text><text x="338.000" y="159.143" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">C</text><text x="177.857" y="300.286" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">D</text><text x="462.143" y="300.286" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">E</text></svg>

lines.say: Type three — the hourglass.

lines.label: Two triangles between parallel lines in an hourglass appear

lines.say: Two parallel lines, AB parallel to DE, closed by two crossing lines. Two triangles.

lines.draw: Draw the Z between the parallels and mark the equal angles

lines.say: Parallel lines — the angles are equal. α equals α: that's the Z between the parallels.
It looks more like an S — we still call it Z, it's a zigzag that helps us see the equal angles.
And the angles at C are vertical angles — equal too.

lines.label: AB ↔ ED, AC ↔ EC, BC ↔ DC appears

lines.say: The table: the two bases match. And notice — here a side matches its own continuation through C.
AC matches EC. BC matches DC.
So that's how triangle similarity shows up on the exam: parallel to the base, the altitude to the hypotenuse, and the hourglass.

lines.say: Now similarity in other shapes that aren't regular — rectangles.
To know two rectangles are similar I must check BOTH the ratio of the widths and the ratio of the lengths.
If the width grows 2 times but the height 3 times — the rectangles are NOT similar.

lines.draw: Write × 2 by the lengths and × 2 by the widths

lines.say: 5 to 10 — times 2. 3 to 6 — times 2. Same ratio — similar.
Another way: compare inside the same rectangle, length to width. 5 to 3 — and 10 to 6, which is also 5 to 3.
Length ratio 1 to 2 — so the area ratio is 1 to 4.

items.t: Length $:$ width is the same in both rectangles
Leftovers too: subtract matching lengths from matching totals

lines.say: On the psychometric, rectangle-similarity questions usually look like this —

lines.label: A small rectangle on the diagonal of a big rectangle appears

lines.say: A rectangle, a diagonal through it — and on the diagonal, another rectangle.
Then the two rectangles are similar. We could prove it — let's skip that and understand what it means.

lines.label: Length : width equal in both appears

lines.say: The ratio of length to width in the big rectangle equals the ratio in the small one.

lines.draw: Shade the right triangle APQ and mark its two legs

lines.say: A right triangle forms here — its legs are the small rectangle's length and width.
Sometimes it's about leftover pieces: the top part to the bottom part equals the right part to the left part.

lines.label: Leftovers too: use matching remainders appears

lines.say: Just subtract matching lengths from matching totals — a width from a width, a height from a height.
So when you see a rectangle inside a rectangle with its corner on the big one's diagonal — they're similar.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Match sides opposite equal angles — make a small–big table
On the exam: parallel to the base · altitude to the hypotenuse · hourglass
Rectangles: both dimensions use one factor
Also similar: 3 proportional side pairs — or 2 pairs and the angle between them

lines.say: Two equal angles — similar.

lines.label: Match sides opposite equal angles — small–big table appears

lines.say: Match by the angles — and make the table.

lines.label: Parallel to the base · altitude to hypotenuse · hourglass appears

lines.say: The three exam pictures.

lines.label: Rectangles: both dimensions, one factor appears

lines.say: Rectangles: both dimensions, one factor.

lines.label: Also similar: 3 proportional sides, or 2 + the angle between appears

lines.say: And from the course, two more ways to prove it: all three sides in the same ratio, or two sides in the same ratio and the angle between them equal.

beats.title: Similar Triangles Question

lines.say: Let's solve an example.

lines.say: In triangle ABC, DE is parallel to BC. AD is 3, DB is 2.
What's the ratio of the small triangle's area to the TRAPEZOID's area?
Careful — the second shape isn't the big triangle. It's what's left, the trapezoid below.
The common mistake: the length ratio is NOT 3 to 2.
That 2, DB, isn't a side of the triangle at all. It's a side of the trapezoid.
As always, the best way to check what matches: which angle is each side opposite?

lines.draw: Mark the equal angles at D and at B

lines.say: AD is opposite the angle at E. In the big triangle, the side opposite the matching angle — the whole AB.
AD is 3. AB is 3 plus 2 — 5.
So the length ratio between the triangles is 3 to 5 — to the WHOLE AB.

lines.say: From here, the area ratio is easy.
Length ratio 3 to 5 — area ratio squared: 9 to 25.

lines.draw: Write 9 in the small triangle and 25 beside the whole triangle

lines.say: Say the small triangle is 9. The whole big triangle is 25.
What's left is the trapezoid: 25 minus 9.
16 — so that the big triangle really is 25.
Small triangle to trapezoid: 9 to 16.
Choice four.
9 to 25 is a trap: that's small against the whole, not against the trapezoid. And 3 to 5 forgot to square.

lines.say: Start with a regular shape in 3D — the cube.
It's easy to see that all the cubes in the world are similar — like all the squares in the world.

lines.label: A big cube built from 3 × 3 × 3 small cubes appears

lines.say: A small cube, and a big cube whose edge is 3 times longer. Length ratio 1 to 3.
How many times does the small cube fit into the big one? Let's count.
One layer — 3 by 3 — 9 cubes.
And three layers. 27.
Length 1 to 3. Area — squared — 1 to 9. Volume — cubed — 1 to 27.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Cubes: count them" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Cylinders: check both

lines.say: The cube was easy because it's regular.
A cylinder or a cone isn't regular — so they're not always similar.

lines.label: Two cylinders: radii 2 and 4, heights 4 and 8 appear

lines.say: Cylinders are similar only if the ratio is the same for the radii AND for the heights.
And when I say cylinders — the same goes for cones.

lines.draw: Write 2 : 4 by the radii and 4 : 8 by the heights

lines.say: The radii: 2 to 4 — 1 to 2. The heights: 4 to 8 — reduce the fraction — also 1 to 2.
The same ratio in both. These cylinders are similar.
So the areas are squared — 1 to 4. And the volumes cubed — 1 to 8.
Very important with cylinders and cones: check that the shapes really ARE similar.
If only the radius doubled — not similar, and the cube rule doesn't apply.

beats.title: Similar Solids Question

lines.say: Let's see an example of a question.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Area → length

lines.say: The area of one face of a big cube is 16 times the area of one face of a small cube.
How many small cubes fill the big cube?
They're mixing us up a little: we're given not an edge, but an area — an area ratio.
And at the end they ask about volumes. I need an in-between step.
First: cubes are similar shapes. Area ratio equals the length ratio squared.
The area ratio is 1 to 16.
To go from an area ratio to a length ratio — take the square root. The edges: 1 to 4.

beats.title: Length → volume

lines.say: Now that I have the length ratio, 1 to 4 — to get the volume ratio I raise it to the power of three.
1 to 4 cubed: 1 to 64.
You can see it: a layer of 4 by 4 — 16 — and 4 layers. 64.
So if the small cube's volume is 1, the big cube's volume is 64. 64 small cubes fit in.
Choice three.
16 is the area ratio — not the volume. 256 is sixteen squared — the mistake of using 16 as the edge.

beats.title: Volume Changes

lines.say: Volume ratios.
Questions that ask about a change in volume — how many times it grew, how many times it shrank.
In most cases we can tell without really plugging the data into the formula — just by understanding how the change affects the volume.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: Cube edge × 4

lines.say: The edge of a cube is made 4 times longer. How many times does the volume grow?
Length, width and height — each is now like 4 cubes.
One layer: 4 by 4, 16 cubes. And 4 layers — 64 cubes.
Now let's understand why — with the formula.
The volume of a cube: the edge cubed. Make the edge 4a.
Open the brackets: the 4 is cubed — 64. And the a is cubed — a cubed. That's the original volume.
So the original volume grew 64 times. The 4 itself went to the power of three.
When you enlarge a cube's edge by some number — the volume grows by that number cubed.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Cube edge × 4" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Height only

lines.say: A cylinder or a cone: the volume changes according to what they changed in the radius and the height.
It won't always be cubed or squared. It depends what they changed, and by how much.

lines.label: A cylinder made five times taller appears

lines.say: If they changed only the height, without touching the radius — the volume changes in direct proportion.
Imagine a soda can. Make it twice as tall — put another can on top. The volume? Also twice.
Another can on top — three times the height, three times the volume.
Here, five cans stacked: height times 5, volume times 5.
As long as I don't touch the radius, the volume changes exactly like the height.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Height only" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Radius only

lines.say: Our problem is when they change the radius.
When the radius changes, the volume changes by the SQUARE of the change.
Radius times 2 — volume times 2 squared: 4. Radius times 3 — volume times 9.
Here it's hard to see — the original cylinder sits inside the wider one. So let's see it in the formula.
The volume of a cylinder: π r squared times h.
The new radius is 2r. Open the brackets with the power — every term inside is squared: 4 r squared.
Take the 4 outside: 4 times π r squared h — and π r squared h is the original volume.
Where did the 4 come from? I took the 2 and squared it. Brackets first — or you lose a 2.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Radius only" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

lines.say: By the way — a cone works the same way.

lines.label: A cone with radius r and height h appears

lines.say: With a cone it's hard to see even with the height.
In the cylinder I could see cans stacked. In a cone — hard. But it's true.
The cone's volume is the cylinder's divided by 3. Make the height 5h, take the 5 outside —
5 times the original cone. The divide-by-3 is in both, so it doesn't matter.
Height times 5 — volume times 5. Radius times 2 — volume times 4. Same as the cylinder.

beats.title: Both change

items.t: Both $\times k$ $\rightarrow$ $k^2\cdot k=k^3$ — the similar-solids rule

lines.say: From the course — what if both change? Just multiply the separate factors.
Radius twice: 4. Height five times: 5. Volume 20 times.
Halve the radius — a quarter. Triple the height — three quarters. Taller, but LESS volume.

lines.label: Both × k → k² · k = k³ appears

lines.say: And if both change by the same k — k squared times k, k cubed. That's the similarity rule again.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Both change" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Factor vs percent

lines.say: Last thing — read what they ask.
Four times the volume is an increase of three original volumes — 300 percent.
Three quarters of the volume — a decrease of 25 percent, not 75.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Cylinder or cone: check what changed, and by how much
Height $\times n$ $\rightarrow$ volume $\times n$ $\quad$ Radius $\times n$ $\rightarrow$ volume $\times n^2$

lines.say: Let's sum up.

lines.label: Cube: edge × n → volume × n³ appears

lines.say: A cube — the volume grows by the change cubed.

lines.label: Cylinder / cone: check what changed appears

lines.say: A cylinder or a cone — I must check what changed and by how much.

lines.label: Height × n → × n · radius × n → × n² appears

lines.say: If the height changes — the volume changes in exactly the same way. If the radius changes — squared.

lines.say: Twelve identical cubes, edge 1, are joined into a block. Which arrangement has the smallest total surface area?
Notice — this is a minimum–maximum question in geometry.
Surface area is the sum of ALL the faces — including the ones we can't see: the back, the bottom.
Instead of formulas — let's count. One small face is 1 square centimetre.
And every block is symmetric: what you count at the front is also at the back. Top equals bottom. Right equals left.
So count three directions — and double.
Choice one, 1 by 3 by 4: front 12, top 4, side 3. 19, times 2 — 38. Remember it.
Choice two, 2 by 2 by 3: 6, 6 and 4 — 16, times 2 — 32.
Already smaller than 38. We want the smallest — so choice one is out. Out of time? You already know that much.

lines.draw: Next to choice 3 write 2(12 + 12 + 1) = 50 and cross it out

lines.say: Choice three, the long stick 1 by 1 by 12: 12, 12 and 1 — 25, times 2 — 50. Bigger. Out.

lines.draw: Next to choice 4 write 2(12 + 6 + 2) = 40 and cross it out

lines.say: Choice four, 1 by 2 by 6: 12, 6 and 2 — 20, times 2 — 40. Also out.
Trial and error: we checked, we counted — choice two, 32. Not hard. But long.

lines.say: Now let's solve it with understanding. A psychometric flash.
When is the surface area smallest? Think backwards — when is it the LARGEST?
Each cube has 6 faces. Twelve cubes lying apart — 72 faces. Nothing is lost. That's the maximum.
Now start pushing them together. Every time two cubes touch —
— two faces disappear. One from each cube.
So the more they touch — the smaller the surface area.

lines.label: Most compact → smallest surface area appears

lines.say: Smallest area = the most compact shape — the one closest to a cube.
Which of the four is closest to a cube? 2 by 2 by 3. Choice two — without counting a single face.
Got it in advance? Well done. Now you have — next time, no hard work.

lines.say: A sample question — a hard one.
Inscribed and circumscribed — we met these in circles, and they show up in 3D too.
Three approaches: full math, plugging in numbers, and estimating.

beats.title: Approach 1 · Full math

lines.say: A cylinder is inscribed in a box. The square base has side 2a, the height is 3a. What fraction of the box is outside the cylinder?
Cylinder volume: base area times height. A straight solid.
We want everything in terms of a — no r. So look at the base.

lines.draw: On the top view, mark the diameter along the side 2a

lines.say: The circle sits inside the square: the side of the square is the diameter. So 2r = 2a — the radius is a.
Pi a squared, times the height 3a: 3 pi a cubed.
The box — multiply the dimensions: 12a cubed.
Outside is box minus cylinder. Divide by the box — a cubed cancels. 1 minus pi over 4.
Choice three. That's the full solution — and it's long.

beats.title: Approach 2 · Plug in numbers

lines.say: We learned it in circles: inscribed–circumscribed? Plug in numbers — don't fight with letters.
Usually we'd think 1 is the easiest number.

lines.label: a = 1: choices 1, 2 and 3 all become 1 − π/4 appears

lines.say: But look at the answers: with a = 1, choices one, two and three all turn into 1 minus pi over 4. It can't separate them.
So pick a convenient number that isn't 1. a = 2.
Box: 4 by 4 by 6 — 96. Cylinder: radius 2, height 6 — 24 pi.
Outside over the box: 1 minus pi over 4.

lines.draw: Cross out choice 1 (1 − π/8) and choice 2 (1 − π/2)

lines.say: Now put a = 2 in the answers. Choice one — 1 minus pi over 8. Out. Choice two — 1 minus pi over 2. Out.

lines.draw: Cross out choice 4 and circle choice 3

lines.say: Choice four has no a — 1 minus pi over 2. Not ours. Choice three. The recommended approach — the safest.
