beats.title: Approach 3 · Estimate

fig.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="189.7 49.7 260.6 284.6" role="img" aria-label="Top view: a circle inscribed in a square of side 2a"><title>Top view: a circle inscribed in a square of side 2a</title><polygon points="215.714,284.286 424.286,284.286 424.286,75.714 215.714,75.714" fill="#edf3f7" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><circle cx="320.000" cy="180.000" r="104.286" fill="#d5f1ed" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="320.000" y1="180.000" x2="424.286" y2="180.000" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5"/><circle cx="320.000" cy="180.000" r="3.2" fill="#203344"/><text x="372.143" y="162.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">a</text><text x="320.000" y="308.286" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">2a</text></svg>

lines.say: Third approach — psychometric thinking, estimating sizes.
Remember the rule from circles: make the shape bigger or smaller — the ratio stays the same.

lines.label: Volume ÷ volume: a must cancel appears

lines.say: Volume over volume — the a's cancel and we get a fixed number. Same for area over area, perimeter over perimeter.
So any answer with an a in it is a distractor. Choices one and two — out.
Choice four: pi over 2 is about 1.57. 1 minus 1.57 — negative. A part of the box can't be a negative fraction.

lines.draw: Cross out choice 4 and circle choice 3

lines.say: Choice three. And it makes sense: pi over 4 is about three quarters — the cylinder is about three quarters of the box. A quarter is outside.
Three approaches: full math — not recommended. Plugging in — the safest. Estimating — depends on the answers.
Here the estimate knocked out all three. Sometimes it only knocks out some.

lines.say: A pyramid is cut out of a cube: its base is the whole bottom face, its apex on the top face. 54 is left. What was the pyramid's volume?
Build a scheme: cube minus pyramid equals what's left.
No edge is given — call it a. The cube: a cubed.
The pyramid — a pointed solid. With the same base and the same height, it's a third of the cube.
Solve: two thirds of a cubed is 54.
a cubed is 81. And here — a isn't even a whole number. But we don't need a! The pyramid is a cubed over 3: 27.
Choice one.

The pointed solid is a third of the straight solid. So what's left — two thirds.
In ratio units: the pyramid is one unit. The whole cube — three. What's left — two.
What do we know? What's left is 54. So two units are 54.
One unit — divide by 2. 27. Done.
Choice one. Simple and easy.
Volume ratios are a tool that really helps on the psychometric.

lines.draw: Draw the diagonals of the base

lines.say: The diagonals cut the square into 4 silver triangles — right and isosceles.
From hypotenuse to leg — divide by root 2. 2 root 2 over root 2 — 2. So OB is 2.
Leg 2, hypotenuse 5. Not a triple we know — so full Pythagoras.
h squared plus 4 is 25. h squared is 21.
21 has no whole root: h is root 21.
Choice two. That's the math solution.

lines.say: Now the psychometric solution — estimating sizes.
Look at the height. If the lateral edge is 5 — must the height be less than 5?
The height is the SHORTEST distance from the apex to the base. The edge is slanted — longer.
So the height is less than 5. Our anchor: root 25 is exactly 5.
5 root 2 — root 2 is about 1.4. About 7. Too big. Out.
Root 21 — less than root 25. Possible. Not certain yet — but possible. Don't cross it out.
Root 29 — more than root 25. More than 5. Out.
3 root 3 — that's root 27. Also more than 5. Out.
Three out — mark the fourth. Choice two.
Two ways: full math — and here the psychometric solution was much shorter.

lines.say: The edge of the cube is 3 root 2. What's the area of triangle BDG?
Triangle area: base times height over 2. Take BD as the base, and drop a height from G to BD.

lines.draw: Mark M, the midpoint of BD, and draw GM

lines.say: BD is a diagonal of the bottom square. Square diagonal — a silver triangle: side times root 2.
3 root 2 times root 2 — 6.

lines.draw: Draw CM and mark the right angle at C

lines.say: Now the height. The edge CG — 3 root 2 — stands straight up, so it's perpendicular to CM on the base. A right triangle.
The diagonals of the square halve each other: CM is half of 6 — 3.
Leg 3, leg 3 root 2. Not golden, not silver, not a triple — full Pythagoras. 9 plus 18 — 27.
The height is 3 root 3.

items.t: Edge and a diagonal of another face $\rightarrow90°$
Edge and a diagonal of the same face $\rightarrow45°$

lines.say: Let's use this question to meet three situations worth knowing — angles between lines in a cube.

lines.label: Edge ⊥ a diagonal of another face → 90° appears

lines.draw: Mark the right angle between CG and CM

lines.say: One: an edge and a diagonal on the face it stands on. The edge is perpendicular to the base — 90 degrees.

lines.label: Edge and a diagonal of the same face → 45° appears

lines.say: Two: an edge and a diagonal on the same face. A diagonal in a square — 45.

lines.label: Two diagonals of different faces → 60° appears

lines.say: Three: two diagonals on different faces, from the same corner. Always, always, always 60.
Why? Connect the third diagonal — all three are equal, an equilateral triangle — just like BDG.

What is this triangle made of?

lines.draw: Label AE 'edge', EG 'face diagonal', AG 'body diagonal'

lines.say: AE — an edge. EG — a diagonal on the top face. AG — a diagonal through the inside of the cube.
The edge is 2.
EG — a diagonal on a square with side 2. Two silver triangles: leg to hypotenuse, times root 2. 2 root 2.

lines.draw: Mark the right angle at E

lines.say: And angle AEG is 90 — we just learned it: an edge and a diagonal of another face.
So a right triangle. Two legs — Pythagoras: 4 plus 8 — 12.
Root 12 — 2 root 3.
Perimeter: 2 plus 2 root 2 plus 2 root 3.
Choice four.

We built two right triangles — a face diagonal, then Pythagoras. There's a simpler way. Why?
In a cube all the edges are equal — so there's a fixed ratio between the edge and the diagonal.

lines.label: Face diagonal = a√2 · body diagonal = a√3 appears

lines.say: The inner diagonal is always root 3 times the edge.
How to remember: a diagonal in a square — root 2. A cube is a 3D square — root 3.
A similar question was on the exam: edge 5, what's the diagonal? 5 root 3. Instantly.
The other way round? Diagonal 18 — divide by root 3. Our method: ignore the root, 18 over 3 is 6, attach the root — 6 root 3.

lines.say: What about a box?
Unlike a cube, the edges aren't all equal — so there's no fixed ratio.
What we do: build two right triangles, like we did in this question.
A box: 6 by 8, height 24. How long is the inner diagonal?
First the diagonal of the base: 6, 8 — the right angle there — a 3-4-5 triple times 2. 10.
Now with the height, another right triangle: 10 and 24. 5-12-13 times 2 — hamsa, bat mitzvah, bar mitzvah. 26.
In a cube — a fixed ratio. In a box — split into two right triangles.

How many times does the cube's edge go into the length, the width and the height?
3 into 10 — 3 full times. The remainder — ignore it.
3 into 7 — twice. Ignore the remainder.
3 into 8 — twice, with 2 left. A third layer won't fit — ignore it.
Multiply: 3 times 2 times 2 — 12.
Choice two.
And the trap: dividing volumes — 560 over 27 — about 20.7. Choice four, 20, is waiting for whoever treats cubes like water.

solve-geo35-g132.title: Removing a corner cube: volume and exposed faces

beats.title: 3D Questions II

lines.say: A sample question — medium.
We call these 'Rubik's cube' questions. The idea comes back quite a lot on the psychometric.

beats.title: Volume, then surface

lines.say: 27 cubes with edge 2 form a big cube. One corner cube is removed. What happens to the volume and the surface area?
Start with the volume. Take one cube out — the volume goes down. No doubt.
Choice one says the volume is unchanged — out. The others all say it drops by 8, one small cube.
Now the surface area — a bit harder to see.

lines.draw: Mark the 3 visible faces of the corner cube

lines.say: What does the corner cube give the surface? 3 faces.
Remove it — it looks like we lose 3 faces.

lines.draw: Mark the 3 faces that become exposed

lines.say: But the moment it's gone, 3 other faces show — faces of the cubes it was hiding.
We lost 3, we gained 3 back. The surface area doesn't change.
Choice two.

beats.title: Three situations

lines.say: In Rubik's cube questions there are three situations to tell apart.
The corner — the one we just solved. Lose 3, gain 3.
Now a cube in the middle of an edge. Think: bigger, smaller, or the same? It shows 2 faces. Take it out — 4 faces are exposed. Up by 2.
Last — the centre of a face. It shows just 1 of its 6 faces. Push it in — 5 appear. Up by 4.
Whoever noticed: lost plus gained always completes to 6.

lines.say: A cone-shaped container, radius root 7, height 9, full of water. Which of the containers can hold all of it?
What do we do? Calculate the volume of the cone — how much water there is.
Then find a solid whose volume is bigger than the cone's, or equal. Once we find one — we mark it.
How do we calculate the volume of a cone? A cone is a pointed solid — one third of the straight solid.

lines.draw: Draw a cylinder around the cone

lines.say: If we put the cone inside a cylinder — the cylinder's volume over 3 is the cone's volume.
Base area πr squared, times the height, over 3.
Root 7 squared is 7. 9 and 3 cancel to 3. 7 times 3 — 21π.
How much is that roughly? 21 times 3.14 — 63 plus 2.94. About 65.9. Remember that number — it's the water.

The most important thing: straight solid or pointed? Straight — base area times height. Pointed — the same, over 3.
Choice one: a box, 7 by 3 by 3. A straight solid. For a box — just multiply all the dimensions.
63. Less than the water.
Choice two: a square pyramid — a pyramid whose base is a square. Base edge 6, height 6. Pointed.
Base area 6 squared, 36. Times the height 6, over 3 — 6 and 3 cancel to 2. 36 times 2 — 72.
72 is more than 65.9. This pyramid can hold all the water.
Choice two. On the exam — we mark and move on.

The cube: better to remember a cube is just the edge cubed. 4 cubed — 64. Just below the water. Eliminated.
Careful — that one's close. If you round π to 3, the water is 63 and the cube suddenly looks big enough. Use 3.14.
The cylinder: a straight solid. Root 5 squared is 5, times the height 4 — 20π. Less than 21π. Eliminated.

lines.say: A cone and a cylinder with equal bases. The cone's volume is twice the cylinder's. The cylinder's height is h — what's the cone's height?
Let's start with the mathematical solution. We build an equation.
The cylinder's volume — a straight solid, base area times height: πr squared times h.
The cone: a pointed solid, one third of the straight solid. Same base — πr squared.
Its height isn't given — let's call it H.
The cone's volume equals twice the cylinder's volume.

lines.draw: Cross out πr² on both sides

lines.say: πr squared appears on both sides — the base area cancels.
Multiply by 3: H is 6h.
Choice two. Not complicated at all.

items.t: Same base, same height: cone $=\frac13$ cylinder

lines.say: Now the psychometric solution — through a volume ratio.
Some students read the question and already know the answer — without solving anything. How?

lines.label: Same base, same height → cone = ⅓ cylinder appears

lines.say: The cone and the cylinder have the same base. If they also had the same height — the cone would be one third of the cylinder.
In a cone, if I double the height — the volume doubles too. Triple the height — triple the volume.
So to reach one whole cylinder — multiply the height by 3: 3h.
But we want TWICE the cylinder — so double that again: 6h.
Careful — 3h is a trap choice: it's the height for EQUAL volumes.
Choice two. This principle — volume ratios — helps a lot in more advanced questions.

lines.say: A box with volume 216. AM to MB is 1 to 2. What's the volume of the shaded triangular prism?
Start with the math. The box's volume is 216 — a straight solid: base area times height.

lines.draw: Write x on AM and 2x on MB

lines.say: The only given is the ratio. So AM is x and MB is 2x — the box's length is 3x.

lines.draw: Write y on AD and z on the height AE

lines.say: Nothing about the depth or the height. Let's add unknowns: depth y, height z.
What we do with this is not clear yet — but it's given, so we'll need it at some point.
What did they ask? The shaded solid. Straight or pointed? Its bottom base equals its top base — straight. A triangular prism.

lines.draw: Mark the right angle at A

lines.say: Its base is the triangle. The angle between x and y is 90 — the base of a box is a rectangle.
Triangle area — x times y over 2 — times the height z. Half of xyz.
Now it clears up: 3xyz is 216, so xyz is 72. Half of 72 — 36.
Choice three. That was the math — not simple.

lines.say: There's a much, much simpler solution — a psychometric one, rooted in symmetry.
Look at the box from above for a moment.

lines.draw: Draw the base from above: rectangle ABCD, the line through M parallel to AD, and the diagonal MD

lines.say: If I asked you: the shaded triangle — what part of this whole rectangle is it?

lines.label: Strip = ⅓ of the rectangle appears

lines.say: The line through M cuts the rectangle into x and 2x — three equal parts. The left strip is one third.

lines.label: Triangle = ½ of the strip → ⅙ appears

lines.say: The diagonal cuts that strip in half. So the shaded part is half of a third — one sixth.
And it's true in the box too — only instead of a line, we pass a wall. Same height, so the volume ratio is the area ratio.
One sixth of 216 — 36. Choice three.
The psychometric solution was much shorter. That's the essence of the psychometric: there's almost always a shorter way.
Spot the shortcuts — and you pave your own way to success.

lines.say: A right prism whose base is a right triangle: a leg of 5, a hypotenuse of 13, height 4. What's its lateral area?
Lateral area — the sum of the faces, without the two bases, top and bottom.
The first approach — the formula: the perimeter of the base, times the height.
The base perimeter: one side 5, the hypotenuse 13. We need the third side.
A right triangle, hypotenuse 13, leg 5 — the other leg is 12. The Pythagorean triple 5, 12, 13.
5 plus 12 plus 13 — 30. Or: the average of the three sides is 10, so it's 3 times 10.
The height is given — 4. 30 times 4 — 120.
Choice one.

lines.say: The second approach: calculate the three faces one by one.

lines.draw: Shade the three side rectangles, one at a time

lines.say: The first face — 5 times the height 4. 20.
The next one — 12 times 4. 48.
The last one — 13 times 4. 52.
Add it all up: 48 and 52 make 100, plus 20 — 120.
Careful: adding the two triangle bases gives 180 — that's the total surface area, a trap choice.
Choice one — either way. Pick the approach that's comfortable for you.

beats.title: Solids: Surface and Volume

lines.say: Three-dimensional geometry — definitions and formulas.
3D on the psychometric is a topic a lot of students are afraid of — they don't remember it from school, or never learned it.
And that's a shame. The questions here are usually not hard.
A simple formula or a simple idea — and you solve them pretty fast.
Stick with me through the lessons — it's much simpler than it looks.

items.t: Edge $=$ a length $\cdot$ face $=$ a wall $\cdot$ base $=$ bottom or top face

lines.say: First, basic definitions — so we share one language.
An edge is a side of a 3D solid. We measure it in length units — like a side.
A face is a side wall — like a wall of a room. Right face, back face, left face, front face.

lines.draw: Shade the bottom and the top faces

lines.say: And the bottom face and the top face — we also call them bases.

lines.label: Edge = length · face = area · base = bottom or top face appears

lines.say: Bottom, top — those are our bases.

items.t: Prism: two identical bases — one straight above the other

lines.say: A prism is a solid whose two bases — the bottom and the top — are identical polygons.
Take a triangle — that's the bottom base. To make it the top base too, lift a copy straight up.
And — hop — we've made a prism. The bottom base and the top base are identical.

lines.label: Prism: two identical bases, joined straight up appears

lines.say: Same with a rectangle: lift it up and you get a box. That's also a prism — a right prism.

items.t: Cylinder: two equal circles — one straight above the other

lines.say: On the exam we also have the cylinder.
Take a circle and pull it straight up.

lines.draw: Shade the bottom circle and the top circle

lines.say: A bottom base and a top base — both circles. That's a cylinder.
You know it — any can, a tin of food, a roll.

lines.label: Cylinder: two equal circles, joined straight up appears

lines.say: Lateral area — the lateral surface is what wraps around the solid.
If we peel this cylinder — everything that wrapped it is the lateral surface.
Think of a toilet-paper roll. Tear off one full turn and stretch it out.

lines.label: The cylinder's side, unrolled into a rectangle appears

lines.say: What do we get? A rectangle.
The area of a rectangle — base times height.

lines.draw: Mark h on the rectangle's height

lines.say: The height of this rectangle is the height of the cylinder.
And its width? Imagine wrapping the cylinder again — it's the whole way around. The circumference: 2πr.

lines.label: Lateral area of a cylinder = 2πr · h appears

lines.say: So the lateral area of a cylinder is 2πr times h — the perimeter of the base times the height.

lines.say: Now a box. What's its lateral surface? Everything around it.

lines.draw: Write a, b and c on the three edges (c = the height)
Shade the right and left faces

lines.say: Right face and left face — each one is b times c. We have it twice.

lines.draw: Shade the front and back faces

lines.say: Front and back — a times c. Twice too.
No top, no bottom — only what's around, like we wrapped the cylinder.
Take c out as a common factor: 2a plus 2b, times c.
A cube: four side faces, each a squared. 4a squared.

beats.title: Perimeter × height

items.t: Lateral area $=$ perimeter of the base $\times$ height
Any prism — any base: perimeter $\times$ height

lines.say: Instead of remembering a different formula for every shape — there's one general formula.

lines.label: Lateral area = perimeter of the base × height appears

lines.say: Lateral area equals the perimeter of the base, times the height.
Check it on the box: the perimeter down there is a plus b, plus a plus b in the back — 2a plus 2b. Times the height c.
The cube: the perimeter of the base is 4a. The height is a. 4a times a — 4a squared.
And a prism with any base — same thing: the perimeter of the base times its height.
Remember this one — and you can always calculate the lateral area of any shape they give you.

lines.say: Total surface area is the area of the solid from every direction.
That's the lateral surface — plus the bases, bottom and top.

lines.label: A cube net with six equal squares appears

lines.say: Look at the cube: the bottom base, the top base, and 4 faces around.
Around it we had 4a squared. Add the bottom and the top — 6a squared. 6 faces.

lines.draw: Write a, b and c on the three edges

lines.say: The box: the front face is ac — we have it twice, front and back.
The right face is bc — right and left. And the bottom is ab — bottom and top.
Twice each of these faces.
And it's the same idea: the lateral (2a plus 2b) times c, plus two bases of ab. Open the brackets — 2ac plus 2bc plus 2ab. Exactly this.
The cylinder: 2πrh — the lateral surface we calculated — plus two times πr squared. One base is πr squared, and we have a bottom and a top.
So in every shape: total surface area is the lateral area plus the two bases.
Remember that — and you don't need the specific formula of each shape. You understand it.

beats.title: Volume

items.t: $1\text{ cm}^3$ $=$ a cube $1\text{ cm}\times1\text{ cm}\times1\text{ cm}$

lines.say: Volume is the content of the solid — its capacity, what's inside it.
Imagine a can of cola. All the liquid inside — that's the volume.
It always says on the can: 330 millilitres. That's a volume unit.

lines.label: 1 cm³ = a cube 1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm appears

lines.say: A cubic centimetre is 3D: a centimetre by a centimetre by a centimetre. A tiny cube, every edge one centimetre.

lines.draw: Draw a flat rectangle, then stack more and more rectangles on top of it

lines.say: Look at this rectangle. It has no volume — only area. a times b.
Now add another, and another, and another — lots of rectangles, one on top of the other.
Each one alone was only an area — its height was negligible. But together we got a box. It takes up space now.

beats.title: Base area × height

v.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="84.1 53.6 471.8 252.8" role="img" aria-label="Rectangular box with hidden edges shown dashed"><title>Rectangular box with hidden edges shown dashed</title><polygon points="110.125,280.375 429.500,280.375 429.500,143.500 110.125,143.500" fill="#f8fbfd" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><polygon points="429.500,280.375 529.875,216.500 529.875,79.625 429.500,143.500" fill="#d5f1ed" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><polygon points="110.125,143.500 429.500,143.500 529.875,79.625 210.500,79.625" fill="#e8eefb" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><line x1="110.125" y1="280.375" x2="210.500" y2="216.500" stroke="#71818d" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="7 5"/><line x1="210.500" y1="216.500" x2="529.875" y2="216.500" stroke="#71818d" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="7 5"/><line x1="210.500" y1="216.500" x2="210.500" y2="79.625" stroke="#71818d" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="7 5"/></svg>

lines.draw: Write a, b and c on the three edges

lines.say: So what's the volume of the box? The area of the base — a times b — times the height.
As if we had the area c times: area plus area plus area, c times.
Length times width times height.
A cube is a special box — everything is a. a times a times a. a cubed.
The cylinder: the area of the base, πr squared, times the height.

lines.label: Any prism: V = base area × height appears

lines.say: And any prism — the area of the base times the height. In every one of these shapes.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Lateral area $=$ perimeter of the base $\times$ height — what wraps around
Total surface area $=$ lateral area $+$ the two bases
Volume $=$ base area $\times$ height — what's inside
Pointed solid (cone, pyramid): the same volume $\div\,3$

lines.say: Let's sum up.

lines.label: Lateral = perimeter of the base × height appears

lines.say: Lateral area — everything that wraps around the solid. The perimeter of the base times the height.

lines.label: Total surface = lateral + the two bases appears

lines.say: Total surface area — what wraps around, plus the bases.
Volume — everything inside. The area of the base times the height.
And a pointed solid: the ordinary volume — divided by 3. Always. Cone or pyramid, triangle base, square base, rectangle base — it doesn't matter.
That's it for 3D definitions and formulas. From here — psychometric questions.

lines.say: ABC is an equilateral triangle. The line DE passes through vertex A, and F is on the extension of side BA.
Two angles are marked: p and q. We need to express q using p.
There are several ways to solve this. First way: the angle sum in a triangle.
Look at the highlighted triangle ABE, and let's express its angles using the givens.
First given: ABC is equilateral. All sides are equal, all angles are equal — and each one is 60 degrees.
So angle B is 60.
Next, angle BAE. It's vertical to q — and vertical angles are equal. So it's q too.
Last angle: AEB. It completes p to 180 — so it's 180 minus p.
Now: the angles in a triangle add up to 180. Write it as an equation.
A plus in front of the parentheses doesn't affect them — we can simply drop them.
180 cancels on both sides.
Move minus p across, move the 60 across — and q equals p minus 60.
Choice one.

And an exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior angles not next to it: q plus 60.
Move the 60 across and isolate q: q equals p minus 60.

lines.say: One more way — psychometric thinking: plugging in numbers.
As we learned in geometry questions with unknowns: plug numbers in for the unknowns, and the question gets easier.
Which unknown? The one that appears in the answers — here, p.
In the figure, p is an obtuse angle. So choose a comfortable obtuse angle: 100.

lines.draw: Write p = 100° next to the figure

lines.say: p equals 100. Now find q.
The exterior-angle way again: 60 plus what gives 100? 40.
You could also go through the big triangle — lots of ways. Either way, q is 40.
Now plug 100 in for p in every answer. Anything that isn't 40 — eliminate.
Choice one: 100 minus 60 — 40. Keep it.

lines.draw: Next to choice 2 write 50 and cross it out

lines.say: Choice two: 150 minus 100 — 50. Eliminated.

lines.draw: Next to choice 3 write 80 and cross it out

lines.say: Choice three: 180 minus 100 — 80. Eliminated.

lines.draw: Next to choice 4 write 80 and cross it out

lines.say: Choice four: twice 100 is 200, minus 120 — 80. Eliminated.
Three answers out — choice one.

lines.say: Given: alpha is bigger than beta, and angle B is 40 degrees.
The angles in a triangle add up to 180. If B is 40, alpha and beta together are 140.
That's our first conclusion from the givens.
Next given: alpha is bigger than beta. What does that mean?
If alpha were equal to beta, each would be 70.
But alpha is bigger — so alpha is more than 70, and beta is necessarily less than 70.
So alpha is bigger than beta, and bigger than 40 too. Alpha is the biggest angle in the triangle.
Careful: beta is below 70, but it could be above or below 40. So here we can't order all three angles.
We don't need to. We only need the longest side.

items.t: The sum of any two sides is always greater than the third side.

lines.say: ABC is an obtuse triangle: angle C is more than 90 degrees. And AB is 6.
Which of the answers could be the perimeter?
It should be clear: there isn't enough information to calculate the perimeter exactly.
So this is a minimum–maximum question in geometry.
There's a minimum the perimeter has to be bigger than — and a maximum it has to be smaller than.
Start with the minimum. One of the most basic triangle rules is about the range of the sides:

lines.label: The sum of two sides is greater than the third appears

lines.say: So AC plus BC has to be more than 6.
How does that affect the perimeter? The perimeter is 6 plus AC plus BC. 6 plus something bigger than 6 — more than 12.
Any answer that is 12 or less — eliminated.
22.5, 13.5 and 18 pass. 12 is too small — eliminated.

lines.say: Now we just need the maximum… actually, not so fast.
Some students already see the answer, with a min–max insight. How?
Out of the answers, some are eliminated for being too small — and some for being too big.
Put them in order. 12 is already out — too small.
So two of the three left must be too big. Which ones can be too big?
Could 13.5 and 18 be too big, while 22.5 is the right answer? Impossible.

lines.draw: Draw a number line: lower limit 12, an open upper limit, and the choices on it

lines.say: Picture it: a valid range. The lower limit — 12. An upper limit we haven't calculated yet.
If 22.5 were inside the range, 13.5 — which is above 12 and below 22.5 — would be inside too. Two right answers.
So necessarily the smallest answer above 12 is the right one. 18 and 22.5 go over the upper limit.
13.5 — choice two.

We learned: opposite the biggest angle is the longest side.

The other two angles are less than 90, so AC and BC must each be shorter than 6.

beats.title: Isosceles properties

lines.say: Let's recall the properties of an isosceles triangle.
In an isosceles triangle, the two legs are equal — and the base angles opposite them are equal.
Also, the altitude to the base is a line of symmetry: it's also an angle bisector and a median.

lines.draw: Write: legs equal ⇔ base angles equal

lines.say: Now let's check the answers. We'll start where we can decide quickly.

beats.title: Go through the answers

lines.say: A triangle with angles 76 and 52. Find the third angle: 180 minus 76 is 104, minus 52 — 52.
Two equal angles means two equal sides. It's necessarily isosceles — eliminate.
Next: an altitude that also bisects the angle.
If the altitude is also an angle bisector, it's a line of symmetry — so it's also a median, and the triangle is necessarily isosceles.
Eliminated.
Choice one: a median of 6 to a side of 4. It's a median — it splits the side in two. But it isn't given as an altitude or as a bisector.
Honestly, it's not very clear what to do with these numbers. So skip it — go to the next answer and hope to eliminate that one.
Choice four: a median that's perpendicular to the side it meets.
Sometimes the right angle is hidden: two equal angles alpha and alpha at the foot of the median. Two alphas make a straight angle, 180 — so alpha is 90.
Either way, the median is also an altitude. That's a line of symmetry — the triangle is isosceles. Eliminate.
Three answers out — so we mark choice one, the one that wasn't clear.
Why can it fail? A median reaches the midpoint, but it can lean to one side. Its length doesn't make it perpendicular — so the two sides can be different.

lines.say: ABC and ACD are right triangles. What's the area of quadrilateral ABCD?
In a right triangle, when two sides are given, we can always find the third with the Pythagorean theorem.
But we also learned a shortcut: Pythagorean triples.
Start with triangle ABC. One leg is 6, the other leg is 8.
That's 3, 4, 5 times two — so the hypotenuse AC is 10. No need for the full theorem.
On to the second triangle. The leg AC is 10, and the hypotenuse is 26.
Another triple we learned: 5, 12, 13 — times two, that's 10, 24, 26. We have the leg 10 and the hypotenuse 26 — the missing one is 24. So CD is 24.
Now, how do we find the area of ABCD? Notice: it's made of the two triangles together.

lines.label: Area of a triangle = (side × altitude to it) ÷ 2 appears

lines.say: The area of a triangle: a side times the altitude to it, divided by 2.
Triangle ABC: 6 times 8 is 48, divided by 2 — 24.
Triangle ACD: 10 times 24 over 2. Cancel first — 24 over 2 is 12, times 10 — 120.
So the quadrilateral's area is the sum of the two triangles: 24 plus 120 — 144.
Choice two.

lines.say: ABD and BCD are right triangles, and AD is 12. What's the perimeter of ABCD?
Look at triangle ABD. Angle A is 30 degrees, angle B is 90 —

lines.draw: Write 60° at D in triangle ABD

lines.say: — so the angle at D is 60. A golden triangle: 30, 60, 90.

lines.label: Golden triangle 30-60-90: sides x, x√3, 2x appears

lines.say: The hypotenuse is 12. To go from the hypotenuse to the short leg in a golden triangle, divide by 2.
So BD, opposite the 30, is 6.
From the short leg, opposite 30, to the long leg, opposite 60 — multiply by root 3. So AB is 6 root 3.
Now triangle BCD. It's a silver triangle: 45, 90, 45 — a right isosceles triangle.

lines.label: Silver triangle 45-45-90: sides x, x, x√2 appears

lines.say: Careful: BD was a leg up there — here it's the hypotenuse, opposite the right angle at C.
From the hypotenuse to a leg, divide by root 2. How much is 6 over root 2?
The method we learned: ignore the root — 6 over 2 is 3. Stick the root 2 back on: 3 root 2.
So CD is 3 root 2, and BC is 3 root 2.
Now the perimeter — the outside only, not BD: 12, plus 6 root 3, plus 3 root 2, plus 3 root 2.
3 root 2 plus 3 root 2 is 6 root 2. So it's 12 plus 6 root 3 plus 6 root 2.
Choice three.

lines.say: AE is the altitude to BC, D is on AE, and DBC is equilateral. BE is 3 and AD is 2 root 3. What's the shaded area?
Shaded areas are pretty common on the exam. The main way to handle them: subtracting areas.
We need to see what the shaded area is made of — or what minus what gives it.
Take the big triangle ABC and subtract the white triangle DBC — that's exactly the shaded area.
To calculate the areas, first complete the data.
If BE is 3, EC is 3 too. Why? DBC is equilateral, and an altitude in an equilateral triangle is also a median.
Now the altitude DE. It splits the equilateral triangle into two golden triangles, 30-60-90.
The short leg, opposite the 30, is 3. Multiply by root 3 — DE is 3 root 3.
Now we have everything: the big triangle minus the small one.
Big triangle: the base BC is 6. The height is 3 root 3 plus 2 root 3 — 5 root 3. 6 times 5 root 3 over 2 — cancel by 2 — 15 root 3.
The small white triangle: base 6, height 3 root 3. Over 2 — 9 root 3.
Is there another way to get that area? Yes — it's equilateral, and there's a formula using only its side.
a squared root 3 over 4. Put in 6: 36 root 3 over 4 — 9 root 3. Exactly the same.
All that's left is to subtract: 15 root 3 minus 9 root 3 — 6 root 3.
Choice four. That's the standard way.

lines.say: But this question has a flash-of-insight way — a shorter one.

lines.draw: Turn the figure so AD is horizontal (or tilt your head)

lines.say: To see it, rotate the triangle. The shaded area is made of two triangles: ADC and ADB.
For the area of ADC we need a base and its altitude. The base is given: AD, 2 root 3.
Where's the altitude to AD from vertex C? The triangle is obtuse, so it's an outside altitude — extend the base and drop it.

lines.draw: Extend AD down to E and mark EC = 3 as the altitude

lines.say: And we know it too: EC is 3 — the same as BE.
2 root 3 times 3 over 2 — 3 root 3. That's one shaded triangle.
The other triangle is completely symmetric to it — again 3 root 3.
Twice 3 root 3 — 6 root 3.
Choice four — with almost no calculating.

lines.say: The area of ABC is 32, and DC is 3 times BD. What's the difference between the areas of ADC and ABD?
Let's start with the math. The base isn't given and neither is the height — so define them with unknowns.
BD is x. DC is 3 times BD — so DC is 3x.

lines.draw: Drop the altitude h from A to BC

lines.say: Drop an altitude h from vertex A to the base BC.
The area of ABC: the base BC is 4x, the height is h — 4x times h over 2. And it's given as 32.
Solve: cancel by 2 — 2xh is 32. Divide by 2 — xh is 16. Keep that.
Now ADC with x and h: base 3x, height h. 3xh over 2 — 3 times 16 over 2 — 24.
Now ABD: base x, height h. It's obtuse, so the altitude falls outside — but it's the same altitude. xh over 2 — 16 over 2 — 8.
The difference: 24 minus 8 — 16.
Choice one. That's the math way.

items.t: Same height: the ratio of the areas equals the ratio of the bases.

lines.say: This question also has an insight way — through understanding area ratios.

lines.label: Same height ⇒ area ratio = base ratio appears

lines.say: What's an area ratio? Two triangles with the same base and the same height have the same area.
And if they have the same height but one base is 3 times bigger — its area is 3 times bigger too. Exactly like here.
DC is 3 times BD, and the height is the same height, because it's the same triangle.
So the areas are 1 to 3. Together 32 — four parts of 8. The left one is 8, the right one is 24.
The difference — 16. Choice one.

lines.draw: Split DC into three equal parts and join them to A

lines.say: You can also see it another way: split DC into three pieces, each as long as BD, and join them to A.
All four triangles have the same base and the same height — so the same area: 32 over 4, 8 each.
ADC has three of them, ABD has one. The difference — two pieces: 16.

lines.say: Four squares with side 3 are joined as shown. What's the perimeter of AEF minus the perimeter of AFG?
Full math first: find the perimeter of AEF, find the perimeter of AFG — and subtract.

lines.draw: Write 3 on the sides of the small squares

lines.say: The four squares are identical, so every side is 3.
Now the length AE. It's made of two diagonals of the small squares.
A diagonal splits a square into two silver triangles. The legs are 3 and 3 — so the diagonal is 3 root 2.
And the second one is 3 root 2 too — so AE is 6 root 2.
Now AF. It's the hypotenuse of triangle AGF: one leg is 3, the other is 6. Pythagorean theorem.
36 plus 9 is 45. AF is root 45 — 3 root 5.
Perimeter of AEF: 3 root 5, plus 3, plus 6 root 2.
Perimeter of AFG: 3 root 5, plus 3, plus 6.
Subtract: 3 root 5 minus 3 root 5 cancels. 3 minus 3 cancels. 6 root 2 minus 6.
Choice two. That's the full solution.

lines.say: One more nuance. Say you reach this question at the end of the exam, with 10 or 20 seconds left.
Sometimes you can eliminate answers by estimating the size.
Root 3 is about 1.7. Root 2 is about 1.4.
Choice three: 3 root 3 is about 5.1, minus 3 — positive. Can't eliminate it.

lines.draw: Next to choice 4 write < 0 and cross it out

lines.say: Choice four: 3 minus 5.1 — negative. Impossible: AE, the diagonal, is longer than AG.

lines.draw: Next to choice 1 write 6 − 8.4 < 0 and cross it out

lines.say: Choice one: 6 root 2 is about 8.4. 6 minus 8.4 — negative. Eliminated.
Two answers out already. Here the two left are close — about 2.5 and 2.2 — so the estimate alone won't finish it.
But with no time left, you're down to a fifty-fifty guess. It's a trick that does show up on the exam.

lines.say: Two equilateral triangles: the big one has side b, the small one has side a.
The bold line is twice the perimeter of the small triangle. What's a over b?
As usual, we start with the math.

lines.draw: Write a on all three sides of the small triangle

lines.say: The small triangle is equilateral — if one side is a, all its sides are a.

lines.draw: Write b on all three sides of the big triangle

lines.say: The big one too — all sides are b.

lines.draw: Write b − a on the bottom bold pieces

lines.say: But how long is the bold line along the bottom? It's b minus a: the whole side of the big triangle minus the side of the small one.
Now the given: the bold line equals twice the perimeter of the small triangle — twice 3a, 6a.
A plus doesn't affect the parentheses. Move the minus a across — 3b equals 7a.
And stop here. Most students get tangled at this point: how do I get from here to a over b? You don't really need to.
It's clear the ratio is 3 to 7 or 7 to 3. On the psychometric exam, you usually won't find both orders as answers — but here you do!
So the trick eliminates 3 quarters and 1 — but not 7 thirds.
Then use the given a is smaller than b: a over b is less than 1. 7 thirds is out.
If you insist — not during the exam — divide everything by 7b. On the left, the b cancels: 3 sevenths. On the right, the 7 cancels: a over b.
3 sevenths — choice four.

lines.say: Another way to solve this question: plugging in the answers.
If the ratio is 1 — a equals b. Could a be 1 and b be 1? They defined a big triangle and a small one — the sides can't be equal. Eliminated.
Next: 7 thirds means a is 7 and b is 3. Could a be 7 and b be 3? No — b is bigger than a. No point checking. Eliminated.

lines.draw: Next to choice 1 write a = 3, b = 4: 12 − 3 = 9 ≠ 18, and cross it out

lines.say: 3 quarters: a is 3, b is 4. Looks fine — but we have to check the bold line. 4 plus 4 plus 4 is 12, minus 3 — 9. Twice the small perimeter: twice 9 — 18. 9 isn't 18. Eliminated.

lines.draw: Next to choice 4 write a = 3, b = 7: 21 − 3 = 18 = 2 · 9 ✓

lines.say: 3 sevenths: a is 3, b is 7. Bold line: 21 minus 3 — 18. Twice the small perimeter: twice 9 — 18. It works.
Choice four.

lines.say: Last lesson was the general triangle — angle sum 180 and so on.
Now: special triangles.
You probably remember them a little from school: the right triangle, the isosceles triangle, the equilateral triangle.
Let's get to know them.

lines.say: First: the isosceles triangle.
An isosceles triangle is a triangle with two equal sides.

lines.draw: Mark equal ticks on the two equal sides and write 'leg', 'leg'

lines.say: These two equal sides are called the legs. The third side is called the base.

lines.draw: Mark the two base angles as equal

lines.say: In an isosceles triangle, the base angles are equal — the two angles sitting on the base, between the base and each leg.
And the angle left at the top is called the vertex angle.
If the vertex angle is 44 — the base angles share the other 136 equally. 68 each.

items.t: To the base: median $=$ altitude $=$ angle bisector

lines.label: To the base: median = altitude = angle bisector appears

lines.say: In an isosceles triangle — the median to the base.

lines.draw: Draw the dashed line from the vertex angle to the midpoint of the base

lines.say: It bisects the base,

lines.draw: Mark equal ticks on the two halves of the base

lines.say: it's perpendicular to the base,

lines.draw: Draw the right-angle mark at the base

lines.say: and it also bisects the vertex angle.

lines.draw: Mark the two halves of the vertex angle as equal

lines.say: Bottom line: what we have here is a symmetric triangle.
The line of symmetry from the vertex angle down to the base — it's the altitude, the median and the angle bisector. All one line.
Only this line — not a median from one of the other vertices.

items.t: Isosceles $=$ symmetric: right side $=$ left side

lines.say: This line divides the triangle into two congruent triangles — two identical triangles.
Imagine a piece of paper, and you fold it along the dashed line.

lines.draw: Draw a curved arrow folding the right half onto the left half

lines.say: Take this vertex and move it over here — the two triangles land exactly on each other. Mirror images.
So all the rules we saw are really contained in one understanding: it's a line of symmetry.

lines.draw: Write 90° and 90° at the foot of the line

lines.say: The legs are equal, the base angles are equal, the median bisects the base — and here we have 90 and 90, because together they make 180.
So instead of memorising all the rules of an isosceles triangle — we're not writing a formal proof here —
just remember: an isosceles triangle is symmetric. Draw the symmetry line — everything on the right equals the left.

lines.label: An equilateral triangle with three 60° angles appears

lines.say: The next one: the equilateral triangle.
Just like its name — all its sides are equal.

lines.draw: Mark equal ticks on all three sides

lines.say: In an equilateral triangle, all the angles are 60 degrees. Why?
The sum is 180 — we know that from last lesson. 180 divided by 3: 60. All angles equal, all sides equal.
An equilateral triangle is really like an isosceles triangle — only from every direction.
An isosceles triangle has right equals left from one direction. Look at it from another side — it's not necessarily isosceles.
An equilateral triangle — however I place it, flip it, flip it again — it's always isosceles.
So all the properties of the isosceles triangle hold for it too — just from every direction.

lines.say: The right triangle.
It has three sides. Two sides are perpendicular to each other —

lines.draw: Write 'leg' on each of the two perpendicular sides

lines.say: they're called legs. Leg and leg.

lines.draw: Write 'hypotenuse' on the side opposite the right angle

lines.say: And the third side, opposite the 90-degree angle, is called the hypotenuse.
The hypotenuse is the longest side. It's longer than each leg separately — it's opposite the largest angle.
Tip: find the right-angle mark first, then look across from it. That's the hypotenuse — however the triangle is turned.

items.t: Median to the hypotenuse $=$ half the hypotenuse

lines.label: The right triangle with the median to its hypotenuse appears
Median to the hypotenuse = half the hypotenuse appears

lines.say: There's a rule about the right triangle — the median to the hypotenuse.
It's very rare. We almost never use it on the exam. We'll learn it anyway.
Draw a median from the right angle to the hypotenuse.

lines.draw: Mark equal ticks on the two halves of the hypotenuse and on the median

lines.say: Of course it bisects the hypotenuse — and not only that: it's also equal to half the hypotenuse.
Hypotenuse 14? The median is 7.

lines.draw: Shade the two small triangles in two colours

lines.say: So we get two isosceles triangles: here — these two sides are equal. And here — these two sides are equal.
Like I said — very rare on the exam.

beats.title: Recap

items.t: Isosceles: symmetric — base angles equal; median $=$ altitude $=$ bisector
Equilateral: all sides equal, all angles $60°$ — symmetric from every direction
Right triangle: two legs, hypotenuse opposite $90°$ — the longest side
Median to the hypotenuse $=$ half the hypotenuse (rare)

lines.say: ABC is an equilateral triangle. D is a point on side BC.
We're given: DC is 6, and angle DAC is 30 degrees. What is AB?
We're really looking for the side of the triangle.
We know ABC is equilateral — so all its angles are 60 degrees.

lines.draw: Write 60° at A, and 30° in the other part of angle A

lines.say: The whole angle at A is 60. So what's left here — is also 30.
So AD bisects angle A: 30 and 30.
And in an equilateral triangle — just like in an isosceles one — once we have an angle bisector, it's also perpendicular, and also a median.

lines.draw: Mark equal ticks on BD and DC; write 6 on BD

lines.say: If it's a median — DB equals DC. Each one is 6.
Together: 12. That's the side of the triangle. And AB is a side — so AB is 12.
Choice three.

lines.say: In triangle ABC, D is a point on side AB.
Given: angle BAC is 24 degrees.
Also given: BC equals CD.

lines.draw: Mark equal ticks on BC and CD

lines.say: So here I have an isosceles triangle.
And AB equals AC — the big triangle is isosceles too.

lines.draw: Mark equal ticks on AB and AC

lines.say: What is angle ACD? Let's start.
Triangle ABC is isosceles — so its base angles are equal. Angle B equals angle C.

lines.draw: Write (180° − 24°) : 2 = 78° at B and at C

lines.say: How much? Subtract the 24 — 156 — and split it in 2. 78 and 78.
So the whole angle at C is 78. That already lets us eliminate the 78 choice — only PART of that angle can't be 78 too.
Now triangle CBD — also isosceles. So its base angles are equal too.
Angle BDC is also 78. Mark it.
78 and 78 — by the angle sum, the angle here at the bottom of C, angle DCB, is 24.
And now we can find the marked angle: 78 minus 24 — 54.
Choice one.

lines.say: Area of triangles.
Before we talk about the area of triangles — let's first understand what area even is.

lines.say: Until now, for units, we talked about units of length — a line, a distance, a side. Centimetres.
Of course we can also measure in metres, kilometres and so on.
Area we measure in square centimetres. Square metres, square kilometres.
What does that mean? Take a square whose side is 1 centimetre.

lines.draw: Shade one little square and write 1 cm on two of its sides

lines.say: One side is a centimetre, the other side is a centimetre. Its area is 1 square centimetre.

lines.say: Now take that square and turn it into a rectangle.
This rectangle is made of little squares like that — 3 rows, and in each row 5 squares.
So to find the area of this rectangle: take its width, 5, times its length, 3. 5 times 3 is 15.
Why? 3 rows of 5 squares, each one 1 square centimetre. 1, 2, 3… up to 15.
That's how we find the area of a rectangle.

lines.label: A right triangle inside a rectangle appears

lines.say: Now the area of a right triangle.
A right triangle is really half a rectangle.
The area of the rectangle is width times length — or here, we can call it base times height. A side times its height.
The right triangle is exactly half of that rectangle.
So the area of a right triangle is the product of the legs, divided by 2.
Why? The legs are like the length and width of the rectangle.
Legs 6 and 3? The rectangle is 18, the triangle is 9.

lines.label: A triangle inside a rectangle with the altitude CH appears

lines.say: Now an ordinary triangle. We can put it inside a rectangle too.
But is it really half the rectangle? With the right triangle it was easy to see — we drew a diagonal and saw two equal parts.

lines.draw: Draw the altitude from the top vertex down to the base

lines.say: Let's drop an altitude from the vertex to the base.

lines.draw: Shade the left half-triangle; write '=' between it and the white part beside it

lines.say: Now we have two rectangles. In the left one, the shaded area equals the white area — exactly half.

lines.draw: Do the same in the right rectangle

lines.say: And in the right one too — two equal parts.
So all in all, the triangle is half the rectangle.
And the height of the rectangle is really the height of the triangle.

lines.label: Area = side × height to that side ÷ 2 appears

lines.say: So the area of a triangle is base times height over 2 — or more correctly: a side, times the height to that side, over 2.

beats.title: Any side as base

lines.say: Why do I call it a side and not a base?

lines.draw: Draw a curved arrow: rotate the triangle

lines.say: Because we could look at this triangle from another direction — from here, or from here. We can turn it.
A triangle doesn't really have a base. The base is just the direction I'm looking at it from.
What matters: the side and the height that goes to THAT side.
Side 8, the height to that side 5 — area 20. Any correct side-and-height pair gives the same area.

lines.say: Points A and B lie on one line, and C, D and E lie on a parallel line.
Given: DE is 4 times CD. What is the area of BDE divided by the area of ACD?
Look — there's no data here. No area, no length, nothing. How do we start?
Simply by the givens.

lines.draw: Write x under CD and 4x under DE

lines.say: DE is 4 times CD. So CD is x, and DE is 4x.

lines.draw: Draw one altitude from A and one from B; write h on each

lines.say: The height we don't know — but let's drop it anyway, and call it h.
Because the lines are parallel, the height of ACD is exactly the height of BDE. Same height.
Now calculate the expression. Area of BDE: its base, 4x, times the height h, over 2.
Same for ACD: base x, times h, over 2.
Dividing fractions — multiply by the reciprocal. Flip the bottom fraction.
Cancel the xh, cancel the 2 — we get 4.
Choice four.

lines.say: Now another way — without any of that calculation.

lines.draw: Split DE into four equal parts x, x, x, x and connect each point to B

lines.say: If DE is 4x, we can split it into x, x, x, x — four triangles, each with a base of x.
The area of a triangle is a side times its height over 2.
So now we have five triangles — ACD and the four small ones.
All of them have the same base, x. All of them have the same height, h. So all five have the same area.
BDE is made of 4 of them. ACD is 1 of them. So the ratio is 4.
Choice four.

lines.label: An equilateral triangle with its altitude appears

lines.say: We need a side times a height — so we drop an altitude.

lines.draw: Write a on the two slanted sides

lines.say: Every side is a.
Once we drop the altitude — it's also a median. So it splits the side opposite it into two equal parts.

lines.draw: Write a/2 on each half of the base

lines.say: a over 2 and a over 2.
To find the height, we use the Pythagorean theorem — we'll learn it properly in a moment.
a squared — that's the hypotenuse — minus a over 2 squared, the small leg, gives the height squared, the big leg.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The height" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Simplify

lines.say: Open the parentheses: a squared over 4. Both the top and the bottom get squared.
Multiply both sides of the equation by 4: 4a squared minus a squared equals 4h squared.
So 3a squared over 4 equals h squared.
Take the square root — the height is root 3 times a, over 2.
So far we've only found the height.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Simplify" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Area formula

lines.say: Now the area. What does it equal? A side, times the height to that side, over 2.
The side is a. Times the height, over 2.
Simplify: bring the a up into the numerator — a squared.
We have divide by 2 and divide by 2 — instead of dividing by 2, multiply by a half. A quarter.
So: the area of an equilateral triangle is a squared times root 3, over 4.
Why learn this by heart? Because finding the area of an equilateral triangle on the exam is pretty common.
And we don't want to do the whole Pythagoras process every time — find the height, then the area. Remember the formula.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Area formula" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: a-two-three-four

lines.say: At first sight the formula looks a bit complicated. But there's an easy way to remember it.
Think of a dance teacher counting the beat: a-two-three-four! a-two-three-four!
That's our way to remember the equilateral area.
a — squared — root 3 — over 4.
Side 8: 8 squared is 64, times root 3, over 4 — 16 root 3.
A little practice, and it'll stick.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "a-two-three-four" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

lines.say: ABC is an equilateral triangle with perimeter 18.
D and E are the midpoints of AB and BC, respectively.
What does 'respectively' mean? The first point named goes with the first side named. D is the midpoint of AB — not of BC.
What is the area of quadrilateral ADEC?

lines.draw: Write 6 on each side of the big triangle

lines.say: First: the perimeter is 18, so each side is 6. 6, 6 and 6 — 18 together.

lines.draw: Write 3 and 3 on the halves of AB and of BC

lines.say: If AB is 6, here we have 3 and 3. Same on BC.
And the little triangle DBE is equilateral too. Why?
BD is 3, BE is 3 — isosceles — with a 60-degree angle. So the other two angles are 60 and 60 as well. Equilateral.
Let's find the area of the big triangle ABC — and subtract the area of the small triangle DBE.
What's left is the quadrilateral we want.
Area of ABC — by the formula: a-two-three-four. The side is 6: 36 root 3 over 4.
We could simplify the 4 — but let's leave it. It'll help with the subtraction later.
Area of DBE: the side is 3. 9 root 3 over 4.
Now subtract. You see why I kept the denominator? Same 4 — no common denominator needed.
36 minus 9: 27 root 3 over 4.
Choice one.

lines.say: One more way — from the formula itself.
The small triangle has half the side. In the formula, the side gets squared — so a half becomes a quarter.

lines.draw: Write S(DBE) = ¼ S(ABC), S(ADEC) = ¾ S(ABC)

lines.say: So the small triangle is a quarter of the big one, and the quadrilateral is the other three quarters.
Three quarters of 36 root 3 over 4 — 27 root 3 over 4. Same answer.
Choice one.

lines.label: Triangle ABC with the median and the altitude appears
Median → two triangles of equal area appears

lines.say: A median in a triangle divides it into two triangles with equal area.
This doesn't have to be a special triangle. Not equilateral, not isosceles, nothing. Just a triangle.

lines.draw: Mark equal ticks on the two parts of the side cut by the median

lines.say: We draw the median — so the two pieces of that side are equal.

lines.draw: Shade the two small triangles in pink and green

lines.say: We get two triangles — the pink and the green.
They have equal bases. And the same height —

items.t: Same base $\cdot$ same height $\Rightarrow$ same area

lines.draw: Trace the altitude and the dashed extension of the base

lines.say: — this altitude is the height of BOTH triangles. The left one, and the right one.
One of them is obtuse — so its height is outside the triangle. That doesn't matter.

lines.label: Same base · same height → same area appears

lines.say: Area is a side times the height to it, over 2. Same base, same height — same area.
Careful: same area does NOT mean the triangles are congruent. Their shapes can be very different.
So — if you see a median, you automatically know it cut the triangle into two triangles of equal area.
That's it for the area of triangles.

beats.title: Triangles

lines.say: Triangles.
In this lesson we'll get to know the rules of triangles — sides, angles,
the connection between them, and a few special lines that are important to know.
Let's start.

lines.say: The first line is called a median.
A median is a segment that joins a vertex of the triangle to the midpoint of the side opposite it.

lines.draw: Draw equal ticks on AM and MB

lines.say: Here we've drawn a median from the top vertex to this side — and it splits the side into two equal parts.
That's all it promises: equal pieces.
It doesn't promise a right angle, and it doesn't split the angle at C in half.

lines.say: An altitude is a segment from a vertex to the opposite side — that makes a 90-degree angle with that side, or with its extension.

lines.draw: Point to the right-angle mark at H

lines.say: Here the triangle is acute, so when we drop the altitude, it's perpendicular to the side opposite it — inside the triangle.
It does not promise that H is the midpoint. An altitude gives a right angle, not equal pieces.

lines.label: An obtuse triangle with the altitude CH outside it appears

lines.say: Now an obtuse triangle.
The altitude from this vertex goes down to the extension of the side opposite it.
I can't drop it inside the triangle — it would come out slanted. It has to be perpendicular. 90 degrees.

lines.draw: Draw a dashed extension of AB out to H

lines.say: So it meets the side only on its extension.
The altitude here is outside the triangle — but it's still the altitude of the triangle. That doesn't change anything.

lines.draw: Draw a floor line under AB and an arrow up along CH

lines.label: Triangle ABC with angles α, β, γ appears

lines.say: The sum of the angles in a triangle is 180. Alpha plus beta plus gamma equals 180.
I'm guessing most of you know this rule — and never thought about how to prove it. Let's do it quickly.

lines.draw: Through C, draw a line parallel to AB

lines.say: Draw a line parallel to this side of the triangle.

lines.draw: Draw a Z from A and copy α next to C

lines.say: Between parallel lines — look for the Z. Small angle and small angle. This one equals alpha.

lines.draw: Draw a Z from B and copy β on the other side of C

lines.say: Same thing on the other side. Another Z — this one equals beta.
And now look along the new line: alpha, gamma, beta — they sit on one straight line.

lines.draw: Draw a half-circle arc over the three angles at C and write 180°

lines.say: A straight angle. 180. So the three angles of the triangle add up to 180.

beats.title: Exterior angle

v.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="139.5 35.5 395.8 286.1" role="img" aria-label="Triangle ABC"><title>Triangle ABC</title><polygon points="189.459,278.531 450.541,278.531 366.894,81.469" fill="none" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><text x="171.459" y="295.531" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">A</text><text x="468.541" y="295.531" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">B</text><text x="366.894" y="61.469" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">C</text><path d="M 215.567 278.531 A 26.108 26.108 0 0 0 206.929 259.128" fill="none" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2"/><text x="231.524" y="259.802" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#087f83" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18">α</text><path d="M 440.340 254.498 A 26.108 26.108 0 0 0 424.433 278.531" fill="none" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2"/><text x="412.144" y="253.116" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#087f83" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18">β</text><path d="M 349.424 100.872 A 26.108 26.108 0 0 0 377.095 105.502" fill="none" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="224.485" y1="81.469" x2="509.302" y2="81.469" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5"/></svg>

items.t: Exterior angle $=$ the two interior angles not next to it

lines.label: Triangle ABC with angles α and β appears
Exterior angle = sum of the two remote interior angles appears

lines.say: An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior angles that are not next to it.
First of all — what is an exterior angle?

lines.draw: Extend side AC past C, and mark the angle outside as γ

lines.say: It's the angle between one side of the triangle and the extension of another side.
It's outside the triangle — so it's exterior.
The rule says: this exterior angle equals alpha plus beta. We need to show gamma equals alpha plus beta. Let's prove it.

lines.draw: In the interior angle at C, write 180° − γ

lines.say: The angle inside is 180 minus gamma — they're adjacent angles, it completes it to 180.
And by the angle sum: alpha plus beta plus 180 minus gamma is 180.

lines.draw: Cross out 180° on both sides; write α + β = γ

lines.say: Drop the parentheses, cancel 180 on the left and on the right.
We're left with alpha plus beta minus gamma equals zero. Move gamma across — alpha plus beta equals gamma.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Exterior angle" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Two routes

lines.say: Honestly — we don't use this rule a lot on the exam.
And we don't really need it: many times we can just find the angle next to the exterior angle, and use the angle sum.
But if we know it — it can save us time in some questions. Look.
With the rule: 47 plus 68 — the exterior angle is 115. One step.
Without it: the third angle is 180 minus 47 minus 68 — 65. And the exterior angle completes 65 to 180 — 115 again.
Same answer. The shortcut just saves a step.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Two routes" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Side vs. angle

items.t: Larger angle $\leftrightarrow$ longer side opposite it

lines.label: Larger angle ↔ longer opposite side appears

lines.say: In every triangle, the largest side lies opposite the largest angle.
And the smallest side lies opposite the smallest angle.
Here we have three angles. Let's order them: 40 is the smallest, then 60, then 80.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow from the 40° across the triangle to the side opposite it, and write 'shortest'

lines.say: Opposite the 40 — look across, to the side that doesn't touch that vertex. That's the shortest side.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow from the 80° to the side opposite it, and write 'longest'

lines.say: 80 is the largest angle — so the side opposite it is the longest.
And the 60 is in the middle — so its side is in the middle.
It works both ways: opposite the longest side is the largest angle. Exactly the same thing.
And it makes sense. Imagine opening an angle wider and wider — the side opposite it gets longer.
Close the angle — and the side opposite it gets shorter.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Side vs. angle" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Two sides > third

items.t: Any two sides together $>$ the third side

lines.label: 'Any two sides together > the third side' appears

lines.say: The sum of two sides of a triangle is always greater than the third side.
Let's understand what that means.
Suppose one side is 10. And the other two sides are 4 and 6 — exactly 10 together.

lines.draw: Draw a segment labelled 10; from its ends draw sticks 4 and 6 lifting up without meeting

lines.say: Watch what happens when I try to close a triangle. I lift the 4 to one side, the 6 to the other —
— and they don't reach. Lying flat, they're exactly 10. The moment they open up, a gap appears between them.
To close a triangle, I'd have to make one of them longer — or both.
So for this to be a triangle, the two sides together must be MORE than 10. Strictly more.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Two sides > third" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: The shortest path

v.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="139.5 35.5 361.1 286.1" role="img" aria-label="Triangle ABC"><title>Triangle ABC</title><polygon points="189.459,278.531 450.541,278.531 366.894,81.469" fill="none" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><text x="171.459" y="295.531" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">A</text><text x="468.541" y="295.531" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">B</text><text x="366.894" y="61.469" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">C</text></svg>

lines.say: There's another way to see it.

lines.draw: Write 'home' by A and 'sports club' by C

lines.say: Say this is my home, and this is the sports club.
If I want to walk from home to the club — obviously the shortest way is to walk in a straight line.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow straight from A to C

lines.say: Let's send two friends from home to the club, each by a different route.

lines.draw: Draw a second arrow from A to B and on to C

lines.say: The first walks straight. The second makes a stop at B on the way.
Who arrives first? The straight one — his road is shorter. The one who went through B walked more, and he's not there yet.
So two sides together are longer than the third — it's simply a longer route.
A straight line is always the shortest distance between two points.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The shortest path" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Between diff and sum

lines.say: Let's see an extension of this rule.
c is less than a plus b — two sides together are greater than the third.
But c and b are also two sides — so together they're greater than a.

lines.draw: Move b across: write c > a − b

lines.say: Move b to the other side — and we get c is greater than a minus b.

lines.label: a − b < c < a + b appears

lines.say: Put them together: a side of a triangle is less than the sum of the other two sides — and greater than their difference.
And both signs are strict — it can't be equal to either end.
For sides 7 and 12: more than 5 and less than 19. We'll use this in a moment.

lines.say: In triangle ABC, the marked angle outside the triangle is vertically opposite the interior angle at A.

Now we know the sum of the angles in a triangle is 180.
So 2x plus 3x plus 4x together have to give 180.
That's 9x equals 180. Divide by 9 — x is 20.
Choice four.

lines.say: In the figure, the angles at A and C are equal.
What is the value of p plus q over 2?
We have an expression to calculate. And notice — the figure has u, p and q.
To calculate the expression, I have to end up with ONE unknown. Not stuck with u, p and q.
So let's use the exterior-angle rule. Why? Because p and q are both outside the triangle.
p is adjacent to the angle at A — so p is 180 minus u.
q is an exterior angle. It equals the two interior angles not next to it: u plus u. 2u.
Now I can calculate the expression.
p is 180 minus u. And q over 2 is 2u over 2 — just u.
Minus u and plus u cancel. We're left with 180.
Choice one.

lines.say: In triangle ABC, AC is 7 and BC is 12.
Which of the following could be the length of AB?
So AB is x in the figure — and we want to know what its length could be.
How do we do it? The rule we just learned: a side is greater than the difference of the other two, and less than their sum.
So x is less than 12 plus 7, and greater than 12 minus 7.
x is between 5 and 19.
From the choices, I'm looking for something between 5 and 19. 21 is too big.
5? x can't equal 5 — it has to be greater than 5. And the same for 19 — it can't be equal.
10 is the only one inside. Choice two.

lines.say: That's it — we've gone over the rules of triangles: sides, angles, and the relation between them.
Large side opposite large angle, small side opposite small angle.
The most important rule to take from here: the angles in a triangle add up to 180. Most of you remember it already.
If you already remember that — take the exterior angle too: it equals the two interior angles not next to it.
You can solve without it, but it's recommended — it can save a few seconds.
Next: special triangles.

beats.title: The Pythagorean Theorem

lines.say: The Pythagorean theorem.
A very important theorem — we'll use it again and again, all through geometry, at least everything on the psychometric.
Pythagoras was a Greek philosopher and mathematician — over two and a half thousand years ago.
His followers were almost a cult that believed in mathematics. Read about him sometime — fascinating stuff.
They proved many important things. The most famous one is his theorem.

lines.say: Right triangle ABC. Angle B is 90 degrees. AB is 8, BC is 15. What is AC?
Before we start solving — look at the choices. We have 15 and 8 there.

lines.draw: Mark AC as the hypotenuse — it's opposite the right angle at B

lines.say: The right angle is at B, so AC is the hypotenuse.
And in a right triangle, the hypotenuse must be the longest side.
So it has to be more than 8 and more than 15. It could be 15.01 — but it must be more than 15.
So 15 and 8 are out. They can't be the answer.
And 23? That's 8 plus 15. A side of a triangle must be shorter than the sum of the other two.
Out too. Only 17 is left — but let's find AC exactly, with the theorem.

lines.say: Pythagoras: AB squared plus BC squared equals AC squared.
Put in the numbers we know: AB is 8, BC is 15. AC stays.
64 plus 225 is 289. That's AC squared — not AC itself.
To find AC, take the root. 17 squared is 289. So AC is 17.
A length is positive — the negative root isn't a side.
Choice four.

lines.say: The same triangle — just different numbers. AB is 4, BC is 7. What is AC?
AB squared plus BC squared equals AC squared.
16 plus 49 is 65. That's AC squared.
Last time we got a nice round number. Here — not.
No problem. Take the root of both sides. The root cancels the square — and we're left with root 65.
Keep it exact. No decimals.
Quick sense check: 8 squared is 64, so root 65 is a bit over 8 — longer than the leg 7, shorter than 4 plus 7.
11 just adds the lengths. 65 forgot the root.
Choice three.

fig.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="155.8 23.2 324.5 321.6" role="img" aria-label="Right triangle ABC, with right angle at B"><title>Right triangle ABC, with right angle at B</title><polygon points="209.772,63.200 209.772,296.800 430.228,296.800" fill="none" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><line x1="209.772" y1="279.164" x2="227.409" y2="279.164" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="1.7"/><line x1="227.409" y1="279.164" x2="227.409" y2="296.800" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="1.7"/><text x="195.772" y="49.200" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">A</text><text x="191.772" y="310.800" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">B</text><text x="448.228" y="310.800" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">C</text><text x="187.772" y="180.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">8</text><text x="320.000" y="318.800" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">x</text><text x="340.000" y="176.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">11</text></svg>

lines.say: Same triangle again. But this time we're not given two legs to find the hypotenuse.
We're given a leg and the hypotenuse — and we need the other leg.
AB is 8, and AC — opposite the right angle — is 11. We need BC.
So instead of adding the legs, we subtract.
Think of it as moving a squared to the other side: hypotenuse squared minus one leg squared gives the other leg squared.
Put in the numbers: 11 squared is 121. 8 squared is 64. 121 minus 64 is 57.
Take the root of both sides: BC is root 57.
Not 11 minus 8. We subtract the squares, not the lengths.
Choice two.

lines.say: First — the geometric meaning. What is a squared?

lines.draw: Draw a square on leg a and write a² in it

lines.say: a squared is the area of the square that sits on leg a — a square whose side is a.

lines.draw: Draw a square on leg b and write b² in it

lines.say: b squared, the same way: the area of the square on leg b.

lines.draw: Draw a square on the hypotenuse and write c² in it

lines.say: And c squared — the area of the square on the hypotenuse.

lines.label: 'Area on a + area on b = area on c' appears

lines.say: So the theorem says: the two squares on the legs together have exactly the area of the square on the hypotenuse.

lines.say: Let's see it visually first.

lines.label: A big square appears: four right triangles around a square of side c

lines.say: Take a big square and put four copies of our right triangle in its corners.
The hypotenuses make a square in the middle. Its area: c squared.
What's not covered by the triangles is c squared.

lines.label: The same big square appears, with the four triangles moved

lines.say: Now slide the same four triangles into new places — same big square.
What's uncovered now? A square of side a and a square of side b.
We didn't change the big square. We didn't change the triangles. So the uncovered area didn't change either.
The squares on the legs cover exactly the area of the square on the hypotenuse.
That's the geometric meaning. It's not a mathematical proof — but it's nice to see it once. We use this theorem so much.
