beats.title: Count the area

v.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="179.9 39.9 280.1 296.1" role="img" aria-label="Area proof of the Pythagorean theorem"><title>Area proof of the Pythagorean theorem</title><polygon points="205.938,294.062 434.062,294.062 434.062,65.938 205.938,65.938" fill="none" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><polygon points="205.938,294.062 297.188,294.062 205.938,157.188" fill="#d6e9f5" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><polygon points="434.062,294.062 434.062,202.812 297.188,294.062" fill="#dcebd6" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><polygon points="434.062,65.938 342.812,65.938 434.062,202.812" fill="#f5e7ca" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><polygon points="205.938,65.938 205.938,157.188 342.812,65.938" fill="#e8ddf4" stroke="#203344" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><polygon points="297.188,294.062 434.062,202.812 342.812,65.938 205.938,157.188" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#087f83" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><text x="320.000" y="180.000" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="27">c²</text><text x="251.562" y="310.031" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">a</text><text x="365.625" y="310.031" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="#203344" font-family="DejaVu Sans,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="20">b</text></svg>

lines.say: Now the math.

lines.label: The big square with the four triangles appears

lines.say: Here's our square on the hypotenuse, and around it four triangles that make one bigger square.
What is the big square made of? The middle square — c squared — plus four triangles.

lines.draw: In one corner triangle write ab/2

lines.say: Each triangle is a right triangle. Its area: leg times leg over 2. a b over 2. And there are four of them.
But the big square also has a formula of its own: side squared. Its side is a plus b.

lines.draw: Along one outer side write a + b

lines.say: So its area is a plus b, all squared.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Count the area" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Cancel 2ab

lines.say: Two expressions for the same area — so they're equal. An equation. Let's solve it.
Open the brackets with the short multiplication formula: a squared plus 2ab plus b squared.
On the other side: c squared plus 2ab — the 4 cancels with the 2.
And 2ab is on both sides — just cancel it.
What's left?
a squared plus b squared equals c squared. The Pythagorean theorem.
That's it — much simpler than you thought, I guess.
Next: Pythagorean triples, and after them the special right triangles.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Cancel 2ab" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Pythagorean Triples

lines.say: Pythagorean triples.
A shortcut for the Pythagorean theorem — when the numbers are whole.

beats.loads: Clean title slide: the sidebar (nothing highlighted yet) and one massive centred title. Nothing else.

beats.title: What a triple is

lines.say: Pythagorean triples are three whole numbers that satisfy the Pythagorean theorem.
Remember the theorem: a squared plus b squared equals c squared.
When three whole numbers satisfy it — we call them a Pythagorean triple.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "What a triple is" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: 3-4-5 and 5-12-13

lines.say: Example: 3, 4 and 5. Put them in as a, b and c — 5 is the hypotenuse, because the longest side is always the hypotenuse.
3 squared plus 4 squared is 5 squared. 9 plus 16 is 25. It works with whole numbers.
Another triple that shows up on the exam: 5, 12 and 13.
25 plus 144 is 169. It works.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "3-4-5 and 5-12-13" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Most pairs: a root

lines.say: This is pretty rare. In most cases it won't work out.
Legs 2 and 5: 4 plus 25 is 29 — so the hypotenuse is root 29.
Almost any pair of numbers gives a root somewhere — in one of the legs or in the hypotenuse.
Nothing wrong with that answer. Don't force a whole number.
What makes the triples special: everything is whole.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Most pairs: a root" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: NITE loves triples

lines.say: And that's exactly why NITE loves them.
No messy calculations with roots — whole numbers all the way.
They're common in psychometric questions.

lines.draw: Draw a star next to both triples

lines.say: Most of the time, the exam uses these two.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "NITE loves triples" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: 8-15-17: rare

lines.say: There's another triple that's often taught.
Honestly — there's no real need for it. It's not that it can't appear, but it's very, very rare.
If you meet it — the ordinary calculation still works.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "8-15-17: rare" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Multiples

lines.say: Notice: the triples define a ratio between the sides.
Those colons — that's a ratio. 3 to 4 to 5.
What does ratio mean? That we can scale it up — and it still holds.

lines.draw: Write '× 7' over the arrow from 3-4-5 to 21-28-35

lines.say: Multiply everything by 7: 21, 28, 35. Exactly the same ratio — so it's also a right triangle.

lines.draw: Write '× 3' over the arrow from 5-12-13 to 15-36-39

lines.say: We can keep multiplying — by 2, by 4, by 10 — it's always kept.
The same factor multiplies all three sides.
And it's important: the longest side is always the hypotenuse. The other two are the legs.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Multiples" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: How to remember

lines.say: So how do we remember the triples?
3, 4, 5 — simple. Three numbers in a row.
5, 12, 13? A hamsa, a bat mitzvah, a bar mitzvah.

lines.draw: Under 5, 12, 13 write: hamsa · bat mitzvah · bar mitzvah

lines.say: Five fingers of the hamsa, a bat mitzvah at 12, a bar mitzvah at 13.
8, 15, 17 — you really don't need to memorise. There are tricks: 8 times 2 is 16 — minus 1 is 15, plus 1 is 17.
But don't bother yourself with it.
Just remember 3, 4, 5 — and hamsa, bat mitzvah, bar mitzvah. That's enough.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "How to remember" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Why scaling works

lines.say: Why does multiplying keep the triangle right-angled?
Square the scaled sides: 9k squared plus 16k squared is 25k squared.
Every square has the same factor k squared. So any positive factor works — even a fraction.
Half of 3, 4, 5. Not whole numbers — but the same right-triangle ratio.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Why scaling works" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Match the positions

lines.say: One trap. You see 15 and 20 in a right triangle.
If both are legs — that's 3 and 4 times 5. The hypotenuse is 25.
But if 20 is the hypotenuse — they're not in the same positions. The triple doesn't fit.
Find the right angle first. Then match the triple.
Now a sample question.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Match the positions" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

lines.say: We're given three right triangles, as in the figure — stacked one on another like this.
Based on this information and the figure — what is CD?
Look at the givens. In triangle ABC, we already have two sides.
A leg and a hypotenuse. It's a right triangle — so we can find the other leg.
But instead of doing Pythagoras — 26 squared minus 10 squared — notice the triple.
10 and 26 are 5 and 13 times 2. It's 5, 12, 13 — so AC is 12 times 2: 24.
Now look at triangle ACE. Again a right triangle — with legs 18 and 24.
After some practice, 18 and 24 should jump out as familiar: 3 times 6, 4 times 6.
So CE is 5 times 6: 30. It's the 3, 4, 5 triple, scaled by 6.
Now we're left with CD.
No triple here — the legs are 30 and 30.
There's actually something for this — we'll learn it next lesson. For now, Pythagoras.
30 squared plus 30 squared. Instead of adding to 1800, I write 2 times 30 squared — I know it'll simplify.
Take the root: root 2, and the root of 30 squared is 30. So CD is 30 root 2.
Choice one.

AC squared is 26 squared minus 10 squared. Add 18 squared for CE squared. Add 30 squared for CD squared.

lines.label: A right triangle with 30° and 60° appears, with its short leg and hypotenuse

lines.say: So we have its short leg — a. And its hypotenuse — 2a.
We need the long leg. How? With Pythagoras.
Hypotenuse squared minus leg squared gives the other leg squared.
Open the brackets: 4a squared — the 2 is squared too, don't forget!
4a squared minus a squared is 3a squared. Take the root —

lines.draw: On the long leg write a√3

lines.say: — and the long leg is root 3 times a. a root 3.

lines.label: The 30°-60°-90° triangle appears with sides a, a√3, 2a

lines.say: We got it with no numbers — with a variable, a.
So there IS a fixed side ratio in the golden triangle, and it's important: a, a root 3, 2a.

lines.label: short leg : long leg : hypotenuse appears

lines.say: Short leg, long leg, hypotenuse.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow from 30° to the side a

lines.say: The short leg is opposite 30. The long leg — opposite 60. The hypotenuse — opposite 90.
Identify them by the angles, not by how the drawing is turned.

lines.draw: Write 'a = ½ · 2a' by the short leg

lines.say: Notice: the short leg is always half the hypotenuse. Say it's 3 — I know right away the hypotenuse is 6.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow from a to a√3 and write × √3

lines.say: From the short leg to the long leg: multiply by root 3. 5 becomes 5 root 3.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow back from a√3 to a and write ÷ √3

lines.say: And from the long leg back to the short leg: divide by root 3.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "The ratio" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: One side is enough

lines.say: Let's practise a bit. All of these are golden triangles — 30, 60, 90.
The advantage here, compared with all the Pythagoras we did so far:
Until now we always needed two sides to find the third.
Here, one side is enough to find the other two.

lines.label: Short leg 7 → long leg 7√3, hypotenuse 14 appears

lines.say: Short leg 7: the hypotenuse is 14 — double. The long leg: times root 3 — 7 root 3.
With two sides I could use Pythagoras — but I don't want to. I just multiply by root 3.

lines.label: Hypotenuse 18 → short leg 9, long leg 9√3 appears

lines.say: Hypotenuse 18: the short leg is half — 9. From short to long, times root 3: 9 root 3.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "One side is enough" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: From the long leg

lines.say: Now I got a 2 — but this 2 is opposite 60. It's not the short leg.
So I can't say the hypotenuse is 4, or the long leg is 2 root 3.
It's the long leg. To go from the long leg to the short leg — divide by root 3.
So the short leg is 2 over root 3.
The hypotenuse: double the short leg. Instead of 2 over root 3 — 4 over root 3.
Doubling works from the short leg — never double the long leg. It's the most common mix-up.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "From the long leg" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Dividing by a root

lines.say: One last example.
9 — opposite the 60. So 9 is the long leg. To get the short leg: divide by root 3.
9 over root 3 — a bit harder than before. There's a nice method.
To divide a whole number by a root: ignore the root for a moment.

lines.draw: Cover the root sign with your hand: write 9 : 3 = 3

lines.say: 9 divided by 3 — 3.
Now just attach the root 3 back. 9 over root 3 is 3 root 3.
This method always works. Ignore the root, divide by the number under it, attach the root.
Why? Multiply top and bottom by root 3: 9 root 3 over 3 — that's 3 root 3.
So the short leg is 3 root 3, and the hypotenuse is double: 6 root 3.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "Dividing by a root" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: A root that cancels

lines.say: Sometimes the long leg already has a root 3 in it.

lines.label: Long leg 12√3 → short leg 12 → hypotenuse 24 appears

lines.say: 12 root 3 divided by root 3 — the roots cancel. Short leg 12. Hypotenuse 24.
Looks harder — but it's actually shorter.
That's the golden triangle.

lines.say: One more triangle — and it comes straight out of the golden one.

lines.label: An isosceles triangle with 120° at the top and 30° at each base angle appears

lines.say: An isosceles triangle with 120 degrees at the top. The base angles: 180 minus 120 is 60 — split in two, 30 and 30.
It's NOT a right triangle. But watch what happens when we drop the altitude from the top.

lines.draw: Draw the altitude from A down to the base; mark D and the right angle

lines.say: It's isosceles — so the altitude is also a median and an angle bisector.

lines.draw: Write 60° and 60° at A, on both sides of AD

lines.say: It splits the 120 into 60 and 60, and the base into two equal halves.
Now look at each half: 30, 60, 90. Two golden triangles, back to back!
The leg a is the hypotenuse of each golden triangle.
The short leg — opposite the 30 — is half of it. a over 2. That's the height.

lines.draw: Write a√3/2 on BD and on DC

lines.say: The long leg: times root 3 — a root 3 over 2. And the base is two of those —
— a root 3. So the side ratio is a, a, a root 3.
Leg, leg, base. Nothing new to memorise — just cut it in half and it's golden.

beats.loads: Sidebar with "30°-30°-120° triangle" highlighted; the main canvas is completely blank.

beats.title: Using 30°-30°-120°

items.t: Where it shows up: a rhombus with a $120°$ angle — the long diagonal cuts it into two of these.

lines.say: Same deal as before: one side is enough.
Legs 8: the base is 8 root 3. The height — half a leg — 4.
Base 6 root 3: divide by root 3 — each leg is 6. Height 3.
And the area: base a root 3, height a over 2, divided by 2 — a squared root 3 over 4.
Look familiar? Same as an equilateral triangle with side a!

lines.label: Where it shows up: a rhombus with a 120° angle — its long diagonal cuts it into two of these

lines.say: Where do you meet it? A rhombus with a 120 degree angle: the long diagonal cuts it into two of these triangles.
Now let's solve a sample question.

lines.say: Right triangle ABC. Angle B is 90, angle C is 30, and AB is 6. What is the perimeter?
So we have a golden triangle here: 30, 60, 90.
The side ratio in a golden triangle: a, a root 3, 2a.
You don't really have to write it. Once you've practised enough, you write it straight on the triangle.

lines.draw: Draw an arrow from the 30° at C to AB

lines.say: AB is opposite the 30 — it's the short leg. So a is 6.
The hypotenuse, of course, is 12.
And the long leg: 6 root 3.
If it's still hard: a is 6, so a root 3 is 6 root 3, and 2a is twice 6 — 12.
The perimeter: just add the sides. 6 plus 12 is 18 — and the 6 root 3 stays separate.
18 plus 6 root 3. Not 24 root 3 — only one term has the root.
Choice four.

lines.label: The same triangle appears, legs a and a

lines.say: Its sides keep the ratio a, a, a root 2. Let's see why.
One leg is a — so the other leg is a too, because it's isosceles.
How do we find the hypotenuse? Pythagoras.
a squared plus a squared: 2a squared equals the hypotenuse squared. Take the root —
— root 2 times a. The hypotenuse is a root 2.
The ratio in the silver triangle is always a, a, a root 2. Two legs and the hypotenuse.

beats.title: Leg ↔ hypotenuse

lines.say: From a leg to the hypotenuse: multiply by root 2. From the hypotenuse to a leg: divide by root 2.
Say a leg is 7. To get the hypotenuse, times root 2: 7 root 2. And of course, the other leg is also 7.
And once I have the hypotenuse — to get the legs, which are equal — divide by root 2.
Remember the method from last lesson: pretend there's no root.
16 divided by 2 is 8 — and attach the root 2. 8 root 2.
So each leg is 8 root 2.
And a square's diagonal? Same triangle: the side is a leg, the diagonal is the hypotenuse.
Let's solve an example.

vr-active-reading.title: Active reading: make meaning as you go

beats.title: Read for a small picture
beats.script: Think about reading a message from a friend. If it says, ‘The café is closed, so meet me at the library,’ you immediately picture a changed plan. You do not memorize every word and hope the meaning appears later. We want that same habit with an unfamiliar exam paragraph. The subject may be a museum, a scientific study, or a disagreement between two writers. Our job is to build a small, accurate picture as the sentences arrive. At first, we will practice this slowly. Speed comes from understanding without repeatedly starting again. A minute per question is a useful training target for many short questions, not a rule that every question or every passage must fit. Longer passages share their reading time across several questions.

beats.title: Pause at the full stop
board: The council increased parking fees, but traffic did not fall.
My words: Parking cost more; traffic stayed about the same.
beats.script: At the end of a sentence, take a tiny pause and say its message in your own words. Here the council raised parking fees, but traffic did not fall. My version is: parking cost more, yet traffic stayed about the same. That is enough. I am not writing a second essay, and I am not translating every English word into another language. I am checking that there is a thought in my head. If your paraphrase is just the original sentence with two words replaced, ask what you would tell a younger sibling about it. If the sentence contains several clauses, you can make this pause at a meaningful comma instead. During early practice, say the paraphrase aloud. Later, it becomes a quick mental check.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → Keep the words that control the claim]

beats.title: Keep the words that control the claim
beats.script: Shorter must still mean the same thing. ‘Some visitors disliked the exhibition’ does not mean ‘visitors disliked it’ if your shortened version makes you imagine everyone. ‘The treatment may help’ does not promise that it will help. And if a price did not fall, it might have stayed unchanged; it did not necessarily rise. Keep these small words attached to the claim. They are often the whole reason one answer is right and another is wrong. A useful paraphrase removes decorative detail, not logical limits. Names can become ‘the researcher’ and a long place name can become ‘the town,’ as long as there is only one researcher or town to keep track of. With two researchers, give them separate labels so their views do not get mixed up.

items.label: SOME
items.detail: At least one; not necessarily all

beats.title: Give the sentence a voice
board: Although the plan was CHEAPER, it took LONGER.
The word although tells us what is surprising.
beats.script: Read this in your head as if you are telling a bedtime story to a younger sibling: although the plan was cheaper, it took longer. Let your voice lean on ‘cheaper’ and ‘longer.’ There is a small disappointment in that contrast. We expected one advantage to come with another, but it did not. This dramatic reading is a way to notice structure. It is not permission to invent the writer’s feelings. A neutral report remains neutral unless the wording supports a stronger tone. Try a second version: because the plan was cheaper, it was chosen. Your inner voice should now make the second part sound like a result. The words are steering you. Hear the change from a contrast to a reason and a result.

beats.title: Make a tiny visual
beats.script: When the text says taxes increased, a small upward arrow above ‘taxes’ can save you from rereading that direction. If shop visits fell, add a downward arrow. Put the arrow beside the thing that changed; a loose arrow in the margin may become meaningless a few sentences later. Suppose the text says visits fell after taxes rose. We can draw the two changes in time, but we should not automatically draw a proven causal arrow between them. ‘After’ gives us an order. It does not by itself explain why the visits fell. This distinction will matter in strengthening, weakening and scientific reasoning. Your markings should preserve what the writer actually said, including what the writer has not established.

visual.text: After local taxes rose, visits to the shopping district fell.

beats.title: Circle the turn
beats.script: You do not need to underline half the paragraph. Choose the words that tell you how its parts fit together. ‘However’ signals a turn; ‘because’ introduces a reason; ‘for example’ usually gives an illustration of a point already made. These labels are clues, not a replacement for meaning. Two sentences can disagree without using ‘however,’ and a writer can describe someone else’s explanation without accepting it. Try drawing a small bend beside a contrast and writing ‘example’ beside an illustration. If your page starts to look like a coloring exercise, stop adding marks. A few useful marks are faster to read than a paragraph covered in ink.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → Track the owner of each opinion]

beats.title: Track the owner of each opinion
beats.script: Here a critic calls a design impressive and an engineer calls it impractical. Those views can both be true: appearance and usefulness are different questions. More importantly, the writer may only be reporting them. Write C beside the critic’s claim and E beside the engineer’s claim, or simply think ‘one person’ and ‘the other.’ When you meet ‘she,’ ‘this view,’ or ‘such an approach,’ point mentally back to its owner. Do not give the writer an opinion merely because the writer included a quotation. Questions often ask which claim belongs to whom. Keeping that ownership clear now is much easier than untangling it after reading four tempting answers.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → Prediction is a check, not a guess]

beats.title: Prediction is a check, not a guess
board: A paragraph says a method is useful but limited.
Keep reading if the text takes a different turn.
beats.script: Once you understand a sentence, ask what kind of sentence might follow. If a method is described as useful but limited, I expect either an example of its usefulness or an explanation of its limits. That small expectation keeps me alert. It is not a licence to finish the paragraph in my imagination. If the next sentence goes somewhere else, I update my picture. In sentence completion, predicting the direction of a blank helps me reject a phrase that goes the wrong way. In a passage, predicting the job of the next paragraph helps me notice a change of topic. Stay flexible: the text supplies the evidence, and your prediction only helps you organize it.

beats.title: Use a five-word margin label
beats.script: After a paragraph, give it a short label. ‘An old explanation.’ ‘Evidence against it.’ ‘A more cautious account.’ Five words are often enough, and there is no need to count them. The point is to remember the job of the paragraph as well as its subject. Three paragraphs might all discuss birds, but one introduces a puzzle, one describes a test, and one limits the conclusion. A label such as ‘birds again’ misses that structure. These labels become a map for reading comprehension. When a question asks why a study was mentioned, you can return to the paragraph that does that job without scanning every sentence from the beginning.

beats.title: When a word is unfamiliar
board: Keep its role if its exact meaning is not needed.
Return if the distinction decides an answer.
beats.script: You will occasionally meet a word you do not know. First ask whether you need its exact meaning. If the sentence says a device is expensive but reliable, and the device has an unfamiliar name, ‘the device’ may be enough. If an analogy depends on the difference between reluctant and unwilling, the vocabulary is central and you must be more careful. Context can suggest a meaning, but do not turn a guess into a fact. Mark the uncertainty lightly and continue if the next sentence may clarify it. A useful reader knows both what is understood and what is still uncertain. That is better than pretending every word is clear or stopping at every unfamiliar word.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → Match the technique to the question]

beats.title: Match the technique to the question
board: Passage: label roles and return to evidence.
beats.script: The same active reading habit will look a little different in each topic. For an analogy, your paraphrase is a relationship sentence. For formal logic, it becomes a condition and a result, with ‘only’ kept in the right place. For a scientific argument, you separate what was observed from the explanation proposed for it. For a passage, you keep a short map of the writer’s steps. We will practice all of those applications. You do not need to perform every technique on every sentence. Choose the smallest action that makes the meaning clear. Often a quiet paraphrase is enough. Add a diagram or a written label when the structure is harder to hold in your head.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → Build accuracy, then shorten the pause]

beats.title: Build accuracy, then shorten the pause
board: Finally: time a short set and review the error.
beats.script: Start with a few untimed questions. Read each sentence, paraphrase it and compare your version with the original. Did you lose an ‘only’? Did ‘some’ become ‘all’? Did a possible explanation become a proven cause? Correct that habit before chasing a faster time. Then shorten the pause until the check happens almost automatically. When you start timed sets, review more than the score. Ask where the meaning changed in your head. If you understood the text but chose a tempting answer, practice evidence checks. If you had to reread because you lost the subject halfway through, practice short clause summaries. Speed improves when you repair the actual source of delay.

solve-vr39-g001.title: A contrast without an invented cause

beats.title: Your question
beats.script: A town reduced bus fares. Passenger numbers rose, but the number of cars entering the town center remained unchanged. Which of the following is necessarily true?

beats.title: Three facts, three short notes
beats.script: Read the three observations separately. Fares went down. Passenger numbers went up. Car entries stayed the same. Notice how much easier that is to hold in your head than the complete wording. Now keep one detail from the question: necessarily true. We are looking for something the passage commits us to. We are not looking for the most interesting explanation for it. People might have switched from walking to buses, or more people might have made trips. None of that has been stated. Our little set of arrows is a record of observations, not a story about causes.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → The word but is doing work]

beats.title: The word but is doing work
board: BUT no reduction in car entries
beats.script: The contrast tells us why an obvious story may be too simple. We might have expected cheaper buses to mean fewer cars, but that expected change is not in the figures. Still, we cannot jump to the opposite extreme and claim that the policy changed nobody’s behavior. Some drivers could have changed while other drivers began entering the center. What survives without any added assumption is the reported rise in bus use. That is our answer. This is active reading in action: compress the sentence, preserve the contrast, then check the strength of the claim.

beats.title: Choose the matching answer
board: More people used buses after the fare reduction.
beats.script: The answer is choice 3: More people used buses after the fare reduction.. The passage directly reports that passenger numbers rose. It gives no information about the previous travel habits of those additional passengers and does not establish the cause of the increase.

solve-vr39-g001.navLabel: A contrast without an invented cause

beats.title: Your question
beats.script: Mara calls the archive valuable because it preserves ordinary people’s letters. Theo agrees that the letters are worth keeping but argues that the archive’s catalog makes them difficult to find. Which of the following best describes Theo’s position?

beats.title: Agreement first; disagreement second
beats.script: Theo is not simply for or against the archive. He agrees about one thing and complains about another. Read ‘agrees’ with a small nod, then let your inner voice turn at ‘but.’ The letters are worth keeping; the catalog is difficult to use. If we paraphrase his whole view as ‘Theo dislikes the archive,’ we erase the agreement and become vulnerable to the first distractor. A fair summary keeps both parts. This is especially useful when a question presents two named thinkers: write down the exact point on which they differ, rather than imagining two completely opposing camps.

beats.title: Choose the matching answer
board: He values the material but criticizes the way it is organized.
beats.script: The answer is choice 2: He values the material but criticizes the way it is organized.. Theo explicitly accepts the value of the letters. His criticism concerns access to them through the catalog, not whether they deserve preservation.

vr-analogy-method.title: Analogies: start with the word that needs the other

beats.title: A relationship, not a shared subject
board: A clock is an instrument that measures time.
beats.script: Time and a clock are connected, but ‘connected’ is far too broad to solve an analogy. We need a sentence that tells us how they are connected. Start with the word that is easier to define through the other word. Here that is clock. A clock is an instrument that measures time. Time does not need a clock in order to exist, but our definition of a clock needs the idea of time. This is what we mean by the dependent word. We are looking for a useful defining relationship, not debating whether an object could physically exist in a world without its partner. Our sentence now gives us a clear test for another pair.

beats.title: Keep the printed order
beats.script: We started the definition with clock, the second word, but we have not reversed the printed pair. Our rule is still: the second thing measures the first. Temperature and thermometer fit that order. A thermometer measures temperature. Thermometer and temperature would put the roles in the wrong places. You can draw an arrow from the word you define to the word you use in its definition. What matters is that you carry exactly the same roles into the answer choices. Starting with the dependent word makes the sentence easier to form; it does not give us permission to rearrange a pair when we check it.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → Try the definition with every role intact]

beats.title: Try the definition with every role intact
board: A medicine may relieve a symptom; a diagnosis identifies it.
beats.script: Try hunger and meal. It is easier to define the meal’s role through hunger than to define hunger through a meal. A meal can satisfy hunger. Notice the word ‘can.’ Not every meal completely satisfies every person, so our relationship should not make an unnecessary guarantee. Now compare a remedy and a diagnosis. A remedy aims to relieve a problem; a diagnosis identifies it. Both belong to the same general world of problems and responses, but their jobs differ. We want the closest relationship, not just two words from a similar subject. A good definition is precise enough to make that distinction and modest enough to stay true.

beats.title: When dependence is not obvious
board: Do not force a tool or purpose into every pair.
beats.script: Sometimes neither word clearly depends on the other. Scarce and plentiful are opposites. There is no need to invent a story about one producing the other. Use the dependent-word approach as your first question: which word can I define naturally through its partner? If that does not reveal a useful direction, test another simple relationship: opposites, similar meanings, stronger degree, part and whole, action and result, or prevention. The method should make the pair clearer. It should never force you into an awkward sentence just because every previous example began with a tool. We will practice a range of relationships so that the first question becomes a flexible habit.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → A true definition can still be too broad]

beats.title: A true definition can still be too broad
board: A forest contains trees, but it is not a storage facility.
beats.script: ‘An archive contains documents’ is true, but a forest contains trees and a box contains shoes too. If more than one answer fits, sharpen the sentence. An archive is a place or collection organized to preserve records. That gives us something more useful than ‘contains.’ Do not add irrelevant details simply to force a favorite option. We do not need to specify the archive’s opening hours or the color of its shelves. We refine the relationship itself: storage, preservation, membership, material, cause, or purpose. A useful check is to ask whether your extra detail belongs to the meanings of the words, rather than to one example you happened to imagine.

beats.title: Cause, purpose and result differ
board: Do not turn an intention into a guaranteed result.
beats.script: A warning is intended to help someone avoid a danger. It does not guarantee that the person will listen. An injury, by contrast, tells us that harm has occurred. This difference is easy to lose when we define every pair with a vague verb such as ‘makes.’ Ask whether the second word is the aim of an action, its necessary result, a possible result, or a state the action tries to prevent. The English exam pairs often rely on exactly that small distinction. Your relationship sentence can use ‘aims to,’ ‘can,’ ‘results in,’ or ‘prevents’ as appropriate. Choosing the right verb is part of solving the question.

beats.title: Small part or weak degree?
board: A component is not the same as a mild form.
beats.script: A crumb is a small piece of a loaf. A drizzle is a light form of rain. Both suggest something small, but they do not have the same structure. One is a component of a larger object; the other is a weaker degree of a phenomenon. A letter and a word would fit the component relationship, not the intensity relationship. When two choices seem close, name the difference in plain English. ‘A piece of’ and ‘a mild form of’ are already enough. You do not need a technical label before you can solve the question. The labels simply help you remember a distinction you have understood.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → Let the pair choose the meaning]

beats.title: Let the pair choose the meaning
board: An eye is the opening through which the thread passes.
Do not keep an unrelated sense of eye.
beats.script: English has words with more than one meaning too. In eye and needle, eye does not mean a seeing organ. The partner word selects the relevant sense: the small opening through which thread passes. The relationship in the pair helps us choose among possible meanings. Here is the reasoning move: select the sense that makes a precise relationship, then keep that sense while checking the answers. If every choice fails, revisit the definition before assuming that the vocabulary is impossible. Sometimes the words are familiar and the first interpretation was simply the wrong one.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → Use the choices to repair a definition]

beats.title: Use the choices to repair a definition
board: Change the rule for all choices together.
Never bend it separately for each answer.
beats.script: Usually, define the pair before looking closely at the answers. But if you cannot get a useful definition, the choices can suggest the kind of relationship you missed. Perhaps you called an anchor ‘something on a boat’ and then notice that the options all concern preventing an unwanted event. That can prompt a better definition: an anchor prevents a vessel from drifting. Once you revise the rule, apply the revised version to every choice. Do not give one answer ‘prevents,’ another ‘treats,’ and a third ‘detects,’ then say they all fit. That is three different rules. The goal is one sentence with the same roles and the same strength.

beats.title: Vocabulary without panic
board: Use word families and context cautiously.
Do not assume unfamiliar words are synonyms.
beats.script: A difficult-looking word may express a simple relationship, but unfamiliar words are not automatically synonyms of their partners. If you know one meaning confidently, use it. A word family can help, and the answer choices may help you recognize a sense, but mark any guess as a guess in your own thinking. During practice, keep a vocabulary note with the word, a short definition and a sentence showing the relevant sense. A bare translation is often less useful than that sentence. In a timed set, make the best supported choice and move on when further staring is not adding information. Afterwards, repair the vocabulary gap separately from the reasoning mistake.

beats.title: A short answer check
beats.script: Before choosing, run three quick checks. Does the answer keep the same roles: tool and task, producer and product, or problem and response? Does it keep the same direction in the printed pair? And does it preserve the strength and specificity of the connection? A possible result is not a guaranteed result, and a place where an action happens is not necessarily a place into which the action puts something. In early practice, explain why each distractor fails. Under time pressure, the explanation can be just a few words in your head. Those few words should identify a real mismatch, rather than simply saying that one answer feels better.

beats.title: Your question
beats.script: crest : wave

beats.title: Define the relationship
board: A crest is the highest part of a wave.
beats.script: A crest is the highest part of a wave. Start with crest, because its meaning here depends on the wave whose top it names. A summit is the highest part of a mountain. The answer preserves a particular part of a whole, not merely two related objects. Say that relationship once in your own words before looking for the answer. The useful part is the verb or phrase that connects the roles. We can change the subject matter completely and still preserve that connection. Carry the printed order with you even if your definition starts with the second word.

beats.title: Test the closest-looking alternatives
beats.script: The matching pair is summit : mountain. Consider oar : boat. An oar is equipment used with a boat, not its highest part. Consider harbor : ship. A harbor shelters a ship; it is not a part of the ship. Consider rain : cloud. Rain may come from a cloud, but it is not the cloud’s highest part. If you chose one of those alternatives, compare the exact relationship you used with the one in the original pair. The correction is usually a small change in the defining sentence, not a need to memorize the entire question.

beats.title: Choose the matching answer
beats.script: The answer is choice 2: summit : mountain. A crest is the highest part of a wave. Start with crest, because its meaning here depends on the wave whose top it names. A summit is the highest part of a mountain. The answer preserves a particular part of a whole, not merely two related objects.

beats.title: Your question
beats.script: to inspect : inspection

beats.title: Define the relationship
board: To inspect is to carry out an inspection.
beats.script: To inspect is to carry out an inspection. To select is to make a selection. The second word names the action expressed by the first. Sleeping may involve dreaming, but a dream is not simply another grammatical form naming the entire action of sleeping. Say that relationship once in your own words before looking for the answer. The useful part is the verb or phrase that connects the roles. We can change the subject matter completely and still preserve that connection. Carry the printed order with you even if your definition starts with the second word.

beats.title: Test the closest-looking alternatives
beats.script: The matching pair is to select : selection. Consider to rest : fatigue. Rest can relieve fatigue; fatigue does not name the act of resting. Consider to sleep : dream. A dream may occur during sleep, but the two do not name the same action. Consider to arrive : invitation. An invitation may lead someone to arrive; it does not name arriving. If you chose one of those alternatives, compare the exact relationship you used with the one in the original pair. The correction is usually a small change in the defining sentence, not a need to memorize the entire question.

beats.title: Choose the matching answer
beats.script: The answer is choice 2: to select : selection. To inspect is to carry out an inspection. To select is to make a selection. The second word names the action expressed by the first. Sleeping may involve dreaming, but a dream is not simply another grammatical form naming the entire action of sleeping.

beats.title: Your question
beats.script: to straighten : bent

beats.title: Define the relationship
board: To straighten an object is to remove its bent state.
beats.script: To straighten an object is to remove its bent state. To dry an object is to remove its wet state. Define the action through the state it changes: the first word makes the second description cease to apply. This is more precise than saying the words are opposites. Say that relationship once in your own words before looking for the answer. The useful part is the verb or phrase that connects the roles. We can change the subject matter completely and still preserve that connection. Carry the printed order with you even if your definition starts with the second word.

beats.title: Test the closest-looking alternatives
beats.script: The matching pair is to dry : wet. Consider to polish : shiny. Polishing tends to create or increase shininess, rather than remove it. Consider to describe : detailed. A description may be detailed, but describing does not remove that property. Consider to whisper : quiet. Whispering is quiet speech; it does not make something stop being quiet. If you chose one of those alternatives, compare the exact relationship you used with the one in the original pair. The correction is usually a small change in the defining sentence, not a need to memorize the entire question.

beats.title: Choose the matching answer
beats.script: The answer is choice 2: to dry : wet. To straighten an object is to remove its bent state. To dry an object is to remove its wet state. Define the action through the state it changes: the first word makes the second description cease to apply. This is more precise than saying the words are opposites.

beats.title: Your question
beats.script: trickle : flow

vr-sentence-meaning.title: Understanding sentences: scope, emphasis and implication

beats.title: Find the main action
beats.script: A sentence can become difficult without containing a single advanced word. ‘He never missed a chance to avoid the meeting’ is built from ordinary words, but several actions and negatives are nested inside one another. Start with the main subject and action. Then unfold the added phrase. In this case, he took every opportunity to avoid the meeting. That tells us about his repeated attempts or choices, not necessarily whether he managed to avoid every meeting. Plain English is our tool, but the plain version must keep that distinction. When a question asks what can be inferred, we need the meaning supported by the sentence, not an attractive extra story.

beats.title: Unpack from the inside out
board: Avoid attending → try not to attend
Never missed a chance → used every opportunity
beats.script: Take the smallest difficult phrase first. Avoid attending means try or arrange not to attend. Now put back ‘never missed a chance.’ He used every opportunity to do that. This inside-out method works better than counting negatives. Some negative-looking verbs express prevention or refusal, and their meanings do not cancel mechanically. If the sentence instead said he failed to avoid attending, he attended despite trying not to. Say the small phrase naturally before rebuilding the full sentence. You should be able to point to which action actually occurred and which one was only attempted, wished for or prevented.

beats.title: Only changes what is excluded
beats.script: These sentences do different jobs. Only Maya praised the design excludes other people from praising it. Maya praised only the design limits the objects of her praise. Maya only praised the design may contrast praising with doing something more, such as funding it, and context can matter. Do not move ‘only’ around while paraphrasing. Attach it to the part it restricts. If a sentence is genuinely ambiguous, a question may ask which interpretation is possible or which revision removes the ambiguity. We should not pretend that English always has just one scope reading. Look at what the wording and surrounding context actually settle.

beats.title: Separate fact from attitude
board: An event and an opinion about it are different.
beats.script: ‘Unfortunately, the proposal was rejected’ reports an event and expresses a negative attitude to that event. ‘The proposal was not rejected without reason’ says there was a reason for rejecting it; it does not tell us every reason was good. These small qualifications often decide an answer. Ask two questions: what happened, and what does the speaker think about it? Someone may dislike a decision yet accept that it had a reasonable basis. Someone may support a decision without being pleased about all its consequences. Keep those judgments separate rather than forcing every sentence into a simple approval-or-disapproval label.

beats.title: Compare exactly what is compared
board: More useful than the old version
Does not mean useful in every respect
Less expensive does not mean inexpensive
beats.script: Relative words compare things. A revised manual can be clearer than the old one and still be confusing. A cheaper ticket can still be expensive. When you paraphrase, keep the comparison partner and the direction. If an answer turns ‘more accurate than’ into ‘completely accurate,’ it has made the claim stronger. If it drops ‘for beginners,’ it may have widened the group to which the comparison applies. These are small edits with large logical effects. Your active-reading mark can be a simple greater-than sign, but place the two things and the quality beside it so you remember what is being compared.

beats.title: Replace a phrase without changing the claim
board: Check subject, time, scope and certainty.
A true statement may still change the meaning.
beats.script: Some questions ask which replacement changes the meaning, or which sentence expresses the same idea. Do not merely ask whether the replacement sounds plausible. Compare it with the original in four respects: who is acting, when the action occurs, how wide the claim is, and how certain it is. ‘Could have arrived’ is not ‘arrived.’ ‘Everyone did not agree’ may be less clear than ‘not everyone agreed.’ ‘The doctor brought the actor to the clinic’ assigns roles differently from ‘the actor brought the doctor.’ Read each complete version once in a natural voice. A role or time change often becomes obvious when you picture the scene.

vr-paragraph-method.title: Understanding paragraphs: evidence, purpose and scope

beats.title: Ask what each sentence is doing
board: A topic is not the same as a purpose.
beats.script: A paragraph about a railway may describe its construction, defend a decision to build it, or challenge a popular explanation of its failure. ‘Railway’ is the topic in all three cases. The paragraph’s purpose is different. After each sentence, give it a small job label: claim, reason, example, opposing view, or qualification. You do not need all five labels in every paragraph. The point is to understand how the thought develops. A question asking why an example is mentioned wants that job, not just a description of what the example contains.

beats.title: Literal information and inference
board: Implied: connect what the text actually supplies.
Neither: do not add a missing premise.
beats.script: Some questions ask what is stated. Others ask what follows or is implied. For a stated-information question, find the relevant sentence and compare the option carefully. An inference may combine two statements, but it still needs support. If a paragraph says a device is cheaper to produce and more expensive to maintain, it does not tell us which device costs less over ten years without more information. Do not confuse a plausible answer with an entailed one. The safest inference often sounds less exciting than the distractors because it respects what remains unknown.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → Keep two views in separate boxes]

beats.title: Keep two views in separate boxes
beats.script: When two thinkers are presented, use separate boxes or labels. They may agree on an observation and disagree only on its explanation. Or they may agree that a policy has a benefit while disagreeing about its importance. Ask what each person would accept and what each would reject. A broad answer such as ‘they disagree about science’ is rarely enough. We want the precise point of disagreement. The same habit helps with a writer who quotes a critic: the critic’s words belong in the critic’s box unless the writer explicitly endorses them.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → An example can test a boundary]

beats.title: An example can test a boundary
board: Does the case support, limit or challenge it?
beats.script: Examples are not decorative. A paragraph may use one to make an abstract idea concrete, show an exception, or expose a weakness in an argument. Read the sentence before and after the example. If the writer says ‘yet this account cannot explain...’ the example is a challenge. If the writer says ‘for instance,’ it is likely an illustration, but still check what feature is being illustrated. A distractor may accurately describe the example and still give the wrong reason for including it. The question is about its role in the paragraph’s reasoning.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → Unknown terms can have clear roles]

beats.title: Unknown terms can have clear roles
board: A defined term gets its meaning from the paragraph.
Do not substitute a familiar but different meaning.
beats.script: A paragraph may introduce a technical term or an unfamiliar artistic movement. Read the definition supplied there. You usually do not need outside knowledge. If the text says a technique combines ordinary speech sounds to imitate an action, use that description even if you know a related term from another context. In a language-based example, pay attention to the specific feature the definition names. What matters is the same reading task: understand a supplied definition, recognize a case that fits it, and reject a superficially similar case that lacks the defining feature.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → Check scope and the negative demand]

beats.title: Check scope and the negative demand
beats.script: A negative question deserves a small visible mark. If it asks which statement is not supported, three options may be true paraphrases. Do not choose the first true-looking statement out of habit. Beside each answer, mentally put supported, contradicted, or not established. A not-supported answer may be false or simply go beyond the evidence; read the exact demand. Keep the paragraph’s scope: a finding in one setting is not automatically a rule for every setting. At the end, point to the sentence that supports your choice, or the precise extra claim that the text never supplied.

vr-comparison-method.title: Parables and comparisons: match the roles

beats.title: Translate the story into a relationship
board: What are they trying to achieve?
What goes wrong or stays the same?
beats.script: A speaker may answer a practical argument with a story about a gardener, a ship or a broken road. The objects are not usually the point. Ask who acts, what they are trying to achieve, and which relationship the comparison highlights. If someone criticizes painting over a damp wall without fixing the leak, the point is treating a visible symptom while leaving its source. An answer about a gardener trimming damaged leaves while ignoring the cause may fit even though it contains no paint or building. We are looking for the same reasoning pattern under different scenery.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → Give every important role a partner]

beats.title: Give every important role a partner
board: Reason the response fails ↔ same reason
beats.script: Map the roles one at a time. The leak is the continuing source of the problem. The stain is its visible effect. Repainting is a response to the effect that leaves the source untouched. A good parallel must preserve those roles and their connection. A distractor may mention a wall too but describe a completely different issue, such as choosing an expensive color. Shared nouns are not enough. In harder questions, two options may both concern prevention, but only one preserves the timing or the dependence that made the original comparison work.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → Find what the speaker is answering]

beats.title: Find what the speaker is answering
board: Read the claim before the comparison.
Is the reply agreement, criticism or qualification?
beats.script: A comparison gets its force from the claim it answers. Suppose a manager wants to reward a team before the project is completed. A colleague says this is like counting fruit before the tree has flowered. The reply challenges treating an uncertain future benefit as already secured. If the preceding claim instead concerned choosing the wrong kind of tree, the intended point would be different. Read the short conversation as a conversation, with a natural change of voice between speakers. Then paraphrase the reply without any of its story objects. That abstract sentence becomes your answer test.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → Do not add an extra lesson]

beats.title: Do not add an extra lesson
board: The comparison makes one relevant point.
Do not import every property of its objects.
beats.script: A ship may have a captain, a crew, an engine and a destination. A comparison involving a ship does not automatically use all four. If the speaker compares a leader following public opinion to a person walking in front of a crowd while copying its turns, the relevant issue is apparent leadership versus actual direction. The weather at sea or the skill of sailors has nothing to do with that point. Keep the map as small as possible. Adding properties from your own experience can make a wrong option seem rich and convincing while moving away from the text.

beats.title: Watch the direction of cause
board: People gather where music is played.
Does music attract them, or do performers choose crowds?
beats.script: Comparisons can test causal direction. A busy place may attract performers rather than become busy because performers arrived. Both accounts connect the same two things, so an answer that simply mentions the association does not preserve the distinction. Draw the arrows in each story. If the original reply reverses an assumed cause, the correct parallel should reverse an assumed cause too. This connects the comparison topic with strengthening and weakening: we are looking underneath a familiar story to see which inference is being challenged.

beats.title: Check the closest distractor
beats.script: After finding a plausible parallel, compare it with the closest rival. One may describe prevention before a problem occurs; the other repairs damage afterwards. One may reward a result before it is secured; the other merely make a plan in advance. Planning is not the same as pretending the plan has succeeded. A few precise contrasts like these let you reject an attractive answer without a long essay. During practice, write the abstract relationship in a single sentence. Under time pressure, keep that sentence in your head and test the roles in the same order.

vr-argument-method.title: Strengthen or weaken: find the gap

beats.title: Separate the observation from the conclusion
board: Conclusion: the product became less reliable.
Gap: were more products in use?
beats.script: Repair requests increased, so the product must have become less reliable. The first part is an observation; the second is an interpretation. Ask what would have to be true for the observation to justify that interpretation. If twice as many products were in use, a larger number of repair requests might coexist with the same or a lower failure rate. We have found a gap. Do this before reading the options closely. A short paraphrase such as ‘more repairs means worse quality’ lets you see exactly what an added fact would need to support or challenge.

beats.title: Strengthening is not proving
beats.script: A strengthening fact need not prove the conclusion beyond doubt. It should make the argument more persuasive relative to what we knew before. If the number of products in use stayed constant, that removes one alternative explanation for more repair requests. Other explanations might remain. This is why the answer can be right without settling every imaginable question. Focus on the specific conclusion in the stem. A fact that praises the company or confirms an unrelated detail does not necessarily support the reliability claim. Ask which part of the gap the new fact addresses.

beats.title: Weakening leaves the observation intact
board: Challenge the step from result to explanation.
beats.script: For a weakening question, usually accept the stated observation and challenge the inference drawn from it. If sales fell after a shop changed its hours, the fall is still a fact. A road closure that prevented customers reaching the shop gives another explanation for that fall. It weakens the claim that the hours caused it. We do not need to pretend sales rose instead. Some options directly contradict an explicit premise and therefore do not function as a useful explanation of the given situation. Look for information that can coexist with the observation while making the proposed conclusion less secure.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → Counts, rates and who was observed]

beats.title: Counts, rates and who was observed
board: More failures, but how many items?
Fewer complaints, but who could complain?
A survey of attendees misses nonattendees.
beats.script: Three checks are especially useful. First, a count needs a denominator when the conclusion is about a rate. Second, reports depend on whether people notice and report a problem. Third, a sample can exclude the very people whose experience matters. A meeting-time survey of attendees may miss those unable to attend. These are not automatic objections to every argument. Use them when the facts make them relevant. A correct weakening option should identify a concrete alternative route from the situation to the observed result, rather than merely say that all research is uncertain.

beats.title: Draw the rival arrows
beats.script: If the conclusion is causal, sketch its arrow. Does music improve concentration, or do people who already concentrate well choose music? Could a third factor explain both, such as having a quieter workspace? The alternatives correspond to reverse causation and a shared cause. An option strengthens the original account when it makes a rival less plausible, perhaps through a fair comparison or a sequence that rules out the reverse route. An option weakens it when it supplies a credible rival. Keep the measured outcome fixed while you compare these stories.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → Read the demand one last time]

beats.title: Read the demand one last time
beats.script: A fact can be relevant and still point in the wrong direction for the question. Circle the demand, especially when it contains ‘not.’ In a does-not-weaken question, three choices may raise real doubts and the answer may be neutral or supportive. In an explain-the-finding question, look for a mechanism that makes the reported result less puzzling. Do not answer a different question simply because an option sounds like a familiar criticism. Before choosing, say the effect in one line: ‘This removes the attendance explanation,’ or ‘This makes the sample less representative.’ That line should connect the option to this argument.

vr-completion-method.title: Sentence completion: hear how the parts fit

beats.title: Read a sentence, not a row of holes
board: Choose the completion that creates a coherent whole.
Read one option into all the blanks in order.
beats.script: A sentence with several blanks can look like a pile of disconnected fragments. Give yourself a complete version to work with: read an answer choice into the blanks in order. The first phrase goes in the first blank, the second in the second, and so on. You can start with the first option, or begin with an option whose opening you understand quickly. The important thing is to read a real sentence and follow its logic. Do not choose an answer because its first phrase sounds good. A later phrase may reverse the claim or make the example contradict the point it is supposed to illustrate.

beats.title: Keep a short skeleton
board: But, only, not and unless stay.
beats.script: Suppose a long sentence describes a historian with an unfamiliar name who wrote several books in a city with an unfamiliar name. If the issue is whether she accepts a particular explanation, your mental version can simply say ‘the historian accepts the explanation.’ But do not remove the word ‘partly,’ ‘only,’ or ‘not.’ Those words change the claim. Think of this as keeping the sentence’s skeleton: who takes which position, why, and what turns or limits that position. Use it to reduce memory load, not to flatten all the interesting logic out of the sentence.

beats.title: Predict the direction
board: Because X → expect a reason that fits
For example → expect an instance of the claim
beats.script: Once the first clause makes sense, predict the direction of the next one. If the sentence says a device is reliable but something else is true of it, expect a limitation or a contrast. If it says ‘for example,’ the example should illustrate the claim just made. This is not a rule that contrast words always join a positive word to a negative word. ‘Although the team lost, the coach was pleased’ contrasts an event with an unexpected reaction. Read the ideas, not just plus and minus signs. Your prediction is a quick check: does this completion take the sentence where its connective promised to go?

beats.title: Read the turn with emphasis
board: The plan was CHEAP, yet INEFFECTIVE.
The plan was cheap and THEREFORE ATTRACTIVE.
beats.script: Use dramatic inner reading here. Let ‘yet’ sound like a turn and ‘therefore’ sound like a conclusion. In the first sentence, low cost comes with a disappointing limitation. In the second, low cost explains why someone finds the plan attractive. Saying the sentence naturally can expose a completion that looks grammatical but has the wrong relationship. Do not overdo the performance or read aloud during a timed exam. The point is a small shift in your inner voice that makes the link between clauses easier to hear. If a sentence still feels unclear, pause after the clause and give yourself a plain-language paraphrase.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → An example must demonstrate the point]

beats.title: An example must demonstrate the point
board: Example: a predicted rise became a fall.
A correct prediction would not illustrate failure.
beats.script: Here the claim is that predictions sometimes fail. The example should show a prediction that did not match what happened. If an option makes the example a perfectly accurate prediction, the sentence may be grammatical but it does not support its own point. This is one of the most useful checks for a long sentence. Ask what job the last clause is doing. Is it an example, a reason, a qualification, or an opposing view? A completion can fail because it fills the wrong job even when each separate phrase sounds reasonable. Internal coherence is the target; specialist knowledge about an actual historical forecast is not required.

beats.title: Counterfactuals: separate the imagined case
board: Had the guide arrived, the tour could have begun.
Do not invent a complete history from this sentence.
beats.script: Counterfactual wording asks us to consider a situation different from the one being discussed. ‘Had the guide arrived’ means ‘if the guide had arrived.’ ‘Had it not rained’ means ‘if it had not rained.’ First rewrite that condition simply. Then read the result with its exact strength: would, could, or might. Be careful here: we should not automatically negate both halves and claim to know the whole real outcome. The sentence may leave another route to the outcome open. If the question explicitly tells us the guide did not arrive and the tour was canceled, those are facts we can use. Otherwise, keep the imagined relationship separate from unstated history.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → Untangle one negative at a time]

beats.title: Untangle one negative at a time
board: Did not fail to object → did object
Not every visitor complained → at least one did not
beats.script: Some negatives cancel neatly, but others do not. ‘She did not fail to object’ says she objected. ‘Not every visitor complained’ says at least one visitor did not complain; it does not say no visitor complained. ‘Not impossible’ means possible, not certain. Work from the inside out and keep the scope of each negative clear. When the wording becomes awkward, replace one small phrase at a time with plain English, then reread the sentence. Do not count negative-looking words and decide that an even number must make the whole sentence positive. Natural language contains different verbs, quantifiers and scopes, so that shortcut can produce the wrong meaning.

beats.title: Test similar openings efficiently
board: Same opening meaning → reuse the understood clause
Different ending → check the new connection
Finish the whole sentence before deciding.
beats.script: If two options have essentially the same opening, you can reuse the understanding you already built and focus on where they differ. This saves effort without skipping a logical check. Once one completion makes the entire sentence coherent and you have a clear reason for rejecting the serious rival, do not keep rereading out of anxiety. In untimed practice, inspect all four so you learn the traps. In timed work, avoid unnecessary checking, but never stop after a promising first clause while later blanks remain untested.

beats.title: Check the final message
board: Which clause supports or challenges it?
Did every blank preserve that connection?
beats.script: At the end, give a one-sentence summary of the completed sentence. ‘The critic expected a weak performance, but the performance changed her mind.’ ‘The survey supports a limited claim, not a universal one.’ If you cannot state that message, the option may only feel familiar rather than make sense. This final paraphrase is especially useful with reported opinions: the writer may describe a belief without accepting it. Keep the owner of each claim attached to it. Then choose and move on. The practice sets will gradually add longer clauses, counterfactuals and multiple speakers while preserving the same basic routine.

vr-logic-condition-result.title: Deductions: condition → result

beats.title: Treat the rule as a promise
beats.script: Every blue badge is magnetic. Think of that as a promise about anything that meets the condition: if it is a blue badge, it must be magnetic. Blue badge goes on the left of the arrow, and magnetic goes on the right. These are the condition and the result. The arrow does not have to describe a cause or a sequence in time. Being a blue badge need not cause magnetism. It simply tells us which combination the rule allows. For this question, accept the rule as given even if an invented world behaves differently from the real one.

beats.title: Condition present: result required
beats.script: If I show you a blue badge, the condition has been met. The promised result must follow: the badge is magnetic. We are not guessing from how most badges behave. We are applying a rule that says every blue badge. This first case is the straightforward direction of the arrow. When a longer problem gives several rules, look for a fact that starts one of the arrows. That fact lets you move forward. If the new result starts another arrow, you may be able to continue. We will build those chains in a moment, but every valid chain begins with this same small step.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → Condition absent: the rule is silent]

beats.title: Condition absent: the rule is silent
board: A red badge may still be magnetic.
beats.script: Now I show you something that is not a blue badge. Does it have to be nonmagnetic? No. The rule made a promise about blue badges, and we have stepped outside that condition. A red badge might be magnetic too. The result is undetermined, which means the information allows more than one possibility. It does not mean the object has no definite properties in reality; it means this rule does not tell us which properties it has. This is one of the two common traps. Denying the condition does not let us deny the result. We should be able to imagine a non-blue magnetic badge without breaking the original rule.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → Result present: the condition is not guaranteed]

beats.title: Result present: the condition is not guaranteed
board: Many different objects could be magnetic.
beats.script: Suppose we are told only that an object is magnetic. Must it be a blue badge? Again, no. The original promise did not say that blue badges are the only magnetic objects. A result can be shared by several conditions. A helpful everyday comparison is: every square has four sides, but not every four-sided shape is a square. In the invented badge world, a magnetic red badge is a perfectly good counterexample to the reverse claim. We use such a counterexample to show that a conclusion does not have to follow. We are not claiming the counterexample actually exists unless the question says it does.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → Result absent: the condition is impossible]

beats.title: Result absent: the condition is impossible
board: Not magnetic → not a blue badge
Otherwise the promise would be broken.
beats.script: Finally, an object is not magnetic. Could it be a blue badge? It cannot, because a blue badge must be magnetic. If we labeled this nonmagnetic object a blue badge, we would break the rule. This is the valid backward move: reverse the arrow and negate both sides. In plain English, if the promised result is missing, the condition cannot have been met. Do not remember this as merely ‘reverse the rule.’ Reversing without changing both sides gives the invalid case we just rejected. The meaning is the safest memory aid: a blue badge with no magnetism is the one forbidden combination.

beats.title: The four cases together
beats.script: Here are the four cases in one place. Condition present: result required. Condition absent: no conclusion about the result. Result present: no conclusion about the condition. Result absent: condition ruled out. Instead of memorizing four unrelated lines, keep the promise in mind. The rule forbids condition yes with result no. Every other combination can occur. This gives us a second method: draw four small boxes for the two yes-or-no properties and cross out only that forbidden box. The two methods agree. Use arrows for quick chains and the boxes when you need to check whether a proposed counterexample is actually allowed.

beats.title: Only points to a requirement
beats.script: Only trained staff may enter. Ask: if someone may enter, what must be true of them? They must be trained. That puts permission to enter on the left and trained on the right. The phrase immediately following ‘only’ names the required group here. It is not automatically the condition on the left. A trained person might still lack a pass, so training alone does not guarantee permission. Rephrase the whole sentence as an if-then promise before drawing an arrow. This is especially useful with ‘only if’: the gate opens only if the code is correct means gate opens, therefore code correct. It does not by itself say every correct code opens the gate.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → No and none exclude an overlap]

beats.title: No and none exclude an overlap
beats.script: No silver tokens are square. Draw two circles that cannot overlap, or write silver implies not square. The valid reverse-and-negate version is square implies not silver. Notice that this does not say all tokens are silver or square. A round bronze token fits the rule perfectly well. The rule excludes one shared region; it does not describe the whole universe. Now consider ‘There is no blue badge that is not magnetic.’ The forbidden thing is a blue badge without magnetism, so this is another way of saying every blue badge is magnetic. Remove the double negative by identifying the combination being forbidden, not by crossing out every word ‘not’ you see.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → If and only if gives two arrows]

beats.title: If and only if gives two arrows
board: Access if and only if approved
beats.script: If and only if is a stronger statement than a one-way rule. It says each condition is enough for the other. If a file is accessible if and only if it has been approved, access implies approval and approval implies access. We can move in either direction because both directions were supplied. The same idea appears in wording such as ‘all approved files, and only those files, are accessible.’ Keep the word ‘only’: without it, we would have only one arrow. When a question asks whether a feature lets us decide a second feature completely, this two-way relationship is often what is needed.

beats.title: Chain at the matching middle
beats.script: All couriers are registered, and all registered people carry a pass. Registered is the result of the first rule and the condition of the second, so the arrows join. A courier must carry a pass. Compare that with courier implies registered and gardener implies registered. Those two arrows end at the same place. They do not tell us that couriers are gardeners. A shared result is not a bridge. Before linking two rules, check that you are leaving one arrow exactly where the next arrow starts. If a negative version would create the match, write the valid reverse-and-negate form first, then connect it.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → Some gives you a real witness]

beats.title: Some gives you a real witness
beats.script: The word ‘some’ tells us that at least one example exists. Take that example with you through a rule. Some musicians are cyclists, and every cyclist wears a helmet. The musician who is a cyclist must therefore wear a helmet. We may conclude that some musicians wear helmets. We cannot conclude that all musicians do. Nor can we combine ‘some musicians are cyclists’ with ‘some cyclists are painters’ and assume it is the same cyclist. The two ‘some’ statements may refer to different people. Give the first witness a small dot or an imaginary name, then track that same witness rather than silently replacing it.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → A universal rule does not supply an example]

beats.title: A universal rule does not supply an example
board: This alone does not establish a moon gardener.
beats.script: A rule about all members of a group does not, by itself, tell us that the group has any members. ‘All moon gardeners wear purple’ may be a perfectly consistent rule even if there are no moon gardeners. This matters when an answer begins with ‘some.’ To establish that someone exists, look for a stated example or a statement such as ‘there are’ or ‘some.’ The ordinary fact that real humans exist should not quietly fill that gap in a made-up logic question. We are checking what follows from the information supplied. Once an example is supplied, use it confidently, but keep its properties attached to that one example.
beats.nextCue: [NEXT → Disprove a rule with one forbidden case]

beats.title: Disprove a rule with one forbidden case
board: Rule: all amber stones are smooth.
beats.script: To contradict ‘all amber stones are smooth,’ we need one amber stone that is not smooth. A smooth stone of another color is irrelevant. An amber smooth stone follows the rule rather than contradicting it. This is the same forbidden combination from our four cases: condition present and result absent. If a question asks for one object that disproves two claims, write the forbidden combination for each claim and combine them. Check that your chosen object violates both, not merely one. A very short table with one row per claim can prevent a long, tangled sentence from taking over the problem.

beats.title: Distinguish certainty from possibility
board: Must be true: every allowed case
Could be true: at least one allowed case
Cannot be true: no allowed case
beats.script: Before testing an answer, read the question’s demand carefully. A ‘must’ answer survives every allowed arrangement. A ‘could’ answer needs just one allowed example. A ‘cannot’ answer fails in every allowed example. These are different jobs. For a must question, one valid counterexample is enough to reject an option. For a could question, one working example is enough to accept it. We will use this habit again in rules and arrangements. Your active-reading note can be as small as circling MUST or CANNOT. That one mark is often more valuable than underlining every noun in the premises.
